TODAY'S PROBLEMS BY R. O. HUGHES DIRECTOR OF CITIZENSHIP AND SOCIAL STUDIES PITTSBURGH PUBLIC SCHOOLS With the good wisher of R. O. Hughes 

ALLYN AND BACON BOSTON ATLANTA NEW YORK SAN FRANCISCO CHICAGO DALLAS

KE 22425 HARVARD UNIVERSITY

FOREWORD 

For the second time in a generation the United States is at war. 

We have been told that the pressure of events is the wave of the future and that we need only allow ourselves to be carried along. 

Such an attitude assumes that problems will solve themselves. Of course something will happen even if we do nothing, but to insure a right solution of the day's problems, we need to act. 

Many of yesterday's problems are still not permanently solved, but often they have taken on new aspects, and others which once did not seem so vital have attracted attention. Today's Problems undertakes to discuss the outstanding issues and questions which young men and women need to understand as they approach the time when their vote and their influence are recognized as forces in making public opinion and determining the policies of government. 

A free people can remain free only so long as they are free to think and act in accordance with their best judgment. Never has there been a time when the schools of the United States of America were more competent to help people understand freedom and provide the means of preserving it. In spite of what critics sometimes assert, American teachers and American pupils are free to consider the problems of their time and of the days to come. We must insist, however, that teacher and pupil shall hold to the democratic point of view. 

Call that indoctrination if you wish, but unless our own country indoctrinates for democracy, we can hardly hope to save ourselves from countries that indoctrinate their people with its opposite. 

We admit that there are problems difficult ones. We offer fundamental facts on which honest thinking must rest. We consider conflicting suggestions for the solution of our problems. We urge thoughtful conclusions upon them. We emphasize the general welfare rather than selfish gain as the great objective of all truly democratic methods and ideals. We try to talk over the live problems of today with young people who realize that these are problems they themselves must face and who want to be prepared to meet them. 

Few problems can be solved in a week or a year, and some people, as time passes, form such fixed ideas about things as they are or as 

iii

iv 

FOREWORD 

they ought to be that there is little use in urging them to consider different possible solutions. Our hope lies in the youth of our country. 

If they are wise and brave, they will be neither helpless nor hopeless in facing the future.

In the spirit of loyalty to our democratic institutions and in the belief that youth will respond to opportunities to understand and defend those institutions, the author presents this effort to help in meeting Today's Problems. 

R. O. HUGHES

TODAY'S PROBLEMS

TODAY'S PROBLEMS PROLOGUE  

1. Worlds to Conquer. - A young man once lamented, "There are no more worlds to conquer.' He did not know that he had not conquered even a quarter of his own world. Yet if he had lived in our time, he could not have been President, because he died too young. He was 

Alexander the Great, one of the notable conquerors of history. 

Do we sometimes feel as he did that all the great things have been done and there is nothing left for us?

On the other hand, do we think the world is going to ruin so fast that there is no hope of stopping it? The fact is we do have worlds to conquer. 

We do have problems to solve. Wars, misunderstandings, ill will, suffering, still afflict us. Even when we know what we should like to do, we are not sure of the best way to do it. 

If these problems are to be solved or these worlds conquered, it will have to be done by those who live beyond the time of those who are now running the affairs of humanity. The boys and girls now in school will soon have to tackle a job that has proved pretty tough for their elders. We need not worry about having nothing to do in the future. 

H. Armstrong Roberts

THINKERS 

These high school students want to understand the world they live in and to prepare themselves to do their part in making it what it ought to be.

PROLOGUE 

There are three ways by which we can prepare ourselves for our opportunity: (1) We can become so well informed about things in general that nothing important in the future will seem entirely strange to us. (2) We can learn the reasons why present conditions have come about, for in that way we should get some suggestion about avoiding the evils of the past. (3) We can set up such worthy purposes and ideals that we will not be satisfied with anything mean or low.

A critic of our time said recently that if you want to interest high school pupils today, you must start with the mess we find ourselves in at any particular time. "They are not concerned," he said, "with what anybody did years ago, and they are pretty nearly convinced that everything has gone to the dogs." Doesn't that statement put a challenge before the readers of this book? The writer is far from believing that they think nothing in the past is of any value, that there is nothing worth living for today, or that we look ahead down a dead-end street.

Which is harder, to build up a nation out of parts that have grown up separately, or to hold a great nation together after it has been built up? Do you imagine that people complain about conditions today more or less than they did 150 years ago? Are young people of today looking for something soft, or are they willing to face odds in order to make things better? Have there been other periods in history in which the world seems to have been as upset as it has in the last few years? 

2. Some Inheritances of Ours. Our forefathers had never heard, "You can't take it with you," but it was true, and they left behind much for us. 

"All we have of freedom, all we use or know, This our fathers bought for us long and long ago." 

Kipling wrote that about England, but it would have been equally true of the United States, for our love of freedom and many other good features in our life came from the same source that they came to the English people.

We have inherited a rich land with most of the natural resources that any nations possess. We have inherited a love of liberty and free government which makes us feel distressed when we see great nations submitting to dictators who laugh at freedom and despise

democracy. We have inherited flaming ideals and sacred memories. 

These ideals you can read in our Declaration of Independence and in the Preamble of our national Constitution. These memories recall to us the sacrifices that have been made in the past by those who were willing to give their lives that this nation might come into being and might be kept united. Are we going to be worthy of them?

If you can answer this question fairly, how do you think our national inheritance compares in brilliancy or worth with that of other great nations? 

Harris & Ewing

A MEMORIAL TO A GREAT AMERICAN 

Thomas Jefferson was a believer in democracy at a time when many had no use for it. His influence on the thinking of the American people was great in his time and continues to our own day.

Another inheritance that we sometimes undervalue is the inheritance of experience. Others have saved us the necessity of worrying through some problems because they found the answer first. On the other hand, young people are sometimes accused of being in too much of a hurry, and not being willing to permit time to work its own cure of some diseases. As one citizen might speak to another, let us listen to the voice of experience, (1) Let us not expect to straighten out every difficulty in a little while. It is just as true of nations as of men and women that longstanding habits and customs are not easy to change in a few years.

PROLOGUE 

(2) We must set the general good above the selfish advantage of any person or class. Sometimes we are in such a hurry to benefit a few that we fail to see the whole distance and attempt many things only to have to undo them later. (3) Co-operation is essential for a happy world. We must not only work for others but with them if even good things are to be accomplished with ease and satisfaction. (4) Success individual or national — will depend in large measure upon intelligence. It is well to have heroes, but not profitable to be merely imitators of them. What is good for one age and one time may need to be adjusted to later conditions. (5) Lasting achievement is founded upon sound morals. Brute force and injustice sometimes seem to succeed for a while, but one who puts himself in power by cruelty makes himself hated in the next generation. The successful practicer of clever trickery gets by for a time, but when his methods are known, he is despised. "Experience is a hard teacher, but fools will learn from no other," it has been said. 

But who would be a fool? 

It has been said that the misinformed are especially anxious to lead the uninformed, and the uninformed seem particularly inclined to follow their leadership. Have you ever seen any examples of that kind of foolishness? 

Why is taking advice so hard for some people? 

3. Our Many-sided Democracy. - Life is so many-sided that if we are to understand much of it we shall need to call upon many sources of information. When we study human relations as they have gone on in the past, we call the story history. When we consider the relations of people with their government, we call it civics or political science. 

When we think of the lives of men and women as they are affected by their physical surroundings, we call our study geography. If we emphasize the way people earn their living, we speak of our field of interest as economics. If we give particular attention to the relations of people in social groups, we refer to the study as sociology. If we are concerned with the right and wrong of human relations, we are dealing with ethics. 

All of these together we often speak of as the social sciences or the social studies. Not one of them is entirely separate from the rest. 

We shall need the help of all to understand the life of people and nations today. Surely there will be nothing monotonous or dull in the adventure on which we have started.

Why do you suppose years ago studies like those just mentioned had only a small place in the programs of the schools? Take some current question the first you happen to think of - and see how many of the fields of interest just mentioned have a bearing upon it. 

We shall have to call upon all these fields of learning and experience if we are to understand fully that cherished possession that we call democracy. Democracy is not an easy word to define, as you would discover just by looking in your dictionaries. We think of it most often in connection with government, but it is much broader than that. GEGE 

James Sawders

HEROES OF THE PAST 

In the Hall of Fame at New York University one may see such memorials as these of men and women who have served our country in the past. Their careers should be an inspiration to us.

It is a way of life which seeks to give every person a fair share in the making of the society to which he belongs. It has at least four elements. 

We should not ignore any of them. 

When we look at it as political, we think of a kind of government in which the people rule themselves, or, at least, choose their own rulers.

PROLOGUE 

When we consider it economic, we have in mind a form of life and work in which each one shares in rendering services and is entitled to a fair return for doing so.

When we regard it as social, we are considering a relationship in which everyone enjoys the chance to make a place for himself suited to his talents and effort.

When we think of it as moral or spiritual, we look upon every man and every woman as an individual, with equal rights before God and their fellow men. 

THE FOUNTAIN OF YOUTH THIS SPRING WAS DISCOVERED IN 1513 AND WAS RECORDED A LANDMARK IN A SPANISH CRANT. 

Harold M. Lambert THE FOUNTAIN OF YOUTH 

We may visit in St. Augustine today what is said to be the spring which Ponce de Leon discovered more than four centuries ago. A more valuable means of keeping young is to be constantly alert toward what is going on right around us and in other parts of the world. 

Does democracy show itself in speech, manners, and attitudes? If so, how? Can a rich man be democratic? Do we fully appreciate the value of our democracy?

Ask some of your friends to define democracy as they think of it. After getting all the definitions you can, work up for yourself the best one you can formulate.

4. "The Truth Shall Make You Free." One of the surest things you can know is that "the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth" is the least with which we should be satisfied. We cannot expect to know all there is to know about anything, but at least we can try to keep our minds clear as far as we do go, and be willing to change them if any evidence should make it necessary. 

We do not need to think, for instance, however much we love our own country, that no other country has done anything well. We may very definitely believe that our political party is better than any other, but all parties when in power in this nation have done some good things. Some rich men have blessed the world with their wealth. 

Some have gained it by brutal oppression of their workers. Some poor men have lived worthy lives in unattractive corners of the earth. 

Others have wasted the opportunities they did have in shiftlessness and dissipation. It is seldom fair to pass snap judgment on any class. 

So if we are going to obtain the best results from the work in which we are starting, we must go at it not with a vacant mind or a closed mind, but with an open mind. That does not mean that we should have no convictions, but it does mean that we should constantly be seeking for more light so that we may keep always in the right path. "Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free" - if we faithfully use it when we find it. Thus speaks from experience one citizen to another. 

Why do pupils from different high schools often tell quite different stories about a football or baseball game in which the teams representing their two schools participated? Why do people in politics or in some other kind of public life call each other names? How far should anyone be influenced by that sort of alleged argument? Why is it sometimes hard to get at the facts, even when we sincerely try to discover them? How much exaggeration is there in the advice, "Believe nothing of what you hear, little of what you read, and only half of what you see"?

SOME SUGGESTIONS 

I. Draw up a code to be observed in discussing questions in your class or elsewhere about which there might be differences of opinion. 

2. Make a list of the values which should come to you as a result of your study of the topics discussed in this book. 

3. Mention individuals or classes of people who might desire to know less than the whole truth about some current problems. What cautions can you set up for your contacts with them?

PROLOGUE  

co-operation problem opportunity inheritance freedom; liberty experience success history civics geography economics sociology ethics social studies democracy 

(Some of these words have not been given formal definitions in these pages, but they are used so often that we should understand just what we mean by them.) 

Blackington A RICH INHERITANCE 

As one looks into this valley near Pownal, Vermont, he realizes the varied natural inheritance which is ours to use.

PART I  

In every community or nation we shall find its people showing at least three kinds of interests. They want to live and that means food, clothing, and shelter; they cannot, in these days at least, live alone and that means various kinds of social contacts; since few individuals could protect themselves indefinitely unaided, people have united in order to set up governments — and that means the making of laws and the enforcement of them by public officials. Since the main facts about the form and work of government are simpler to state than those concerning the broad fields of society and industry, we may find it easier to take up first the principles and activities of government. 

We may not think much about the beginnings of our government, but the roots of its life reach far back into the past. Some features and principles of our government have been common to all governments all through human history. These universal ideas, as well as some that are distinctive to us, are the foundation on which our country, the United 

States of America, rests.

Some Questions: 

1. What is government and why must we have it? 

2. Why did we adopt the form of government that we have? 

3. Under what circumstances was our present federal Constitution adopted? 

4. What do we find in this Constitution, and what has it done for us? 

The most convincing reason is 

5. Why We Have Government. 

that we cannot do without it. Human beings in all stages of their growth and civilization have found some sort of authority necessary. 

By government we mean the work of laws and officials in carrying on activities which concern the general welfare. (1) Government must determine the rights of individuals and protect individuals in enjoying life, liberty, and property. If John Smith and I

IO 

disagree, some authority must decide who is right and stand by the decision. Government does that. (2) Government must define the duties of individuals and punish those who disregard them. With every right there goes a duty. Those who are unwilling to perform their duties may be compelled to accept their responsibilities, or treated as unworthy of liberty if they disregard the rights of others. 

Harold M. Lambert GOVERNMENT IN ACTION 

Perhaps you can guess what this young man did. It may not have been serious, but unless the law is enforced equally on everybody, no one can be sure that justice will be done. (3) Government must do whatever is necessary to promote the health, morals, and general welfare of the people. We often speak of this as the police power. It differs from the function next mentioned, in that the police power deals with establishing conditions for living, while the other concerns the providing of conveniences and comforts. (4) Government may carry on useful services which could not so well be performed by individuals. We could not depend upon individuals to maintain public highways, for instance, even in front of their own houses. We could not safely allow anybody and everybody

II 

to deal as he pleased with the government of other countries. As the years pass, we expect governments to do more for us than once anyone would have thought of asking governments to do. 

Mention five ways in which today you have consciously or unconsciously depended upon some government for some service. Why have we fallen into the habit of depending more and more upon government to do things for us? 

Does that seem to be, in your opinion, a desirable tendency? 

6. Forms of Government the World Has Tried. Whatever the form of a government, somebody must possess sovereignty, or supreme political power. It may be in the hands of one man, of a few, or of all the people.

Primitive people usually depended upon one-man rule. 

They needed a leader for war, and if he succeeded in that activity, they were willing that he should direct other features of their lives. That was the beginning of the absolute monarchy, a government in which one person possessed unlimited authority.

In the past such men often expected to pass on their power from father to son. Today we have dictators in several countries who have seized authority and exercise it as arbitrarily as did any absolute monarch of the past. 

What will happen to the governments of dictators when the dictators pass on we can tell later better than while they live. Governments such as these, which claim that the state has full right to control every feature of the life of its people, are sometimes called totalitarian or authoritarian. 

In several countries in the past, certain families or groups of individuals came to dislike or distrust the power of their monarch, and sometimes took authority into their own hands. Such a government

the rule of a few - is known as an oligarchy or, perhaps, if in the hands of a class who think they are superior to ordinary people, an aristocracy. 

If a monarch or his family is allowed to continue to hold office and perhaps exercise a few powers, we have a limited monarchy. If a constitution is drawn up, it may be called a constitutional monarchy. 

Under such a government the people may have most of the privileges and liberties that people could have under any kind of rule. That is

The goose step and the authority wielded by a dictator symbolize a theory of government entirely contrary to our own ideals. the case in Great Britain and was in many of the smaller countries on the continent of Europe, as Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, while they were free. 

If the will of the people of a country is exercised by direct vote or by entrusting power to persons elected by the people, we have a democracy or a republic. We may rightly use the word democracy to mean the spirit of a government in which the people's will prevails (83), whether in form it is a limited monarchy or has a chief official with some such title as president. If the chief public officers are elected by the people and then given considerable responsibility, the government becomes a republic or representative democracy. That

theory of government is seen in our own country as well as in little nations like Switzerland.

So the world has tried at least four types of government the rule of one man, the rule of a small part of the people, rule by direct vote of the people as a whole, and rule by officials whom the people choose. 

Pure democracy, in which authority is exercised by direct vote of all the people, is out of the question for governing a big country. There,

A SYMBOL OF DEMOCRACY 

This town hall at Georgia, Vermont, is one of many in New England where the people come together regularly to make their own decisions on public questions. government must be conducted by those whom the people elect, and whom we call representatives.

We should mention another contrast between forms of government. 

Some national governments are centralized, with all important powers in the hands of national officials. Great Britain and many others belong in that group. But some countries are composed of parts, which may be called provinces or states, and which have considerable responsibility for their own government. A government formed by a union of these parts is called a federation if large powers

are given to the central organization, a confederation if the separate units keep the greater power in their own hands. The great British dominions of Canada and Australia are federations, and so is little Switzerland. Our country went through the confederate stage first, under the Articles of Confederation, but became a real federation under our present Constitution.¹ Germany went through a similar change from a confederation to a federation, but Hitler knocked out the federal idea and centralized all power in his own hands. 

Several countries in Latin America tried to imitate our Constitution when they made their own. Brazil calls itself the United States of 

Brazil. Mexico thinks of itself, too, as a federation and today is composed of twenty-eight states and one territory. But the Latin- 

American countries were handicapped by having no long tradition of self-government or democracy to guide them after they became free, and some of them could not serve as shining examples of either republics or federations. 

May one who has never lived under any form of government except his own be able to judge intelligently the desirability of other forms? Does the fact that some absolute monarchs have tried to do well by their people justify absolute government or dictatorship today? What changes in the form of governments, if any, have taken place within the last year or two? 

7. Our Political Background. - American liberties are English liberties transferred into a New World. We in the United States are deeply indebted to England for most of the principles and ideals that underlie our own government. Our own struggle for independence against a misguided king had its earlier parallel in the struggle of the barons who forced King John to accept Magna Carta in 1215. 

Another struggle for liberty in England occurred in the seventeenth century. After a period of arbitrary rule by the Stuart kings, the climax of the conflict was reached in the passage of the famous Bill of Rights in 1689. When King William III signed that document, he put an end to all the theories of personal rule that any of his predecessors on the throne of England preached, for it definitely forbade numerous things which several kings had done. that Bill of Rights you will find in the Constitution of the United States today almost word for word, if you read the first ten amendments, which now are as much a part of the Constitution as the original document itself. 

Several of the notable features of our form of government also were suggested by those of England. Partly because England had a king as the official head of the government, we have a President in the same situation. England's

Parliament is composed of two houses, and so is our Congress. 

We had other reasons for that arrangement, but English precedent helped us to accept it. 

English courts had not been looked upon as standing on just the same plane with Parliament and the king, but their separate duties helped to establish the belief that there were three great functions of government-legislative, executive, and judicial law-making, law-enforcing, and law-interpreting. When governments were set up in the English colonies, English principles of law were usually observed. When the colonies

If George III had pursued a wise policy toward his North American colonies, do you think today we might be citizens of the British empire? Why do you suppose we often speak of the United States as America when there are twenty other independent countries in North and South America? Do those countries have any right to object? 

8. The Making of Our Present Constitution. A constitution, as you probably know, is a fundamental document which explains the form and powers of a government. In other countries and sometimes we do so too the word state is used to mean an independent political organization. But today in this country and in some others, such as Australia, the word "state" is used to mean one of the members of a federal government instead of a completely independent organization. 

Your study of history has told you that our country did not get along very well under the Articles of Confederation. The central government which the Articles set up had practically no power to compel the states to do anything they did not care to do. Within the states conditions were very bad, and the states seriously disagreed with one another about some things. Some of the ablest men in the states then began to ask themselves, "What are we coming to?”

Congress twice proposed to the states that the Articles of Confederation be changed to give a little more power to Congress, but each time the proposition failed because all the states had to agree to such changes, and one state held out.

At a conference held in 1785 at George Washington's home at Mount Vernon between representatives of the two states of Maryland and Virginia, it was suggested that the states should be invited to send delegates to a meeting at Annapolis in 1786 to consider what might be done to improve conditions. Only five of the thirteen states cared enough to be represented there, but out of the meeting came the proposal to get a convention together from all the states of the 

Union which would meet in Philadelphia in 1787.

Things turned out better now. All but the one state of Rhode 

Island sent delegates to this famous Philadelphia convention. They kept at their job for four months, finishing on September 17. They went far beyond the original purpose for which the meeting was called, which was to revise the Articles of Confederation. Instead they built a whole new Constitution.

This convention had several big decisions to make and, as events turned out, acted very wisely. It set up a strong central government with a three-fold organization of authority- a Congress of two houses to make the laws, a President to be the chief executive, and a Supreme Court which would be the highest judicial body in the land. Since the work involved compromise over several important matters, nobody was fully satisfied. Out of the fifty-five delegates who attended the convention, there were only forty-two left when its meetings closed, and three of those refused to sign the Constitution. 

The Constitution had to be submitted to the states to be ratified that is, accepted—before it could go into effect. In each state special conventions were held to act upon it, and it was to go into effect when nine states accepted it. Some states accepted it promptly, but in others the fight over ratification was close, even bitter, especially in Massachusetts, Virginia, and New York. By the time it went into effect in the early part of 1789, eleven states had accepted it. 

North Carolina and stubborn little Rhode Island held out until later. 

Apparently there could have been no Constitution made without compromise. Are there any matters in which one should not compromise? Is compromise always better than for one person or party to insist on having its own way? If you had been Patrick Henry or George Mason in 1788, do you think you would have refused to favor the ratification of the Constitution? 

When is the most favorable time to propose extensive changes in government or anything else, when conditions are rosy or when they are dark? 

9. Some Distinctive Features of Our Government. - The makers of our Constitution "builded better than they knew." Benjamin 

Franklin admitted there were things in it which he did not like, but supported it because he was sure they could do no better under the circumstances, and what they had done might be the best after all. 

As things have turned out, no far-reaching change in the nature of our government has taken place from that day to this. (1) The Constitution established a federal government. No other kind could possibly have worked out, for the states would not give up their separate existence, and the inefficiency of a weak confederation had been shown by experience. (2) The Constitution established a definite system of checks and balances. It provided two houses in Congress, each of which could check the other by refusing to pass bills which it did not like. The

President could check Congress by vetoing measures passed by that body, though Congress could come back at him, if it wished, by passing a bill over his veto by a two-thirds vote. The courts could check both the President and Congress in that they could decide whether either of them had gone beyond the powers which the Constitution granted. Perhaps some would say that our system of government 

H. H. Rideout OUR NATIONAL CAPITOL 

Probably no picture is better known than one that represents the meeting-place of our lawmakers at Washington. No textbook on American problems would be complete without it. carries the check-and-balance idea too far, but it was established to preserve liberty, and liberty has been preserved. (3) The Constitution set up a republican form of government. The right to decide who should vote was left in the hands of the states, and most of them were not very liberal in granting it at first. But public officials were chosen by those who did have the right to vote, and that is what we mean when we talk about a republican form of government. (4) The Constitution established a fairly definite distribution of powers between state and national governments. Some powers are specifically granted to the national government, and some are denied

to the states. A few also are prohibited to both the national government and the states. But on the other hand, many powers may be exercised by both the national government and the states. 

Might a country have a constitution and still not be a democracy or a republic? Of the four special characteristics of our government mentioned, are there any which in the course of time might seem less important than they did in 1787? 

10. Keeping Our Constitution Up to Date. - Perhaps we can agree that a constitution should include all the fundamental facts and ideas which are necessary to set up an effective government, but that matters of minor detail or provisions that clearly might need to be changed later on should be left to be dealt with by laws from time to time. Of all the republics in the world that have constitutions, ours has the shortest. (1) The first part of a constitution is regularly the preamble. This explains the reasons why the constitution is made or states the principles underlying it. If you have forgotten the Preamble of our 

Constitution, turn to it and learn it again right now. (2) Constitutions usually contain a bill of rights, which is a list of powers and privileges that the people say their government must not take away from them. The makers of our Constitution thought that none was needed, because the government was to have only the powers granted to it anyway; but people in general thought otherwise, and the first ten additions, or amendments, that were made were nothing else than a bill of rights. (3) An outline of the organization of the government is essential. 

This need not be detailed, but will include a list of the chief officials, a statement of the way they are to be chosen, and a summary of their powers and duties. (4) Special provisions relating to certain important matters are found in most constitutions. 

In ours, for instance, the relation of the states to one another is mentioned. There is more variety in constitutions in regard to this fourth item than any of the others, because what seems important to the makers of one constitution will not stand out particularly in the minds of another group. (5) Provisions for changes in or additions to the constitution are desirable. We call such changes amendments. We should not expect any constitution to be completely fool-proof, or suppose that the

members of any constitutional convention will be clairvoyant enough to see everything that is going to happen in the future. (6) A schedule explaining the conditions under which the constitution will go into effect is usually necessary. In only a few cases do conventions drawing up constitutions have the right to declare their constitution in effect as soon as they finish their work. 

Look at your state constitution and see whether it includes the six items just mentioned. If you were making a constitution, would you include in it such matters as the salaries of public officials, the size of the law-making body, the length of term of judges, the powers that the law-making body might exercise?

To bring a constitution up to date, amendments which might either add to it, make changes in it, or cut out parts of it are likely to be necessary. Twenty-one amendments have been made to our national Constitution up to the present time (1941). 1933 1933 You will notice that all these amendments were made within three periods of a limited number of years. Maybe that means that our people have rather prolonged periods of thinking that our Constitution

is pretty nearly right, interrupted by shorter spells in which they are in a mood to make changes. The process of amendment cannot be unreasonably hard if you notice that the last six were made within. a period of not much over twenty years.

In amending our Constitution, two steps or stages are needed. 

First the amendment must be proposed, and then it must be ratified. 

The ratification must be made by the states. 

All amendments thus far made have been proposed by a twothirds vote of both houses of Congress. Congress also is required by the Constitution to arrange for the holding of a national convention to propose amendments if the legislatures of two thirds of the states ask to have it done. This second plan has never been used. 

Before an amendment can go into effect, ratification must be given by three-fourths of the states. In submitting an amendment to the states, Congress decides whether it will be considered by the state legislatures or by special conventions held in each state. Though the 

Twenty-first Amendment was the only one adopted by the convention method, this method has the advantage of allowing a decision to be made on the merits of the amendment alone, instead of by a state legislature which might have been elected when many other things than a constitutional amendment were in the minds of the voters. 

The Constitution fixes no limit as to the amount of time that states may take to act on an amendment after it has been submitted to them. In two amendments it was definitely provided by the amendment itself that unless it were ratified within seven years, it would not go into effect. An amendment was submitted by Congress to the states in 1924 which was intended to give Congress the power to make laws about the labor of young people up to the age of eighteen. Since it has not received the approval of three-fourths of the states, it is still up in the air. 

Do you think the process of amending our federal Constitution is too difficult, too easy, or about right? What would you think of having a direct nation-wide popular vote on amendments instead of having ratification given in the way in which it is given now? 

11. Adjusting the Constitution to New Needs. Constitutions may also be kept up to date without actually changing the constitution itself. Some of these are the result of the natural working out of provisions already in the constitution, and some of them are the 

---

result of changes in customs or conditions which could not be foreseen. (1) Making laws to carry out the details of powers given by the constitution to the government is one means of adapting it to new conditions. For instance, our Constitution said that there should be a Supreme Court, but did not say how many members it should have or what other federal courts there might be. Neither does it make any special provisions about the amount of money that shall be raised by taxes or the kinds of taxes that may be used to bring revenue into the federal treasury. This method of adaptation is commonly referred to as adjustment by statute - which is another word for "law." (2) Adjustment may also take place by usage or custom. People get into the habit of doing things a certain way until that method is followed without anyone's thinking much about it. Our Constitution does not mention the President's Cabinet, but every President has one.

The Constitution says nothing about the number of times a person may be elected President, but no President was elected for a third term until 1940. Customs which are regularly followed for a long time we sometimes speak of as our unwritten constitution. (3) A third means of adjusting the constitution is through judicial interpretation. In Great Britain when Parliament passes a law and the king signs it, it is constitutional. With us, it depends on our courts whether some laws will go into effect or not. Courts have no right to take anything out of the Constitution or put anything into it of their own accord, but if a law has been passed whose meaning is not perfectly clear to everybody, the courts have to decide what it shall be taken to mean. One may believe that Congress has no authority to pass a certain law, but the Supreme Court has the final word as to whether Congress did have the right to do it or not. The 

Constitution gives Congress, for instance, the right to regulate commerce "among the several states.' But what is interstate commerce? Does it include radio messages and letter-writing and the production in factories of goods that may go into another state some time? The interpretation put upon such items by the courts may really determine under some conditions how the Constitution itself shall operate.

In the early days of our history under the Constitution, there were

big arguments over strict construction as against broad or loose construction. Was Congress limited to the particular powers mentioned in so many words in the Constitution, or could it pass laws that might be suggested by some of the powers that were definitely stated? For the acceptance of the broad or loose construction of the Constitution as the proper policy, we are much indebted to John Marshall, who was Chief Justice of the Supreme Court for thirty-four years (18011835). If the opposite view had prevailed, our national Constitution could hardly have been equal to changing times and circumstances to the extent that it has been. 

The makers of the Constitution showed a fine amount of practical wisdom in drawing upon the experience of England and of the states rather than working up something entirely original. Perhaps the 

Englishman Gladstone was exaggerating when he said that it was the greatest document ever struck off at a given time by the brain and purpose of man, but its making was certainly a wonderful achievement. 

Why do you suppose it was so much work to get the Constitution adopted if it was such a remarkable document as we think it is today? In the business world we do not have such checks and balances as are provided for our government in our national Constitution. Is there any reason why there should be a difference? Is it well to have some customs that might be properly called an unwritten constitution? 

12. Democratic Government at Home and Abroad. - Pure democracy was looked upon by many people in George Washington's time as a rather wild notion. Some still feel that way about it. The growth of democratic practices has been slow in some places, though until within a few years we would have said it was steady. 

When our Constitution was made, most of the states set up restrictions on voting based on property-owning or taxpaying, or even on religious belief, which cut down greatly the proportion of voters to the whole population. The first half of the nineteenth century, however, witnessed numerous steps in advance. Requirements of propertyowning and taxpaying were reduced or abolished so that by the middle of the nineteenth century white men had the right to vote for most offices in most of the states. As a result of the Civil War the vote was extended to colored men on the same basis as to the white. 

Not till after the close of that war did any part of the country permanently give women a right to vote on the same level with men.

Utah,

Wyoming did that first in 1869, while it was still a territory. 

Idaho, and Colorado followed in the 1890's. In the early part of the twentieth century more states gave women the vote, and the World War gave the necessary push to put over woman suffrage for the country. The Nineteenth Amendment, which went into effect in 1920, finally put the proposal into the Constitution. 

CAIL 

Acme Photo THE PRESIDENT VOTES 

The President on Election Day is just one of the voters in his home district. 

Here he is setting an example which too many citizens whose votes would count as much as his fail to follow.

But now that we do have in this country representative democracy for all citizens over twenty-one, we may ask ourselves, How has it worked? Dictators in several countries have ridiculed it. "It is decadent," they say. Here are some arguments sometimes offered for and against the principle of democracy. We may think a little about them right here, and then, after we have carefully observed our ways of living and working, come back to the question again, and see what experience has told us. If any principle of government is really sound, it surely will stand free discussion.

For 

(1) People progress best when they make choices for themselves. (2) Democracy gives the individual citizen a sense of responsibility and a desire to make good. 

(3) Democracy promotes peace. 

Free, self-governing peoples are much less ready to go to war than those who are dominated by one man or a selfish class. (4) The loss of liberty is too high a price to pay for tyrannical efficiency. Besides, tyrants can make blunders.

Against 

(1) Democracies may delay in times of emergency. The dictator need not wait. (2) A majority vote is not necessarily on the right side. Majorities may be tyrannical and changeable. (3) In democracies leaders may be chosen not on real merit but because they make big promises to ignorant voters. (4) To be well governed is more desirable than to have the privilege of making ignorant mistakes. The authoritarian government is efficient. 

British Combine Photos, Limited A DEMOCRATIC ROYAL FAMILY 

The King and Queen of Great Britain, with their daughters, Elizabeth and Margaret Rose, are a royal family because their people want them to be.

Great Britain and her dominions, little Switzerland, and the Scandinavian countries believe in democracy as well as we do. Until calamity came in 1940 we were including France, and we would like to include Latin America, in that statement. In the countries whose rulers despise democracy, such as Germany and Italy, we find peoples who either never pretended to try it or, if they did, did not succeed in giving it a square deal. We need not pretend that our democracy has been perfect, but our experience thus far has made us like it better than any other kind of government we have heard of. 

Point out some steps taken in our own history that today seem to have been mistakes. Was democracy to blame for these mistakes, or would they probably have been made under some other form of government? Can we profit by the experience of other people with their particular type of government?

The British people have the reputation of moving "slowly down from precedent to precedent," as Tennyson put it, but the British government of today, as compared with that of 1787, has shown more change than that of the United States. France, in the same time, has changed from an absolute monarchy to a radical republic, an empire, a kingdom, a second republic, an empire, a third republic, and now what? For a young and growing nation, our government has certainly proved itself unusually stable, and demands for change have been surprisingly few.

II  

Government rests upon constitutions and laws. But they are just words on pieces of paper until some machinery gets to work to change them into living and working forces. Important parts of this machinery in our country, as in all other democratic countries, are political parties. 

Why we have them, how they work, and how the people control their government when they want to do so - by using them are things we need to understand if we are really to appreciate how our government actually works. 

Some Questions: 

1. Of what use are political parties? 

2. What do political parties want and how do they get it? 

3. How are candidates for office nominated? 

4. Who may vote and how do they do it? 

5. How may honest voters get honest and efficient government? 

13. Politics and Parties. Politics is a perfectly good word. It means the practical working of government. But why do we often speak of "a politician" as someone who deserves no particular respect?

Simply because we have let the work of government too often fall into the hands of men who use it for what they can make out of it themselves. And we call them politicians. It would be far better if every citizen should think of himself as a politician. If he would do that and then determine that as far as his influence should go government should be honest and capable, the words "politician" and "politics" would cease to smell bad. "Politics is dirty," says one man and will have nothing whatever to do with it. "What can I know about politics? It is all run by a few people anyway," remarks another and lets the matter drop. Are those people and others who refuse to vote justified? Think of certain people to whom the word "politician" has been applied. What sort of reputation did they have? 

How did they get it?

Politics touches every extensive interest of the people, in the home, on the street, in business, in school, and anywhere else, because govern- 29

ment itself touches all those interests. If politics is unsound in a community, business men lose confidence, graft and unfairness may prevail in the dealings of citizens with their own government, and even schools may be controlled by persons who want jobs for their own friends. If politics is clean, every class and group can go ahead without being disturbed over anything except the honest disagreements that arise among even the best of citizens. Because differences do arise among citizens, we use political parties to help settle these differences and keep things moving. 

By a political party we mean a group of people who think alike about some matters, and who wish to have their views adopted as the policy of the government. Parties may differ considerably in size, because one set of opinions with reference to the tariff, foreign relations, control of business, or something else, may be held by a much larger number of people than the opposite views. But it is a misuse of words to talk about having just one political party, as the rulers of such countries as Italy, Germany, and Russia do today. At any given time, there are likely to be groups which disagree, if for no other reason than that one group is in office and wants to stay in, while another is out and wants to get in. 

Parties render some service, else they would not be found in all democratic governments. (1) They help to bring together those who think alike and increase the chances of getting their views adopted. 

One thousand individuals, with each one working by himself, might make considerable trouble, but they would not be likely to accomplish anything constructive. (2) Parties help to crystallize people's thinking about the questions of the day and make conflicting opinions clearer. (3) Parties help to reduce the number of candidates for office and make it more likely that those who are chosen really represent the preference of a considerable portion of the people. (4) Parties may accept responsibility for getting the policies they advocate put into effect after an election has been held. 

On the other hand, noticeable evils have appeared as a result of parties. (1) Since parties, to be successful, need to be organized, their leaders may be tempted to conduct the party's affairs in their own interests. In order to get or hold jobs for themselves and their friends, they may agree to do almost anything. (2) When parties have been in existence for some time, voters may assume that everything done

under their own party name is desirable. They may vote for a crook or an ignoramus just because he is running on their ticket. (3) Parties may overemphasize the benefits or dangers in some particular program, and create unnecessary ill feeling. The best solution of many a disputed question may be one which takes into account the views of both sides. (4) Parties may try to win elections by forcing officials to act unfairly, bribing voters with money or promises of jobs, or other dishonorable means.

This is a picture of the convention in Philadelphia in June, 1940, at which the Republican party nominated Wendell Willkie as its candidate for the presidency. 

The main floor of the hall is reserved for delegates. The galleries are for visitors. 

What, then, should a voter think about parties? In many states a voter must declare himself publicly to be a member of a certain party or else he can have no voice in nominating candidates for office. He should try to decide which party, on the whole, most nearly represents his own opinions, with the full understanding that no law can bind him to vote for a candidate whom he believes to be unfit. The voter may sometimes think he has to make a choice of evils, but may not that be sometimes true in other fields than politics?

How do the parties in your community or state compare in strength? 

What is the reason for this situation? Give examples from your own acquaintance or knowledge of conditions or events that illustrate the statements made in this section. After an election, is it hard for the losing side to accept peacefully the result? Why? 

14. Parties in National Politics. Not a word was said about parties in the Constitution. Just as soon, however, as the Constitution itself was before the people for discussion, party division began. 

People were for the Constitution or against it, and called themselves Federalists or Anti-Federalists. When the Constitution had been ratified, the controversy between those who wanted a strong national government under the Constitution and those who did not became so bitter at times that in Washington's famous Farewell Address he warned his countrymen against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party." Unfortunately, people were not willing to listen to that advice.

The Federalist party wanted a strong central government, and the Anti-Federalists thought the states should exercise the bulk of the power of government. After a while the Federalist party disappeared. 

The Anti-Federalists changed their name to Democratic-Republican and then Republican, and then new divisions occurred. One party, led for a time by the famous Andrew Jackson, and claiming to represent the masses of the people, called themselves Democrats. Their opponents took the name of Whigs. 

When the slavery question came forward, the Whig party tried to escape taking sides on it, and the Democratic party emphasized the right of the states to deal with such matters. Then came the new 

Republican party, which declared that the central government should do as it pleased with slavery in the territories. The Civil War followed its victory in 1860. By no means were all Democrats against the Union, but the Union victory weakened the Democratic party in the North for some little time. The South, however, supported the 

Democrats pretty solidly.

As times change, so do policies and parties, though parties do not always realize how they shift sides themselves. Under Woodrow 

Wilson and later under Franklin D. Roosevelt the Democratic party undertook policies that could be justified only by a very broad construction of the Constitution, while the Republican party, forgetting

its political past, opposed both Wilson's "New Freedom" and Franklin 

D. Roosevelt's "New Deal," partly because, they said, it interfered with the rights of the states. 

E PLURIBUS 

During most of our national history there have been only two parties that had any chance of winning a national election, but there were other parties, too, variously known as "third parties" or "minor parties." In 1854, for instance, the Republican party was a "third party." Another one that drew a good many votes was the so-called People's party of the 1890's, and still another the Progressive party, headed for a while by Theodore 

Roosevelt at a time when he had lost his control of the Republi- 

The Prohibition party for many years regularly nominated candidates on the one issue of getting rid of the liquor traffic. "Third parties" rarely grow into permanent organizations. 

When a third-party issue seems likely to succeed, usually one of the two leading parties takes it up. cans. 0910 

UNUM Temple in New Orleans "Times-Picayune" THE ELEPHANT AND THE DONKEY 

Especially in years when important campaigns occur, cartoonists have fun with the leading parties by picturing the animals which have come to represent them. In this cartoon Uncle Sam is urging both the 

Republican elephant and the Democratic donkey to forget their differences as far as possible in the interests of the nation as a whole.

Though often the opposition of parties to each other seems childish, the existence of at least two parties seems to be necessary for democracy to succeed. 

Dictators do not allow any party except their own. Just as in England the leader of "His Majesty's Loyal Opposition" is recognized as a really important personage, so in this country, as in any other democracy, it seems important to have somebody looking for mistakes in what the party in power undertakes. Probably many more mistakes would be made than are made if it were not for the

faultfinders, but they should be constructive rather than nasty about their activities.

What party names are used in European countries that have popular government? Is a party likely to have a long existence if its activities center around one strong leader? What men who held high places in our political life were outstanding on their own account? Did they make parties take certain courses, or did parties give them their opportunities to become famous? 

15. How Parties Get What They Want. Since in a free country no law can command any individual to belong to a party, the formation and organization of parties is, to a considerable extent, a private affair. 

On the other hand, since political parties are formed for the purpose of electing officials and influencing the policy of the government, a government is justified in making laws that will regulate party activity in such a way as not to harm the cause of good government. 

The large national parties have a national committee made up of one person or perhaps a man and a woman from each state. They have a national chairman, a secretary, and a treasurer, and are particularly active in the years when a presidential election is to be held. 

The national committee has to adopt the plans for the nominating convention in years when a President is to be chosen, and make arrangements to get funds to pay the bills of the party. 

In each state there are committees similarly made up, though parties in every state are not always organized in exactly the same fashion. 

In the local communities in each state there are also committees city, county, borough, ward, and even precinct- and upon them the party depends for a great part of the work needed to win votes and get voters out on election day. There is nothing wrong in such party activity if it is done honestly and openly, and not simply for the purpose of getting favors for oneself. Indeed, a man or woman may really be rendering a worth-while service in trying to keep voters from neglecting their duty to go to the polls on election day. 

As far as your knowledge goes, do parties in your neighborhood use dishonorable or questionable means to get support or to win elections? Should a young voter as soon as he is twenty-one definitely consider himself a member of some particular party?

Sometimes contests for nomination as party candidates produce as much bitterness as fights between one party and another. It is often hard for an independent to beat "the ring" or "the machine," as a

well-established party organization is sometimes called. Occasionally one man really becomes the boss of a party in either a city or state. 

He does not always ask for a high office himself, but may prefer to put up some respectable figurehead who will do as he is told. 

Party organizations get some of their support by doing little courtesies or kindnesses. Getting a fellow out of jail who has got into trouble, giving a Christmas basket at the appropriate time, getting a job for someone who is out of work things like these may mean not only the vote of the individual who is helped, but of all his relatives. 

One reason why a party machine is often hard to overthrow is that a great many voters, though they may get excited while a campaign is going on, forget about it after the shouting is over. By the time the next election comes around, the organization has strengthened its position so that it is just as solidly intrenched as ever. Sometimes a great change, like the depression of 1929, turns people en masse from one party to another without any reason for doing so except that one group was in office when the calamity came on. 

In the history of your state or local community have there been examples of party machines or boss rule? If they were overthrown, by what means was the change brought about? Do you know of cases when politicians shifted from one party to another simply because they thought a certain party was going to win an election? Is that sort of thing good citizenship? What kind of political work do you consider really justified on the part of party workers? 

16. Selecting Candidates for Office. Nomination means the put ting up of candidates to be voted on; election means the choice by the people of persons who are to hold office.¹ Be sure you understand the difference. Some kind of formal nomination before an election is usually desirable. To leave the final choice to election day might result in the total vote being so widely distributed that the winner would really represent the preference of only a small part of the people. 

Besides, when nominations are made ahead of time by recognized parties, voters have a chance to consider these candidates and what they stand for and choose more wisely than might otherwise be the case. 

Several ways of nominating candidates have been used. In the past conventions were a common method. A convention is simply a meeting 

1 The word "nomination" is also used when Presidents, governors, or other such officials propose the names of people for certain offices which have to be approved by a senate, a city council, or some such body.

of persons who come together for a particular purpose. Such a convention might be a mass convention, which any interested person might attend, or a representative convention, made up of persons regularly chosen to participate in its actions. A meeting of members of a party in a ward or voting district might be called a caucus. That word is also used when the members of a legislature or Congress who belong to a certain party get together to talk over party problems. 

Because of a feeling that caucuses and conventions are too easily controlled by party bosses, a direct primary system has been adopted in most of the states, which allows all the members of a party to have a voice in deciding who the party candidates shall be. Primary elections are so called because they are the first or primary step in the process of electing officials; they are direct primaries, if the voters take part in them in much the same way as in a general election.

ATTORNEY GENERAL Vote for ONE HOWE COOLIDGE AMEE OF 285 HARVARD STREET, CAMBRIDGE CLARENCE A. BARNES OF 79 RUMFORD AVENUE, MANSFIELD FRANK F. WALTERS OF 70 CHANDLER STREET, BOSTON~~~~~ A PRIMARY BALLOT 

On this ballot, used by the Republican party in Massachusetts in a recent year, appear the names of all the persons who would like to have the party's nomination for certain offices. Each voter picks out his choice among the various candidates for nomination. At a primary election each party has a separate ballot. 

Each state may make its own laws about primary elections. Separate ballots are provided for each party. 

Some states have an open primary, in which a voter on primary election day simply asks for the ballot of the party in which he wishes to vote. 

Then he marks his choices among the list of persons who want to be candidates of that party. Other states have a closed primary. A voter may not participate in nominating the candidates of a party unless he is registered as belonging to that party. He does not have

to enroll in a particular party, but if he refrains from doing so, he can have no voice in nominating any party's candidates. There is room for argument as to whether better candidates, on the whole, are obtained through the direct primary than through the old-time conventions. With the direct primary, however, the majority of the voters in a party can have their wishes fulfilled if they will only turn out on primary election day. 

In many states the winner is the candidate with the largest vote, whether a majority or not.¹ In several southern states, if no candidate gets a majority of all the votes cast for nomination for a certain office, a "run-off" primary is held. Then the two highest candidates fight it out at a second election.

Let no one think the primary is unimportant. In states where one party regularly wins, the primary may be even more important than the final election. If no party puts up a strong candidate, the voter's final choice may have to be made between two unworthy politicians. 

In most states it is possible for a person to get his name on the ballot on election day after primaries or nominating conventions have been held, by means of a petition signed by a certain number of persons. 

Sometimes the law requires that candidates running in that way shall adopt a party name for that election. Voters are also permitted, as a rule, to write on the ballot the name of a person not nominated in advance. Occasionally persons nominated by independent movements, or even those whose names have to be written in by the voters, succeed in winning, but of course they are under a handicap. 

A few states have laws forbidding a person to run as the candidate of more than one party. What do you think of such a law? Would your answer to this question be the same for all kinds of offices? Which do you prefer, the open or the closed primary?

Some would like to have all candidates run for office without using any party name, especially in local elections. Others think that since judges ought not to be partisans, they at least ought to be chosen without reference to party. Independent voters are more likely to favor 

1 Be sure you understand the difference between "majority" and "plurality." A majority is more than half the whole number of votes cast. A candidate has a majority when he has more votes than all other candidates put together. A plurality is simply the lead of one number of votes over another. If John Smith gets 4,000 votes, James Brown 3,000, and

Bill Black 2,000, nobody has a majority, but John Smith has a plurality of 1,000 votes over 

James Brown.

To what extent, if at all, do you have non-partisan elections for any offices in your state? If you do have them, are they satisfactory? Do you approve of them? 

17. Convincing or Fooling the Public. The period between the 

.nomination of candidates for office and the final election is often a time of great excitement. Each side may carry on a lively campaign to get the support of voters, either by argument or by other means. 

A special committee of a party may draw up a platform, which is a statement of what the party does or is supposed to believe. The various clauses or propositions in the platform are referred to as planks. Usually a party platform in a state or national election is submitted to the party convention for approval. 

Sometimes the personality or opinions of the leading candidate of a party really become the "issue" of the campaign. It is easier, for instance, to ask oneself the question, "Do you want Franklin D. Roosevelt for President?" than, "Do you believe in parity payments to farmers?" or "What is your opinion of social security?" Sometimes there is one big question to be settled, as in 1896, when the presidential election turned to a great extent on the question of whether the United States should or should not adopt the free coinage of silver at the ratio of sixteen to one. Almost always parties include in their platforms some statements about which nobody would disagree or which are intended to get the good will of some particular group. Indeed, voters sometimes suspect, as has been said, that a political platform is like a platform on railroad cars — intended to use to get in but not to stand on after one does get in. 

If the platform of every party contains statements or proposals with some of which a voter does not agree, what should he do on election day? Would you prefer to vote for a personally honorable candidate on a poor platform or a weak candidate on a good platform? Why?

There is doubtless much less outright buying of votes today than at some times in the past. There is less spending of money for torchlight processions and other spectacular ways of stirring up enthusiasm. 

Billboards are plastered with all kinds of statements about candidates. 

The radio is overworked with candidates' speeches. Newspapers discuss candidates and issues on their editorial pages, and some of

them write their news stories in one-sided fashion. A short campaign is more economical than a long one, and probably in most elections everything that needs to be said can be written or spoken in three or four weeks. When long periods of time intervene between the primaries and the final election, it is hard to arouse sufficient interest in the primaries. 

To reduce the likelihood of using money improperly in an election, most states now have laws requiring political parties and candidates to report exactly how much they receive and spend during the campaign, and also what they spend it for.

Laws, both state and national, forbid parties to take gifts from corporations. The public as a whole really wants elections to be carried on honestly, but we have not yet reached the time when voters can be influenced only by appeals to logic and common sense, and not by appeals to selfishness, prejudice, or ignorance.

Should limits on the amount of money that might be spent for a candidate or by him be set? Would it be desirable for governments to print at public expense the chief arguments offered by various parties and candidates and distribute them to all voters? Are really high-grade men always the strongest possible candidates? Why or why not? 

18. Who Shall Have the Right to Vote? In a real democracy, we look upon voting as a right which any well-behaved citizen should be able to obtain. In a dictatorship we shall probably be told that voting is a privilege which the dictator grants or takes away in accordance with his own sweet will.

Some limitations are reasonable. A definite age requirement is usual — Russia says 18; several other countries, including our own, say 21. There are requirements of residence, also, and in this country

citizenship in the United States. In Section 12 we pointed out steps by which the right has been extended from a rather limited number who had it when our national existence began. You can read a similar story in the history of the English and other free peoples. 

We sometimes speak of the right to vote as suffrage, or the franchise, and of all the voters taken together as the electorate. Enfranchisement is the giving of the right to vote, and disfranchisement means taking it away. One who shows himself by criminal acts or other evidence to be an unworthy citizen certainly should not be allowed to have a voice in the government.

Granting the right to vote in our country has always been chiefly in the hands of the states. They set whatever qualifications they please, with the exceptions found in the Fifteenth Amendment (1870), which declares that one may not be denied the right to vote on account of "race, color, or previous condition of servitude," and the Nineteenth (1920), forbids suffrage laws to make any distinction on account of sex. The national Congress does not determine who may vote. 

Residence requirements vary considerably among the states. Some require that a voter, if he was not born in the state, must have lived there at least a year. Additional restrictions in regard to residence in his voting district, or his city or township, are also customary. 

Why are residence restrictions and the possession of citizenship in this country reasonable requirements? Would it be better if a definite clause were added to the national Constitution making the qualifications for voters uniform all over the country? What arguments might have been offered for demanding taxpaying as a necessary qualification for voting? A smaller proportion of women vote, in most places, than of men. 

What do you suppose is the explanation? Is it sensible? Why not cut down the voting age in this country to 18?

What are the specific requirements in your state as to residence, taxpaying, and other possible restrictions on the right to vote? What happens if a person in your state moves from one voting district into another inside of the residence limit for voters prescribed by your laws or constitution? 

Many states require registration of voters. An official list must be prepared which contains the name and residence of every voter, and a person whose name does not appear on this registration list is not permitted to vote. Different methods are used for getting voters registered. (1) Local officials, perhaps known as assessors or registrars, make up voting lists of the residents of their town or district.

4I (2) Voters may be required each year on a definite day or days before election to register as voters, giving such distinguishing facts about themselves as their age, street and number, political party, and other statistics. (3) Permanent registration lists may be made up by requiring voters to register when they become 21 years of age, or when they move into a new neighborhood, and then as long as they continue

If he moves from one voting district to another, he must see to it that his change of residence goes on the official cards or other lists. 

Do you have permanent registration of voters in your state and community, or yearly registration? If you have neither, by what means are your voting lists made up? Why have states sometimes required personal registration of voters in cities when they did not demand it in rural districts? 

Some states think that voting is important enough to justify requiring voters to be able to read and write English. Various kinds of tests

What do you think of such an arrangement? 

19. How Voting Is Done. - The Tuesday after the first Monday in 

November is the regular election day for state and national officers in every state but Maine, which chooses state officials on the second Monday of September in even-numbered years. The choice of a 

President is the one election that occurs on the same day in every state of the Union. That comes on the regular day in the years divisible by four. It is just an accident that leap years are "presidential years," but since the President's term is four years, the elections naturally have to come four years apart. 

Some states hold city and other local elections in other months of the year than November. Other states try to serve the same purpose by having local elections in odd-numbered years, while the state and national officers are chosen in the even-numbered years. Primary elections, as we have already noticed, are held some weeks or months before the regular election. 

What do the laws of your state provide with reference to election days? 

Would you recommend any change? If so, what?

Counties or cities are divided for voting purposes into districts or precincts. In a thinly settled township all the voters can be accommodated in one place. In each voting district there is an election board with, usually, three to five members representing at least two political parties. Since fraud or serious error in one voting district might upset

Numerous changes have taken place in the method of voting.

voting was more likely to be honest and thoughtful if done in private. 

So gradually all the states introduced a system of voting by paper ballots, provided by candidates or parties. That in turn gave way to the system known as the Australian ballot because first used in one of the states of Australia. Massachusetts was the first entire state in this country to adopt it.
