NOONAN CLASSING ORDERGEPORT WALDMAN MacCRATE LAUN STRONG A NEW YORK VOTING MACHINE 

The setup of candidates shown on this machine was that which appeared in a recent election in the State of New York. The voter made his choice for different offices by pulling down the lever that indicated the candidate he favored. He would do the same thing on the questions that appeared above the candidates' names, voting "Yes" or "No" on each one. The New York ballot, like the form used in

Massachusetts, does not permit one to vote for all the candidates of one party by pulling one lever or making one cross. putting all the candidates of a certain party in one column, and perhaps having at the top of the column a square or circle within which the voter may make one cross and have it count for all the candidates of one party. Sometimes a certain symbol is used to indicate each party so that if a voter cannot read, at least he can recognize the Republican eagle, or the Democratic star, or some other party symbol. 

Paper ballots are still the most common means of voting in the country as a whole, but a number of states, including New York and

Pennsylvania, have introduced voting machines on an extensive scale. 

These machines are set up in such a way that the front of the machine looks somewhat like an enormous paper ballot. Instead of making crosses, however, one has to turn a lever or a button to record his choice. The voting machine has the advantage of counting each vote as it is cast and having the returns ready promptly when election is over. If something goes wrong with some part of the works, it is just too bad for a candidate whose counter has failed to record votes for him; but it is doubtful whether anything like as many errors are made that way as through incompetent or dishonest counting under the ballot system. 

Does your state use voting machines? What objections might be offered cost of introducing, danger of machinery not working, or something else? 

How do you like the arrangement of names on the ballot in your state as compared with arrangements used elsewhere? 

20. Ways of Securing Public Officials. There are three recognized methods of filling public office-popular vote, appointment by an elected official or board, and by holding a competitive examination. 

In a democracy the most important executive and legislative positions. should certainly be filled by election by the people. Appointment by a governor, a President, a mayor, a board of judges, or some other official or officials is common for some positions, since the general run of voters could not be expected to realize all the considerations that should be taken into account in filling certain offices. Besides, it seems fair that an important executive officer should have persons with whom he can work in harmony as the heads of the principal executive departments under him. If they do not do a good job and he allows them to continue in office, he can be held responsible. 

For positions requiring some kinds of expert knowledge, and for routine positions that do not require the adoption of new policies, but chiefly honesty and faithfulness in definite duties, students of good government recommend the so-called merit system of making appointments on the basis of a rank gained through examination. This may be wholly in writing or may include also an investigation of one's previous record.

We have in our national government now a Civil Service Commission, made up of three persons appointed by the President, and representing more than one party. They arrange for examinations for

many positions, including postmasters, postal clerks and mail carriers, railway mail clerks, stenographers, typists, and various other kinds of clerical positions in the city of Washington and elsewhere. The candidates who have taken examinations are arranged on an eligible list in the order of their accomplishment. Then when a vacancy occurs, an appointment is made from the three highest on the list. Some of our states and cities, New York in particular, have similar arrangements for their civil service appointments.¹ 

In contrast with the merit system to which we have just referred, the spoils system has been altogether too common. The phrase refers to the custom of throwing out of office after an election many of the office holders who did not belong to the winning party, and substituting persons who had supported the winning ticket. Andrew Jackson did not invent the practice, but he introduced it into our national politics. 

Presidents of all parties continued it for a long time. After President 

Garfield was assassinated by a disappointed office-seeker, Congress passed the Pendleton Act of 1883, which established the Civil Service Commission and gave the President the right to designate certain offices which would be filled after competitive examinations. Since that beginning the number of positions filled that way has been increased many fold. (See the graph on page 86.) 

In city and county governments, the ordinary clerical or other jobs have usually been treated as spoils, and promises of jobs have been one of the means by which candidates sought to get votes. Presidents, governors, and mayors have also made use of the spoils system in strengthening their own political position. The power they have to make appointments to office is often referred to as patronage. Since executive officials cannot possibly know the personal fitness of everyone who applies for an appointment, they depend on advice given by members of Congress, state legislators, or plain ordinary politicians. 

Sometimes they use this power of patronage to get support in Congress or state legislatures for laws they want to have passed. They may, for instance, refuse to appoint to office persons recommended by a Congressman or state legislator unless that lawmaker will support measures the executive wishes to have passed. 

1 Be sure you understand that civil service means all officials of the government outside of the army and navy. We sometimes use the expression as if it referred only to positions filled after examination. Such positions are often referred to as the classified service.

Has the spoils system ever caused any embarrassment in filling positions in your local government? Make a list of four or five offices for which you would consider a knowledge of law a special qualification; for which you would stress business experience; for which you would prefer someone who had an advanced education; for which you would want someone who was a good mixer; for which ability to speak or write would be particularly desirable. 

Students of politics have complained that voters are often asked to choose among so many candidates for so many offices that it is utterly impossible for them to know the qualifications of each candidate. As a remedy for this difficulty, the so-called short ballot has been proposed. 

This does not refer to the size of the paper but to the idea of having only a few officers chosen by popular vote, and allowing those few to have large responsibilities for selecting persons to hold offices under their authority.

An effort to permit the mass of the people to have a closer share in the control of government is proportional representation, called P. R., for short. If in a certain election the Democrats cast 55% of the vote, and Republicans and all others 45%, and this margin is rather evenly distributed all over a state or city, the chances are that at least 90% of the members of the legislature or city council will be Democrats. 

Would it not be fairer, it is argued, if in the state legislature or the city council the distribution of members among parties were in proportion to the total vote cast by each party? 

Under the so-called Hare system of proportional representation, voters mark the different candidates in the order of their preference a figure I after their first choice, 2 after their second choice, and so on. After the total number of votes cast in the election has been determined, a quota is figured out, which is the smallest number that could be received by any candidate and still have him a winner. For instance, if in a small election 

100 votes were cast and five persons were to be chosen, the quota to elect anyone would be 17, because there could be no more than five persons getting 17 first-choice votes out of 100 votes.

The ballots are first separated in such a way as to determine how many first-choice votes have been received by each of the various candidates. 

Those who have received the quota are declared elected. If any of them have received more than a quota, their excess votes are given to other candidates in accordance with the way they were marked for second choice. 

As soon as a candidate gets the quota by adding second choice votes, he is also declared elected. The ballots cast for those who had only a small 

---

number of first-choice votes are similarly distributed to their second choice. 

Thus step by step the shifts go on until enough votes have been transferred to second- or third-choice candidates to give a quota to the necessary number of winners.

Perhaps this sounds complicated, but it has been used in a number of well-governed cities. Even New York City now has it. Some say that the count is too cumbersome, and they believe that voting will not be done any more wisely than in the days when voting a straight ticket was a common practice.

An interesting experiment is to draw up a list of prominent personages in public life with party names attached to them and hold an election for some imaginary office. Then, taking the same list, vote for them by the method of proportional representation described here and see whether there is any difference in the result. 

In a few states the state has been divided into districts which might elect two or three representatives to the legislature, and then each voter is allowed to cast as many votes as there are persons to be elected from that district. If there are three to be chosen, voter John Smith might cast three votes for one candidate or distribute them among three individuals. Sometimes, also, when two or three persons are to be chosen to a certain position, a voter may vote for less than the entire number to be chosen, with the idea of giving the leading minority party one of the commissioners, councilmen, or whatever officials might be involved. 

21. Ways of Getting Rid of Public Officials. - Occasionally it is even more important to get rid of an official than it was to fill the office in the first place. Sometimes the trouble is incompetency, sometimes it is dishonesty, sometimes it is inability to work with one's colleagues or to obey proper instructions from one's superior officer, and sometimes it is just plain laziness. 

When an office is filled by appointment, the simplest way to remove its occupant is to have the official who made the appointment ask for the appointee's resignation, and if that person does not give it, to "fire" him. Usually officers appointed after civil service examinations, however, may not be removed without a hearing. No government should tolerate dishonesty, immorality, or inefficiency. But officials who have earned their positions through their own achievements deserve to be protected from unjust treatment or removal for insufficient cause.

What shall we do with officials who are elected by popular vote, or,

as in the case of United States judges, appointed for "good behavior" which often means as long as they live? One method that may be used in many cases of this character is impeachment. In the national government the House of Representatives may bring formal charges against a President or other executive official or judge who is accused of misconduct in office. Then the accused person is given a trial before the Senate.¹ The Senate, after hearing the charges and the testimony, votes "guilty" or "not guilty." In order to prevent a conviction for mere partisan reasons, it takes a two-thirds vote of the Senate to find the accused guilty. 

In 150 years under our Constitution there have been only 13 impeachment cases, only 4 of which resulted in conviction. An official who is convicted is automatically removed from office. The Senate may or may not impose the additional penalty of disqualifying the accused from ever holding any other office under the United States. 

Each state has its own method for dealing with similar situations in its own government, but does not necessarily follow the exact procedure described here. 

None of the methods thus far mentioned, however, reach members of Congress. They may be removed from office only by a vote of the house to which they belong. It is assumed that they represent their constituents and are entitled to remain in office even if they do make nuisances of themselves. This tolerance, however, would ordinarily not extend to actual dishonesty or crime. Similar provisions apply in state governments to members of their law-making bodies. 

Some states allow officials to be removed by the process known as the recall. In states or local communities where this procedure is permitted, a petition may be drawn up and signed by a certain percentage of the voters, asking to have a special election held to determine whether a certain official shall continue in office for the remainder of his term. According to one method, the voters vote simply "yes" or "no" on that question. According to another, other candidates may run against the incumbent, and if one of them beats him, the victor takes the incumbent's place. 

The recall gives the voters a direct hold upon those officials who might be subject to it. But many think judges should not be subject 

1 The Vice President, who is the regular presiding officer of the Senate, presides over such trials unless the President is impeached. In that case the Chief Justice presides.

to it, because public sentiment or prejudice might be aroused against a judge because of a decision that the law forced him to make. 

What might be the effect on a public official's attitude toward his work if he knew that he might be subjected to a recall election at any time? Have there been any recent occasions of removal from office of important officials in your state or local community? If so, what was the cause of them? What do you think of the recall?

Sometimes a community's worst problem about office-bolding is that an unnecessary number of persons hold public jobs without having to do much work. When such waste of public money is discovered, public opinion ought to be strong enough to cause the state legislature or whatever body established these unnecessary jobs to abolish them. On the other hand, the public sometimes does not realize the nature of worth-while service performed by officials whose names never get into the papers as doing anything big. 

22. Making Politics Clean and Intelligent. Some people in politics expect to make something in addition to their regular salaries. 

We commonly think of graft as some sort of gain that one gets which he could not have if he were not an office holder. If an office holder accepted a thousand dollars for getting a contract given to one firm rather than another, that would certainly be graft. Congressmen sometimes vote themselves mileage for expenses home and back to Washington between one session and another, and take the money whether they go anywhere near home or not. A mayor may get his expenses paid to an international conference in Rome or some other place a long distance away. A county official may get public workmen to build a road on his own farm. 

Some think our governments would do better to pay higher salaries to public officials, for it has happened that when an officer made a good record in settling a labor dispute or accomplishing something else that deserved publicity, he was promptly offered by a private organization a salary perhaps double what he had been getting as a public officer. But, on the other hand, many persons holding public jobs get much bigger pay than they could earn in private business. Probably democracies would do well, on the whole, to pay their officials good living wages, but not enough to make people too anxious to get a job for the money alone. 

Special groups may be very embarrassing to honest public officials.

Suppose, for instance, that a law were proposed to limit the activities of labor unions. Officials of certain business interests might use all kinds of influence to get it passed, but it would be violently opposed by the leaders of labor unions.

Sometimes such special interests are accused of actually paying money to members of law-making bodies or other public officials to get them to act or not to act in some particular way.

An official sometimes makes the mistake of thinking that after he gets into office it is his duty to favor in any way possible the interests of those who voted for him, and to do nothing even to protect from wrong the property or interests of those who supported his opponent. Every official ought to consider himself the servant of all the people and not of some group or faction.

Mr. Willkie made a very favorable impression by the fine spirit he showed in accepting the result of the presidential campaign in which he was a candidate. That was true democracy. 

Do you have any "corrupt practice act" in your state to forbid the kind of things just referred to? Have you had in your state any examples of influence sought or achieved over public officials for selfish purposes? Do you know of public officials who became unpopular because they did what they felt was their duty? Did they then or later receive appreciation for their conduct?

One difficulty in securing intelligent appreciation of government has been that, in drawing up laws, such technical language has been used that they can be understood only by lawyers. The average legislator may not know what other laws, if any, have been enacted on a subject in which he is interested. To help such people and citizens in general, a state may establish a legislative reference bureau. Those in charge of such work can draw up for a legislator a bill in proper form after he

tells them the idea he has in mind. They may give advice to state officials or to men and women interested in public affairs about the form and practices of government. Sometimes college professors or others with expert information may be invited by heads of governments to assist in gathering information that will be helpful in making wise solutions of public problems.

Should teachers in public schools take an active part in politics in their own communities? To what extent are your own views influenced by those you believe your teachers hold on current questions? 

23. Direct Lawmaking by the People. Some people believe that on big matters of public policy, it may be well to permit a vote by the people as a whole, instead of leaving all the responsibility to the lawmakers. Such means are often referred to as direct legislation. 

Under the process known as the initiative, a certain percentage of the voters of the state may draw up a petition asking the lawmaking body to enact a law which the petitioners think is desirable. This is in vogue in only a small number of states. 

The process known as the referendum is much more common. This consists in submitting a measure to popular vote for approval or disapproval after it has been formally drawn up. Sometimes a measure drawn up by initiative petition may be submitted directly to the voters, but the referendum is used in many states where the initiative plays no part at all. Almost all states, for example, require that a new state constitution or proposed amendments to the state constitution must get the approval of the voters before they go into effect. Frequently, also, proposals to borrow money, whether by the state or the local government, have to be submitted to popular vote. Sometimes the recall, to which we have previously referred (§ 21), is tied up with the initiative and the referendum and the three referred to as the I. R. and R. You can see, however, that any one of the three can be used without the others.

There is considerable difference of opinion about the merits of these measures. Some will inquire, "What is the use of having representatives if all they can do is to draw up bills to submit to popular vote?" It is also argued that the mass of the voters often are not well enough informed to make it wise to submit important propositions to them.

On the other hand, it is asked: "In a democracy, why shouldn't

the will of the people be discovered?" Representatives in a legislature, it is said, can be played upon by special interests more easily than the whole public. Besides, it is urged that referring to general public decision matters of real significance is so educative itself as to justify it.

On the whole, sentiment in general favors the use of the referendum on such matters as constitutional amendments, big bond issues, and that kind of thing. In regard to regular lawmaking many think it is best to use it only as a sort of reserve measure when, for some reason, a legislature's acts or failures to act are disapproved by the majority of the people.

To what extent are the I. R. and R. used in your state or community? 

Perhaps you have one or more of them if not all three. Do you favor introducing the same sort of procedure into the national government? 

Do you have proportional representation in any form in your school elections? How do you think you would like it? 

24. What Are You Going to Do about It? - Perhaps you ask, "What can we do about it until we are 21 years old?" Of course you can't vote at elections, but you can learn enough about the issues of elections to have some real convictions on them. Perhaps you can talk with voters who are over 21 and win them to your way of thinking. 

Have you realized how many voters over 21 don't bother to take part in elections in this country? In some other countries than ours 

85 to 90 per cent of the voters regularly turn out at elections. 

If 60 per cent of the voters in the United States take part in a presidential election, it is better than usual, though in 1940 that percentage was considerably exceeded. If a state is very one-sided politically and the outcome of the election is a foregone conclusion, there is not much to bring a lazy voter out. In Belgium and Australia a person may be fined if he stays away from the polls on election day unless he has a very good reason for doing so. That may be one way of getting out a large vote, but isn't it still better if voters go to the polls because they take a sincere interest in the outcome? 

One way in which a good citizen can show his fair-mindedness is in the way he acts toward members of different parties or groups. If he belongs to the winning side, does he try to rub it in on his opponents? 

Does he recognize good things that are done by individual members of the opposite group? Should he vote for the candidates that seem

most likely to serve his selfish interests, or should he take into account the welfare of his whole community, state, or nation? Should he habitually vote a straight party ticket, or should he regularly try to find out what individuals are best qualified for the various positions to be filled and then "split his ticket" so as to support the best man? There is plenty of opportunity for one to be a good sport in politics. Every voter should give reasonable respect to the holder of an office, unless that official shows by his conduct that he is not trying to give a fair and honest administration. politics politician political party plank issue campaign names of leading parties voters in our history boss "the organization" Republican? Honest man?

After all, if we get incompetent or otherwise undesirable public officials, who are to blame in a democracy? Representatives will not be much better than the people who elected them. If the wrong kind of representatives are regularly chosen to office, it is pretty good proof that the wrong kind of voters are in the majority in a community or state. major party; minor party electorate "third party" party committee ring machine

III  

There are two theories about the way we should approach the study of the forms of government. One person says, " Begin with the activities that are right around you. Get acquainted with them and then go on with the larger units." That sounds well in theory, but ask yourself, "In practice, which do we read and hear the most about—the government of our local community, the government of our state, or the activities that are centered in the city of Washington?" So let us make sure that we understand the form and activities of our national government. That should furnish a good background for comparison when we study state and local government. 

Some Questions: 

1. How do free governments do their work? 

2. Who compose our national law-making body, and what do they do? 

3. What is the place of our chief executive in our federal system? 

4. How does the administrative side of our government operate? 

5. What is the place of our federal courts in our political scheme? 

6. How well adapted is our government to meet present and future needs? 

25. How Two Free Governments Serve Their People. We have already referred (§§ 7, 9) to the three-fold, check-and-balance organization of government which is characteristic of our way of doing things. 

It rests upon the belief that the three great activities of any government are to make laws, to carry out laws, and to deal with misunderstandings and violations of laws. The founders of our nation, impressed by the way obstinate George III and some of his predecessors tried to make Parliament simply a tool to carry out their own ideas in government, were determined that this should not happen here. So, while they patterned the national government they established after the British form, they made some notable shifts in the distribution and possession of power.

The British king still personifies the government of his country, but he signs every bill that Parliament passes, whether he really wants it or not. George VI enjoys the deep respect that any free people would 

58

give to a gentleman of courage, honor, and intelligence, whose chief ambition is to serve his people, but the great decisions of his government are made by others. Our President may be not only the chief executive, but first also in establishing policies and setting up ideals for the nation.

The British Parliament now has in its own hands, as representing the people of the nation, all final authority. The ministers who com- 

THE HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT 

In this building the two branches of the British Parliament hold their meetings. 

In the tower you see the face of Big Ben, whose tones have been heard all over the world. pose the Cabinet and carry out the will of Parliament hold their positions only as long as they can control the House of Commons. 

That House, elected by the people, has practically entire control of lawmaking, for the House of Lords rarely attempts to go contrary to the will of the Commons. Our Congress still has its two houses of equal standing in lawmaking, but the laws it passes must not conflict with the powers given it under the national Constitution. 

British courts have a high reputation for efficient work, and for doing justice between man and man, but they do no more than to apply the law as handed down by tradition or enacted by Parliament. 

They do not question the laws they apply. Courts in the United

States try cases brought before them, as in Britain, but they exercise a far greater power. They may even question the law itself, and if they believe a law to be contrary to the Constitution they refuse to put it into effect. No President and no Congress will dare to do anything else than accept the ruling of the federal courts on the constitutionality of the law.

So here are two great free peoples, with institutions derived from the same source, each putting into effect in its own way its ideals of liberty and ordered government. Law in both cases is made and administered by the representatives whom the people have chosen for that purpose. One builds its institutions on traditions and customs developed through the centuries, and does not feel the need of a written constitution to guide it. The other looks to its Constitution as the guarantee of its freedom and cherishes it deeply. And each may well respect the other's way of putting into effect their common ideals of freedom.

Is there more need of a written constitution in a federation than in a centralized government? If Britain should be so unfortunate as to have another 

John or Charles I or George III on the throne, what do you think might happen to him? Could a President of the United States be removed from office for the same reason that cost Edward VIII his throne? ________ 26. The Make-up of Our Congress. Should a lawmaking body be unicameral - composed of just one house, or bicameral - composed of two houses? With only one legislative body more bills would probably be passed than when a measure has to get through two houses - but should we have more good bills or more bad ones?

The friends of the one-chamber idea say that with only one chamber its members would feel more responsibility to be careful about the laws they did pass, and of course it would cost less to have one house than two. The two-chamber advocates, however, believe that we get a wider representation of the whole people by our present method, and that if a bill has to get through two houses before it becomes a law, its weak points are more likely to be shown up and corrected. 

The Senate represents, in theory, the states of the Union as states. 

Each sends two senators to represent it at Washington. To be qualified for the Senate, a person must be thirty years old, a resident of the state which he represents, and a citizen of the United States for at least nine years.

Senators are chosen for terms of six years, but their terms are so arranged that only one-third of them expire at the same time, and that the regular terms of the senators from any given state do not end in the same year. When vacancies occur by death or resignation, the governor of the state may appoint someone to fill the vacancy temporarily. 

An election will then be held on the next regular election day for the remainder of the uncompleted term.

Under what circumstances could two senators from the same state be chosen at the same time?

Senators were for a long time chosen by the state legislatures, but in 1913 the Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitu tion was adopted, requiring them to be chosen by popular vote. It would be hard to prove, though, that the quality of senators is much higher today than it was when they were chosen by the state legislatures. 

The members of the House of Representatives have always been chosen by popular vote. They are all elected at one time for a term of two years, except when a special election has to be held to fill a vacancy. Members of either house may be re-elected. Some have spent over thirty years as members of one house or both. Representatives must be twenty-five years old, must have been citizens of the United States for seven years, and must be residents of the state which they represent. Usually they live in the district within the state from which they have been elected. 

The number of representatives from any state depends on its population, except that each state has at least one. After each ten-year census of the United States has been taken, Congress is supposed to pass an apportionment bill declaring how many representatives each state shall be entitled to. It has now been agreed that the total number in our national House of Representatives shall be 435. These are distributed in accordance with a fixed plan, as reported to the President by the Director of the Census, unless Congress itself adopts some other method.

A state is regularly divided into as many districts as it has representatives, and each district elects one representative.¹ Sometimes 

¹ If, after a new apportionment takes place, the number of representatives from any state has been changed and the state legislature has either failed or had no opportunity to make a new division of the state into districts, the whole list of representatives or any additional representatives that the state has gained, may be chosen by a vote of the whole Such a person would be referred to as a congressman-at-large. state.

state legislatures divide the state into districts of queer shapes or uneven size so as to make it likely that a certain party will control as many as possible of the districts. This practice is known as a gerrymander.

The salary of members of Congress is $10,000 a year. In Washington's time they started with $6 a day while Congress was in session, but like most other things, their wages have gone up since then.

THE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES 

The number on each state shows the number of representatives whom that state will send to Congress in the years 1943-1953. When a state's representation was changed as a result of the 1940 census, the number previous to the change appears, enclosed in a circle.

Besides their official salary, Congressmen get an allowance for the services of secretaries and other helpers, and mileage to and from Washington for each session of Congress. They also have the "franking privilege" -the right to send mail free if the Congressman's signature is written or printed on the envelope or wrapper. 

Who are the senators from your state? How long have they served?

Had they any previous political experience before they were elected? Who is the representative from your district? What political experience did he have before he was chosen? Do these men seem to be recognized as outstanding in Washington or among their constituents at home?

What qualities would you consider in supporting candidates for the United States Senate or for the House of Representatives? Do you think women have as good qualifications for service in Congress as men? When the last apportionment of representatives was made, what states gained or lost? 

Do you think the equal representation of the states in the Senate is fair? 

Is there any likelihood of its being changed? (See Constitution, Article V, last clause.)

If there are disputes over the election of members to either house, the house which is directly concerned decides who has been elected. Do you consider that a wise feature? 

27. How Congress Works. The Vice President is the regular presiding officer of the Senate, and the House elects one of its own number as Speaker. The Senate also chooses one of its own number as President pro tempore. He presides in the absence of the Vice 

President, and in case of vacancy in that office becomes the regular presiding officer.

Each of the houses of Congress makes its own rules of order, and they differ in several respects. The theory of the Senate has been, for instance, that there should be no restriction on the length of time members should speak.¹ Since the House is so much larger than the 

Senate, cloture rules are necessary, which limit the amount of time members may use in debate. There is a Committee on Rules which makes decisions as to the length of time that may be consumed in discussing bills, and at times may have considerable to say as to whether a bill shall be brought up for consideration at all.2 

The records of the two houses are kept under the direction of the Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House. Official stenographers take down every word that is spoken during the sessions of either body, and these remarks are printed in the publication known as the Congressional Record. Congresses are referred to by number, counting from the first one in 1789. Constitution has fixed that date for the beginning and end of the terms of members of Congress. Each year a session of Congress begins on that date and continues until the two houses agree on a time to adjourn. 

If they are unable to agree, the President has the right to fix the time for an adjournment, but he has never had to do that.¹ The President has the right to call special sessions of Congress between the regular sessions.

You understand that Congress does not have to exercise any given power just because it is given the right to do so, and that it authorizes other officials to carry out the laws it makes, rather than executing them itself.

(6) General

Much argument, as you know, has occurred at times over the powers of Congress. There is no doubt, for instance, of the right of Congress "to lay and collect taxes" for the purpose of getting revenue. But may it levy taxes on manufacturers of agricultural products in order to pay bounties to farmers, or may it levy such heavy taxes on certain articles that nobody would care to produce or import those articles? 

On the other hand, many measures have been passed to which nobody has cared to object, even though not specifically authorized in the Constitution, such as laws describing the form and proportions of the national flag. The last item in the list of powers is sometimes called 

1 This means to authorize privateering. Civilized nations no longer do it.

the elastic clause, because it can be made to cover a good many exercises of authority not specifically mentioned.

Go over the laws passed by Congress at a recent session, or if Congress is in session, those that have been considered or are under consideration right now at this session. Connect each one with the particular power mentioned in the Constitution which would justify that law but do not try to excuse too many of them by referring to the elastic clause. 

But there are also some things which Congress may not do. The 

Constitution definitely says that no bill of attainder nor ex post facto law shall be passed,¹ and that no title of nobility shall be granted. 

These three restrictions also apply to state governments. No tax may be laid on articles exported from any state, nor any regulation be established which would give advantage to the ports of one state over those of another. No direct tax may be laid except in proportion to population (but this provision has been modified by the Sixteenth Amendment, so that income taxes may be collected without regard to population).

Some other very important restrictions on Congress are found in the First Amendment, which undertakes to guarantee freedom of religion, of speech, of the press, of assembly, and of petition (§ 83). Other provisions in the first eleven amendments are not so worded as to be aimed directly at Congress, but without them there would be the chance that sometime laws might be proposed that would violate important rights or privileges. Article X makes a rather sweeping statement: 

"The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people."

Two of the later amendments also impose a limit on the power of Congress with reference to the right of voting. This matter never was included within the range of the powers of Congress, but Amendments XV and XIX declare that the United States shall not deny citizens the right to vote because of race, color, previous condition of servitude, 1 A bill of attainder would be an act passed by a lawmaking body condemning a person to punishment without giving him a trial in court, and perhaps imposing some additional "attaint" upon his family. An ex post facto law is one under which a person might be punished for doing something that was not contrary to law at the time it was done. Congress would have the right, for example, to pass a law in 1941 requiring everybody who traveled from one state to another after that year to pay for a federal license on his car; but if it undertook to punish those who went from one state to another in 1940 without a federal license, it would be an ex post facto law.

or sex. Many other matters which are neither granted nor prohibited to Congress, as far as the national Constitution is concerned, have been handled mostly by the states, such as education, the granting of the right to vote, the care of health, the construction of highways, and the protection of workers in industry. But in late years Congress has enacted laws about some of these matters which the Constitution does not forbid it to handle, and has been justified by our courts in doing so. 

29. How Congress Does It. Any bill may be introduced by any member of either house, except that bills for raising revenue must be introduced in the House of Representatives. If it passes the house in which it is introduced, it then goes to the other house, and if it passes that house, it is sent to the President. The President, if he approves the bill, may make it a law by signing it. If he does not like it, he may veto it (in Latin veto means "I forbid"). In that case he fails to sign it and sends it back to the house in which it was introduced, with a statement telling why he does not approve it. If both houses of 

Congress pass it again by a two-thirds vote, it becomes a law anyway. 

A few important measures have become laws over the President's veto, but comparatively few laws are passed which it is known in advance that the President disapproves. If, after he receives a bill, he keeps it ten days while Congress is in session and does nothing one way or the other, the bill becomes a law without his signature. But if during those ten days the session of Congress comes to an end, it does not become a law unless he signs it. Refusing to sign it under those circumstances is referred to as a pocket veto. 

But now what happens when a bill is going through either the house where it is introduced or the other house? 

(1) Introduction 

This usually involves no particular formality. When a member introduces a bill, either because he really wants it to be passed or because someone has asked him to introduce it, it is slipped into a box on the desk of the 

Secretary or Clerk. 

(2) Reference to Committee 

The bill is then referred to the standing committee which considers that kind of bills. If a majority of the committee are opposed to it, they do nothing more with it and the bill dies right there, unless a majority of the members of the house require the committee to make a report on it. If a majority of the committee favor the bill, they will report it back to the

house. They may make changes in it and sometimes alter its character considerably. Only a small part of all the bills introduced by members ever get back to either house of Congress for formal consideration. Though the standing committees doubtless act unwisely at times, they furnish the only suitable means of sifting out from the thousands of bills that are introduced the ones which are most likely to be approved by Congress. 

To totum A CONGRESSIONAL HEARING 

When an important bill is before Congress for consideration, the committee of one house or the other may hold a public hearing to get the opinions of people with reference to it. In this picture Joseph P. Kennedy, seated near the center of the picture, is testifying before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in regard to the 

Lend-Lease Bill of 1941. 

Acme Photo 

(There are 30 or 40 standing, or permanent, committees in each house, selected at the beginning of a new Congress, and ranging in size from 3 members to 35. In the House of Representatives the Committee on Ways and 

Means, which considers all bills for raising money, is very important, and its chairman is looked upon as the most important personage except the Speaker. Other leading committees are those on Interstate and Foreign 

Commerce, the Judiciary, and Appropriations, and in the Senate the Foreign Relations Committee. Every member is on at least one committee, but if he happens to belong to the minority party, he may be assigned to some committee of little importance. Members of the majority party control all the chief committees, and those who have been members of either

house the longest time get the most favored assignments. The more important committees are usually much larger than the less important ones.) 

(3) The Bill on the Calendar 

If a bill is reported back to the house by the committee to which it was referred, it is placed on the calendar and then usually must wait its turn before it is considered. Certain kinds of bills may be taken up only on a certain day of the week, unless unanimous consent is given by the members present at any time to take up a bill out of its natural order. The Rules 

Committee in the House has much to say about the order in which bills shall be considered. 

(4) Discussion 

When the time arrives for the consideration of the bill by the house, arguments may be offered both for and against it, and amendments may be proposed. If a proposed amendment gets a majority vote in its favor, the original bill is then changed accordingly. Sometimes a bill is referred back to the committee which considered it, either with instructions to amend it further, or else with the intention of letting it stay there. That is one way of defeating bills. 

(5) Final Vote 

After debate and possible amendment, the bill is voted on. Sometimes if there is no objection to it, no roll call is taken, but in most cases the "yeas and nays" are recorded. The names of the members are called in alphabetical order, and each one answers "Aye" or "No" in accordance with his feeling concerning the bill. If it is supported by a majority of those present, the bill is passed and is sent over to the other house. 

After a bill has gone from one house to the other, it is often amended by that other house and then passed in its amended form. In such cases, unless the first house accepts the amendments that the other house has made, the bill is sent to a special committee, known as a conference committee, made up of members of both houses. They try to harmonize the differences between the two houses with reference to the measure, and sometimes make rather extensive changes. A bill does not go to the President until it has passed both houses in just the same form.

Sometimes even the President tries to influence Congressmen by the use of his power of patronage (§ 20). A governor may do likewise with state lawmakers. Congressman White may promise to support a bill Congressman Smith wants to pass if Smith in return will vote for or against some other measure in accordance with White's wishes.

That sort of thing is referred to as log-rolling, from the practice of frontiersmen in agreeing to help one another move logs or do some other service.

Congress and the President sometimes work at cross purposes, especially if the President belongs to one party and the majority of Congress to another. In such cases, or when one of the two houses is controlled by one party and the other by a different one, it may be hard to get anything of importance done. 

What unpleasant things might a Congressman have to deal with? Congressmen are sometimes said between sessions to go back home and "mend their fences." What do you suppose that means? What change would you make, if any, in the process of lawmaking as described here? If you as a private citizen wanted to have Congress pass a certain bill, what could you do about it? Refer to recent newspaper accounts for specific examples of any of the matters mentioned in this section. 

According to the Constitution, each of the two houses has certain powers which it exercises separately. (1) Only the House of Representatives may introduce a bill for raising money, though after the Senate gets such a bill, it may treat it like any other bill. (2) The 

House of Representatives may bring impeachment charges against public officials. (3) If in an election for President no candidate has a majority of the electoral votes, the House chooses one from the three highest candidates.

The Senate has four powers of its own. (1) It tries impeachment cases. (2) It selects the Vice President from the two highest candidates when no one has received a majority of the electoral votes. (3) Many appointments made by the President do not go into effect unless approved by the Senate. (4) The Senate must consider all treaties with foreign countries, and they will not go into effect unless approved by a two-thirds vote. (§ 96) 

30. The President and His Powers. The office of President was an original idea with the makers of our Constitution. Citizens of the United States were sure they did not want a king, but experience had also taught them that they needed some one person to head up the operation of the government. Lawmaking comes first, and so we talked about Congress first. But laws need people to enforce them. 

The President was made much more powerful than the English king was, even in 1787, though possibly the members of the Constitutional

Convention did not realize it. Because he was to be elected instead of inheriting his job, there would not be the same objection to bestowing considerable authority on the position. There are at least ten ways in which the President may influence the policy and progress of the country. 

Acme Photo SIGNING A BILL 

In this picture Secretary of War Stimson, Representative May of the Military Affairs Committee, General Marshall, Chief of Staff of the Army, and Senator Sheppard, then Chairman of the Military Affairs Committee, look on as the President attaches his signature to the Selective Service Act of 1940. (1) The President must "take care that the laws be faithfully executed." 

His attitude toward public affairs determines the spirit of the entire government. (2) The President appoints thousands of persons to help in carrying out the laws, as well as all federal judges. Most of his appointments have to be approved by the Senate. No federal officers are fully in possession of their offices until they hold commissions signed by the President. He may also remove from office most of the persons whom he appoints, except federal judges. (3) Every bill or resolution of Congress must be submitted to the President. If he disapproves a measure, it does not go into effect unless passed over his veto by a two-thirds vote of each house.

(4) The President may recommend measures for Congress to enact, and sometimes uses various kinds of pressure to get them adopted. He usually "recommends" them by sending or delivering in person a “message." It may, as the Constitution says, give Congress "information of the state of the Union," but a message may also set forth a policy of lasting importance, as one of Monroe's did in 1823. Thomas Jefferson, who was not a good public speaker, established the practice of sending messages to be read by the clerk or the secretary, which was continued until the time of Woodrow Wilson. Wilson thought that a message would get more attention if spoken in person. Since his time, both methods have been used. (5) The President may call Congress into special session whenever he thinks circumstances require it, or may call either house by itself, and if they cannot agree as to the time to end their sessions, he may fix the time. (6) He has no direct judicial authority, but does have the right to pardon persons convicted of violating federal laws, except in the case of officers who have been tried by impeachment proceedings. His indirect influence over the courts may be considerable, however, since he appoints federal judges, and is likely not to appoint people who disagree seriously with his own views. (7) The President is commander-in-chief of the army and navy and of the state militia when they are called into federal service. He does not actually command armies or ships in person, though there is nothing in the Constitution forbidding it. In every war of any account Congress has always handed over to the President powers which it would have no desire that he should exercise in times of peace. (8) The President decides whether a particular person shall be received in this country as the official representative of some other government. 

Ordinarily that is a matter of no great importance, but sometimes it might make a considerable difference. When our government is dissatisfied with the policies of some other country, or the acts of an official representative of that country, the President may send home that person or even all the official representatives of that government who are in this country. (9) The President also makes treaties with foreign countries, which must have the consent of two thirds of the Senate before taking effect. 

Regularly the President does not draw up the treaties himself, but there is nothing to prevent his doing so if he wishes. (§ 96) (10) The President has the right to ask the opinion of the principal officers under his authority as to the work of their respective departments. 

Their opinions and desires are frequently accepted by the President and recommended by him to Congress.

Why is the President not given authority to pardon persons convicted by impeachment proceedings? Summarize ways in which the President is checked by other departments of the government and ways in which he may assert influence or restraint upon them. Could a President of the United 

States make himself a dictator? Why or why not?

The Constitution lays down only three requirements for the Presidency: (1) he must be 35 years old or more; (2) he must be an

American citizen by birth; (3) he must have lived in the United 

States for fourteen years, in case he was born here and afterward spent some time outside the country. Parties and voters take other things than these into account, however, in making their choices. Rarely do we favor one who is very young or very old. William J. Bryan, nominated in 1896, was only 36 at the time, but he never reached the presidency. Theodore Roosevelt, who became an accidental President when he was not quite 43 years of age, was the youngest actually to hold that office. An old man, we may think, could not stand the strain of campaigning, and the office of President itself is one of the hardest jobs that a human being can undertake, unless he is as thickskinned as a rhinoceros and is able to keep calm and poised in spite of living always in the limelight. 

To assist the President in the routine duties of the Executive Office, he has, besides his office secretaries, six Administrative Assistants, the Bureau of the Budget, the Office of Government Reports, and the 

National Resources Planning Board. 

Most often the candidate comes from a large state or one which does not regularly favor one party. New York and Ohio have had far more than their arithmetical share of presidential candidates. 

Race and religion, in practice, also do make a difference, though there is nothing in the Constitution to suggest it. Previous experience in public office usually counts, though not always. Governors of New 

York or some other well-known state have a much better chance of being selected as party candidates than members of Congress or persons who have never been in politics to any extent. 

31. How a President Is Chosen. - The Constitution declares that each state shall choose a number of presidential electors equal to the total number of that state's senators and representatives in Congress, and that they shall meet in their respective states (they do meet in their state capital) and vote by ballot for President and Vice President. 

---

That is all perfectly true, but these constitutional provisions have now become a mere formality. The real choice of a President is not mentioned in the Constitution at all. 

The actual first step is the nominating of candidates by the various parties. They hold national conventions in the summer of the years when an election takes place, and there they adopt a platform for the party and pick out their candidates for President and Vice President. Each convention is attended by twice as many delegates from each state as there are presidential electors to be chosen in November of the same year.¹ The Republican party has always required only a majority vote of the delegates to nominate its candidate. The 

Democrats used to demand a two-thirds vote, but do so no longer. 

The choice of presidential electors is made on the regular election day, the Tuesday after the first Monday of November, in every state.

The original intention was that outstanding people would be chosen as electors, and after they were elected, would use their own personal discretion in selecting men to vote for as President and Vice President. 

But now they are simply "stooges" who are morally pledged to vote for the candidates for President and Vice President who have been nominated by the party they represent. In fact, some of the states do not put the electors' names on the ballot at all, and most of those which do print them allow a person to vote for the entire list of one party by making just one cross.

This arrangement gives the big states an even greater influence in the choice of a President than their population deserves, because a whole block of votes 47 from New York or 35 from Pennsylvania will probably be cast for a candidate who may not be supported by more than a few thousand more voters than his nearest rival. In 1876 and 1888 the party whose candidate won the majority of the electoral vote was actually supported by fewer voters throughout the country than the candidate of the other leading party. The margin between the winning and the defeated candidates in the electoral vote is often much greater in proportion than in the popular vote. Every now and then some plan is proposed to make the electoral vote more nearly correspond to the preferences of individual voters the country over. But it is hard to get people to think about this matter oftener than once in four years, and then the winning side is likely to be satisfied with the result. 

1 A few delegates from the District of Columbia and from the territories and possessions may also be included.

If no candidates for President or Vice President receive a majority of the electoral vote, the House of Representatives chooses the President and the Senate the Vice President. In taking such votes in the 

House the representatives from each state vote as a unit, and to be elected a person must receive the votes of a majority of the states.¹ 

In the Senate, however, when choosing a Vice President, its members vote as individuals.

STEPS IN THE CHOICE OF A PRESIDENT 

1. Nominating convention in some large city in the summer of "presidential years." 

2. Campaign, between the nominating convention and election day, carried on as political campaigns usually are. 

3. Choice of presidential electors by popular vote in each state the 

Tuesday after the first Monday of November. 

4. Voting by the electors in each state on the Monday after the second 

Wednesday of December. Six reports made out and sent to various officials. (The electors all taken together are sometimes referred to as the electoral college.) 

5. Counting electoral votes in the presence of both houses of Congress on the following sixth of January. Congressmen do not take this ceremony very seriously for unless the election has some very unusual feature everybody has known for two months what the result was. 

6. If the successful candidate at the regular election should die before being inaugurated, the regularly chosen Vice President would be sworn into office in his place. Congress has the right to provide for the case when both the newly elected President and Vice President are unable to serve, but has not yet taken action on that subject. 

For a long time March 4 was inauguration day for the President.

THE OFFICIAL HOME OF THE PRESIDENT 

This building does not belong to our Chief Executive, but he and his family have the use of it during his term of office. and probably had no thought of preventing anyone else from being President for more than eight years. Thomas Jefferson undoubtedly could have been elected to a third term but refused. His refusal gave a definite start to the tradition that two terms were enough for any President, which was not broken until the people chose Franklin 

D. Roosevelt for a third term in 1940. 

What are the leading arguments for and against a third term? Would it be better to elect a President for six or seven years and forbid him to be reelected? What states have furnished the greatest number of persons to be nominated or elected to the presidency? What qualities would you take into account in selecting a presidential candidate whom you would support: age, religious beliefs, ability to speak, ability to write, being a good mixer,

interest in athletics, family relations, education, wealth or the lack of it, experience in public office, experience in business, opinions on public questions, ability to earn a living?

The Constitution declares that the Vice President shall become President "in case of the removal of the President from office, or of his death, resignation, or inability to discharge the powers and duties of the said office." We have joked about the Vice President as if he were of little importance. He presides over the Senate whenever he cares to do so, but he may vote only when the Senate itself is tied. 

On the quiet, however, a capable man in the office may have considerable influence. President Roosevelt's assignment of Vice President Wallace to important work in connection with national defense may be a step toward making the office one of real significance. 

Too often parties pick their vice presidential candidates so as to please a faction of the party or a section of the country different from that which their candidate for President represents.

What do you think would constitute "inability" on the part of a President serious enough to warrant the Vice President's taking charge of the office? 

No definite rule has ever been made on that point. 

But what if there is no Vice President when the President is unable to serve? (If the office of Vice President becomes vacant during a regular term, it remains so until the end of the term.) For a time the provision set up by Congress was that the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives should be next in line for the presidency. But in 1886 the Presidential Succession Act was passed which is now in force. This provides that if there is a vacancy in both the presidency and vice presidency, the Secretary of State shall become President, and so on down the line of Cabinet officers as far as they existed in 1886 - the Secretary of State, of the Treasury, of War, the Attorney-General, the Postmaster-General, the Secretary of the Navy, and of the Interior. Since the Secretary of State on becoming President will appoint a new Secretary of State, it is improbable that any one further along in the Cabinet will become President by accident, unless there should be some wholesale massacre or other misfortune affecting the members of the Cabinet. 

Study recent nominations of the leading parties for the office of Vice President to see whether they seem to have been picked because of any outstanding service they had rendered, because they themselves qualified to be President, or because they were merely "available" for some other reason.

Several times men who could have had a nomination for Vice President declined to take it. Why do you suppose they did so? What can you find out about the present Vice President? 

32. Our Cabinet and Other Cabinets. Perhaps it was an oversight, but you cannot find the word "cabinet" in our national Constitution. Perhaps it was because cabinets in Great Britain at the time the Constitution was made were not as influential in government as they are today. In two places reference is made to the "heads of departments," but otherwise nothing is said about those officials whom we refer to as our President's Cabinet. 

UNITED STATES 

1. The members of our Cabinet may not be members of Congress.

At this point let us list the chief differences between our own Cabinet and that of Great Britain and numerous other countries. Sometimes we distinguish the two arrangements by calling one the presidential system and the other the cabinet or ministerial system. 

2. Our Cabinet officers are appointed by the President and usually belong to his party. 

3. Our Cabinet members are appointed, as a rule, for four years, but may be removed by the President. 

4. Individual members of the Cabinet may disagree with other members.

The Cabinet is a unit only in the sense that all are subordinates to the 

President. 

GREAT BRITAIN 

The members of the Cabinet regularly are members of Parliament and are responsible for trying to secure the passage of all important bills.

The members of the Cabinet belong to the party that controls the House of Commons. If that party loses control, a new Cabinet will come into office representing a different party or group. 

Members of the British Cabinet have no fixed term, but the King may not remove a Cabinet officer simply because he disagrees with him.

The British Cabinet acts as a unit, with the Prime Minister as the leader of the Cabinet and the real head of the government. If a member of the British Cabinet should seriously disagree with his fellow members, he would expect to resign.

Both in Great Britain and in our own country the Cabinet, however it works, has come into existence by custom and not by any law. 

Most countries that have Cabinets with real authority have followed the British pattern rather than ours.

Members of the President's Cabinet have two definite functions: (1) Each one is the head of a department and is responsible for overseeing its work, subject to the approval of the President. Sometimes

a Cabinet head is content to hold the office and let abler men in positions of lower rank do the actual work of the department, but a person with real executive ability at the head of a Cabinet department may make a name for himself by efficient and successful management of his department. Officially there is no superiority in rank of one department over another, but the Secretary of State has at least an unofficial standing at the head of the list and is recognized as the first Cabinet member to be in line for the presidency after the Vice President. 

As the country has become bigger and countless additional responsibilities have been accepted by the national government, more and more varied duties have been put under the administrative departments, and many separate boards and commissions have been organized, sometimes without much logical relationship to one another. 

In 1939 Congress authorized the President to make extensive adjustments and redistributions of work. The chief activities included under the various departments and agencies today (1941) may be stated as follows: 

The State Department has the oversight of foreign affairs and keeps the official seal of the government and the original copies of treaties, laws, proclamations, and the like. Besides the Secretary of State, the department has the Undersecretary, a Counselor, three Assistant Secretaries, and numerous advisors, chiefs of divisions, and the like. 

The Treasury Department has the general oversight of the financial activities of the government. It has an Undersecretary and two Assistant 

Secretaries. Its chief activities include the Fiscal Service, under which are the Bureau of the Public Debt and the Treasurer of the United States, the Bureaus of Customs, of Internal Revenue, of the Mint, of Engraving and 

Printing, of Narcotics, and the Secret Service Division. 

The War Department is responsible for the entire defense of the country by land. The highest official in the army itself is known as the Chief of 

Staff, and most of the other high personages in the department are army officers. The Secretary of War, however, is regularly a man from civil life, and so are the Undersecretary and other administrative assistants. 

The Department of Justice is the law department of the national government. The Attorney-General is the chief legal adviser of the President and other officials, and the Solicitor-General usually is responsible for the direction of important criminal cases in which the government is interested. 

The department includes the Bureau of Prisons, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Immigration and Naturalization Service. 

The duties of the Post Office Department are to carry the mail and operate other activities connected with that work. Besides the Postmaster-General there are four assistant postmasters-general, each of whom is responsible for overseeing certain branches of the work of the department.

The 

The Navy Department looks out for our national defense on the sea. highest officer of the navy itself is known as the Chief of Naval Operations, but there are an Undersecretary and numerous chiefs of bureaus who have the direction of special phases of its management. There has been considerable difference of opinion as to whether the air service should be organized entirely apart from either the army or navy. Up to the present, however, it has been divided between the two, on the principle that both the army and navy need the cooperation of an air force.

The duties of the Department of the Interior are hard to state briefly. One might almost say that they cover everything concerning the internal affairs of the national government that is not handled by some other department. It also includes the Division of Territories and Island Possessions. It has an 

Undersecretary and two Assistant

Secretaries, besides commissioners or directors at the head of the

General Land Office, the Office of Indian Affairs, the Bureau of Rec lamation, the Bureau of Mines, the Geological Survey, the National 

Park Service, and the Fish and

Wildlife Service.

Uncle Sam's postal service reaches far out into the country, and even the younger members of the family have the benefit of it.

The Department of Agriculture was created for the purpose of giving direct service to the farmers of the country. Besides the Secretary of Agriculture, there is an Undersecretary, an Assistant Secretary, and other assistants. The Agricultural Adjustment Administration naturally belongs in this department, as well as the Farm Credit Administration and the Rural Electrification Administration. In it are also found the Bureaus of 

Animal Industry, of Agricultural Economics, of Home Economics, of Dairy 

Industry, and of Plant Industry, besides the Commodity Exchange Administration, the Forest Service, the Soil Conservation Service, and the Surplus 

Marketing Administration. 

The Department of Commerce has the oversight of various interests related to the commerce and business of the country. Besides assistant secretaries, the department includes the Bureau of the Census, the Bureau

of Standards, the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, the Coast and Geodetic Survey, the Patent Office, the Weather Bureau, and the Civil 

Aeronautics Board. 

The Department of Labor was the last to be organized up to the time this is written. Besides the Secretary of Labor, there are as usual assistants and heads of various bureaus. These include the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Women's Bureau, Children's Bureau, the Division of Labor Standards, Acme Photo A SERVICE OF THE WEATHER BUREAU 

On this machine the direction and velocity of the wind and the amount of sunshine and rainfall are registered, so that they can be noted every hour of the day. the United States Conciliation Service, and the Wage-Hour Division. This is the first department to have had a woman at its head. 

The Federal Security Agency was brought into existence by order of President Roosevelt in 1939, along with the Federal Works Agency and the Federal Loan Agency. These agencies either took out of some of the 

Cabinet departments work which had been under their supervision, or brought under their authority activities that had been outside the Cabinet. 

The Federal Security Agency includes the Office of Education (§ 169), the Public Health Service (§ 154), the Social Security Board (§ 162), the Food and Drug Administration (§ 154), the National Youth Administration

(§ 158), and the Civilian Conservation Corps (§ 158). All these activities were thought of as promoting the general welfare of the people of the country.

The Federal Works Agency oversees the activities under the federal government that deal with construction of highways, buildings, and other public property. It includes the Public Roads Administration, Public Works Administration (§ 158), Work Projects Administration (§ 158), the United States Housing Authority (§ 130), and the Public Buildings Administration. 

The Federal Loan Agency has the oversight of most of the activities of the federal government that have to do with lending money to private individuals or corporations. It includes the Reconstruction Finance Corpora tion (§ 269), the Electric Home and Farm Authority, Export-Import Bank of Washington (§ 241), Federal Housing Administration (§ 130), and the Federal Home Loan Bank Board (§ 130). 

If you were President, would you rather have strong capable people with minds of their own as members of your Cabinet, or people who would expect to do as you told them? How many members of the present Cabinet had you ever heard of before they became members? 

34. Independent Boards and Commissions. Some independent offices have no necessary relation to any particular Cabinet department and could do their work just as well while acting separately. 

Longer terms than four years have often been the case with these boards. Besides, Cabinet officials have often been looked upon as administrators and nothing else, while many of the separate commissions have had duties that were somewhat like those of judges as well as of administrators. Several of these commissions or boards have been definitely intended to be non-partisan. 

First of these independent bodies was the Civil Service Commission (§ 20). 

It was brought into being by the Pendleton Act of 1883 after the assassination of President Garfield. It has three members, who must not all belong to the same party, and has the oversight of the giving of examinations to persons who seek positions in the federal government that are filled by that means.

The Interstate Commerce Commission (§ 266) (eleven members appointed at different times for terms of seven years) was started in 1887. It is responsible for the supervision of railroads, bus lines, express companies, sleeping car companies, and oil pipe lines, as far as their activities are of an interstate character.

The Federal Reserve Board (§ 237) was organized in 1913. Its membership was later fixed at seven members appointed by the President for terms of fourteen years. These terms begin at different times, and no person may have two terms. It is now technically known as the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and has very important duties with reference to the twelve Federal Reserve Banks in the country.
