EMPLOYEES OF THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT 

The proportion of those who must take an examination before being eligible for appointment is greater today than ever before. The graph points out this proportion, and also how the numbers of federal employees increased from earlier dates. 

The Federal Trade Commission (§ 264) has five commissioners appointed by the President for terms of seven years, not more than three of whom may belong to the same party. This commission, established in 1914, was given authority to prevent unjust competition between corporations, and to order them to put an end to unfair methods of carrying on business.

The United States Tariff Commission (§ 263) was organized in 1916. It has six members appointed for terms of six years, and not more than three of them may belong to the same political party. The commission has the duty of investigating the administration of the tariff laws of the country. 

The Federal Power Commission (§ 268) was organized in 1920. At first it consisted of the Secretaries of War, Agriculture, and the Interior. Ten years later it was made a separate commission of five members appointed in separate years for five-year terms. Not more than three of them may belong to the same party. This commission has authority over the water power on public lands and navigable streams. 

The Securities and Exchange Commission (§ 235) was created in 1933. It has five members appointed by the President for terms of five years, beginning in separate years. It may issue regulations with reference to the conditions under which stocks and bonds may be offered for sale, and through the enforcement of these regulations may do much toward bringing about honesty in such matters. 

The Federal Communications Commission (§ 266) came into existence in 1934. It took away from the Interstate Commerce Commission the oversight of telegraph, telephone, and cable lines in the United States, and added the work which for seven years previous had been handled by the Federal Radio Commission. It is composed of seven members appointed by the President in separate years for seven-year terms. 

The National Labor Relations Board (§ 255), also composed of three per sons, was created in 1935 to look out for cases arising under the operation of the Wagner Labor Relations Act, which provided for its establishment. 

The main purpose of the act was to protect labor unions in their right to organize and carry on their activities without interference from employers. 

Some other agencies have no responsibility for the making of policies, but render valuable services nevertheless. The Government 

Printing Office, for example, is the greatest organization of its kind in the world, and the Library of Congress is one of the largest to be found anywhere.

Some argue that to have all the various governmental agencies headed up in the office of the President and subject, more or less directly, to his authority, would permit a President to make himself really a dictator. What do you think about it? What activities of the federal government of which you know seem so distinctive in character that they should be kept separate from other departments or boards? Why? 

35. The Plan of Our Federal Courts. The Constitution simply says that there shall be one Supreme Court and such other courts 

---

"as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." The number of judges in these courts and the distribution of duties among them was left for Congress to determine, because neither the makers of the Constitution nor anybody else could foretell the extent and kind of judicial service which the country might need in later years. 

The first act passed by Congress in carrying out this power - the famous Judiciary Act of 1789-was one of the most thoughtful measures ever enacted by it. Its chief author was Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut. It set up a plan for the organization of the courts which is, in its essentials, followed today. 

The foundation of our federal court system is the series of district courts which are so arranged that there will be at least one in every state. The larger states have two, three, or even four districts as in the case of New York and Texas. Each district court has at least one judge, a district attorney, and a United States marshal. The 

Constitution requires that all judges shall be appointed "for good behavior," but the positions of district attorney and marshal have become political appointments and hold good for only four years. A large proportion of all cases coming into the federal courts under laws of Congress are first tried in the district courts. They have original jurisdiction only — that is, they handle cases that have not previously been tried in any other court.

Above them are the ten circuit courts of appeals, once called simply circuit courts. Three or more states are grouped into a circuit, and from three to seven circuit judges are appointed for each circuit. 

They hear cases which have already been tried in district courts but in which the losing party is not satisfied and asks a higher court to look into the case—in legal language, he "takes an appeal." That is known as appellate jurisdiction, and it is the only jurisdiction the circuit courts have.

The highest court in the land is the Supreme Court. It meets only in Washington, and now holds its sessions in a beautiful new building all its own. Two kinds of cases are tried in the Supreme Court only those in which a state is involved as a state, and those which concern the official representatives of foreign countries. It is assumed that the dignity of the parties concerned in those cases is of such importance that they should be heard in no court of lower grade. Most of the work of the Supreme Court, however, deals with cases appealed 

1

from the lower courts or from the highest court in some state. Any cases that involve the interpretation of the Constitution of the United States or of a law of Congress, or any cases in which it is claimed that a state law conflicts with the Constitution or laws of the United States may find their way to the Supreme Court. The Court decides for itself whether to refuse to hear appeals in cases that have already been WASH.

The number of justices in the Supreme Court started with six, but had been increased to nine by 1837, and has remained there since, except for fluctuations between 1863 and 1873. When President 

Franklin Roosevelt proposed that Congress authorize raising the number to fifteen, violent opposition arose, and the proposition failed. 

Salaries paid to federal judges are not excessively high, considering the ability and experience a judge should have. The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court receives $20,500 and the other justices $20,000. 

Circuit judges receive $12,500 a year, and district judges $10,000. 

But the positions carry with them dignity and prestige, and they are good for life if a judge wishes to work that long. After judges reach the age of 70 they may retire on full pay, if they agree to help out

when their services may be desired in connection with any of the federal courts. Judges may be removed only by impeachment.

In addition to the three grades in the regular court system, there are also special courts. The Court of Claims, consisting of five judges, hears cases in which persons seek to get money which they claim the government owes them. If this court decides in favor of any claimant, Congress usually

36. Our Courts and the Rest of the Government. Does the fact that federal judges are appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate make their positions political jobs? Less often than one might fear, for many Presidents have plainly tried hard to select capable people for judges, sometimes appointing members of a different party than their own. Yet a President, through such appointments, may have a great influence on the interpretation of laws for years to come, especially if he has many chances to make such appointments. 

The Senate usually confirms a President's nominations to judgeships, but some nominations have been rejected. Since the Constitution does not say how many judges there shall be in the Supreme Court or any other court, Congress may fix the number at any point that the amount of court business requires. 

But what about the power of judicial review of acts of Congress which has been exercised by our courts from the time when John 

Marshall was Chief Justice? Should the courts have the power to set aside a law which is desired by both the President and the lawmaking branch of the government? Of course judges should not throw out a law simply because they do not like it. But sometimes executives and lawmakers, in their haste to get something done, may bring about the passage of a law which is not in accordance with the Constitution. Then somebody should have the right to invalidate it, if our Constitution is to have any force. 

In the Constitution itself this power of judicial review is not stated in so many words, but it was assumed by Marshall as implied in the setting up of the government itself. Few other countries vest in their courts as much power in regard to legislation as our courts

exercise, but there is much to make us believe that our people on the whole want it that way. A high-minded Supreme Court is a safeguard against the abuse of power by any party that happens to control the lawmaking or the executive branch of the government. 

Some think that it would be a real improvement if our high courts in state and nation would give advisory opinions on certain policies before laws are passed to put them into operation. As it is now in the national government and in most states, a law must be passed, somebody must be accused

37. Adding New Territory. One question which the makers of our Constitution probably did not think of at Philadelphia in 1787

was whether we might annex additional territory. So much of what we had to start with as an independent country was unsettled that it seemed to thoughtful people as if it might take some hundreds of years to get our land properly occupied. When, in 1803, Thomas 

Jefferson was offered the tremendous bargain which we now refer to as the Louisiana Purchase, he thought at first that he might have to try to get the Constitution amended to authorize him to take it. 

But the argument was raised that any country has the right to annex territory, and therefore we did not need to say anything about it in our Constitution.

Since the acquisition of Louisiana, additional opportunities have come to take over new territory. Usually this was done, as in the case of Louisiana, by a treaty ratified by the Senate, as all treaties must be before they go into effect (§ 96). After the war with Mexico and the war with Spain, new territory was added, and in both cases we paid the defeated country something instead of merely taking the land as the spoils of war. Other acquisitions were made by purchase, as the 

Gadsden Purchase in 1853, Alaska in 1867, and the Virgin Islands in 1917.

What is done with acquired territory when it has been taken over? 

Several different ways of dealing with it have been used. The general principle has been to give it the kind of government which its particular needs might call for. If there was likelihood of its becoming a state sometime, it would be recognized as a territory (§ 39), with a form of government not greatly different from that of a state. If it were not ready for such action, it might be given whatever kind of government seemed most convenient to all concerned. Distant lands which we have not made into territories we most often refer to as possessions. 

Today the Virgin Islands have a governor of their own, usually one sent from the United States. So do Guam, an island in the North 

Pacific, and the islands of American Samoa in the South Pacific. 

Regularly he is an officer of the Navy. Wake and Midway, islands in the North Pacific, are similarly administered. In 1939 Canton and 

Enderbury Islands, to which Great Britain also laid claim, were occupied under a joint arrangement with Great Britain running for fifty years, and as much longer as the two countries wish. The Panama 

Canal Zone is under the direction of a governor who receives his authority directly from the President.

The Philippines have been both a problem and an opportunity for us. They were kept under the American flag only after a struggle. 

Whether the majority of the people of the islands really wanted the United States to take them will never be known. After a while we set up a government with a Governor-General appointed by the President, and a lawmaking body elected by those of the voters who could read and write. In 1916, by the so-called Jones Bill, the islands were promised their independence when they were ready for it. Then

IV  

Few people could describe with accuracy the way their own state government is organized. The average person may know less about his local government than he does about national affairs, but his understanding of his state government is likely to be still nearer zero. Yet we had state governments before there was any organized national government. 

Our federal government is one of the few that came into being through a combination of states already in existence that voluntarily came together and gave up many important powers to a new national government. To understand today's needs and problems we must have some intelligent knowledge of the place of the states in our national life. 

Some Questions: 

1. How did our states come into existence and how may new ones be formed? 

2. What general features of government are common to all the states? 

3. What notable differences are found among them? 

4. What distinctive features make our state what it is? 

5. What relations exist between the national government and the government of the states? 

6. How are the states related to one another? 

7. What problems particularly confront state governments today? 

38. How the States Came into Existence. Our thirteen original states, as you know, started as colonies of Great Britain. These colonies changed themselves into "states," so they thought, by making their Declaration of Independence in 1776, which declared that “these united colonies are and of right ought to be free and independent states." Notice the plural. They acted together, but they were not yet united. They had to find a way to unity before they could expect to stay independent, but they kept on calling themselves "states" after they were united.

The Congress which met in Philadelphia to look after their common problems advised each state to arrange for its own government in such a way as might seem most appropriate. In few years most of the states adopted new constitutions for themselves, though Rhode 

99

Island and Connecticut, which had for that time very liberal charters already, did not bother even to do that. Even the adoption of the 

Constitution under which our government is now carried on did not carry with it any necessary change in the government of the states. 

If your state is one of the original thirteen, make a special study of the circumstances under which it adopted its first state constitution. Was any extensive change made in its government at that time? May there have been more willingness to accept a new national Constitution than if the government of the states had had to be changed in the process?

The year indicated for the thirteen original states is the year when the state ratified the Constitution. 

39. Admitting New States to the Union. "New states may be admitted by the Congress into this Union." So says the Constitution in Article IV, Section 

3, and that means in the same way that any law or ordinary resolution is passed. The only restrictions on this power of Congress are that no new state may be made within any other state nor formed by the combination of two or more states or parts of states unless the legislatures of any states concerned give their consent. Such points have come up only twice. The legislature of Massachusetts gave its unquestioned consent to the admission of

IOI Maine, and a body calling itself the legislature of Virginia consented to the making of West Virginia as a separate state during the Civil 

War. 

Anyone could tell by looking at a map of the United States that no established or uniform area was required of a new state, and census figures would make it clear that no particular population was needed. 

Nevada had only 20,000 people when it was admitted, though it has room for 31,000,000 if the state were as thickly populated as New York. New states, when once in the Union, are on the same legal footing as states that have been there all the time. No state may claim any special privileges just because it was one of the original thirteen. This equality is guaranteed further by the provision that no state without its consent shall be "deprived of its equal suffrage in the Senate."

Territory belonging to the United States but not a part of any state is, under the Constitution, subject to the authority of Congress. The famous Northwest Territory Ordinance of 1787, drawn up before the Constitution of the United States itself had been made, set up in a general way a plan of government for such territory. The name territory came to be regularly used for the kind of government provided for a region that was being prepared to become a state. It was allowed to have a legislature elected by the voters, and a governor and judges appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, as many officers of the United States government are. 

Sometimes there has been a long wait between the organization of a region as a territory and its admission to the Union as a state. Six states, however, never were territories at all, because they either already had some sort of organized government at the time they were recognized as states, as in the case of Vermont, Texas, and California, or were made directly out of territory already in a state, as were 

Kentucky, Maine, and West Virginia.

At present Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico have about the same kind of government that territories have had in the past. Whether they will come into the Union as states, and if so how soon, is something that would be hard to tell just now. The voters of Hawaii have already voted that they would like their island paradise to become a state. Puerto Rico, which did not belong to the United States until 1898, is thickly settled, but by people who for the most part speak

Spanish. Some of them would like to be completely independent rather than become a state of the Union. 

Would it be desirable to have a provision established by law or constitutional amendment setting up a fixed area or population for a region before it could be admitted as a state? Do you think there are likely to be any more states added to the Union by the division of states? Why or why not? Be able to identify on an outline map of the United States each of the forty-eight states. 7001 BETIC www

40. General Features of State Government. - All the states are alike in several respects. They all have a governor, a legislature, and a system of courts. They all have a constitution. They are all represented in Congress by two senators and by as many representatives as their population entitles them to have. They all have a system of executive or administrative offices other than the governor. 

They all have the same rank and authority in comparison with the higher authority of the government of the United States.

That, however, about ends the likenesses. Today the states do not all even have two houses in their legislature, for Nebraska has adopted the unicameral form.¹

Certain executive officers are common to most or almost all of the states. 

Every state has a governor as its chief executive. In most states he has a veto power over acts of the legislature corresponding more or less to that of the President over laws of Congress. There is a tendency in recent years to strengthen the governor's power and reduce the number of officials over whom he has no control, by cutting down the number of administrative departments and making the heads of departments subject to the governor's authority. Three-fourths of the states have a lieutenant-governor who takes the governor's place in the case of death or other inability to serve.

The lieutenant-governor generally presides over the state senate. Every state also has a secretary of state, though in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and Virginia he is called the secretary of the commonwealth. All of the states have a state treasurer. Almost all the states have an attorney-general who is the legal adviser of the state officials and usually is responsible for taking charge of legal cases in which the state is directly concerned. Most states also have an auditor, auditor-general, or comptroller, whose chief duty is to see that no money is spent from the state treasury unless it has been authorized by law.

Acme Photo TAKING THE OATH OF OFFICE 

Governor Leverett Saltonstall is being sworn in for a second term as Governor of Massachusetts.

States usually have also an adjutant-general who has some authority over the state militia or National Guard. Usually there is some such officer as superintendent of education, superintendent of public instruction, or commissioner of education. A state banking commissioner, a commissioner of insurance, a commissioner or secretary of agriculture, a secretary of welfare or assistance, and a public utility commission are also usually included in the list of state executive or administrative offices, besides others which are not found in every state. 

1 Pennsylvania, Vermont, and Georgia originally had only one house in their legislatures, and Vermont did not make its legislature bicameral until 1836.

State constitutions are usually drawn up by a special convention called for that particular purpose. Almost always they have to be submitted to popular vote before they can go into effect. Some states have written into their constitution relatively unimportant provisions, and have made them altogether too long. The first state constitution made that of New Hampshire in 1776 - had only about 500 words. 

That of Louisiana, made in 1898, had 50,000. 

Either at this point or a little later compare the form of government in your state with the facts given in this section and see wherein your state is like or unlike the majority. Would there be any advantage in requiring all the state governments to be uniform in organization? 

41. Differences among the States. - Differences in laws and form of government often result from differences in other respects. States often are not alike in resources, in industries and occupations, in traditions, or in social conditions. 

Some states are mountainous, some are largely in great river valleys; some have rich mines, some none worth mentioning; some have deep, rich soil, some little but shallow and stony land. 

States with great industries and hundreds of thousands of factory workers find their legislatures and governors perplexed with problems that seldom bother the officials of agricultural states. 

States that are largely agricultural have seldom found it necessary to set up governments that cost as much as those of commercial or industrial states.

A state in which hardly anybody but Indians lived until about the middle of the nineteenth century would not be likely to have any extensive political traditions. But states like Virginia, Massachusetts, and others which

have already found excuses for celebrating the 300th anniversary of something, have families whose ancestry goes far back, and whose members still stand high socially, industrially, or politically. It is not a mere accident that our western states are the ones that most often are willing to try something new-perhaps risky in govern- 

ment, industry, and social life.

Race and even religion may also affect social and political life. 

The contacts of white and colored people in the South, and the memories of the Reconstruction era, have produced problems of government and social relations in the southern states which are not exactly paralleled in any other part of the country. States which have received great numbers of immigrants from Europe have also been affected politically, industrially, and socially. Political parties there sometimes show a line-up that rests to some extent upon race, ancestry, or religion. There may be an economic or historical reason why a state usually has voted the Republican or the Democratic

42. Distinctive Features of Our State's Progress. Topics like this our readers will have to work out for themselves. The following suggestions may help you to think things through that will give you a better understanding of your own state-perhaps you call it a commonwealth: 

1. Start a map of the state, marking county boundaries and showing important bodies of water and mountains.

2. Show on this map the location of the principal railroad lines, 8 or 10 important highway routes, and from 15 to 25 important cities or towns. 

3. What are the most important products of this state — agricultural, metal or mineral, manufacturing, etc.? What districts or communities in the state are notable for each of these? 

4. How does the state rank among the states of the Union in area, population, and wealth? Has its ranking always been what it is today? 

If not, how has it differed? 

5. What changes have taken place in the industrial and other economic activities of the people of the state? 

6. Trace the development of political sentiment in the state. What parties have been dominant from time to time? If changes in party leadership are marked at particular times, explain how and why they took place. 

7. What notable events of national importance have occurred within the state? Does it contain relics, memorials, or other remains of notable events of the past? 

8. Are there natural resources, special scenes of interest, or particular institutions in the state notable enough to attract the attention of people from other states? 

9. Mention people who either were born or spent much of their lives in the state, who have been outstanding in politics, industry, education, literature, science, or other fields of interest.

44. National vs. State Sovereignty. Though the federal Consti tution itself declares that the Constitution and the laws and treaties made under the authority of the United States shall be the supreme law of the land, it also provides in Amendment X that the powers not delegated to the United States nor prohibited to the states are "reserved" to the states or the people. You can see how this fact might give rise to violent differences of opinion over the comparative authority of state and national governments. Nobody of importance today would argue, as Calhoun did a century ago, that the Constitution was simply a compact between the states from which a state had the right to withdraw, and that the states were the rightful judges as to whether a law of Congress is in accordance with the Constitution. 

That kind of union would indeed be a rope of sand," as Webster said. We still find differences of opinion, however, on whether particular measures that involve the relation of the national government and the states are wise or constitutional. On such questions the 

Supreme Court of the United States has the last word. 66 The trend of the times is toward transferring authority from the states to the national government. Many things which once could not have been done on a nation-wide scale are so carried on now. 

There is enough common interest and contact among all sections so that anything seriously affecting the welfare of one section cannot fail to show some reaction in almost every other. At the same time, there is considerable objection to letting officials at Washington in time of peace become dictators or even managers of the economic or social interests of all the varied states and districts of the nation. 

Can a person consistently object to the taking over by the federal government of matters hitherto left in the care of the states, and at the same time have no sympathy with Calhoun's theory of state sovereignty? Would 

Calhoun's theory be more dangerous, or less, today than in his time?

III 

45. The States and the Union Today. - The relation between the national government and the states is by no means one-sided. The national government agrees in the Constitution to protect every state from invasion, and also "against domestic violence." The latter obligation does not come into effect unless the legislature or the governor of a state, when the legislature cannot be assembled, asks for help. 

If, however, the President thinks the authority of the nation is being disregarded within a state, he will not hesitate to send troops into the state to enforce the national law, whether or not the governor wants them.

STATE 

The national government also guarantees to every state a republican form of government. 

Once almost anyone would have said that no state would want to set up any other kind. In late years, however, we have seen things done even in our own country which make us wonder whether "it can happen here."

If any group of people in a state, whether they call themselves Communists, Fascists, Silver Shirts, or something else, undertook to say that its ideas and no others should have any voice or expression in government, surely that state would not have "a republican form of government." In one case which came before it, the Supreme 

Court ruled that it was the business of Congress to determine whether or not a state has a republican form of government. The Court itself declined to assume that responsibility.

THE GREAT SEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

Every state has an official seal to signify its authority.

Some powers need to be exercised by both the state governments and the national government, because hardly any government could get along without them. These are called concurrent powers. Levying taxes and borrowing money are important examples of this kind of power. Those which are given in the Constitution to Congress are looked upon as delegated powers. Those which are kept in the hands of the states or the people of the states are reserved powers.

And then there are a few, some of which have been exercised by other governments in the past, which are not permitted to either the states. or the national government, and that may properly be called forbidden powers. We mentioned in Section 28 the delegated powers and the forbidden powers and referred to several of the reserved powers. 

Let us consider some other limitations on the national government which are mentioned in Article I, Section 9, of the Constitution. 

About some of these items some interesting observations may be made. 

1. Congress was forbidden to prohibit the importation of slaves (though the word "slave" did not appear) before 1808. Now there is no such thing as slavery in the United States. 

2. The writ of habeas corpus (§ 84) may not be suspended except in cases of invasion or rebellion, but who may suspend it then? Lincoln thought he had the power to do it during the Civil War and exercised that power. 

3. "No tax or duty shall be laid on articles exported from any state." 

This statement, however, does not say that the export of certain goods may not be entirely forbidden. Congress at one time forbade the sale of munitions to a country engaged in war and has authorized the President to proclaim embargoes on certain goods to certain countries. But in no case may it interfere with the trade of a state by taxing goods merely because they are sent out of the state. 

4. "No money shall be drawn from the treasury, but in consequence of appropriations made by law." This, however, is a restriction on the other branches of the government than Congress, and is hardly a restriction on the national government itself. It is intended to mean that Presidents and other federal officials may not help themselves to public money. 

Congress may authorize its being spent. Only 5. No person holding any office of profit or trust under the United States may, without the consent of Congress, accept any present or honor from any foreign ruler or government. 

Let us now turn to the powers which the Constitution denies to the states. A few of these, as we have noticed, are also forbidden to the national government, but several are not. You will be able to give your own reasons why the states should not be allowed to do some of these things. 

1. Enter any treaty, alliance or confederation. 

2. Grant letters of marque and reprisal. 

3. Coin money. 

4. Emit bills of credit. (This means to issue paper money.)

5. Make anything but gold and silver coin "legal tender" in payment of debts. (Congress has done this, however. If somebody who owes you something offers you paper money to pay for it, he has fulfilled his obligation and you must take it or else release him from the necessity of paying.) 

6. Pass any bill of attainder. 

7. Pass an ex post facto law.

The outer circle includes not only the powers which are exercised by governments in this country, but those which, though at some time exercised by some governments, are forbidden under the Constitution. The first inner circle is divided so as to show the powers exercised by the national government and those exercised wholly or mainly by states. The central circle shows the concurrent powers exercised by both national and state governments. Some of these state powers, such as care of the dependent and defective, and maintenance of highways, could with some justification have been transferred into the inside circle of concurrent powers.

8. Pass any law impairing the obligation of contracts. (Congress has certainly done so; e.g., in permitting debts to be paid in dollars that did not contain as much gold as a dollar did when the debt was incurred.) 

9. Grant any title of nobility. 

10. Lay duties on imports or exports (without the consent of Congress, which is not likely to be given). 

11. Keep troops or ships of war in time of peace (also unless Congress consents). 

12. Enter into any agreement or compact with another state. (Congress has permitted some things of this kind, as when certain states having a common interest in a river that formed a part of the boundary between them, or a harbor which touched upon the shore of two or more states, were allowed to establish a joint "authority" to build bridges, dig tunnels, or do something else intended to be for their common advantage.) 

13. Engage in war unless actually invaded or in imminent danger. 

14. Deny the right to vote on account of race, color, previous condition of servitude, or sex (Amendments XV and XIX). 

In times like the present when men do things that once would never have been dreamed, nobody can tell when new questions may come up affecting the powers of either the national government or the states. Should a federal agency, for example, have the right to forbid the proprietor of a local radio station to use profanity in a talk he might give over his station, just because somebody in another state might listen to it? Should a person who owns an automobile be required to take out a federal license before going from one state to another? Fortunately a very considerable number of provisions in the Constitution have been made flexible and indefinite enough to meet any situations that have thus far arisen, and of course the Constitution can always be amended if enough of the people of the United 

States want to change it.

Many things are of interest to both state and national governments. 

The matter of defense from foreign enemies, for example, is one. The control and prevention of disease is another, for a disease that gets started in one state recognizes no state boundaries as it spreads. And now in late years the federal government has taken on the responsibility of giving money to pay workers who are out of a job in private industry, and states and cities have been falling all over themselves to get handouts from the Treasury at Washington for the construction of public works. Should we also say that a labor dispute which closes

factories in big industries is also a national concern as well as a problem for the state in which the dispute occurs? 

Moreover, some things that states ordinarily do are of benefit to people in other states, or to the country as a whole. 

For that reason, among others, the federal government has made "grants-in-aid" to the states for constructing highways, maintaining vocational courses in schools, supporting unemployment insurance laws, and several other purposes. When such grants are made, it is the custom to require the state either to match equally the amount that the federal government gives it, or in some other way to co-operate with the federal government in getting the thing done. 

Under what circumstances are states likely to be willing to turn over to the national government any authority or responsibility which they have previously exercised? If the federal government decides to help care for unemployed people in a state, should the payment of funds for the purpose, or the supervision of jobs created to make work, be in the hands of the federal government or the states? 

46. The Relation of the States to One Another. In one sense, one state is just as good as another. The Constitution says that every state shall have two United States senators. That equal status in the Senate is the only thing in the Constitution which may not be changed without the consent of every state that would be affected. 

No state has any special privileges over another. No state can buy or force laws to suit itself just because it is large, populous, or wealthy. 

When the Constitution imposes restrictions on the states, it imposes them on all alike. The protection of the federal government is assured to little Delaware as well as to its big sister California on the other side of the continent. 

Since all states are on the same footing, the Constitution requires each state to give "full faith and credit. . . to the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of every other state." Whatever is lawfully done in one state must be recognized by other states as having been legally done. Let Delaware charter a corporation, and other states will have to admit that a corporation has been created and has a legal right to do business. Let Louisiana impose a burdensome tax on chain stores, and other states cannot do anything about it, no matter how much good they may believe chain stores do for their own people. 

In these days when means of transportation make it so easy to eat

breakfast in one state, lunch in another, and dinner in another, it makes some difference to a person what he may have the right to do in one state as compared with another. When John Smith is in 

Pennsylvania, he has whatever rights a citizen of Pennsylvania has no more and no less. He must abide by the laws of Pennsylvania while he is within its boundaries. 

He may drive his auto 50 miles an hour in Pennsylvania, since one may legally do that, even though in his own state 40 miles might be the legal maximum; but if he drives over 50 miles an hour, the motor police may get him, even though his own state would allow him to go 55. 

A state is not supposed to "lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws." This provision was meant to encourage the freedom of trade between the states which has been one of our boasts for years and years. But now some states are discovering needs for "inspecting" all kinds of things and people when they come into the states, charging something for 

Numerous other little incondoing so, and provoking the visitors. veniences arise when one goes frequently from one state to another, on account of minor details in parking, paying sales taxes, or observing daylight saving or standard time in the summer. 

Though state boundaries are often purely imaginary things, they may at times make quite a difference. Suppose a person is accused of breaking into a house and stealing something in Ohio. The instant he gets across the boundary into Indiana or Michigan, he is safe from an Ohio sheriff for the time being. So the Constitution gives the

governor of a state where a certain crime has been committed the right to make a requisition on the governor of any state where the criminal may have gone. According to the Constitution, that governor, upon receiving the requisition, must allow the accused person to be taken back to the state from which he came. At the same time, no way is provided to punish a governor who refuses to comply with the requisition of the governor of another state. Several times governors bave refused to send back accused persons, when they believed that they were being sought for political reasons, or because they thought justice would more nearly be done by letting the accused person stay free than by sending him back to be punished. If a person accused of crime should get out of the country entirely, then this process of extradition, as it is called, would be handled between our State Department and the government of the country to which the accused person had gone, and not by the governor of any state. 

If you have traveled in more than one state, what misunderstandings or embarrassments, if any, resulted from differences in laws or customs? Have you read any news articles recently involving the obligations of one state toward another? If so, discuss the points concerned. 

47. Problems Common to Many States. - It would be hard to find a matter which was of concern to one state and no more. One matter which has been left entirely to the states, but which has been a headache to many of them, is the making of marriage and divorce laws. In one state no one may be legally married without the parents' consent, unless he or she is over 21 years of age, and there may be no legal marriage under the age of 16. In one state two persons planning to get married have to make an application at least three days before they can obtain a license. In some other states there is no wait at all, and even a license may not be required. South Carolina grants no divorces. New York grants divorces for only one cause. 

Nevada tells the country that all you have to do if you want a divorce is to come and live there six weeks. Such differences in a matter of so great social importance have led many people to believe that uniform marriage and divorce laws for the entire country would be distinctly helpful. Yet, of course, we cannot get them without amending the 

Constitution, because Congress ha no power to pass such laws. 

One of the first efforts to bring about co-operation among the states in dealing with their common problems was made during the presi-

dency of Theodore Roosevelt. He became greatly interested in the conservation of natural resources and felt that problems of that character could be dealt with properly only by co-operation among many of the states. So he invited to the White House the governor of every state in the Union to consider this and other matters of common interest. This meeting of the governors got the nickname of the 

House of Governors. It was hoped that the governors, after the

Illinois represents the "strong governor" type of state organization. The legislature and chief judicial officials are, of course, elected by the voters, but most of the administrative heads are appointed by the governor and responsible to him. 

48. Reforms and Changes in State Governments. 

- Not so many years ago it was generally agreed by writers on government that one of the chief opportunities to improve state governments was to make 

---

I 

them more businesslike in their organization, and to reduce the number of officers selected by the people. It was said that responsibility was distributed so much that nobody in particular could be blamed when things did not go right, and that nobody had enough authority to make minor state officials behave themselves if they were inclined not to do so. It was believed that if only the governor and perhaps two or three other state officials were chosen by popular vote, the state would get better results. Several states, notably Illinois, New 

York, Maine, and Virginia, did make useful changes in their state governments, looking toward the centering of more power in the office of governor.

There is no doubt that a more businesslike organization has been brought about by such changes, but risks have come too. Centralizing power in the hands of one officer or a few may give a chance to those who have the power to use it to build up political machines, or to force policies upon a state that displease a great many people. The voters must be on their guard against electing the wrong people to responsible positions.

It remains to be seen whether any other state will follow the example of Nebraska in getting rid of one of its two houses in the legislature. 

That is a proposition which sounds good, but which demands vigilance on the part of the voters to prevent concentration of power in unsafe hands.

The abolition of the spoils system and the substitution of the merit system in selecting minor state officials would certainly be an improvement in many states. When that is done, there is always a temptation for the party in power to get the jobs filled with its own people before the new system goes into effect; and that of course disgusts the other side. It is hard to make any reform without hurting somebody's feelings.

Sometimes changes are made necessary when special emergencies arise. For example, the depression of the 1930's brought about in more than one state the establishment of a department of relief or assistance in the state government, and led to the transfer of power from local governments to the state government in handling the problem. Flood control, the stabilizing of the coal industry, the effects of the "dust bowl," are examples of problems that may vitally and directly affect one state and indirectly many others. How shall

these be handled? Through co-operation of the states? If so, how shall we get it? Must we call on the federal government to take over these problems?

Would a strong man or a weak man as governor like it better to have much authority centralized in the governor's hands? Is your state government organized on a businesslike basis? If not, what changes in it would you recommend? If a proposed change is good in theory, should the fact that one party may profit from it more than another cause one to oppose it? state colony OREGON'S STATE CAPITOL

LOCAL GOVERNMENTS IN THE LIFE OF OUR PEOPLE 

Coming down the line from those activities of government which center in the city of Washington, we reach those which are nearest at hand, and with some of which we come in contact every day of our lives. 

Theoretically we ought to know more about these activities than we do about anything else in the field of government. But do we? Local government was probably the earliest form in which authority was exercised by anybody. The cities, boroughs, towns, townships, villages, and whatnot of today are its successors. Anyway, we cannot afford to ignore their activities or problems now. 

Some Questions: 

1. For what particular reasons is local government important? 

2. Under what forms of local government do we live, and how did they come into being? 

3. What is the importance of county government in general and in our own state? 

4. Why are the problems of city government serious? 

5. What forms of city government may be found in vogue today? 

6. How may we plan to make our local governments more effective? 

49. Why Local Government Is Important. Our state legislature may make laws applying to its entire area, but the state has to have officials living in local governments to carry out its general laws if they are to be properly enforced. If our government is to be a democracy, the authority to administer the affairs of that democracy must not be too far away.

The chances are that local government touches us a dozen times to every once that the state or national government directly affects us.

When we ask a policeman to direct us to the street we are looking for, when we pay taxes on the house we live in, when we attend or visit a public school, when we drink a glass of water or take a bath, we may be taking advantage of some service of the local government or doing something to support it. It is most often the city, the borough, the town, or the village that furnishes street lights and fire 

124

LOCAL GOVERNMENTS 

125 protection, cleans the snow from the streets in the winter, and sweeps them in the summer, if they get such treatment at all. 

Every state is divided into counties, or parishes as Louisiana names them. In many states the laws of a state are actually administered through the county, though in others the counties are chiefly convenient subdivisions for holding courts or looking after some other local need. The punishment of crime, the settlement of important

The farmer from out in the country may meet the state highway patrolman as he drives to market, and may look to the national

Department of Agriculture for advice about planting or to receive payments for not growing more of some crop. But he too depends on his own township supervisor or road commissioner for the care of

the roads that branch off from the main highway, and he votes every so often for the school directors who look after the rural school or the justice of the peace who is a local judge on a small scale. You can't get away from some kind of local government. 

Mention six occasions during the present week in which you have come directly into contact with some government official. How many of these contacts were with local officials, how many with state, and how many with national? 50. The Background of Our Local Governments. Most of the features of local government in this country have a background in some precedent in our own history or that of England. During the colonial period, three kinds of local government took form in the English colonies the county system, the town system, and the mixed or county-township system. In the South where the plantation was the center of interest and where small organizations of local government did not seem so necessary, the county became the type of local organization. Towns grew up in New England, centering around the church or a harbor, and these communities were the typical arrangement for local government there. In the middle colonies, just as one might expect, we have some features of both the county and the town system. The responsibilities of government were more nearly divided between the county and the town or township. There the mixed or county-township system was typical. 

As time went on and people moved West, they took with them their ideas and customs with regard to local government. In the southern part of the Mississippi Valley the states were divided into counties, and the subdivisions of the counties had little importance. North of the Ohio River a different state of affairs developed, and there in many places townships played an important part in local life. In the one state of Illinois, where two lines of immigration came in, one from the northern Atlantic states and another from the southern, we have different forms of local government derived from the two sources from which the early settlers came. 

Since conditions differed so much in different states, the makers of our national Constitution wisely made no attempt to tell the states how they must be subdivided. State constitutions sometimes take care of the matter, and sometimes the state lawmaking body makes

Why might the form of local government in one state or even in one part of a state need to be different from that prevailing in other states or parts of states? In your state are local governments classified? If so, on what basis? 

Is there any notable difference as between one county or other division of local government and another? 

51. Officials in County Governments. Every county has a county seat, which is a sort of center of government for the county. That is where the courthouse and county jail, and perhaps other public buildings, are located. Usually a town somewhere near the center of a county was made the county seat, though today it may not be so important as it was years ago.

Students of government have often ridiculed the condition of county government in the states. The county has been referred to as "the jungle of American politics" because of the lack of order and common sense in the distribution of the work of government. Often so many different officers are elected by popular vote that no one could be expected to have a very good understanding of the qualifications of candidates for the various positions which are to be filled. Sometimes state constitutions or acts of a state legislature have established political jobs in the counties for which there was no real need. 

In many states the most important officials in a county are the board of commissioners or supervisors. They may choose some of the other county officers, fix the rate of taxes for the county, perhaps have charge of highways and other public property, and in general oversee all the county business. These commissioners or supervisors come nearest to being the legislative officials of the county government, and often have much executive authority too. 

Another officer, commonly found in counties all over the country, is the sheriff, whose duty it is to keep order and act as a kind of enforcement officer for the courts. There is almost always a county attorney, state's attorney, or district attorney - the name varies in different states - who is responsible for overseeing the prosecution of criminals and may be the legal adviser to the other county officers. Practically all counties also have a treasurer to have charge of county money, and a county comptroller or controller or auditors to inspect the financial accounts of county offices. Other officials may include a recorder of deeds and other legal papers, directors of 

---

LOCAL GOVERNMENTS 

129 the poor or directors of welfare, and in many states a county superintendent of schools.

Terms of county officers are most often either two or four years. It depends on the policy of a particular state whether these officers are practically all chosen by popular vote or whether some of them are appointed by the county commissioners or county judges. The judges themselves are frequently looked upon as really belonging to the judicial system of the whole state, even though they may be elected by counties. 

In a few states, Maryland for example, something like a commission form of government has been adopted. Under this arrangement there may be from three to five elected officials who have practically all responsibility for carrying on county business. There may be a county manager if a county sees fit to provide for such an official. When such an arrangement is made, the manager becomes responsible for overseeing the business part of county government. In the state of New York the legislature has laid out five plans for county government, and, subject to some limitations, a county may choose any one of the plans that it wishes. 

Be able to compare the system of county government in your state with that of neighboring states, and explain why there is a difference between them, if any is noticeable. 

52. The Subdivisions of Counties. We might have to tell fortyeight different stories if we discussed this topic fully. Read this section through, and then give special attention to the parts that seem most important or interesting. 

We have already noticed that subdivisions of counties in the southern states do not amount to very much. Sometimes they are called precincts, sometimes hundreds, and in Mississippi they are called beats. Once these divisions might have been intended to have something to do with the furnishing of men for the state militia. Sometimes the divisions are for not much more than voting purposes. In the colonies which had an established church, the church parish might be the basis for division. 

The farther north we go, generally speaking, the more important do the subdivisions of the county become. That statement, of course, leaves the cities out of account, because the city is important anywhere. But in the 

Middle Atlantic states and the states of the Middle West, the subdivision called township or town often takes over some rather important functions in such matters as the care of the roads, the government of schools, and other problems that have their local aspect. In the states west of the original thirteen, much local government has been organized on the basis of the socalled congressional township, which originally was merely a basis for measur-

ing and surveying public land. Townships may have such officers as supervisors who look after highways and possibly some other matters, a treasurer, assessors, auditors, constables, tax collectors, justices of the peace, and school directors or school trustees. In New York each town has a supervisor who belongs, with the other supervisors of towns in his county, to the county board which has the general oversight of county affairs. 

The New England town has always been interesting, with the town meeting as its distinctive feature. Every voter in most New England towns has the right to attend the town meeting, though there is a question as to where they would be put if they all came out at the same time. At this town meeting, anything and everything of general importance may be taken up. The tax is fixed by a majority vote. Programs for conducting schools, looking after streets, taking care of parks, deciding what to do with the poor all these and many other matters may be discussed at a town meeting. It is democracy in its most complete form. 

Keystone View Company WHERE TOWN BUSINESS IS CONDUCTED 

In keeping with this idea of democracy, the officers of a New Avon, Connecticut, does not need a big England town are many. Most city hall, but keeps up to date this town hall which is over 100 years old. important probably are the selectmen, who have the general responsibility for looking after the business of the town. There are also justices of the peace, constables, road commissioners, assessors, a treasurer, auditors, jurors, and others. In many cases such officials are elected for terms of only one year, though some of the most important ones, such as selectmen, may have a three-year term, with one or two of the group elected each year. 

Outside of New England, town or township officers are often elected for longer terms, even up to four years or perhaps six for justices of the peace. 

When a town grows large, it becomes hard to handle public business on a perfectly democratic basis, and some sort of representative government takes its place. Brookline, Massachusetts, with about 50,000 people, still calls itself a town, but has a kind of representative town meeting instead of trying to get 25,000 voters or more together in one place at one time. This town and Lower Merion Township in Pennsylvania are among the richest communities in the country per capita. Where the make-up of the people is such that law and order are easily maintained and there is

LOCAL GOVERNMENTS 

131 a high standard of general intelligence, they do not seem to need an elaborate system of government.

Frequently a portion of a town or township will become more thickly settled than the rest of it. It may be willing to tax itself for improvements such as paved streets, street lights, more expensive schools, or something else which the whole town or township would not care to pay for. In such cases, the community may be set off by itself, being either completely removed from the government of the rest of the township, or given the right to handle certain matters which the rest of the town does not care to provide for. Pennsylvania calls such communities boroughs. A borough has as its chief executive an officer known as the chief burgess, and it has a council of perhaps five or seven people to handle the legislative part of the local government. In New York a somewhat corresponding local organization is known as a village, with its chief officer known as a mayor. A New York village remains, for certain purposes, a part of the town within which it grew up. Boroughs and villages, if they keep on growing, may decide to become cities, but many of them do not care to take on the somewhat complicated and expensive features of city government until they have to. 

Besides all these forms of local government, some states have special districts formed for perhaps one purpose only. These districts may levy a special tax, but have no other local responsibility outside of the particular purpose for which they were organized. These may include drainage districts, sewerage districts, or fire protection districts, not to mention the school districts, which in many states are entirely separate in their management from the other local government organizations, even when they cover the same territory.

Would it or would it not be best to have such matters as school control, fire protection, or sewage disposal form a part of the activities of the regular local government? Some people who do not favor many separate local governments believe that schools should be managed separately from other local government activities. Why do you suppose they feel that way? 

53. Local Government in Our Own State. - You will have to work out the main facts on this topic yourself, unless somebody else has been enterprising enough to do so already. You ought to be acquainted with its natural resources, means of communication, industries, and government. You should know how townships or other local subdivisions were laid out, and how new ones may be formed. You should learn the titles and duties of local officials and know who hold those positions. Good citizenship may show itself just as positively through one's interest in his local government as in being concerned about national problems.

In thousands of local communities, there is next to nothing in print which gives in concise form the facts about the organization, officials, and policies of government, local resources and industries, and other matters of local importance. Perhaps your class might do something really creative in working up material which your local newspaper would publish in installments or chapters. In fact, it might be a work of several years, considering the limited time most classes could spend on this part of their work, before the whole ground would be covered. 

Whether or not you undertake anything more elaborate in the study of your local governments, you should arrange in your notebooks, for each local government in which you live, a table as suggested below, and keep watch for changes that might take place during the time that you are studying it.

54. The City in Law and in Fact. Ever since men have been fit to be called civilized, there have been cities. Memphis and Thebes in ancient Egypt, Babylon, Jerusalem, Athens, Rome, have a permanent place in history, and some of them are important today. Cities are likely to be the centers of industry and power. Usually when a country as a whole has been growing, its cities have grown faster than its rural districts, though recently in this country, in many cases, city growth has slowed down or even stopped. 

The word city does not always mean just the same. It often suggests a place of considerable size, but sometimes it means only a form of local government without regard to size. London, which we usually

133 think of as one city- the biggest in the world - includes several communities with separate governments of their own. Any local community with an organized government under a charter or constitution of its own may be termed a municipality or municipal corporation. 

Neither do "city" and "urban community" mean just the same.

55. City Governments and Other Governments. 

City govern ments, you remember, are subject to the authority of the state of which they are a part. Some states find it a problem to know just where to draw the line in distributing the powers of government between the state and the local communities. When a state has one or more large cities that have a great deal of influence in the social and economic life of the people of the whole state, such as Boston in 777

Sometimes this undertaking has been carried so far that the cities themselves claim they are not getting a square deal. At least in the upper house of the state legislature, if not in the lower, the districts from which members are elected are usually so arranged as to prevent the small towns and rural districts being constantly outvoted by representatives from the largest cities.

135 In many states a community has to have a specified population, such as 8000 or 10,000, before it can become a city. In classifying cities, legislatures may fix the population requirements for particular classes at certain points with the deliberate intention of putting some cities into one class rather than another. Some states allow a considerable measure of home rule, by which is meant allowing the people of a county, city, or some other division to decide what kind of government they will have, perhaps choosing from three or four different kinds of local government authorized in advance.

§ 2. Definitions. As used in this chapter, (1) the term "local law" means a law adopted pursuant to this chapter by the local Jegislative body of a city as constituted under section ten, THE BEGINNING OF NEW YORK'S HOME RULE LAW 

If a city finds that its people are moving out from congested districts into pleasanter neighborhoods, it may annex the newly settled territory, if state laws permit. It is often required that a region must give its own consent before it can be annexed to a city. Sometimes people in suburban communities feel that they do not need elaborate

and expensive government and fear that in joining a city the only result might be an increased tax rate for them. 

To satisfy communities that want to keep their own identity and still get some of the advantage of being affiliated with a large city, an arrangement sometimes called a metropolitan district has been proposed. It would include not only the city, but perhaps an entire county or even more of the surrounding country that is tied up with the city in a business way. The former separate communities might retain self-government in many respects, but highway construction, fire protection, and other matters in which all are concerned might be handled by representatives chosen from the whole district. Pittsburgh and Atlanta, at least, have thought of something of the kind. 

What is the largest city in your state? Would there be good argument for setting up a metropolitan district with that city as its center? Would a city sometimes be unwilling to annex territory that wanted to join it? Why or why not? Does your state allow home rule to its cities or other local governments? state. 

56. Types of City Government. The early government of large cities in this country was generally made considerably like that of the There was a mayor corresponding to the governor, and probably two divisions of the lawmaking body, just as the state had two houses in its legislature. But one lawmaking body is usually enough, most often called the city council. If the number of city lawmakers is small, people can keep their eyes on them and the opportunity to get away with graft and other forms of dishonesty is reduced. No longer do intelligent people think that a city government must be closely patterned after a state. Three common types of city government may be observed today. 

The most numerous type, and the one which has changed least from the older forms of city government, is the mayor-council form. The mayor is the chief executive and has powers somewhat like those of the governor or President in the state or national organization. The council makes the city laws, or ordinances, as they are often called. 

There are also usually city judicial officers, who may be called magistrates, or justices, or occasionally aldermen. Sometimes, however, the name aldermen is applied to one house of the lawmaking branch, 1 The term is often used to refer to a region of that kind, whether any change of government is being considered or not (§ 113).

57. Our Own Contacts with City Government. Perhaps you have no direct contacts. It may be you live out in the open country, or in a suburban village or some other small center of population. Nevertheless, there is not one of us who is not affected in some way by what is done in at least one of the large cities of our country. 

If you live in a large city, study it thoroughly. Draw a map of the city, showing its division into wards, its principal streets, the location of railroads, important buildings, and the like. Survey its history. Show how it has grown, if it has, through the development of industries or the annexation of neighboring territory.

Be sure you are acquainted with the chief features of its present form of government. Through what changes in form has it passed, if any? 

How are the leading officials chosen? Who are they? What do they do? 

Under any general form of city government there will be administrative departments. What names are given to them in your city, and who are at present heads of them? What important work is handled by the bureaus or subdivisions into which they are probably divided? Do you have a merit system for choosing these public officials, or are they appointed because they are friends of the mayor or of a political boss? 

What contacts do citizens in general have with city officials? You could work up a series of chapters for a textbook or a set of radio programs that would explain to school pupils and the public the work of the various branches of the government of your city. In it you could discuss problems of your city that seem either more serious than in other cities or different from them. 

If you do not live in a city, perhaps you will have an advantage even over those who do. Then each member of your class can make a study of a different large city along the lines mentioned in the previous paragraphs, and by bringing them together, you might produce a book on cities which would be even more valuable for your purposes than anything Lincoln Steffens wrote. You will probably find some good things about the government of almost every city, though to do that would be easier in some places than in others. One does not need to go out of his way to uncover the dirt that might be found in the government of many cities, but if he is truthful he should recognize its mistakes and weaknesses as well as its strong points. Don't let yourself think that everybody in public life is crooked, however.

What do you think would be the reaction of your local newspapers or leading politicians if you tried to find out and tell the exact truth about government in your community? Would they be likely to try to hide a good many things, or would they say, "Come on and look. We are not afraid"?

58. Special Problems of Local Government. For one thing, how many local organizations of government shall we have? Small though some of the counties are in some of our states, there doubtless was a time when they had to be as small as they are in order to make it convenient for the county seat to be reached from all portions of the county in less than one day's travel, and to enable county officials to be familiar with conditions in all portions of the county. Now that situation has completely changed as a result of the automobile, the telephone, the telegraph, and the radio. Shall we combine the small counties in some of our states and the small townships in others and thus eliminate unnecessary officers, save money, and make administration more efficient? The only honest objection can be that it would be a mistake to take government too far away from the people who pay for it. 

Another problem is to get rid of political corruption and dishonesty. Petty graft occurs in rural districts and small towns as well as in the big cities. The best remedy is to develop in the people of any community or county such a hatred of dishonesty that no official would dare to indulge in it. The holding of local offices should be based on ability. No doubt there are communities so small that they would not care to bother with a system of civil service examinations, but a state could arrange for examinations to be held in different sections and have it understood that no one would be appointed to any administrative position in a county or other local government who had not made a good showing in such examinations. Whenever possible it is well to separate local elections from state and national ones. Then

it is more likely, though of course not certain, that voters will take into account a person's qualifications for the office he seeks, rather than the name of the candidate he supported for President. 

The handling of public utilities — railroads, street railways, electric light systems, water supply, and the like sometimes is a serious problem for local governments. Public utilities corporations have sometimes tried to control officials in cities and smaller districts so as to make sure that nothing was done to harm the interest of the utilities. 

But to turn all such activities over to the mercies of state or local politicians might be still more dangerous.

Just one other problem of local government we will mention. That is the way local officials are elected. There have been altogether too many of them in many counties and smaller communities. Here is where the "short ballot" (§ 20) may come in. If we succeed in reducing the number of officials to be chosen by popular vote, then we shall have to determine whether to have a smaller number chosen by direct popular vote on a party basis, or do away with party names and when possible introduce the much-discussed "P. R." In electing city, town, or village councils, there is much to be said in favor of it. 

How many of the problems mentioned in this section have been discussed to any extent in your community? Is there some outstanding problem in your own community which has not been mentioned here? If so, what? 

Why is it a problem of special importance to you? 

59. Planning for Community and Regional Welfare. When we talk about community planning, we most often think about the arrangement of streets, the location of a civic center, and other things that may be done to improve a city's attractiveness. If a city grows without planning, its streets will probably be narrow and winding, and traffic on its way through may be badly delayed. With modern kinds of transportation and thousands more of people to use all these various kinds, a city which is not planned finds itself sooner or later seriously handicapped.

But with reasonable planning, streets will be laid out with some reference to their relation to other streets. Boulevards and main thoroughfares will be protected by regulations that are intended to make them most convenient and useful to all concerned. Every up-to-date city has its zoning laws, which declare that in one section the so-called heavy industries may be carried on, that in another there

143 may be retail stores and other conveniences for the citizens to meet their everyday needs, and that still other sections are entirely for residential purposes.

Schools, churches, and libraries, however, may have a place in even the so-called best sections of a city. A city may plan, also, with reference to the location of these. What happens if a school board HEL AR 

DENVER'S CIVIC CENTER 

The city of Denver and the state of Colorado have worked together toward the planning of a civic center for the state capital, which has few, if any, superiors in attractiveness in the country. buys land to put up a new building simply where it is cheapest? That may be in the section of the city where few families live any longer, so that there will be few children to take advantage of the new building, or else those that do come will be put to great inconvenience. Many a church has found it necessary to move from the downtown congested districts into the residential portions of a city if it was going to keep its congregation together. So, planning involves not merely laying out streets but considering the future needs of a city in any and all respects and trying to see to it that the city of the future will serve

its people better than the smaller community served its residents in the past. Plans should, of course, permit change if unforeseen developments occur. Once, for instance, communities wanted main highways to go through the business part of a city. Now they will do almost anything to avoid traffic congestion. 

But planning can be done on a larger scale than the local community. A whole county or a whole section of a state may deserve to be planned. No longer do we think that parks are to be placed only in cities. Whole districts may be set aside for a state park or a county park. Plans may also be made for drainage systems and reservoirs to hold back flood waters that might threaten cities and states hundreds of miles away. Land that has the possibility of good use for pasture but not for cultivation can be put to the kind of service which it is best qualified to render. New trees may be planted which in time will help to replace those that are being cut down. In fact, it would be hard to set a limit to the ways in which thoughtful planning may promote community, regional, state, or even national welfare.

As a practical proposition, governments can do very little to promote the people's welfare without spending money. In that respect they are the same as individuals. Also like individuals, they have to get it or get a promise of it before they can spend it. How this money is obtained and how it is spent are topics of vital importance. More than one government has gone to smash because it handled this matter recklessly or dishonestly.
