60. Taxation and Government. Did you ever hear anyone speak kindly about a tax? Seldom, unless he thought somebody else was going to pay it. A tax is a payment, usually in money, which a government demands from persons or organizations for its own use. 

Taxpayers may not like it, if only because they have to pay it, and if the tax is burdensome, there is more grumbling. 

Governments must have money, but governments and nations have been broken over ways to get it and ways of spending it. In Old 

Testament times King Solomon's successor refused to cut down the cost of government, and more than half of his kingdom broke away from him. The barons of England forced King John to agree, among other things, not to collect taxes without the consent of the leaders of the nation. The American Revolution was caused largely by taxesnot high taxes, it is true, but just the demand for them. 

At the very same time, the people of France were getting restless under burdens 148

of taxation and other feudal tyranny, and a drastic French Revolution followed soon after the one in North America. 

Make a list of at least six items or occasions in the history of the United States when the levying of taxes was a serious problem. Make a similar list of problems of today that relate to the getting and spending of public money. 

If taxes cause so much trouble, why do we have them? Well, what would we do without them? Governments cannot be carried on as

Very often the government which is having the work done hires private contractors to do the actual work of construction. Do you consider this a constituent or a ministrant service? charity enterprises. Most of those who work directly for their government need to be paid for their services in order to be able to work at all. Many material things are used in carrying on the activities of government, and somebody has to pay for those. 

The services that governments render are sometimes called constituent and ministrant. The constituent functions of government are those that governments must do if they are to be done at all. We cannot safely leave the punishment of criminals to private vengeance, or the defense of our people to volunteer service alone. When individ-

150

uals disagree about their relations with one another, public authority must settle the matter. There must be a general understanding about the way public officials shall be selected. (Of course you understand that we are talking about democracies. Dictators and absolute monarchs make their own rules, and under them public authority determines everything that private citizens may do.) 

The ministrant functions of government include those things which governments do for the convenience and welfare of their people, rather than because there is no other possible way to have them done. We could get along without public schools, let private citizens carry the mail, or leave sick people and poor people entirely to the charity and sympathy of their families and friends, if any. Ministrant services have steadily increased. More and more we are expecting governments to look after things that once were left to the family, the church, or some other private agency if they were done at all. 

But when a public agency pays for goods or services, there is no such thing as a magic fund that it can draw upon. Whatever a government spends comes from its own people, either as they knowingly pay for services they receive, or lend their savings to the government, or pay higher prices for goods than they would otherwise have to, because producers or previous owners have already paid taxes on them.

61. Problems of Budget-Making. — If you or your family buy whatever you want, whenever you want it, without thinking when and how you are going to pay for it, you will probably reach the end

of a year without having anything on hand to settle your unpaid bills. 

Some families do that regularly. Governments are sometimes the 

If they must get revenue, they simply tax the first convenient source of revenue. The remedy is a budget - a definitely planned arrangement for handling expenses for a given period. Both governments and homes need it. 

European governments had budget systems for many years before we took up the idea here. In England the Chancellor of the Exchequer would bring before Parliament a budget measure which would contain not only an estimate of the expenses of government for a year, but proposals for getting money to meet those expenses. Some of our cities and school districts, but by no means all, undertook budgetmaking before it came into vogue for state governments or our national government. When government budgets are made, they usually cover a period of twelve months, which is known as a fiscal year and which may not correspond with the calendar year. 

In a city the heads of administrative departments usually make up estimates of what they would like to spend during the next fiscal year. 

These estimates are either brought together by the mayor and presented to the city council, or turned over to the city council without any particular summarization by the mayor. In well-managed state governments usually some particular official under the governor's direction makes up the budget, which in turn is submitted to the state legislature by the governor.

In our national government several presidents tried to get the process introduced, but without success until 1921. At that time a 

Bureau of the Budget was established, then connected with the Treasury Department, but now directly under the President. It brings together for presentation to Congress the estimates made by the various administrative offices as to their needs for the next year. 

Congress must decide whether to accept this budget, and how to raise money to meet it; but with a carefully planned budget before it, Congressmen can do more intelligent thinking about levying taxes than they could otherwise. Sometimes lawmakers have some pet project, perhaps in their own home districts, which they would like to put through, and they are tempted to be generous with public money. An official called the Comptroller-General is appointed by the President for fifteen years and is not eligible to be re-appointed.

Balancing the budget means keeping the amount received equal to or larger than the amount paid out. In a normal year that is not so hard, but what if there is a long depression or a threat of war? If balancing the budget is brought about by reducing expenses, those whose salaries are cut or whose jobs are abolished always object. If it is brought about by raising taxes, the public will usually complain. 

But it is certainly not good business to get further into debt every year.

62. Where We May Get Public Revenue. Outside of taxes, the following sources of revenue have been available to some governments at one time or another: 

1. Public land. - Years ago this country got considerable revenue that way, but it no longer amounts to much. 

2. Gift. Once in a while some kind wealthy citizen may give money or property to his government. He may put up a library or a high school building, or leave his estate at his death to be used as a public park. This source is also undependable. 

3. Fees and licenses. Some things that governments do are paid for at the time or soon after in the form of fees. Recording deeds and mortgages, issuing marriage licenses, and the like, are done for a fee that more than meets the cost of the work required, though no great help toward meeting public expenses can be expected in this way. Some revenue may be obtained from licenses which people must pay for if they wish to engage in certain businesses. __________ 

How LOCAL GOVERNMENTS GET REVENUE AND WHAT THEY DO WITH IT 

The citizens of Pittsburgh pay taxes to their city government, to the local school district, and to the county in which the city is located. On the basis of the graph on the opposite page, would you think that the tax and expenditure program for this city is wisely planned? How heavy do you think the burden of taxation on real estate should be? What changes in this program do you think desirable, if any?

4. Fines. 

These are collected from people who break laws; but surely this source of income is not to be encouraged. 

5. Special assessments. — The cost of laying out new streets and sewers, constructing sidewalks, and such projects, is often met, in part at least, by payments collected from the owners of property nearby which benefits by the special project. 

6. Public industries.· In a few cases, profits are made from a publicly owned water or light plant or, especially in other countries than our own, from a monopoly on the sale of a particular product, such as tobacco or matches. 

7. Loans. 

Governments, like private citizens, may borrow money. 

When they do this they usually have to pay interest on what they borrow. 

Loans, therefore, are only a temporary source of revenue. 

Such sources of revenue turn into sources of expense later on. 

8. Eminent domain. The right of eminent domain is the right of a government to take private property for public use. As in the case of a loan, the government does not get it for nothing, for an honest government will expect to pay the fair value of property taken in this way. But the use of this power may enable a government to get more land for a highway or a public building than would otherwise be possible, at the place where it wants it, whether the owner wants to give it up or not. 

Find in the World Almanac or some other dependable source of information the various means by which the federal government obtained revenue during the last year for which statistics have been published. In the same way study the latest reports of financial operations of your city, school district, or other local government. How important are any of the sources of revenue mentioned in this section? 63. Taxes - Good and Bad. Yes, there are well-planned taxes, and others that are poorly planned or unfair. Some characteristics of a good tax may be stated as follows: 

1. A tax should be in proportion to one's ability to pay. A millionaire would not miss a tax of $2000 a year as much as a poor man would miss $20. 

It might seem fairer to tax one in proportion to the benefits he receives from his government, but how can you figure those with any accuracy? 

Many a poor man could not possibly pay the cost of the education of his children in the public schools; and how can you measure the benefits Henry 

Ford receives because of the services of government? 

2. Taxes should be payable at as convenient times and places as possible. 

Even a rich man might find it easier to pay at one time of year than another.

3. Taxes should be definite and clearly stated. One should have no doubt as to the amount he is expected to pay, and the time and manner of payment should be perfectly plain. 

4. Taxes should be collected at the same rate from all who are in the same situation. It would be unfair to tax one person more heavily than another who possessed the same amount and kind of wealth. We do have some taxes levied on the graduated or progressive principle. On that basis, the rate of tax is greater as one's taxable wealth increases. Even then, however, there is no discrimination, because everybody whose taxable income is $50,000 will pay the same amount, even though the percentage is higher than on a $5000 income.¹ 

5. Taxes should be collected economically and spent honestly. To induce people to pay promptly, not only may a discount be allowed for prompt payment, but a penalty added on taxes not paid by a certain date-commonly called delinquent. 

6. A good tax is adjustable to the needs of the taxing power. This is the hardest to realize of all the qualities of a good tax, because the need may not always be known at the time the tax is levied and it would be impracticable to have a tax rate fluctuating from month to month. 

All taxes may be divided into two great classes direct and indirect. 

Direct taxes are those which are collected by a government in such a way that a taxpayer knows how much is being collected and is expected to bear the burden of the taxes himself. Indirect taxes are those whose burden may be shifted to someone else or are collected by the government in such a way that their cost may not be realized at the time. If a man owns the house that he lives in, he is taxed on the value of that house, and when he pays the tax he knows it. If a tax is collected on goods imported into this country, the importer pays the tax to the government; but he shifts the burden to the person who buys the goods from him, by adding enough to the price of the goods to cover the tax he has paid. People object less to indirect, or "hidden," taxes than to direct taxes, because they pay so many of them without realizing that they are doing so. But many think that if a government depends on indirect taxes for a great deal of its 

1 Our federal income tax is a good example of a graduated tax. The income of a married man is not taxed unless it is above $1500, or of a single person above $750, after deducting gifts to churches, charities, and the like, and making certain other allowances (1942 tax rate). If the net income is above $4000, an added tax called a surtax begins, the rate of which increases by steps until those who have incomes over $5,000,000 a year have to pay a surtax of 77% on the amount of their income beyond that figure.

income, it is likely to levy more of them and be more extravagant in using them than if it collected its taxes in such a way that people knew all about them at the time they were paid. 

Some of the state constitutions limit the total amount of tax that can be collected from certain sources real estate, for example for all purposes combined. It has sometimes happened, however, when this has been done, that the state legislature has failed to provide other means of getting the needed money, and schools and other important public services have suffered severely. It is dangerous for the people of a state to be so anxious to keep taxes down that they deny their people services which should not be crippled or wiped out. 

Taxpayers are spiting themselves when they do that. 

How do you think you would feel if you had an income of $500,000 a year and had to pay nearly $300,000 of that to the federal government in the form of an income tax, in addition to other taxes you might have to pay? Does your state constitution limit the amount of taxes that may be collected from any particular source of revenue? What examples of indirect or "hidden" taxes have you heard or seen mentioned recently? Do you think it is desirable to get rid of such taxes? Why? 

64. Levying and Collecting Taxes. The lawmaking body of a government generally has sole authority to levy taxes for the benefit of that government. A tax law once passed continues in effect indefinitely unless the law itself provides that the tax shall end at a fixed time, but it may be changed or repealed the same as any other kind of law. Unless a state constitution makes some special arrangement to the contrary, the legislature levies taxes for the state, and has the right to determine the amount and kind of taxes that may be levied by local governments. Tax levies in counties may be made by county commissioners or similar officers; in cities, boroughs, and villages, by the council or the trustees; by the voters in the town meeting, in states that have it; and in school districts, if they are managed separately from other local authorities, by the school directors or corresponding officers.

In governments of any grade, there is at least one official whose chief or only duty is to receive and properly care for the money received through taxes. He is most often called the treasurer. In some cases special collectors of taxes receive the money and turn it over to the treasurer.

In the federal government, taxes on imported goods are paid at custom houses to a collector of customs. Most other federal revenues are paid to the collector of internal revenue in the district in which the taxpayer lives.

The time when taxes are paid depends upon the law and custom of the state or community where the tax has to be paid. Some taxes may be paid in installments, with a discount if paid before a certain date.

At this point, it might be well to fill out the table on levying and collecting taxes suggested as a project on page 155. 

Now let us see what some of the most common forms of taxes are. 

1. The most widely used tax in this country is often referred to as the general property tax. This is a tax on practically all kinds of a person's wealth. It may include both real estate — lands and buildings that are fixed in character and cannot be easily moved - and personal property· bonds, tools, mortgages, and the like, which can be readily carried from one place to another. Some state governments make no attempt to tax real estate, and many local governments do not tax personal property. 

To determine the amount of this tax, the property to be taxed must first be assessed. In the case of real estate, this is done by county or other local officials known as assessors or listers who decide how much a particular piece of property is worth. Then in many states the tax is fixed at so many mills on the dollar of the value of the property. If a person's real estate were assessed at $10,000, for example, and the tax rate was 20 mills on the dollar, he would have to pay a $200 tax on that property. Personal property taxes are reckoned in a similar way, though in this case the owners of personal property are expected to make a return telling how much taxable property of that kind they own. Some means of checking up on this statement may be employed by the authorities who collect the tax. 

2. Taxes on income are important sources of revenue for the federal government and for some of the states. Federal income taxes are levied on a graduated basis. State income taxes are usually much lower than the federal income tax.

Each individual or corporation that owes an income tax must make a return. Employers have to make reports of all persons to whom they pay wages or salaries above a certain figure. Governments may exchange information as to their knowledge of the income of persons and corporations, and a taxpayer who tries to cheat is taking a big chance. 

3. Taxes on imported goods we commonly refer to as tariffs, customs, or duties. They may be levied on either the specific or ad valorem prin-

ciple. A specific tax is one that definitely fixes the amount to be paid, as 

3¢ a pound, 10¢ a yard, $5 a ton, and the like. Ad valorem taxes call for a certain percentage of the value of the goods. In one sense, the ad valorem tax is fairer but a little more difficult to determine accurately. Sometimes a tax on a certain article will be both specific and ad valorem. 

4. An excise or internal revenue tax is one that is levied on goods produced within a country. State and national governments both use this kind of 

OP Ewing Galloway ASSESSING PROPERTY 

These men with the big books are setting down the value for taxation of the house and lot which they are just visiting. tax. Manufacturers of tobacco, cigarettes, playing cards, and some other things have had to pay such taxes for a long time. long time. During the World

War and in recent years, many excise taxes have been collected on such commodities as automobiles, liquors, radios, and long-distance telephone calls. Gasoline has been hit hard by both the states and the national government, presumably on the theory that a person who can afford to own a car can afford to pay a tax. In some states, the gasoline tax has gone up as high as seven cents a gallon. Excise or internal revenue taxes are often indirect.

The stamps which have to be placed on deeds and other legal papers represent a form of excise tax. Still another is the so-called sales tax, which levies a small amount on retail purchases. 

5. All the states but Nevada, and the federal government as well, collect inheritance taxes. It is argued that the government is justified in taxing inheritances because they could not have been saved up without the protection of the government, and those who receive them have probably done little or nothing to earn them. Generally the tax on small inheritances is lower than on large ones, and less on inheritances going to near relatives than to those that are otherwise distributed. Recently it has become somewhat common to levy taxes on large gifts so as to prevent people from giving away much of their wealth before they die. 

6. In some states a poll or capitation tax is collected from all voters. 

Since everybody pays the same amount, this tax does not agree with the principle of ability to pay; but seldom is the poll tax high enough to be a serious burden to a person who has a job. 

Some sources of revenue may be in reality taxes, though not called by that name.

Sometimes the revenue from certain taxes is "earmarked" set aside to be used for a particular purpose. So-called licenses and fees are often nothing else than taxes, especially when they bring in more money than it costs to collect them. The amount paid for an automobile license, for example, or in some states the amount paid by chain-store organizations, illustrates this fact. When letter postage was increased from two to three cents on letters going from one post office to another, the added cent was really a new tax.

At this point, if you have not started it before, begin to fill out the suggested table on kinds of taxes mentioned in the form found on page 155. 

Would it be helpful or otherwise if all taxes, federal, state, and local, were collected through one office and then distributed to the various governments that are entitled to receive a share of them? Where would you pay any of the kinds of taxes mentioned in this section if you had to pay them? 

65. Can We Do Better about Taxation? It would be too much to expect that any tax system will please everybody. How, then, can we make the tax system we do have as fair as possible? As a whole, taxes today are very much higher than at other times in our history. 

Federal expenses were multiplied by ten during the twenty years after 1913. State and local governments were also spending very much more at the end of that 20-year period than they were in 1913. It has been figured that, on the average, every earner of an income is paying some kind of taxes to the amount of $300, though of course 

---

there are plenty of individuals who do not hand out that amount of money to all governments put together. 

Let us summarize the principal sources of tax revenue received by the various governments under which we live.

Check over this list with reference to your own state, county, and other local governments. Should any items mentioned in this list be omitted as far as your location is concerned, or should any other significant items be added?

The general property tax has come in for a great deal of criticism. 

Some believe that the tax on personal property can be evaded by dishonest people who fail to report all that they actually own. Real estate owners object loudly to bearing the burden of a large part of local taxes. The main reason for such a policy is the fact that land and buildings are in sight and you can easily prove their ownership. 

Students of tax problems agree that it might be fairer to get more of the needed revenue of local governments from other sources, or perhaps even to tax real estate on the income received from it rather than on

its supposed value. But what happens when you propose to tax something else in its place!

Income taxes are popular with those who do not have to pay them, and come near meeting the requirement of "ability to pay." They have the serious disadvantage that when times are hard and incomes are reduced, the amount received from such a tax is cut down considerably, though at such times the government may need to spend more money than usual. No government, therefore, can afford to depend on an income tax as its only source of revenue. It has also been objected that our present income tax laws discourage private enterprise. If a person is going to have to pay to the state or national government a large proportion of any added income he would gain by enlarging his business, what inducement is there for him to do it? 

Another criticism of our tax policy is that income from bonds issued by federal, state, or local governments has been exempt from taxation. 

Tax-exempt bonds have been one of the chief places of refuge for those who wanted to use their savings so as to escape other kinds of tax. 

Bonds already issued with the understanding that they were not taxable could not honorably be taxed now, but Congress has now voted to make income from future federal bond issues taxable, and it is possible that state and local governments will do the same with their own bonds. Yet some fear that if the income from such bonds is taxed, they will have to bear a higher rate of interest in order to induce people to buy them, and maybe not enough added revenue would be received through taxing them to make up for the greater amount that would have to be paid out in interest. 

Sometimes taxes on corporations have been looked upon as if they were a means of getting a revenue that would hit only the well-to-do. 

It does not follow, however, that a corporation is necessarily big or rich. A heavy tax on a corporation just because it is a corporation may be very unfair to small organizations. Besides, if a corporation's income is taxed heavily, it has less money to distribute to its stockholders in the form of dividends, and stockholders are not all rich people.

Taxes may also be used for other purposes than to get revenue. 

Tariffs on imports have been used for "protective" purposes, as a means of encouraging the production of goods in our own country in preference to using imports from other countries (§ 263). Taxes

on intoxicating liquors have often been employed as a means of restricting either the extent of their use or the number of people who could go into the liquor business. Taxes on chain stores have been intended to make the cost of operating such stores more expensive, and thereby to encourage small dealers outside of the chains.

Discussion over the merits of the sales tax has been lively. Some say it is unfair because wealthy people do not spend in retail purchases anything like as large a proportion of their income as poorer people do. 

On the other hand, the total tax to be paid at any one time may not be intolerable for even a poor family. Whether sound in theory or not, sales taxes have been lifesavers for several state governments. At least they bring money into the treasury promptly. The so-called "nuisance taxes" on little things like telegrams, cosmetics, cameras, and other articles have often been criticized as being more annoying than their revenue value would justify. When a government needs money, however, it is inclined to overlook the item of annoyance if a particular kind of tax does bring in needed revenue. 

A very high tax may not be a revenue-producer, however. If the tax makes something cost very much more than it did before, fewer people will use it, and less revenue be received. The effect of any particular rate when a new tax is levied is often guesswork. 

Still another tax problem relates to so-called double taxation. To many it seems unfair that the same source of revenue should be taxed by national and state government alike, and perhaps by some subdivision of the state. Could there be some understanding among the three grades of government, national, state, and local, so that certain kinds of taxes should be left to the federal government alone, and that the federal government in turn should leave to the states and local governments certain other sources of revenue? Income taxes to the federal government, perhaps? Corporation taxes, other than on income, to the states? Real estate and sales taxes to local governments? Maybe these particular examples would not please everybody, but they suggest the idea.

Should taxes be used to help bring about a different distribution of wealth? Some people believe that this is one of the chief reasons for income and inheritance taxes. Some families do have incomes so large that they are meaningless to the ordinary person, and some of the members of such families have made themselves unpopular by their

selfishness and lack of public interest. On the other hand, some rich people are generous and personally likable. Big gifts to charities, to universities, and for other public purposes come from them. In some respects there is a redistribution of wealth when governments provide free education, public libraries, and pensions of one kind or another. To levy taxes, however, with the chief purpose of bringing the fortunate down to the level of the unfortunate is bad business.¹ 

Do people who inherit property ever do anything to earn it? What policy does your community follow in assessing real estate at full value, or at some smaller percentage? Is such a policy sensible? Can your community do better about taxation? Can your state do better about taxation? 

66. Incurring and Paying Debts. There are two real justifications for public borrowing other than to meet temporary payments before taxes come in. (1) If a serious emergency causes expense, like a great flood or a big war, those of later days who share in the security or other gain resulting from such expense should help share the costs of it. (2) When great improvements are undertaken which can be used for a long time, some of those who are to use the improvements later can help pay the cost of them—a concrete highway which should last for many years, a park which will be enjoyed for an indefinite time, a school building which may be used long after those who put it up are dead. Some people say that it is good for a government to have a debt, on the ground that there is more likelihood of economy than if there are no obligations that have to be met in the future; but there is no sense in incurring a debt simply for the sake of having one. Borrowing money to pay current salaries, or to repair streets that need fixing every year, or to mend the roof on the city hall is ordinarily foolish. Some think that even such things as parks and schoolhouses should be acquired through a pay-as-you-go policy. Then, they say, a government gets only what it can afford and does not make those who come later pay for the comfort or extravagance of those who are living now. 

We cannot escape taxes by borrowing money. Unless a government is deliberately dishonest, the money it borrows will have to be paid back, with interest. Sometimes this interest keeps on long after the 

1 An entirely different principle of taxation from any considered in this unit is the so-called single tax. If you are interested in learning about it now, turn to Section 245.

original cost of expense has been forgotten, and the total outlay may be at least twice as great as if the whole cost had been met at the start. 

Borrowing money is usually done by selling bonds or notes, which are really nothing but promises to pay money later, with interest from time to time. In paying off bonds, two ways have been most common. The government issuing the bond may set aside each year a certain amount of money out of its regular income and call it a sinking fund.

This in turn may be put on interest somewhere. When bonds are to be paid off, the sinking fund should have enough money in it to pay the amount due. Another way to arrange for the payment of borrowed money is to issue the bonds in series, so arranged that a part of them would be paid off every year. Out of the regular income of the government, enough would be used to pay off the principal on the bonds that fell due in any given year and interest on the rest of them. 

The Constitution puts no limit on the amount of debt which the national government may incur, except that Amendment XIV forbade the paying of any debt incurred in aid of rebellion. Congress may decide, however, to establish a maximum figure. The Civil War debt of over $2,800,000,000 seemed large in 1866, but the World War raised our national debt to about $25,000,000,000. During the years following the war, it was steadily shaved down until around 1930, but during the depression years it went up to almost $45,000,000,000, and then the threat of war from abroad forced it still higher. In 1941 

Congress set the limit at $65,000,000,000, but no one is sure it will stop there.

Sometimes a state constitution will specify a limit to which a state government may go in incurring debt. Most state debts are not unreasonable in proportion to their wealth, though some states have gone wild over building new highways, and have put more money in them than might have been wise.

Most cities, townships, school districts, and counties also have debts. State constitutions or laws or city charters often put a limit on the amount of debt of a local government perhaps two, five, seven, or ten per cent of the total valuation of property in that community. Sometimes in state and local governments, propositions for incurring large amounts of debt are submitted to popular vote. This practice should be a check on extravagance, but unfortunately too often voters are willing to borrow money when they would not want to pay increased taxes, or when they hope to get some benefit from the borrowed money themselves.

One fact that makes the debt situation not so bad as it would otherwise seem is that a great part of the money borrowed by a government is lent to it by its own people. When those people are taxed to pay

interest on this debt, it is somewhat like taking money out of one pocket and putting it in another, as far as our citizens are concerned. 

Nevertheless, we should think more carefully than we sometimes do, after we have decided that we want a certain thing, whether we should pay for it when we get it or by installments, with interest, for years to come.

Has the debt of your state and local governments increased in recent years? 

If so, what was the money spent for? If a government constantly adds to its debts year by year, should intelligent citizens ask questions about it? Would you justify a government in borrowing money for any of the following purposes to pay the President's salary? to construct the Panama Canal? to build a storage place for the gold owned by the government? to increase the salaries of state judges? to lend to an embarrassed railroad? to build a crossstate highway? to enlarge your school building? to build an electric light plant? to make up a deficit in last year's accounts? If a referendum vote is taken on a proposition to borrow money, should the right to vote on the proposition be limited to property owners? 

67. Some Current Financial Problems. - Both state and local governments have dumped upon the federal government, or at least been willing that the federal government should accept, burdens which once no one would have thought of asking Uncle Sam to take over. There seems to be a notion that somehow the federal government can raise money from somewhere when states and local governments cannot. But Uncle Sam has to get the wherewithal to do what he does from the same people who could get much of this work done through states and local governments if they cared to pay the necessary taxes to them. The chief difference when the federal government assumes those burdens is that the wealthier states can be forced to make contributions to the federal Treasury, which will then pass them over to the poorer states. 

Is it right that the federal government should accept responsibility for dealing with problems which could be handled through the states? How long can a government keep on spending money without getting into trouble? 

With the federal government looking after as many things as it does, is there anything left for states to spend money on? Oh yes, plenty.

Handling local finances may be at the same time simpler and more difficult than those that operate on a larger scale. Because often the great bulk of receipts for a local government comes from one source, real estate, the amount of income can be estimated fairly definitely. But suppose your community has been infested with the kind of cheap politician who keeps himself in office by getting unnecessary jobs created or salaries paid to persons whose chief service is getting out the vote on election day! For the same reason as in the case of state governments, much more is demanded of local governments today for good streets, good schools, parks and libraries, and maybe even such things as "free" band concerts, than once one could have imagined. United States.

68. Getting Our Money's Worth. - How should a good citizen feel about taxes? Certainly it is his right to expect the money he pays in taxes to be spent honestly. He may properly expect public officials to give an account of themselves and make reports which tell the truth in such a way that any ordinarily intelligent person can understand them.

But a community with low taxes does not necessarily have good government. Perhaps such a community has neglected its schools. 

Perhaps its streets are not in decent repair. A community, like an individual, may display false economy in not doing the things that would benefit all concerned. 

The good citizen has a right to expect that other people will get no special favors or concessions that would not be given him under the

Rich or prominent people, leaders of a union, club, or lodge, sometimes expect favors from a public official which simply could not be granted to all citizens. The good citizen has a right also to expect that his public servants will work hard and faithfully in the interests of all. In such cases a good citizen will pay his fair share of taxes willingly.

When new expenses of government are proposed, one is not necessarily a "reactionary" or tightwad if he asks questions about the

wisdom of them. Is this proposition for the benefit of the community as a whole, or of just a small portion of it? If it is of value to the community, how much will it cost, and will it bring returns equal to the outlay involved? He must not, however, think solely of whether he himself is better off in dollars and cents. Paved streets, street lights, up-to-date schools, public libraries, pure water, police and fire protection, cost money. Every citizen benefits by these services, in many cases directly, and usually gets them for a much lower price than if he had to provide them all himself. The welfare of the community in the long run brings well-being to all good citizens.

VII  

People do not all think just alike, but often there is a strong balance of opinion on one side or the other of some topic of interest. The majority may be right or may be wrong at any given time, but whatever it is, a democratic government must be controlled by it. One of our most important duties as good citizens is to understand the ways by which individuals and groups try to influence public opinion, and to know how to aid in making that opinion sensible and fair. Our own personal opinions may help to make public opinion correct, or may, perhaps unconsciously, be swayed by it.

Some Questions: 

1. What is public opinion and how is it expressed? 

2. How are personal opinions and public opinion formed? 

3. What agencies are most common or effective in creating or directing public opinion? 

4. How do leaders and groups influence public opinion? 

5. What is the proper relation between public opinion and the government? 

6. How may we help to prevent wrong or ignorant public opinion? 

7. How may we make intelligent public opinion effective? 

69. What Is Public Opinion?-One definition is this: public opinion is the attitude of that part of the people that holds definite views on a given subject. Public opinion is one of those intangible things that are formed in ways we cannot always recognize, for the opinions most loudly expressed are not always the opinions of the majority of the people.

Public opinion is very rarely unanimous. There are people who would amend even the Ten Commandments. Occasionally we find some one who always seems to want to take the opposite side from what anybody else desires. And sometimes, of course, only a few may be wise enough to get a correct understanding of a certain subject. 

On many matters public opinion is not very active. What is the best way to learn the alphabet? What kind of flowers are most satisfactory to grow in a city back yard? How large should a paper dollar 174

be? "Nichevo," millions of people might say, if they knew Russian. 

But on questions that vitally concern the welfare or interests of a considerable number of people, public opinion may take very definite form. 

Make a list of five topics mentioned in today's newspaper that you think unlikely to arouse any strong public opinion one way or the other; five about which there may be strong feeling, but somewhat evenly divided; five about which there can be little doubt as to the weight of public opinion. Does public opinion on a particular subject remain the same indefinitely? 

If we speak of a certain policy as "the will of the people," who are the people and how is this will brought into being? What do we really mean by "the consent of the governed"? Of course, all the governed do not deliberately agree to be governed in a certain way, nor do all the people necessarily approve what at any given time may seem to be the will of the majority. 

But in a democracy we have to accept majority rule that the will of the larger number, other things being equal, ought to prevail. If we do not like what is done, we are free to try to change the opinions of enough people so that our ideals will become the opinions of the majority. Our "consent" may be given silently as well as by voice or action. If, in a particular community, vice and dishonest politics are common, either the majority of the people want that kind of thing to prevail, or do not care enough about it to change conditions. 

Public opinion may express itself by not doing something as well as by taking positive action.

It has been said that "the voice of the people is the voice of God" "Vox populi, vox Dei." No doubt God uses men to carry out His will, but one hates to think that everything human beings have done is divinely ordained. When two parties or nations contend for exactly opposite principles, both cannot be right. No, public opinion may be mistaken and may be foolish, and may lead to acts which good citizens will, later at least, deeply regret. All this may suggest to us that we ought to give some attention to the way public opinion is formed. 

Is there anything in your community which you believe to be tolerated rather than desired by the majority of the people? If so, what? You recall the remark so often credited to Lincoln, "You can fool all of the people some of the time, and some of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time." Give your reasons for agreeing or disagreeing with this quotation or any part of it.

70. How Public Opinion Expresses Itself. - Opinion does not always find utterance in words, but the customs of a people may speak very clearly. Are stores closed on Sunday? If they are, it is probably because most of the people in a community use that day for worship or recreation, or at least want it to be different from the other days of the week. If school buildings are unattractive and teachers 1880. 1890 1900 1910 22 1920 

Keystone View Company WHAT THEY WORE IN THE PAST 

These dresses are said to represent what brides wore at the dates indicated. Can you see any reason for these changes in fashion? are poorly paid, the majority of the people do not care whether their children learn any more than the parents learned when they were in school.

Customs that are long-standing and relate to principles of conduct rather than mere details are often called mores (mō-rēz). Are elderly people, for example, turned out to starve or sent to the poorhouse, or are they treated with care and consideration? In ancient Greece a girl's parents picked her husband for her, and she had little or nothing to say about who he should be. How is it today? 

Short-lived practices about dress or manners, that we refer to as fashions, also show what public sentiment demands or is willing to

tolerate. The ancient Greeks made comparatively little difference in the style of dress of men and women. How is it today? 

Public opinion may also be seen in what a community does not tolerate. Such things we sometimes refer to as taboos. "Woman's place is in the home," most people used to say, including women themselves; so, for a long time in this country women were never elected to public office or even allowed to vote. What is the harm in putting things into your mouth with a knife? None, except that it is socially taboo.

In the realm of ideas rather than of practices, we set up standards and ideals. By a standard we mean a basis of judgment by which thought or conduct may be rated. A person whose standards are high wants to do things in the best way they can be done, and constantly improve himself and the conditions in which he lives. If his standards are low, he has little desire to live well, and probably does not care very much about what other people think or say concerning him. 

Ideals may also be expressions of public opinion. They represent what we would like to become, to know, or to have. An individual's ideals may be distinctly different from those of the group within which he has to live and work. "What do you want to be?" is a question that time after time comes to both individuals and communities. 

Sometimes public opinion shows itself when community leaders get together and pass resolutions saying that they want or do not want something, or that they approve or disapprove some official's actions. Sometimes newspapers make themselves mouthpieces of public opinion. Voting is another way to express it. Sometimes it is concerned chiefly with putting people into office, but often we vote for a candidate not because he is John Smith rather than Bill Brown, but because we like Smith's principles and views better than we do Brown's.

Make a list of five things that you do every day and decide how many of them should be called customs, mores, fashions, standards, or ideals. Make a list of taboos that you recognize in the life of your community. Why do people feel as they do about them? 

71. How Public Opinion Is Formed. Since society is made up of individuals who live and often act together, public, or social, opinion is made up of individual opinions that look in one direction. It gains strength because it has the weight of the group behind it. Group

feeling, or mass feeling, may be of slow growth, or it may arise suddenly. Sudden mass action hardly deserves to be called public opinion. It is rather a matter of doing than of thinking. It is the result of prejudice, misunderstanding, fear, or some other emotion. We should be well informed as to the ways by which real public opinion may be brought into existence. 

Acme Photo TELLING IT TO THE PUBLIC 

In many of our cities speakers make a regular practice of taking a stand in some public place at regular times and talking on a topic in which they are interested. 

There appear to be two audiences in this picture.

Many a widespread belief represented in the first place the opinions or hopes of only a few. 

Recall how men like William

Lloyd Garrison were treated hardly more than a hundred years ago in this country. All the great religious teachers of the world had only a few followers at the beginning. To transform the opinion of the few into the opinion of the many, the few must be absolutely sincere in their conviction or be able to make people think they are. As more and more accept that opinion, it gains strength as a snowball gains in size when you roll it along in the soft winter snow.

There are at least three ways by which believers in some doctrine or policy may enlarge their circle of influence. (1) Some are able to force others to accept their own views, because they have physical, political, or social power. (2) Sometimes people's emotions can be played upon. A skillful agitator may appeal to fear, hate, the hope of enjoyment, or the desire for better times. People who are swayed by such emotions can easily become fanatical and lose all regard for common sense or the interests of others. (3) The most satisfactory way to influence others' opinions is, of course, to convince them that one's ideas are correct. If we are anxious for long-time

achievements or for successes which we shall not have to regret, that is the way to go about it. 

That is not to say it is wrong to consider one's own interests, but sometimes the choice may be between the benefit of a few and the good of many. One of the hardest things is to get people in groups to look beyond their own immediate advantage and appreciate what is really "the greatest good for the greatest number." Permanent benefit is far more important than short-lived immediate gain. 

If one wishes to arouse public opinion on some topic in which he is interested, he may first take advantage of every opportunity to talk to others about it though he must be careful not to make himself a bore. Then he may try to get some publicity for himself or his views in the newspapers or over the radio. If his proposition has a distinct moral or ethical basis, he may interest such agencies as the church and the school. One must not expect to put over a new idea in a little while. Sometimes a victory in the field of ideas is more lasting if it is not gained too suddenly or without a struggle. Opposition to a new idea, if presented fairly and openly, may give the advocates of the idea the best possible opportunity to put up the arguments for their side of the case effectively. 

If you wanted to get a new athletic field for your school, what steps might you take in support of the proposition? Is the sentiment of your class or community inactive or incorrect concerning important topics of the day? 

If so, what can be done about it? 

72. How We Form Our Own Opinions. If public opinion is formed by the accumulation of a large number of individual opinions, we need to find out how we get our individual opinions. Just for example, why do you attend one church rather than another? Why do you call yourself a Republican, a Democrat, a Socialist, or something else? Isn't the chance better than two to one that you do so because other members of your family have done so, perhaps for many years? Maybe your own associations in religion or politics would be the same if you had made a wide and careful study of the differences in belief of churches and parties - but then again, maybe 

not.

All kinds of sources may furnish the foundation for one's opinions. 

Some things are so definitely established as true that there should be no doubt about them. These we may call facts. George Washington

was President. Pennsylvania is east of Ohio. One's belief or opinion is his attitude toward accepting or rejecting some idea or principle. 

We believe that our government should or should not build a bigger navy than it now has. It is our opinion that John Smith would or would not be a good mayor. A theory is an explanation of the probable way in which things take place. It may help us to explain some situation, and if it can be definitely proved to be true by evidence, it will come to be accepted as a fact. 

Other influences on individual opinions may also be strong and yet have little sound support. We may be influenced by a tradition that is, a belief or story handed down from the past that is commonly accepted, though without substantial proof of its truth. We may be influenced, too, by prejudice - we have a feeling in advance that causes us to like or dislike some person or thing. Bias may make us act in about the same way, although this less often relates to persons than to attitudes. We may feel so strongly for or against labor unions that we are for or against anything that a union supports or disapproves.

Somewhat similar to prejudice and bias is the condition that we often refer to as a stereotype. That is a fixed idea with reference to persons or things. Bret Harte wrote a poem in which he represented someone as saying, "The heathen Chinee is peculiar." One who gets that idea may find it hard to realize that there are Chinese men and women as cultured and likable as those of any race or color. It is said that some young people in the South believed until they grew up that "damyankees" was a proper name for all Northerners, and that some northern young people have read so much about southern share-croppers that they think that all Southerners live in dirty shacks. 

How should one reach a conclusion on a matter about which there are differences of opinion? First, he can find out what all who know about the subject admit to be true. Next, he should learn the reasons given for the opinions held by those who disagree about certain aspects of the matter. He may also inquire about the general reputation for fairness and common sense of those who hold one view or the other. 

How many people do you think are willing to go even to this limited amount of trouble? But is it unreasonable?

Why does the fact that in an election campaign more than one question of importance may be discussed make one's individual decision harder than it

might otherwise be? Mention some subject on which you have an opinion but are not conscious of having reached it by any logical process. Would it be possible for you to change your mind on that point? If so, who or what might bring about the change?

What seems to be public opinion may influence the opinions of an individual. A good many of us, perhaps unconsciously, like to be on the popular side of a question or to "get on the band wagon." "One million Americans can't be wrong," you may have heard. Well, can't they? In the presidential election of 1940 either the twentyseven million who supported Roosevelt or the twenty-two million who voted for Willkie made a wrong choice, unless that was one of the rare occasions in which one candidate was just exactly as good as the other. Besides, there is no denying that sometimes the majority is on the wrong side. Anyway, the good citizen cares more for what is right than for the number of people who agree with him. 

What should a person do when asked to sign a petition favoring or opposing some proposition? How much weight do you think a Congressman or member of a legislature should give to telegrams and letters sent to him at a time when some proposition is undergoing a rather lively discussion? 

73. Agencies that Create or Direct Opinion. At least five kinds of agencies certainly have a considerable effect upon the thinking of millions of people — not to mention such influences as family relations, clubs and lodges to which one belongs, contacts in business or among workers in a factory, and personal friendliness or acquaintance. (1) Most extensive and most frequent are newspapers and magazines. They may influence us by their news stories or their editorials. 

Ideally, news is news and should be told just as it happened, but sometimes two ways of telling the same story may create exactly the opposite impression. On the editorial page or anywhere else, when the opinions of the editor or publisher are plainly marked as opinions, it is his privilege to say what he thinks. But we do need to be on our guard against biased interpretations of the news. The owners of "chain" newspapers usually insist that on subjects of wide general interest, all the newspapers in the chain shall take the same attitude. 

Sometimes exactly the same editorial may be printed in all of them. 

Do you think most newspapers care more to create public opinion or to find out what the public already thinks and then follow it? Do you know of any case where newspaper publishers seemed to have been influenced by the

possibility of getting or losing advertising? What do you think of a newspaper which accepts money for political advertisements from parties or individuals with whose ideas it does not agree? Give an example of the way a certain event, such as the resumption of daylight saving in the latter part of April, could be written up so as to convey either a favorable or an unfavorable impression. (2) Another important means of influence upon public opinion is found through books, pamphlets, and similar publications. Agencies interested in a certain cause sometimes circulate pamphlets to persons named on a mailing list that they have compiled, but conceal their real purpose under some intellectual-sounding name. Sometimes totally opposite impressions will be given in two different books on the same subject. There are enough books and pamphlets written by people of thorough scholarship and good intentions to make it unnecessary for one to spend time on crude or biased publications. "Don't believe everything you see in print" is often good advice. 

Consider the standing, the past record, and the probability of a writer's having an axe to grind," before you decide whether to accept at face value everything he writes. 66 Make a list of five books published within the last year that seemed to have some definite objective in influencing public opinion. As between newspapers and books, which do you think has the greater influence on public sentiment? Why? (3) Moving pictures and stage plays reach millions of people every month. Much of their influence is unconscious, but, because we both see and hear at the same time, a double impression is made upon us when we attend such performances. Some plays and pictures are deliberately planned to affect public opinion. In countries where the government uses all kinds of means to stir up favorable opinion toward itself, moving pictures are one of the instruments employed. 

What moving pictures have you seen that changed your opinion in regard to some person or country or proposition? What theatrical performances or moving pictures have you seen that seem to have a definite tendency toward encouraging good conduct and high ideals or the opposite? Do you think such effect, in any case, was incidental or intended? (4) The radio is another vital force for creating and directing public opinion. Perplexing questions have arisen in regard to it. Is freedom of speech to be assured so completely as to permit any kind of

statement and any kind of language whatever? The Federal Communications Commission in more than one instance has denied the privilege of the air to some person or organization who, in its opinion, violated the principles of good judgment and decency. The way governments like those of Soviet Russia, Germany, and Italy try to 40 

11 12 7 6 

Courtesy Columbia Broadcasting System, Incorporated NEWS COMMENTATORS ON THE RADIO 

One of the newest means of influencing public opinion is the radio. What we might call a new profession has started, which includes people who make it their business to report the news and to discuss the meaning of events. These speakers are Bob Trout and Elmer Davis. maintain absolute control of the use of the radio in their own countries is sufficient proof as to what might be done by other governments that were so disposed.

One disadvantage or advantage of the radio, depending on one's point of view, is that one speaker may make an impression on listeners that is hard to counteract if no opponent who debates with him follows him closely. It would be hard to say whether the radio has made it easier or more difficult for the average person to come to a fair decision on questions about which there is a difference of opinion.

Is it an advantage to a candidate for office to be able to speak effectively over the radio? Why? Do you think public officials such as a president, governor, or mayor should regularly make use of the radio to discuss governmental problems? (5) The church (meaning, of course, religious bodies of all kinds) surely is intended to influence people's conduct and ideals for the better. It fails in its duty if it does not stand firmly for right principles. To speak boldly against dishonesty in public life or private business is doubtless fully the privilege of a preacher in the pulpit. 

But what is the effect when he undertakes to influence people's opinions on matters that are not plainly of a moral or religious character, especially if he constantly takes one side in social or economic controversies? Some preachers have gained thousands of devoted listeners through their activities over the radio, and perhaps have made bitter enemies at the same time.

Make a list of five preachers, not all of the same denomination, who are frequently mentioned in the newspapers. How have they gained their prominence? Should the religious affiliation of candidates for office make any difference with one's attitude toward them? 

74. The School as a Factor in Public Opinion. One important influence on public opinion is the school. In using the word here we mean to include all kinds of educational organizations. Education ought to help one to think more clearly, to form more intelligent opinions, to become more valuable to his community. But does the school have the right or duty to try to induce its pupils to take one side rather than the other of disputed questions? 

Trying to teach certain definite views about a certain topic is sometimes referred to as indoctrination. We could hardly blame a private school founded by a religious organization for trying to "indoctrinate" its pupils with the belief that the particular teachings of that church are correct. But what about public schools, maintained by taxes on almost everybody? Surely it is not wrong for a public school in the 

United States to teach that democracy is the principle on which we want our government to rest. 

But should we teach that one political party is better than another, or that the activities of our business men are either wicked or impeccable? 

Every little while we hear some question about academic freedom. 

Most of us would agree that it is the right of an instructor or pupil to

think freely and to discuss frankly topics that pertain to the work of a class. If corporations are the subject for discussion, for instance, academic freedom would call for free consideration of the advantages and disadvantages, the achievements and the mistakes of corporations. 

But should the instructor present to his pupils only the side of a disputed question which he believes in himself? Some have even said it is the duty of the school to plan for a new social order, and teach its pupils to work for the substitution of this new social order in place of what we have now. Would it not be fairer to give pupils the chance to learn the most important facts bearing on current problems, to understand the different points of view concerning them, and then encourage pupils to use their own brains in deciding what their own attitude should be?

Many believe that our political, social, and economic troubles will be much reduced if we can only get people to come together and talk things over, giving everyone a chance to meet face to face those who agree or disagree with him. They have great confidence in open forum discussion, in which all who will speak courteously may express their opinions and ask for light on points which seem to them to need explanation. Commissioner of Education John W. Studebaker has referred to this method of forum discussion as "the American way." 

Have any of your teachers ever tried to make you accept a certain point of view or theory to which you had an honest objection? Is there any possibility that you were as stubborn in not wanting to be convinced as they were in trying to convince you? If the public forum idea has been tried in your community, how did it seem to work? 

75. How Pressure Groups Work. We often use the term pres sure group to refer to an organization or group of people who have united for the purpose of trying to get the things done that they wish. 

Often they exert their "pressure" upon members of a lawmaking body to get a law passed which they want or prevent the passage of one they do not favor. Sometimes an organization not formed for that purpose feels an urge to do it in the case of some particular matter. 

Church assemblies, the American Legion, teachers' organizations, associations to encourage or prohibit the use of intoxicating liquor, not to mention labor unions and associations of employers, have all done so. They may simply use honest argument in behalf of the cause they believe in, but some have been known to offer money to

legislators to vote a certain way, or try to defeat officials who will not take orders from them.

One method used by pressure groups is lobbying. The lobby in a public building is a place where people can meet and talk with public officials, but there are also plenty of other places and ways of getting at them. In some states legislatures have required that any persons who come to a state capital with the purpose of trying to influence legislation should register with a certain state agency or office. Some people even make a living as lobbyists. They get a salary from organizations which they represent, and sometimes the amount of that salary is determined by the success or failure of the lobbyist in getting what he wants.

Should lobbyists and pressure groups be wiped out as if they were vermin? Some of them are at best nuisances, and some are a positive menace to good government; but, on the other hand, some may be interested in the passage of good measures. Sometimes a bill may be introduced about which a legislator happens to know little or nothing. He may be open to honest argument, and who can provide that argument better than those who know the facts? 

Sometimes a regular snowstorm of letters and telegrams descends upon lawmakers whose votes are going to be cast on some matter in the near future. This often means that the members of a pressure group have been told by their leaders to send messages all at the same time so that legislators may think there is a tremendous outpouring of public opinion in favor of or against a particular proposition. It may also mean that some demagogue has appealed over the radio to his unthinking listeners to undertake this kind of mass action. Lawmakers can usually tell whether letters and telegrams come from people who are sincerely concerned about a question. 

The good citizen will be careful not to be dragged into this kind of thing by a pressure group which cares more for its own selfish gain than for the common good.

If you were asked to sign a petition to be sent to a city council, what might you reasonably do before signing it? What examples of the activities of pressure groups have you noticed in your newspaper reading in recent months? What do you think you would do if, as a lawmaker, you were told that a certain organization would try to defeat you for reelection if you didn't vote the way its members wanted you to?

76. The Place of Leaders in Forming Public Opinion. 

Of course we must have leaders. Some people think that one of the weaknesses in democracies is that they pay too little attention to developing the right kind of leaders and to keeping them in office when their abilities become known. "All men are created equal," we quote, though we know perfectly that all men are not equal except in their right to equal treatment before the law and equal opportunity to make the most of whatever talents they have. It would be a terribly monotonous world if all people were alike in talents and interests. 

The crude but common-sense proverb, “What is everybody's business is nobody's business," tells one of the chief reasons why we must have leaders. Someone must be responsible for directing the activities of others. There must be many more privates than generals in an army.

A mass of people may be moved by a worthy impulse, but it must have leaders to propose the next step to take and suggest how fast to move. 

Not everyone has leadership qualities, though some do not discover they can lead until some emergency has forced them to do so. 

A leader must have the faculty of making other people believe in him. 

A wise leader must have vision and judgment, and must understand the best way to work toward his goal. He must be able to restrain as well as to arouse his followers, for there are times when a mob would rush madly into something that would do irreparable damage. 

A leader also must have in a high degree determination and perseverance. He cannot afford to be easily discouraged, for a discouraged leader is not likely to have followers very long. 

At times, wise leaders will move cautiously, for even a well-meaning leader may make a mistake. Those with the best motives do not always know just the best way to attain their objectives. Leaders must have followers, but that leader is most desirable who can show his followers why he wants to go a certain way. 

There is a big difference between a leader and a demagogue. The leader seeks to bring about better things for the group which he leads. 

The demagogue tries to get people to do something which will advance his own interests, though incidentally he may sometimes help to accomplish some good end. A dictator has no place for rivals or even for followers who will not obey him implicitly. He may call himself Der Fuehrer or Il Duce, but he commands rather than leads.

He seldom dares to submit to the risk of an election, except when the election machinery is all set up so that only one result can occur. 

Why do dictators get power? Usually there is some general feeling of grievance among a considerable mass of people, which the dictator promises to relieve. He may arouse a feeling of hatred against some class or group who then become the "goats" for anything that goes wrong. He builds up a collection of followers who have no scruples about doing anything that will make other people afraid of them. If

When war comes, most countries see to it that all mail going into or coming from their own borders is inspected by government agents. he does achieve some well-publicized success, doubters will think that perhaps he has the answer after all. Before long anyone who dares question his authority is treated as if he were a traitor. "It can't happen here," wrote Sinclair Lewis, and then proceeded to tell a story that suggested that it might happen here after all. In any country, large or small, there are numbers of people who never think deeply and who are moved solely by emotion or self-interest. 

Pick out five men in the history of our own country who have been outstanding as leaders not necessarily all in politics. What, in each case, either gave them their opportunity or enabled them to succeed? Give examples from this or other countries of good causes that failed for lack of leaders. What qualities make for leadership in school life?

77. Public Opinion and the Government. A government may wish to create public opinion favorable to itself. To do that, its officials may tell the public how good it is and how valuable its policies are. Millions of pages of printed matter have been printed by our federal government to advertise its activities. Since the radio became a popular institution, Presidents, Cabinet officers, and 

Congressmen have been ready to use the air to publicize their own views or condemn those of their opponents. There is nothing wrong in this, providing the speaker honestly believes what he says, unless he spends public money to promote support of his own private views. 

Some governments attempt to control public opinion by refusing the use of the mails, the newspapers, the schools, or the air to those who disagree with the government's policies. 

If people can hear only good about a person or policy, even though they do not see the good themselves, there is not much else they can believe. So dictators drum into the ears of their subjects over the radio the glories of their accomplishments and the villainy of their opponents. Letters are opened and unpleasant portions are cut out or the letters destroyed. Newspapers, magazines, and books have pages torn out or "blacked" out, or are burned, if they contain anything unpleasant to the government. This kind of censorship is abhorrent to our way of thinking. 

Reasonable censorship has its justification, however. Some of our

Occasionally such censorship brings publicity to an immoral show or book which may make some people more anxious to see or read it. But surely a community has the right to protect its people from acts or words on the stage, or screen, or through the radio or the press which would have a vicious effect upon people of weak minds or morals. 

One way by which our governments, both state and national, may try to prevent improper influence upon individuals is the requirement that printed material in a newspaper or magazine which is paid for by a political party or candidate shall be marked in such a way as to make it clear that it is advertising and not news. 

Too many people are ready to believe everything they read, especially in a newspaper which comes to them regularly. Political committees are now required to make reports of the amount of money they receive for campaign funds, and to publish the names of all those who contribute more than a limited sum. To help protect honest newspaper publishers and editors, it is required that the names of owners and stockholders and others interested in certain publications shall be printed from time to time so that readers may know, if they care to go to the trouble, what interests are back of a certain publication.
