THE UNITED STATES EMBASSY IN OTTAWA 

Our own government has now adopted the policy of maintaining its own establishments for permanent headquarters in the leading capitals where we are represented. tiary, or minister resident. We send "ambassadors" to any country that sends "ambassadors" to us. Our ambassadors and ministers are the official representatives of our government in the presence of another government. There is also a considerable array of consuls. 

A consul is a representative of his government who is stationed in a city or district in another country. His chief duties are to look out for the welfare of citizens of his country when they are in the neighborhood where he is located, to promote the commercial interests of the country

which sends him, and to get any information or do anything which might be of benefit to his country or its citizens. Sometimes a person with the title of consul-general is stationed at the capital city of an important country, and such an official attains almost to the status of an ambassador or minister. By way of contrast, the persons employed as consuls are classified as in the consular service, whereas those engaged as ambassadors or ministers are considered in the diplomatic service.

For a long time positions in the foreign service, whether diplomatic or consular, were simply political jobs filled at the whim of the President who happened to be in office with persons who belonged to his party. Within the last few decades, however, a notable change has taken place, so that now positions in the foreign service may be sought by people who want to make it a life career. Civil service examinations must be taken to qualify for many positions, and the whole foreign service does not change after every new President. Ambassadors who happen to be in office still offer their resignations when there is a change of Presidents, which may or may not be accepted. 

But even in such positions there are frequent promotions or transfers from one city or country to another in order to recognize specially valuable service or make some other desirable change. 

There are several ways in which nations may settle differences of opinion. The simplest is by direct negotiation, when representatives of the nations concerned get together and talk things over. 

If they cannot agree, they may decide on arbitration. Then a representative from one or more other countries will be called in and asked to help settle the question. When there is a World Court, a dispute can be referred directly to it. Formal agreements between nations usually take the form of a treaty. Sometimes such an agreement is referred to as a convention or a protocol, especially if it is preliminary to something else or is an agreement that may or may not be permanent, depending on future developments.

Our Constitution requires that treaties shall be made by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. This consent has to be given by a two-thirds vote. In practice, treaties are seldom made by the President himself, and though President Wilson was quite within his rights when he went to Paris to make the treaty following the World War, he aroused considerable opposition by doing

SO. 

Treaties are sometimes made by a Secretary of State, sometimes by an ambassador, and sometimes by a person specially appointed for the purpose.

This requirement of ratification by our Senate makes treaty-making in this country somewhat more difficult than in most other countries. 

Monarchs or their ministers in foreign governments have often made treaties without any reference to their parliaments. Even when they are so referred, nowhere is a two-thirds vote required. Whether our "two-thirds" arrangement is more likely to cause the failure of good treaties or the adoption of fewer but better ones is a matter of opinion. 

The real importance of treaties depends upon the extent to which they are observed. At present the only compulsion to carry out a treaty is the honor and good faith of the nations that make it. There is not much use in making treaties if they can be set aside by unilateral action - that is, by either party to the treaty at its own will. Treaties need not be everlasting, however. They may be put in such a form as to hold good for a certain number of years with the understanding that at the end of that time they may be disavowed by one or more of the makers. 

Do nations think better of one another when they know each other or when they do not? Inherited misunderstandings and prejudices are hard to get rid of. Differences in language, in money standards, in likes and dislikes about articles of trade sometimes create friction

97. Measures for National Defense. 

that "National defense" is what they all say when nations prepare themselves so that they can take part in a war, but it is not always "hokum." Too often strong, well-armed nations have picked on weaker ones. 

What happened to Ethiopia, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Denmark, Norway, and the rest, which thought they would be safe if they only minded their own business? As long as things like this do occur, just so long will a prudent nation feel the necessity of doing what it can to protect itself. Bryan used to say that if our nation were invaded by a foreign foe, "a million men would spring to arms overnight." But where would they get the arms, and how would they know what to do with them, if there had been no preliminary preparation or training? Armies and navies may also have use in time of peace. When internal disorders or calamities occur, the army may step in and by the use of force make crime unattractive. When few countries had well-organized navies, piracy was profitable and sometimes popular. 

66 

Nice examples in arithmetic can be worked out by asking how many schools or city halls at so many dollars apiece could have been constructed with the money spent during the World War, though the fact is plain that that amount of money would not have been spent on schools or city halls if there had been no war. Benjamin Franklin is quoted as saying that there never was a good war nor a bad peace, yet he himself had considerable to do with promoting one war, and out of that war the United States gained its independence. And was there no gain in the long struggle that was required to upset the tyrant Napoleon in the early years of the nineteenth century? 

Preparing for war or against war is an expensive business. There have been times in our history when from 85 to 90 per cent of the expenses of government were the result of the cost of previous wars or of preparation for defense needed in future wars. Our own country is in a position where it needs a larger navy than most other countries.

No other except the far-flung British Empire has as much coast line as the United States facing on waters in which a navy could travel. 

And who could carry on an honest-to-goodness defense or offense today without an air force?

The right to maintain an army and navy is included in the list of powers given by the Constitution to Congress. Though the President is commander-in-chief of the army and navy, there can be no army and navy for him to command unless Congress has authorized them, and no officially recognized war unless Congress has declared one. 

Except in such great emergencies as the Civil War and the World War, our armies have been extremely small in comparison with those of other countries. Only Great Britain, whose situation is somewhat like our own, has contented itself among the great nations with an army anywhere nearly as small as our own in peace times. In 1939 our army numbered approximately 175,000 officers and men. When a possible danger of war arises, the first step is usually to call into service the national guard of the various states, for the states maintain such a force to protect their people and property. Next would come the enlargement of the regular forces through additional volunteers, and finally, if a great struggle were obviously possible, the drafting of men for service.

The draft was used with only partial success during the Civil War, but on a far-reaching scale in the World War. In 1940, when it seemed as if the flames of war in Europe might spread to our own. hemisphere, we did not wait for war to begin. It seemed fairer to spread the responsibilities of military service on an equal basis to all classes than to depend upon those who were most patriotic or reckless to do the fighting for the rest. In the World War about four million men altogether were called upon through such measures. The Selective Service and Training Act of 1940 required all men within the ages of 21 to 35 to register. Then the effort was made to determine in what capacity each individual could do the greatest good. Those who had persons depending on them for their living or whose services would be of greater use in some other place than in a training camp were put in a "deferred" classification, to be called later if actually needed for military service.

Just as methods of fighting for armies change from time to time, so do other features of warfare. No large navy today would under-

take to get along without a considerable share of many types of fighting machines such as dreadnaughts, cruisers, destroyers, submarines, airplane carriers, and the rest. And much fighting in future wars, as in the present, will be in the air. Anti-aircraft guns, mines, gas masks, and air-raid shelters are means of defense which nations need to use today against the devastating brutality of aggressors. 

Draw up a statement of the types and extent of defensive measures that the United States should maintain permanently.

In October, 1940, for the first time in our history, young men in peace time were asked to register for a period of military training and service. Most of them did it goodnaturedly. 

98. When War Comes. - It has been said that no nation in the world today wants war. But war still occurs because some nations have leaders who, if they cannot get what they want without war, will fight rather than not get it; and other nations that do not want war will fight to defend their lives, property, and liberty. Causes of war might be grouped in four classes: (1) grievances and hatreds inherited from the past; (2) domestic problems or conditions that have international effects; (3) ambitions for conquest or mastery; (4) conflicting theories or ideals of government. 

Some long-standing causes of disagreement have now been outdated, such as the hostility between Great Britain and Russia which led to

at least one war, the Crimean, and the constant fear of others. Racial ill will has been responsible for many years of restlessness and uncertainty among the Balkan countries. The German taking of French territory in 1871 produced a desire for "revanche" which could not forget the past. Hitler defended his own policies by referring to what he called the "diktat" at Versailles in 1919. OLD-TIME IMPLEMENTS OF WAR 

How do you think these would match up against modern military equipment?

Among the domestic policies that have international bearings we may think of high tariffs and trade restrictions. They may not actually have caused war, but they have not encouraged mutual friendliness. Civil war or revolution may also arouse sympathies of outside people for one side or the other, and any civil war interferes with a country's outside trade.

A few years ago it was popular to blame munition makers for stirring up wars and being responsible for most of the unpleasantness between nations. Their agents did try to break up peace conferences and to discredit movements toward harmony and good will among nations. 

But Hitler's rearming of Germany in six years proves that it would be no remedy at all to transfer the making of war materials to governments.

The ambition of nations for expansion outside their own borders has frequently led to trouble. Suppose a neighboring country can produce much wheat, oil, or cattle, and some stronger power would like to make use of those products. True statesmanship would suggest cultivating the good will of that country and encouraging honest trade with it; but since that policy might take a little longer time than the shortsighted politician would like, he and those army or navy men who would rather fight than eat may combine and bring about war with all its unpleasant consequences. Japanese leaders acted that way, first toward China and then toward us. 

The possession of colonies is another sore point with some people. 

There used to be a general belief that colonies were a source of profit to the home country. Today we are not so sure about it. The 

United States has not found the Philippines tremendously profitable. 

Great Britain holds on to India not so much because India brings great profit to Great Britain as for fear of what would happen if she let it go. So when Germany lamented loudly that it was ill treated in having its colonies taken away at the close of the World War, we may be pardoned for wondering whether it was just an excuse for "acting up" about other matters. 

To what extent do you think Great Britain is benefited by having its extended colonial possessions? Why does the submission of one country to a tyrant make it easier for the tyrant to gain more power? What were the causes of the wars in which the United States has participated? How do you regard our record in that respect, on the whole? 

Absolute monarchies or dictatorships are far more likely to be troublemakers than democracies. The dictator must be constantly seeming to accomplish something. If he doesn't, he will lose popularity, and people will ask what they are getting in exchange for tightened belts and the loss of liberty. His war-making methods require prolonged and careful planning with an unscrupulous unity of purpose. 

No democracy could keep a secret long enough to get ready for a "blitzkrieg."

No nation, whether in a war or out of it, can be just the same while war is going on as it was before. When war breaks out, automatically every nation becomes either a belligerent or a neutral. Belligerents are those who take part in the war directly; neutrals are those who do not engage in fighting. Theoretically neutrals show no preference

for either side, but they often make and sell needed material to one side or the other, and sometimes make their sympathies pretty clear. 

When war breaks out, the ambassadors who represented the contending nations go back home and some other country is asked to accept the responsibility of looking out for the interests of the nation whose own representative is no longer present. 

WAR IN LONDON British Combine Photos, Limited 

Special underground shelters were built to provide a safe place when German air raiders came over. The British King and Queen are showing their interest by visiting one of them. Yes, war changes things.

When a war is on, a nation which is engaged in it must make war its first business. Home life, education, trade must go on, but to such an extent as does not interfere with the prosecution of the war. 

Railroads and every other means of transportation and communication would give the government first claim on their services. "Priorities" in the use of necessities and production of goods would be set up, so that the needs of defense would get first consideration. 

Even in peace, if there is a serious riot or some other domestic trouble, when the President or the governor of a state declares martial law

in some particular section, the authority of the head of the national guard, or whatever military force may be on duty, takes precedence over ordinary civil authority. Few people like that sort of arrangement very long, but there are times when it is the only alternative to disorder or even chaos.

One problem that recently has caused considerable difference of opinion among us is what to do when other nations are at war. A few years ago the pacifist feeling was so strong among us that Congress forbade the carrying on of trade in our own ships with nations that were at war, and the selling to either side of anything in the nature of war materials. But what happens when such fixed policies are put into effect? In the very first war that came along, in spite of our desire to keep out, the sympathies of most of us were strongly with one side. And the side that we disapproved had been bending its energies toward getting ready for war, while its opponents were interested in peaceful activities.

That was what happened in 1939, so that we changed our neutrality law so as to permit us to sell to nations whose citizens would come to us and pay for what they wanted and carry it away. Even that seemed to many to be rather hard on nations that were fighting for their very lives against brutal aggression. You see, therefore, that staying out of war is not the simplest thing in the world. In spite of the violent opposition of those who insisted that the United States should stay out at any cost, unless directly attacked, the majority of our people concluded that our duty and interest both called upon us to help Britain and the other opponents of the dictators, whatever the outcome might be. And as things turned out, we were viciously attacked in spite of all our efforts to treat other nations fairly and arrive at peaceful solutions of international problems.

Situations like this try the souls of people, especially young men and women who feel that upon them will rest the burden of future wars if they are to be fought. They do not wish harm to any peaceful people. They hate to spend time preparing for war when so much more good to humanity could be done by peaceful achievement. But one accepts a pretty heavy responsibility if he insists that no matter what happens he will never risk his own life in defense of his country. 

Surely liberty and democracy are worth defending if they are worth having. The surest way to encourage a criminal nation is to give it

the impression that other nations are too soft, lazy, or careless to stand in its way if only it is determined and mean enough. 

What do you think of military training in schools and colleges? What cause of war would you select as at the same time obvious as a troublemaker and also practicable to eliminate? How would you go about eliminating it?

What is the proper policy of the United States when two or more other nations are engaged in war and the United States is not directly concerned?

99. Can We Have Peace? 

Since selfishness and greed in one form or another have always been among the chief causes of war, many think the best we can do is to try to remove any excuse for a nation's thinking that it does not get a square deal. Then if we can set up means for applying the united force of well-disposed nations against those that have no regard for right or justice, we may

hope to have gone a long way toward averting war. We have been told, "In time of peace, prepare for war." What do you think of these slogans also: "In time of war, prepare for peace"; "In time of peace, prepare for still better peace"?

The theory back of it was that the nations which belonged to the League would use their joint strength, when occasion required, first to boycott a nation which broke its pledges and went to war, and, if necessary, to unite forces against

There were two houses in its government the Assembly, which was to meet at least once a year and include in its membership delegates from all the nations belonging to the League; and the League Council, on which originally the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan were to be permanent members, and four other nations were to be chosen from time to time by the assembly. serving on the Council. A vacant chair was kept for the United 

States, whenever it might find its way clear to join. 

The League Covenant required the League to set up the Permanent Court of International Justice, commonly called the World Court. 

At first it had nine justices, and later fifteen, chosen by the League Council and the League Assembly voting separately, and eligible for re-election. A justice would have to give to actual service on the 

Court as much of his entire time as might be needed. The court was supported by funds collected through the League but handled separately from other League finances. It had no power to compel any nation to submit cases to it, but handled with dignity and reasonable dispatch most of the cases that were laid before it. The International Labor Office was another agency of the League, whose purposes are partly suggested by its name. It aimed to circulate among its members information concerning labor conditions and to do whatever it could to improve the standard of wages and work all over the world. 

But what happened to the League? Its first misfortune was the failure of the United States to join. Another cause of weakness was the unwillingness of some of the leading nations that were members to risk something in the way of loss of trade when boycotts were in order. Nothing was done, for instance, when Japan seized Manchuria except to make a statement condemning it. When Mussolini undertook to conquer Ethiopia, the League went a little further, but it would not risk the possible danger in cutting off his oil supplies which an effective boycott would have required.

Dictators have no use for such organizations as the League, the Court, and the I. L. O., for to join them and abide by their conditions of membership would seriously cramp their style. As the conquests of these men overran so many of the peaceful countries of Europe, the League practically had to fold up and transfer to other locations such activities as could be carried on elsewhere. Yet the League accomplished a number of useful things. It did much to find the cause and put a check upon the spread of contagious diseases, and to promote international co-operation through science and literature. It prevented two or three wars between small powers and settled peacefully a number of matters in which the two nations that were directly concerned could not seem to come to an agreement. Too bad that our own country did not join it and help to give it a real chance!

The Briand-Kellogg Treaty or Pact of Paris, accepted by a considerable number of nations in 1929 and afterward by others, pledged its signers to "renounce war as an instrument of national policy" and to agree to settle all disputes "by pacific means." No provision was made, however, as to what would happen if any nation forgot or ignored its promises. So the treaty has been nothing but a pious wish which apparently was not sincerely accepted by several of its original signers.

Not all work for peace is done through the activities of governments. 

There are international peace societies of one kind or another and various private organizations under different names that try to encourage either a complete hostility to war or the establishment of means of settling disputes so that there will be less excuse for war. The Red 

Cross Society, founded by 

Henri Dunant, a fine Swiss gentleman who was distressed by sufferings that he witnessed on a battlefield where French and Austrians fought, has, since its foundation in 1864, grown to be a world-wide organization doing a much needed and often appreciated work whenever other emergencies like fire and earthquake lay waste to a city or country, as well as in time of war. The American Red Cross, whose first president was the famous Civil War nurse Clara Barton, began its activities in 1881. Numerous international conferences are attended by delegates or volunteers from different countries. Even such organizations as 

Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts make their contribution to international acquaintance and good will. International tennis tournaments and "Olympic" games bring representatives of different countries together in peaceful competition. It remains to be seen whether the airplane and the radio will in the future do more to promote mutual under-

One of the sad features of the rise of the dictatorial powers in Europe in recent years is the success with which the heads of those governments have trained their young men and women so that they believe they are doing something smart in backing up the program of their Fuehrer or Duce. They have been willing to make sacrifices for their leader which young people in democracies have cared to do only in times of great stress. We should not blame these young people too much, for in their schooling they have been allowed to hear nothing except those stories that would make other nations appear to be enemies, "decadent," or "sissies,” and have been taught that their own nationality or race was somehow superior to any other on the face of the earth - "young and virile," you know.

Do you suppose there really is anything in the charge of dictators that democracies get soft and do not like to inconvenience themselves? 

There can be no hope for world peace until the spirit which was responsible for the creation of the League and the Court can become an effective force throughout the world. Nations must be willing to risk a little something through united action in behalf of peace rather than undertake to be so aloof from the rest of the world that no one else will bother them.

If a new organization should be formed to put into operation the ideals that led to the establishment of the League of Nations, to what extent would you plan for any differences in organization or program as compared with the League? 

100. Our Responsibilities as a World Power. Is the United 

States a world power? Yes, if by "world power" we mean a nation whose policies and activities influence notably the course of international relations. No country wants the United States to be its enemy, but many would like to have the United States line up in support of their policies. If we build a big navy, even if we have no intention of attacking anybody, other nations may use the fact as an excuse for enlarging their own naval power. If we change the basis of our currency system, numerous other countries will be forced to let their own currencies follow ours up or down. If we buy more or less than usual of the products of some other country, that country's prosperity is promoted or harmed proportionately. 

---

An important early instance of participation by the United States in a movement to prevent war was our response to the invitation given by the Czar of Russia to send delegates to The Hague to consider means of reducing navies and otherwise making war less likely. Out of this Hague Peace Conference, the anniversary whose assemblage on May 18, 1899, has been commemorated as World Peace Day or World Good-Will Day, came the setting up of the so-called Hague

President Theodore Roosevelt was also instrumental in having a second peace conference meet at The Hague in 1907, but unfortunately more time was devoted at that conference to making agreements about ways of carrying on war than actually to making constructive moves to prevent war.

When William J. Bryan became Secretary of State under President 

Wilson, he arranged numerous arbitration treaties or other measures for preserving the peace. One outstanding feature of the Bryan treaties was the inclusion of a time for "cooling off." The signers to these treaties agreed that even after a dispute might have developed between them, they would not go to war over these disputes until after a fixed period — six months or so.

The failure of the United States Senate to accept the Versailles treaty and join the League of Nations in 1920 left the Republican leaders who came into power in 1921 with a choice of playing a lone hand in international affairs, or doing something different from the proposal of the League of Nations to avert war and promote peace. 

In President Harding's time the Washington Conference of 1921-1922 

set up an agreement by which the four leading powers, the United States, Great Britain, France, and Japan would come together and talk things over if any serious difficulty came up between them, and each of the countries concerned decided to cut down its construction of big battleships; but after 1935 Japan refused to have her hands tied any longer in regard to warship construction.

Strenuous efforts were made by our Presidents to find some way by which the United States might join in supporting the World Court, but always a minority of members of the Senate have been able to prevent the obtaining of the necessary two-thirds vote to approve a treaty for that purpose. Nevertheless, from the very beginning one of the judges of the Court has been a citizen of the United States. 

They have included such able men as John Bassett Moore, Charles E. 

Hughes, Frank B. Kellogg, and Manley O. Hudson. The Briand 

Kellogg Treaty of 1928 and 1929, to which we have already referred, was a well-meant but ineffective undertaking. Conferences held at 

Geneva and London failed to accomplish anything important, and after Hitler's and Mussolini's activities had begun to alarm other

governments, it was not an appropriate time to talk about disarmament.

It would be a great mistake for us to assume, when any question arises that threatens world peace, that we need to do nothing, and that all wars are "imperialistic," whatever that means. Possibly it signifies simply the extension of authority by a strong country over regions that are weaker or more backward, whether for its own good or theirs. Great Britain when he wrote "The White Man's Burden," but every thought in it is just as applicable to the United States as to Great Britain not that white men should seek to rule the world, but that those who have ability, influence, and power should use it rightly and not make excuses for failing to do so. Disputes over foreign affairs should end "at the water's edge," it has often been said. It is very unfortunate if a political group, to gain some temporary advantage, is willing to compromise our influence for peace and good will among nations.

We are devoted to the principles of freedom and democracy. We want to be strong not for the sake of beating up anyone else, but so that until all the great nations of the world are willing to practice peace, we shall not be in danger, and when that longed-for time shall come, that we may join in being firm against any who would disturb through selfishness or blundering the well-being of mankind. The United 

States has a reputation for desiring peace, for believing in the square deal among nations as well as among individuals, and for at least in our own day-acting with unselfish motives in its attitude toward other countries. We cannot afford to lower the standard we have already set up. It does make a difference what other nations think of us. 

And why shouldn't we be proud to take the lead in making the world better when the opportunity comes to us to do so? Our own self-interest should cause us to do this, if there were no better reasons.

PART II  

One very important reason why we have governments is to protect our relations with one another in families, schools, churches, and other groups. Many of these groups came into existence without any act of government. Unless we understand why these groups are formed and how people act in connection with them, we may fail to realize the truth about many matters which directly touch our personal lives. In fact, such topics as these, along with the activities related to earning a living, make up the greater part of all our natural interests. 

SOCIAL LIVING 

As early as there were people to meet one another, those relations and associations began which we refer to as social. Without anybody's planning it, a social background has been set up which we need to appreciate in order to understand the life we live today. The whole body of people who live this common life we refer to as society. The study of the facts and principles that explain our relations with one another in the groups to which we belong, we speak of as sociology. 

Some Questions: 

1. What is the nature of the society in which we live? 

2. What is civilization? How much of it do we have? 

3. What forces outside of ourselves and within us influence human progress? 

4. What may the individual do to promote his own welfare? 

5. How is he likely to be controlled by the groups to which he belongs? 

6. What hope is there for a better society than that in which we live? 

101. What Kind of Society Do We Live In? The society we live in is not fixed or static. Never before was it just as it is now, and probably it will never be just the same again. Sometimes we talk about a normal society, meaning by that a way of living that seems to be satisfactory to the general run of men and women. But there is not and is never likely to be a state of affairs which will not change 

267

greatly over an extended period. Because our society has within itself a capacity to make improvements we sometimes call it dynamic. 

Neither society as a whole nor the individuals who compose it always make good use of their powers, but they have them, nevertheless. 

We often use the term social order to mean the established arrangements and customs which characterize our lives. A social order comes into existence without the making of any constitution or law. Some people have tried to direct it to their own advantage, and others have gone along with it because it was the easiest way to go. Neither all the good things nor all the bad things in society were deliberately planned. In fact, some people say that that is one of the things that is wrong with it. But there is a social order, and not merely what some smarties would call a social disorder.

Give two or three reasons for thinking that our present social order is neither the best nor the worst possible. can we

If our social order is not perfect and who says it is? build a new and better one? Maybe we do not know just what will be the best social order twenty-five or fifty years from now. Maybe it would be better sense to set up ideals as to the kind of society we should like to have, and then just try day by day to take whatever step ahead is possible then and there. We may have to change our methods and even modify our objectives as unforeseen conditions appear; but at least we will not have jumped blindly into a program that may not turn out at all the way we expected. 

We need to keep an open mind toward new ideas. Granting that the world could be much better than it is, it could also be far worse. 

Probably some of the ideas we hold today will be modified a little by our study of the topics that are just before us. But we need not assume that everything our parents have taught us is out of date, or that the new world of fifty years ahead will be totally different from the one in which we live. 

In the study of topics in sociology, should we aim chiefly at discovering facts, or discussing problems, or try to do both? Are we better able to discuss sociological topics now than we were a year or three years ago? Why or why not? Recall the distinction among fact, belief, opinion, theory, and conviction, with reference to attitudes and understandings. What is the importance of suspended judgment at times?

SOCIAL LIVING 

269 

102. Are We Civilized? 

One definition of civilization is that it is the condition in which man exercises a purposeful control over nature. 

Today most of us live more comfortably than any except the wealthiest families lived a hundred years ago. Many who are not rich have their own radios and automobiles. We make electricity and many other natural forces serve us in surprising ways.

Unfortunately, however, some men use their power over natural forces in such ways as to wreck civilization rather than advance it. 

Never before were there so many ways to kill people as there are today, and never before was war so expensive. That is nothing for civilization to brag about. Moral advancement and material accomplishment plainly do not always go side by side. 

Another word closely related to "civilization" is culture. Sometimes we employ it in a special sense. We speak of a person as "cultured" if he is interested in music, art, literature, and the finer things of life generally. But when we speak of a culture, we usually have in mind the stage of development of a people. Their culture might, therefore, be either advanced or backward, high or low, depending upon their attainments and interests.

There are certain wants which all men wish to satisfy. Food, clothing, and shelter represent material wants; education, religion, and a chance to make a living represent a different sort of human interests. These did not mean the same to a primitive savage that they mean to us today, but they were real enough even to him. The civilized man or woman wants very much more, and wants many more different things, but may or may not feel any more keenly about them.

Make a list of five items in common demand among us which neither 

George Washington, Julius Caesar, nor Abraham Lincoln would have expected to enjoy. Make a similar list of things useful to both them and us. Mention several things in present-day life which, in your opinion, will have to be eliminated before civilization can be thoroughly satisfactory. 

103. A Changing World. Nobody can fix the date when civilization began. By the year 4000 B.C. people in ancient Egypt and probably in Mesopotamia were doing some of the same things we are doing They had begun to keep some kind of records of what they were doing, and that is one of the surest evidences that a people have made progress. In most peoples, if we trace their history back far now.

enough, we shall find evidences of five epochs or stages of progress, which you have probably heard of already. There was no clear-cut date to separate one from another. Neither did all people go through the same stage at the same time.

When new stages of progress came into existence, their activities were added to those already existing. 

Ewing Galloway

LOVE IN ZULULAND 

This young fellow is putting a cow horn into the hut of the girl he loves. It is supposed to bewitch her and make her like him. 

1. In the earliest stage, the hunting and fishing age, men depended for their food and clothing upon the birds, fish, and animals which they could kill. 

2. The second period is called the pastoral stage. Men learned to keep animals together in flocks and herds so that they were handy when needed. Here we have evidence of organized planning, which was surely a notable step in advance. 

3. Then came the agricultural stage. Now men added to their control over animal life a control over plant life. Here, too, came an important change in that people had to settle down in one place and stay there some little time if they were to get the benefit of the grains and fruits which they planted. 

4. Next we come to the fourth, or handicraft, stage. People had already been making tools, garments, tents, and the like, but now manufacturing became important. At first it was just what the word really means in 

Latin-making by hand. During this period division of occupations became marked. Some people continued to be farmers, some to be herdsmen, some to be fishermen, but many others began to make their living by manufacturing tools and weapons for others to use. 

5. Finally came the machine age, in which most of the world finds itself today. Now we depend not merely upon the skill of hand and eye to manufacture things, but on enormous factories with machines costing immense sums. This tremendous transformation dates chiefly from the eighteenth century. We call it the Industrial Revolution. It began in England and

SOCIAL LIVING 

271 spread gradually from England to the continent of Europe, to the United States, and finally to almost all parts of the world, so that in India and Japan today are factories of the same kind that have sprung up in Birmingham, in Manchester, in Pittsburgh, and in Gary.

No civilization or culture is entirely different from that of every other. "East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet" so you have probably heard. It is sometimes hard to understand how people can think and act so differently from the way we do. 

Yet how many things the people of both East and West have in common! Our own American life has been tremendously influenced by contributions from widely different sources. Very true is it that "We are the heirs of all the ages, ""and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." We can be sure only that we shall not always be what we are now. 

What is your reaction to the statement, "Youth is a savage in civilized society"? Do you recognize any problems of today which our people find more difficult to solve than other peoples do? If so, what and why? What problems of civilized people, if any, are distinctly European or Asiatic rather than American?

The influences which bring about change are not always realized at the time. You may have heard it said of some person, "He was a self-made man." But was he? Are you? Ask yourself the question and be honest about the answer. A subject for debate which is as old as the hills concerns the relative influence of "heredity" and "environment," or "nature" and "nurture." Both sides win may or neither. Environment itself includes both the people with whom we associate and the surroundings in which we live. 

104. How Geography Affects Human Progress. - Geography has had a tremendous effect upon the history of nations. Switzerland's mountains have helped to make her free. England's island situation forced her people upon the sea and aided her to become a great commercial nation. A warm sun makes men lazy. Frigid climates tax their energies unduly. In the temperate zones have been found the peoples who have made world history. 

Point out other natural conditions which directed the development of great nations in ancient and modern times. Has Australia lost anything by reason of her isolated location?

Geography also makes a difference with an individual. A boy or girl in rural Georgia or North Dakota has fewer choices of occupations than a young person in New York or Philadelphia. A farm boy may stay on the farm either because he feels it his duty to do so, or has little chance to do anything else, or because he actually likes it; but he also may go into the city and make good there. Yet people out of a job in our large cities often absolutely refuse to go out in the country to work even when they can get it. They will live on other people's charity instead. They are in the clutches of their environment and cannot or will not break away.

Some natural disadvantages we have learned to overcome. Desert lands can be irrigated and made to grow abundant crops. Canals may even cut continents apart, as at Panama. We are still careless with our natural resources, but we do use such by-products as coal tar, cottonseed oil, and paraffin which once went to waste. We can make ice in Africa and with electricity turn darkness into light in northern

Sweden and in Little America. But it is not likely that we can profitably grow bananas in Alaska or rubber in any of our forty-eight states. Some natural conditions we do better to accept rather than try to change.

The United States has been exceedingly favored by Nature in almost every respect. We have over 3,000,000 square miles of territory, stretching from one great ocean to another, and with almost every kind of soil and mineral resource. All of the largest mass of our huge territory is in the temperate zone. 

We have plenty of harbors, 18,000 miles of navigable rivers, and smaller streams which can furnish an unmeasured amount of power. 

The fertile Mississippi valley and the neighboring southern states raise three fourths of the world's cotton, three fourths of its corn, and from one fourth to one third of the world's wheat. We still have rich forests. Even at that, other countries are better supplied with certain things than we are, and we might as well admit the fact and adjust ourselves to it. 

Primitive men- and don't we do the same? - sought those places to live which enabled them to get along in comfort with the least amount of toil and trouble. That is why the earliest civilizations grew up in warm climates and in river valleys. rain or too much of it are alike unfavorable.

105. How Biology Affects Human Progress. - We can easily list the respects in which man and the lower animals are alike and those in which they are different. The structure of the human body has considerable in common with that of many animals. 

Many animals 

James Sawders

PITTSBURGH FROM THE POINT 

Pittsburgh's location where two large rivers meet made it early a center of trade and travel and brought business to its doors. can do things that you cannot, but none can do everything that you can. Man can think, plan, and organize. Some of the lower animals appear to do so on a small scale, but men can plan for the improvement of the whole human race. There is no evidence that any horse or dog has tried to bring about a better standard of living for all horses or dogs, or that he could if he tried. It is not to man's credit that i he has used his great powers to create instruments of destruction and to kill his fellow men by the thousands, but these facts do show men's almost illimitable capacity.

The argument over "nature" has at least two sides, with something to be said on each side. Perhaps you do not need to look outside

SOCIAL LIVING 

275 your own home to find plenty of evidence that many characteristics and qualities are inherited. Do you look totally different from any other member of your family? Are there no interests whatever in common between you and your parents and more distant relatives?

By a principle discovered by a monk named Mendel, and known as Mendel's Law, it can be determined with some accuracy how frequently certain definite characteristics in human beings or animals will be passed on to their descendants. Some characteristics, it is true, disappear after a few generations. These are referred to as recessive qualities, but others, known as dominant, will appear in every generation.

To explain why certain qualities, certain races or groups of people, or certain forms of plant life survive, while others disappear, we turn to the principle of "natural selection" or "the survival of the fittest." 

This does not mean that those individuals or groups that survive are the best in all respects, but that they are best suited to the conditions under which they have to live. Some kinds of birds and animals that once lived have wholly disappeared. They could not defend themselves from a bad climate or from enemies, either men or beasts. 

Trees cannot grow in a desert, except in the oases where water is found. 

Tropical plants will not live in cold climates outside of greenhouses. 

Perhaps you will say that this is the effect of environment; but since some animals and plants do live in cold climates, there must be something in those living things that enables them to survive while others perish.

As human beings, we are influenced also by other than physical factors. Instincts cause us to do things either unconsciously or without taking time to reason about them. It is natural for us, for example, to eat, to sleep, to defend ourselves when attacked, and to like or dislike persons and things. We have a nervous system which closes our eyes against a sudden flash of light or pulls a finger away from a hot stove or steampipe. Such means of response to outside conditions are known as reflexes. 

Feelings, wishes, and emotions also may make us do things without reasoning why. By a feeling we mean in general the sense of pleasure or displeasure that is connected with some particular situation. We are comfortable or uncomfortable when the thermometer shows a certain temperature or when we are in the presence of certain persons.

Sometimes we need to learn to restrain these feelings, if we are to act in ways that will work out for lasting good rather than mere temporary comfort. 

It has been said that four wishes tend to dominate people in general: (1) for security from want, sickness, or misfortune; (2) for response or appreciation from those with whom we associate; (3) for adventure or new experience; (4) for distinction or superiority. Naturally all people do not possess all these wishes to an equal degree. But those who are seriously disappointed in connection with any one of those wishes seldom make great achievements in life or enjoy continued happiness. By emotions we mean those impulses which make us feel or act in certain ways. The three primary emotions are said to be fear, anger, and love. One sees these in the very young child, and as he grows older others come into evidence, such as sympathy, gratitude, and jealousy. Emotions, like feelings, often need to be kept under restraint, both for one's own good and the good of others. 

You have probably seen how both violent temper and foolish love can bring about most regrettable results. 

To say "we are born that way" is no excuse for continued objectionable misconduct. But through knowing how feelings, wishes, and emotions operate, we can understand people better and make ourselves more successful or likable. Biological forces do play a great part in human life. 

H. Armstrong Roberts

106. Group Relations That Influence Us. - With many of us, our social environment is much more significant than our physical environment. "Birds of a feather flock together," we are told. But the

SOCIAL LIVING 

277 acts of the flock may also determine what a single bird will do. Only a strong-willed person can force himself to do something, no matter how good he believes it to be, if most of those with whom he associates wish him to do otherwise. It may be hard to tell how many of the things we do result from the fact that others habitually do those same things. Social groups, therefore, play a tremendous part in society. 

Not all social groups, however, are alike. One distinction that may be made is between primary and secondary groups. A primary group is one in which the members have regular and direct contact with one another, such as the family, a small school, or one's personal friends. Secondary groups are usually larger, and offer fewer close personal contacts, though sometimes their influence may be considerable, as a political party, a religious denomination, or an army. 

Another distinction that may be drawn is between voluntary and involuntary groups. Voluntary groups are those to which we belong because we choose to do so; involuntary, those about which we have no choice. The church, in this country, is a voluntary organization. 

A school is an involuntary group, until we get beyond the compulsory attendance age. Voluntary groups may have more than one object. 

A person may join a church both to help himself to live a better life, and to assist in supporting an organization that will benefit the community. One may help support a community forum both because he enjoys the discussions that take place there, and because he thinks they aid others in understanding current problems. 

A third kind of classification is between majority and minority groups. These may exist within other groups. In some religious denominations, as the Methodist, Presbyterian, or Baptist, there may be rather strong differences of opinion about certain things; before the Civil War their members disagreed vigorously on whether it was right to hold slaves. In some parts of our country, one political party may be much more numerous than another. In Mississippi most people call themselves Democrats; in Vermont, Democrats are much scarcer.

Groups may influence individuals through the force of group solidarity and group loyalty. One thinks of solidarity when an action is decided upon and every member is expected to act in the same way in order to exert as much force as possible. Group loyalty appears when the members act together not so much for the purpose of forcing

people to do or not to do some thing, but to accomplish something for the benefit of the whole group. Members of a family can quarrel violently with one another, but let someone from the outside undertake to harm a member of that family and see what happens to the kibitzer. 

Group co-operation makes possible far greater accomplishments than the individual members could bring about separately. Small groups acting separately will often be less effective than if they go together. 

That is why we have "community funds" or "community chests" in many of our cities. The charity organizations that compose them

Many of our social and political groups are the outgrowth of evident needs or wants. The family was the simplest and earliest of them. 

Families in early times enlarged into associations of families, which might be called clans. Clans, in turn, combined into tribes, and several tribes, either through conquest or voluntarily, might have formed nations. Each step in the process of combination was to somebody's advantage, and the rulers or leaders in each group were supposed to protect the interests of all the members. 

Group activities may not always result in social benefit. When tribes or nations make war upon each other; when members of a

SOCIAL LIVING 

279 political party think more of its interests than of the welfare of a city, state, or nation; when a social club encourages its members to acquire extravagant or harmful habits then we see the bad effects that groups may produce. Besides, an individual who belongs to several groups may find that the interests of the majority of one group conflict with those of another. That does not mean that we should try to abolish groups, but rather to direct their energies into useful channels. 

Group organizations are not necessarily permanent. Some may serve a very good purpose for a while and then disappear, like the old-time village singing school. Political parties may go to pieces after they have accomplished what they first undertook. But organizations which plainly do benefit their members and also promote the welfare of society are likely to continue indefinitely, even though they may not work in just the same way forever.

107. What Institutions and Customs Do for Us. The word 

"institution" may be used in different senses. If we speak of a college as an "institution of learning," we mean an organization established to help people learn something. But we also speak of beliefs, practices, and agencies which become established and generally accepted, as institutions. Marriage is a social institution; the church is a religious institution; the state is a political institution. Such institutions, when once definitely established, are not readily changed and give a permanence and substantial nature to society which it would not otherwise have. The methods and even the ideals of these institutions may change, but while they exist institutions have a significant place in our life. 

Institutions may be preserved through custom and tradition, and then may be established by law. A state legislature may command children to go to school until the age of sixteen or some other time, because of a belief that to educate children is for the good of society.

People get into the habit of driving on the right or the left side of the street. Then a law comes along and says you must do that. Sometimes, of course, it is hard to tell how a custom or tradition originated and why it has come to be generally accepted. 

If a custom ceases to appeal to people as desirable, it may gradually disappear. If the majority come to think of it as definitely hampering 09.06

AN HONORED CUSTOM 

On Commencement Day the alumni, faculty, and graduating class of Brown University march around the campus in a winding procession, while the band plays the "Commencement March" heard only at this time of year. Then the line moves down the hill to the old Meeting House built "for the worship of God and for holding commencements in." These annual exercises stir again in the alumni the spirit of loyalty to the University and suggest to the graduating class that they are entering into a priceless heritage. their happiness or progress, they will probably sooner or later get rid of it. Particularly if a custom comes to conflict with the majority's idea of right, it will not be tolerated any longer than is necessary. 

The institution of human slavery existed for centuries. As long as people looked upon the buying and selling of slaves as simply a business procedure, there was no particular objection to it. One did not have to buy a slave unless he could use him. But when in our own country people's consciences began to be disturbed over the matter,

SOCIAL LIVING 

281 they became anxious to do something about it. They were not satisfied merely to refrain from buying slaves themselves, but they insisted that others should not be allowed to own them, even though those people might feel that it was a social or economic necessity. 

Every social group has its idea of value, but the values set upon certain customs or practices may be altered from time to time. What is right? What is desirable? Will any person answer all such questions in the same way all through his life? Once it was believed, for instance, that a very few years of schooling were enough for the average person. Now we believe that everybody ought to have two or three times as much schooling as once anybody had except in the learned professions.

Sometimes waves of sentiment sweep over a country and it becomes very popular temporarily to take a certain attitude about some particular proposition. When business conditions are not good, public sentiment blames the party in power and turns it out of office. In war years a people may feel bitter hostility toward another nation. A few years later some will be crying "Keep out of war" so loudly that the leaders of the nation cannot get money to spend on reasonable preparations for defense. Such unsound and unreasoning changes of opinion are much like a mental epidemic and may do as much harm as one of the periodic visits of measles or influenza. We should change customs and institutions, of course, when they need it, but let us do it through reason and common sense and not in hysteria. 

Would a custom be likely to become generally accepted that did not benefit a considerable number of people? Might one's conscience justify him in doing things that others would believe to be distinctly wrong? Give examples if you think that is possible. 

108. What Can One Person Do?- That depends. You are only one out of about two billion people in the world. Yet some individuals have either changed the history of the whole world, or else have been the agency through which a people changed their own destiny. 

Among primitive people one person stood out only when he was the ruler or master. Some have argued that the great changes that have taken place in the development of humanity came through the "lengthening shadow" of one man. They would say that history is the story of what great men have achieved, and that the world largely

stood still during the time that it had to wait between the appearance of one great man and another. 

What determines a person's standing in the groups to which he belongs? Personality surely has much to do with it- and by personality we mean those often indefinable qualities that distinguish one person from another. Some have plenty of it, some almost none. 

You meet Mary Smith, and forget her. You meet Sarah Brown, and the word or the glance she gave you comes back to you over and over again. She may or may not be exceptionally brilliant in mind, but there is something in her that attracts attention. Such a person can exercise a force for good or harm that could hardly be measured. If any of us find that we have this gift, let us use it to make life happier and better, and let us not refuse to accept the responsibility that goes with the power.

But those of us who do not seem born to command need not think that we are to be useless. Perhaps in a quiet way we can accomplish a great deal by co-operating with others. Indeed, the person who often gets into the limelight may have to face jealousy, if not outright hostility. The everyday work of the world will have to be done chiefly by the millions who never get into Who's Who. You know 

Lincoln's remark that the Lord must have loved the common people because he made so many of them. 

The welfare of an individual gets much greater consideration today than perhaps it ever has received before. The handicapped child in school gets special attention. Women workers have laws passed for their special benefit. The "forgotten man" becomes a center of political interest. No longer do we believe it is inevitable that human life shall be ended in great numbers by epidemics and wars simply because there are too many to feed. We talk about "social" security, but we really mean the protection of one individual after another against misfortunes that once it was thought we could not expect to escape. How far may an individual rightly demand that society shall look out for his particular interests? Who can be sure? Some individuals have already got to the point where they demand help rather than ask for it.

If an individual thinks he is not getting a square deal from his associates, what can he do about it, in school, in industry, or in some social relationship?

109. Controlling Our Destiny. - A person or a community may perhaps avoid worry by spending no time on efforts or plans, accepting what comes, and making the best of it. Yet careful planning brings more chance of gaining desired conditions than not to plan. We have considerable to say these days about social control, by which we mean the extent to which society directs human conduct or the course of events along definite lines, and about social planning, by which we mean the specific undertakings which society makes to bring about certain definite results. There may be social control, for example, of those who have criminal tendencies, and social planning with the idea of removing conditions that lead to crime. 

Changes will usually come with less discontent and inconvenience if brought about step by step, rather than by a sudden overturn. In other words, evolution— gradual change is in principle much to be preferred over revolution — sudden overthrow of previous forms or conditions. Revolution can be justified only when some minority group has so established itself in power that ordinary peaceful processes cannot succeed in getting what the majority want. Some revolutions have been justified; but revolutions often tear up things by the roots, instead of simply transplanting them from one location to a better one. Revolutions may also disturb people and things that do not deserve to be disturbed. 

Evolution as a means of change also has the advantage that improvements can be made one by one as their desirability is proved, instead of allowing evil conditions to drag on to such a point that everything good is threatened with disaster. A situation of that kind we might refer to as a crisis. Occasionally it takes a crisis to make people realize the seriousness of undesirable conditions. 

Times of crisis, too, give dictators their chance. Der Fuehrer or 

Il Duce says he knows what ought to be done, and people will accept him as their master in order to avoid what seems a worse fate. People who believe in the democratic idea of government should certainly work for steady improvement by gradual reform, so that extreme measures may never be necessary. 

Changes may not take place at the same speed in all phases of life.

When change has proceeded extensively in one field and not in another,

the sociologist may speak of the former as an example of culture acceleration and the latter as culture lag. For example, the ways of making things by machines have advanced much more rapidly than the provision we have made for giving people who wish to work a fair chance to do so. We could be so interested in discovering ways to deal with disease after it appears that we might not realize the importance of removing the conditions that encouraged the disease in the first place. 

Several forces may interfere with the bringing about of social change. 

The strongest, perhaps, is the force of custom and precedent. If 

James Sawders

REFUGEES FROM THE DUST BOWL 

On the outskirts of Boise, Idaho, these people took refuge from farms that would no longer support them. Does this suggest civilization going in reverse? people have always done things in a certain way, it is hard to get them to do differently. Ignorance and mental or physical laziness are other handicaps. The self-interest of those who might be inconvenienced by change is also hard to overcome. The building of railroads put stagecoaches out of business, and the automobile has ruined railroads.

An unwillingness to accept criticism may also stand in the way of progress. Criticism, be sure you understand, does not necessarily mean 'fault-finding. The Greek word from which that term comes meant simply passing judgment. A critic may find some pleasant things to say about a person or thing as well as the opposite. But if

SOCIAL LIVING 

285 someone honestly thinks that he has been doing a good piece of work, he may look upon all criticism as inspired by ill will. The critic's motives or proposals, too, may be misunderstood, if his criticisms are presented tactlessly.

To bring about improvement, several forces need to be brought into play to counteract the influences that hold back people and communities. The most effective of these is, of course, education. The more we know, the less likely are we to hold to methods and ideas no longer useful. A spirit of co-operation is another essential, so that the controlling motive will be "the greatest good for the greatest number." 

With reasonable planning, changes may come without irreparable harm to very many people. The stage driver, for instance, might be given a job on the railroad, and the conductor whose railroad stopped running might learn to drive a bus. Leadership is a third essential. 

Seldom does a desire to make a needed reform seize a whole community at once. Individuals and clubs interested in social welfare may have to talk and urge for a considerable period before the change they wish is brought about.

When we talk about social change there may be a temptation to "call names." One who thinks things are in pretty good shape after all may speak of an advocate of reform as a radical, implying that he is one who wants to destroy society. One who is very enthusiastic about making society over may call a person a stand patter or a reactionary just because the latter believes we should be sure that a change is good before we make it. The terms conservative, liberal, and progressive may mean much or little, depending on who uses them, and the real opinions which these words represent may not differ greatly. 

The conservative emphasizes the importance of moving slowly and surely in making changes, and insists that much that has been done in the past is good. The sincere liberal lays stress on the importance of being willing to listen to new ideas and undertake new policies that seem good. The true progressive is simply one who wants society to be constantly bettering itself. 

In spite of all the unpleasant things that have occurred in the past, in spite of wars and panics and epidemics, much social improvement has taken place, particularly within the lifetime of people of today. 

We have a right to protest against such types of social planning as would make it possible for someone in authority to tell everybody just

how he must live, exactly what he is privileged to say, or precisely what he may do for a living. That is regimentation, and free people do not like it. But it does not follow that everybody has the right to oppose any social change which interferes with his own convenience or requires him to make a new adjustment. Successful efforts at human progress require willingness to work with one's fellow men, to try new things that offer a hope of improvement, and to be openminded toward new ideas.

In thinking of our social background, we have had in mind humanity as a whole — and most of us do that too little. But certainly we ought to know the important facts about the people of our own nation, their relationships, and their problems. Then we may also understand other peoples better, for people are people wherever we find them. Only in the matter of race relations is the situation somewhat more mixed with us than it is in other great civilized countries. 

Some Questions: 

1. How many people have we in this country and where do they live? 

2. Where did our people come from in the first place? 

3. How important has immigration been in the making of our nation ? 

4. What influences upon our history and life have been produced by the relations of races among us? 

5. What should we think in regard to the relations of our people in the future? 

110. Numbering the People. Nobody knows how many people there are in the world, though there are probably around 2,000,000,000. 

No accurate count was ever made of the population of China and several other parts of Asia, of most of Africa, and of some regions in the Western Hemisphere. We and most other civilized nations, however, like to know the facts. 

Our Constitution requires us to take a census every ten years. The information is gathered by enumerators who go around from house to house, is reported to city or county supervisors, and passed on by them to the Bureau of the Census, which is a division of the Department of Commerce at Washington. There the figures are tabulated by local divisions, by states, and for the whole country. Of course conditions change somewhat between one year and the next, but it is rare that the changes are so extreme in a short time as to make the census information unreliable. A few of our states have taken a census in the fifth year between the national censuses.

Most of the nations have shown a tremendous increase since the eighteenth century until recently. Why? Except for the World War and an occasional famine, there have been no major calamities to wipe out any large number of the people at any given time. There used to be a considerable margin of births over deaths in most of the leading countries, except possibly France, though this margin is not nearly so great today as it has been. Besides, we have learned how to cure sickness and guard against disease to such an extent that people on the average live much longer than they used to. In a few countries, as in the United States, there has been a great volume of immigration to add to the other forces that tended to increase the whole population. Such additions to the United 

States meant subtractions from other countries, but they were not great enough to overcome the effects of the tendencies at work toward an increase of population. 75,994,575 91,972,266

It is not merely inquisitiveness that is responsible for the taking of a census. In this country the distribution of the number of representatives in Congress among the states is based on population. We also can meet many of our problems and responsibilities much better if we know the facts about such matters as the number of foreign-born residents, people of foreign ancestry, or people of different races and colors, the number of children in school and the number who ought to be, the distribution of people in cities, small towns, and rural districts, family incomes, or the number in different occupations.

within the families of the country were asked in connection with the taking of the 1940 census that some people allowed themselves to become excited about an imaginary interference with the private rights of citizens.

What difference might it make to a school board to know how many children there were in a certain community of various ages? To a firm thinking of starting a new factory? What difference might it make to anyone to know how many people of foreign birth or how many naturalized and unnaturalized persons over twenty-one there were in a community or state?

Seldom has such distribution come because anybody planned it that way. Our population has never been evenly distributed over the country, and the westward movement of the people into unoccupied territory has been one of the tremendous influences upon our history.

113. What Great Cities Mean to Us. - The increase in the number and size of cities raises several questions. Are we better off morally, spiritually, or otherwise because of these great cities? Or may a city be so large as to make it hard for any one person to mean much to more than a very few people? Is it well to have factories crowded together in comparatively few places? Would it be better for industry to quit trying to build up enormous unwieldy establishments and encourage more factories of moderate size decentralize, as they say? Then would the individual worker feel more of a personal interest than now in the success of the industry to which he contributes ? 

We do not need today nearly so many farmers in proportion to the whole population as once we did, because we have learned to use

machinery on the farm, and a much smaller number of workers can raise a considerably greater volume of products. Instead of expecting that the large cities will absorb the surplus farm people, would it not be good sense to make use of them in smaller manufacturing centers?

Perhaps by the right kind of planning, with government and business interests working together, conditions might be brought about which naturally would attract workers to the places where they can work to the greatest advantage for themselves and everybody else. City problems loom large to the social worker of today. Consider particularly the problem of congestion. Sometimes a city may grow too fast for its own good. Early factory workers naturally liked to live within walking distance of the place where they worked. When houses became scarce, rents went up, and crowding in tenements and apartments became worse than before. That meant slum districts. When we were admitting immigrants without much restriction of numbers, they crowded into the parts of the city in which some of their fellow-countrymen already were. So there grew up in our large cities little Italys, little Russias, or other distinct settlements, and the languages and customs of the old country were perpetuated. 

Cities became notorious for political corruption and bad government, for the newcomers were game for crooked politicians.

The city has also suffered from lack of opportunities for play. What chance did the average city man or boy have for hunting, fishing, skating, or playing baseball? Sitting down with his pipe in the evening or going to bed was the choice many a factory worker had. The

The 1940 census reports astounded some of us, when they showed that city after city, including some of our biggest ones,. had lost population during the previous ten years. Why was this? One reason was a declining birthrate among us, of which we shall speak later (§ 119).

Other causes were the great depression and resultant decline of city jobs, and the falling off of immigration because of depression here and disturbed conditions abroad. 

Moreover, today people often prefer to live in the suburbs of a city even when their work or business interests may be in the city. Suburban neighborhoods may be much quieter, more open, and pleasanter otherwise.

During most of our national history the farmers have seemed to be moving into the city. If conditions continued, however, as they were at the time of the 1940 census, the parade seems almost ready to stop. 

114. Living on the Farm. We used to think of the city as offering comforts and advantages which only a few people could ever hope for in the rural districts. Perhaps we should not be too sure that the farmer has the worst of everything. 

The most serious problem we connect with the farmer is his isolation and the resultant difficulty of co-operation. Especially on the great farms of the Middle West and Far West the farmer must work by himself or with only a very few helpers most of the time, and it may be miles to the nearest house. His hours of work cannot be regulated by schedule so much as by what must be done when it can be done. 

In the summer, now and then, they may run from dawn till dark. 

The country school and the country church have also come in for

much criticism. Pupils of all grades from at least one to eight might be found in one room, often without satisfactory books or other equipment. Teachers were poorly paid, and the term was sometimes not more than six months in a year. The country church was perhaps one of three or four served by the same minister, for otherwise no minister could live on the salary these churches could pay. In many parts of the country, even this arrangement has gone out of vogue, and in some states hundreds have closed their doors. 

Chicago Aerial Survey Company.

A WELL-KEPT FARM 

This farm scene from Indiana may not suggest wealth, but it does indicate rural comfort.

The country home has too often lacked the most ordinary conveniences of present-day dwellings. Bathtubs and running water and electric lights and telephones are still in some sections conspicuous by their absence, and the farmhouse was sometimes less well cared for than the barn. And, of course, no ordinary farmer ever expected to handle a great deal of money. 

But more and more miles of hard-surface road are being built every year in almost every state. Electric light and power lines are reaching all over the farming sections, and the radio works just as well on the farm as it does in town. Farm machinery has reduced the backbreaking toil of the men and boys, and with electricity coming into

de 3 1 nd of the home the farm wife and farm girl are going to have an easier time of it. Bathtubs and indoor toilets are more numerous. 

Rural free delivery of mail helps considerably, and in some sections there are more telephones in proportion to population than in some of our largest cities.

Another helpful influence, as far as the farm is concerned, is a changed attitude toward education. The one-room "little red schoolhouse" is gradually disappearing. Buses carry pupils to central or consolidated schools, where the enrollment is large enough to permit reasonable salaries to teachers. Even those one-room schools that are left are sometimes reasonably well equipped. No longer do we think that the country high school must offer just the same kind of courses that the city high school does. 

Many a farmer has found his state college or university ready to arrange special courses for him, and the country high school plans to help its boys and girls be happy.

The county fair may be the big event of the year.

If the weather is too unpleasant to drive into town for the movie, there is at least the radio. A boy or
