115. The Village and the Small Town. - You can hardly give an exact definition for either of these terms. In some states the word "village" means a community with a recognized local government, perhaps with a mayor or trustees at the head of it. In other places

出​社 ​חור rd It es a village is simply a group of houses, perhaps at a crossroads, including at least one store, today a gasoline station and probably a church, and maybe a post office, unless the post office is inside the store. From such a small group of buildings a village may expand until it has a distinct community life of its own. The small town may be still less easy to identify in words. Any place not big enough to be classified by the Census Bureau as urban would certainly be a small town or rural neighborhood, and people who live in large cities would be likely to call any town small unless it had 5000 people or more.

The small town has some of the problems of both the farm and the big city. Its people may not have the healthful outdoor work of the farm nor the conveniences of the larger community. Recreation may take the form of loafing at the corner store or in a pool room, if the place is large enough to have one. The small-town church may not have the inspiration of even a rural "meeting house," and the schools may have just enough pupils to make them wish they could get the same service that pupils obtain in larger communities. People who are brought up in such places are sometimes narrow-minded and prejudiced. Some years ago Sinclair Lewis in Main Street gave us a picture of small-town life which some have taken as typical ever since.

Often the people of small towns include a much more than average proportion of older persons. The farmer who thinks he has put in his share of hard-working years moves into town and settles down.

116. Our National Origins.-Up to our own Revolution, and during the period that followed our Revolution and the French Revolution, immigrants to this country came largely from the British Isles. 

When we became independent, about 85 per cent of our people were of English ancestry, and a considerable number of the rest came from Ireland and other parts of the British Isles and from northern or western Europe. Until 1819 our laws did not require us even to take the trouble to count the number of immigrants. But after the wars of 

Napoleon were over and conditions had quieted down both in Europe and in this country, we began to receive them in greater numbers.

The period of the 1840's was marked by a tremendous rush of immigrants. The Irish famine sent a million Irishmen out of their country, most of whom came to the United States. The failure of attempted revolutions in Germany in 1848 and 1849 caused many Germans to come to this country. A little later many thousands of Swedes, Norwegians, and Danes came. The year 1882 is often looked upon as a sort of dividing line with reference to our immigrants. We sometimes refer to those who came before that date as the old immigration, and most of them were from northern or western Europe. 

The new immigration, which came after 1882, was in many ways different from the old. It came largely from southern and eastern 

Europe from Austria, Italy, Hungary, Poland, Russia, Greece, Serbia, Czechoslovakia. Its people had less acquaintance with the ideals and practices of democracy than did many of the old immigrants, and there was more difference in social and religious interests between these newcomers and those who were already here than had been the case with the majority of those who had come earlier. 

When in 1926 Congress passed a law putting immigration on the basis of the "national origins" of those already here, a special committee of investigators had to determine what our origins" were. 

Their conclusion was that over 41 per cent of the white people of the country in 1921 had ancestors who had come from Great Britain or North Ireland, and that those of German origin and Irish ranked second and third in number. The law required them to work out a distribution as to the quota, or number of people, who may be admitted from particular foreign countries as immigrants in one year, taking as a basis the figure 150,000 as an approximate total of immigrants in any year. The purpose of those who passed the law was to keep the national and racial background of the white population of the country just about the same as it was when the law went into effect (1929). 

Have we, then, a distinct people with characteristics that would be recognized anywhere else? The fact is that we are not so much alike that anywhere we might go one would pick out a citizen of the United States by his looks or manners, though if we could hear him talk, it would help. Since the people of the United States today have backgrounds reaching into many and varied sources, we find among them traits and characteristics belonging to most of the civilized people of the world. Even though the children of immigrants easily learn 

---

to adopt the ways of children of native Americans, it will take some time before all evidence of foreign ancestry disappears, if it ever does.¹ 

Both white and Negro are admitted on equal terms, under our present immigration laws, but few Negroes will be found in the list of immigrants from the countries mentioned in the tables below. At least 90 per cent of all the Negro people in the United States were born in this country and their parents were also native here. Among the whites, on the other hand, as late as 1930 somewhat over 38,000,000 of our people were either born in a foreign country or had one or both parents born abroad.

Do the cartoonists' drawings of Uncle Sam, John Bull, and representatives of other countries, suggest anything in the line of national characteristics? 

Are there any particular national groups sufficiently prominent in your community to deserve special attention? Do you think it is desirable to keep the population of this country about the same as it is with reference to national origins? 

117. What Immigrants Have Done for Us. In 1907, the peak year for immigration in our history, enough immigrants entered the United States to have made up a city as large as Philadelphia was at that time. How did they, and the millions who came in other years, affect the life and progress of this country? 

When immigrants began to come to this country in large numbers, factories were just becoming prominent. Perhaps the immigrant took some less desirable work and let the native American man or woman become a factory hand. Perhaps he filled a place left by one who went West in the years after 1840, if it needed filling. Then, by hundreds of thousands, immigrants got factory jobs themselves;

they made a large part of the steel and the ready-made clothes of the country; they did most of the hard work of building railroads; they mined a large share of all the coal. Only a minority of the immigrants, either "old" or "new," went on farms. Some Germans did so, however, and many Swedes, Norwegians, and Danes. In more recent years, French Canadians have crossed the line from Quebec and taken up farms in northern New England which native New Englanders had deserted.

Immigrants have also contributed to the cultural progress of this country. From immigrant peoples, especially those from southern 

Europe, have come more than their fair share of musicians and artists. 

Carl Schurz rose to a place in the cabinet of President Hayes and held other notable positions. Men like Jacob Riis and Edward Bok did much for social improvement. People such as Charles P. Steinmetz and Michael Pupin were famous in science and invention. 

On the other hand, immigrants have brought serious problems. 

Except for certain sections of the South, the largest proportion of illiteracy in our country has been found in cities with many people of foreign birth. We have already mentioned the crowding of newly arrived immigrants into quarters of our cities already occupied chiefly by foreigners. Such neighborhoods sometimes became slums. When the immigrant did take out citizenship papers, he was too often played upon by politicians who could tell him how to vote on election day. 

Such evil conditions were not entirely the fault of the immigrant. 

Often the native American did not care to associate with the newcomer, who then had to go with his own kind or else be intolerably lonesome. Sometimes native landlords got rich out of the rents they collected from immigrant families who had to live in tenements that were constant fire hazards and breeders of disease. 

Much of the story of immigration to this country is economic. 

Though some came in order to escape military service and others because they heard that people in this county were freer than elsewhere, the largest number came in the hope of being better off financially. Low wages here might have been high wages in Europe. 

Immigrant labor has been blamed for keeping wage standards low and thus making living conditions poorer on the average for all workers. 

The tide of immigration went up and down in accordance with the presence or absence of business prosperity in the United States.

Sometimes immigrants retained a marked loyalty for the country which they left when they came here. Even those who could read and write their own language were sometimes not anxious to learn English. Foreign language newspapers and other factors sometimes kept alive racial hatreds brought from the Old World. 118. What We Have Done for Our Immigrants. Our present 

National Origins Act does not apply to immigrants from Canada and Latin-American countries of the New World. To use a technical phrase, these are non-quota countries. But what a change this act represents from the time when we were glad to have everybody come here who wanted to do so! When opposition did begin, it was largely animated at first by religious feeling. Some Protestants began to fear that the country would fall under the control of the incoming Catholics from Ireland and Germany. The coming of the Civil War, however, checked immigration so much that it was not until after that period that any restrictive laws were passed. 

Immigration has not always affected different sections of the country in the same way. Before the Civil War the South had little place for immigrants because there were slaves to do the kind of work that native whites did not want to do. In the Middle West there was opportunity for people to settle on farms, and unskilled laborers could find work in the cities. To this part of the country the German, Swedish, Norwegian, and Danish immigration went in large numbers. 

Eastern factory towns and some of the other large eastern cities also took care of a large number of immigrants. The Far West had its own peculiar immigration problems, because of the Chinese and later the Japanese, of whom we will speak later. Several hundred thousand 

Mexicans have also crossed the border into the states of the Southwest. 

Our first law-restricting immigration was enacted in 1875 and called for the exclusion of people who had already shown themselves to be undesirable in their own country, such as criminals and immoral women. Then in 1882 a tax (now eight dollars) was levied on each immigrant to cover the cost of handling them at the ports of admission, and lunatics, idiots, and other people "likely to become a public charge" (L. P. C.) were excluded. In that same year the first general law against Chinese immigration was passed. 

In 1888 a law was passed forbidding the bringing in of contract laborers that is, workers hired abroad in large groups and brought here to work on some railroad or in some factory at very low wages. 

Then came prohibitions against immigrants who had contagious diseases and against polygamists. The assassination of President 

McKinley caused a law to be passed excluding anarchists. 

For years there was argument over the establishment of a literacy

test. Those who opposed it said that the main thing we wanted in an immigrant was character, and we could not test that by a person's ability or inability to read. Others maintained that anyone who lacked the ambition to learn to read and write would be unlikely to become a good American citizen. Three Presidents vetoed a law setting up a literacy test, but the third veto, given by President Wilson in 1916, was overruled by Congress. The law of that year required that an immigrant must be able to read forty words in some language or dialect.

After the World War a tremendous rush started toward the United States from Europe. Congress then decided to limit immigration sharply. After enacting two preliminary laws, the policy already mentioned of admitting immigrants from various countries in accordance with the present "national origins" of our people was adopted. 

We might harm ourselves more than anybody else if we should never admit any more immigrants. China and Japan followed that policy for some centuries, and if you have read their history, you know what happened to them. On the other hand, we certainly have a right to insist that those who come here to live should adjust themselves to our ways of living rather than expect us to adopt theirs, if there is any difference.

Would you be willing to make physical health and a clean moral record the sole tests for immigrants? Is a new country or an old country more likely to encourage immigration? Do you think Canada and Mexico should be under the same quota law that applies to other countries? 

The United States is not the only New World country to receive immigrants. Canada has its own immigration problems, but has had a relatively smaller number of applicants for admission from the countries of southern Europe. People from Italy and Spain have gone to South America. Argentina has received a good many immigrants from Europe, and so have Chile and Brazil. In Argentina some of the immigrants have proved themselves capable of rising to places of leadership in the business and political activities of the country. 

The making of an alien into a citizen is not a matter of law alone. 

There ought to be a real transfer of loyalty and spirit from the mother country to the United States. It is not easy for a person to get rid of the marks of language, habits, and ways of thought which one acquired in the country of his birth. Perhaps, therefore, there ought

to be a more kindly attitude on the part of native-born citizens to help all they can.

The public schools do much to make alien families into Americans. 

Go into a school today in which children of foreign-born parents and children of native Americans sit side by side, and you may not see a thing that would enable you to tell them apart. Through the schools adults also may find opportunities to learn English and a love for our institutions. Religious and social organizations may also help. 

Acme Photo IT'S MUTUAL 

The famous scientist Einstein is pleased to receive his final papers as a citizen of the United States, and the judge of the court which granted the papers seems equally pleased at receiving the new citizen. 

Special exercises when foreignborn men and women complete a course in "Americanization" and take the oath of allegiance as citizens of the United States may be made very impressive. 

To what extent does your own community engage in Americanization work? Has race or nationality been used in your community as a means of influencing votes?

Mention several people of recent foreign origin who have become prominent here in music, science, literature, sport, or some other field. Do you think our present immigration laws are too strict, too lenient, or about right? Why? 

119. Figures on the Future. 

Until within a few most years, of us assumed that the United States was going to keep on growing at about the same rate as in the last two or three decades. We were reassured by being told that our entire present population could settle in the state of Texas without having it as thickly populated as some of our states are already. But in the past some students of social problems feared that population might naturally increase too fast for the general good. About a century and a half ago an Englishman, Thomas R. 

Malthus, came out with the theory that population tended to increase at a greater rate than the means of supporting it, and that war, epi-

demics, and other misfortunes were a biological necessity in order to keep the population down. 

Recently, however, we have realized that contrary trends have set in. Two reasons in particular are noticeable. First is the restriction of immigration of which we have already spoken. Second is a very noticeable decline in the birth rate, which is observed also in other advanced nations. In 1915 for each 1000 people in the country there were on the average 25 births. In 1920 that ratio had come down to 23.7, in 1925 to 21.5, and in 1931 to 18. It is true that this decreasing birth rate is balanced in part by a decreasing death rate. More infants live to grow up than was formerly the case, and older people do not die so soon, on the average. The death rate for all ages combined has gone down in twenty years from about 14 to less than II per thousand. If the birth rate continues to go down, it may reach a point where it will no more than equal the death rate. Then we should have, except for immigration and emigration, an exactly stationary population. Our Census Bureau has announced, as the most satisfactory estimate it has seen, a statement that our population will probably increase slowly until about 1985 and then may start to go down.

It seems certain that in the future society is going to be considerably different from what it has been in the past. About 1800 there were in the United States 20 people under the age of 20 for every 10 people over that age. Throughout the nineteenth century that difference closed up, until in 1900 there were only about 18 people under 20 for each 20 over 20 years old. In 1935 the ratio had gone down to about 14 to 20, and in 1975 it is estimated that it will be about 10 to 20. 

Meantime the proportionate number of people who live to be over 

60 will be much greater. (See the graph on page 316.)

Such figures are significant in many ways. Already the enrollment of our elementary schools has declined, and the high schools are beginning to notice the effect. Industry will be affected by the fact that society will be asking for the things needed and desired by adults more than for the things children want. Something might happen to check or even reverse some of these trends; but if they continue, we must plan for the future on the prospect of a population that will gain very little and perhaps decline.

Is this anything to frighten us, or are we gradually moving toward

an optimum or most satisfactory figure for the population of the United States? A population that changes little from year to year should be rather easy to plan for in almost every respect. Middleaged and older people are likely to be interested in living comfortably without making great changes in their surroundings. The highest standard of living conditions in general today is found in those parts of the country in which there are small proportions of children as compared to adults. Progress hardly ever depends upon quantity of either people or things so much as on quality.

120. The Colored Man among Us. We have in this country at least a few representatives of every race. Race means, as used here, a division of the human family marked by characteristics of color, distinctive features of face, hair, and the like, which are passed on from one generation to another. In the United States there are today about 12,000,000 people of the Negro race, whom we often, for con-

venience, call "colored." Our Census Bureau in some of its statistics groups together all who are not white. On that basis there were in 

1940 in this country over 118,000,000 white and over 13,000,000 "non-white" persons.

In the whole world there are probably about as many yellow or Mongolian people as there are white or Caucasian. The Negro race numbers about one-sixth of the white race, and the Malay and Indian, if we count them as separate, are about and 10 of the whole population of the world, respectively. Asia and its neighboring islands have a much larger proportion of yellow and brown races than any other parts of the world. Negroes are found more extensively in Africa than elsewhere, yellow men in the Far East, and white in Europe and the New World, with a considerable representation in other continents.

For many years relations between white and colored seemed to offer problems almost solely in the South. Recently colored people have moved North to work in mills, and some of the same questions have appeared there. In the South colored people may work for whites as they did in white families in slavery days, but the southern white man thinks that schools, churches, railroad cars, and public places of all kinds should offer separate accommodations for white and colored.

Colored people have not always agreed about this point. Some of them, of whom Booker T. Washington, perhaps the most famous of all American Negroes since the Civil War, was a representative, feel that the colored man would do best to try to succeed as a colored man and not insist on mingling socially with white people. Others have insisted that there should be no discrimination between white and colored, even if the separate privileges provided for colored people were as good as those intended for the white which was not always the case.

In northern communities colored children usually attend the same schools as white children. When colored people are numerous, however, in a certain section, they are likely to have separate churches, and one or more schools may be composed wholly or largely of colored children. 

Think of the situation in general of the colored people of the United States at the close of the Civil War, with a background of 250 years of slavery, and then suddenly set free. Outside of a chance to earn a living for themselves, what they needed most was an opportunity

for education. Yet it has been asserted that colored schools in the 

South have often received less attention and care than the white schools, and that often colored children seemed to care very little whether they went to school or not. Illiteracy among the southern colored people, however, went down from about 70 per cent in 1880 to 16 per cent in 1930.

Outside of the public schools, a number of private institutions, some of them established as missionary enterprises by northerners, have

The two most famous schools for Negroes are undoubtedly Hampton Institute in Virginia and Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, founded by Booker T. Washington, himself a graduate of Hampton. Men like Booker T. Washington and his successor, Robert R. Moton, had qualities that would fit them for leadership anywhere.

Colored people have risen to prominence in the professions. In 

1930 there were over 25,000 clergymen among them, 4000 artists,

nearly 4000 physicians and surgeons, more than 50,000 teachers, more than 10,000 musicians and music teachers, and a considerable number of lawyers and dentists. Jesse Owens and Joe Louis represent achievement along physical lines. The great bulk of the Negro workers, however, were employed on farms or were engaged in some kind of domestic service or manual work. 

Colored people in the North sometimes feel that industrially their opportunities are limited. The occupations open to them are perfectly honorable, but an ambitious boy or girl may be pardoned for moments of discouragement. But after all, what would have happened if colored people had all stayed in Africa? Perhaps they should not be too greatly discontented over what they do not have here.

One special cause of bitterness on the part of the colored man has been the lynchings of people of his race. It is a kind of lawlessness which no decent person will defend, but special legislation against it in Congress has thus far failed. Thinking people, white or colored, North or South, realize the need of a square deal and understanding between people of different colors. Special efforts have been made through commissions and organizations of various kinds to study the problems affecting white and colored alike, and try to reach a fair solution.

121. The Yellow Man among Us. Black men were forced to come here from Africa; yellow men came of their own accord from _____

Asia. Colored people number one in ten of our whole population, Chinese and Japanese about one in four hundred. The problem of the yellow man is difficult only on the Pacific coast. 

During the gold rush to California in 1849 Chinamen were welcomed, for when the white men rushed off to hunt for gold, Chinese could be useful in doing less exciting things that were even more necessary. When more Chinese wanted to come to this country, loud outcries against them were raised by those who said that "Chinese cheap labor" would ruin American workers. A treaty with the 

Chinese government in 1878 authorized the United States to "regulate" Chinese immigration into this country. In 1882 Congress "regulated" it by passing the Chinese Exclusion Act, which completely forbade the immigration of Chinese laborers. This first act was to cover a ten-year period, but it was later renewed, and now the exclusion of Chinese immigrants is a part of our permanent policy. 

Most of us in the East know the Chinese as laundrymen, storekeepers, or college students for a considerable number of Chinese have attended our colleges and universities and have usually been keen and interested learners. Some Chinese have become skillful as physicians and surgeons and as teachers and office workers. In 

California most of the Chinese own or work on farms or own or work in restaurants and lunchrooms.

At first there was not the same feeling against the Japanese as against the Chinese, but as the Japanese kept on coming, were quick to learn, and would do acceptable work for low pay, they too faced hostility. In 1907 President Theodore Roosevelt arranged a "gentleman's agreement" with Japan under which each government refused to issue passports to laborers who wanted to go to the other country. 

This arrangement "saved the face" of the Japanese, but was of course really very one-sided, for no American laborers wanted to go to work in Japan. A few years later California passed a law forbidding any alien to become a landowner if he could not become a United States citizen. This restriction provoked the Japanese considerably, but the climax came in the provision of the immigration law of 1924 which forbade the admission to the United States for permanent residence of people of any country who were not eligible to become citizens. 

Many Americans felt that this slap at the Japanese was unnecessary, for if the immigration of yellow races had been limited by the same

What are the chief arguments against Chinese and Japanese immigration? Those who favor exclusion say that Asiatic standards of wages and living conditions are such that our own people cannot compete with them except by lowering our standard to theirs. It is asserted: "We have one race problem already; let's not have another."

Today most of us feel more kindly toward China than toward Japan. 

Why? Because we have seen Japan "pick on" China and help herself to territory on the mainland of Asia in a way contrary to solemn treaties which Japan had signed along with the other great nations. 

Some have also feared that if Japan did succeed in bringing the whole Far East under its control, it might then turn around and tell the white

nations "where to get off." That was the so-called "yellow peril."

Japan's leaning toward the same ideas in government as those of Germany and Italy has also caused us to think less of them. It is a shame that a people who have shown so much ability should not have realized that they could have won from China by friendship the leadership in the Far East that they desire and have held our good will at the same time.

Do you, whatever your own color, have any unpleasant feeling toward people of another color? If so, what do you think is the cause of it? Do you think sensational stories or moving pictures have any effect upon the feeling of races toward one another? What Far Eastern policy would you recommend for the United States at the present time? What other Asiatic people than Chinese or Japanese have caused some dissatisfaction among white people? 

122. The Original American. —No, he was neither Christopher

Columbus nor George Washington. No one has proved where the people whom we call Indians came from, if indeed they did come from anywhere outside of America. The story of past relations between white men and Indians is one which we do not care to brag about today. 

White men helped themselves to whatever land they wanted, broke treaties with the Indians, and made whole tribes leave their native homes and move hundreds of miles to reservations which the white man probably thought were not worth much. 

Happily, things are better today. There are now over 300,000 

Indians in the United States, maybe more than when Columbus came, and every one of them is considered a citizen. The Indian is no longer "the vanishing American," as we once thought it was smart to call him. Indian wars, we hope, are all over. Many Indians live in all respects the same as their white neighbors. Half of the children of 

Indian families were in 1930 enrolled in the regular public schools. 

Indians served in the World War and contributed to Liberty Loans even more generously than the average white man. 

Since by far the greater part of the Indians of the United States are engaged in farming or ranching, the land is still the Indian's chief source of support. Many of the Indians live on reservations set apart for their exclusive use. Most of these are in the West, but even 

New York State has its Indian reservations where a few thousands of the original native Americans live.

People of many faiths and different ancestries helped to found and develop the colonies which grew into our nation. People of still more faiths and ancestries live under the Stars and Stripes today. 

In this country, whatever we may think about equality of all men in practice, the theory is that all men are entitled to equal rights under the law. It is sometimes hard for people to believe that another man's ideas in religion, politics, or economics can be held with sincerity, but in a free country we have to admit that such differences are possible, and that he has a right to hold them. 

With no disrespect to people of other colors, perhaps there is such a thing as "the white man's burden." White nations have been in the lead in making the history of the world. If the white man's example is what it ought to be, it must be one of good will and the square deal. There can be no real contentment when one race sets out to show its mastery over others, and the others feel oppressed or snubbed.

Understanding one another as individuals and as nations ought to bring peace and good will. Loyalty to one's own convictions and to his associates is a real virtue, but there is a difference between loyalty, prejudice, and hate. To "agree to disagree" is sometimes one of the finest evidences of good citizenship.

XII  

Of all the groups or associations to which we belong, the family comes first in time, and for most of us continues to rank high in importance. 

No substitute for it has yet appeared that satisfies any considerable number of people. Yet, like almost everything else, it has its problems. Its members are individuals and are not always able to get along harmoniously. Outside influences may strain the bonds that hold it together. 

But if anything happens to the family as an institution, society will have to be rebuilt on a different foundation. 

Some Questions: 

1. What is the place of the family in social life? 

2. What changes in family life have taken place? 

3. How does family life mold the characteristics of its members? 

4. How is family life influenced by its material surroundings? 

5. How may government and society safeguard family life? 

6. What are the prospects for future successful family life? 

124. What the Home Does for Its Members. It is said that only six languages have a word for home, though every tongue has a word for house. A house is a building in which one may live. A home is the life lived in a house or associated with it. A family is the group of people whose associations make up a home. Our Census 

Bureau defines it as "a group of people related by birth, marriage, or adoption, living together as one household." Father, mother, and children compose the ordinary family, but often other relatives form a part of the group. 

The care and training of children rank high among family activities. 

The average boy or girl knows little of life during the first few years except what he gets through the home. There we receive those first impressions which are so hard to wipe out. Indeed, those who establish the home pass on their own characteristics to their children. 

In the home the child learns to talk and to acquire the habits and customs of civilized society. If he does not in the home learn to obey, to co-operate, to sympathize, to help, and to be loyal, it is 

329

just too bad for him and for his associates. The home protects the child when no other agency would care about him. It helps its members to act together to serve their common interests, and to have a place of encouragement and refuge in trouble. No other institution touches life at so many points or can do so much to build character and cultivate personality. 

Harold M. Lambert ALL OUT FOR THE PICNIC 

This group suggests that family life is happy for all of them. 

How many things that now form a regular part of your daily activities did you learn first outside the home? Under what circumstances might children's interests be better looked after outside a home than in it? Could one person constitute a family? 

125. Homes of Yesterday. Even primitive parents brought up their children and protected the members of their families in accordance with their own standards of life just the same as today. 

Some of the relationships found among human families in primitive times, however, we do not approve today. For example, today we consider the best relation between man and wife to be monogamy · one husband and one wife. We can find numerous examples in history, however, of polygamy, which might mean a relation in which 

---

either one husband has several wives or one wife has several husbands. Most often the father has been recognized as the head of the family, but we can find instances in which the mother had first place-patriarchal and matriarchal families, respectively. 

Among the first civilized peoples that we know about, such as the Egyptians, the Hebrews, the Greeks, and the Romans, the family was extremely important. The father had a place of dignity and 3.2-3-4 3.5-3-7

Among the ancient Romans, the patria potestas, or the father's authority, permitted him even to put a child to death for what he considered sufficient reasons. The father was, among many peoples, a sort of priest as well as a family leader. 

Families of yesterday were much larger, on the average, than today.

Once the family was largely self-contained and self-supporting. 

Food was raised and prepared by the same household that used it. 

Clothing was spun and woven by the people who wore it or their fellow workers in the home. Fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, worked and occasionally played together. Even young children had chores to do which made their little contribution to the family

Philip D. Gendreau comfort. The mother probably taught the children their "letters" and the girls how to sew and cook. Children's first religious ideas might come through saying their prayers at mother's knee or listening to the saying of grace at the table.

The typical home of the old days, even at its best, would seem crude in many respects. A hundred years ago the richest family could not have electric lights, washing machines, or vacuum sweepers, and probably did not have a bathtub. Early to bed and early to rise was the regular practice in all well-managed families. There was not much encouragement to read by the artificial light available in

colonial days, even if one knew how. Yet all these things were not wholly disadvantages. People had to learn to be self-reliant and to be ingenious in making use of their limited means for comfort and convenience. 

When people go out camping today, do they find out how people in general had to live a hundred or a hundred and fifty years ago? Is it possible for a family to live today on the same basis as a medieval family or one in our own colonial times? 

126. Modern Trends in Family Life. The Industrial Revolution brought about numerous changes in family life. Opportunities for work outside the home were multiplied, and dozens of conveniences introduced into the home. Few would be willing to work as many hours of the day as almost every worker once expected to put in. 

Not only children but adults complain if they do not have some kind of amusement. Some people even think they are being abused if they do not have the chance to spend money to go to a show on Sunday. "Why bother," the housewife might say, "to put up fruits or vegetables when I can buy them in cans? Why waste my energy baking bread when I can buy it from the corner grocer? Why wear myself out with a needle when I can find almost everything readymade at the department store or even the 5-and-10?" But it is still useful for a girl to know how to cook and sew and knit. 

Hardly anybody except the mother regularly spends a large part of the daytime at home. If the family is "well fixed" financially, probably one or more maids will do the housework. In our towns and cities, the father and the older boys and girls may be out working. 

The children spend a good share of their waking hours at school or at play outside. Father may have his lodge or club for the evening. 

Even mother may have her bridge club, church activities, or other outside interests. And there are always the movies. 

Let us recognize, however, that these outside interests may give a welcome variety to life. Boy Scout and Girl Scout organizations may build character as well as provide interesting recreation. The occasional bridge party, dinner-out, or something else, may take the place of the family calling which occurs now so seldom. 

The automobile and the radio have also had a great effect upon family life, but have they intensified or counteracted the influences that once were drawing families apart? The family can all go out 

---

in the same car, though they do not always do so, and they do not even have to go out to listen to Charlie McCarthy or Jack Benny. 

Let us be thankful if there are some forces that help to strengthen home ties. It is too bad if a person is considered abnormal if he really prefers to be at home rather than somewhere else.

Have changes in family life equally affected large communities, villages, and rural districts? Which kind of community seems to you to offer the best opportunities for desirable family life? Is it a sign of progress or otherwise when the members of a family depend on people outside their own number to furnish the ordinary comforts and necessities of life? 

127. Building Personality. The home can do much to develop in its members a colorless or a striking personality, and to encourage the children of the family to become men and women whose acquaint-

ance will be considered desirable by others. Among the personal qualities which vary considerably among individuals are the following: 

1. Vitality. A person may be "full of pep," active, eager to go somewhere or do something new. Someone else might be listless or lazy, would work only under some kind of compulsion, or would be unable to stand very much strain or expenditure of energy. And in between them there might be many who would not be notable in either direction. 

2. Resourcefulness. Some people are able to look out for themselves. They are willing to try new things, to be pioneers. They can readily adapt themselves to new situations or emergencies. Others prefer to follow somebody else's example. They wait to see what "they" are doing before they make up their minds what to do themselves. Sometimes they can do reasonably well a thing that can become a matter of habit, but they always remain "routineer" rather than pioneer. 

3. Sociability. Here we may distinguish four grades. The social are those who like to be with others, and whose company others enjoy. 

The non-social have no particular liking for the company of others. 

They are uncomfortable in meeting other people, except in a casual or routine way, yet sometimes, when by themselves, can think and plan with considerable success. The pseudo-social are those who do not care for other people, but who, for the sake of what they can gain by it, are willing to pretend to a sociability which they do not actually enjoy. They can be "glad-handers," on occasion, but are out of place in situations that require a sincere and honest interest in one's fellow men. The anti-social are those who are against society as they find it, and may even try to overthrow it. In this class also belongs the extremely selfish person, who does not care what happens to others so long as his own comfort or profit is secure. 

4. Intelligence. This quality relates to one's natural ability to learn, rather than to the amount of things he knows. The I. Q., or intelligence quotient, which was given you after you took an intelligence test, was intended to compare your learning ability with that of others. It is expressed in figures on a basis that takes 100 as a sort of average. One who is ranked 130 or more is distinctly superior; some might rate him as a genius. There are few such. If the I. Q. is from 110 to 130, one may be classified as bright. He ought to do a

high quality of work in school and get along well in his outside activities. I. Q.'s from 90 to 110 are average. 

Within this range come the great bulk of people, young and old. An I. Q. from 70 to 90 indicates one who does not learn easily but is not hopelessly lacking in capacity. Such people are often classified as dull normal. An 

I. Q. below 70 indicates that a person is seriously lacking in mental ability. He may be able to do passably well things of a routine character, or those that require only manual skill or physical strength. 

There has been considerable argument lately as to whether one's I. Q. changes as he grows older or whether when once determined it can be considered fixed for the rest of his life. Some experiments indicate that the kind of training given in infancy has much to do with the mental capacity which one shows after getting beyond that stage. As one's information and experience increase, he probably would be able to show up somewhat better on some intelligence tests. But the fact remains that there are the various grades of ability which we have already pointed out, and as far as we can tell, they will always be found.

Another element that sometimes is significant in personality is the attitude one takes toward others. It may be the attitude of superiority shown by one who thinks he is better than other people and indicates it in his manner and speech. He may need to seek advice oftener than he is willing to take it. Such people, however, may succeed in politics and business because their confidence in themselves sometimes makes others take them at their own estimate. 

The inferiority attitude, on the other hand, may be a distinct handicap. A person may feel that he is less capable than he really is, and always wait to be told by someone else what to do. Occasionally these superiority and inferiority "complexes," as they are often called, lead to unexpected results. The person with a superiority complex may fail to prepare himself properly for some situation, and may antagonize others by his display of self-assurance. The person with an inferiority complex sometimes tries to conceal it by acts of bravado or violence. He may indulge in profanity to impress people with the idea that he is "hard boiled." Sometimes physical cripples, when put into a position of authority, have exhibited vindictiveness and brutality that would not be understandable except on this explanation.

A wise parent or teacher will watch for evidence of these various qualities and seek to encourage or restrain them, as may be needed. 

One may also do something toward developing or restraining his own attitudes or tendencies, when he discovers what they are. 

Is distinctive individuality to be encouraged or discouraged in a person? 

What do you understand by rugged individualism? Is there any advantage or disadvantage in being the oldest child, the youngest child, a sibling (a single brother or sister), one of twins, an adopted child?

In considering the physical stages of life, five periods are commonly marked out: (1) Infancy is the period when the child is too young to do anything important for himself and has to be constantly cared for by older people. 

It commonly is thought of as covering the years up to 5 or 6. (2) Childhood covers the period from 5 or 6 to about 12. 

The child can look out for himself to a certain extent, can control himself physically to a greater extent than the infant, and should be able to realize his responsibility for the welfare of others. (3) Adolescence includes the ages from about 12 to 20. Rapid growth physically takes place during this period, and mental and emotional changes also occur, sometimes rapidly, sometimes slowly. It is a period when selfcontrol and self-responsibility ought to be developed, but which frequently needs good advice and occasionally restraint. (4) Maturity is the period when one has reached approximately his full growth physically and has become fully responsible before the law and otherwise for his conduct. The age of maturity runs from 21 to 60 or 70. (5) Senescence, or old age, is the last of these five periods. By this time physical strength has reached its peak and started downward. Mental capacity may be just as vigorous at 80 as at 40, but in some cases it weakens along with physical decline.

The dividing lines between one of these five stages or periods and the next are not just the same for everybody. Some adults never show much mental capacity or stability of character. Many a high school or college student under 21 would vote on election day much more seriously and intelligently than half those whose votes are counted. Some people are old at 50. Others are lively at 80, like 

King Gustav V who still enjoyed his game of tennis at that age. But the five stages which we have already pointed out are typical, and in the lifetime of the average individual they appear rather definitely.

How large a part of the life of man is included in the three earlier periods as compared with the corresponding part of the life of such an animal as a horse? 

Why is the difference important? Which of these five stages, in your opinion, is or ought to be the happiest? Which is or ought to be the most satisfying?' 

128. Women and Men in Society. Homes without women would surely be much less satisfactory than they are now, for it is rare that one finds a man who takes naturally or kindly to the various duties of home management. Among many people, both ancient and recent, the idea has prevailed that "women's place is in the home." Even the last of the German Kaisers is said to have declared that Kinder, Kirche, und Küche represented women's function in life — children, church, and the kitchen. Prehistoric women, it is true, planted grain and helped to harvest it—and some do yet. 

But as city life has developed, there has been a steadily increasing tendency for women to do less of the outdoor manual work, while at the same time their fields of activity in factories, stores, and offices have greatly broadened. Among the ancient civilized people, Hebrews and Greeks gave woman a place of honor in the home, but seldom thought she should do much outside of it. Among the ancient 

Egyptians and Romans women were sometimes given places of leadership in society as well as in the home. What the Hebrew wise man thought were good qualities in women are listed in the thirty first chapter of Proverbs. Read it. 

Nature has seen to it that the number of men and women the world over does not differ very greatly. In the longer-settled communities the number of women may be slightly larger than the number of men. 

That is true in some of our eastern states. In pioneer communities we find a considerable margin in the other direction, as in the mountain states of the West. In 1940 Nevada had about 124 men for every 100 women, but in the District of Columbia the figures were 

91 to 100 in favor of the women.

Outside of the home women's work has taken them particularly into the field of teaching, where some people think they have a larger place than is really desirable. Women somehow have a knack of dealing with little children that many men do not have, but when the children are grown up to junior high school age or higher, many think that they should be in contact with men as much as with women. 

Those who believe in separate education for girls and for boys may

not agree with that statement, for in such schools the tendency is for the faculty to be of the same sex as the pupils. 

For the change in the way society as a whole looks upon women's life, women are probably more responsible than men. Women felt that there was no reason for classifying them with insane, idiots, and children. So they have gained places in professions other than teaching, and some positions of prominence in the business world. nurt

The expectation which some had that women would clean things up in politics has hardly been achieved. But there is no good answer to the argument that simple justice allows women to express their opinions on how we are governed as well as men. 

Family life today may be more of a partnership proposition than it was in the days when women were either set up on a pedestal to be adored or else made household drudges. Women have not yet in every state acquired equal rights in the ownership and disposal of property with men, but such equality will probably come in time.

Mail reaches this family's home in the Smoky Mountains, but they are cut off from many contacts with the rest of the world. They have "all outdoors" but not much else. may apply these principles in their dress, their home equipment, and otherwise.

The worst places to live in are, of course, the slums. The word suggests at once a neighborhood where streets are narrow and dirty, where houses are old and in poor repair, where light and ventilation are absent or scanty, where cleanliness is difficult and perhaps unpopular, and where disease finds it easy to get a foothold. One finds such conditions most frequently in the older portions of towns and cities. It is unfair to blame all such conditions on the landlord, for

in too many cases the people who live there make no effort to do any better. Using the bathtub to keep coal in and throwing waste paper over a front lawn are practices that we may joke about but are too serious to treat lightly. Social workers today often insist that any suitable living quarters must have provisions for heating from a furnace or other central plant, running water, and sanitary toilet facilities, as well as reasonable light and ventilation. Most of our cities have ordinances requiring any new tenements or apartments to meet with standards of decency in these matters, but it has not been easy to get rid of the old kind. 

Not all slum conditions are in the large cities. In our small towns and out in the country are plenty of places even yet without running water, and with no better sanitary facilities than farms had a century ago. It is easier to arrange for facilities of that character in cities with modern sewer systems than where each farmhouse has to install its own equipment.

To set up desirable conditions for clean and happy home life is a matter of both education and finance. Some of us who are too lazy to be willing to shovel snow or care for the furnace and to whom flowers and grass mean nothing prefer to coop ourselves up in an apartment with perhaps dozens of other families. But when some families have looked for places where they could be clean and have some respectable home life of their own, they have not been able to find them except at a cost which they could not hope to meet. 

What, in your opinion, are the relative advantages or disadvantages of hotels, apartments, tenements, or single houses as places to live in? If there are slum conditions in any portion of your own community, how did they come into existence? Is there any possibility of getting rid of them? 

In your community is the cost of rents a real handicap to decent living for any large number of families? 

130. Some Housing Problems. When a family lives in a house which it owns itself, it is likely to feel a much keener interest in keeping it in good condition than if it depends upon a landlord to make all repairs or improvements. Home-owning gives one a settled feeling that he cannot have when each May I or September 1 may mean a new change of address. The home-owner is a part of the community such as the renter cannot expect to be. A community with many home-owners is likely to be a pleasant place to live in. 

01 23 2

But home-owning sometimes has its difficulties. Some families do not know when the head of the house will be sent to a different town or city to live. What if they had invested in a dwelling house that they could not sell? A home-owner does not have to pay out money for rent every month, but he does have to meet tax bills and be responsible for repairs and improvements. Communities differ greatly in the proportion of their residents who own the places where they live. Manhattan Borough in New York

Efforts to provide improved housing facilities for our people, especially in the cities, have received a great deal of attention in recent years. Some believe that private corporations should be formed to undertake extensive housing projects, perhaps with government help, but others insist that governments, national, state, or local, should construct such communities themselves. As examples of what might be done, the so-called Resettlement Administration started in 1933 to build some "model communities," of which Arthurdale in West Virginia and Greenbelt just outside of

Federal Home Loan Banks was started, to make loans to building and loan associations and other agencies engaged in lending money to home-owners on mortgages. Then in 1933, as a means of saving many homes that were mortgaged and in danger of being lost by their previous owners, the 

Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) was organized. 131. Making a Successful Home. A home could hardly be called successful unless it was marked by these three characteristics: happiness, comfort, and decent morals. Happiness is not merely a matter of money, as many rich men have found to their sorrow, but the question of income is a thing to be taken into account in planning for the establishment of a home. There is no use in imagining that two can 

1914 Fairchild Aerial Surveys, Incorporated A MODEL VILLAGE FOR MILL WORKERS 

These dwellings have been put up by the company which employs many of the members of the families who live in these houses. live as cheaply as one, but careful planning for the spending of what one does receive can do wonders to make a small income go a long way. 

A successful home is characterized by friendliness and respect on the part of its members toward one another. Children obey their parents, but parents are careful not to be mere tyrants. Every member of a family has a right to expect when he is doing his best that every other member has confidence in him and wishes him well. 

Some of the difficulties in family life come from the fact that the weaknesses and blunders of members of the family are discovered at such close range as to make it hard to overlook them.

Good health has much to do with family happiness and contentment. That is one reason why decent housing conditions are important. If one or more in a family suffer from prolonged ill health, old age, or other misfortune that keeps them completely out of participation in the activities of ordinary people, a perplexing question is sometimes raised as to whether such people are really better off in the home of their children or grandchildren or in some institution where they will associate with others in the same situation as they are.

Responsibility for the success of a home is not limited to the older members of it. Children who are old enough to think and act for themselves certainly cannot escape their share of obligation. Sometimes parents are overindulgent. Father should be something else than a walking checkbook, and mother should have other recreation than washing and ironing the family clothes. Children have a right to expect father and mother to give them the care and affection that parents ought to show to welldisposed children, but the relationship works both ways. Children may not be able to add very much income to the family treasury, but there are plenty of little things around the home which even a young child can do, and many courtesies that make a hard day's work less tiresome.

What is the reasonable responsibility of young people toward parents or grandparents who are no longer able to care for themselves properly? In a successful home, do you suppose money matters would be a frequent subject of conversation? If so, in what respect?

132. The Home and the Law. In every civilized country laws have been enacted for the protection of family relationships. In this country our Constitution has given Congress no power over such matters, with the result that each state has its own laws on the subject and those laws sometimes differ in a rather embarrassing way. 

Especially is this true of laws which concern getting married or getting unmarried.

Not only here but elsewhere, marriage may have both a religious and a civil aspect. The Roman Catholic church considers marriage one of the seven sacraments, and desires that it should be performed in the church. Most other religious bodies also wish the marriage ceremony to be performed by a clergyman. In some European countries a "civil" marriage is required before some public official. 

In such cases two ceremonies are often performed. Laws in the 

United States accept either a religious or a civil ceremony. Any recognized priest, rabbi, or minister, or such official as a mayor, justice of the peace, or alderman, may perform marriages. 

Practically all states have an age requirement for marriage, which frequently is twenty-one years for the man and eighteen for the woman, with exceptions under those ages permitted if one or both of the parents consent. Some states also ask for physical examinations and do not permit the marriage of people with dangerous diseases. Usually the marriage of persons closely related by birth is forbidden. 

Most states require the taking out of a license in advance, and some demand that this shall be done some days ahead of time in order to prevent runaway marriages on the part of people who could not be married in their own state. 

Details of divorce laws in the states are at least as diverse as those of their marriage laws. In South Carolina no divorces whatever are granted. In New York the only recognized ground is adultery. 

But in some states ten or more reasons are accepted by law, and these may be so worded as to cover almost any situation drunkenness, incompatibility, physical or mental cruelty, desertion, or misrepresentation of facts at the time of marriage. 

The lack of uniformity in marriage and divorce laws has produced a great deal of confusion and many awkward situations. A person may be considered married in one state and divorced in another a situation which may lead to all kinds of difficulties in regard 

---

to property holding, the rights of children, inheritances, and many other matters. Some states have disgraced themselves by passing easy marriage and divorce laws in order to make a little money out of people who will come there to take advantage of them. It has been proposed to amend our national Constitution so as to give Congress the power to pass nation-wide marriage and divorce laws, but public sentiment has not yet become strong enough to force any action on this subject.

Some of our laws touch the home directly or indirectly, at other points than with reference to marriage and divorce. Laws requiring husbands to support their wives, and parents to support their children, have some value in keeping homes together. Laws requiring school attendance or forbidding child labor have a relationship to home conditions, as do laws regulating the hours and conditions of women's work outside the home, mothers' pension laws, and the like. Divorces HOW TIMES HAVE CHANGED 

Do you think the increasing proportion of divorces to marriages indicates a lower standard of married life or a greater willingness to let disagreements become publicly known? disapproval, in recent years there has been one divorce for every six or seven marriages. The record of the United States in this matter is the worst of any nation that keeps statistics on the subject. 

The fact that a very large number of divorces occur within five years after the marriage indicates that hasty marriage and lack of preparation for home-making is one of the most frequent reasons for broken homes and resulting divorces. When the husband's income will not spread over two people satisfactorily; when the wife has no idea of the way to take care of a home properly; when either or both are accustomed to having their own way; when either or both are jealous, something unpleasant is likely to happen. The number of moving picture or theatrical stars who obtain divorces suggests that a career such as they are engaged in is not conducive to happy married

life. Sometimes when women are employed outside the home, they lose interest in home affairs or cannot care properly for the children in the family. And if they can get outside jobs, they may not be ready to put up with unpleasant conditions at home. Almost two thirds of all divorces are given to women. That does not necessarily mean that women are more ill-treated than men, for it frequently happens that when both parties are discontented, the man permits the suit for divorce to be entered by the woman rather than do it himself.

One of the saddest features of divorce cases or broken homes for other causes is the effect upon children. In 1930, 38 per cent of all divorce cases on record involved children. What ideas of married life can they have when they have seen their own family break up and perhaps find themselves forced to spend part of the year in one place and part in another, or to face other awkward situations resulting from the public knowledge that their parents had been divorced? 

The attitude of religious bodies on divorce is not uniform. The 

Roman Catholic Church refuses to grant divorces, though sometimes it will "annul" marriages which it is believed should not have been performed in the first place. Protestant churches for the most part have no fixed rules, but many Protestant ministers will not perform the marriage ceremony for divorced persons. If a marriage was a mistake in the first place, or a man and wife are hopelessly unhappy together, it ought to be possible to make some adjustment. In many cases a legal separation, rather than a divorce that would permit a divorcee to marry immediately, might be the best way out. But certainly some strengthening of sentiment against easy divorce is essential.

Would you expect a decline in religious interest to be accompanied by an increase in the number of divorces? Should a "career" for married women be any different than for married men? How do you explain the fact that there are almost no divorces among women who are college graduates? 

When, if at all, is the payment of alimony justifiable in a divorce case? When, if at all, should divorced persons be allowed to marry again? 

134. Substitutes for the Home. Many things which were once done in the home are now done better outside the home than they probably would be performed in it. Schooling, for instance, seems to come under that head. Today we expect the school not only to 

---

teach the three R's, but also to furnish the shop training, domestic science, and the like, which once children naturally picked up at home without thinking it was education. The laws of our states even put the teacher "in loco parentis" — in the place of the parent. 

That is, the teacher, during the time that children are lawfully under his control, has the authority over them that the parent has elsewhere.

Many families no longer feel any direct responsibility for religious training. Churches, Sunday schools, and young people's organizations of various kinds are expected to look out for that. Of course the ultimate responsibility for this rests upon the home, for no outside body can compel children to receive its services contrary to the wishes of parents.

The state has also taken over much of the responsibility of the family for the health of its members. It may even quarantine a person against his will and sometimes insists that insane and feebleminded people should be put into institutions instead of having them cared for ineffectively at home. Many of our cities and towns also provide means of recreation instead of assuming that children can amuse themselves. 

Will an outside institution do better for children than their home would do? Certainly not in every case. Can the very best of "scientific care" take the place of the affection and personal interest that a good parent feels for his own children? Can any child who is just one of dozens or hundreds in an institution receive consideration as an individual that he could get as a member of a family? 

We must have our institutions, however, for children who need them. Children who have lost their parents, and those whose families do not know how or are unable to look after them properly, will be better off under the care of kind-hearted matrons and nurses. The modern juvenile court often provides foster homes for those whose own home life is lacking in proper conditions. Some of our children's homes and asylums, and institutions like Girard College and Mooseheart, have put many unfortunate youths under great obligation. 

If you have visited a children's home or similar institution, did you get the impression that the children were really happy? Do you think adopted children appreciate home life more, or less, than children who have never known anything else? Do you think the assumption by the province of

Ontario of the education of the Dionne "quints" was a suitable example of the interference of a government in private family life? 

135. Young People and Their Elders. It was once an accepted theory that "children should be seen and not heard," even though in the times when that theory was common young people left the home and went out to earn their own living sooner and more often than they do today. The ideal relationship, however, is not one in which the older members of the family constantly have to appear to be holding the younger ones back from something.

Young people sometimes do not realize their own responsibility for the maintenance of a happy home life. They talk about their right to "self-expression" and about "living their own life." They are too often not willing to learn from those who have been through just such experiences as their own. A suggestion that it would be better not to do a certain thing may result in the adviser's being called an old fogy or mid-Victorian. 

If there could be the same quality of cordiality, friendliness, and good will between parents and children as between children and their chums of equal age, conditions in many homes would be much better than they are. Sometimes when misunderstandings arise, the cause seems to be that modern conditions do not permit children and parents to have many things in common. A member of President 

Hoover's Cabinet once said that he could find nothing for his boy to do at home except keep the garage door shut. If the family has a maid, little is left for the girls to do.

Naturally one might think it unreasonable if he were expected to stay at home all the time and play checkers or croquet when he liked tennis, baseball, or swimming better. But there are all kinds of things that both the older and the younger members of a family might do together. If the young people of a family do not learn to adjust. themselves rightly to family and community life, they are not getting very good preparation for the time when conditions will be reversed and they will be the members of the family whose advice may be disliked by those who think they want to be "modern."

What are some features of home or social life which interest young people that were uncommon or unknown a century ago? Do you suppose boys and girls of today think more, or less, about the social, economic, and political problems of the time than boys and girls did a half century ago? It has been

said that every generation thinks that the young people of its day are going to the dogs. If that were true, who would be to blame? What examples, if any, have you seen of parental neglect or of conduct on the part of young people which brought misfortune or unhappiness to a whole family? 

136. Training for Successful Home Life. — Very few boys or girls leave high school or college with a deliberate intention of never marrying, and some of those few change their minds. Three out of four men and women do marry at some time or other. Since home life is the normal future to which such a large proportion of us look forward, surely preparations for that home life should be a part of one's education. 

Certainly the school can help to train both boys and girls to be self-reliant and to have an understanding of the world in which they live, and to encourage thrift and economy. In some homes, older children naturally learn how to care for younger ones, but where that opportunity is not afforded at home, the school and perhaps the church may be expected to help parents in this important feature of family life. It is not a bad idea for boys as well as girls to be able in emergencies to cook an eatable meal, to sew on buttons, and to know how and when certain other features of home routine should be done.

XIII  

Solving problems of any character involves both an understanding of the facts relating to those problems and the right attitude toward their solution. Some of the dark events in history occurred not only because people in general did not know the truth, but because their leaders did not want them to know it. How, then, may we set up proper standards to judge our own conduct and the conduct and policies of others? What forces may work toward the establishment of the good life among us? 

Some Questions: 

1. How do we set up standards and why are these standards important? 

2. Why is crime a serious problem and what can we do about it? 

3. How may we establish sound moral standards? 

4. What ideals and attitudes should we hold with reference to the development of our own talents and our proper relations to others? 

5. How important is religion in our life? 

6. What should be the relation between religious organizations and the community or the nation? 

7. What hope do we have for establishing the good life for individuals and society? 

137. Standards and Who Sets Them. Perhaps you have heard a person say, "There ought to be a law about that." Perhaps there ought, but community standards are sometimes more powerful than laws. If somehow a law is passed with which the majority in a community do not agree, it will be almost impossible to enforce it. 

A standard, as we have seen (§ 70), is a basis of judgment by which thought or conduct may be rated. It may concern personal habits, practices in business, personal relations between individuals, or the policy of a community. Community standards may not represent the individual will of every member, but they do indicate the feeling or ideals of the community in general. 

Now who determines what these standards shall be? One important influence is precedent, habit, or custom. Will stores keep open evenings? In some places, "No" for the big ones but "Yes" for 

359

many small ones. In others not at all except as a special individual favor. If you ask why, the only answer may be, "We've done so as long as I can remember."

The home is the place in which most of us get our first ideals with reference to anything. The school and the church come next. The newspaper and the movie may also have a vital part in determining both individual and community standards. Community leaders 

ANOTHER NEW ENGLAND TOWN 

This tree-shaded street in Woodbury, Connecticut, is a type of those that make so many New England towns attractive to their own people and to visitors. How would community standards here be likely to compare with those in other places that you know? may exert considerable influence upon community standards of conduct, though sometimes one makes himself a leader by coming out strongly in favor of what the majority of the community want anyway.

It is often hard to decide how some particular habit, practice, custom, or ideal originated. It may have been the result of preaching and instruction in church and school. It may be a merely temporary fashion or fad which has become popular for no particular reason.

It may represent a practice or a point of view that served the selfish advantage of some individual or class and was unconsciously accepted by those who were not benefited, because they could not help doing So. To adhere to community standards or try to change them may or may not be a creditable act, depending on the standard and the circumstances. One cannot escape his own responsibility for doing serious thinking as to when it is his duty to conform and when it is his duty to object.

It was said once of Senator Borah that he never was for anything in his life. 

Yet he was elected to the United States Senate by his state term after term. 

What do you suppose it was that gave him his place of leadership in Idaho?

Of the elements or forces now at work in society, which do you consider to be, on the whole, beneficial? 

138. Questionable Influences and Conditions. When the force and authority of social institutions have become weakened and new or better ones have not developed to take their place, a condition exists which is sometimes called social disorganization. It may be nobody's fault in particular. We have social disorganization in industry if there are many people willing to work and not able to find jobs. We have social disorganization in community life if disobedience to law, rowdyism, and disregard of the comfort of others is common. We have social disorganization in government if people are elected to office not because of what they believe, but because some particular group expects to be better off if those people are in power. 

We have no right to be satisfied if there is ill will and strife between classes, if any considerable proportion of the population does not get a square deal, or if many people are willing to be supported at public expense without working. 

One thing we ought particularly to guard against is the development of the mob spirit. When is an individual not an individual? 

A foolish question, maybe, but the answer is, When he is in a crowd. 

By a crowd we usually mean a considerable number of people assembled in one place. If that crowd has become excited and is carried away by a spirit of vengeance or destructiveness, it becomes a mob. A crowd easily yields to suggestions. Its members do not take time to think soberly. They act on sudden impulses or emotion. You may get up and yell when your favorite player hits a home run with the bases full, or pound your neighbor on the back when your pet 

---

halfback makes a fifty-yard run. Such acts are relatively harmless, but most lynchings, riots, and destruction of property during labor troubles are the result of the operation of the crowd or mob spirit in a more disastrous form. Political speakers who are demagogues make use of the same psychological influences to stir up enthusiasm or hostility toward someone else. 

Acme Photo STIRRING UP THE CROWD 

This union leader is threatening to tie up the port of San Francisco unless his demands are listened to. It is easier for such a leader to get his way with a crowd than if he were to take these men one by one. 

This same "crowd psychology" may be played upon for a good purpose. It has been done over and over again in religious revivals. 

Campaigns for community funds and other worthy causes are likely to get more and larger contributions from a crowd than would be secured if those same individuals were approached one by one. 

We need not over-emphasize the disagreeable side of what we see. 

There have been wars, crime, injustice, ignorance; but we ought to do more thinking about what can be done to set things right than mere complaining about unpleasant situations. It is not true that every-

body is influenced by pure selfishness or other unworthy motives. 

In our study of social, political, and economic questions, we should remember both that humanity is imperfect and that there have been very many people who, with all their faults, tried on the whole to do the right thing by their fellow men. P

ANOTHER KIND OF CROWD
