139. Crime and Criminals. Among all the great civilized nations, our record in personal crime is worst. Every year in the United 

States 12,000 people are murdered and that would make a rather fair-sized community. Since 1900, the proportion of murders with reference to the whole population has increased 350 per cent, while the population of the country has not doubled. The average number of people murdered in the United States out of every 100,000 is far greater than in such countries as Italy, England, and Switzerland.

Figures on other crimes than murder probably would be about as unfavorable to us. J. Edgar Hoover, head of the Federal Bureau of 

Investigation (the F. B. I.), has put it this way: "There is a murder in our United States every 44 minutes; a major felony every 21 seconds." 

In the strict legal sense, any violation of law is a crime. One might commit a crime without knowing he was doing it if he did not know the law which he was breaking. Some crimes, therefore, are actions not wrong in themselves. There is nothing morally out of the way, for instance, in driving a car, if you know how; but if the state commands you to carry your driver's license with you, you had better do so, unless you want to become a criminal. When we talk about crime in general, however, we commonly think of those acts which are harmful to individual or community. 

We should also distinguish between crimes and other undesirable activities. If one indulges in a habit which is harmful to himself, he is practicing a vice. One who violates what is believed to be a law of God is guilty of sin. Hating another person without cause would be a sin, but would not in itself be a crime, though it might have a vicious effect on the person who indulges in it. An act that resulted from a misunderstanding or from lack of information might be a blunder or error, with disastrous results, but would not necessarily be either a sin, a vice, or a crime. 

Crime itself is also divided into two classes, based chiefly on the seriousness of an offense. Offenses of a minor character are commonly referred to as misdemeanors, such as parking in a forbidden place, or being noisy and disorderly in public. Offenses of a more serious nature, affecting life or property, are called felonies. 

These include such acts as burglary, embezzlement, and murder. 

The total cost of crime is enormous, though the money damage resulting from it can only be estimated. It has been figured all the way from $3,000,000,000 to $16,000,000,000 a year in the United States. The latter amount would pay the entire expense of our schools for six years or more. It includes: the actual loss of money and destruction of property resulting from certain crimes; the salaries and other expenses of officers whose duty it is to arrest and punish criminals; the maintenance of courts which, though not entirely the result of crime, is to a considerable extent caused by it; the support of prisons, jails, reform schools, and the like; the robbing of people

through dishonest practices in business; and the cost of protective agencies and services like detective bureaus, burglar alarms, and other things of that character. 

What shall we say, also, of the social effect of crime? The families of criminals often suffer keenly. An entire community may have a bad reputation if it makes no serious attempt to suppress criminals. 

The moral attitudes of children and even older people are sometimes entirely upset by their association with vicious or criminal characters or by seeing criminal acts apparently successful. 

But what makes people become criminals? Once it was believed that there is a natural criminal class with the tendency inherited from criminal ancestors, and that one might distinguish a criminal by his looks or by some other physical characteristics. In certain families there is a much larger proportion of criminals than in others, but what causes this to be true is not entirely certain. 

Some people may commit one crime and then stop, especially if they are caught at it. That is why "first offenders" are often treated leniently. Others, especially if they "get away with it," become recidivists, or repeaters, and go from one criminal act to another. 

Nearly two-thirds of the arrests reported to the F. B. I. in any given year are of persons who had a previous criminal record. A few become "habitual criminals" and try to make a living that way. 

1. One common cause of crime is the desire for money or possessions. 

Crimes ranging all the way from stealing a loaf of bread or a package of cigarettes to robbing a bank come under this head. So do gambling, picking pockets, stock swindling, and graft in public office. Poverty and unemployment have no doubt induced people to commit crime when they would not have done so under other circumstances. 

2. Poor home conditions and lack of education are often responsible. 

A family broken by divorce or other unpleasantness or living in vicious or unsanitary surroundings may get the wrong slant upon life. Some parents do not know how to get right ideas into their children's minds, or else neglect doing so until too late. Lack of proper religious training is often responsible for the establishment of wrong ideas. Education itself is no sure guarantee of honest living, for some criminals have had more than average intellectual training. 

Neither does it follow that we should blame society for all crime, nor be sentimental about excusing criminals for their wrongdoing.

3. The establishment of vicious habits, such as the use of liquor and drugs, is also responsible for much crime. The drug habit in particular seems to induce a complete weakening of moral standards which leaves the victim with no backbone to do anything right but with a violent will to do whatever is necessary to get his drug. 

4. The development of a gang spirit, especially among young people, has been blamed for a considerable amount of crime. If their social interests cannot find harmless or helpful ways to express themselves, they may transform a group into a gang and encourage its members to do things that as individuals they would never think of doing. 

5. A low standard of law enforcement in a community also leads to crime. Who has much encouragement to obey law if the public officials either are "in cahoots" with the criminals or are too lazy or cowardly to enforce the law? 

6. Descriptions of crime in newspapers, radio programs, and moving pictures have been blamed for suggesting criminal ideas. 

Even though in such stories a criminal gets what he deserves in the end, he is sometimes played up as a hero to a certain extent, and the observer may be tempted to think that he could figure out more crafty ways to commit some particular crime. 

7. Weakness in lawmaking or law-enforcement is another cause of crime. If laws are not drawn up carefully, a criminal may find a tricky lawyer not only to defend him in court, but to find ways to get around the law. The long delays which sometimes occur between the commission of a crime and the trial of the offender make it possible for witnesses to die or disappear or to be bribed to give untrue testimony. Besides, if a judge is more particular about observing technicalities than about getting at the truth, a criminal may escape justice in that way.

The deliberate planning of criminal conduct as a means of making a living sometimes exhibits itself in most distressing fashion. One racketeer will threaten a business man with damage to his property or with personal danger if he does not pay something for "protection."

Another will take advantage of labor troubles to get himself into a place of influence, and by threats of strikes or destruction of property try to get money out of employers or even out of the union which he uses as his tool. A particularly reprehensible offense is kidnaping. 

This kind of case is doubly hard to deal with, because the anguish

of the relatives of a child or older person who has been carried away is such as to make them willing to submit to the demands of the kidnapers in order to get their loved one back. Improvements in firearms have unwittingly aided reckless criminals, as also has the development of the fast automobile. 

Does an increase in crime warrant the belief that schools and churches have failed to do their work effectively? Is a lawyer justified in defending in court some one who he knows is guilty? What remedies can you offer for the evils mentioned in this section? 

140. What Shall We Do with Criminals? Any of four purposes might animate one who has to deal with a criminal vengeance, punishment, reformation, prevention. Among primitive men vengeance was a natural motive. The criminal had wronged another individual or family, so the whole group got back at him and made him suffer what he had made others suffer. You see that spirit to a certain extent in the old practice of "an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a life for a life." 

Punishment, which means imposing some inconvenience or suffering upon one who has committed a wrong, was not intended merely to get back at him, but also to deter others from committing the same crime. If the crime brought pain rather than pleasure, people would be less likely to do it. Very severe penalties, however, often produced a contrary result from what was desired, for it sometimes led to sympathy for the one who was punished. Experience has proved that certainty is much more effective in this connection than severity. 

Reformation of the criminal is a motive much more recently emphasized than the earlier ones, but certainly more important. A reformed criminal will plan no more crime. One who has been merely punished might be more vicious than ever.

Conviction for a minor crime or misdemeanor may be punished by levying a fine on the offender. Sometimes a brief jail sentence is added, and sometimes a certain privilege is taken away. Drunkenness, for instance, may be penalized by a fine, the amount depending on the discretion of the judge or magistrate, up to the limit allowed by law. But for repeated offenses a jail sentence of ten days, thirty days, or even more, might be added. Often when a fine is assessed, an additional charge for "costs" is added, to cover the expense of the arrest of the offender and the conducting of the trial. An automobile

driver who breaks the traffic laws may have his license suspended or taken away as well as given a fine. For more serious offenses, there may be much larger fines or longer prison sentences or both. 

To take care of persons whose offenses are considered serious enough to deprive them of their liberty there are at least three kinds of institutions. A jail may be used to hold some accused persons while they are waiting for trial, or as a place in which prisoners sentenced for a

Another element in the treatment of criminals is the use of such measures as probation, parole, and the indeterminate sentence. 

Probation works in this way: a penalty is imposed, but suspended for a given period with the understanding that if during that time the convicted person breaks no law, the penalty will not be enforced. 

The criminal is expected to report at regular times to a probation officer who will check up on whether he has kept his word and is

complying with the requirements of the court. Under parole, a prisoner who has served part of his sentence is released on his promise to conduct himself properly. He also must report to a parole officer and give evidence of good behavior. An indeterminate sentence is one that has both a minimum and a maximum period. It may read, for example, "from five to ten years." The conduct of the prisoner will then determine whether he will be released at the end of five years or kept there for the full time. In some prisons a merit system is set up which gives special privileges to inmates who conduct themselves well.

Sometimes an outright pardon is given before the full term of a sentence has been completed. 

Pardons are supposed to be granted only when it appears that a person has repented for his wrongdoing or has paid as heavy a penalty as society ought to ask. Pressure is sometimes brought from undesirable sources upon officials who have the power to grant pardons, especially if the crime involved some act connected with politics. In some states the governor must assume entire responsibility for granting or refusing a pardon. To make things easier for him other states have a Board of Pardons, which may be composed of three or four state officials, who must recommend a pardon before the governor may issue it. In the case of offenders who have been convicted of breaking federal laws, the President has the power of pardon, but this power of his does not extend to cases coming under the laws of the states. The President usually asks the advice of his Attorney General and probably other people whenever cases in which a pardon has been requested come before him.

141. How Can We Wipe Out Crime? As long as the characteristics of human beings remain as they are, there will probably be some who will not be influenced by laws or by appeals to worthy motives. But some conditions do exist which either explain or are used as excuses for crime. If we could do away with slums and give every child a good education and every grown-up a chance to earn an honest living, we should prevent many crimes. Warden Lawes, former head of Sing Sing prison, said, "It costs over $400 a year to keep a criminal in prison. It costs less than $100 a year to keep a child in school." (These figures are averages for the entire country and not accurate for every community.)

The percentage of arrests for robbery, burglary, larceny, and auto theft by such persons runs from 28 to 53.

If public sentiment would give needed support to churches, schools, social welfare organizations, and the like, many more boys and girls

It has been said that in England sympathy is with the prosecution, in America with the criminal. One reason why the racketeer sometimes gets away with his nefarious business is that people from whom he collects money are afraid to say anything about it. 

We may also help in preventing criminals by refusing to ask special favors ourselves. If our city has an ordinance against leaving cars parked on the streets all night, we have no business to do it. Persons of social or business standing should expect no particular favors when they break the law. Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty, they say.

142. Establishing Sound Moral Standards. Our standard of morality consists of the ideas of right and wrong that we set up for ourselves or for others. Sometimes we use the word "ethical" in referring to what is suitable and proper in the relations between one person and another. A physician might say, for example, when asked to prescribe for a person who is already under the care of another physician, “That would not be ethical." When an honorable newspaper man is told that a certain piece of information is "off the record," he feels bound not to publish that information, no matter how interesting it might be to the public.

How do ideals and practices of a moral and ethical nature originate? 

By divine authority, many would say. Jew and Christian will both point to the Ten Commandments and declare that those are principles which God has laid down for the guidance of man's conduct. The 

Christian will also add the Sermon on the Mount, and no doubt the Jew will equally recognize its moral force. To Mohammedans, the teachings of the Koran are binding. 

Are moral and ethical standards changeless? Not necessarily.

Said the apostle Paul in one of his letters, "Women should not speak in churches." But what would happen to many of our churches if that advice were considered binding today? Paul did not consider slavery a thing serious enough to argue about. Christians once thought it was wrong to accept interest for lending money, but today it would not be hard to persuade most Christians to take it. 

In the long run, the acceptance of a certain principle as moral or ethical depends on how it works. It is the experience of society that monogamy is better than polygamy. Even those who do not observe the Sabbath Day as a holiday from work because of religious scruples will usually agree that using one day in the week differently from the other six is good for most people.

Once in a while someone gets a little temporary publicity by attacking some moral principle that is accepted by most sensible people. 

Bertrand Russell may say that it makes no difference whether a husband or wife is true to the other or not. But whatever a particular individual may think or say will be tested by the experience of society 

---

as a whole. Changes that take place in regard to moral conduct are just as likely to set up more rigid standards for the individual as less. 

Most of the practices once considered moral that time sets aside were established in the first place through human selfishness and ignorance. 

We think much about success. What constitutes success anyway? 

Was the storekeeper successful who made profits by selling a poor quality of goods? Was the society woman successful who put on the most expensive party of an entire season? Was the colored bootblack successful who used his own savings to send nine or ten boys to college? 

Was the Englishman Robert Scott successful who died on his way back from the South Pole? You see, there are many angles to this matter of success. Many of us need to guard against the notion that notoriety and money are the chief evidences of success. 

A few years ago a boy wrote to the editor of a well-known magazine, asking the editor to give him proof that it actually pays to be honest. 

The boy mentioned one person who seemed to be popular and yet was, in that boy's opinion, utterly tricky and dishonest, and said that a perfectly honest man whom he knew had failed in business. One of the boy's errors was that he did not realize that the honest man might have failed in business not because of his honesty, but because of mistakes in judgment. Besides, the supposedly successful dishonest man could not have been popular if everybody knew he was dishonest. 

He must have done some good things in order to make anybody like him. 

Standards do change from age to age for the better, let us hope.

It is one of the glories of the human race that we can steadily rise " "on stepping stones of our dead selves to higher things." 

"New occasions teach new duties; 

Time makes ancient good uncouth.

They must upward still and onward 

Who would keep abreast of truth."

Are we content with standards lower than our ideals? Should we be? 

Is there any inconsistency between the Golden Rule and going into business for profit? Should a pupil who would not himself cheat refuse to do anything to restrain another pupil who does cheat? 

143. Developing One's Interests and Ideals. - The interests of individuals may be of three kinds. John and Bill may like to do the same things and may do them successfully. Their interests are said

to be common if both enjoy the same activities and neither is harmed or handicapped by what the other does. Suppose Tom and Jim, however, have planned to be dentists. What will happen if both try to practice in a small town which has just about enough work to keep one dentist busy? Interests which cannot be served for one person without detriment to those of another are said to be conflicting. 

Still other kinds of interest are independent, when one does not in any material way affect the other. In this same small town there would be little rivalry between the dentist and the barber, for example. 

What would be a person's duty in promoting his own interests may depend upon circumstances that would not be the same all the time or in every place.

And one's interests, like his standards, may change from period to period. Compare what you liked to do most when you were seven years old with what you like to do now. 

Do you think you will have changed any when you are the age of your father or mother? Sometimes one's interests are affected by unexplainable whims and preferences. Why does John like to go fishing when Frank thinks it is the dullest thing in the world? Of course, there is no particular reason why Frank should like fishing. The two boys are just different. 

Certainly it is one's duty to develop to the fullest possibility any special talents or capacities he has, as far as he can do that without wronging anyone else. If Harry has it in him to become a great scientist, or Mary has the qualities that can make one a successful teacher, the world will be worse off than it needs to be if Harry decides to be a grocery clerk or Mary a salesgirl in the 5-and-10. 

Such work, we admit, is perfectly honorable and useful, but others could do that work equally well, while they could render some uncommon and distinctive service.

If one finds obstacles in the way of the attainment of his interest or ideals, should he let these obstacles cause him to change his plans, or should he persist in going ahead with them? If a person is fortunate enough to find that he can do two or three things rather well, how would you advise him to decide between them? 

144. Doing the Right Thing by Others. - One's attitude toward others may show him to be either an introvert or an extrovert. The introvert thinks a great deal about himself, the way he shall act toward others, and the way they act toward him. He cares very little for

social affairs. The extrovert is much interested in things outside of himself. He likes to be with others. He may be "the life of the party." He likes to be doing things rather than thinking about them. 

Of course one does not need to be extreme in either direction. In fact, if one finds himself that way he might properly ask himself whether he might profitably adjust his habits and manners a little one way or the other. He could be an ambivert, exhibiting a moderate amount of both tendencies.

Two other contrasting types of personality may be classified as those of ascendance and submission. The ascendant type is the kind of person who likes to be responsible for something. He enjoys being chairman of a committee or a candidate for office. If there is a discussion, he takes an active part in it and is likely to be sure that his point of view is the only right one. The submission type follows what others are doing — the kind of clothes they wear or the shows they go to. In an argument he says nothing or is easily squelched. In politics he will "climb on the bandwagon." What we really need are not people who want to boss others, but who are willing to accept responsibility when the proper time comes not a great mass of people to take orders from a self-constituted leader, but many thousands who think sanely for themselves and make up their own minds. 

In developing one's own interests and talents, we have hinted that sometimes they might come into conflict or competition with some other person's ambitions or achievements. The two terms are not just the same. Conflict may imply that one is to win and the other to lose. Competition may mean the effort of two or more persons to reach some desired goal, but under such circumstances that no one actually fails, but some accomplish somewhat less than their rivals. 

Two Sunday school classes may have a contest to see which shall have the higher average attendance over a given period. One class may win, but neither side really loses, because both have probably brought out a larger attendance than they would have otherwise had. "Competition is the life of trade," it used to be said. When two men in the same kind of enterprise try to get all the business each can by honorable methods, both may succeed in getting more than either would have had without this competition. But if competition is carried to the point where one competitor seeks to beat another by any possible means, it is no longer the life of trade but may be the

economic death of one of the competitors. So in developing individual ambition, one should think of what he may accomplish himself rather than what he may prevent somebody else from accomplishing. 

This year there might be a perfectly friendly competition between Mary and Grace for the leadership of their club; but if Mary insists on keeping Grace out of the presidency year after year, then this competition has ceased to be helpful and has become unsocial. 

Philip D. Gendreau LEARNING TO BE SELF-SUPPORTING 

School programs are sometimes criticized as not giving practical preparation for life. These boys in the Brooklyn Technical High School cannot well complain of the training they are receiving. Will their training be likely to turn them in the direction of conflict, competition, or co-operation?

Another important social quality is co-operation. Some things, it is true, can be better handled by a committee of one, two, or three than by ten or a dozen. But if one member of a club, one clique in a school, one racial group in a community, should try to get all the honors for itself, the life of that social group would inevitably be handicapped. 

What do you think of a basketball team on which four boys of one nationality refused to pass the ball to the fifth member of the team

who was admittedly the ablest single player in the group? You can doubtless think of many instances which would illustrate the effect of a lack of co-operation or of a square deal. 

Sometimes in matters of politics and business relationships people have been known to say, "Ideals have no place there. I believe in doing things in a practical way." The idealist does indeed make a mistake if he thinks that all one has to do with a good idea is to announce it. Great reforms are not brought about without work on somebody's part. "Let George do it" is a poor way to accomplish even the most desirable end. But back of every social gain and every practical improvement in government or industry is somebody's hunch or somebody's ideal of a happier or more wholesome human relationship.

Is there any harmful effect in giving prizes for achievement in scholarship, athletics, or any other field in which young people take an interest? 

What do you think of a marking system in school which gives only two grades, passing and failing? Suppose a person has worked hard for a good cause but has not succeeded in securing its adoption. How should he feel? Can the reform of individuals take place apart from the reform of society in general? 

145. What to Do about Habits. There is no use advising people not to form habits. We cannot help it, if by habit we mean a customary way of doing or thinking which tends to become automatic. 

Habits differ from instincts, however, in that the instinct is inborn, while the habit has to be acquired. 

It has been said that "Each of us is a bundle of habits." You probably never tried to count the number of things you do without deliberately thinking about them. It is hard to say what kinds of habits are easiest to form, because individual differences might have considerable effect. Though it would not always follow, a boy whose father smoked cigarettes would probably find it considerably easier to form the habit than one whose father never used them. If your close friends regularly attend religious services, it is easier for you to adopt the same habit than if they do not. 

Excellent advice on habits is, Make sure that a certain thing is good and then set about the formation of a habit of doing it. "When in Rome, do as the Romans do" is not necessarily good sense. Maybe the Romans are doing something just because they always have done it and have never had the intelligence to make any change. At the 

---

same time, do not be different just for the sake of showing your alleged independence. If a school fails to help its pupils to acquire the ability to distinguish between what is good and what is bad, or to aid them in establishing helpful habits, it is neglecting one of the most important parts of true education. 

Make a list of the things that form a part of your daily routine which have become habitual, and of those about which you have to give definite thought and consideration each day. What kinds of habits are the hardest to change? Give examples from people you know. 

146. Religion in Life. - A 

most powerful force in human life and conduct is religion. Is religion any different from morality and ethics? In some respects no, in others yes. Like morality and ethics, religion sets up standards to govern one's thinking and conduct. But religion deals particularly with man's idea of a power higher than himself and of his relations to that power. 

It has been well said, "Man is incurably religious." At any stage in the history of human progress, you find something that represents religion. Primitive man thought of propitiating evil spirits or getting on the right side of good spirits. The Greek who saw divinity in streams and winds, in ocean and the sun, was recognizing forces outside himself which he could not control. Too often religion has been looked upon as a sort of magic, something which, if one observed it, would keep him out of trouble. Religion has often called for the performance of certain rites or ceremonies. Some of these, as performed in ancient times, like the throwing of infants into a red-hot idol's arms, seem utterly inhuman. Others, which appear in modern religious services, are neither moral nor immoral in themselves, but may be given a

definite significance by the participants, such as the use of bread and wine in the Lord's Supper or taking a trip to Mecca.

What would your own community be like if every religious influence and every religious organization were removed from it? Few people would deliberately choose such a place to live in. The services of the 

Church, by which we mean organized religious work under any name, are many. dit valon_

One very important service of the Church is as a center of worship. 

It is true that one can worship anywhere, but most people find it much easier in favorable surroundings. Religion encourages right living, if for no other motive than to please God. Every church or synagogue tries to set up for its members better ideals of living than they would be likely to seek by themselves. It preserves examples of righteous living in the past. The Roman Catholic Church makes a considerable point of confession to a priest. Other pastors render the same kind of service but perhaps in a different way. Preaching sermons is an important part of almost every regular service of worship, especially in Protestant churches.

The Church encourages its members to be kind to one another and to relieve the distressed. It often speaks out with reference to some condition in society that needs correction. Critics of religion frequently point to so-called hypocrites in the church. But how much worse they might be if there were no influence to make them behave as well as they do! The number of people whom everybody would recognize as good but who have no religious faith whatever would not take very long to count. 

The influence of religion and religious organizations is not limited to their adherents. Many a person who does not go inside the church door five times a year accepts the service of the church in the great events in his own life and the life of his family. Few will refuse the prayers and consolation of a pastor in time of trouble, even though they forget him and his work when things are going well. Hospitals, schools, and many other organizations for social benefit had their beginning, in a very large number of cases, in activities connected with religion.

Would it be correct to say that religion is a thing of the spirit and morality a thing of conduct? Mention institutions in your community, outside of churches and synagogues, that owe their existence to the activities of religious bodies or persons connected with them. 

Churches also are helpful as community centers for social service and for recreation. Some church organizations do not like to have their main auditoriums used for anything but regular services, but they may provide a separate parish house or social room for other purposes. Some maintain special workers to visit and help people in their own homes.

The service of the church in education must not be overlooked. 

One is never too old to grow morally and spiritually. Bible schools or Sunday schools in some churches are limited largely to young people, but in others there are classes and activities for people of all ages. Robert Raikes, who started the Sunday school idea in England in 1774 in order to get rowdy boys off the streets, did not realize the significance of the work which he was thus beginning. 

Parochial schools maintained by the Roman Catholic Church and a few other religious bodies for the purpose of guaranteeing that their children shall have religious education as well as any other kind may include both elementary and high school classes. There are also

Catholic colleges and universities. Most other religious organizations, though they have founded academies and colleges, are not so inclined to insist on providing schooling for their young people at their own expense.

If your church maintains a Sunday school or Bible school, is it planned for young people alone or people of all ages? Could you tell, with no more than a few minutes to think about it, the main doctrines and features of the church to which you belong? If not, why not? 

III Harold M. Lambert "TRAIN UP A CHILD" 

If boys and girls when very young learn the right kind of ideas and ideals, most of them will carry these all through their lives. Sabbath school is one of the ways to help them.

One other notable religious activity is the work of missionaries. 

Christian nations have not always practiced Christianity in dealing with other people. But many unselfish men and women have left all the pleasant things of home behind them and gone to give their lives to the uplift of people who were not always glad to see them. 

Missionaries have been, time after time, the forerunners of civilization. Their work has not always begun with preaching. Some missionaries have had to spend some time learning the language of the country where they expected to work, and in a few cases have even invented a written language for people who had none. Other mission-

aries start by relieving the sick and doing the work of a physician. 

When, by such means, an approach has been gained to the hearts of men and women, it is easier to talk about purely religious ideas. 

David Livingstone in Africa and Wilfred Grenfell in Labrador are notable examples of workers whose activities brought them honors from others as well as the appreciation of those whom they served. 

Many a priest or pastor in a little parish at home has worked for a lifetime at just enough salary to keep him alive. 

Today many think that the time has come in many lands when the missionary from Europe or America should, after training native workers to take his place, turn over the work to them and come back home. That might be the proper policy in some cases, but not in others. When it is possible to do this, there is pretty good evidence that the missionary's work has been built on a solid foundation. 

Religion had much to do with the opening up of the New World, for some wished to carry Christianity to those who did not have it, and others wished the opportunity to practice their own brand of Christianity in the New World when it was not comfortable to do so in their native country. Religion was responsible as much as any one factor for the overthrow of human slavery, and it has done more than anything else to encourage charity and sympathy for those in need. 

Does the religious denomination with which you are affiliated maintain home or foreign missionaries? If not, why not? Mention special benefits that have been rendered by religious organizations of which you know. Would these services have been performed if there had been no such organization? 

Do you think there is ever likely to be another war in which religion will be one of the causes? Why or why not? 

147. Religious Organizations. - Division among people on the basis of religion is obvious and extensive. Though many religious bodies agree on certain fundamental moral principles, they are kept apart by questions of theology or form or ceremony. 

The oldest of the religious bodies that include any large number of people today is the Jewish. In a remarkable fashion, Jewish people have kept their religious and national integrity through a period of more than thirty centuries under all kinds of experiences. 

Christianity came out of Judaism. Its essential difference is the recognition of Jesus Christ as not only a worthy religious teacher, but possessing special merit as the son of God.

Earlier in their origin than Christianity are the eastern religions — Buddhism, Brahmanism, Confucianism, Taoism, and Shintoism—which are professed by people of the thickly settled Asiatic regions of India, China, and Japan. Mohammedanism started a separate existence with the Hegira, or flight of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina in 622 A.D. Mohammedanism teaches a belief in one God as forcefully as do Judaism and Christianity, but it lays special emphasis on Mohammed as the last and greatest of the prophets. There are still people whose religious beliefs or practices are almost as primitive as those of prehistoric man. 

About one-fourth of the Jews of the world are found in the United States. 

The Eastern Christian church, chiefly Greek and Russian in its origin, has about 1,000,000 people. One guess at the division of the rest of our population between Protestant and Roman Catholic affiliations puts it at about 

75,000,000 to 40,000,000. Christian Scientists and Mormons are examples of distinctive religious bodies that began in this country. 

A few outstanding differences of religious beliefs and practices may be pointed out. The Bible of Jews, Catholics, and Protestants, as far as the same books are included in it, differs only as translations from the original Hebrew or Greek might differ if not made by the same people. To the 

Jews, the New Testament has no binding authority, and the Talmud supplements the Old Testament as a source of instruction. The Roman Catholic 

Bible includes certain books which do not appear in the versions used by Protestants. Catholics accept the decisions of church councils and precedents established in the past as having authority which is not recognized by Protestants.

All Roman Catholics, but not Protestants, believe that the Pope should be recognized as the head of the Church on earth, and that his authority in matters of faith and morals is not to be questioned. The Roman Catholic 

Church has an extensive and thorough organization. Some non-Catholic bodies, like the Church of England, otherwise known as the Protestant Episcopal Church, continued a good deal of the original church organization after they broke away from the authority of the Pope.

A HOME FOR THE RELIGIOUS 

This scene is in the garden of the old Spanish mission of San Juan Capistrano in California. Some of these missions have a long and interesting history. 

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that an actual transformation of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ takes place in the service variously known as the Mass, Communion, Eucharist, or Lord's Supper. This doctrine is known as transubstantiation. Protestant bodies look upon that service as a memorial or symbol only. Baptists maintain that immersion is the only proper form of baptism, and that only those old enough to have an understanding as to what the ceremony means should be baptized. Most of the other leading religious bodies baptize infants and are more likely to use sprinkling or pouring as the method of baptism. The

character of church services also varies greatly, ranging from the rather elaborate forms used in the Roman Catholic Church and "High Church" Episcopalian to the complete lack of formality found among the Quakers, or Friends, who do not even have ordained ministers or priests. 

Among Protestant bodies in the United States, the most numerous are the Baptists and Methodists. Baptists lay stress on the authority of the individual church as compared with bishops, church councils, or other superior dignitaries. Presbyterians and Lutherans also are influential in some sections, and Congregationalists in others. 

If you have attended religious services in other churches than your own, what differences did you observe in the ways the services were conducted? 

Do you like a considerable amount of form and ceremony in a religious service? 

Can you understand why other people might feel exactly the opposite about it? 

148. Changes in Religious Thinking. Some religious people emphasize what might be called theology, while others prefer to stress what they call the social gospel. In other words, is it more important to talk about such matters as the divinity of Christ or the relief of suffering among human beings? Of course one can also think that both are important. In the past, millions of people accepted unpleasant conditions as something to be put up with, and looked upon one of religion's greatest services as the offering of the hope of a future heaven where everything will be happy. Today, however, many preachers have much to say about slums, sweatshops, the promotion of peace, and the practice of the Golden Rule in industrial and social relations. 

James Sawders

A FAMOUS OLD VIRGINIA CHURCH 

Inside this church which many tourists visit, Patrick Henry delivered his famous speech, "Give me liberty or give me death."

Until very recently we would have said that the days of persecution for religious reasons were over in civilized lands. Recent events,

however, make us less sure about it. Take, for example, the persecution of the Jews in Germany and the futile effort to destroy religion in Soviet Russia. In our own country, though some sincerely deplore a seeming decline of interest in the church and religious activities, there is no hostility on the part of the government to any religious group whose teachings do not call for disobedience to lawful authority or for some undesirable social practice. 

We have already mentioned (§ 73) the difference of opinion as to whether a church or its pastor should take an active part in politics and economic disputes. Some pastors unquestionably believe that this is practical Christianity, but others think that if a church, by mixing up in political or economic quarrels, forfeits the good will of a considerable number whom it might serve, it is doubtful whether anything has been gained either for the church or for the community. 

Try to recall the central theme of the sermon or address of your pastor, priest, or rabbi at regular services during the last ten weeks and list the central ideas of his remarks. How often would you classify his theme as distinctly one of theology, one of personal living, one of social relations, or of some other distinctive character? Are people more likely to think more seriously about religious matters in times of prosperity or in times of adversity? 

To many the division among religious organizations seems unfortunate. Though few communities could have too much religion, some are "overchurched" in the sense that they have more religious organizations than are needed to serve the number of people in the community. To get away from such an embarrassing situation in many small communities, "federated" churches have been formed which are attended by most or all of the people who used to go to separate churches. In the larger communities, one finds today, much more often than formerly, union services during the summer time and on other special occasions, in which churches of several different denominations join. Ministers often exchange pulpits with pastors of another denomination. In their missionary work in foreign lands, Protestant denominations frequently agree to divide up a certain territory so that two Protestant denominations will not be working in the same field. 

149. Religion and the Government. In your study of history, you have probably noticed three attitudes on the part of governments toward religious bodies: control, toleration, and religious freedom. 

Under the policy of control, the government has been closely tied

up with one church or religious organization and has forbidden the use of any form of worship not supported by the government. Back of such a policy is the idea that there is only one true faith, and that people should not be diverted from it by the practice of any other. 

From one point of view, a much more practical policy is that of toleration. When this practice prevails, there is still an established church associated with the government, and perhaps supported in 

James Sawders

RELIGIOUS SERVICES IN A LABOR CAMP 

These men are employed by one of New England's railroads, but religious opportunities are not denied them.. part by public taxation. But other religious bodies are allowed to worship freely, and an individual may belong to any church he wishes. 

In Great Britain, for instance, the king or queen must be a member of the Church of England, but anyone else is free to follow any religious faith or none at all. Persons belonging to Presbyterian, Baptist, Catholic, and Jewish societies have risen to high places under the 

British government. 

Under the third policy, which we may name religious freedom, no preference is shown one religious body over another, and there is no official connection between the government and any one sect. Each

maintains itself by the contributions of its own members. Religious requirements are not demanded for voting or office holding. The First 

Amendment to the United States Constitution declares, "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." The original Constitution also provided that "no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification to any office or public trust under the United States." 

At the very time the national Constitution was ratified, and in some cases for many years afterward, religious qualifications were demanded with reference to the right to vote or to hold office in some states. 

Those have now all been done away with, as far as they involve adherence to any specified religious body. That is not saying, however, that people never let religious preferences influence them in voting. Who would deny, for example, that religion played some part in the presidential election of 1928? 

Religious intolerance on the part of a government usually reacts sooner or later against that government. In the past there was a close tie-up between the Orthodox Greek Church and the government of the Czar in Russia. The revolutionary leaders then used that fact as an excuse for ridiculing and interfering with all religion. Of course, the crushing of the church by the state is to a liberal-minded person at least as indefensible as compelling people to support it. 

At times there has been considerable effort in certain states to provide money from the public treasury to help support parochial schools, but such aid has usually been limited to free transportation of pupils to school or occasionally to the furnishing of textbooks. 

Many states have refused to allow public money to be given to hospitals maintained by religious denominations except on the understanding that such money was to be used to support free services on the part of the hospital. 

The Bible is used in the inauguration ceremony of Presidents, governors, and the like, and in taking oaths in court, but people who prefer to do so may "affirm" rather than "swear" in such cases. 

Religious organizations need not pay taxes on property definitely used for religious purposes. If a church owns and rents an apartment house, however, it would pay taxes on that like everybody else. 

The belief that religious instruction is necessary to complete education has resulted in a few places in a kind of co-operation between the

public school authorities and the local churches in providing it. One plan is to set aside one period a week as "released time" within what would regularly be school hours and allow that period to be used by pupils to go to their own churches for special religious instruction. 

School credit is sometimes given for properly certified religious education.

Laws in regard to the observance of Sunday have caused dissatisfaction in some places. These so-called "blue-laws" have depended for their effectiveness upon the sentiment of each particular community. 

The West has never been marked by the same feeling toward Sunday amusement as the East, and now even in the East the tendency is to legalize outdoor sports or theatrical performances on Sunday at hours that do not conflict with the morning church service. But if, for the sake of rest and health, it seems desirable for most people not to work seven days in the week, it may be unfair for some people to be allowed to make seven days' profit by conducting their businesses all the week while others are limited to five or six days. 

A minister once declared in a sermon, "Church property should be taxed." 

What arguments might he offer in support of that attitude? Does the principle of religious freedom carry with it the right of public officials or university professors to belittle religion or particular religious bodies? What policy prevails in your community and state in regard to Sunday observance? 

150. Making the Good Life. What is the good life? Is this an acceptable statement? The good life is one which brings true satisfaction to the individual who practices it, and general well-being to the community where it prevails. Though some may not agree, it seems more likely that an individual can live a good life himself if his community helps him to do so than if he must accept the entire responsibility himself. Why should anyone be subjected to temptation just for the sake of seeing whether he is strong enough to resist it? At the same time, no individual has the right to blame others for misfortune if he himself has not tried his best to develop his own talents to the highest possible level. 

How much, if at all, do you think your own community falls short of having achieved the good life for its people? Do you see any difference between what might be called the "good" life and the "abundant" life? Mention six conditions that would exist in a good society, in your opinion, and six of a different type which would not exist there. How can a community be induced to work for the establishment of the good life among its people?

It may be good for young people to think about this question: 

Whom would you be like? Perhaps you would not want to be exactly like anybody. But most of us can find in the lives of those who have already been "through the mill" something that will help toward setting up right standards for ourselves. Of course we can overdo the business of imitation. 

An actress has her hair cut in a certain style. Immediately thousands of high school girls do the same thing. That an advertiser has paid some baseball player or other person of prominence to endorse something to eat, drink, or smoke is no sufficient reason why thousands of other people should follow his or her example.

Conserving natural resources has received much attention in the last few decades, and that is right. But is it not even more important to conserve human resources? If human life is to be comfortable and happy, the people who compose society must be able to live and work efficiently. 

How far does that condition exist today, and what more may be done to make it general?

Some Questions: 

1. How may we guard against disease and promote health? 

2. How much responsibility in this matter belongs to the individual and how much to the community? 

3. How may we best care for the physically or mentally handicapped? 

4. What shall we do to relieve or prevent poverty? 

5. How shall we take care of the places where people work and the people who do the work? 

6. What safeguards against accidents may we set up? 

7. How far shall we go in the field of social insurance? 

8. How and how much should we play? 

151. The Battle with Disease. Some sick people have accomplished much, but would not they have liked to be free from their handicap! Ill health often means lack of ambition, inability to do things well, and a constant state of discontent. Good health means more than we can measure in the enjoyment of life and a very great deal also in what we can achieve. 

Once diseases, even great epidemics, were looked upon as visitations that must be accepted. Now we are sure that much of the individual suffering of the past and human misery in general was unnecessary. 

A New England deacon once declared that everybody ought to wash himself all over at least once a year. Today would any church elect such a man as a deacon?

Recall cases, if they have occurred, when you undertook something important when you were sick. Did the result satisfy you? What other motives, if any, than improved health may lead one to be interested in personal cleanliness? 397

Today we are not satisfied just to relieve disease without finding out what caused it and how to prevent it. The Frenchman, Pasteur, and the German, Koch, both worked on the causes of disease and came to the theory now generally accepted that bacteria or germs do the dirty work. If we can find the kind of germ that caused the disease, we can give it the particular treatment it deserves. 

Not all bacteria are harmful. Some good germs fight the evil germs. 

One style of attack on disease has been to introduce into the system germs that would counteract harmful elements which had already gained a foothold or which might find their way in later. 

On that principle we have learned to use anti-toxins of various kinds not only to prevent sickness, but to make recovery much more probable if the disease does come. Since we learned about the use of anti-toxin in diphtheria cases, death occurs in only 5 per cent of the cases, whereas once 20 to 

30 per cent died. 

Since, in many cases, having a disease once gives immunity against repetition of it, another practice has been to introduce into the human system a serum which will develop just enough of the disease to furnish this immunity without causing any real danger. It is on that principle that vaccination works against smallpox. Similarly, one may take a "shot" against typhoid fever or some of the other diseases which may be carried by impure milk, water, or other food. 

Since a sick person in a home can often not be given the necessary care without completely upsetting the family life, hospitals come into the picture to render an exceedingly valuable service. There the sick person is under the charge of people who make that work their life profession. Medical inspection in school may discover disease before the sufferer realizes he has it, and even young children can learn about common sicknesses and form proper health habits. CCC #EXT 

Keystone View Company TAKING A BLOOD TEST 

Modern doctors have many ways of judging whether a person is healthy. This young lady seems to know what it is all about.

What provisions does your own community make for disposing of garbage, rubbish, and other refuse? Where does your family get its milk and water supply? What assurance do you have that they are safe?

Combating disease is on a much more scientific basis than ever before. A doctor may have to try more than one medicine or treatment on a person, because all kinds of treatment may not be equally appropriate for every individual. But at least the physician has a wider knowledge of what has succeeded in other cases than medical men did in the past. Experimentation is constantly going on to find out new facts about both the cause of disease and the treatment of it. Work under the direction of such agencies as the Rockefeller

Foundation has accomplished wonders. Our knowledge about health and disease is further improved by the careful keeping of vital statistics.

Records of births, deaths, and marriages are now regularly required by law in most of our states.

INCREASING LIFE EXPECTANCY 

This graph indicates the average length of human life in the United States at the year 

Can you explain indicated at the bottom. why people on the average live so much longer now? 1935 Rarely do terrible epidemics sweep the world as they once did. 

The Black Death of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, which we now identify with the bubonic plague, would probably be checked today soon after it started. Yellow fever has virtually been blotted out from the United States, and even in tropic lands like Cuba, Panama, and Africa it has either been removed or brought under control. Tuberculosis is still with us, but not to the extent that once was common.

Measures such as these have added marvelously to the average length of human life. Once some people thought, from the fact that 

Jesus was on earth about thirty-three years, it would always be a

typical life period for human beings. In 1800 it actually was about that figure. Now, however, the average "expectancy” of life among us is 60 years or more. Much of this higher average is the result of the fact that many more children than formerly live to grow up. 

Investigators can come very near telling the total number of people who will die in any given period. Insurance companies cannot tell what particular people of those whom they insure will not live long, but they can make their plans on the basis of averages. 

Some things medical science has not yet achieved. Cancer still carries away many. Physicians can tell a person not to strain his heart, but they have not learned how to strengthen a heart that is naturally weak. Infantile paralysis sometimes strikes without warning, and we have not learned how to prevent it. That perennial nuisance, the so-called common cold, produces more discomfort than any other disease. Even doctors still grow old and die. A surprisingly large number of army draftees are rejected on account of physical deficiencies. 

Would it be desirable to have everybody live to be 90 or 100 years old? 

How much fun. or self-reliance do old people have? Are experimenters justified in using living dogs, mice, and other animals in their experiments? 

What have anesthetics and the X-ray done for medicine and surgery? 

152. Send for the Doctor. - Among primitive people there have almost always been "medicine men" or workers of magic who have made their living by pretending to do something for the afflicted. 

Strange medicines were prescribed as cures for disease. In spite of the cruelty which men displayed in warfare and in punishing criminals, they did not dare to study the human body, alive or dead. It was once believed that the arteries carried air into the body, and not until 1694 did the Englishman Harvey make clear the facts about the circulation of the blood.

It is much less than a century since our states have required proper study and experience before a person might set himself up as a physician or surgeon. Now he must get a diploma from a recognized medical school, and usually that will not be given without actual practical service in a hospital. Today it is said that four out of every fifteen physicians are specialists. The physician in the country or the small town can hardly expect to make a living in that way. He must be able to deal with almost anything that comes along.

Some doctors do not live up to the ethical standards that the profession as a whole insists upon. In the days of national prohibition, some would sell whisky prescriptions to people who they knew wanted it only to drink. Others do not practice what they preach. The 

American Medical Association, to which most physicians belong, has sometimes been criticized as dictatorial in its policies. But it has done much to keep physicians in touch with the latest developments in their field of work and to set up worthy standards in the field of medicine.

But how many people there are who will not consult a doctor as long as they can stay on their feet, and how many there are who are willing to spend their hard-earned wages on widely advertised patent medicines! "Has cured others, will cure you" is a fatally weak kind of logic. How much was Mrs. Jones paid to sign a letter saying that she was greatly improved by using Dr. Fixit's Health Compound? Do you really believe that when a famous actress was tired, she smoked a certain cigarette and immediately felt better? 

Everyone ought to learn to recognize the symptoms of common diseases and to know what to do in the case of the most frequent emergencies. But let us not depend too much on the drugstore. 

Sometimes relief from one inconvenience is obtained at the risk of acquiring some other dangerous habit. "Send for the doctor" is excellent advice for anyone who has the slightest question as to what is wrong with him. 

But you may ask, “What if we have no money to pay doctor bills?”

Doctors are said often to adjust the size of the bill to the customer's pocketbook. Yet "doctor bills" may sometimes become a serious burden to people in the so-called middle class and it may take years to pay the cost of a single operation. People who know they cannot pay doctors' charges have two choices. They can go to free clinics and accept care in the free wards of hospitals, which must be maintained when hospitals get aid from the government-or they may get along without medical help. 

To relieve such embarrassments, plans have been formed in recent years by which groups or associations are organized, the members of which pay a comparatively small sum each year or month and then, if necessary, they have the right to go to hospitals which have been interested in the forming of such organizations. Of course, if a person

is not sick, he gets nothing back for his money, but many people are perfectly willing to pay for the sense of security that they get, just as they may pay for fire insurance. 

Some have even recommended the "socialization" of medical care. 

Under such a plan some physicians would be paid a salary by the government, state or local, and then the public physicians could be consulted by anybody who needed advice. Some physicians are very 

Acme Photo TRAINING FOR NURSING 

A practical nurse may not need to have the complete training that a registered nurse receives, but she should know how to provide suitable nourishment for invalids and to use properly instruments that might be needed. much opposed to such procedure. They say they would rather give their services, as they often do to poor people, than to make themselves public officials and introduce into the profession the evils often connected with politics. They say that the confidential relations between a physician and his patient are something that cannot be properly maintained if a physician becomes a public official. 

Try to find out the details of any plans for hospital or medical service through organized groups which have come to the notice of any people whom you know. Country villages have been known to advertise for a physician to come and settle there. What advantages or disadvantages might a physi-

cian find in such a place? Which do you think are more common, people who make themselves sick by thinking that they are, or people who do not seek medical advice when they ought to do so? Would it be a sensible arrangement to pay a doctor a regular fee for keeping you in good health but making him take care of you free when you are sick? 

153. Protection against Vice and Bad Habits. Is there a single good reason why people indulge in habits they know are harmful? 

Shall we let such people ruin their health or weaken their usefulness otherwise just because they want to do so? It is not purely a matter of individual liberty that is involved. If indulgence in a habit, whether actually vicious or merely annoying, deprives other people of comfort, has an individual the right to claim liberty to engage in it? 

Sumptuary laws, as they are sometimes called those that try to control what people shall eat, drink, or wear are not unconstitutional. The only practical question is whether they are unreasonable and whether they can work.

Take the matter of "dope." A person who acquires this habit is not master of himself while he is under the influence of the drug. He may become a distinct menace to the comfort or life of any one he meets. The first federal law on this subject, the Harrison Drug Act, passed in 1914, required that strict records should be kept of all sales of dangerous drugs and forbade their sale at all except under physicians' prescriptions. To exercise proper control over this matter, we have a Bureau of Narcotics in the Treasury Department. The 

Public Health Service in the Federal Security Agency is also interested in this problem. 

Three principal causes for the drug habit have been discovered. 

More than two thirds of the "addicts" got that way by learning from others; about one fourth took it up as relief from personal suffering; the rest began it out of curiosity or from other varied motives. Some addicts may be restored to normal life under proper treatment, but the dope habit is about the hardest of any to break. 

The liquor problem is as old as the human race. Some people probably can "take it or leave it." Some do not care for anything stronger than beer or wine and take them as many people drink coffee. 

But others must have something strong whisky, rum, or gin - and when they get it they may be almost as bad as if they had taken drugs. 

In addition, the distress of their families, who often have to suffer 

---

for the lack of the things that the money wasted on liquor could buy, should be enough to make thoughtful people feel the need of some kind of restraint upon the liquor business. 

Two means in general have been proposed to do this. One is by a license system, which is virtually a tax upon manufacturers or sellers of liquor, in the hope of reducing the number of people who will engage in the business and thus making it a little more inconvenient for drinkers to buy their liquor. Another policy is to make it illegal to sell the stuff for beverage purposes at all. This may be done by local option that is, allowing each town, city, or county to decide for itself whether it will permit the sale of liquor within its limits — or by state or national prohibition. 

Until well toward the middle of the nineteenth century, there was no effective restriction of the liquor business in the United States. The first "temperance" movements were carried on by people who tried to get individuals to take a pledge of total abstinence. The state of Maine adopted prohibition in 1846, and Vermont and New Hampshire a few years later. 

In the 1880's Kansas and North Dakota adopted it. 

After the beginning of the twentieth century a real national movement for prohibition became popular, especially in the South. By 1920 two thirds of the states had their own prohibition laws. Ever since 1872 there had been a Prohibition Party, but it got very few votes on election day, for many people could not bring themselves to vote on that issue and no other. 

The World War brought the situation to a head, and when grain was in demand for food, it seemed an awful waste to use it for making liquor. In 

1917 Congress proposed the Eighteenth Amendment, forbidding the manufacture or sale of liquor for beverage purposes in the United States. It was ratified by the necessary number of states in January, 1919, and went into effect one year later. For a few months it seemed to work well, but then evasion and disregard of it began to be common and bad politics interfered with the enforcement of it. Little by little the opponents of prohibition began to gain strength, until in 1932 the Democratic platform and candidate for the presidency demanded repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment.

The next year (1933) another constitutional amendment, the Twentyfirst, repealing the Eighteenth, was presented to the states and ratified by the necessary number before the end of the year. The Twenty-first Amendment puts matters back where they were before 1919, except that it contains a provision that liquor must not be sent into a state whose laws do not permit its sale there. Only three or four of the states still have statewide prohibition. Even Maine has abandoned it.

In several states, state stores have been set up which have a monopoly of the sale of liquor within the state, except that it may be sold by hotels or restaurants with meals. Under one guise or another, drinking places have in some states become common, and in them some women may be found as frequently as men. Probably we have not discovered the final solution of the liquor problem yet. 

Other vicious habits also call for prohibition or restraint. Gambling has meant loss and suffering to children as well as to adults, whether it takes the form of an actual organized lottery, or selling numbers, making baseball pools, betting on horse races, or operating slot machines. Some have even advocated lotteries as a means of revenue for this country. Wouldn't it be intelligent, though, for people who complain about taxes to be willing to pay unknown amounts for chances in a lottery, most of which would never bring any money to anybody!

Local governments often have their problems with public dance halls, cabarets, roadhouses, and places of that character, which allow or even encourage indulgence in all kinds of bad conduct. 

Intelligent laws, strictly enforced, would do much to limit such evils, but the surest remedy goes back to the individual. There are some things about which it is never safe to take a chance. 

What is the policy of your state with reference to the sale of liquor? What do you think of the logic of the liquor seller who said that he never asked anybody to buy a drink, but if people were going to buy it, he might as well profit as anybody? Do you know any instances in which gambling has had a bad effect upon sports? 

154. Public Responsibility for Health. There are some things which no government and no private organization can do for the individual. They cannot easily make him brush his teeth or take a bath. They can make it easy for him to get pure water, pure milk, and pure food. They can force him to keep himself or his family from contact with others when there is contagious disease. Such restraint is a matter of enlightened selfishness on the part of the community, because if disease is not checked, it may spread to many other people than the ones who had it first. 

The promotion of health in a local community is the reason for quarantine laws in cases of disease, and the inspection of milk, meat, and other food. In a great many cities, boroughs, or villages, there

is a Board of Health though not always under just that name with power to enforce local or state laws. Cities or counties may also maintain hospitals for the care of those suffering from contagious diseases, insanity, and other difficulties.

No up-to-date city today would think of maintaining an impure water system. Pasteurizing milk is essential for a city, for the city resident cannot know where his milk comes from. It is a rural problem, too, for impure well water and milk from diseased cattle

This furnishes a considerable part of the water supply for New York City. have both caused unnecessary sickness and death. Along with such preventive measures go the proper disposal of garbage and rubbish. 

New York City used to dump its refuse out in the ocean, only to have some of it washed up against the shores of New Jersey. Now it has its own disposal plant. Even then, the location of such a plant is sometimes embarrassing, for who wants to live near a garbage-disposal establishment? Besides, there is often argument over whether the municipality shall collect and dispose of garbage and rubbish itself or pay private companies to do the work. 

A large school system will have its school physicians and dentists

who are responsible for discovering when pupils need special treatment or shall even be kept out of school. Health instruction may be given through a department of hygiene or in connection with physical education and athletics. Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts can learn how to give first aid in the case of cuts, bruises, or broken bones, or even when one is in danger of drowning.

State laws can be more farreaching than local ordinances because they can apply to everybody within the state's boundaries, though sometimes local regulations are more strict than the state would dare enact. A state may enact inspection laws with reference to live cattle and to milk and meat. It passes quarantine laws and other regulations to deal with epidemics. 

A state will have a state Board of Health or Department of 

Health, perhaps with one person having the title of Director of 

Health, or something similar.

States often maintain institutions for the tubercular, the insane, the feeble-minded, or the epileptic, and may also give money to private hospitals or institutions which in return offer services to those who cannot afford to pay for treatment. 

The national government's responsibility for health comes largely from two sources. Immigration, like the admission of goods into the country, is a part of foreign commerce. All who come into the country as immigrants or tourists receive medical inspection, so that if any of them have a contagious disease, they may either be excluded entirely or not admitted until the danger is over. 

The Public Health Service in the Federal Security Agency co-oper ates with the states in matters relating to health and issues bulletins giving advice and information on matters of general interest. The Food

It is responsible for the administration of the Foods and Drugs Act, which requires labels or brand marks to carry truthful statements of the contents of a bottle, box, or other container, and demands warnings in the case of drugs that might have harmful results. The Federal Trade Commission also has the power to interfere with the activities of those who seek to make sales by untrue or unfair methods in advertising. The 

Bureau of Animal Industry in the Department of Agriculture inspects cattle transported from one state to another. 

World-wide co-operation for the sake of health is possible chiefly through such organizations as the League of Nations and private societies like the Red 

Cross. The League gathered statistics about health conditions, the existence of epidemics and means of combating them, and made it easier for nations to protect themselves against diseases from outside. It tried to put an end to the so-called white-slave traffic, in which women and children were sometimes taken from one country to another to be engaged in immoral occupations, and to abolish the opium traffic. 

Community responsibility is not solely a matter for governments. 

Private individuals may co-operate in various ways to protect health and to relieve the sick. Hospitals have been founded by churches or charitable organizations. Social organizations of various kinds now frequently combine in one yearly campaign for money, as you know, and the money when collected is referred to as a welfare fund, community fund, or community chest, and distributed to members of the group in accordance with a carefully prepared budget. Sometimes a community maintains a community nurse who gives help in homes and perhaps co-operates with school medical inspectors. Large business firms maintain a medical department of their own for the care of
