National associations supported by private gifts work hand in hand, when occasion requires, with the local health authorities. The 

National Tuberculosis Association gets money, among other ways, by selling Christmas Seals. The American Child Health Association is interested in many things that concern the well-being of children. 

The Red Cross Society, both the American organization and the international society, assists in almost any kind of emergency arising from fire, flood, or other disaster. The Rockefeller Foundation, working with money given by John D. Rockefeller, maintains an experimental hospital in New York City and has carried on a number of investigations in many parts of the world to find ways of improving health conditions. One of these achieved marked success in relieving the people of Puerto Rico and the southern states of this country who were suffering from hookworm.

Are the hospitals of your community, or if there are none there, the ones which might serve your people, publicly or privately supported? In hospitals which have "free" and "pay" departments, is any distinction made in the nature of the service rendered? 

155. Aiding the Handicapped. By the handicapped we mean people who, through some misfortune, have been deprived of the means of living a happy, comfortable life or who were born lacking some of the natural faculties of normal human beings. In helping them to make full use of whatever talents and faculties they do possess, we may relieve the burden upon others of their care. Included under the "handicapped" are those people whom we technically call defectives. They were either born without full possession of ordinary human faculties, or through accident or illness have lost some of these faculties and powers. Under this head come the blind, the deaf, the dumb, and the crippled. Those who are unable to care for themselves wholly or partly and must be supported or looked after by others are known as dependent. Those who, while not necessarily deficient physically or mentally, have not been able to enjoy the ordinary comforts and conveniences of life, are sometimes called underprivileged. And those who, for any reason, do not seem to be able to take the responsibility for themselves which the average man or woman should accept may be called socially inadequate. 

---

Few people would fail to feel deep sympathy for the blind. According to the 1930 census, there were 643,899 blind people in the United States. Partial blindness, especially with increasing old age, is fairly common and sometimes results from accident or serious illness. A considerable number were born blind. Now every state helps in some way to care for the blind, and the federal government, under the 

Social Security Act, also assists, besides not requiring postage to be paid on books sent to or by blind people. 

Acme Photo THE SEEING EYE 

Seeing-eye dogs have learned to render most helpful service to their masters and mistresses. They go through a training almost as thorough as any other student in school. In this picture the man is extending his own good wishes to the girl who is blind like himself, as she and her dog have finished their course in school. 

Blind people are by no means helpless. They learn to make many things, such as baskets, brooms, and ropes, and are often gifted with a musical sense which enables them to be excellent piano tuners or organists. 

Blind people learn to read by the use of raised letters or a system of marks known as the 

Braille System. Special books, magazines, and musical compositions are published for their benefit. Several blind men have served in the United States 

Congress. Most famous of all blind people in this country is probably Helen Keller, who, through illness when only nineteen months old, became both blind and deaf, but was able to graduate with honor from Radcliffe College and has been a successful author. 

There are almost as many deaf people in the United States as blind. 

Frequently we think of them as both deaf and dumb, but that impression often results from the fact that they do not talk because they do not hear other people. Deaf people learn to understand others through the use of either sign language or lip reading or placing a hand upon a speaker's face or throat. Sometimes they become so expert

4II that by looking directly at a person, they can understand him almost as easily as if they could hear his voice. Deaf people can do more different things than blind because they are not handicapped in getting around as blind people are.

A still larger number than either the blind or the deaf are those who are physically crippled. These may be the result of such disease as infantile paralysis, or of accident, or they may have been born with parts of the body illformed. Medical science has enabled many such people to regain much of their physical strength. Some people learn to be surprisingly expert in doing certain things in unusual ways. 

The special care needed by crippled persons is provided both by private contributions and public aid. Special schools are often maintained for crippled children, though the older ones are frequently taken to regular high schools and means provided for them to get around. 

Crippled soldiers are under the special care of the United States government through the Veterans' Administration. Many who were injured in the World War received special training for a trade after their return to this country, and those who are unable to do much for themselves are cared for in government homes.

One important consideration for defective people is to help them to overcome any "inferiority complex" that might result from their misfortune. The best way to do this is to help them to be as nearly self-supporting as possible. On the other hand, it is bad business to let cripples or blind people beg on the street. It surely should be no more unpleasant to a person's pride to accept help in an institution than to sit on the sidewalk and hold a tin cup. Public institutions for

handicapped people are often under the supervision of the state Department of Health or Department of Welfare. Sometimes states or counties find it costs less to pay for the care of handicapped people in private institutions than to operate a separate establishment themselves.

156. Dealing with the Mentally Sick. People can be sick in mind as well as in body. The treatment of such people is nowadays usually referred to as mental hygiene. It deals particularly with the two classes known as insane and feeble-minded. Insane people are those who once had normal mental powers but have lost control of them, either wholly or partly. A person may be insane on one or two subjects while apparently rational enough about other things. The feeble-minded are those who never had a full mental equipment. About one-third of those who become insane may be 

---

restored to mental health, but a feeble-minded person can never become the mental equal of a normal man or woman. 

In the past insane persons were sometimes chained to cells or put into strait jackets. It used to be thought that they were "possessed of the devil." They were sometimes thrown into jails with the worst criminals.

Today we realize that these unfortunates need special treatment. 

There are private institutions for the insane, and others wholly or partly supported at public expense. Sometimes a county, sometimes a state, sometimes a city, has its own institutions to care for the insane or feeble-minded. New York State has a Department of Mental 

Hygiene in its government, which has the oversight of all public institutions that look after such people. Other states may include such work under their Department of Welfare. Sometimes hospitals have special departments for the insane where they do not mingle with other patients. It is particularly important that insane or feeble-minded people should not be allowed to marry. The chances are strong that many of their children will not be normal. 

Feeble-minded people are of three classes: the idiot is a person whose mental powers never get beyond those of a two-year old child; the imbecile is a person whose mental capacity ranges between two and eight years; and the moron is one whose mental development corresponds to that of a normal child between eight and twelve. 

Idiots are virtually completely helpless. They cannot talk intelligently or understand what others say to them. Imbeciles can do some simple activities but cannot live independently or earn a living of their own. Morons are much more numerous. Since a moron can do some ordinary kinds of work well enough, he may be mistaken for a person who is sound mentally but a slow thinker. The real moron, however, is easily induced to do wrong things. His education should be directed chiefly toward training for unskilled or other simple trades.

Does your state maintain institutions for the insane or feeble-minded, or does it provide for their care by other means? Do you think the intelligence tests given in schools are a fair basis for judging a person's mental capacity? 

Does your state allow insane or feeble-minded people to vote? Should it?

Abnormal mental conditions may take many different forms. Any serious mental disorder may be known as a psychosis. One may suffer

from an hallucination in which he thinks he sees or hears a purely imaginary person or thing. Others suffer from delusions which they hold, usually in regard to themselves. A person may think he is 

Napoleon, or that other people are always talking about him or trying to injure him. Others suffer from illusions. They actually see certain things but believe them to be something else, as happens when one mistakes a piece of rope for a snake. Other difficulties are classified as obsessions. These are ideas that one cannot get rid of even if he tries. Perhaps you have known housewives who could not help thinking that a room must be dirty, whether there was any reason for its being so or not. Sometimes people may suffer from alternations of depression or excitement. An uncontrollable desire to do a certain thing, especially if it requires an exceptional amount of energy or effort, may be referred to as a mania. 

Acme Photo OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY 

One way to help those who have been mentally upset in regaining sanity is to give patients something useful to do while they are recovering from treatment.

People who are not really insane may suffer from various difficulties that some physicians might call neurosis and others nervousness. 

Perhaps you know people who are easily stirred up over little or nothing, who constantly think they are being slighted or abused, and who indulge in very annoying nagging or faultfinding. Hysteria is a condition into which such people sometimes get, in which they display great excitement and talk excitedly, usually with the purpose of getting attention for themselves. Others actually do suffer from a nervous exhaustion known as neurasthenia. Such a person gets tired very easily and may feel too exhausted to have any interest in much of anything. Others suffer from constant worry, hesitation, and discontent. 

Some believe that some of these unfortunate conditions result from the speed and excitement under which so many of us live in these days, though that cannot be the entire explanation. It is asserted that one person out of every ten becomes mentally ill at some time, though not more than half that number go to hospitals. Usually sufferers

from mental diseases are most in need of understanding and sympathy, yet their own words and actions are often such as to make it difficult for any one to feel kindly toward them. Possibly, too, another reason why cases of this kind seem more numerous than formerly is that we now think of such people as really sick, rather than simply possessing a mean disposition. Cases of mental abnormality now come to the attention of physicians and public officials that were once kept quiet and put up with in families in the best way possible under the circumstances. 

157. Poverty, Pauperism, and Their Causes. More people have probably suffered from poverty than from any other handicap except ignorance. Poverty does not mean merely a condition in which one cannot enjoy everything he would like, but rather a state in which one must live at a standard below what is necessary to health and comfort. Pauperism is a still lower level of existence, when outside assistance is required in order to preserve life. It has been estimated that even in so-called good times at least 25,000,000 people in the United States are living on one or the other of these levels. 

Poverty and pauperism are a handicap to society as well as to individuals. The poor cannot contribute much to community welfare, and the goods or savings of the more fortunate have to be drawn upon to care for the unfortunate. Social ill will may develop between the prosperous and the unprosperous, the rich and the poor. The distress of underprivileged individuals or groups may be turned by demagogues or other trouble-makers into personal hate against those who are not themselves to blame for the misfortunes of others and whose own success may have been honestly obtained. Why, then, does poverty exist?

One set of causes that we may call physical includes such misfortunes as earthquakes, fires, floods, and drought, which may affect a large number of people at once and for which neither they nor society may be in any proper sense responsible. Other causes might be classified as social. Business depression or hard times will throw a great many people out of work. Others have been held back by lack of opportunity or a general low standard of living in their particular neighborhood. Some may have lost their jobs when a new machine was introduced into a factory-we have learned to call this kind of thing technological unemployment.

Still other causes might be classified as individual. Sickness may use up all a person's savings and make it hard for him to do first-class work after he recovers. Some have neglected to take advantage of their opportunities. Others are just plain lazy and willing to live on the generosity of the government or the charity of kindhearted people. 

Some are extravagant and wasteful. Some become poor because they have put their savings into some foolish investment and lost all of it.

Sometimes, too, several causes may operate at the same time. The very fact that one gets into poverty may handicap him in trying to better himself. Sickness and unemployment may come at the same time. Poverty is or is not a disgrace, depending on what caused it. 

If one's own laziness or worse is responsible, he must not take it out on society. But if society has not given the person a chance to make himself "socially adequate," then he may rightly expect society to do something to make things better.

From your observation, do you think poor people are more likely to use money unintelligently than others? Make a list, using numbers or letters instead of names, of persons or families in your acquaintance who probably should be classified as poor. In each case what do you think is the cause? 

158. What Shall We Do about Poverty? As long as poverty exists, we shall have to do something to relieve it, though it would be far better to prevent it. We should see that the people who need help get it, and that then they do not waste it. Churches have always done much to relieve the unfortunate among their own members. Some organizations, such as the Salvation Army, that work particularly with "down-and-outers," maintain mission stations in the poorer sections of cities, and by public appeals on the streets try to revive a spirit of self-dependence in them. Lodges and social orders of various kinds also try to take care of their own members and of their families. 

Every large city has some organization known as a Public Charities 

Organization, Association for the Improvement of the Poor, the Help ing Hand, or something else of that character, to which people who are homeless or out of work may apply. Sometimes they care over night for transient unemployed people — otherwise known as hoboes. 

At other times they offer a chance to work in a shop or other establishment and thus to earn something to pay the cost of board and lodging. 

---

Many believe it is a distinctly undesirable policy to give money to a "panhandler" or a beggar at the door. 

Sometimes the same individuals or the same families may get help from several different sources at once. To avoid this difficulty, in all large cities there are now co-operative organizations known as Associated Charities, United Charities, the Federation of Social Agencies, or something of that kind. They maintain a central system of card cataloging and co-operate with public officials who have the responsibility of giving aid to the needy. 

In cities such assistance is usually given through a Department of Charities or a Department of Welfare. In counties and states now such agencies are sometimes referred to as the Department of Assistance, and this activity has become so extensive that in some cases it has been organized as if it were to be a permanent part of a city, county, or state government. In the last few years much responsibility for the relief of the needy has been taken over by state governments and even the federal government. Whether this change is permanent and whether it is even desirable are points about which people differ.

Some cities, counties, or towns maintain poor farms, or "homes," as they are most often called today. Such places may take care of the "unemployables" who cannot work for their living and who have no one who can properly be held responsible for them. When there are children in a family, it is often desirable to prevent the breaking up of the family group. Mothers' pension funds, provided by state law and the federal Social Security Act, help to keep families together. 

Help given outside public institutions is known as outdoor relief; assistance given in a poorhouse or similar place is indoor relief. 

The federal government's activities in the relief of the needy began in 1933, as a result of the nation-wide business depression. 

The Civil Works Administration (the CWA) put about 4,000,000 people on the public payroll for a few months doing all kinds of things. Then came the PWA (Public Works Administration) which was given large amounts of money to use in the construction of public buildings or other projects that would require the employment of people and the purchase of materials but that otherwise would not have been undertaken at the time. 

PWA money was lent or given to states, counties, cities, and school districts to construct roads, build schoolhouses, and do other things they would

not have undertaken without this assistance. Then came the WPA (now the Work Projects Administration) which undertook work that would call for less expense for materials but more for wages, as compared with the PWA. All kinds of things were attempted under the WPA, from building roads and sidewalks to writing state guidebooks and even putting on theatrical performances and maintaining orchestras. 

Numerous problems came up in connection with the sudden development of federal aid to the unemployed. Local politicians tried to use WPA jobs

as a club to get votes which they could deliver. Labor unions sometimes insisted that the WPA should pay the regular union wage per hour, though they were willing to let a person work fewer hours. You can see how such an arrangement might make loafers out of WPA employees. Finally it came to be the rule that a WPA employee must put in at least 130 hours per month if employed that long, and that after 18 months on the WPA he must wait a while before going on the WPA rolls again.

A considerable amount was also set aside for the NYA (National Youth Administration). Pupils in high schools and colleges were paid by the hour for work done in connection with the institutions which they attended. 

The work of the NYA was later extended so as to provide help for those who had graduated from a high school and who were unable to find any employ-

ment. They were frequently aided in training for some skilled trade. The 

CCC (Civilian Conservation Corps) was another effort to look out for young men whose families were needy and who could not get work themselves. 

Camps were set up, where these young men engaged in work connected with forestry or some other service of public benefit. The greater part of the wages which they received had to be sent to the homes from which they came. SEGAN EFF EFFE  OUT OF WORK 

These men have had no luck in finding employment or else did not try very hard. 

They are sitting here sunning on a dock along the Hudson River. 

No system that permanently pauperizes any large number of people can be defensible, nor any plan of relief that gives people the notion that they will be looked out for, whether they try to do anything for themselves or not. Sometimes social workers find that some people possess an illogical kind of pride. A man might be too proud to tell anyone that his family did not have enough to eat, but willing to steal a loaf of bread if he thought he would not be caught. A boy whose father is out of work might run away from home and ride trucks or trains, living on what he could pick up by the way. Some become

just plain "chiselers," willing to take all they can get, whether they need it or not.

Something is wrong, of course, when in a country as rich as our own such conditions could exist, whatever the cause might be. No one class of people, bankers, business men, politicians, or anyone else, can properly be blamed as being chiefly responsible for them. But we have shown too much selfishness in approaching these problems. 

Too often one interested party has been afraid that somebody else would get a larger proportion of benefit or credit than he did out of any reform measure that might be undertaken. Perhaps more than anything else we need a truer knowledge of the facts of the situation and a better co-operation between the government, business organizations, labor unions, and private social agencies. Want in the midst of plenty does not speak well for our national intelligence. 

Do you think the federal government should permanently be responsible for any considerable proportion of "relief"? What "red tape" would an individual or family have to go through in order to get help from local agencies in your neighborhood? 

159. The Places Where We Work. Workmen today in some of our factories find more healthful conditions there than they do at home good light, ventilation, and other conveniences for cleanliness, health, and comfort. A doctor and nurse may be on hand to care for a sick worker or other emergency case. Workers are not obliged to stand up at their work if they can do it just as well sitting down. Men who are engaged in processes which might cause them to inhale poisonous gases or get particles of metal in their eyes or lungs must wear protective appliances to guard against such injury. 

We should not be too harsh on the employers who founded the early factories. Competition was pretty severe, and the employer felt obliged to get all he could out of his workers with the smallest possible expense. Besides, neither at home nor at work did the average family a hundred years ago think of asking for the comforts which the majority of us want today. Both workers and employers understood that when a worker accepted a job, he took his own chances on it. If he got hurt while at work, it was just too bad, and if the employer did anything for him, it was out of his own kindheartedness. 

Undesirable conditions often prevailed in places called sweatshops. 

These are not really shops or factories but simply places in which 

---

people work under conditions that violate the recognized principles of sanitation and comfort. Perhaps in the same rooms at home in which they spent their free hours and their nights, women and children have rolled cigars, made artificial flowers, and worked on ready-made clothing. Even in shops or factories wages may have been set at such standards that only the fastest workers could make a living income. 

Fifty or sixty cents a day has been good pay in some sweatshops. 

Conditions such as these sometimes got even worse when business was affect red W

Philip D. Gendreau IN A VIRGINIA COTTON MILL 

The women are inspecting the cloth for flaws. Not hard work perhaps, but rather tiresome, if one stands up all day. How do working conditions here impress you? not good, for then even well-meaning employers might have to choose between paying small wages for part-time work or closing their plants and letting nobody get any wages or profits. 

One great change with reference to workers is in the hours of labor. 

When factories were first established they took over the long working day that was common on the farm in the summertime and made it, to a considerable extent, an all-year-round schedule. Twelve hours a day or more was common in factories in this country and others at the middle of the nineteenth century. Then it was discovered that when workers had to keep at a job so long that they were completely worn out, they could not do as good work and accidents were much

more common. It was believed that in a shorter working day, workers would be able to work faster and more efficiently and get practically as much done as in a longer time. Of course there are limits to such condensation of effort. But employers did find it possible to operate their establishments on a ten-hour day instead of a twelve-hour, and then on an eight-hour day instead of a ten-hour. 

When business was rushing, it might be necessary to run two or three shifts a day, instead of one.

Following the acceptance of the eight-hour day have come the halfholiday on Saturday or some other day and a reduction in many cases to a total of forty hours a week. In fact, the Fair Labor Standards 

Act of 1938 set that figure as the goal for all workers to whom it applies, after October 24, 1940. Improved machinery has made it possible to get a volume of production, even with shorter hours, that once would have been out of the question. But to set up a uniform rule which must never be set aside by any industry or in any emergency would be unfortunate. Various influences have been responsible for this kinder treatment of workers. Labor unions have done much, but social workers, intelligent lawmakers, educators, and church leaders have all contributed.

Take some factory or other industrial establishment with which you are familiar and observe its working conditions with reference to lighting, ventilation, cleanliness, noise, and hours. Suppose some manufacturing company's business was not very lively but it was able to keep all of its regular force working part time or half of it working all the time. What policy would you recommend? 

160. Who Should Work? Really, is there anyone who should not?

But some kinds of work cannot be done well by some kinds of workers. 

When factories became common, they provided new work for women as well as for men. Since many of the machines did not demand great muscular strength to operate them, many women and some children went to work in English factories. Women and children also worked in or around mines, sometimes in conditions almost unbelievable. 

By the time factories had become numerous in the United States, laws of Parliament had corrected some of the worst evils that had appeared in England, and this fact probably helped to limit the spread in this country of the worst features of factory and mine employment. 

But the hours of the early factories were long, even though women ____________

often felt that when the factory work was over, their time was their own, whereas housekeepers hardly knew that there was any end to a day's work. Usually women were paid lower wages than men. If women, especially when young, worked long and hard, would that weaken them physically, and how would such weakness affect the children of later generations? Besides, since there were many kinds of work they could not do as well as men, the economic pressure they could exert when it came to fixing wages was considerably less than men could bring to bear.

Such problems have led to the passage of laws intended particularly to protect working women. Usually these limit the total number of hours of work per week and frequently specify the hours within which women may work at all in factories or stores. In some industries the employment of women is completely forbidden. In others women under a certain age may not be employed. 

Minimum wage laws for women also are now common, usually setting a figure which is considered the least that a woman or girl could live on if she had no other means of support. For a time most court decisions called such laws unconstitutional, on the theory that women did not need that kind of special protection, and that any worker had the right to make a contract to work as long as he pleased. 

Today, however, the trend is in the opposite direction, and the United States Supreme Court has sustained a state minimum wage law for women.

Outside of the items of wages and working conditions, a number of other social questions have arisen from the very fact of women's going out to earn their own living to a steadily increasing extent. At least a fourth of all women over 16 are now gainfully employedthat is, doing work for which they receive pay in money. Why do they do it? 

Some must, in order to support themselves or others dependent on them. Some want to get away from the humdrum life within a home where perhaps only one woman is needed to do housework. 

Some have natural talents which cause a real demand for the kind of service they can render.

In the 1830's or earlier a woman who had to earn a living might teach school, take boarders, take in washing, or do dressmaking, but not much else. Today there are at least three classes of occupations in which thousands of women engage outside the home: factory work,

work in offices and stores, and professional services. For certain types of office work, for nursing, and for teaching young children, girls and women have talents that few men possess in the same degree. 

And in almost every occupation or profession except those requiring hard physical labor, some women have been outstandingly successful. 

But has this enlarged opportunity for women's work outside the home had any undesirable effect on their interest in the home and on home life itself? Because women's wages have averaged lower than men's, has their industrial activity tended to lower the wage standards for all workers? Should there be any difference in pay between men and women for the same kind and quality of work? Should married women whose husbands are able to work hold jobs that other girls and women would like? Asking these questions, to which not all readers will probably give just the same answers, is one way of suggesting that the expansion of women's work may both help solve some problems and start new ones.

What are the laws of your state in regard to the employment of women? 

What girls or women among the members of your family or acquaintances are gainfully employed? How do they like it? Why are girls and women often unwilling to work as maids or helpers in private homes? Should they be?

Children need protection even more than women. 

Women are grown up and to a considerable extent able to look out for themselves, but that is not true with the child. He has neither reached his full strength nor had education and experience that will enable him to understand industrial problems.

The effects of child labor are almost uniformly bad. Outside of helping out the family treasury and sometimes giving restless children something to do, child labor brings few benefits to anyone except the employer who has work to do that does not require long experience or skill. A child who is regularly employed cannot go to school, and in these days lack of education is a pretty serious handicap. If a child works all day he is likely to be too tired to think of studying in the evening. If a child is regularly employed he may be thrown in with all classes of workers, some of whom have no morals. 

In the national Department of Labor, which was established in 1913, a Children's Bureau was set up which gathers statistics and issues pamphlets to keep the country informed about the problem of working

children. In President Wilson's administration a law was passed providing that the products of child labor should not be carried in interstate commerce, and another which put a tax on such products when so carried. But both these laws were declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court on the ground that this was a matter that belonged to the states. Congress then submitted to the states in 1924 an amendment to the national Constitution proposing to give Congress the power to regulate and prohibit the labor of all persons under the age of eighteen. But that amendment has not received the approval of the necessary three-fourths of the states. President Hoover, who is much interested in social problems, was responsible for calling a national conference on child welfare which met at Washington and drew up a "children's charter" listing provisions which were declared to be the right of every child.

Others than factory owners have opposed child labor laws. Sometimes parents want their children to go to work as soon as possible so as to help out the family budget or even enable the parents to loaf. 

Children themselves may think it is smart to leave school. Farmers have been afraid that child labor laws might knock them out of the help of their own children on the farm. Some churchmen have feared that such laws might be extended so as to dictate the kind of education persons under the age of eighteen should receive. 

The states, however, have little by little enacted and then strengthened child labor laws. Such laws usually prohibit the employment of children at all in some industries, such as coal mining, and in others forbid them to work beyond eight or nine o'clock in the evening or beyond a certain number of hours per week or per day. A maximum of 48 hours has been a fairly frequent provision, with the understanding that four hours of these forty-eight would be spent in a continuation school. Besides, it has been commonly provided that a child must be at least fourteen years old (now more often sixteen) before he could be employed regularly at all, and must have finished the sixth grade in school. If children have to be in school they cannot possibly be fully employed. And certainly if children are not to be allowed to work, school is the best place for most of them. Compulsory school laws go hand in hand with child labor restrictions. 

When, under the National Recovery Administration (1933), codes were drawn up to regulate all kinds of working conditions, it was easy

enough to put provisions into them limiting or forbidding child labor because there were plenty of people over sixteen who had no jobs. 

Such measures as the Wages and Hours Act work in that same direction, because if a child worker must be paid the same as an adult, there is little inducement to employ child workers when adults are unemployed.

There may be some danger of being over-sentimental about child labor. If a boy can deliver newspapers and groceries outside of school UGE 200 

GOOD CEWOOD NEWS WORK AFTER SCHOOL Philip D. Gendreau 

Each of these boys has his own paper route. Do you think such work does them any harm? hours and before dark, his job may keep him out of mischief and do him actual good. Boys or girls of fourteen or fifteen may actually be better off for having some responsibility instead of being forced to loaf. 

We need not be too ready to accept the notion that children should have nothing to do but play. 

Have you ever worked for pay? If so, were you harmed by doing so? Are there kinds of work that young people of the ages of fourteen or sixteen can do particularly well? What are the child labor laws of your own state?

a human agent. As much harm and suffering might result from an accident as from an act criminal in itself. It is proper, therefore, that in conserving human welfare a program of accident prevention should be included. 

One numerous class of accidents we call industrial, because they occur in the carrying on of recognized occupations or industries. To reduce such events, our states generally have enacted laws requiring the safeguarding of machinery in one way or another so that workers

Just now the automobile is the worst menace to human life and safety among all the agencies of transportation. You know all about the campaigns for safe driving, against jay-walking, and such things. 

Since most high school seniors of today either know how to drive a car or hope to learn soon, it is particularly important that they take such matters seriously. Safety for pedestrians can usually be secured by proper care on their own part. They, as well as auto drivers, should respect traffic lights. 

Children should not play in city streets except when a block is definitely set apart for them to do so or when few cars have occasion to drive

there. Stepping out into the street from between or behind cars when drivers cannot see that the child is coming is a careless act which has brought misfortune to a good many children. 

Accidents also occur in places that we usually think are perfectly safe. Mark Twain said once that the most dangerous place for a person was in bed because more people die there than anywhere else. 

About as many lose their lives through falls, burns, explosions, and poisoning at home as are killed in automobile accidents. Fireplaces or gas stoves not properly protected by screens, electrical appliances left where children may tinker with them, cleaning fluid and medicine placed where children may help themselves these are examples of carelessness that no law could stop. 

Some bad accidents have resulted from running or suddenly opening doors in school.

The worst calamities in school have resulted from fire. State laws now insist upon regular fire drills so that pupils will know what to do and where to go when an emergency arises. Most new school buildings these days are reasonably safe, as far as danger from fire is concerned. Getting school children across dangerous streets is another safety problem which pupils themselves can help to solve.

Outside of schools fire is still one of the most distressing sources of loss of life and property. In some years more than half a billion dollars' worth of property has been destroyed by fire in this country and from 10,000 to 15,000 lives lost. It might be going too far to fine people if a fire occurs in their houses, shops, or stores; but we can put the burden of proof upon them to show that it could not have been the result of their carelessness. 162. Programs for Social Insurance. By social insurance or social security we mean measures taken by society as a whole or some part of it to provide for special needs on the part of certain classes of people. 

The emergencies which it is intended to meet, such as unemployment or old age, are not, as a rule, the fault of the sufferer. Society must meet the cost of caring for the needy by sending them to poorhouses and similar institutions, or giving them public or private charity. One 

---

argument for social insurance is that it helps to make charity unnecessary because it has provided in advance for meeting a need. Another way to put it is that if one works faithfully until he is sixty or sixtyfive, he has earned the right to live quietly and comfortably during the rest of his existence. Those who have contributed to the social security funds can claim their share of later benefit not on the ground of charity but as a right.

Once arguments of that character might have been looked upon as pure socialism. When Bismarck was running things in Germany, he took a few ideas from the socialists for the very purpose of weakening their political power and causing Germans to look to the government for help, rather than depending upon the activities of any party. 

Some time later England, under the leadership of Lloyd George, took up with such ideas as unemployment insurance and old-age pensions. 

In one sense, laws governing the hours and conditions of work, especially for women and children, foretold the development of social security legislation in this country (§ 258). Unemployment insurance is discussed elsewhere. Workmen's compensation acts were the earliest kind of social insurance provision to be adopted in this country. Such laws usually provide that a worker who is injured while on duty or made sick by work that his job requires may receive compensation for a certain number of weeks. Both the state and the employer may have to contribute to a fund for such a purpose. Such laws are now practically universal in this country. 

Those laws reverse the old-time theory that the worker was responsible for what happened to him while he was employed. Another tradition was that if the worker was injured as a result of the carelessness or criminal act of another worker, that was a chance that he took along with the job, and that the employer was not to be blamed for the act of a "fellow servant." The modern theory is that industry, rather than the unlucky individual, should stand the burden for such losses. If this means that the employer is going to charge a little more for his product in order to make up for the extra expenses which such laws cause him, the public could afford to pay that at least as well as to let an injured worker and his family become an object of charity.

Arguments against old-age pensions and unemployment insurance rest, to a considerable extent, on two grounds. They do unquestion-

ably increase the cost of government or of private industry. In the second place, some people who otherwise would do their best to take care of themselves will become extravagant and lazy. In answer, the advocates of such measures say that abuse of them is a thing much less to be worried about than the distress that is caused by the lack of provisions of that character. It is urged that the support of old people would cost more in public institutions or "homes" than through pensions, but that is not fully proved. Old-age pensions could be very expensive if they were accepted by everybody over the customary age line. If people who did not need them did not take them, the cost would probably not be in any proper sense objectionable. It has been a disappointment to many to see how states that have tried to be very generous to their old people have had that class in the community exhibit as large a proportion of grafters and chiselers as any other group.

Many states have programs for pensioning teachers, policemen, firemen, judges, and sometimes other officials, who retire after serving a considerable number of years. It is argued that salaries paid to public servants are not excessive and do not enable them to save up very much, though many public officials could not earn as much outside of public jobs as they earn with them. But in many cases the officials who are to get the benefit of them later have had to make regular payments into the pension funds out of their own salaries. 

There was considerable argument about constitutionality when it was proposed that Congress should enact a national Social Security law as was done by Congress in 1935. But the Supreme Court sustained the law and it is now in operation. Details may be changed from time to time, but the principle of federal help to the states for the various classes of people covered by the law is not likely to be abandoned.

The Social Security Act as amended in August, 1939, makes provision for ten classes of people. The Social Security Board, now under the Federal 

Security Agency, which administers the act, is composed of three persons appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. 

One phase of the Act, technically known as Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance, is operated by the federal government alone. The funds are obtained by a percentage of a worker's wage paid by the employer out of the worker's earnings, and duplicated by the employer himself. Each worker

has a social security card bearing a number which refers to himself alone. 

Benefits from this portion of the act go to the worker when he reaches the age of sixty-five and stops regular work, to his wife at the age of sixty-five, and to children until they are sixteen, or eighteen if still in school. If the worker dies before the age of sixty-five, his widow and young children, or dependent parents if he left no other survivors, receive "survivors' payments." Only the first $3000 of a worker's yearly wage are counted as the basis of the payment made for him, and when he is receiving benefits, $85 a month is the limit. 

The exact amount depends on numerous details which would take too much space to mention here. 

The other services provided by the Act are carried on through cooperation between the federal government and whatever agency the states may have to engage in the same kind of work. These features

of these cases determined by the state law or by administrative officials representing the state.

To what extent has your own state enacted various kinds of social insurance? Do you think that the general adoption of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance systems will tend to make people lazy? Should a state maintain an insurance system against accidents, illness, and other emergencies to be supported by voluntary payments from those who might benefit by the plan? What effect would that have on private insurance companies? Can farm laborers, domestics, and seasonal workers be brought under social security laws? 163. "All Work and No Play."- An occasional change helps us to do our daily work better and to get more enjoyment out of life. 

We have become convinced there should be in our lives a place for what we call recreation. The term comes from the Latin and means "re-creating" or "making anew." In other words, it is a rebuilding of the vigor of mind and strength of body. 

Some words are nearly but not quite synonymous. 

Leisure is time

Amusement is somein which there is nothing which we have to do. thing that we do or experience for the fun there is in it. Sport is active exercise, usually physical, that is carried on either for amusement or for recreation. Relaxation differs from sport in that it means simply letting go of the ordinary routine of daily work and taking things as easily as possible. Merely doing nothing, for example, may bring rest but is not necessarily recreation. Neither is overexertion in games and other activities that are not a part of our regular daily lives. 

More people are getting leisure time these days than ever before. 

Sometimes it comes involuntarily, as when one is out of a job, but hardly any labor contracts or agreements are now made that fail to permit some time for something else than work, eating, and sleeping. 

Merely having nothing to do for two or three hours may mean added opportunity for mischief. Leisure in itself is, therefore, either good or bad, depending on how it is used.

Most real recreation should be a contrast to one's regular work. 

To people who do physical labor, recreation might mean rest or reading, attending a play, a game, or a lecture. To those who do mental work, some physical activity is usually of value, such as golf, tennis, swimming, or gardening.

Recreation ought to have moral values as well as physical. Character may be developed through playing games. Self-control, loyalty, co-operation, presence of mind, and many other valuable qualities may thus be encouraged. Music, art, nature study, and the right kind of books also help to develop the finer elements in one's make-up. There is nothing inherently wrong in games like pool and billiards, but they are often played in in undesirable surroundings. When so-called recreation takes the form of indulgence in reckless driving, late hours in roadhouses, and all that goes with such things, there can be little doubt as to the harmful results that follow. But in the long run the old proverb is sound: "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy." The right kind of play brings change to our bodies and minds that enables them to take up their regular activities again more efficiently.

164. How Shall We Play? If recreation is important, how are we going to get it? We ought to be able to furnish a good deal of it ourselves. James Sawders

NEW YORK'S MOST FAMOUS RESORT 

On Sundays people go out to Coney Island by the hundreds of thousands. Many of them find health as well as recreation here. 

Community forums, musical societies, Y.M.C.A.'s, and similar organizations which admit to membership practically any interested person at a small cost will help him to find one or more forms of recreation. They are not conducted to make a profit. The activities engaged in are such as the members of the organization want, and not what somebody else thinks they ought to want or out of which he can make money.

Recreation or amusement furnished for pay offers numerous varieties. Professional baseball is one of the oldest of such amusements;

football and tennis have also become partly professionalized. A team that stands at or near the top of a league is likely to be a big money maker. Probably more people get out-of-doors than otherwise would in order to witness professional sports, and there is, if not relaxation, at least change for those who are too old or too lazy or too inexpert to take part in a game themselves.

The moving picture theater outnumbers by far the professional sport organizations, both in the number of establishments concerned and the number of people who attend them. The physical environment in a stuffy theater may be weakening rather than otherwise, and the nervous excitement that is sometimes aroused by certain types of pictures may also be unfortunate. At the same time, they are the most convenient means of amusement available for millions of our people, and probably moving picture theaters are better equipped, as far as ventilation and other physical conditions are concerned, than ever before. The "legitimate theater" as a means of recreation still has its place for some, but the small town and rural district can have little of it except through the summer theaters that are found in some places.

Do you think the movies are harmful to children? How can the public get moving-picture producers to put out pictures of high quality? Classify the last ten moving pictures you have seen, with reference to the nature of the story, the probable effect on observers, their value from the social viewpoint, and the classes of people for whom you would recommend them. 

Turning now to means of recreation supplied by public expense, we may begin with the local community and its parks and playgrounds. 

If parks in large cities are to do the good they ought to do, the city must try to have several of them conveniently located, rather than to try to make everybody go to one park, however big it may be. 

Playgrounds are primarily for children, of course, though older people enjoy baseball, tennis, and mushball there. A few cities have facilities for the old-style bowling "on the green," rowing on lakes and rivers, swimming in public pools. Golf and archery on other public grounds are features that either have now become common or are rapidly being made so. Occasionally a community will furnish free movies and band concerts in the summertime, and a very few are fortunate to have a community music hall where programs of a high type are presented either by a community orchestra or by a paid organist.

State and national facilities for recreation at public expense usually take the form of state parks, forest reserves, and national parks. 

The construction of good highways has been a great encouragement to people to get outdoors for automobile rides which otherwise would never be taken, though the prime purpose of constructing highways is convenience rather than pleasure. Many of the states have set

WINTER SPORTS 

These are the mountains above Sun Valley, Idaho, which has become a winter sport center, for those who can afford it. Skiing, snowshoeing, and skating appeal to many. apart extensive areas of forest or other public land and provided facilities for tourists to stay over night in cabins or their own trailers if that is the way they prefer to travel. We all know about the national parks and national monuments which the federal government cares for through its National Park Service in the Department of the Interior. 

Many thousands of our people visit such places yearly by auto or by train and find in doing so not only a healthful change but a means of education.

There are plenty of hobbies that an individual may take up and provide in this way for his own relaxation or amusement. Stampcollecting is fun not only for boys but for President Franklin Roosevelt. 

One may live on the top floor of a New York City apartment and still find through photography or one of the many forms of collections some kind of engaging occupation for his spare time, and the same may be said of the farm boy or girl whose chance for recreation outdoors is far superior to that of the city "cave dweller." Anybody anywhere, when he is tired, may at least relax in a chair and turn on the radio, if he has been able to save up the small amount needed these days to own one.

It is not necessary for any person, young or old, to go to some gambling "club" or other undesirable place for amusement. A caution one might well keep in mind is to avoid overdoing anything. Too many people use a vacation for such reckless rushing around that at its end they are in no better shape than when they left, and may even need several days to get going right again. So-called hunting and fishing clubs have been actually carried on in such a way as to turn them into liquor and gambling resorts. Let us have our recreation, but let us make it something that will build us up and not harm us morally or physically.

Do you personally have any difficulty in securing all the recreation you need? Mention hobbies that have been found interesting by people that you know. XV  

Preparing for useful citizenship or even for the wisest use of our own talents is a thing that few of us can do successfully by ourselves. Much of our skill or knowledge comes to us through associations with other people. That is why we have schools. The whole course of experience that prepares us for our place in the world we call education. It is not merely book-learning, though books have an important service to render. When education goes beyond the mere necessities of life and brings us into contact with finer interests we gain culture. No one should be satisfied until he has acquired a fair measure of both. 

Some Questions: 

1. How much is education needed? 

2. How is education provided? 

3. How are schools and school systems organized? 

4. What opportunities do schools offer their pupils? 

5. How may we get education and culture through reading? 

6. How may we get education and culture through music? 

7. How may we get education and culture through art? 

8. In what ways is education available for everybody? 

165. How Much Do We Need Education? Primitive people usually were satisfied when they had enough to eat and some sort of protection from cold and enemies. Each family provided for most of its own needs, and what family B did made little or no difference to family A as long as B let A alone. Yet education had a place among them. A child picked up what he could from the natural activities of family life. Boys and girls learned what their parents knew and probably added to it, little by little, from their own new experiences. 

Today everyone's interests are affected by the activities of other people thousands of miles away. We need to know many things even to look after our simplest wants properly. Nobody's wants are so simple as they once were, and no one could wants himself. possibly meet all of his 

To know how to read and write is one of the most ordinary needs of today. But as late as 1930, out of every 100 people in the United 444

States there were four who were ten years old or more who could not read and write. That was the standard our national Census Bureau used to define illiteracy. Our record for illiteracy is not at all to our credit, though it is steadily going down. It is much worse than that of any of the nations of western and northern Europe or even of Japan. 

In comparison with our 4 per cent, England's mark was 1.8 per cent, and the Scandinavian countries of Europe definitely below I per cent.

Illiteracy in this country has been too common in some southern states among both 

Negroes and poor white people. 

Mexican immigrants in parts of the Southwest and European immigrants in some of our northern cities have kept their records down.

SSSSSSSS SSSSSS SSSSS 

Each figure represents 1% 1910 1920 1930 

Education is particularly important in a democracy. Any fool can obey orders, if he is watched closely enough. But if we are allowed to have opinions and cast a ballot as we please, illiteracy may be dangerous. 

The ignorant are at the mercy of demagogues and self-seeking agitators. One who can read and express his own opinions clearly can ask his own questions and demand sensible answers. The farmer who cannot read about improved methods of agriculture, for instance, or who does not know enough to discover how his products stand in the markets of the world, is seriously handicapped. One who wants to keep up with the procession in any field of work must have his own means of knowing what is going on. 

What a mess you would be in yourself if you could not read and write — and that is only a small part of education! 

ILLITERACY IN THE UNITED STATES 

We are evidently improving in this respect. The 1940 census began to ask the number of years of schooling individuals had instead of merely whether they could read or write.

Make a list of twenty interests or activities which are likely to concern you directly when you are twenty-one years old. Mention at least one way in

which education will help you to attend to those interests better. Is the kind of education needed today the same as that needed by earlier peoples? 

166. How Much Education Do We Need? The answer to that question depends on what we are going to do with it. If all we want is merely to exist, we can get by with a comparatively small amount of formal schooling. But if we wish to live comfortably, to understand other people and the conditions under which they live and work, or to appreciate the treasures of art, literature, and music then there is hardly any limit to the amount of education that can be useful to us.

Soufoto 

A RUSSIAN RURAL SCHOOL 

We may not approve of everything that Russian school children have been taught, but at least many of them have the chance to go to school now. 

Years ago a commission under the direction of the National Education Association made a famous report in which they listed seven cardinal objectives of education. Probably you have heard of these before, but never mind! Their seven great objectives were the following: health; command of fundamental processes (by this they meant such basic ideas as the three R's); worthy home membership; vocational education; wise use of leisure; citizenship training; ethical character. If any one of these has been left out of one's early experiences, his preparation for life will be incomplete.

Some people can never learn as much as some others, and we do not all need exactly the same kind of education. One who is planning to be a physician will need a much different kind of learning and experience than one who expects to be an electrical engineer, and both will need a much wider training than a motorman on a street car. But all of them need the fundamentals covered by the seven cardinal objectives.

There is little likelihood that anybody will ever get too much education, though he may get more of a certain type than he needs. 

One person said: "I am not sorry that I know something about Greek, but I am not sure that other things which I might have studied while I was learning Greek would not have been more valuable." Perhaps the most important item is to be in earnest about what we do, for then we shall get as much benefit as possible out of the things we do undertake.

In the list of seven cardinal objectives, were any included that you would not have in advance expected to find there? If so, what and why? Let each of ten members of the class select a different kind of occupation and make a list of perhaps six educational studies or experiences that will be needed for it. 

After the separate lists have been brought in, observe which items were included in more than one of the lists. 

167. Who Should Provide Education? Education is not something apart from other interests in life. Helpful experiences may come from many sources. The family, the church, business, and other agencies add their own particular contribution. But schools can arrange for that definite planning of instruction that is likely to bring the best results, and through schools most formal education comes. 

Among many people and at many times education was mainly a function of the church. Religious leaders had to know more than the mass of the people, or at least make them think they did, in order to command respect. For several centuries during the Middle Ages the Christian Church was chief promoter and guardian of education. 

Along with the instruction which would be of value in many activities, the Church taught the religious ideas which it believed were essential. 

But suppose we have a country in which there are many kinds of religious beliefs, with no one of them large enough or ambitious enough to dominate the rest. No one religious organization can then provide

the broad training which the young people of a community or nation need, and presumably only a few well-to-do families can afford private tutors for their children. If "all the children of all the people" are to be decently educated, the community must pay for it just as it pays for other desirable things. A democracy in particular must see to it that its people are educated in ways that will not be harmful to the general good. So in every progressive nation today a public school system is found that provides at least elementary schooling for all. In the United States so many more pupils attend public schools than go to any form of private school that we may properly give first attention to them.

If all the people of a country belonged to the same religious faith, would it be desirable to have the schools of that country carried on by the church? 

How can you reconcile the previous bad record of the United States in illiteracy with its emphasis on democracy in government? Are there any people today who would really like to see either public schools or private schools done away with? If so, what motives might actuate them?

Let us make sure that we understand just who or what supports public education in this country. The words "school" and "education" do not appear in the Constitution of the United States, though that document does refer to "the promotion of science and useful arts." The support of schools like those at West Point and Annapolis is not for the purpose of education in general but with the idea of training officers for the army and navy. In many countries, however, education is considered a national job. In such countries there is likely to be a cabinet minister who is responsible for the general oversight of education.

In this country the state government is responsible for whatever system of public education is set up within its jurisdiction. It may provide for public schools by collecting taxes itself for the support of the schools, or compelling the subdivisions of the states, as counties, cities, and towns, to finance them. The amount of money that comes out of the state treasury for public education varies from 7 per cent to 8 per cent in a few states to 85 per cent in one; but in most cases the lion's share of the cost of the schools rests upon the local governments.

The federal government has been responsible for public schools in the District of Columbia and in the territories and possessions, because

the Constitution gave Congress full authority over those places in all matters. When our western states were thrown open for settlement, one of the thirty-six "sections" in each "township" (later two sections) was set aside for the support of schools in that township, but that took no money directly out of the federal treasury. In 1917 an act (known as the Smith-Hughes Act) was passed by Congress which provided for the spending of federal money to support schools within 22

Some demand that appropriations from the federal treasury be made to the states to support all kinds of education and not merely that of a vocational character. They say that since some states are so much poorer than others, it is to the interest of the whole nation to have educational opportunities more nearly equal everywhere. 

That argument appeals more strongly to the poorer states than to the other states which would have to contribute, through taxes, to build up the schools in less fortunate sections. On the other hand, federal support of local schools might result, it is argued, in having courses of study and school policies dictated from Washington, regardless of the needs of any particular state or community. Leaders of Roman 

Catholic parochial schools have been particularly disturbed about this possibility.

In your state how large a part of the cost of public schools comes out of the state treasury? Some states at one time authorized communities to provide free instruction in schools only for those who declared that they could not afford to pay for it. What do you think of such a policy? 

168. What We Pay for in the Schools. Public schools are some times the largest single item in the cost of local government, and why not? A country which can spend billions of dollars a year on moving pictures, cosmetics, cigarettes, and pleasure cars ought to be able to find quite a little for schools. For a country whose total wealth is commonly estimated to be between $250,000,000,000 and $300,000,- 000,000, to spend not more than $2,500,000,000 a year on public schools is certainly not extravagance. As an investment in good citizenship they are cheap at that price.

Taxes in some form are the chief means of getting the necessary money. It is only once in a great while that a wealthy man puts up a high school building in the town where he was born or makes some other notable gift. Sometimes a parent-teacher association or some other local group will raise money to equip a gymnasium or do something else which the regular school taxes have not made possible. 

But that again is the exception. 

In some places a tax on real estate brings in most of the school In some cases sales taxes have been collected for the special purpose of providing money for schools. In other cases the support revenue.

for education comes out of the general budget, and several sources of revenue may be drawn upon to meet the items in that budget. Just as taxes that are used for the care of streets are collected from all people who are taxed in a community, whether they ever use particular streets or not, so school taxes are levied on all taxable persons whether they have children attending school or not. 

School support includes at least three general objects: school buildings and grounds; teachers and other officers; books, maps, machines for school shops, and other materials used in school work. In a live community school buildings are not used solely for children. Especially in rural districts, the school house may be the community center for old as well as young. A solid, substantial, fire-proof structure that will be safe, convenient, and large enough to accommodate all those in the community who want to use it is a community investment well worth making.

No school can be carried on without teachers, supervisory officials, janitors, and other helpers, who should not be expected to work for nothing. A teacher must be constantly learning if he is going to keep ahead of his pupils. New ideas are always coming up in connection with education, and a successful school person must keep informed about these. A community that tries to economize on the cost of education by hiring people simply because they will take low salaries is likely to suffer in the long run and regret its stinginess. 

The cost of books, maps, and such material is a much smaller item in the expense account of schools than many people realize. Machines and other shop equipment are more expensive. But if our schools are to meet the educational needs of all classes of people, we cannot be content with book-learning alone. Besides, if the school is going to give suitable preparation for the wise use of leisure time, and for the side of our interests which we call culture, it must provide for instruction in such subjects as music, art, and other fields of interest which once had little place in the program of studies of the school. 

What is your local school tax rate? Who determines it? Do the people of your community find fault with the cost of public schools there? Do you think there is any justification for criticism? 

169. Organizing Public School Systems. We need to make a distinction between a school and a school system. One good definition for a school is "a group of teachers and pupils working together in a 

---

definite location for educational purposes." There are a considerable number of one-teacher schools still left in the United States, although many states have been trying hard to get rid of them. A school system, however, includes all the schools in a certain community under central supervision, or perhaps all in an entire state. 

Every state has some official or board with state-wide responsibility for public education. If one person is at the head of the organization he may be called the Superintendent of Education or the Superintendent of Public Instruction. Sometimes there is a State Board of Education or a State Council of Education made up of five or more people. In New York State the board that supervises the whole public school system is known as "The Regents of the University of the State of New York." This "university," however, is not any one institution but the whole school system of the state. 

The superintendent is in some states chosen by popular vote and in some states appointed by the governor or the State Board of Education. Sometimes the state authorities are given complete control over the schools throughout the state, even to the extent of choosing textbooks for all the schools of the state. In other cases the greater part of the responsibility of actual management is left with the subdivisions of the state, and the state authorities are more like advisers than officials with positive power. 

There is a great difference among the states as to the importance of the counties in school management. In the South and West, particularly, the county may be the basis of administration for all the schools within it, except that very large cities are usually allowed a good deal of leeway in handling their own affairs. In the northeastern states the actual management of schools is likely to be in the hands of officials in the separate cities and towns. Sometimes two or more of those local governments are allowed to go together for purposes of maintaining better schools than any one could maintain separately. 

Often each city, borough, town, or township is a school district, with its own school board, or board of school directors, or school trustees whatever the local name may be. In the majority of cases these local school boards are elected by popular vote. Their number is usually from three or five up to perhaps fifteen. When they are not elected by popular vote they may be appointed by the mayor of a city or the judges of a county. The local school directors or boards of education 

---

are responsible for electing superintendents, principals, teachers, and other school officials, for fixing the tax rate, for adopting textbooks, for borrowing money to put up school buildings or make other improvements, and sometimes for helping to support local libraries and playgrounds. A state legislature may impose restrictions on the activities of the local boards. For example, it may compel them to levy a certain amount of tax or put an upper limit on that amount. The state legislature may set up standards that must be met by persons to be chosen as teachers. It would be a pure accident if this book's description of the organization of the state or local school system happened to fit your community exactly. Find out the facts about your local school management the same way you would find out the facts about any other feature of local government.

In spite of the lack of responsibility on the part of the federal government for public education, it does feel a growing interest in that field, especially when it involves training for vocational efficiency or national defense. There is in the Federal 

Security Agency a division known as the Office of Education, with a Commissioner of Education at its head. It includes people who make studies and issue bulletins that furnish useful facts about education, and has been given increasing responsibility in helping to see what is done with the federal appropriations for educational purposes. 

States and local school districts may find this federal money very helpful in balancing their own budgets. Citizens in general may profit by the educational information that comes out of Washington.

170. Those Who Conduct the Schools. Most students of education believe that the actual management of a local school system should be in the hands of the superintendent, principals, and teachers, and that boards of education and school directors should not attempt to dictate the details of management of the schools. The best kind of school directors are public-spirited men and women who take those positions not because of any desire for prominence, but because they want to render a public service. School directors are seldom paid salaries. Unfortunately they are sometimes elected for political reasons only, rather than because they take a sincere interest in boys and girls. 

In states where the county is the unit of school organization, there is a county superintendent who has the general oversight of the schools of the county, with perhaps one or more assistants. A city regularly has one superintendent of schools, and probably, in large places, assistant superintendents. Sometimes the supervision of buildings and grounds may be under a separate superintendent. He may also have the oversight of the custodians, janitors, and other helpers in caring for these buildings. Perhaps there may be a superintendent of supplies who will be responsible for the purchasing and distribution of all the various kinds of materials that are used in the operation of the schools.

In many well-managed school systems that are not too large, the

superintendent recommends the adoption of courses of study, selects the teachers whom he would like to employ and presents their names to the school directors, and advises the directors on all kinds of matters concerning the welfare of the schools. His advice may not be taken in every case, though if a superintendent is not able to get his school directors or board of education to agree with him most of the time, it is likely that either he will look for another place, or the directors another superintendent. Superintendents are sometimes elected for periods of four or even six years.

Principals and teachers must be formally elected by the directors or board of education, but, as we have said, the superintendent of schools likes to feel that he has the right to recommend the ones who are to be chosen. The principals and teachers are the ones who meet the pupils day after day in the schoolroom and who direct their study, play, or other activity. Every state has some system of granting certificates to its teachers. The particular certificate a teacher has may depend upon the nature of his college training and his teaching after getting his college degree.

Teachers like to feel that their own positions are secure as long as they do a good quality of work. That is why in so many states they have tried to get state legislatures to pass "tenure" laws guaranteeing them their positions permanently as long as they conduct themselves properly. In a good school system today few teachers will get positions who have not had a four-year course in college or state normal school, and few high school teachers will hold their positions indefinitely without some additional advanced study. Only men and women of high quality should be teachers. At the same time, it is only fair, if we are to expect much of them, to be considerate and reasonable in our attitude toward them.

In addition to a teacher's record in college, what else would you take into account in judging the probability of a teacher's success? Would there be any advantage in avoiding the use of party names in choosing school directors? 

Draw a plan that will show the organization of the schools of your community or county. What regulations are observed in your school district in regard to the choice of teachers? Would you like to make teaching your life work? 

Why or why not?
