172. Meeting Individual Needs. —No two people are completely unlike or completely alike. For that reason there ought to be a considerable number of studies or experiences which should be a part of every one's training, and also plenty of others which might be taken or not in accordance with the different needs and desires of pupils. This fact is taken into account in the division of school work into required subjects and elective subjects. The work of the elementary grades is largely the same for all, because it is believed that a common foundation of the three R's and some other desirable subjects is needed for everybody.

One expert in the study of school programs has said that there are five "core areas" which should be represented in every school program: language arts; social relations; home and vocational arts; creative and recreative arts; nature, mathematics, and science. 

All the way through your course you have probably been required to study some phase of English. You have had, or should have, all the way, geography, history, civics, and other social studies, because an

understanding of the world we live in and the people you have to meet or read about is exceedingly important. All who must make their own living or assist in providing it need some sort of training in the third field that was mentioned. Such activities as music and art represent an element in life that is essential to a thoroughly rounded character and training, and of course the material world that you live in as represented by "nature, mathematics, and science" should not be ignored by one who wants to understand his own environment. 

When one gets far enough along really to understand his own abilities and interests, he may properly begin to spend more time on the things for which he has a natural talent and give less attention to those for which he has no particular qualification. To help him make wise choices, every high school needs one or more people who devote much or all of their time to helping pupils make selections of courses and subjects. In fact, every teacher ought to feel some responsibility for such guidance or counsel. 

Some pupils learn quickly; others cannot or will not. It is generally assumed that the average person fourteen years old belongs in the eighth or ninth grade in school. If he is at any point behind the grades in which the majority of pupils of his age are found, he is said to be retarded. If he is younger than the general run of pupils in his grade, he has been accelerated. Retardation may be the result of slow learning, laziness, unfortunate transfers from school to school, sickness, or other reasons. Acceleration usually means that a pupil has been promoted at a faster rate than one grade to a year. The wisdom of pushing pupils ahead and jumping them a semester or year in school work just because they are brighter than the average boy or girl of their age is open to question. Special studies or other supplementary school experiences for talented pupils might be much better than to put them in grades among pupils considerably older than they are.

Pupils are sometimes classified in accordance with their intelligence as indicated by tests. This practice is referred to as homogeneous grouping. People are not all agreed as to whether this is wise or unwise. Some say that to have pupils of all normal grades of intelligence in one class is a much more natural situation than to separate them into different groups, and that the resulting experience they will get in school will be more like that in everyday life. Others say that

a slow-learning pupil mixed in with those who learn quickly might get discouraged, and that the brighter pupils may be held back if they are in groups with slow learners.

In some cities separate high schools are provided for pupils training for commercial work, for some kinds of skilled trades, or even for particularly talented persons in the field of music or art. Others prefer the so-called cosmopolitan high school, in which provision is

A good high school no longer insists upon a "lockstep" which forces everybody to do practically the same kind of work and to go through a set procedure, regardless of his distinctive interests or talents, nor will it give its chief attention only to those who are going to college. 173. How Schools May Educate. We may learn from books, we may learn from experience in meeting other people, we may learn from doing things of a practical character. Most schools today are interested in the development of every proper interest of a pupil. If a pupil will not respond to the efforts to help him make the most of himself, who is to blame?

Just notice, for example, what schools are now doing in the field of physical education. Once a school might have a football or baseball team which included among its players not only regular pupils, but members of the faculty, and perhaps outsiders, but nobody else got into the game. Now many schools require of all their pupils a definite amount of work in the gymnasium or in some other form of exercise, unless they are suffering from some physical disability. Games between groups in the school may be given almost as much advertising as games between the school team and teams from other schools. 

Another way in which schools of today try to educate their pupils is in the field of citizenship. Knowing the Constitution is good, but merely reciting its language will not necessarily make a person a good citizen. He should feel respect for law and order and gain some experience in having responsibility himself. In our best schools today there is opportunity for students to learn democracy by participating in the handling of the everyday affairs of the school. Committees have definite daily duties in the school. A school council or assembly

co-operates with teachers and principals in maintaining a proper spirit in the school and in suggesting ways to make it still better. 

Contacts with agencies in the community are provided which will supply first-hand information about the way the public affairs of one's own community are managed. New York City, for instance, has taken the pupils in its civics classes for boat tours on the Hudson River and East River which permit them to get a view of the manifold activities of that metropolis. Addresses at school assemblies by inspiring speakers bring to pupils a new point of view, or help them to understand the many features of people's life and work. The planning and publishing of a school paper, the support of many kinds of clubs these and many other activities in the modern school give a great variety of helpful experiences. 

Social life and character training are other interests of a good school today which once schools did not particularly bother about. If the influence of the home or other outside contacts of pupils is bad, the school has to try in six or seven hours of the day for not more than forty weeks in a year to overcome the harmful forces at work in a considerably larger part of the pupils' time. Sometimes pupils misbehave at games or indulge in other conduct that reflects upon their school. Much of the education pupils get in the school comes from one another and is not merely the result of what the faculty undertake. The school can do most for its pupils and for the community only if all who are connected with it feel a responsibility for its accomplishments and its good name.

To what extent can pupils properly exercise responsibility or authority in school administration? What examples, if any, have you seen of overemphasis upon athletics in school life? What provision should a school make for social affairs? Why in the ordinary school is there less interest in interscholastic debates or literary and scholastic contests in other fields than in football or baseball? Does your school have slogans or traditions which help to maintain a high morale among its pupils? Is there a spirit of unity among the pupils in your school, or are disagreements between cliques and factions common?

Often they deal with each pupil on an individual basis and may have no fixed time for the completion of a course. Some private schools make a special effort to do something new or different in method, curriculum, or something else. Public schools, especially those with large enrollments, cannot so easily undertake experiments with new and untried methods. 

For some pupils some of these types of private schools may have definite advantages. Those whose families have been broken by death, divorce, or other misfortune, those who have been kept out of school by illness or other irregularity until they are much older than other pupils with whom they might have to associate, pupils from foreign lands who want to learn English at the same time that they become acquainted with other subjects - these are a few kinds of pupils who may get more out of a small private school than out of some public schools.

Two temptations face private schools to tolerate low standards of conduct or work in order to get the money that comes from a pupil's tuition fees, and to encourage a feeling of snobbishness. Really highclass private schools know better than to commit such errors. There are schools in this country that have a reputation somewhat comparable to that of Rugby and Eton in England. Indeed, masters of private schools sometimes maintain that if it were not for the standards some of them set, the public schools would be content with a much lower quality of service.

177. Going to College? - Some people should and some people should not. Those who would not try to profit by college opportunities and whose chief interest is athletics, fraternities, or amusement might save money for their parents by not going. There are at least three good reasons for going to college: to obtain a foundation of general culture and to broaden one's intellectual equipment; to gain social experience through contacts with others that may help one to be more effective in business or other capacities; to obtain preparation directly leading into specific professions. College men have had many times their numerical share of high positions in government, whether as Presidents, members of the Cabinet, judges, or Congressmen, and the

proportion of people who get to the front in the business world today without a college education is not great. 

Today there are in the United States 795 colleges and universities, not counting such institutions as teacher training schools, business colleges, and others organized for special purposes. Unless we count the junior colleges, which do the work of the freshman and sophomore class of the four-year college, the number of these advanced institutions has begun to decline. Some have either quit completely or combined with others. Many have found it hard to compete with other institutions that had a bigger endowment.

There are three chief sources of financial support for colleges and universities- tuition fees, which often meet less than half the expense of running the institution, income from endowments, and government aid. A "university" sometimes differs from a "college" in nothing much but name, but if there is a real distinction, the college limits its offerings to either a so-called liberal arts course, giving general education, or devotes itself to preparation for some particular type of occupation, as a teachers' college or a medical college. A university is an institution that is composed of several departments representing different fields of learning. It may be composed of several so-called "colleges" or schools. 

A few of our colleges have been exceptionally lucky in piling up large endowments. Harvard has by far the largest of all. Others, like Leland Stanford and Duke, owe their chief support to the gifts of one very wealthy man. Some colleges receive yearly contributions. from many of their alumni. 

Every state has at least one institution supported in part by the

178. Education for Everybody. Education should never end for anybody. Not even school days need to end. Adult education today is often talked about even more than education for children. People already employed may want to become more competent in their profession or trade. Others may wish to have a better understanding of current problems in which all good citizens should be interested. 

Some find leisure time on their hands and want to use it profitably. 

Some, especially farmers, can afford time in the winter to use for study and discussion of topics which will be valuable to them during the busy time of their year. 

The "people's schools" of Denmark have attracted special attention because of the opportunities they offer for adults to learn. England has also tried to give special opportunity for its citizens to improve themselves through special classes. In the United States the chief opportunity thus far given has been through evening classes in high schools and colleges, though during the depression of the 1930's daytime classes were arranged for the unemployed. In this country

correspondence schools have also been developed to a large extent. "Get your knowledge through the mail" has been a helpful suggestion to many thousands. At first these schools were largely developed as private undertakings, but some of our best-known universities, such as Columbia and Chicago, have engaged in correspondence work on a rather extensive scale. Newspapers, except the very poorest, can hardly help containing some instructive features, and the radio always offers a wide range of selection.

A community forum can be very helpful in making possible the intelligent discussion of significant topics in a rural community, a village, or a small town as well as in the city. When it is clear that the people of a community want to keep themselves mentally alive and informed about the things that are going on in the world, they can usually find somebody to help satisfy their demands. 

When you are forty or fifty years old will you be willing to admit that you can still learn? If you know anyone who has taken correspondence courses, what was his reaction to them? By what means not directly connected with any school have you improved yourself in some way during the past year? 

179. Education and Culture through Reading. — Our people have considerable of a reputation as readers, but what do they read? Back in colonial days the Bible was more commonly read than anything else. 

Books were few and most of them had to be imported from England. 

Many people in those days could not read, anyway. The first newspaper in the country that had a continued existence for any length of time was the Boston News Letter, which began publication in 1704. 

One of the most famous trials in our history occurred in New York City in 1736 when Peter Zenger was prosecuted because he had said something in criticism of the government of the colony. When he was acquitted the event was looked upon as a notable milestone for freedom of the press in the colonies.

Reading must always be one of our principal sources of information. 

Intelligent people do not believe everything they see in print, but if it were not for the printed page, ignorance would be dense. There is so much printed matter of all kinds that one who wants to waste his time through reading can do it just as readily as one who wishes to put in his time profitably in that way. 

In 1938, according to the best statistics available, there were in the United States about 25,000 newspapers, including both dailies and weeklies. There are not so many newspapers as there were even a few years ago. As the wages of employees have gone up and newspaper chains have been formed which can furnish material for every member at comparatively low cost, it has been difficult for some papers, even in our big cities, to come out even. Advertising is what keeps most newspapers going, anyway.

You know that newspapers vary greatly in make-up and quality.

ליי Some appeal to readers of intelligence. Others play up to those who want scandal or sensation.

Some load their pages with cartoons. 

Some make much use of "columns" or other "syndicated matter" which is sold to perhaps dozens of papers at the same time. 

In reading newspapers one must use judgment and common sense. 

When we find what the particular bias of an editor or columnist is, we may make allowance for it in our reading. A good newspaper will

Too few of us read the editorial page. Maybe it is best for us to form our own opinions, regardless of what the editor or publisher

wants us to think. But those editors who do write thoughtful articles with literary skill deserve a wider appreciation than they receive from the millions of people who prefer the tabloids with their big headlines and sensational pictures. 

Magazines are far more varied in character than newspapers, though fewer in number. A magazine may serve any of some dozens of purposes. It may be a weekly news magazine, like Time or Newsweek, a combination of stories and special articles, like Collier's or the Saturday Evening Post, or it may represent some religious, educational, or scientific interest. Monthly magazines are frequently of a high quality. The National Geographic, the Atlantic Monthly, and Harper's, for example, are valuable for all kinds of readers, though only the most intelligent people do read them. The Reader's Digest is an example of another recently developed kind of publication which meets the needs of a great many people. 

New books to the number of 9,015 were printed in the United States in 1939. They, too, come in infinite variety. They include textbooks, scientific publications, histories, biographies, poetry, and fiction. Most public libraries find that about 75 per cent of their total lendings are of fiction. Perhaps this means that more people read to be amused than to be informed, though some novels that have had a very wide sale - Gone With the Wind, for example gave an interpretation of history that meant as much to many readers as the story itself.

Many books, like tunes and moving pictures, have a brief vogue. 

They are popular for a little while and then forgotten. A very few, either because of the subject with which they deal or the manner in which they are written, become classics. Uncle Tom's Cabin was one of these which played an important part in our history. It was not a great work of literature but dealt with a great social problem at a time and in a way that appealed to the emotions of its readers. 

Every taste, intellectual or stupid, depraved or cultured, can find what it wants in the output of American authors and publishers. One sometimes wonders why books go out of their way to deal with the disagreeable and ugly side of life to the extent that they do. Many works of foreign authors have had a prominent place in the world's literature, and some of these are read, as you know, by students in modern language courses in our own schools. Today, however, most

things worth reading in any language will sooner or later be translated into English. Some books of this kind, like All Quiet on the Western 

Front, get an even larger sale in the English translation than they did in their original form.

Many of us cannot afford all the books we should like to read, and others who could afford them do not care to buy them for permanent ownership. The modern library not only collects books but provides facilities for obtaining information from all kinds of sources. A large community can stand the expense of maintaining a library of half a million books better than most individuals could afford a thousand.

180. Education and Culture through Music. 

"A primrose by the river's brim A yellow primrose was to him 

And it was nothing more." 

Thus Wordsworth characterized one who might be a type of some millions of people today. To many millions music is just noise, perhaps in rhythm, but beyond that it means nothing. To others paintings and drawings are only splashes and marks. Yet music, art, and their related interests, such as drama, may contribute greatly toward education and culture on the part of those who can appreciate them. 

Who is to blame if our people do not appreciate music as much as those of some other countries? One reason is that we are still, as compared with many other peoples, a young nation, and in the early periods of a nation's life people have to spend so much time on the material side of things that they do not pay great attention to cultural interests. Our schools in the past seldom tried to develop musical or artistic talent in their pupils to any great extent. Perhaps that is one reason why some today look upon music and art as "fads and frills" and do not want school money spent on them. 

Music is another means by which the people of any race or nation can develop a common feeling. Whatever the nationality of a composer, be it Bach, Mozart, Chopin, Gounod, Tschaikovsky, Sibelius,

Elgar, Foster, or Sousa, when we hear the composition we may or may not think of the name of the composer, but we can catch the spirit of the music. There is nothing wrong with brass bands. They have their place in the world of music. But there is something lacking in us if the only music we can appreciate is the kind that has noise and swing.

There are millions of us to whom so-called classical music means little or nothing, but who are thrilled by a song that expresses religious feeling or patriotism or the humble sentiment of a folk melody. There is no reason why we should discredit these kinds of music, but it is important in our schools that our pupils be helped to appreciate all kinds that are likely to have lasting merit. 

Kaufman-Fabry Photo EDUCATION OR RECREATION? 

Do you think this crowd at the Chicago Civic Opera are there for a good time or because they enjoy music and are benefited by listening to the opera? 

Practically every large city of Europe has its symphony orchestra and music hall, and its people throng by the thousands to the concerts which are given at reasonable prices. In the United States, symphony orchestras in our large cities have had to compete with so many less expensive kinds of recreation and amusement that they have sometimes lost out in the process. Today one sees evidence of a revival of interest in music of the better kind. Perhaps that is a result of the attention given to music in our schools. Some would not favor introducing competition into any kind of art, but if recognition is given for talent and achievement on the part of an orchestra, a chorus, or a pupil soloist

as well as to a track team or a halfback, we may put a fairer value on some things in school life. 

Only a large city can afford grand opera. Only a church that has a fairly well-to-do congregation can pay for a first-class organ. But there is no excuse for doing less in these matters than we can afford to do. 

Can a love for music be cultivated in one who does not naturally feel it? 

How many outstanding musical compositions could you name if a significant strain from a dozen or fifteen of them should be sung or played? Name living composers or others of recent years whose work you think will last.

181. Education and Culture through Art. Under the head of 

"art" or "the arts" a variety of talents and interests may be included. 

Painting and sculpture, of course, belong there, and some would include drama as well. Sculpture and painting in this country have never attained the heights of the work of the great artists of several European countries. But we do have outstanding names of artists in this country, such as Gilbert Stuart, Winslow Homer, Cecelia Beaux, Augustus St. Gaudens, John W. Alexander, Frederick MacMonnies,

Lorado Taft, and Gutzun Borglum, to mention just a few. 

Sometimes we are moved to ask the question as to what is really art in painting. We have our modernistic kinds of painters, the 

---

cubists, the surrealists, and others, who seem to take pride in making pictures that look unlike anything that was ever seen in real life. 

Then they tell us that if we cannot interpret these there is something wrong with us. Perhaps a picture should make us think and not merely give us nothing to do but look. But surely art that pictures things as they are means more to the average person than something that has little significance except in the artist's mind. 

James Sawders THE UNION STATION IN LOS ANGELES 

There is hardly any kind of building construction today that ignores artistic treatment; yet few railroad stations exhibit just this kind of architecture. 

Can artists be made or do they have to be born? Genius can hardly be worked out by formulas and instruction. Certainly, however, in our schools we should give our pupils a chance to express themselves in other ways than by words, and not keep genius concealed, if it exists. Art is no longer limited to classical or traditional forms. 

There is art in advertising. There is a kind of art in the cartoon that suggests strikingly a thought that might take pages to express in words. 

There is art in the decoration of one's own home. Even a mechanical gadget can be made to look attractive. Anyway, one can learn to appreciate artistic talent in others.

In the United States we have given to architecture a turn which had not previously found expression elsewhere. The construction of business buildings, schools, and other great edifices in such a way as to give the greatest amount of light, convenience, and usefulness for the space that is used is a valuable contribution. Does the skyscraper represent an ideal in building construction worthy to be perpetuated? 

We are not yet sufficiently accustomed to some of these new ideas to prevent some of our "modernistic" residences and buildings from seeming strange. Only the future will tell whether these new features of architecture will prove so satisfactory that almost everybody will adopt them. At least they display a creditable originality. 

Let us add a few words on another kind of art - the art of effective speech. Drama and music, both as a means of livelihood and as an expression of artistic taste, suffered a terrible shock when the talking picture came in which could reproduce both voice and music mechanically. Hundreds of musicians lost their means of livelihood, and other hundreds of actors and actresses lost also the chance to display their talent.

In some places, however, the decline of professional drama has encouraged amateurs to do something for their own amusement and the entertainment of their friends. In many places "little theaters" have been established where in a renovated barn or school or some other place not meant for theatrical purposes groups get together and present plays. Especially does this happen in the summertime. 

Perhaps in the long run such groups may revive an interest in the "legitimate" theater which may regain for it some of its lost popularity. A few talented men and women continue to present on the stage plays of quality from historical, literary, and artistic standpoints. 

Some, however, have done nothing in any of these respects — and that is one reason why the theater has not been a more uplifting social force. 

Public sentiment is what can make the stage, concert hall, or the art gallery contribute most fully to the improvement of a community. 

In the long run people in a free country can get what they want in the field of culture as well as in the field of government. 

How does your community stand with reference to its interest in art of any character? How important is art in the program of your schools? Compare the typical new home or office building of today with one of forty or fifty years ago.

XVI  

When a definite portion of a great undertaking is completed, or a good stopping-place is reached, it is often well to look back and see what has been accomplished. This may be a good place to do just that. Such a backward look may help us in correcting our faults and moving ahead in the right direction and at the right speed. There is little hope for a person or a nation that is perfectly satisfied with what has been accomplished.

Some Questions: 

1. What progress have we made in personal living? 

2. How far have we succeeded in understanding and controlling nature? 

3. Wherein have we failed and why have we failed? 

4. What hope is there that peace and justice may be established in the world? 

5. What are the next steps we should take in the direction of social control? 

6. How in our personal thought and study may we think and act intelligently? 

7. How much right do we have to expect a better society? 

182. Better Ideals and Ways of Living. — If we compare the way the cave men acted toward one another with the way men act today, we may be tempted to say that the principal difference is that now we kill people more scientifically and speedily than primitive men did it. Wars no longer are carried on by one small group against another small group, as in the days of primitive man, but the excuse sometimes given for making war is to set up a new society for a whole continent. At their best men do plan for the improvement of life for all the people of a community or a nation. A group acts in the supposed interest of all of its members, even though that activity may be perverted to brutal uses. 

If we can keep our thoughts upon what men think at their best rather than what they do too much of the time, we shall agree further that our ideals of character and conduct are much higher than those 490

of primitive man. Longer experience has helped us to distinguish more clearly between what is helpful and what is harmful. More people realize that a harmful thing is wrong, and even when brute force prevails, it is seldom justified except by those who make use of it.

Religion in our time seeks to discover ways to realize our noblest ideals of the relationship of man with man and of man with God. 

International News Photo ONE WAY TO MAKE CHANGES 

Hitler has come into Czechoslovakia and is telling the people what's what. Not so long ago we were thinking that perhaps the time was over when brute force would decide in what direction the world would move. It has been a rude awakening. Is there any way to reverse this backward trend? 

Thoughtful men no longer consider it a means of appeasing a heartless divinity or an attempt to divert disaster by some sort of magic. 

Forms and ceremonies may encourage reverence, but no longer do we imagine that rituals can take the place of right living. 

We cannot take time to survey all that has been accomplished in improving human life and comfort. The fact that the average length of life for men and women in this country is nearly twice what it was at the beginning of the last century should be evidence enough. The work of our hospitals, the relief of pain through anesthetics, the care

we give to the cripple, and our truer knowledge of how to look after our bodies, represent tremendous gains over even the recent past. 

We have found means of storing up knowledge and learning both in books and in the minds of men and women. We are not satisfied to let them pick up what they can get haphazardly by watching the misfortunes or achievements of others; but in our country at least, and in a good many others, “all the children of all the people” are not only given the opportunity to learn, but required to be exposed to schooling. And how much better equipped we are than ever before to learn what is going on all over the world and to be informed of the discoveries of ways to adapt the gifts of nature to pleasanter living. 

Too many have failed to appreciate their opportunities for the finer and better things in life, but the opportunity is open to many more than it was even in our grandfathers' time- not to mention the days when nobody even thought of culture. 

The men and women who make up society today have learned more than men and women knew in any other generation. They travel on the wings of the wind and talk with the speed of lightning from one continent to another. All of this we have achieved, even though in some respects we have lamentably failed to measure up to our opportunities.

5000 years ago, 1000, 400, and 100. 

183. How We Learn about Nature. Our world owes much to discoverers, scientists, and inventors. The discoverer is one who finds something that was not known to him or his group before. The scientist puts together in some kind of orderly fashion facts that have been discovered about nature and people. The inventor takes advantage of these discoveries and this knowledge and works out new ways or new tools or machines with which to do things. 

There are two great classes of science. Natural science deals with the forces of nature and the way they work. It includes such special fields of interest as biology, physics, and chemistry. Social science deals with human life in its various relationships. As we have already learned, it covers geography, history, civics, economics, and other related subjects. The two fields are not separate, and there is so

much in them that rarely does one mind seek to grasp anything more than a moderate proportion of both. 

The true scientist never claims to know it all. New facts are being constantly brought to light. Sometimes a scientific notion is modified or displaced through practical experience. Natural science is somewhat easier to organize and to express in the form of definite laws and principles than social science, because we can rarely be quite so sure about what human beings are going to do as about the way nature acts under a given condition. 

From your observation of people, do you think it would be correct to say that some are more interested in things than in people and others are the other way? Offhand, how much do you think a scientist should know about history or a student of the social sciences about the natural sciences?

Primitive man had to learn pretty nearly everything from experience. He could see and feel the effects of the forces of nature wind, cold, heat, and moisture and could see the movements of of the heavenly bodies, but could not do much else than accept them and learn to adapt himself to them or protect himself from them. One who tried to delve into the mysteries of nature might be looked upon as in league with the evil one, or else, if he had sufficient ability to bluff, make himself a man of magic or a priest who claimed acquaintance with the will and power of the gods. 

Some ancient peoples, however, learned scientific facts and methods. 

Ancient Egyptians figured out ways to mark off flooded lands again

The chemist of today helps in countless ways to make improvements possible in practically every phase of human life. 

This man is studying how to make more effective a kind of insect poison. Business firms often pay the salary of a laboratory worker for a year or more who will do nothing else but try to find ways to improve things that they produce.

after the yearly overflow of the Nile had gone down. They could move enormous stones to use in building their pyramids. They as well as priests of Babylon learned about the movements of some of the planets. Means of measuring time were developed — the year, the month, and the week. 

Because the best new ideas come in an atmosphere of freedom, it was natural that among the Greeks sciences made the greatest headway in ancient times. Greeks like Pythagoras, Aristotle, and Euclid thought as keenly about many things as any of the masters of thought do today. The Romans were more likely to be what we sometimes call pragmatists. If a thing worked, it was good. But during their time facts of science were discovered and theories set up which helped toward an explanation of things. 

If you had lived about 200 A.D., do you think you would have believed that the sun goes around the earth? Would it be natural for people who cared as much about conquest as the Romans to think a great deal about science? 

184. How Science Went to Sleep and Woke Again. 

What we call the Middle Ages were a bad time for science. Many of the leaders of the Christian church believed that since scientific ideas were not emphasized in the Bible, it was wrong to try to go into that kind of study. So during the medieval period, from around 500 to perhaps 

1300 A.D., scientific knowledge made greater progress among the 

Arabs than any others, because they were not handicapped by this wrong interpretation of one's attitude toward the world. They learned something from earlier Greek philosophers and scientists, and developed remarkably well their studies in mathematics and astronomy. Though they did not invent them, they brought into 

Europe the "Arabic numerals" which we find so convenient today. 

Not all medieval Christians were opposed to science. In some of the monasteries and cities were men who would have been scholars in any day. Most famous of the medieval monks, as far as science is concerned, was the Englishman Roger Bacon, who lived from 1214 to 1294. He wanted people to find out things for themselves and not to hesitate to raise questions about what those in authority declared to be the truth. He had to spend several years of his life in prison because he was looked upon as a dangerous character. But he was keen enough to foresee in principle even the steamboats, automobiles, and aircraft of our time, though he could not describe them in detail. 

---

The latter part of the medieval period and the early modern days were marked by some notable new ideas and methods. The compass which enabled people to know where they were on the sea became familiar to mariners of Western Europe, and the Portuguese used it in creeping along the continent of Africa toward India. Westerners learned something about gunpowder, and with it they felt safer in going into unfamiliar regions and meeting the natives who lived there. 

One great handicap from which scientific knowledge suffered for thousands of years was the difficulty of spreading new ideas after anyone had them. Try to copy even one chapter of this book by hand and you will get some notion of what it meant to make a dozen copies of a work on any subject. 

But during the Middle Ages Europeans learned how to make paper, possibly getting this idea from the Chinese, as they may have learned of the compass and of gunpowder. Then about 

1440 Europeans began to print with type. We know that John 

Gutenberg of Mainz in Germany set up a printing establishment around 1450. Within thirty years after that date Dutchmen, Italians, and Englishmen were also doing the same kind of thing. Those printing presses were not much like ours, but they were a tremendous improvement over handwriting.

The period from the twelfth or thirteenth century to the sixteenth, which we commonly call the Renaissance, was marked by a great advance in science as well as in almost every other field of thought. 

As happened in so many other fields, science had a rebirth. Not only were old scientific opinions revived, but when they were found to be wrong, sooner or later somebody had the courage to say so and prove it. 

Gladys Miller

AN OLD-TIME PRINTING PRESS

Much that passed for science during the Middle Ages was something else. The astrologers of ancient Chaldea had their successors who for centuries encouraged people to believe that the stars controlled the development of human life. A belief in alchemy also was common that a way could be found to change other metals into gold, not realizing that if we could do that, gold would cease to be more valuable than the other things. But we need not be too harsh on those people, Lawrence H. Miller A PRINTING PRESS OF TODAY 

Compare it with the one of 1745 in size, speed, and other respects. for there are plenty today who visit fortune tellers, crystal gazers, and others who know no more about the future than do their dupes. 

During the period from the sixteenth century onward such far-reaching changes in people's knowledge and attitudes took place that we often speak of the new mode of thought as the Scientific Revolution. 

It had much to do with bringing about that other vast new movement which we call the Industrial Revolution. Sometimes it was necessary to fight wrong ideas, just as truly and just as vigorously, though in a different way, as other revolutionists have had to fight

tyrannical rulers. Sometimes the new thinkers made themselves unpopular by being so sure they were right that they made enemies, just on that account.

For instance, there was the Frenchman who called himself Voltaire. 

He rendered a great service in being willing to criticize things that deserved to be changed, but in his smart-aleck fashion he did not always distinguish between things that should be attacked and those that were helpful. In the nineteenth century, too, Charles Darwin gave out the new theory of evolution. This was merely the principle which seems to be established by experience and observation that higher forms of life have developed out of simpler ones. But when some interpreted this theory to mean that men are merely highly developed monkeys, it seemed so contrary to the teachings of the Bible that many were not willing to see any truth in evolution at all. The 

Scientific Revolution is still going on, and no real scientist will claim that anywhere nearly all the facts are known about the world and its origin and the people who occupy it. 

Do you think most people enjoy getting new ideas? Why or why not?

Have you found any superstitions that people today believe just as positively as anyone could have believed them 500 years ago? If you think you can grasp it, ask somebody to explain to you Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. 

Mention some things which you would like to know about nature and its operations, but which no one can explain with certainty today. 

185. How Science and Discovery Have Explained the Universe. 

To tell this story we must go back again to the sixteenth century. 

In 1543 Copernicus published his theory of the relationship of the sun and the planets which reversed the general notion about such things. He was followed by such men as Galileo, who gave new force to the theories of Copernicus, and who used the telescope to get a closer view of the moon, the planets, and other heavenly bodies. 

Others invented or improved scientific instruments such as the microscope, the thermometer, and the barometer, and gave to scientists instruments of immense importance. In the latter part of the seventeenth century Isaac Newton gave to the world the idea of gravitation, along with numerous other new thoughts. Since those times two planets have been added to the list of the sun's satellites - Neptune and Pluto, which Galileo did not know about. A few of our great cities have planetariums in which spectators can actually see pictured

before their eyes the movement of sun, stars, and planets on a small scale, just as they do travel in their vast courses. 

Our thought of the make-up of the world itself has changed. Once we were told that everything was composed of atoms and that the atom was the smallest particle in nature. Now we learn that even the atoms are made up of electrons which are constantly moving about, and that therefore all nature is moving and not still. Perhaps some of the new scientific ideas do not seem to have any very direct practical relation to our everyday life, but anything that bears upon the constitution of the universe must have some significance. 

Discovery has brought to us knowledge about previously unknown parts of the world. In some respects the great age of discovery ended with the seventeenth century, for by the end of that century wellinformed people had some general notion of the size and shape of the western continents. But in the eighteenth century Vitus Bering, a 

Dane in the service of Russia, visited the strait and sea named after him, and James Cook, an Englishman, went to Australia and New Zealand, which had first been found by the Dutch, and also brought to the knowledge of Europeans the islands which he named after his patron Lord Sandwich, and which we know today as Hawaii. 

Nineteenth century explorers opened up new parts of North America and some of the interior of South America, Africa, and Asia. Progress was also made toward the North Pole. It remained for our own century to furnish such men as Peary, who first reached the North Pole, Amundsen and Scott, who got to the South Pole, and Byrd, who flew over both of them. There are still parts of the earth which have been visited by comparatively few from Europe or America, and there are mountains whose tops have not yet been scaled. 

We must admit that there is plenty yet to learn about our own earth and its neighbors in the solar system, and about the rest of the universe. 

What are the cosmic rays, for instance, that are believed to be bombarding the earth from the distant ranges of the stratosphere, as that portion of space that surrounds the earth and its own atmosphere is called? We are not even sure that some of the scientific ideas which we thought to be definitely established are so completely certain as we imagined. Much of what we believe to be true may depend for its truth on whether something else is true also — and that may have to be proved.

Of what value other than the satisfaction of inquisitiveness is a knowledge of the regions around the North Pole and the South Pole? Does it make any real difference to us whether the earth is bombarded by cosmic rays or not? 

Do you suppose it will ever be possible for people to exchange visits between the planets?

An 186. What Science and Invention Have Done for Industry. 

up-to-date young man or woman does not need to be told that the machine age has brought about all kinds of changes in the way things are done. The type for the book which you are reading was probably set up by machine the same as it is on the great newspapers. Once every single letter had to be picked out of its case by hand - and you know how wonderful an invention was the idea of movable type. 

Our Patent Office at Washington celebrated in 1940 its 150th anniversary. In the first year of its existence only three patents were issued, but in its 150th year the number was 43,030.

Make a list of a dozen things that play a part in our everyday human interests and activities. Then go back in imagination a hundred years and see how many of them were in common use. Contrast, also, the methods of communication and transportation today as compared with those of a century ago. What means of lighting have come into use since then? 

Perhaps the last century-and-a-half deserves to be called the power age just about as truly as the machine age. Man power, horse power, wind power, and water power had all been used, and steam power was becoming common in the early nineteenth century. Electricity has brought its marvelous convenience to us within much less than a century. Press a button or turn some other little contrivance and you either have light where you want it or start the machines of a great factory. Since Edison made the electric light practical in 1879, people in all kinds of communities, urban and rural, have learned to depend upon it. Electricity not only furnishes the force to make industry move, but brings convenience into every household that is wired for the purpose.

New machinery and new methods have made an immense difference in the production of certain vital commodities. When men first learned to use iron for tools and weapons, they had achieved something of vast importance. But when Bessemer and Kelly found out how to make steel, the usefulness of the metal was tremendously

increased. The same was true of rubber. Until about 1852 it had almost no practical use, for it could not be kept hard enough to be suitable for warm temperatures. Then Goodyear found out how to vulcanize rubber, and you can hardly count its possible uses today. 

Another phase of the Industrial Revolution appears in the improvements in transportation and communication. Once the best you could do in getting from New York to Philadelphia was two days. 

Now you can go by train in an hour and a half. Once it meant months to cross our continent. Now it takes not many more hours 400

Now we can learn about either peace or war at an earlier hour by the clock than it is made or broken in Europe, and hear the addresses of presidents, dictators, and prime ministers perhaps more clearly than if we sat in front of them.

The machine age surely has given us immense facilities for comfort and convenience, and produced problems once not imaginable. 

Factories have brought masses of people together to work in one

187. Science and Natural Resources. When we think of the . 

Industrial Revolution, natural resources are involved, because raw materials are used in all industries. Changes in farming that began. about the same time the Industrial Revolution started in England were not so spectacular, but were important nevertheless. An Englishman named Townsend tried to improve the quality of vegetables, grains, and plants by scientific breeding. The same idea was also developed in connection with farm animals, so that cattle and pigs might have good size and weight instead of being mostly bones. Rotation of

crops, so that by planting different crops in a certain area in different years the same drain on the soil might not take place all the time, was another advance step in farming. 

Machinery turned out to be useful to farmers as well as in factories. 

Eli Whitney's cotton gin gave a new turn to the agriculture of our southern states. McCormick and his reaper did the same for the great farms and ranches of the Middle West. Today farm after farm is using electric power for power for many things, even to milking the cows, not to mention the radio and telephone. 

R. I. Nesmith and Associates CONTOUR FARMING 

You see how by plowing and planting in the right way, hillside farms in this California Valley may be kept from loss through soil erosion. 

Some facts about the use of natural resources we did not learn soon enough, or if we learned them, we did not put them into practice. 

European countries realized the importance of not destroying forests recklessly and making careful use of every square foot of soil long before our farmers appreciated their situation. Scientific study has now told farmers to prevent or reduce erosion, or wearing away of the land by rains and wind, by that kind of contour cultivation that runs furrows across a hillside instead of up and down. When the World 

War created an unusual demand for wheat to feed our soldiers and the people of our Allies, land was plowed for the purpose in the drier districts of our western states that was never meant to be so treated.

A little later, when dry years came, the winds picked up the top soil and carried it away. The tragedy of this "dust bowl" for some years was one of the saddest things in our whole economic history. 

We can make new varieties of plants as well as of tools and machines. 

Our patent laws have been so changed as to recognize this fact and allow the producer of some new variety of plant, flower, or vegetable, to be protected in the same way as the inventor of a new machine. 

Luther Burbank is the foremost example of those who have not only improved the quality of plants and vegetables already known, but even brought into existence new kinds. 

Many have the impression that farmers are not as progressive and ready to receive new ideas as city people. What is your observation on that point? 

188. Science and Health. You have already learned the fact that epidemics no longer take the toll of human life that they once did, and that the average length of life has been almost doubled in a hundred years. Science did this. The makers of moving pictures honored Louis Pasteur, indeed, before they did Thomas A. Edison.

One of the earliest of the modern group of scientists in the field of health was Joseph Lister, an English physician, who in the 1780's discovered the use of antiseptics which we now employ to prevent infection from blood poisoning, lockjaw, and numerous other causes. 

About half a century later at least three men in the United States learned how to put a patient to sleep so that he would not suffer while an operation was being performed. The use of anesthetics has now been so refined that in many cases we can simply treat only part of the body without making a person completely unconscious. Pasteur's and Koch's contributions to the methods of treating diseases were of vast service to humanity. 

In the overcoming of disease many have gained fame, though some have lost their own lives because of their heroism. Yellow fever, for instance, in the past might afflict almost any community in warm climates, but now it has been almost completely wiped out wherever men have gone who have known how to handle the situation. Dr. 

Walter Reed in Cuba after the Spanish War was responsible for putting to the test the theory that a mosquito was the carrier of the disease. Jesse W. Lazear became a martyr to the experiment, but his sacrifice, as well as the bravery of those who lived through the

test, have made possible the saving of no one knows how many other lives.

The discovery of the so-called X ray by the German scientist Roentgen is another extremely valuable achievement. By it physicians and surgeons can see conditions that previously they could only guess at. The possibilities of radium not yet fully known, of course were first told us by 

Professor and Madame Curie,

French and Polish, respectively, by birth. 

Science and invention have done many things to preserve food from decay. Refrigerator cars in which meat, milk, and vegetables are transported keep them virtually fresh for weeks and months. The canning industry has made vegetables and fruits available in good condition at all seasons, and has

We have not yet succeeded in keeping living things alive indefinitely, or in giving life by artificial means, but experiments have been made even in that direction. 

We think this girl does not mind washing dishes. What conveniences does she have which her mother did not have at her age? 

Have any of the scientific achievements we have mentioned been of service to you or someone that you know? If so, when and how? Compare the bill of fare of the average family today in the winter with what it would probably have been a hundred years ago.

Surely, on the whole, people are healthier than they were before science and invention accomplished so many extraordinary things. 

With their furnaces, hot and cold water in their houses, bathtubs, electric light and power, they live more comfortably though there are still a considerable number of houses that do not have all of these,

and some that have none of them. Many more kinds of recreation and amusement are available, even for the poor. But are we happier? Offhand we ought to be, but a century ago a good many people thought they were happy. Some would say that we have become so used to comfort and convenience that we are soft and lazy. 

People like that often do not realize when they are well off. 

Dr. Urey, a Nobel prize winner, once made some startling statements to a meeting of scientists: "Chemistry can and perhaps will destroy our European civilization. . . . There is little doubt that much of the unrest of the civilized world resulting in revolutions, new systems of government, and world-wide depressions is all rather closely related to the productive capacity largely brought about by science." He hoped that science would work harder through peaceful means to make humanity better, since so many of its activities had made more frightful the destruction of life. 

One other unfortunate outcome of scientific expansion is the conflict in the minds of some between science and religion. Many scientists of high rank are deeply religious. Perhaps the trouble is that those who have not thoroughly understood either science or religion have encouraged misunderstanding in both fields. God could work, for instance, through the process of evolution in bringing into existence the forms of life which we see and know. 

As far as you can judge, who are more contented, those who want many things or those who want few? Would society be better off if no more patents should be granted for ten years? Give examples that will show that there are some things a scientist cannot really know at present. 

189. Social Failures and Social Lag. A while ago (§ 109) we referred to the fact that progress or change does not always move with equal speed in all fields. We have just had a fine example of the fact that there might be both acceleration and lag in different fields of human interest. Science and invention have made possible many conveniences and luxuries that were once not dreamed of, but they have not brought peace among nations or happiness to even all good people. 

Several reasons might be given for this difference. Sometimes we have not realized our neglect of some important interests. Sometimes we have blundered when we were trying to do some good thing. 

But more often, somebody's selfishness has been responsible for the

development of injustice and discontent. One man is so eager to get rich that he takes no thought of the effect of his business methods upon others. Some group of politicians is so anxious to keep itself in power that it will misuse public money and keep out of office competent people so as to give jobs to its own followers. Success in the minds of individuals and of nations has too often meant beating or destroying a competitor, rather than simply setting up a better standard of living for themselves or accomplishing something that would benefit all humanity.

Another cause of individual or social failure has been the lack of co-operation between those whose interests were really alike. Surely a family is most happy and prosperous when all its members try to make their relations with one another pleasant all the time. The collapse of the League of Nations gives negative evidence of the same character. Enough was accomplished under the League to prove that it was capable of a high order of service to the world. But some of its members were not willing to take a little risk to support the League's authority when its principles were being violated. And the United States was unwilling to take the slight chance involved in even being a member. 

Almost the hardest social lesson for people to learn is that of interdependence. Of all peoples, citizens of a democracy must realize that their own welfare depends on working together. Sometimes the idea has been encouraged by writers as well as by heads of nations that a nation, or at least a continent, could become entirely self-sufficient, though no national group has been able to provide over any long period all the things necessary to maintain its national and individual welfare on a high plane. The man or woman today who tries to live entirely by himself not only becomes a social outcast, but must spend his days in what most of us would consider discomfort and distress.

No doubt we can overemphasize the social lags which we see as we look about us in the world. Perhaps our sense of frustration comes partly from the fact that some of us wanted to do so much better than we have been able to accomplish. Just as material comforts are possible today that could not have been enjoyed by anybody even a few years ago, so have ideals of peace and national brotherhood been given words as never before. When national selfishness and

brute force seem to be prevailing over loftier ideals, we may forget that there have been dark days before. Some of the social dangers which threaten us today are the result of our own carelessness. We have paid no attention to the warnings of those with open eyes who told us we were taking things too easily. Worthy wishes must be accompanied by brave action if the good is to prevail over the evil. 

Mention examples from the history of our own country when individuals, parties, or other groups failed to act as wisely as they could have acted. 

What examples have you seen of the failure of a worthy enterprise because of lack of co-operation? How should one feel who realizes that he has not succeeded in doing all the good he would have liked to do? 

190. War as a Social Lag. — That is a rather mild word to apply to war, for it not only is an example of the failure of the world to deal with its problems sensibly, but it causes a needless waste of life and property, and may build up hates that generations cannot forget. 

We can count war's cost in billions and then be sure that no amount of money can make up for the physical suffering, the mental anguish, and the loss of spiritual ideals that no money system could measure. 

Thinking people have asked themselves over and over again why this kind of thing goes on, but when we try to fix the blame, it is rare that we can put our finger upon one or two causes and say they tell the whole story.

We have simply got to keep on trying to convince even selfish warlords that if they are as efficient as they want people to believe, they can win glory for themselves by wise planning of home industry and foreign trade at far less expense than by threats, bullying, or war. 

In the long run good will is much more profitable than hate. We used to think that the printing press and the radio would make it possible for the peoples of the world to convey to one another messages of friendliness and to understand one another's needs and problems. 

But it is just as easy to tell a lie by these means as to tell the truth. 

If for years you heard only one side of a story of a dispute and were prevented, except by accident, from hearing anything that your supposed foes had to say for themselves, it would be strange if you did not some time come to believe at least part of what you were told. 

Just as long as any strong government refuses to be honest or to submit to the peaceful decision of impartial judges its grievances, real or imagined, just so long will there be danger of war. There are no

disagreements that cannot be settled peaceably between well-meaning nations. A century and a quarter of peace between the United 

States and Great Britain has proved that. 

But if some governments respect nothing but force, other nations may have only two choices to arm to the extent of their utmost need, or to submit to whatever a brutal foe sees fit to hand them. 

If liberty and democracy and the right to mind one's own business are worth having, a war of defense is certainly justifiable. It is too bad to take perhaps a quarter of a nation's income and spend it on instruments of war, even in self-defense, but in the long run that may be necessary insurance in some cases. Sometime the whole world may realize the folly of war. Until that day arrives there seems to be nothing for us to do but follow the advice Theodore 

Roosevelt made famous: "Speak softly, and carry a big stick." In other words, talk peace and pray for peace, but meantime watch and be ready for those who are too foolish or selfish to be reasonable. 

As you look back upon the policies of the British and French governments in the years from 1933 to 1939, how do you explain their lack of preparedness for the great crisis that came in 1940? Why is war so much more costly today than it was 75 or 100 years ago? 

191. Proposals for New Kinds of Social Control. Surely any understanding person will admit that more can be done for human betterment than has been done. But how shall we go at it? We used to think that it was up to the individual to make what he could of himself. In that way we believed the strength of character and purpose that one had was given a chance to develop, and those who most deserved success would get it. "Rugged individualism" was praised as the principle that had enabled the people of the United States to conquer so much of a continent. . 

Others do not see the situation in that light. often the strong have made the weak suffer just individual was strong and the other was weak. is the duty of society to take into its own hands the control of those activities that touch the welfare of all, and to carry these on as group activities in the interest of all. That theory, in contrast with the doctrine of individualism, is often referred to as collectivism. 

Many programs might be called collectivism and yet differ greatly as to motives and methods. We shall have more to say about these

They assert that it

later, after we have given more attention to the economic side of human interests, but we ought to look at their outstanding political and social features right here. One of the best-known of such ideas bears the label socialism. Socialists believe that the fundamental industries are so important that they should not be carried on for individual profit, but should be operated by the government in the interests of all the people. Not only water systems and electric light and power systems, which are frequently found under public operation, but railroads, banks, and the great industries that provide food supplies, are examples of activities which, the socialist thinks, should be brought under the power of the state. By "state" here we mean whatever grade of government could do the job most effectively. 

Socialism and its more extreme comrade, communism, have been advocated by some people who wanted to destroy organized religion and break up family life. But there is nothing in socialism that is contrary to the teachings of Christianity, and there have been some perfectly sincere "Christian Socialists."

The most famous of all socialists was the German, Karl Marx, whose book Das Kapital, published in 1867, is sometimes referred to as the "Bible of the Socialists." Marx believed in what is often called the "class struggle❞— that a conflict between the capitalist class and the masses or the proletariat is inevitable, that it would ultimately wipe out the middle class, and that then the masses would take possession of the instruments of production and operate them collectively. England, in the early part of the nineteenth century, had a manufacturer named Robert Owen who was interested in what is often called Utopian Socialism. He dreamed of a place, as the name suggests, where everybody would be happy, and even tried to put his dream into practice in a socialist colony at New Harmony, Indiana. Like all such projects, however, it did not work the way it was anticipated.

Communism carries the "collective" principle still further than socialism. The socialist does not intend to take away one's rights to own the things that he will use for his personal welfare or comfort, and perhaps not the place he lives in. The communist, however, says that there should be no such thing as private property. That right should be in the hands only of the people as a whole. "What's mine is yours, and what's yours is mine" is one way to express their

theory, though usually the communist has not much to share with anybody else. A few experiments at communism have been undertaken in different times and places, but they never have lasted very long. Those who sincerely set up such communities have found before very long that the loafers were perfectly willing to let honest, faithful workers support them. JIL Under communism the government would not only have the power and right to take the property of an individual away from him and divide it or give it to somebody else, but to tell him how many rooms he might have to live in, and what he should get as pay for whatever work he did. Many communists have no scruples about the means they use to put their ideas into effect. Sabotage-which means the damage or destruction of an employer's property while pretending to work for him seizure of private savings so as to get money for the public treasury, and, if necessary, vio Soufoto lence to life, are proper things for communists to do, if we may judge by the actions of many of them.

Some European peoples are great on mass performances of various kinds.

There are all kinds of socialists and communists. Some of them have been men or women of deep sincerity who would not do violence to anyone in order to get their views adopted, but would depend upon argument and winning their way at the ballot box. Some of them believe in moving slowly

toward the goals which they seek, making changes step by step in such a way as to upset society as little as possible. 

Still another radical group are those sometimes called syndicalists. 

They want to unite all workers in one big union, paying no attention to political governments. By such measures as the general strike they would force their power upon a community or nation and then operate industry in the interests of themselves. 

Don't confuse socialists and communists with anarchists. Both socialists and communists want to give to the government a vast measure of power. Communists would, if Russia is any example, allow no other party except their own, and make that party and the government almost one and the same thing. The anarchist, on the other hand, wants to do away with all organized government. It is in government, he insists, that tyranny arises. After overthrowing the government now in existence, he would let different groups come together in whatever way would serve their own interests and then work out their own career by whatever means were at hand. Socialism much industrial power in the hands of the government; communism - all power in the hands of the government, theoretically representing all the people as a whole; anarchism - no organized government at all. All these we sometimes lump together as radicalism or "left-wing" ideas. 

What groups or classes in a country would be most inclined to accept such ideas? What groups would oppose them? Why are members of radical groups often the dupes of demagogues? 

192. The Totalitarians. — Another governmental principle, held by some who once professed to be greatly disturbed by the activities of socialists and communists, in practice seems to work out in much the same way. Fascism, put into effect by Mussolini in Italy, was one form of it. Fascism preaches the totalitarian idea that the state is all-powerful and individual citizens have no rights apart from those which the state grants or guarantees. Under Fascism private property is not abolished, but the dictator at the head of the country decrees what private business men or other citizens may do. It took its name from the bundle of sticks with an ax in it which centuries ago represented public authority in the Roman republic. 

Adolf Hitler and the National Socialists or "Nazis" in Germany hold very similar ideas. Private living and property may go on,

but under strict rules that the government lays down. The policies of Der Fuehrer or Il Duce are not open to question. The state controls all education and expression of opinion through the press or radio and permits the advocacy of only the ideals of the Fascist or Nazi leadership. Labor unions are forbidden, and employers and employees may be organized in "corporations" in accordance with the kind of work they do. Representation in a perfectly futile 

Chamber of Corporations or Reichstag, as the case may be, is based on these groups. Soufoto 

THE STORE ON A RUSSIAN COLLECTIVE FARM 

As we have already noticed (p. 510), the communist idea is to have the state the source of everything which it thinks the people need. This store seems to carry a variety of goods, but compare it with one of our "five-and-tens." 

The nearest thing to a communist system on a large scale is found, of course, in Soviet Russia. Russia does not call itself Communist, for the U. S. S. R. means the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

The Russian system operates through soviets, which are bodies representing various industrial classes. The Soviet government has not insisted on complete communism in every detail. It does even allow some private buying and selling. But in Soviet Russia no one has any right against the government to hold private property of any kind. 

If the government wants to use your house as a dormitory for soldiers

or public officials, it just takes it. Mines, waterways, railroads, banks, and every important economic organization are controlled by the state, and their managers are state officials. 

Under all of these systems of dictatorship what we commonly think of as the finer things of life get little or no consideration. Newspapers, magazines, art, and music, must glorify their rulers or else. Religion is either made the tool of the state or, as recently in 

Russia, forbidden to be taught to those under the age of 18, and discouraged, though not wiped out, for older people. If one does not care to think for himself, to have any material influence in determining his own way or place in life, or to be anything more than simply a subject of a ruthless government, a form of dictatorship might relieve him of some worry. Those who operate these totalitarian systems as tools of the dictators are well satisfied, of course, for as long as they do not offend the head of the state, they have the pick of whatever there is in society and government. But woe unto the one who dares to criticize his government out loud or to seek by even peaceful means to make any changes in it that the dictator does not approve. 

What conditions in a country would be most favorable to extreme change toward either "left-wing" or totalitarian ideas? Might the same kind of conditions at one time or place lead in one direction and at another in the opposite direction? What kind of political background or history would be most favorable to the setting up of dictators? 

193. Next Steps in a Democracy. — Under dictatorships, with a ruler at their head without principle or scruples and supported by men of clever brains, almost anything can be accomplished that the leader sets out to do. By contrast, a democracy moves slowly, often uncertainly, and may make changes when they are not needed as well as when they are. Is it possible to build up in a democracy some intelligent direction of community and national life so that it may not be open to the charge of weakness, hesitation, and failure to accomplish worthy things? To do this we need at least three things: general education to make all citizens capable of intelligent thinking; the development of a keen-minded leadership which knows what it wants but is willing to lead rather than drive its fellow-citizens; and a spirit of co-operation in place of quarreling or negligence on the part of the masses of the people.

Perhaps what democracy needs we mentioned some time ago under the term social planning. Progress must not be left to be a hit-ormiss procedure. Since many things take years to work out most satisfactorily, we must not expect to bring about on a week's or a year's notice the reforms and changes which we may conclude to be good. 

And where shall this social planning be done and who shall do it?

If we are to give such authority to our government, we must find some way to take out of politics the elements of selfishness, corruption, and carelessness.
