Is there any danger that in trying to set up effective social planning in a democracy we shall have to adopt the methods of dictatorship or some other totalitarian principle? Can the rights of individuals be preserved at the same time that we put authority into the hands of public officials? Mention specifically but fairly the reasons why you do not care to substitute any form of totalitarian authority for a government based on the principle of democracy. 

194. Securing Sound Thinking and Action. The methods of the scientist can be of great value to one in any walk of life. The real scientist not only goes at his studies without a set notion that he is going to prove some particular thing, but works patiently collecting all the evidence he can until he has enough to justify him in drawing a conclusion. Of course a scientist may have some idea where his investigations may lead him, for his experience and his knowledge may justify him in setting up a hypothesis or supposition which seems to have a sound basis of truth. But this hypothesis does not become accepted as a scientific law until sufficient proof is at hand. Proof means, of course, evidence that a certain statement is or is not true, or that a certain event did or did not happen. 

In reaching conclusions one's line of reasoning may be deductive or inductive. Deductive reasoning starts with a generally accepted principle and argues that if that is true, other conclusions less farreaching must follow. Inductive reasoning works the other way. It takes a considerable number of instances which all seem to point in the same direction and from them draws up a general statement. 

The information which is gained in the course of such a process we often refer to as data. They are the facts or ideas which are discovered or agreed upon and which serve as a basis for judging or reckoning.

Let us make clear next certain steps in a definite process of scientific thinking. They will illustrate what is often referred to as the scientific method. We may suspect that something is true or may have no clear idea as to whether it is true or not, but in either case we want to find the facts.

(1) Observation. We find as many pieces of evidence as possible that apply to the study we are making. We may have to make experiments under conditions which we arrange carefully so as to make sure that our observations really do apply to the problem that we are trying to study. 

Observation also may require accurate measurement or judgment. Sometimes it may make a considerable difference whether a certain thing happens 1100 times or 1200 times, or whether a distance is two feet or two feet and a half. (2) Comparison. We may then bring together the facts we have just discovered and compare them with the results of some similar study which we made at some other time, or which someone else has made under the same conditions as ours. If we find that the results of these two or more studies are similar in character, we have reason to conclude that we are on the right track, and that our discoveries are not merely something that happened to occur at a particular time. (3) Generalization. This means the working out of the conclusions that we have a right to draw from our observations. Sometimes the best we can do is to conclude that certain results are likely to take place, but occasionally we find that the same thing happens every time. At this point we are at least justified in saying whether the hypothesis with which we started, if we did start with one, appears to be sound. If it does, we are justified in continuing to work along the same line. If it does not, we may have to start over again, working in a different direction. (4) Classification. If we have assembled a considerable amount of information or a great number and variety of data, it will probably be desirable to arrange these items in some such way that they can be readily referred to without having to repeat or mention the entire list. The classification may be made along any of several different lines. For example, we may give attention to the sequence or order in which things occurred, count the frequency or the number of times one thing happened as compared with another, or may put in definite categories or groups of items these which have some similarity to one another. (5) Verification. We may now feel fairly certain that we have proved something, but we ought to try out our supposition in a new situation and see whether the outcome is the same. If our conclusion holds in a variety of different cases, we may feel rather sure that the process by which we reached our conclusion was sound. 

In gathering information needed for reaching conclusions, different methods may be employed, depending on the circumstances under which the study is carried on or the nature of the problem which is to

be worked out. The case method, for example, takes several typical instances, as in suits at law, and by studying those tries to present a general impression as to what does or should happen under similar circumstances anywhere. The historical method studies the past with the purpose of finding out examples that apply to the matter now under consideration and tries to determine what is likely to 

James Sawders

MODERN BUSINESS ARCHITECTURE 

Who would expect to have these buildings described as freight stations and storage warehouses for railroads? What kinds of information and observation probably were employed before it was decided to put up buildings like these? happen if a past situation is repeated. The comparative method tries to see what happened under different circumstances and then to decide whether similar results are obtained or not. The statistical method seeks to list or enumerate all the examples of a certain condition or event, so as to have as many facts as possible on which to base a conclusion. We might wish to know how many people of different ages there are in the country, the number of strikes that have occurred in a particular industry, or the proportion of the people of a com-

munity who have had a high school education. The laboratory method tries to set up a situation as nearly like a normal state of affairs as possible and then observe what happens.

At certain times we may not be so much concerned with reaching a conclusion as with knowing what the facts are about something or other. In that case our study may take the nature of a survey. This is or should be a far-reaching inspection of all kinds of pertinent facts, customs, or conditions. To decide upon the best program of studies for your high school, for instance, a survey might be made to find out the family incomes represented among the pupils, the proportion of pupils who are likely to go to college, the occupations by which the heads of families represented in the school make their living, and the probabilities of changes in industry or living conditions in the community. To the information thus gathered, reference can be made when some change in the school's program is proposed, and conclusions reached as to whether the proposal would be of benefit to a sufficient number of pupils to justify its adoption. 

To be convincing, a survey should cover as wide a range as possible of persons and conditions in the field in which the survey is made. 

Statisticians often think, however, that it is not necessary to go to the trouble of gathering information about every single individual or location that may be involved. They put considerable trust in the process known as sampling, to which we have already referred (§ 77). 

By taking individuals from different social or economic groups or different religious faiths or some other recognized community grouping, the facts can be gathered about this limited number. Then it may be assumed that these individuals really represent the groups to which they belong, and that the whole number would probably show about the same distribution of opinion or of circumstances. One cannot be sure of the meaning of a "straw vote," however, if one newspaper, for instance, samples only its own readers, or if questions are asked only of members of labor unions or chambers of commerce. 

Give examples from your own reading or experience of the use of any of the methods of getting information described here. Were the results in accord with what turned out to be the facts later on? If not, what may have been the trouble? Can such studies be satisfactorily made by people who have very strong opinions of their own? Is the publication of political "polls" before an election likely to encourage doubtful voters to "get on the band wagon"?

These scientific procedures are not to be thought of as entirely for the benefit of the social scientist or the college professor or the newspaper man who may get some pleasure out of studying his fellow citizens. There may be numerous occasions in the life of any one of us in which we do not have and perhaps should not have any fixed opinions in advance as to what we ought to do as individuals, or what our community might do to its own advantage. Perhaps if we are trying to reach some conclusion as to the proper policy to follow in our own personal living, we may not want to go into any study on an elaborate scale, but the attitude and method set forth here may be thoroughly valid.

Do you think many people consciously follow through such a series of steps as has been indicated in this section? Take some specific topic in the field of society, industry, or government, or some personal problem about which you do or might wish to reach a conclusion. Set down step by step what you might do in trying to reach a sincere and correct conclusion on that topic. 

195. Hopes for the Future. Surely we do not want to be fatalists, and assume that whatever happens, will happen regardless of anything we may do. Neither do we want to be quitters and accept as final the failures of ourselves or of society to make life as happy and productive as it could be. Sometimes failure, whether individual or social, has come because too much was expected in a short time, or because too little preparation was made for carrying out some hopeful plan. 

Obstacles may have to be overcome in putting through even the most promising programs. Sometimes misunderstanding, sometimes ignorance, sometimes selfishness may stand in the way, and any of these three may be pretty stubborn on occasion.

There may be three points of view as to how one should feel with reference to existing conditions or to what should be done to bring about change. The pragmatist is likely to be most concerned about the question, Will it work? If things seem to be going reasonably well as they are, he is not inclined to be enthusiastic about change. 

He may even be willing to accept something less satisfactory than he would like if by so doing he can see a program actually in operation and not creating any serious discontent. The logician may ask, Is it reasonable? If we accept a certain fact or condition as correct, does the thing that is proposed naturally grow out of given conditions, or does it comply with accepted rules of procedure? He may be as

much concerned about the way by which something is done as about the achievement which comes about in the end. The third point of view is that of the idealist. "What is the best thing?" he asks. "Do we have it? If not, we ought to. We should be satisfied with nothing less." If he has sufficient appreciation of human weaknesses to realize that the ideal is sometimes slow of attainment, he will be a leader who never lets his followers feel satisfied with what they have accomplished, but will always urge them on to something greater and

They not only hear but also see the lady at the piano. better. Sometimes, however, he fails to reckon with the frailties of human beings, and either becomes discouraged or urges his fellow men to undertake something for which they are not prepared. 

After all, we do need all three of these points of view. We must be practical, we must be reasonable, we must be content with nothing less than the best. If that three-fold attitude of mind keeps us constantly stirring and refuses to let us rest, even when we have accomplished something worthy, it is still in accordance with the way the world was made. Every phase of social study proves to us that change is inevitable. H. G. Wells has often been quoted as saying,

"Civilization is a race between education and catastrophe." Sometimes we worry lest the race has been lost, but fortunately if those of us who want a better world are unlucky today, there will be others who can take up where we have left off. 

It has often been said, "Youth are the hope of tomorrow." That is why we need not be too much alarmed about the misfortunes of today. Youth is eternal. When some individuals have achieved all that is within their power and have to leave the scene of action, youth still comes on with hope taking the place of despair, and promise overlooking failure. Old age sometimes thinks we have failed. We hope that youth will say, "We can still achieve.” 

Are the problems of today more serious or less than George Washington or Abraham Lincoln had to face? What do we have to use in facing these problems which they did not have? If a problem seems impossible to solve completely in our time, should we or should we not do anything about it?

PART III  

It would be hard to think of any matter of general interest which could not be approached from three points of view — social, economic, and political. Take, for instance, the subject of housing. The conditions in which people live are first of all social. The cost of providing any kind of housing, good or bad, is an economic proposition. Whatever regulation or control a government exercises over private dwellings or public housing projects brings it into the political realm. Which of the aspects of the problem is most important? Sometimes one and sometimes another, probably. The main reason why we often postpone the study of economic problems in school until near the end of the course is to have as mature a point of view and as wide a background of general understanding as possible before we tackle such questions. About them it is easy for a poorly informed person to have crazy ideas. We should approach them with an open mind and without prejudice. 

XVII  

Some terms connected with our economic life are used so carelessly that two persons may not mean anywhere nearly the same thing when they employ them. Much depends, also, on what we accept as facts. 

Before we consider problems about which there is room for difference of opinion, we had better agree on the meaning of terms we shall use over and over again, and also see if there are any economic facts and principles that all intelligent thinkers accept.

Some Questions: 

1. What does economics include? 

2. How may we get dependable economic facts? 

3. How have economic conditions influenced the history of our own and other nations? 

4. How important in our welfare is the ability to satisfy wants? 

5. What principles has experience taught us are wise in using goods to satisfy wants? 524

196. What Is Economics? We have already hinted at a definition like this (§3): Economics is the study of the activities of people related to the earning of a living. We could call it "the science of work." Some people have called economics "the dismal science," because in studying it we cannot help coming upon some conditions that do not seem right. 

If those stand out above everything else, we may get a rather gloomy view of the proposition; but if we think of it as giving us ideas that will help us to live better, it need not be a dismal science but a very interesting and forward-looking one. 

Economics is a living science, because it deals with living people and events that are going on every day. It is not only living but dynamic, for it deals with the forces that influence people's lives and suggests ways to make things better. Since it deals with human beings, economics cannot be an exact science. Some economic laws have been established by experience, but as we have already discovered, “laws" in any field of social science are likely to mean trends or tendencies rather than fixed and unchanging facts. 

In dealing with economic problems, we shall draw on every one of the other social sciences. History will tell how certain conditions came about. Geography will show how nature has influenced the progress of men and of nations. Civics will explain how economic problems are attacked by government. Besides, any study that has to do with human interests must find some place for psychology and ethics. 

What do you consider the three most important events or developments in the last two months? To what extent is each one of them connected with money, trade, or labor, and is therefore economic in character? Look at the page or column headlines of the first two pages of the morning paper. Which of these had anything to do with money, trade, or labor, and in what way? 

197. Economics and Life. - Every one of us is surrounded by some kind of environment, physical or personal. Even our individual activities are controlled, to some extent, by what can be done in our own community. There are no miners in New York City, and few fishermen in Pittsburgh. Nobody in Chicago grows grain for a living, although a considerable number have something to do with buying and selling it. But out in North Dakota or Kansas thousands of people depend for a living on the wheat crop. Another sort of environment is made up of the people with whom we must or choose to associate. Often we cannot pick our own fellow workers.

This matter of environment shows itself in the history of nations, too. Great Britain's history has been largely influenced by her island location. It has forced the British people to be active in commerce, and, until these days of airplanes, has enabled them to control, to a considerable extent, their own relations with the continent of Europe. Our own country has provided wide opportunities for many different ways of earning a living. Some think that one of the most 

Associated Screen News MAN USING NATURE'S RESOURCES 

The largest quartz gold mine in the world illustrates man's taking wealth out of the earth. This mine is at Juneau, Alaska. potent influences in our whole history is the fact that years ago people who were dissatisfied where they happened to be could move out and take up new land for a very small cost, and that today that opportunity is almost completely closed. 

Economic conditions may not determine everything in life, but with many of us they tell much of our story. Life for the average person runs through three periods. He starts out as a totally dependent infant. His dependency continues until he has had enough training and experience to enable him to earn his own living. The

law calls people infants until they are twenty-one years of age. Minor is a term not quite so unpleasant for nearly grown-up young people. 

In these days it has become increasingly difficult for the majority of young people to take entire care of themselves much before they reach voting age. Perhaps, for most, we should extend this age of dependency at least to the age of eighteen, and, for many, for three or four years beyond that time.

Then comes the working age, which may include the whole period from eighteen or twenty-one to sixty, sixty-five, or even a little later. 

During that time society expects us to look out for ourselves, if we are able. The housewife might not be able to live independently on the cash she handles, but she earns her living all right. Those who are in this working age may have to take care of both youthful dependents and those who are too old or feeble to work. 

The third of these economic periods is that of retirement or elderly dependence. Those who have been able to have laid by enough to live on comfortably may find this time one of much pleasure. Many, however, either can not save much, or waste what they could save. 

They must, in turn, become dependent once more. Once we would to take care of have expected their relatives — children or others them. Now it is popular to advocate systems of old-age pensions or other forms of payments so that those who are no longer able to work as hard as they once did may not starve or otherwise suffer unduly, or become a burden to those who may be struggling to get along themselves.

If, during at least a third, and with many at least a half, of one's life he is dependent upon the labor of others or his own savings, it ought to make us realize the extreme importance of economics to us. One who realizes such facts will, if he is any good, try to handle his affairs in such a way that whatever he gets after he ceases to do his regular daily or weekly turn he can look upon as a reward for early planning and faithful service. We are told that out of one hundred people who are earning their own living at the age of twenty-five, only fifty will be doing the same at the age of fifty-five, and only ten at the age of seventy-five.

Can a person understand the world he lives in if he is ignorant of economics? 

Can such a person be a good citizen or an intelligent voter? It has been charged that "we are a nation of economic illiterates." Do you think that

is true? Will everyone who studies economics become rich? May a person be successful without becoming rich? 

198. Getting Economic Facts. Students of economics have no right to do any unnecessary guessing. Statistics and terms which are used in discussing economic issues should not be open to question. 

How many tons of coal did the United States export in 1925 as compared with 1935? Somebody should know. What is the difference between a corporation and a monopoly? What is capitalism as compared with communism? On such pieces of information there should be no disagreement. But too often we are ready to accept any statements that agree with the position we have already taken. 

If someone belongs to a different political party from ours, we may be too ready to misinterpret his motives and his views. 

"Consider the source," is often good advice. Textbooks ought to contain only incontrovertible statements, except when they make it clear that they are quoting one side of an argument. Books written by followers of the "New Deal" may be helpful to any student if they are read with a full recognition of their general attitude. Publications like Nation's Business and United States News frankly represent the business or the conservative point of view. Publications of union labor organizations give their side of questions in which labor is interested.

Independent newspapers, such as the New York Times, may express fairly positive opinions on their editorial pages, but they are respected as being sincere, and as trying to tell the truth in their news columns. 

Bulletins issued by government departments, banks, business service organizations, and the like, probably will state facts as nearly accurately as possible, but may sometimes put their own interpretation on them. Observation may bring useful information, too. see factories and mills in operation, study the way offices are managed, watch developments in strikes, read stories of conferences held by government boards connected with industry, and observe at first hand events of all kinds. 

A student of economics should be able to read and use various kinds of statistical information. Probably every kind of graph ever invented has been used sometime or somewhere in presenting economic statistics. You will find on page 166 and 645 of this book line graphs used to represent a certain type of information which seemed easiest

to indicate in that way. Information showing comparative facts about different countries or industries, populations, salaries, and the like, might be represented in the form of bars, either horizontal or vertical (page 255). Circles might be used for graphic purposes when it is desired to show how much of an entire industry or entire output comes from different countries or is used for particular purposes (page 168). In recent years much use has been made of "pictorial statistics" in which one figure of a man, a barrel of flour, or something else is allowed to stand for 10,000 men or 10,000 barrels, and then as many of these figures are used as are necessary to show the total number involved (page 445). Any of these methods may tell the story more directly and clearly than tables of figures, though one should be able to interpret numbers without having to draw a picture for the purpose. 

One needs to be careful even in the use of statistical facts and graphs. 

One could set up a graph, for instance, showing the total wealth of various nations, but sometimes might it be much more meaningful if we showed the per capita wealth of the nations rather than the total wealth? "Figures don't lie but liars can figure" is a common quotation. People can also make graphs for their own purposes. In any case, let us be sure to have our statistics accurate in themselves, even if different people might use the same figures to draw different conclusions.

Try several of the graphic methods used to represent the growth of population of the United States from census to census and see which one you like best. 

Are any of them more easily comprehensible by relatively uneducated people than others? How much space does the newspaper you regularly read devote to trustworthy information on economic topics? What publications does your state government or the national government get out now that might be useful as a basis for the consideration of economic topics? 

199. Steps in Our Economic Progress. 

Considerable depends on our definition of progress. If we mean increasing comfort and improved means of satisfying our wants, we are better off today than ever before-speaking in general terms, of course. Very much of this improved comfort has been gained within the last century, or even within the last half century. 

You recall the five stages of man's economic development (§ 103). 

Some people are still making a living in almost the same ways that

primitive men did, but few people have failed to profit in some way by the economic advancement of society as a whole. From almost complete dependence upon nature in the hunting and fishing age, men learned, in the pastoral age, to keep flocks and herds ready at any time to serve human needs. The agricultural stage brought about more settled homes, and out of the handicraft stage manufacturing became a definite means of support for people, and towns grew up.

200. Man and Nature. - Man today exercises a control over nature which was once impossible or even unthought of. We take water into the deserts and drain it out of swamps. We have made the water and the wind and now the marvelous power of electricity work for us. In fact, the extent to which man has made himself the master of nature measures largely his own achievement in better living for himself. 

I CELL Courtesy United States Army, Corps of Engineers ONE EXAMPLE OF FLOOD CONTROL 

A channel has been built for the Los Angeles River which will hold it in check when it goes wild.

Not always, of course, does man master nature. It is no sign of mastery for man to kill off all the passenger pigeons or the heath hens or the dodos, or to fish a brook to death. It is much more intelligent to preserve bird and animal life and make it helpful to man. This notion that nature and man should work together we often call conservation. Conservation does not mean refusing to use the gifts of nature but using them wisely so that they will both serve present needs and be kept for future service.

There are forces of nature that man has not yet brought under control. He thinks he has learned how to do something about floods,

but floods have not been ended. We have not developed a successful modern nation in a hot climate. Fire, as always, "is a good servant but a bad master." Lightning takes its toll every year. Bugs and some birds are pests for the farmer. In the process of learning, science and economics can work together. Economic success in the past can furnish money, and science in its laboratories and factories can go on investigating and experimenting. Man would be foolish either to pretend that he knows everything or to admit that nature has licked him.

Mention any natural factors with which you have come in contact which in your opinion could be made less disagreeable than they are. 

What pros pects do you see for control of those elements in nature which still are too strong for man when they care to exert themselves? 

201. Features of Our Economic Order. Our economic order means simply the policies and forces that control the business or work of our lives. People sometimes talk about it as if it were some devilish scheme worked out by a few selfish men and somehow imposed upon the rest of suffering humanity. Nothing could be further from the truth. Its practices began because at some time they fitted the existing situation. The very fact that methods which came into use years or centuries ago have continued to the present time is fairly good evidence that they never were hopelessly bad. We can doubtless transform many features of our present economic order so as to make them serve better the needs of people today. But the wise man will not assume that merely because some program is not working perfectly it should be thrown out bodily.

Everything of an economic nature is connected with one of four phases of economic activity: consumption, production, exchange, and distribution. The four really make an economic circle. Each one leads to the next. 

Since for convenience we must begin somewhere, let us start with consumption. This means simply the use of goods to satisfy wants. 

By goods the economist means anything that will satisfy a want. It may be irreparably harmful in its actual use, just as intoxicating liquor is for the majority of people who use it, but the economist frequently does not bother with the moral aspect of the thing. 

Since goods cannot be consumed until they exist, production becomes fundamentally important. It means the providing of goods so that

they may satisfy wants. It includes the growing of grain and the raising of cattle, the manufacture of chairs, boxes, steel beams and rails, and thousands of other things. It also includes the rendering of services that meet human needs or wants. The lawyer who handles the legal business for an automobile factory is probably as necessary to the production of autos as any machine or any other employee. 

Exchange is the transfer of the right to possess or use goods. All the manufacturers of automobiles would have a hard time using these cars themselves. They must transfer either their ownership or the right to use them to other people or they would have no inducement to keep on producing cars. Exchange, as we shall see, may mean the actual swapping of one kind of goods for another, or it may be carried on by the use of money.

Distribution, as the term is used here, does not mean passing out something, but the sharing of the returns from production among those who have had a part in it. Since the automobile manufacturer's returns sooner or later take the form of money, the distribution he makes among those who have helped to produce the cars is most often in the form of money. His factory workers usually get their share in the form of wages before the goods they have helped to produce are actually sold. 

You see, then, how these four activities do form a circle. Goods are produced because it is believed that somebody will use them. After they are produced they change hands so that people may get them who can use them to satisfy their own needs. As a result of this exchange the returnsusually in the form of money can be divided among those who have had a part in producing the goods. Because they have received this money this return for working they can use, or "consume" the goods that somebody had produced. Then this consumption of goods creates a call for more production, and so the economic circle keeps on going or if it doesn't, something unpleasant happens.

THE CIRCLE OF ECONOMIC ACTIVITY 

EXCHANGE 

---

One standard feature of our present economic order is the right to acquire and own goods. That right is known as property (§ 85). 

Applying the word so as to mean the goods themselves, we classify property as either real property or personal property. Real property, or real estate, is that which is substantially fixed so that it cannot readily be moved. Houses, office-buildings, and the land on which buildings may be constructed or crops grown, are common examples of real property. Personal property includes those goods that can be moved fairly easily from one place to another. Hay and grain after they are cut become personal property. The clothes you wear and the table, chair, or desk you use for study, are other examples. 

Often this personal property is in the form of bonds and stocks, which of themselves will never keep anybody warm or feed him, but which represent other kinds of property, and are valuable on that account. 

Another classification of property distinguishes between private property and public property. Private property is that which belongs to an individual or a group of individuals for their own use. There are limits to the way in which one may use private property, just as the owner of a house has no right to turn it into a gambling joint, or the owner of a revolver to threaten the lives of people whom he meets. But as long as the use of the property does not harm others, there is practically no restraint upon it. The law will not require you to live in your house, for instance, if you find it more to your advantage to lease it to somebody else and live in a hotel. Public property is that which is owned by some agency representing the people as a whole, such as the community, the state, or the federal government. A courthouse, a state forest reserve, a highway, the 

Panama Canal these are examples of it.

Many believe that the right to acquire private property is the chief spur to enterprise. Though many of us will gladly do a kindness to someone else that may involve work, few people will work indefinitely unless some gain to themselves results from their labor. The only people who are opposed to private property are those who are against all organized society or communists who assert that everything should belong to the group as a whole and not to individuals. 

Property may be acquired in three ways — through original production, through gift, and through sale or exchange. The farmer who grows wheat on his own land may usually be justified in claiming that 

---

the wheat is his, for instance, or the clothing manufacturer the garments he makes. But after wheat or clothes have been produced they may be given away or may be exchanged or sold. 

We have already pointed out (§ 189) that we do not always realize the interdependence of individuals and groups of people. Could you live comfortably one day without making use of goods or services which someone else provided? Could your community get along for any extended period without making use of the products of some other community? Has any nation ever amounted to much which did not use at least some of the products of other nations? Only because of this co-operation among individuals, groups, and nations can we have the many conveniences and comforts which we enjoy. 

This statement might be offered as an example of an economic law. 

No Congress or Parliament ever passed it, but it has grown out of the experience of life, and is a law that practically enforces itself. Political laws may be more specific in individual cases, but will come to nothing in the long run if they go contrary to those economic laws which nature and man's experience have combined to make. 

Show how a business depression is an example of the failure of the circle of economic activity to operate smoothly. Classify the following with reference to the kinds of property they represent — personal, real, private, public: the 

White House; the textbook you are using; the President's hat; a street railway; trees in Yosemite National Park; milk on the table. In how many ways today have you co-operated with others or made use of community co-operation in the use of property? 

202. Motives and Means for Achievement. 

Economic activities, as described in print, by letter, or in conversation, often seem utterly selfish. The impulse to do things in the expectation of some return in money or satisfaction is often referred to as the profit motive. 

Some people condemn it as unworthy and blame it for most of the injustice in the world. In contrast to this profit motive such people set up what they call the service motive. People should run railroads, they say, because the community will receive benefit thereby. The doctor should prescribe for a patient because he wants to relieve suffering rather than because he expects to make any money by doing so. The steelworker should go at his daily job because somebody will receive advantage from the use of the steel he is helping to produce, rather than because he is paid five or more dollars a day.

This service motive is fine and surely deserves all the encouragement it can get. The two motives are not inconsistent, after all. By all means we should want our work to bring satisfaction to somebody. 

But most of us like to see some other return than just a "Thank you," if the rendering of our services is the only way we can make a living. 

The soundness of any society rests upon the ability of a large proportion of its members to support themselves through the making of goods or the rendering of services which are useful to someone else. If doing that for compensation involves the profit motive, it does- that's all. 

Now, what conditions best promote achievement? Where will one find the greatest encouragement to make something of himself? 

In a community where every individual is free to think for himself and form his own opinions, to do what he pleases so long as he does not interfere with the equal right of others, and to make such arrangements as seem good to him for the work he will engage in? Or in a community where every relation of one person with another, even to what he may think and say, is prescribed for him by some dictator or other power at the head of his government? Most of us would say that the general welfare and the happiness of the individual will be best served by individual freedom. Most of us will take a chance on democracy and its blunders in contrast with mechanical obedience to a dictator or absolute monarch. 

Another encouraging condition is the existence of opportunity to make use of any distinctive talent we may have. If one has inventive genius, exceptional talent for music or art, or some other greater-thanaverage ability, the community is better off, as well as this outstanding individual, if he is able to make full use of his talents. 

Still another essential feature is security of life and property. The community where public authority is respected only by those who are too weak to defy it, where people feel free to take personal vengeance upon those whom they dislike—who wants to live in a place like that? It is in communities that try to promote the health and safety of their people and to encourage those who are thrifty that most of us want to live. 

Is competition a desirable economic incentive? (§ 144) If it means merely beating out someone else, perhaps not; but if it encourages one to do better work than he otherwise would, all concerned may be better off.

Personal qualities are also important in leading to success or failure. 

A pleasing personality, for instance (§ 127), gets things for one person that another equally competent in many ways would not obtain. 

There is nothing wrong in making oneself likable, unless one thinks he can substitute a pleasing personality for the ability to do a good job. 

Physical well-being is another important element. For the lack of this you yourself may not always be responsible, yet it will be your own fault if you indulge in harmful habits. Ambition and high standards of life and thought have taken many a person far ahead of others 

J Courtesy Ford Motor Company THE END OF THE ASSEMBLY LINE 

Working together, each with a definite job to do, these workers assemble a Ford promptly and efficiently. equally able but lacking in enterprise and perseverance. To be content with merely "getting by" is all too common. 

Two very useful qualities are efficiency in doing one's work (§ 223) and the ability to co-operate with others in doing it. "Every day, in every way, I am getting better and better" is a pretty good motto.

The one who, without lowering his own standards, can work in harmony with others and adapt himself to new surroundings without great difficulty, will be far more likely to succeed than one who refuses to do anything except when conditions are just right.

One has no business to blame our economic order for his own lack of success if he has failed to do his share. Occasionally somebody suffers from terribly hard luck, but few people are pursued by hard luck forever. One with the right stuff in him has no reason for thinking that it is all over when he has experienced one failure. Something is wrong with a community or a country if any considerable number of its people get in the habit of saying "the world owes me a living" and waiting for someone to come along and hand out soft jobs to those who are too lazy to go after them.

Make a list of ten occupations or industries that are familiar in your community. To what extent are both the profit motive and the service motive back of their activities? Is the community better off for what they do?

Are the personal qualities mentioned in the latter part of this section inherited or can they be acquired? 

203. What Wants Do for Us. We all want things, and there is nothing wrong in that. In fact a want is such a natural thing that it is hard to give a definition of it. It represents a feeling or impulse which can be satisfied only by some good or some service. Another word that means almost the same thing is desire; but a desire may represent a wish for something which may not be very intense and may not lead to any positive action on our part to get it. 

By contrast, a need represents the call for some good or service which is essential to life or well-being. Demand carries the idea further. 

Demand suggests not only a desire or need but the ability to satisfy that need. Sometimes in common speech we use the term as signifying simply a very strong pressure placed upon someone, but in economics we always attach to the word the suggestion of ability to obtain the thing we want if it is available.

In speaking of wants, we need not mean mere selfishness. People may want things in order that they may prepare themselves for greater service or usefulness. It is creditable to you if you want this book so that you may learn something you did not know. It is because men have wanted things in order to live better that mankind has made progress.

Of course wants can be carried to excess. People can be too anxious to get along without working or to obtain extravagant luxuries or even things that cause harm. Sometimes, too, we feel that we must have certain things, even though we should wish it otherwise. Very few 

---

of our people want to spend money on armies and navies for the sake of going out and beating up some other people. But the majority of us think we would be foolish not to prepare ourselves so that we can defend our lives and our rights against possible enemies. 

Wants are sometimes classified as primary, or personal, and secondary, or material. Primary or personal wants are those which, if gratified, would contribute to our own immediate satisfaction. Food, James Sawders

This is hard work at best, but men have learned to use tools to do many hard jobs. 

They were made as a result of needs or demands. What kind of wants do they represent? clothing, a house to live in, means of travel, are examples of this kind of wants. Our secondary wants express themselves in calls for material things that will enable us to gratify our primary wants. Stores, railroad trains, trucks, and office buildings, might be a nuisance rather than a help if they did not contribute toward the satisfaction of some of our primary wants. What could you do with a railroad engine if someone gave it to you?

Still another classification of wants distinguishes between individual wants and community wants. The individual want satisfies a par-

ticular person. The community want will be of benefit to many people at some time or other. Broadway may not be of any use to John 

Smith, but New York knows that many people will use a street right where Broadway is. John Smith may never need to be arrested by a policeman, but his community knows from experience that if it had no policemen, the lives and property of its people would be much less safe. 

Make a list of fifteen of your own wants. Include in the list five which represent positive needs, five which represent things you could get along without, and five for which you can assert demand in the economic sense. 

Which of these are primary, and which are secondary? How have other people's wants helped to make possible the activities by which members of your family earn their living? 

204. Laws about Human Wants. - The wise man learns how to satisfy his wants so as to get the most pleasure and benefit out of them. 

Why don't you take advantage of the experience of the past? If you do, both you and society will be better off. 

1. The law of unlimited extent. There is no limit to the total amount of human wants. Perhaps you could make a complete list of all the things you care much about at the present time, but if we should total up all the wants of all the members of the class, we should have a list much greater than that of any one member. Mary may want a tennis racquet, but you may prefer golf or baseball or motor boating. The old saying, "The more we have, the more we want," is a real economic truth. That does not mean that you, like Hitler, after having one want gratified, become more determined to have everything else within reach. But the satisfaction of one want brings a new condition and possibly a new appreciation of things. Perhaps when you left the eighth grade you thought you would like to quit school right away. 

But the state and your parents wanted you to keep on for a while, and because you satisfied that want on their part your own attitude may have changed, and you may have even decided to go to college. 

Another reason why there is no fixing of a limit to human wants is that the wants of individuals and of communities change over periods of time. You certainly do not care for exactly the same things today that you did when you were eight years old or twelve years old. 

Some communities that once welcomed street cars with enthusiasm now are anxious to get rid of them and ride on buses instead.

2. The law of variety. Satisfaction may be increased by variety in kind, form, or quality. Possibly you like bread and butter, potatoes, chicken, and ice cream, and out of those you could make a very satisfactory meal. But what if, instead of having those five items included, it was all bread or even all ice cream? Few people would be equally satisfied with such an arrangement. No matter how much you like baseball, you would not want to keep at it ten hours a day, every day

ANOTHER THING TO SELL 

Every new invention means, if it is really worth making, a new opportunity for business activity. It is another thing that people may want. Improvements sometimes are as effective in making a sale as the original invention itself. in the year. You enjoy it more when it isn't a steady diet. So human wants in general ask more often for variety than for one constant, particular kind of satisfaction. 

3. The law of harmony. A combination of goods may give greater satisfaction than the same goods used separately. Put butter on bread and most people like it, but few care for butter separately. There is no fun in roller skating out in a pasture. You want a hard surface to travel on. In the manufacture of many articles each one of a dozen

or even fifty workers puts himself in harmony with others so that he may do his part of the job when it will best fit in with what some other worker has done or is going to do. Some things simply do not go well together drinking liquor and driving automobiles, for example. 

4. The law of diminishing utility. As the number of units possessed of a commodity increases, the satisfaction derived from the use of any one unit decreases. One suit of clothes brings a high degree not only of comfort but of community approval. But if you had a hundred suits you would not get 100 times the satisfaction that you do out of having one suit, and the community may not care a rap how many suits you have beyond the first one. If you are hungry, one roll or one sandwich seems for a minute to be about the best thing on earth, but after two rolls or three, you begin to take no more interest in rolls, and if somebody compelled you to eat six, you might want no more for a month.

Along with this principle of diminishing utility, consider the idea of marginal utility and consumer's surplus. Suppose you take the case of a man with his golf clubs. Most people who play the game like to have more than one, because one kind will do better for driving the ball a long distance and another for short shots. But not even a golf champion or his caddy will carry a hundred clubs around.

Let us take a situation where a player carries six clubs. 

2 

Xx DIMINISHING UTILITY 

A diagram will illustrate this. 

Let the usefulness he gets out of the first one be represented by the rectangle marked 1. The usefulness of a second club will be represented in the same way by rectangle 2 and perhaps will be almost as great as that of the first. The usefulness of the third club is shown by rectangle 3, of the fourth by 4, and in the case of this particular player, the last one that he cares to carry around has its usefulness represented by rectangle 5. 

For him another club would be a nuisance. One of those clubs may be more useful to him, on the whole, than any other, but each of the additional clubs brings usefulness for its particular kind of shot. Any one of these adds something to the total usefulness of the whole outfit, but, barring perhaps the first one, any one of them may bring no more added usefulness than any other one. The added usefulness of the last one which this player 3 4

will bother to carry around is its marginal utility, for in economics we use the word "utility" more often than we do " usefulness." The principle of marginal utility, then, is that the utility of one of a series of similar goods is measured by the utility of the last one that will be used under given conditions. 

But the total utility of all the units is greater than the utility of the marginal unit employed that number of times. If we draw a line xy from the top of the rectangle representing the marginal unit straight back across the rectangles of the earlier units, then the total amount in those rectangles above this line is what we call the consumer's surplus. That is the amount of satisfaction he has received out of the use of all of a series of articles above that of the last one multiplied by the number of articles used. The total volume of the five rectangles added together (roughly indicated by the line ab) is plainly considerably more than five times rectangle 5. 

5. The law of economic choice. Under normal circumstances one chooses those activities or goods that will give him the greatest satisfaction in proportion to their cost. That cost may be measured in money, in labor, or in time, or perhaps all three. A corporation is thinking of enlarging its facilities for production. It may add a new variety of product to those that it puts on the market, or it may enlarge its factory, or it may construct a new factory in a favorable location. If it is not in a position to do all three of those things at once, it will decide which of the three it will do in 1942, for example, on the basis of which will probably bring the greatest returns then in proportion to the expense and trouble involved. Perhaps you have a chance during a summer vacation to work for someone at an occupation which you have thought of going into for your own life work later on. 

That same summer you may have a chance to take a long auto trip and see a good deal of the United States. Which will you choose? 

Which will do you the more good in the long run? 

That is your economic choice. Every one of us is likely to have the chance to observe in his own experience the working of each one of these five laws. 

What else, beyond the satisfying of physical wants, is necessary to make life most useful and happy? Give examples from your own experience that will illustrate the five laws stated in this section. Is it possible that sometimes in making his "economic choice" one may have to decide whether he will temporarily ignore one of the other laws — the law of variety or of harmony, for example? 

205. What Makes Goods Desirable? Goods are wanted for thousands of different purposes.

Free goods are those which exist 

---

in such abundance that everyone may have all he wants. Economic goods are those which do not exist in unlimited abundance, and for which some compensation must be made in effort or money. The list of free goods is not now very long. Most free goods are forces or gifts of nature. For most of us air exists in a greater quantity than any of us needs for himself, though not always in the kind of temperature and humidity that we should like. Water might seem another example of free goods, though in many places water for drinking purposes costs money, and perhaps is obtained for any use only with effort. 

There was a time when, in many parts of this country, one could have all the wood he wanted by simply going out and cutting down trees. 

Now just try that even in rural districts and see what happens. 

The extent to which goods are limited is referred to in economics as scarcity. To say that a certain good is scarce does not necessarily mean that there is little of it in existence, as such substances as helium and radium. But anything is relatively scarce if its supply is not equal to all the possible demands that could be made for it. 

Another classification of goods marks them as producer's goods or consumer's goods. The manufacturer of steel needs the iron ore, the various chemical materials, and the factory equipment which can transform that ore into steel. Those goods which are useful to the steel man but would have little or no value to the public at large would be producer's goods, because they would be needed for the purpose of producing something else. After the factory has transformed the raw material into steel rails, or steel beams, or even watch springs, then they can be used by a railroad in constructing its tracks, or by a building contractor in putting up a school or an office building, or by you and me in telling the time of day. Those things which have become commodities of daily and regular service are consumer's goods as contrasted with the other type. 

A third classification of goods thinks of them as either perishable or durable. Perishable goods are those whose usefulness ends the first time they are used or lasts for only a few occasions. Durable goods are those which may be employed over and over again for the same purpose or similar purposes. In this matter, of course, some conditions are relative. A tennis racquet can be used much longer than a tennis ball if the same ball is used as often as the racquet is, but neither is as durable as an automobile or a railroad car.

The qualities in goods that enable them to gratify wants we speak of as utilities. One article may possess several utilities at the same time. 

Another may possess some of them at one time and some at another. 

We commonly think of utilities as being of five kinds—natural, time, place, form, and possession. Natural utilities exist when there is some quality in the good itself without which it would fail to be of use. An apple has natural utility for eating purposes. Wood has natural utility for making many articles. A rose has natural utility by reason of its beauty and fragrance.

Time utility exists if a good is available when it will render service. A sled has very little time utility in August in our country, but in some places it may have very high utility at certain seasons. 

Place utility exists when a good is in a situation where it can be of service. If I go out to the tennis court and forget to take my racquet along, that racquet has no place utility whatever until I go back and get it. A boat has place utility only when it is on or near water deep enough to permit one to travel in it. 

Form utility results from the shape given to a commodity which permits it to render particular service. A limb of a tree has certain utilities, but it would have to be given a considerably modified form before it could render any service as a baseball bat. Cotton has to pass through several changes before acquiring the form utility needed in making a piece of dress goods for a girl. 

Possession utility exists when one has the right to use a certain article or good for his own purposes. A perfectly good automobile may be turned out of a factory in Detroit or Flint, but it means nothing to me until by some process it has been turned over to my use so that I may drive it or let others drive it. 

Perhaps these seem like minor points, but there are times when the presence or absence of any one of these utilities may make a big difference economically to any person. Some occupations are concerned very definitely with providing certain kinds of utilities. The railroad, for example, provides time and place utilities for thousands of articles; the department store makes possible time, place, and possession utilities for thousands of people; and every factory has something to do with giving form utilities to the goods it produces. 

What goods did the early explorers or settlers of this country probably look upon as free goods which now we would not classify under that heading?

Are there any free consumer's goods today? May certain goods be either producer's or consumer's goods? Under what circumstances could an apple be either? Some people think that wholesale dealers and brokers do not provide any kind of utility for goods. Is that true? 

206. Wealth and Work. 

which are often used inacccurately. The economist thinks of wealth as meaning the sum total of one's possessions whose value can be estimated in money. Money itself is not necessarily wealth, not even the money in a bank. That money represents what someone has left in the bank, or something that the bank has received from an agency of the federal government in exchange for notes or something of commercial value. Money for the bank is simply a convenience, just as that which we carry around is for most of us. But if the bank owns the building in which it carries on its operations, then that building is a part of its wealth. 

There are many valuable possessions whose value we cannot estimate in money, and therefore cannot count as wealth. The education you have already received is one of them, and so are such perfectly desirable things as health and common sense. But houses and factories and tools and books can be given a money value, for at least we know what it would cost to replace them, if they could be replaced, or what someone else would pay for them if, like a painter's masterpiece, they are not the kind of thing that could be duplicated.

To measure wealth we make use of money, and to have this money mean something definite we take a certain amount of it and give it a name as a standard of measurement. In this country we call that standard a dollar. In Great Britain the standard is a pound, in 

Italy it is a lira. Not even a dollar will buy just the same amount of things at all times and in all places; but at least it gives us something to refer to in expressing what things are worth. 

A few terms that concern wealth are income, assets, and liabilities. 

Income is the money or its equivalent which one receives for goods or services. That part of this income which he does not spend may be added to his wealth, which will then be correspondingly increased. 

Even some that he does spend may have been used to purchase certain things which stay with him after the year is over, and will make him a wealthier man at the end of the year than he was at the beginning. 

Assets represent all that a person has in the form of wealth, plus 

- Wealth is one of several economic terms

whatever is owed to him from others. A bank's assets may include the building in which it does its work, if the bank owns it, the funds in its possession which belong to it and which enable it to carry on its daily business, and whatever is owed to the bank by people to whom the bank has lent money from time to time. Liabilities, on the contrary, are the financial obligations one owes to others. One may have borrowed $10,000 from some kindhearted person in the course of a year and lived "the life of Riley" during that time. But even though he has spent some of the $10,000 for articles of permanent or long-time use, he still owes $10,000, and that amount must be included in his liabilities.

A person may have a considerable amount of wealth in any given period but no income. He may have both assets and liabilities at the same time, and his net wealth is represented by the difference between the assets and the liabilities. Similarly, a nation might have large

amounts of natural wealth in the form of forests or unmined metals, but if nothing has been done to turn those natural resources to use, the people of that country might to a considerable extent be living in poverty.

The distribution of wealth is a most important problem. A country which has people with more wealth than they can possibly use, while at the same time millions can hardly keep alive, has something wrong with it. The wrong may be with the country, its laws, or its economic system, and not necessarily with the wealthy individuals. They may not have done a single illegal thing in their lives. 

It is easier to say this than to tell what ought to be done about it. 

We need not expect to be better off as a nation by taking away the wealth of Rockefeller and Ford and giving it to people who never had the enterprise or ability to earn a decent living. Our effort should be not to make rich people poor, but to give all who are willing to do an honest day's work the chance to provide for themselves.

Many things contribute to human happiness besides wealth. The few who have had to administer a great fortune tell us truthfully that it brings vast responsibility and heavy burdens. It is not wrong for one to desire to be free from worry about where the next day's meals are coming from. The evil in the possession of riches is in possessing them without feeling any sense of responsibility or any desire to use them in a way that will be socially beneficial. Probably the happiest nation in the world would be one in which all of its people had something to do which would provide them a respectable living, and in which each citizen wanted to do his share toward his own and his country's welfare. 

Why do people work, anyway? There are several reasons, some of which will fit some people much more than others. And of course several motives for work may influence one person. 

1. Most people must work in order to obtain the necessities of life, such as food, clothing, and shelter. 

2. Most people are willing to work in order to have comforts and conveniences beyond the bare necessities of living. 

3. Some people will work just for the pleasure they get out of it. Why do some wealthy society girls get jobs in department stores? Because they are better satisfied in doing something than in living at home in idleness.

4. Some people work because they feel that in doing so they are rendering service to others. 

5. Some people work because it brings prominence or power which they could not otherwise enjoy.

Whatever the motive is, wealth cannot be created without work. 

Work is not all physical. Some men must plan, some men must write, some must watch and see that others do their assigned duties. 

Why some who work hard get little wealth is another story. But somebody's work was essential in order to permit anybody to acquire wealth.

When a government borrows money from its own people, is the wealth of that nation affected? Are there many people who have no wealth whatever?

Is it true that "there never has been an absolute overproduction of goods"? 

What problems does a rich man have to face which never bother a poor man?

Give examples of people you know who illustrate the motives for work mentioned above. How many motives for work are illustrated by the pictures on the next page? 

207. The Problem of Using Goods. Here we may think of a few foundation ideas with reference to consumption which we need to keep in the back of our heads as we discuss the next few units. 

Later on (Unit XXII) we will go into this matter in some detail. 

Consumption may be final or it may be productive. In final consumption the good is used in the last form which it will take. Food when used disappears as food. Houses are used as places to live in and not for any further economic purpose if they are houses and nothing else. Productive consumption is the use of goods in producing other goods. The manufacturer of flour buys wheat, and the wheat is then used in productive consumption in the making of flour. The manufacturer of clothing buys the woolen or rayon or cotton goods and then consumes those things productively in making something to wear. 

Consumption goods are also sometimes classified as necessities, comforts, and luxuries. The words almost define themselves. Perhaps this would be a fair distinction a good serves as a comfort when its use is not strictly necessary but not out of line with the ordinary standard of living of the person who happens to be consuming it. It becomes a luxury when it is used for a purpose distinctly outside the ordinary range of that consumer's method of living.

James Sawders 551

Whether consumption is wise or unwise may depend upon the familiar saying, "Circumstances alter cases.' For a wage-earner getting no more than $1200 a year, a Cadillac car would unquestionably be a luxury. In some circumstances a second-hand Ford or 

Chevrolet might be a justifiable convenience for him, but unless used by the worker directly in earning his own living, it would be a "comfort" rather than a "necessity." Conditions also change in the course of time. Even fifty years ago who would have thought of telephones as a necessity for a farmer? But now many farmers think So, and often with considerable reason. The quality of clothes one is justified in wearing will vary somewhat with what he has to do. 

An office worker will want a different kind of outfit from what a farmer would wear. If a woman worker has to meet people of all classes daily, she will want to dress better than if she works in a factory where expensive clothes are no more serviceable than cheap ones. 

Be sure to distinguish between consumption, destruction, and waste. Goods may be "consumed" without at any given time any noticeable change in their appearance or condition being noticed. 

A chair is "consumed" day after day, and it may not look noticeably different after three or four years of use than it did in the first place. 

Destruction, however, involves the disappearance of the good from its original condition. If a chair is tipped over and broken, or burned, its usefulness as a chair is probably destroyed. If you observe the steps in your school building in the morning and again in the evening, you will probably notice no particular difference. But if you saw them when the building was first opened and then came back years later after hundreds of pupils every day had gone up and down them, you would actually see some marks of wear. Some destruction may take place gradually, simply as a part of ordinary justifiable consumption.

Waste is the consuming of goods extravagantly or without care for their protection. If you use twice as much paper as you really need, there is waste. If a city government hires 200 street cleaners to do the work that could be done by 150, there is waste. If farm tools are left where they will rust or rot, there is waste. A true economist dislikes to see such things.

We have heard considerable in recent years about consumption as not only an individual but a national problem. If people cannot

or will not consume certain goods, they will not long be produced. 

When goods cannot be sold, business managers will neither enlarge their business activities nor hire more workers than they absolutely need. A nation's ability to consume will determine in the long run how much it will produce. 

Consuming goods is something that most people do not like to do under orders, or to be forbidden to do, unless there is a very evident reason. Laws relating to the consumption of goods are sometimes collectively referred to as sumptuary legislation. Even when such laws are enacted with the very best of motives, as was the Eighteenth Amendment, they meet determined opposition from some people just because of the principle that is involved. Laws intended to compel people to spend money would be just as unpopular. As a general thing, it is better to show people what is or is not wise consumption than to depend too much on law. 

If people are willing to pay for some article, is it the duty of business or society to produce it? Since the destruction of property would call for labor and the consumption of goods to replace it, would it be socially and economically wise to burn down all buildings that do not provide a desirable standard of living for their occupants? Would laws against the sale and use of fireworks be an example of desirable sumptuary legislation? XVIII  

Leaving consumption until we know more about what there is to consume, let us turn to that great phase of economic activity which we call production. Without the production of goods, human wants cannot be satisfied. Since production aims to satisfy every kind of human want, its range is immense. We shall need to consider the different factors that take part in production and give attention to the way those factors are organized and used in the work of preparing goods to satisfy wants. 

Some Questions: 

1. What does production include and what factors have a part in it? 

2. How does each of these factors aid in production? 

3. What special conditions or problems pertain to labor in production? 

4. How does capital make production possible? 

5. What services does management render in production? 

6. What forms of organization are used in conducting business and what problems have arisen from any of them? 

7. What relatively new features of business organization or management have come into prominence? 

208. Production and Producers. Production takes place because people have wants and need goods or services to satisfy them. It includes a great many activities, though some people seem to think that unless a person operates a machine or works with his hands or other muscles he is not a producer. What would happen if we dropped out of a business organization the people who keep the records of purchases and sales, or those who oversee workers to see that processes are carried on in the right way and at the right time, or those who have to make plans and decisions in regard to what shall be made or sold and where raw materials shall be bought? Moreover, even those of us who do not take part in planning to produce material things render services desired and needed by those who make or execute plans. 

Lawyers, physicians, teachers, professional people generally, render services that make possible the carrying on of the production of material things. They all help in the common effort. 

556

One definition of production is the giving of utilities to goods. Nature puts a certain utility into an apple. Men come along and carry that apple to a place where people can use it to satisfy their own wants. 

Time, place, and possession utilities have been added to the original natural utility, and all who have helped to add these utilities have had a part in the "production" of apples, in the economic sense. 

Every producer supplies one or more of the four fundamental factors in production. These four are land, labor, capital, and management. 

The first two are often called primary factors because we must have them in order to make the others possible. In that respect capital and management are secondary to land and labor. That does not mean that they do not contribute in a vital way to production, but simply that they have no chance to do anything until land and labor have done at least part of their work. 

By land we mean any gift of nature which has a part in production. 

The soil in which seeds are grown is land. In the economic sense, water is a gift of nature often used in production, and so are the animals, such as cows or truck horses, that render a service in production. Labor means any form of human energy that is used in producing goods. It may be physical, it may be mental, it may be a combination of both. One who uses a typewriter may be just as much a laborer as one who digs a ditch or operates a loom. Capital is the product of past industry which is used in producing more goods. Past industry made a railroad and the engines and cars that run on the tracks. 

They are now capital, and so is the shovel which a ditch-digger uses. 

Management is the activity which plans and makes use of the other factors in production. Once economists included it as a kind of labor, but since it involves the exercise of responsibility and the possession of a distinct kind of talent and effort, we usually consider it a factor apart from labor.¹

Every occupation, trade, or profession makes use to some extent of every one of these four factors in production. A dentist's office is located in the building which rests upon land. His office equipment and instruments of torture are a part of his capital. His own services and those of an office girl furnish the labor part of the occupation. 

His plans for operating his office and keeping in touch with new ideas ¹ Some economists prefer to use the term "risk-taking" or a term derived from the 

French, "entrepreneurship," for this field of work (§ 216). Take your choice.

and methods in the field of dentistry, and the decisions he has to make as to where his office will be located, the hours he will keep, and the charges he will make, all come under the head of management. 

Each factor is not equally important in all industries. Land is a much more vital factor to the farmer than to the dentist, because the farmer depends upon land for the growth of his product. These four factors, as in the case of the dentist, may be contributed by one and the same person. The proprietor of a small store may work alone and provide all four of the factors himself. There are all sorts of relationships among the four factors. Sometimes the capital and the management are furnished by the same person. Sometimes the land is supplied by a landowner who has no other connection with a particular enterprise or activity.

209. The Work of Land in Production. - You are welcome to speak of natural resources instead of land, but the economist knows "land" is shorter, and understands what he means by it. To speak of water power, fish in a brook or the ocean, and animals as "land" is not very common with other people, however. 

Three kinds of services are rendered by land. It is fundamental, as we have already noticed, because it furnishes standing room for

every kind of economic activity. Even the ocean liner has to have land at both ends of its trip, and no airman stays up all the time. 

Land also furnishes raw materials out of which many things are manufactured. Out of the soil come our gold and silver, our iron and coal. The trees in the forests that are cut down to make chairs and tables are land in the economic sense. 

ONIONS AND SPINACH 

Market gardening near a large city should be profitable. This scene is in Westchester County, New York, one of the richest counties in the state outside the Big 

City. Intensive cultivation !

In the third place, natural elements and forces are land to the economist. Water power, wind power, electrical power- all these come in the first place from nature. Man can direct or control them, but he did not put the power into the water, or the air, or whatever medium was used to control or direct it. Sometimes we use the term "made land," meaning land which has been given its present form through the purpose of man. We fill in a swamp and on it we locate a baseball park or even a series of homes. But what we have really done is not to make the land, but to move some of nature's own creation

from one place to another, or to do something else with it that makes it more useful.

One of the chief services of land is, of course, for the cultivation of growing crops, such as grain, fruits, flowers, and vegetables. The land has the chemical elements which these products need in order to grow. Just how the land shall be used will depend in part upon the crops that are to be grown. mm
