HOW THINGS MAY BE DONE ON A WESTERN FARM 

This is an example of extensive cultivation, with a tractor pulling a harvester. 

This was taken in the state of Washington. Could this kind of machinery be used on the typical farm in the East?

Two general methods of cultivation are widely practiced. When we take a large area of land and plant it, usually with just one crop, such as wheat or oats, and largely leave the land to itself to furnish the return, we have extensive cultivation. The amount of labor and capital employed in proportion to the total area of land is much less than in the other kind. In intensive cultivation there is a great deal of time, labor, and perhaps money employed in working a comparatively small piece of land. The market garden, which furnishes

vegetables and flowers for our large cities, is a notable example in this country of land which is cultivated intensively. The Japanese are masters of this kind of thing too. Otherwise they could not make their mountainous country do as well as it does in supplying the needs of many millions of people. 

An economic law which shows itself particularly in the working of land is the law of diminishing returns. According to this law, in the cultivation of land, in the working of a mine, and to some extent in any activity, a point will be reached beyond which the employment of a given amount of labor and capital will not bring in as great returns as before. It may still be profitable for land to be cultivated after the point of diminishing returns is reached, though not as much so as before.

A diagram may help to make this law clearer. 

Suppose in the diagram below we represent the returns from $1000-worth of labor and capital on a certain piece of property by rectangle 1. Now suppose on that same piece of land we make use of another $1000-worth of labor and capital. Perhaps it will bring more than the total returns from the first application (2). Suppose we go a little further and put on a third $1000-worth of labor and capital. Perhaps here we shall still see additional returns as great or even greater than came from the use of the first $1000-worth (3). Suppose we try again. Now perhaps we find that the extra returns derived from the fourth $1000-worth of labor and capital (4) are not as great as were added when we put on the second $1000-worth and the third $1000-worth. 

If we do find that to be true, we know we have reached the point of diminishing returns, and if we keep on employing more labor and capital on that same piece of land (rectangles 5 and 6), we may expect less and less for each additional $1000-worth. If we should find, for example, that when we put on a sixth $1000-worth of labor and capital we added to our total returns only $1000-worth of products (6), we should have reached what would be known as the margin of cultivation, where the returns just equal the cost of obtaining them. Beyond that point it would mean an actual loss to continue, and people will not do it voluntarily. 1 2 3 $1000+$1000+$1000+$1000+ $1000+$1000 b 4 x 5 6

This principle of diminishing returns may work even in matters far removed from land cultivation. Suppose a person enlarges an office building. He may be able to rent all the new offices which he adds at a figure which more than pays him for the cost of providing this extra space, but there surely is a limit to the extent below ground or above ground that one can add rooms to an office building and find people willing to rent them. When the point is reached where, for any reason, the opportunity to make profitable use of the extra space comes to an end, we have reached not exactly the margin of cultivation, but at least the margin of gain in that particular building. 

Are the following land in the economic sense: a state forest in your state; a market garden; a coal mine; a railroad tunnel; a vacant lot; a flower garden; a farmer's mule? What examples can you give of so-called made land? What actually was done in the process? In your part of the country do you see more of intensive or extensive cultivation of land? Why? 

210. How Important Is the Farmer? - We often speak of our present economic era as the machine age, but what are people going to live on who operate the machines? So, even though the farmer uses machines today more than he ever did before, and on that account fewer people are needed to live on and work the farms, there will always, as far as one can tell, be need for farmers. The farmer is the landed proprietor par excellence of our whole economic set-up, but in our own country, as in a good many others, there are plenty of people working on farms who do not own the land. They either work for wages or cultivate the property on shares, or may even be somewhat like the serfs of the Middle Ages. 

The economic welfare of these people is of more importance to people in the cities than the latter sometimes realize. If the farmer's family no longer make their own clothes or tools, they must get these from the city. To buy these, they must have money, and so they must get enough through the crops they raise to keep themselves alive and earn some money besides. If the farmer who ships milk into 

New York or Chicago or Boston cannot get a fair price for his milk, he cannot afford to buy as much as he otherwise would from the catalogues of the mail-order houses. Neither the city man nor the farmer can suffer without loss coming to the other. 

Farming has special problems of its own. Weather makes a tremendous difference to the farmer. A sudden frost or a long period

of too wet or too dry weather may make the difference between profit and serious loss. Plagues of grasshoppers and various kinds of bugs and worms may come upon the farmer without warning and eat up half his crop.

The farmer also has his problems of marketing and of labor. Few farmers produce anything in sufficient quantity so that they can profitably market their products themselves. They have to depend 

ADIO Acme Photo WHAT GRASSHOPPERS CAN DO 

These Kansas grasshoppers evidently took a fancy to one kind of crop rather than another. They are an example of the things with which farmers have to contend. upon commission merchants in the cities or upon the activities of a co-operative society which may handle the marketing business for all the farmers in a considerable area. Farmers, more than any other group, have wanted the government to guarantee them a certain price for their produce, for if the cotton crop is larger than usual, for example, it will not sell for so much a pound as when the crop is smaller. We shall have more to say later about the recent attempts on the part of our federal government to do something for the farmer.

One of the farmer's labor problems is that at certain seasons of the year he needs little or no help, and at other seasons he needs it mightily for a little while. Such labor is not easy to get, especially on the farm. 

Ask some farmer what luck he had when he needed help during the haying or harvesting season and tried to get unemployed workers from the city to come out and work for him. The farmer also often must board and lodge his employees. If that is included as a part of their wages, he will not want to pay them much money besides. The reduced amount of money a farmer handles on that account often gives a false impression as to the real returns that a farm laborer receives for his services.

Yet in times of depression when things go wrong in the city, the farmer can usually raise enough to live on. A cow and a few hens will give him milk and eggs, and a vegetable garden will provide him with a considerable portion of his food. If he has only a work suit and a 

Sunday suit, nobody thinks the worse of him on that account. Politicians have sometimes found it profitable to play for the farm vote. 

In the depression period of the early 1930's, some people who had gone into the city to get rich found that back home they could at least get a living, and a "back-to-the-farm" movement of some proportions went on for a while. This movement was just the reverse of the one that had been going on pretty rapidly for a long time previously, when the census figures showed a rapid decline in the rural population as compared with the urban. For years many farm boys thought that work was easier and better paid in the city, and there was a wider range to choose from.

Some counties in our eastern states had a larger population a hundred years ago than today, and in some parts of the East one could have seen at one time farmhouse after farmhouse deserted by its former inhabitants and left to the mercies of the elements. More recently foreigners who were used to farming in Europe or in Canada and were willing to work harder than the natives have taken up some of these abandoned farm properties. City people in considerable numbers have found that the country in the summertime is far pleasanter than the hot, congested city. Some of them have even moved out to the country permanently. 

In your state do farmers have much or little influence in politics? Does the nearest farm neighborhood to you cater to summer visitors and tourists?

211. Labor and Laborers. Next to land, labor is, of all the four factors in production, the most essential. Next to land? Yes, because without the land there is no place for the laborer to work, though it is also true that without laborers the land may not do a great deal for a nation.

Be sure to remember that labor may be either physical or mental. 

Factory workers and farmers sometimes say the teacher has an easy job because he gets two or three months' vacation in the summer, and gets through with his work - so they think at three o'clock in the afternoon. But let those same critics of the teacher go through the nervous strain of teaching, besides the routine demands upon a teacher's time and energy! Probably the teacher would find seven or eight hours a day in a steel mill more distasteful than the same length of time in a schoolroom, but let neither the teacher nor the millworker think that the other has a soft job. 

Both work or play may use just the same muscles or gray matter. 

What is the difference? Primarily this, that work is done to earn a living and often under the compulsion of personal or family responsibilities, while play is done for change or amusement. Some people, of course, get paid for doing things that others would gladly do for nothing, like the professional baseball player. Yet if he is under a contract, he must obey orders; he must do things at a specified time; he is liable to be fined if he fails to do what he is supposed to. Some of you probably enjoy, writing and find it fun to work on a school paper. But for many reporters writing becomes a task. They must go where they are sent and write up stories in which they may feel no particular interest. If they fail to do reasonably good work, their job disappears. The same activities may at some times be work and at other times play.

Labor has a right to expect a return for what it contributes to production. But labor differs from some other things for which compensation is made in that you cannot separate it from the one who furnishes it. A carpenter may make a box and sell it or give it away, and it may be used by people miles away from him. The product of his

labor was separable from him, but the work he put on that particular job was his own special service. Another distinctive fact about labor is that it cannot be stored up and laid by as a surplus for future use. 

It must be available at the time that it is needed. The labor that you could have employed on something yesterday, but did not, is lost forever.

Some of the terms we use in speaking of labor have a distinctive meaning. 

Occupation, for example, is a general term that may be applied to any of dozens of activities. But when we speak of a trade, we are thinking of a kind of occupation which commonly involves a considerable amount of manual work and calls for some skill in doing it. A profession, on the other hand, makes less demand for manual work, requires as a rule a rather long period of preparation, and has in it a distinct personal element for instance, the relations between a physician and his patient, a lawyer and his client, a teacher and his pupil. By industry we commonly mean organized business activities that have something to do with manufacturing. We sometimes employ the term in a more or less general fashion, but we seldom cover under this term agriculture or the professions.

The Bureau of the Census finds ten classes of what it calls "gainful occupations." Trade, as the Bureau uses the term, means an activity that has to do with buying and selling. A storekeeper or a "clerk" in a store, a real

estate agent, or even a banker would come under the head of trade, because to provide means of buying and selling is the reason for the existence of their occupations. Domestic and personal service refers to people who are employed at wages in homes and hotels and who are engaged in such work as that of barbers, beauty shops, tailors, and similar activities. Clerical occupations refer to those which have to do with writing. Private secretaries, bookkeepers, and stenographers are examples of this type of occupation.

Ought we to think of "labor" as carrying with it the idea of unpleasantness or distress? In the list of occupations tabulated by the Census Bureau, where would you place such people as florists, baseball players, janitors, ticket agents, druggists, policemen, teachers, newsboys, bootblacks? Are inventors laborers? How important to the welfare of business or industry or laborers as a class has inventive genius been? 

212. Ways of Working. 

Whenever primitive man found something to be done, everybody concerned was supposed to help. When a group of men were trying to get the better of some big animal, each one might have had some particular responsibility, but it was probably pure accident what any single individual had to do. This kind of work is often called simple co-operation. 

As people's ability to do things improved, the practice which we call the division of occupations began. Some people made it their duty to look after the flocks and herds, since it was probable that they had to move around from one place to another. Others settled down where grain was planted so that they could care for it properly. 

Among those who lived near a seacoast or riverbank, some might become boat builders, and others would engage in trading between one place on the river and some other place, or even between one country and a neighboring region. Division of occupations was not entirely mechanical, either. Some few became priests, scribes, or medicine men among early people, and out of them has grown the professional class of today.

The next step was the division of labor within occupations. One could be a skilled tradesman doing woodwork, another could work in bronze, another could carve stone. In many occupations the work could be divided up so that different steps or parts of the job could be done by different people, and if one's interests and talents appeared to qualify him to do well some limited feature, a worker might give his entire time to that.

The last stage of development of this character may be referred to as specialization. In making automobiles, very few workers have anything to do with more than one part of the machine. The fellow who helps to make tires will have nothing to do with making the engine. Each worker who helps make parts or who shares in the job of assembling the car may have just one little job to do which he does over and over again, day after day.

In the professional field specialization has also appeared. Many physicians, especially in cities, make no attempt to handle all kinds of diseases. Physicians rarely perform operations themselves, and both physicians and surgeons may specialize in treatment of particular parts of the body, as the throat, the stomach, or something else. 

There is still a place, of course, for the general practitioner, because in small towns there is not enough work for specialists who deal with different kinds of ills, and some people do not care to tell their troubles to half a dozen different doctors.

Division of labor has the advantage of enabling a worker to do a particular kind of job in which he takes an interest, or which he finds he can do more skillfully than somebody else. A disadvantage, especially when it is carried to the detailed type of specialization we find in some industries, is the probable narrowing effect of it. It may be hard to get much enthusiasm about making a car if all you do is turn a nut a thousand times a day.

Besides, this detailed specialization in industry may make it possible for a few workers who perform some given part of a process to tie up a whole job if they refuse to work or do not do their work properly. Except in the professions, this method of handling detail may reduce considerably the amount of preparation or practice needed by a worker for his job. It does not take long to learn one motion or just a few. Even some workers who have a variety of things to do may be trained in a few months. 

The problem of adjusting the supply of workers to the amount of work to be done is not always easy to solve. You remember Malthus's theory that under ordinary circumstances a country's population tends to increase faster than the means of providing for it, and that in order to keep these numbers within control, it was inevitable that there should be famines, disease, and war to carry away the surplus population. With so much improvement in providing food through

agriculture, it seems now as if Malthus's fears in that respect were not well founded. If at any given time many workers are unemployed or starving, it is not because we do not have the resources to care for them, but because we have not shared wisely what we do have. 

But who shall do what, and who shall say what one shall do? Back in the Middle Ages when the domestic system of work was typical, only a few workers were brought together in any one shop to make hats or shoes or spears.

The master and the rest all did much the same things. When factories took the place of small shops and several hundred workers might be employed in one establishment, a different type of supervision was needed.

Each part of the shop was put under its boss or foreman, who would oversee the work done in his part of the plant. One of the "higher-ups" in the organization might make it his special responsibility to oversee the overseers, so to speak, and make sure that the bosses knew their jobs and treated properly the men who were under their authority. rimis

H. Armstrong Roberts

APPLYING FOR A JOB 

Many firms have a definite set of questions which they wish to ask of those who 

I would like to work for them. Do you see anything unreasonable in being asked to fill out such an application?

Today almost every large-scale business has its personnel department, with people in charge who have the entire responsibility for "hiring and firing" within the organization. One who wants a job must satisfy that department that he can do the work for which he applies. Inefficiency or other reason for discharge or lay-off may also be a problem for that department, though the boss or foreman of a particular shop must have the right to pass judgment on the quality of the work done by those directly under him. With the growth in power of organized unions, elements have come into this matter of "hiring and firing" which will be considered later on.

Is there any advantage or any danger in being a jack-of-all-trades? Is increased specialization in industry likely to reduce the amount of time required in preparation for one's lifework, or to result in a higher standard of preparation and experience for almost all kinds of work? How far do moral qualities enter into labor? Is all productive labor honorable? How much right does a personnel official have to inquire into the moral character of a person who seeks employment? 

213. Kinds and Classes of Workers. A significant element in the performance of work concerns the grades or levels of work to be performed. These we often distinguish under the name of unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled, and expert or scientific. The unskilled worker is one who can do what he is asked to do with very little preparation. Ordinary farm labor, street cleaning, and certain jobs in factories are examples of this kind of work. 

Semi-skilled workers require some experience and practice, but anyone with ordinary intelligence needs only a short time to get it.

CAREFUL WORK 

This factory at Waltham, Massachusetts, makes watches. This man is testing wiring

Under that head might for a spring only one half of a thousandth of a centimeter thick and six thousandths of a centimeter wide. Manufacturing, you see, may require many kinds of workers and machines. 

Do you call this man an expert? 

James Sawders come streetcar motormen, truck drivers, salespeople in stores, and filing clerks in offices. The skilled worker needs special training for his job. He needs to know why certain things are done as well as how to do them, and to be able to adjust a job to a particular situation. The carpenter, the plumber, the paper hanger, the auto mechanic, are examples of the skilled worker, and so is one who operates a typewriter or other office machines. 

The expert or scientific worker needs a still higher mental qualification than the average skilled worker, because he must not only be able to do effectively things that have been done before, but by investigations and experiments to find ways to do them better. 

Workers in chemical laboratories, and experimenters in the field of

electricity, for instance, may be employed in this capacity. Most inventors come from this class of workers, though occasionally one from a lower group has a bright new idea. 

The more detailed is the knowledge that is required and the greater is the experience demanded, the smaller will be the number of workers who can fill the bill. Sometimes a skilled worker finds that the particular type of skill which he learned ten years ago is no longer needed, because of some new invention or some change in method. 

If he can adapt himself to the new requirements, very good. If not, he is out of luck, though in these days he may be able to earn as good wages for relatively unskilled work as he once did in his old-time skilled trade.

Economists and lawmakers alike used to go on the theory that all grown-up male workers were real he-men and perfectly able to look out for themselves, and that laws were not needed to protect them. At first the same attitude seemed to be taken even toward women and children, but in judging practices of the past with reference to the work of women and children, let us not be too harsh. The opening of factories came like a godsend to some women who had found home work monotonous and apparently unrewarding, or who actually were not needed at home. If their pay was small, it at least was more than they had ever had to spend before. And some child workers did not feel nearly so disturbed about their lot as those who became weepy or poetical over them. But today the prevailing sentiment rightly is that tired, overworked women cannot play their proper part in society, and ought to be protected, perhaps even against themselves, and that immature children certainly need the safeguards of the law (§ 160). Neither are we so ready as we once were to let men be employed under conditions that might ruin their health. 

In this country it has been in the South that regulation of labor by law proved most difficult to secure. Many a family with several children had never known a high standard of living; so when factories came into the South and offered to hire whole families, even at very low wages, the total money returns were far better than anything those families had previously received. Besides, some factory owners had moved their factories to the South or put up new factories there in order to take advantage of cheap labor. So proprietors as well as workers were often opposed to restrictive labor laws.

Labor problems have developed some of their most unpleasant aspects in connection with migrant workers who travel from one part of the country to another as the demand for workers changes with the seasons. In such occupations as the growing of beets for beetsugar factories, in the canning of fruits and vegetables, and in the harvesting of wheat and other products, there is a special demand at certain seasons for workers that does not exist at other times in the year. When unattached men do this kind of work, they can move from one place to another over a period of three or four months with perhaps relatively little inconvenience. But when whole families do this, and women and children work twelve or fourteen hours a day in such places as canning factories for five or six weeks, the situation is not at all desirable. Normal family life or regular education of the children is practically impossible. This condition is much more of a problem to some states than others. Yet the work must be done at a certain time, if it is to be done at all, and people who are employed at year-round jobs cannot be expected to give them up to do it. We certainly must try to find some way out of the difficulty. 

Be sure to familiarize yourself with any labor laws that apply particularly to your own state in regard to the work of women and children. Are there any features of those laws which you would like to change? Does the problem of the migrant worker seem serious in your state? 

214. Capital and What It Does. Here is a topic about which we need to do some clear thinking. Too many people have the idea that capital and selfishness are synonymous, and that all capitalists wish to sponge on the average worker and make a living by exploiting people who are unable to look out for themselves. As a matter of fact, industry cannot exist without capital. Even primitive man could use the same club time after time in defending himself against animals or killing them for food. The more advanced industry becomes, the greater is the importance and necessity of capital in its operation.

We may want to make a distinction between capital and capital goods. Capital may be used to mean the total investment in a business which represents the products of past industry. We may think of it as an abstract term. Capital goods, however, are the particular things that are used in producing more goods. Factories, railroad tracks, saws, shovels, machines of all kinds, are examples of capital 

---

goods, as well as the seed which the farmer grows, leather which is made into boots, or pig iron which goes into the mill. Since even the most durable kinds of capital goods will wear out in the end if not kept in repair, in any well-managed business a replacement fund is maintained to take care of this situation. In reckoning the value of a business, account is always taken of depreciation, which is one of the inevitable costs. Any machine which has been used a year is likely to have suffered some sort of wear which will not make it quite as serviceable, at least without repair, as it was in the first place. 

James Sawders

THE OLD AND THE NEW IN FARMING 

They are plowing land for cotton in the San Joaquin Valley in California. One man runs the tractor plow, the other still uses his team. Are they capital goods? 

Before capital can be obtained for use in a business or profession, three conditions are necessary. First, there must be a surplus of goods produced in the past which were not used or which has been derived from the sale of previously produced goods. Then, this surplus must be saved up instead of being paid out for everyday expenses or given away. In the third place, there must be a willingness to use these savings in creative investment that is, to put them to work in an industry. 

Savings, when they are available, may be obtained in three different ways. The simplest way, though not always the easiest, is for

people who have accumulated a surplus to put it into a business which they themselves will conduct. Since many people have savings, perhaps of small amounts, which they cannot conveniently put into their own business, a second means is available. A corporation, as we shall see a little later, issues stock which can be bought in shares by people who are willing to invest their money in the work of the corporation. This gives them a right to participate in the profit of the business. A third means of getting capital is through borrowing. 

Many who would not take the risks involved in putting money directly into a business will lend it on interest to those who do manage it. 

If a corporation borrows under these circumstances, it very often sells bonds just as governments do. These bonds are simply promises to pay back the amount borrowed at a fixed time, with interest at regular intervals.¹

The amount of capital available for business purposes varies with conditions and localities. In those parts of the country where business activities have been greatest and opportunities for saving most extensive, such as New York and other eastern business centers, the supply of funds for use as capital is greatest. Borrowers are most willing to obtain capital by this means when there is a good prospect that business will be lively and good returns will come in. Those who have money to lend are less fortunate when business is slack, for then business men are likely to hesitate about starting anything new. 

The amount of capital necessary for a business may vary considerably with the nature of the business. If only a relatively small investment is required for machinery, factory buildings, and the like, and a product is manufactured for which there is a great demand, large profits may be possible on a relatively small capital investment. One grievance against some capitalists has been that their business was so profitable that they wanted to conceal their percentage of gain, and so gave themselves new stock on which dividends were to be paid, but which did not represent any new investment in the business. 

That kind of stock is often referred to as watered stock. We cannot

Review the distinction previously made between wealth, money, and capital. Take the first ten businesses or occupations that occur to you and mention two or three ways in which capital is used in each one. Why might a person be willing to lend money to a corporation and receive a bond for it when he would not put the same amount of money into the corporation through the purchase of stock? 

215. What We Should Think about Capitalists. Capitalists are not parasites. Capitalists are perfectly human personages like you and me who have either inherited or have saved up through their own energy and good luck wealth which they are willing to use in producing goods. They expect to profit by it the same as we expect to be paid for doing work not required by courtesy or personal obligation. If capital were not supplied for industry by private citizens, the government would have to see that it was provided, because no industry can get along without it. 

By capitalism, as we commonly use the term, we mean the ownership and use of capital by private citizens for profit. It is a system which grew up from necessity and was not deliberately planned by anybody. But it would be just as silly to say that because capital has been abused, we should therefore try to abolish it, as to recommend that we should stop eating because we may have sometimes eaten unwisely. 

Some people may be capitalists without realizing it. Anyone who owns a share of stock in a corporation engaged in business is, to that extent, a capitalist, for his savings - the product of past industry are used in producing something more. As soon as one gets an interest in the profits of a business he is likely to feel some concern about the success of that business. That is one reason why some of our most wisely managed corporations, such as the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, have tried to get stock into the hands of their employees and the general public. In addition to furnishing what is on the whole a rather high grade of service, they thus secure a background of good will which has gained more favorable consideration for them than many other large-scale businesses have enjoyed.

One thing that the modern capitalistic system has made possible is what is known as round-about production. Today when machinery is used to do so many things-making shoes, for instance - the machines have to be made before the shoes can be given shape. So, as a first step toward the making of the shoe, somebody makes a machine. Sometimes that machine may itself be given its form and structure through the aid of a previous machine. So, by roundabout production we mean the whole series of steps that takes place in order to provide a finished product for consumer use. This can be done only if sufficient capital is available to make possible these various steps in production, and if the preliminary steps, such as the making of the machines which in turn make other machines, are taken before there is an actual occasion for their use.

How STRONG IS PAPER? 

All kinds of products have to be tested to see if they come up to standard. This worker is punching holes in the paper with a machine to test its strength. Perhaps this is a phase of roundabout production. 

Are you a capitalist? Is a capitalist necessarily connected with a big business? Which do you think is more likely to lead to steady improvement in industrial methods, letting capital for ordinary business activities remain in private hands, or having the government furnish the capital needed for all of our fundamental industries? 

216. Managers and What They Do. - A little way back we pointed out the fact that management is a kind of labor. With the tendency, however, to separate planning from performing, we have apparently pretty generally agreed that management should be considered a factor in production by itself. The manager does the planning for an industrial activity. He decides how much capital is needed, where it can be employed to the best advantage, how many employees of any kind it is desirable to have, and in what ways and where the land which every industry needs can be used so as to bring in the greatest returns.

The manager may also furnish all or a considerable part of the capital that a business needs. This happens often enough, in fact, so that some people fail to draw a distinction between the two. Perhaps the manager owns the land that is needed in the industry. Then, of course, he gets a return for that also. 

Every business or profession has a place for management. The professional man is his own manager, as a rule, because he usually knows better than anyone else what he wishes to do and what he can afford to do. Sometimes, however, as you have probably observed, professional people such as concert singers and movie stars hire people to do their managing for them to arrange contracts for public appearances, for taking part in the making of pictures, fixing the compensation they are to receive, and numerous other details which one does not think of unless he makes a special study of the matter. 

A manager is not necessarily one person. There may be a group of persons engaged in the work of managing a business. A board of directors for a corporation may have the final responsibility for deciding what shall or shall not be done. In practice, however, when it comes to working out details, it generally seems better for one man to be responsible for the direction of a certain definite portion of a large undertaking, so as to prevent misunderstandings and other difficulties resulting from differences of opinion or lack of co-operation. 

But whether it is a group or an individual, there is management. 

A French word we sometimes use to represent this activity of management is entrepreneur. Translating the word literally from the French, it would mean undertaker. The entrepreneur, whether he is one person or several, is the one who "undertakes" the work of planning and managing of a business. Most farmers are entrepreneurs because they have to plan what crops they will plant, what animals they will raise and keep, what arrangements they will make for selling their products, or when they will buy new tools, and must look after many other details. In a large establishment one person at least, and perhaps several, will have to give their entire time to the work. 

We have used the term "business" several times, taking a chance that it meant to you what it should mean. A business is, of course, an activity commonly carried on for profit. in order to make allowance for the fact that 

We say "commonly" many business men

really do want to benefit society as well as to make a profit out of what they do. A business unit is a single individual or organization engaged in some particular kind of economic activity. The corner grocery or drugstore is a business unit. So is the Ford Motor Company, and in between these two extremes there are business units of all kinds and sizes. 

One who has never thought about the responsibilities of a business man may have little realization of all that is involved. For example,  THE MANAGER'S OFFICE

217. How Risk Affects Business. Being a business man might be more fun if everything could be worked out in a formula and applied automatically. Any sensible business man will try to avoid the mistakes of other business men and profit by their successes, but he cannot foresee everything that will affect his own business venture. 

A man in a small town on a main highway sets up a gasoline station and repair shop, getting business not only from the people of the town but from tourists and other users of the road. Two or three years later the state highway department reconstructs that part of the highway, and the newly laid road runs a quarter of a mile away from his establishment. What happens to his business?

Early in the twentieth century there seemed to be a great future for electric railroads, and money that amounted to hundreds of millions all told was invested in them. Now what has happened to electric roads? 

In perhaps fifteen years they were not bringing in more than enough to cover expenses, and ten years later the equipment of some roads was sold for what it would bring as junk. 

The entrepreneur the manager has to take the risk involved in matters of this kind and in the direction of business generally. True, others also take risks. The landholder takes a risk in deciding to use a piece of land in one way rather than another. The laborer who agrees to work for a certain employer takes the risk that that business, or his own job in it, may not be permanent. The capitalist takes a risk when he puts his savings into one kind of business rather than another. But the day-by-day responsibility is that of the manager. 

The wise business manager realizes the possibility of change and 

---

tries to guard against loss from that source as well as from such misfortunes as fire. He can follow the markets for general trends in the demands of the public, and watch how his own sales go up or down, or how the demand for his line of products compares with those of others in the same general field. Then he can check up on what may need special attention.

FROM TREES TO PAPER 

In this forestry plot near Georgetown, South Carolina, trees are cut when they can be removed without detriment to the forest as a whole. Here is room for wise management. This corporation produces some of the raw material it uses in its own factories. Any risk here?

One whose business depends upon what may be a temporary fad or fancy will be on the look-out for something to take its place when the popular interest has changed. A manufacturer makes dolls or images of some other kind representing Shirley Temple. Then the popular fancy turns to Grumpy or Mickey Mouse. Sometimes new inventions change the whole situation and make it necessary for a factory manager to install a new set of machines or do something else of a rather far-reaching character if he is going to keep up with his competitors.

Some have maintained that the basic law of business is that a business man endeavors to secure the greatest possible amount of wealth in proportion to the effort or cost necessary to acquire it. Within certain limits that statement is doubtless true, especially if we define "effort" and "cost" properly. Some business men certainly feel it a matter of conscience to tell the truth in selling their goods and to avoid injuring their customers or the general public. The inevitable wear and tear on one's nerves when business conditions in general are not good, or which might accompany the undertaking of a new venture, would all be a part of the "cost" of a business. There are plenty of people who deliberately choose not to be managers. They are better satisfied to take the pay that they get in the form of wages or salaries than to add the worries that attend business management. 

An industry of comparatively recent growth is the manufacture of rayon.

Is the whole insurance business based, to a certain extent, on the taking of risks? How do the insurance companies minimize the danger involved in risks that they take? 

218. Kinds of Business Units. 

A broader definition of a business unit than the one previously given might read, "An individual, group, or organization which has distinctive interests of its own, and which contributes in return for a profit some desirable commodity or service." 

It may consist of but one man operating a little store with only a few dozen customers. On the other hand, it may be a vast organization with 100,000 workers, perhaps with branches scattered all over the United States and even in foreign countries. It is no reflection on a business unit that it is carried on for profit. If it is not so supported, it will either close up or have to be maintained by some generous individual or supported through charity, public or private. 

To be recognized as having the right to engage in business, a business unit must have a "legal personality." If it is a one-man affair, the law will recognize him as having the right to make contracts and to do the other things that have to be done in business. If more than one person is involved in its management, it will have to be recognized as a partnership, or corporation, or some other kind of organization that complies with laws by means of which it obtains this "legal personality." Such a partnership or corporation then becomes an 

---

"artificial person" with the right "to sue and be sued," to buy and sell, and to do the various other things that business requires. Just why charters of corporations so often mention first in the list of rights "to sue and be sued" is a mystery to some of us who would hope that that kind of thing would be one of the last activities a business organization would want to engage in.

The existence of these artificial persons has created considerable legal and constitutional argument. In the Fifth and Fourteenth 

Amendments to our national Constitution are statements to the effect that "any person" shall not "be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law." There is not much doubt that when those provisions were written into the Constitution, individual human persons, especially freed slaves, were the ones that were in the minds of the makers of those amendments. But if a corporation is given in its charter the rights that individual persons have, our courts have argued that it could not in fairness be deprived of the same kind of protection that is guaranteed to individuals. 

One cannot always tell from the name under which a business unit does business who is actually operating it. A plumbing firm continued to operate under the name of A. G. Pease and Company long after 

Mr. Pease was dead. John Wanamaker, the founder of the first great department store in this country, has passed to his reward long ago, but the store still operates under his name. Sears, Roebuck and

Company is now operated by people whose names have not the slightest resemblance to the ones which the company uses for trade purposes. The reputation of the original founders, however, has been of value to their successors.

Select three or four blocks in a business district with which you are familiar and make a list of the names of business organizations in those blocks. Note the kinds of business that are carried on, and observe whether the names actually represent persons connected with the business or even the kind of business that is actually done. Use this list, also, in discussing the kinds of business organization taken up in the next two or three sections. To what extent do you think the risks involved in a large business unit differ from those which are taken by the managers of a small unit?

receives all the profits, if there are any. This is the single proprietorship. Most small stores that are not units in "chains" are of this kind. The single proprietor has nobody to boss him. He makes his own decisions and has to take the consequences. THE SINGLE PROPRIETOR 

He is evidently receiving one of the regular visits of a representative of a wholesale house from which he buys much of his own stock of goods. times, of course, because the amount of capital that a single proprietor can furnish may not be extensive. 

A partnership is a business managed by two or more persons with definite agreements as to what each one contributes to the common activity. Each may go into the partnership on equal terms, but not necessarily. One whose experience is more extensive than his money may be allowed special recognition for that; and if the money investment that the partners make in the undertaking is not equal, their returns may be in proportion to the amount each contributes. Some-

times, indeed, there will be a "silent partner" who will not have any part in the active operation of the business but may have put up much of the necessary money to get it going. Whatever the arrangement is, profits and losses are shared in accordance with a definite understanding, depending on the value of each partner's contribution in money, experience, time, or otherwise. 

A partnership has the advantage over a single proprietor in that there probably will be more capital available and a larger range of experience to draw upon than any one person can provide. If one partner is better qualified for a certain type of work than another, they can divide the work between them in accordance with what each likes best or can do best. There also are disadvantages in a partnership. Usually each partner is liable to the full amount of his personal wealth for the losses of the firm, if they fail to make both ends meet. 

Besides, there is always the possibility of disagreement between the partners. The death of any partner breaks up the partnership. 

Then the survivor or survivors have to make new arrangements. 

Another form of organization seen in this country much less frequently than in England is the joint stock company. The organization of a joint stock company is, in a sense, part way between the partnership and the corporation, described in the next section. In a joint stock company several individuals unite in a company which is organized in such a way as to issue shares of stock which then may be bought and sold like any other property. The joint stock company is more permanent than a partnership, since the death of one member does not break up the whole concern. Sometimes, especially in Great Britain and Canada, under this type of organization, restrictions are placed on the obligation of the members in meeting the debts of the company. In other words, there is "limited liability" on their part, whereas in the ordinary partnership there is no such limitation. 

When the company is allowed to do business on this basis, they are expected to use the abbreviation "Ltd." after the firm name, so that anyone doing business with them will understand this fact of limited liability. 

Go through the list of firms which you compiled in working out the questions after the previous section, and see how many of them belong under any of the types of organization mentioned in this section. What kinds of business activities would you think partnerships might serve rather well? Perhaps

a member of a partnership would talk with you about the reasons why he does business under this form and what he thinks of the desirability of it. 

220. The Corporation and Its Importance. Though the single proprietorship is still the most numerous type of business organization, an enormous proportion of all the business of the country measured in dollars is now done by corporations. A corporation is a group of persons who have organized under a charter granted by the state which authorizes them to issue stock and to engage in such business activities as are permitted in the charter.¹ A corporation is formed by a number of people — in some states the law says at least five, in others three are enough who unite to secure a charter from a state government. Some states have been much more lenient about issuing charters than others. New Jersey used to be a sort of national joke on that account, but that is no longer true. Now 

Delaware is one of the easier states in which to get a charter, and many corporations which do business mostly in other states get their charters from Delaware. 

The charter makes the corporation an artificial person and gives it the same standing at law that a real person would have. It often specifies the amount of capital stock that the corporation may issue. 

Frequently the corporation does not at first issue all the stock which it is permitted to issue, but may enlarge the amount later on. This stock may be held by the incorporators or may be sold to anybody who will buy.

Usually when the stockholders are allowed to vote on electing officials of the corporation or on some matter of policy, they get one vote for every share of stock they hold. Most corporations have a board of directors who are elected by the stockholders and who in turn choose a president, one or more vice presidents, perhaps a general manager, probably a secretary, and such other officers as may be needed.

Of course if you happen to own six shares in a corporation that has issued 20,000 shares, your six votes seldom mean much, and probably you will not go to the trouble of attending stockholders' meetings.

The corporation has several advantages as a form of business 1 There are "municipal" corporations as well as private corporations; but we are not particularly concerned here with municipal corporations, as they are not organized for the purpose of engaging in business activities, though some of them do carry on their own electric-light plants and water systems.

organization. Through the sale of stock, money can be obtained to be invested in the business which would not otherwise be available. 

Persons who have saved only a small amount of money may have a chance in this way to put it to work in industry. The return to the stockholders depends on the extent to which the business is profitable, for the stockholders get dividends, perhaps yearly, perhaps semiannually, perhaps quarterly, depending on the arrangements made in connection with any particular corporation. Sometimes stock is of at least two kinds, preferred and common. Preferred stock carries a definite rate of dividend, and no more, but gets that dividend before any other dividends are paid. Common stock takes what is left after the dividends on the preferred are paid. If the business is very successful and preferred stockholders are entitled to 6 per cent dividend, they get that, and that is all, and when business is booming additional profits may be great enough so that common stockholders have 8 per cent or 10 per cent dividends themselves. 

When business is not good, the common stockholders will probably get nothing, and the preferred stockholders may not even get as much as their maximum dividend. 

Another advantage of the corporation is in its permanency. "Kings and corporations never die" was an old saying. The death of one incorporator or stockholder does not affect the life of the corporation unless he should happen to be a particularly influential individual on his own account. Corporations, however, may come to an end. 

Sometimes charters give a certain definite period of life to a corporation, as 25 years, 50 years, or 99 years. At the end of that time a new charter may have to be taken out or the affairs of the corporation closed up. Especially to corporations whose business affects the public BODI

H. Armstrong Roberts

A SOURCE OF BOTH FUNDS AND OUTLAYS 

Business organizations often get money for expansion by issuing bonds. Of course they agree to pay interest on them. Unfortunately some of these coupons were not paid when they were due.

directly, such as railroad companies, private water companies, and the like, the tendency is now to be very cautious about granting charters "in perpetuity" or for such long terms as 99 years or 999 years, as has sometimes been done. 

Disadvantages as well as advantages result from the corporate form of business. Since a corporation, being an artificial and not a real person, cannot be put in jail, some corporations have engaged in shady practices, without being called to account in any satisfactory way. Sometimes through the ownership of large blocks of stock, persons have been able to use their voting power so as to get special favors for themselves or to compel the adoption of policies which were not beneficial to the public, and perhaps not to the corporation. We have already referred (§ 214) to "watered" stock which directors have been known to issue in order to cover up the high percentage of actual profits they were making. Sometimes persons who wish to control a certain corporation, but without letting it be known that they are the dominating forces in it, have had their private secretaries or other persons elected to boards of directors and then given orders to these people as to the way they should vote at directors' meetings. 

Such a person might be called a dummy director. 

Some people have formed unfavorable opinions of corporations because they bought stock from promoters who organized corporations to develop a Mexican gold mine or Florida land or some other faraway project. Such "wildcat stock," as it is sometimes called, has taken the savings of altogether too many poor but ignorant people who were deceived by the high-sounding advertisements issued by the promoters. It is in part to prevent such kinds of trickery in the marketing of stocks and bonds that the federal Securities and Exchange Commission was organized. Now when new stock is to be sold or bonds advertised, the proposal to do so has to be filed with this commission with all necessary information as to what is actually proposed.

Because some people, under the name of corporations, have engaged in business practices that would be considered inhuman if carried on by an individual, corporations have been referred to as soulless. 

Whether such characterization is deserved will depend upon the character of the persons who compose the boards of directors. If the only real purpose of the corporation is to make as much money

as possible to pass out in the form of dividends, they may try to pay low wages and otherwise carry on business in a socially harmful way. 

Enlightened men today, however, no longer think that is good business. 

They honestly want the corporation to have a good reputation for treating its employees well and giving good service to the public.

Do people from your state go to other states to get corporation charters? 

If so, why? If a corporation has many stockholders, does it follow that it is democratically governed? Would it be desirable to require corporations intending to engage in interstate commerce to take out charters from the federal government? What notable examples in your community or neighborhood do you find of the corporate form of doing business? 

221. What Large-Scale Production Does. Large-scale production or mass production has become a common feature of modern business. 

It means carrying on business with an extensive organization which uses large numbers of men and large quantities of capital and produces goods in great amounts. Do not confuse the idea of large-scale production with what you have learned about corporations. Most largescale organizations are corporations, but many corporations do only a small business. Easy communication and transportation for both raw materials and finished products, and a very considerable amount of capital available for investment in business activities, have made possible large-scale production of the output of both farm and factory. 

Large-scale production has several advantages. If considerable quantities of raw material have to be bought, they can be purchased in large amounts, and the same thing can be said of the disposal of the product. When either purchases or sales are handled in large volume, the cost of production per unit of the goods is much less. Large-scale production permits the division of labor and specialization of work to be carried out in great detail. This ought to mean a higher quality of goods and a greater amount of them in proportion to the cost per unit. The large-scale manufacturer can probably make use of new inventions sooner and maintain experimental laboratories and other facilities which others could not afford. 

Large-scale production also can make use of by-products which in a small-scale business might have to be thrown away. You know they say that the meat-packing concerns use every bit of the animal except the squeal, and the Du Pont people make all kinds of things.

from the deadliest ammunition to cellophane. The bones and other refuse from meat-packing establishments can be used to make glue. 

The large-scale establishment can afford to own its own mines or gardens or other source of raw material. Henry Ford owns not only a railroad to carry much of his products away from Dearborn, but has his own glass factories, forests, and lumber mills from which supplies are obtained to make the hundreds of thousands of cars which he puts out in a year. Ford has laid particular stress in recent years upon making certain parts for his cars in small towns instead of trying to drag them all into the neighborhood of Detroit. 

A particularly notable example of large-scale production is the United States Steel Corporation, which owns or controls iron mines in Minnesota, Tennessee, and Alabama, and has its enormous boats on the Great Lakes with its own docks to load and unload the ore, and railroads even to carry the ore to the factories besides, of course, the great factories themselves. The A and P grocery stores are an example of large-scale business in a different field. Large-scale production will usually make it easier to deal with competitors than small-scale production. It will be difficult for small-scale producers to get out their products as cheaply, and therefore they cannot profitably sell their goods at as low a figure as the large-scale producer. 

Quite likely, however, there is a limit to which large-scale production can be profitably carried. Some products will never need to be manufactured in big factories, as far as anybody can tell. Thumb tacks, paper clips, and other articles of that kind, are used in considerable quantities, but it is not likely that the producers of either of those articles will ever rival United States Steel in its volume of business or the distribution of the establishments engaged in production. "Big Steel," however, might make such things as a side line. 

You remember the law of diminishing returns. It can operate in manufacture as well as in agriculture. Therefore large-scale production, if carried beyond a certain point, may not be the most economical method. Perhaps a single plant may become too large to be supervised efficiently. On the same principle that educators have concluded that 3000 pupils are about as many as a high school can care for most capably, so there probably is a limit to the size of many business activities if we care about using materials most efficiently and treating workers fairly and humanely.

An oversized establishment may exhibit unhealthy social conditions. 

Most of the workers may be utterly unimportant individually, and they may become simply units or cogs in a machine. If one business organization secures such great commercial power through largescale organizations as to ruin competitors by unfair practices or obtain dangerous influence in politics, society as a whole will be harmed and not served. In the third place, since large-scale production inevitably reduces the number of managers and executives in an organization and forces some who have executive ability to become merely hired workers, it may be wasteful of human talent. If the large-scale establishment, through economy and efficient operation, is able to sell its product at a lower price and give consumers in general more for their money, even these disadvantages we have just mentioned may deserve to be overlooked; but one may not always be sure. There is little doubt that the prices of commodities produced on a large scale are generally lower than they would be otherwise, but perhaps not as low as they could be and still give the producer a reasonable profit.

The organization of workers in a big industry has sometimes been compared to that of a great army. Like a commander-in-chief, or, if you prefer, the President and his Cabinet, at the head of a big business is a chairman, president, or general manager, who has been chosen by the board of directors. The responsibility for making the whole system work together successfully is that of the chief executive, whatever his title may be. Under him are managers or superintendents of different departments engaged in some special branch of the work. They tell foremen or bosses what they wish to have done, and these foremen or bosses see to it that the men under their direction carry on in the prescribed fashion. 

The great mass of workers in the industry do the routine jobs that come into the day-by-day processes of production. Some of them may be highly skilled workers. Others may do very ordinary work requiring little or no general intelligence. But each is a part of the whole great machine, and if they do not perform their part suitably, the whole machine may be stalled. It may require an understanding of psychology as well as of economics to run a great industrial concern. 

Workers, being human, will accomplish a great deal more if supervised by people who themselves have not lost the human touch. There can

222. Combinations and Monopolies. Here is another place for clear thinking. Large-scale business may result from the combination of several small-scale businesses, but not necessarily so. Monopolies are not necessarily large-scale affairs, nor are they necessarily the result of combinations. 

You may use the word "combination" for any means for bringing together business units or organizations that previously had been acting separately. Sometimes the combination may not extend much further than the making of a common understanding between two or more producers about marketing their goods or buying raw materials. They might buy their raw materials from the same source so as to get the benefit of reduced prices, or might have a common agency to sell their products. At other times it may actually result in forming a new organization.

Sometimes the agreement between business organizations may take the form of a pool. In such a case the total amount of business that five or six business organizations might get if they worked separately might be treated as a unit. Then orders from a certain part of the country, for example, might be filled by that one of the companies in the pool which could do it most conveniently, and orders from another part filled by a different member of the group.

Railroads have sometimes done this when two or three roads serve the same territory, or at least the same cities at the ends of the lines. Since all business coming to any member of the pool is treated as common property, so to speak, the individual members have no object in competing with one another for business. 

A form of combination now banned by law is the so-called trust. Under this plan several concerns engaged in the same line of business might agree

upon the selection of a certain group of persons as "trustees," and then "entrust" to them the management of all the firms in the combination. 

The trustees would see to it that all of them were handled in accordance with one distinct policy, and that no member of the trust did anything to harm any other member. The Standard Oil Company was the first to be organized on this trust basis. 

Another way to bring about such common management is for each of several corporations to elect several of the same people to their boards of directors. Then these men would see to it that the policies adopted by the separate boards of directors were in harmony with one another. Such an arrangement is known as an interlocking directorate. This also is illegal, but the prohibition is sometimes hard to enforce because it is impossible to prevent the election to a board of directors of someone who will take orders from a person who is a director on another board. 

Another type of combination is by means of the holding company. The holding company is a new corporation chartered like any corporation but only for the purpose of owning stock in other corporations. If the holding company owns 51 per cent of the stock in half a dozen corporations, it will have a majority of the votes of the stockholders when stockholders' meetings are held, and can swing the decisions in whatever way it wishes. 

The most complete kind of combination is the merger. When this occurs, the several separate corporations which have previously been carrying on their own activities cease to exist as separate units and come together in an entirely new corporation. This differs from the holding company, you see, in that the original corporations have disappeared. 

Combinations may sometimes be "horizontal" and sometimes "vertical." 

A horizontal combination is formed from different companies engaged in furnishing a certain part of the materials necessary for a complete product, while the vertical combination is one that attempts to bring into one organization corporations that provide the different items needed all the way through in the production of the commodity. To take the automobile industry which is so handy for illustration purposes, if all the tire-makers were brought together in one combination, you would have a horizontal combination. If the attempt was made to bring together a manufacturer of every little part in an automobile, including the tires, the engine, the spark plugs, the windshield wipers, and everything else you can think of, you would have a vertical combination. 

The attitude of our government in general, and probably of most people in this country, has been somewhat unfriendly toward many of these combinations, though we must remember that such combina-

tions would not necessarily be detrimental to the interests of the consumer. We shall have more to say later (§ 264) about our anti-trust laws. Some countries, such as Germany, have given government support to combinations of producers or importers under the name of cartels. The members of such a combination are given special privileges in regard to the common sale of their products or the goods which they wish to import, and the cartel thus brings to its members the same kind of advantages that have been sought by the makers of trusts and mergers in this country. 

By monopoly we mean such a control of the production or sale of a commodity as will enable the monopolist to fix its price. If no single concern or group of companies has enough control of a certain product to do this, it is plain that there is competition, and when there is competition, there is of course no monopoly. The amount of control necessary to give monopoly power may differ considerably in different cases. 

Monopoly might result from at least five different conditions. 

1. One kind which cannot be prevented is the natural monopoly. Suppose there is a certain kind of mineral spring which supplies water of a chemical content different from any other. Of course the owner of that spring has a monopoly as far as that kind of mineral water is concerned. 

Sometimes there is only one pass through a mountain range which is convenient for the construction of a railroad. The railroad company that gets there first inevitably has a monopoly of railroad traffic in that section of the country. Sometimes a monopoly of the latter character is referred to as a monopoly of situation, but it is a natural monopoly nevertheless. 

2. Another kind of monopoly to which no blame can well be attached is the so-called personal monopoly. If in a certain region there is only one person who is trained to take care of people's teeth, that dentist has a personal monopoly in his neighborhood. Many a country doctor has a similar personal monopoly. 

3. A different type of monopoly is the monopoly of organization. This occurs when several producers get together in order to control the sale and price of the commodity they have to furnish. The formation of a trust or any of the other means of combination we have described might give a monopoly of organization. A monopoly of organization may result also when a labor union obtains control of the supply of workers in either one industry or several. 

4. Another kind of monopoly which is usually conducted on a large scale is a government monopoly. This is an activity carried on entirely

by public officers. In the United States the Post Office is a government monopoly. In practically all countries the coining of money is a government monopoly, and in some countries the sale of widely used articles such as salt or tobacco. Government monopolies usually are the result of the fact that the business thus handled is better suited to government operation than private, or else the government expects to make a profit out of the business. James Sawders

STILL RENDERING SERVICE 

The Erie Canal, first operated more than a hundred years ago, still carries freight, though it is not so important as at one time. These boats are arriving at the Port of Albany. Does the Canal now, or did it ever, have monopoly advantages? 

5. Governments also grant private legal monopolies to such people as inventors and authors in the form of patents, copyrights, or franchises. 

These give to the inventor or composer the sole right to market that particular article for a definite length of time. Patents in this country are good for seventeen years, copyrights for twenty-eight (and they may be renewed for twenty-eight more). Franchises vary in length.

If you look through these examples of possible monopolies you will notice that the monopolist is not necessarily a large-scale producer, though sometimes large-scale production brings about the same kind of benefits that monopoly is intended to secure. There might be such a thing, for instance, as a monopoly in the manufacture of

glass doorknobs, but one could hardly expect it ever to be an economic menace, because if glass doorknobs cost too much we can use other kinds.

The monopolist is, after all, limited by several things. (1) If he tries to get too high a price for his product, he will encourage others to try to become competitors, or else people will simply not buy the highpriced article. (2) Another restraint on the monopolist is the law of diminishing returns. If he tries to get too much of some kinds of business for himself, he will find after a certain point that added business is not sufficiently profitable to encourage him to continue. (3) Besides, there is always the possibility in the case of necessities of life that governments will take action if there is danger that the public at large is going to be harmed by the control of some important commodity, such as flour, sugar, or meat.

It is easy to understand why monopolies in theory are not popular, yet there are times when monopolies may be distinctly helpful to the public at large. There are few cities of any size in which there would be any advantage to the community in having several different streetcar or bus companies furnishing transportation. If they were competing with one another, there would probably be no transfers between one company and another, and if they were forced to give transfers, then competition would be limited to that extent. If, as once was the case in many places, there are two or three telephone companies, you might find that the person whom you wished to call was on a different line. Experience shows that there should be sufficient government restraint to discourage a monopolist from abusing his opportunities for business, but it is also clear that to break up monopolies for no other purpose than to force competition may do more harm than good.

It is through the growth of big business that there has been special opportunity for the kind of person whom we sometimes call a captain of industry. By this term is meant someone of outstanding genius who, either by building up a new industry or by successfully managing an old one, has been able to gain power in the business world and perhaps elsewhere. John D. Rockefeller, Sr., was one of the first of these, and Andrew Carnegie another. Henry Ford would come as near to deserving the title as any living person. 

The value of such men is determined by the net results of their

activities to the country. If they brought cheaper products or greater convenience to the people of the United States, economically we can justify their work. In the early days of big business, however, people made allowances for the use of methods which few would have thought of employing in their own private lives. The wrecking of a competitor's business by any means short of actual destruction of property or life would at one time have been considered entirely permissible. 

Now such means of gaining economic power would be looked upon as both illegal and unethical. 

What examples of any kind of monopoly have come within your observation? Do you think in those cases the presence of monopoly power did any harm? Why or why not? Have there been any notable recent examples of combinations through mergers or otherwise? What advantage was sought? 

Are there any examples of monopoly in your neighborhood? If so, what in general do people think of them? 

223. Some Conditions of Successful Business. In any kind of business, large or small, certain conditions or practices promote success and reduce the chances of failure. Practicing even all of these might not make one's business continually profitable, but certainly the items we are going to mention would help rather than hinder. 

A fundamental essential of all good business is the observance of contracts. Without the keeping of promises in the business world there is no hope for either satisfaction or prosperity. A contract is an agreement between two or more parties, for a definite consideration, to do or not to do some particular thing. Most contracts are put in writing so that there can be no question as to what is demanded under them. An honest business man, however, will keep his word whether he has put it in writing or not. Firms may go so far in dealing with customers as to take the attitude "the customer is always right," whether he really is or not.

Efficiency is another word that in recent years has had frequent mention in business. In one sense, efficiency is nothing more than getting the greatest results from the least amount of labor, time, and expense. In the days when there was only one store in a village or town, good management did not mean so much, because people had no other place to buy. It was not always realized that if a store always had things on hand that people wanted, the store would make more sales than otherwise, or that courtesy on the part of salespeople 

---

would bring customers back who otherwise would not go near the place if they could help it. The recognition of the importance of efficient planning has led to the appearance of a new, and as yet somewhat limited profession-that of efficiency expert. Such a person makes it his job to investigate the way a particular establishment is carried on, and suggest means of getting the work done with less waste of money or labor, and perhaps with greater convenience to customers.

TAKING OUT BIG TIMBER 

Great logs like these, when cut high up in the mountains of western Washington, have to be carried away by rail. Where does efficiency cut a figure in this business? 

This principle of efficient operation is sometimes referred to under the name of scientific management. Once, for instance, would anyone have thought of studying whether there is one type of wheelbarrow which will enable the worker to carry a larger amount of dirt, bricks, or something else with less strain on himself than some other kind? 

Is there a best way to dig a ditch? Is there a best arrangement of a business office? Workers sometimes object to studies of this kind, for they may wonder whether the purpose is to get more work out of

them. In one sense that is often true, but if they can furnish more work with less toil and strain than before, the worker will be better off as well as his employer.

Business men have found ways of promoting their own interests through the avoidance of unnecessary competition. Different firms engaged in a particular line of business as, for example, the production of petroleum or the manufacture of cotton, might form an
