Another form of wasteful competition which has been greatly reduced was the totally unnecessary number of sizes and forms of certain commodities. Plugs for electric fixtures once were of all kinds of shapes and sizes, and if one of them went bad, you might not

be able to duplicate it in any convenient place. There were a great many different sizes and shapes of building brick. It would be hard to tell how many different shapes of shovels were put on the market. 

Some of these differences, of course, are needed to meet different situations, but by standardization of a product, the producer's work has been made easier, and the consumer has been helped to get what he wants when he wants it. 

Another element in successful business is what the business man refers to as good will. You cannot measure it in dollars, but it is worth a good many dollars. Do people like a certain store or business so well that they mention it to others when they can? When a business changes hands or some other important adjustment is made, the item of good will is often listed as being transferred from the previous operator of the business to the new one. That generally means that all the information that the previous proprietor had in regard to his customers, their likes and dislikes, their whims and preferences, would be passed on to the new proprietor, along with a recommendation to previous patrons to keep on coming. Good will cannot be sold in packages, but it may mean even more than the quality of the goods themselves.

Why would an honest person keep his word whether he was bound by a written agreement or not? What examples have you seen of improved business methods in any organization that you know about? What has caused you to trade at certain places rather than others? 

224. Getting Goods to the Consumer. - There was a time when very little attention was devoted by business men to consumer convenience. If you wanted something, it was a case of "come and get it." Delivery wagons were first introduced as a form of competition, on the theory that a firm which delivered the goods would probably sell more than one which forced people to walk or drive to the store to get them. Now we still have the two kinds of store, the one that delivers and the cash-and-carry establishment, but the one that does not deliver usually rewards its customers for the inconvenience it causes them by selling its goods at a lower price. Then it is up to the consumer to decide whether he will carry the goods home from a cheaper place or pay a little more and have them delivered.

As facilities for communication and transportation have increased and business has come to be carried on so frequently on a big scale, new agencies have appeared, so that between the original producer of some commodity and the ultimate consumer the person who finally uses it to satisfy his wants- several people may have had some part in the transfer. Such people we call middlemen. 

Some have thought that the middleman has come to be a nuisance, and that his chief function has been to increase the price which the consumer has to pay. Some manufacturers of shoes maintain small retail stores in at least the larger cities of the country, and thus do their own retailing of their product. Others prefer not to go to the trouble of doing that sort of thing themselves. They let some wholesale dealer or jobber buy their product in large quantities and then let him, in turn, dispose of it to retail stores. Certainly there would be no middlemen if they did not render some service, though it is quite possible that we have more than we need. People do not very long pay others for doing nothing. The chain stores which sell goods at a relatively low price have done considerable to help eliminate the middlemen who were unnecessary. 

Three types of retail organizations have become fairly common in recent years, the department store, the chain store, and the mail-order house. The department store is, in one sense, the old country general store multiplied by 100. The difference is now that it has become a big organization, and instead of having dry goods, hardware, and groceries all bought and sold by one person or under his direction, each class of commodities which the store sells is handled through a department. In the cities and big towns there is the greatest opportunity for the development of the department store. 

The chain store, represented by such well-known firms as the Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company, the F. W. Woolworth Company, and similar organizations, is now found in every sizable community al over the country. Even comparatively small villages may have an A. & P. store or a representative of some other nationally known chain. These are able to sell their goods at low prices because they buy them in enormous quantities. They have been accused of paying their employees low wages, though that charge is often unfounded, and probably they have furnished employment to workers who otherwise might have had difficulty in getting any kind of job. The chain store

is under one central management, but each local store has its own person in charge who is immediately responsible for carrying it on, almost as if he were the proprietor of it himself. 

The mail-order house reaches out into the country and carries into the rural districts some of the same opportunities for the purchase of goods that the city person has at the department store. Montgomery, Ward and Company, and Sears, Roebuck and Company have made themselves virtually national figures. In their big catalogues one may find pictured or described almost everything one could order, from a paper of pins to a prefabricated house. One difficulty is that when the article arrives, the purchaser may discover that there were some things about it that he did not think of when he made the order, or that it is easier to get clothes that fit when you can try them on in person than in ordering them by mail. Nevertheless, rural purchasers have found the mail-order house a great convenience. City people, too, do business with such establishments, and many a small storekeeper has complained about the effect on his own business of buying things by mail instead of from the "neighborhood store." 

But we can hardly blame anyone for buying goods at the lowest figure for which he can get them in satisfactory quantity and quality.

Are any of the members of your family engaged in activities that would properly be classified under the head of middlemen? If so, how does it happen that there is a call for such services? Is it your observation that you get as good service in choice and in quality in a small store as in a big department store? If you have ever done business with a mail-order house, how satisfactory did you find it? 

225. Co-operatives in Business Management. Still another kind of business organization that has gained popularity in this country in late years is the co-operative "co-op" for short. Why should business management be carried on solely for the profit of a few individuals, working either singly or through a corporate organization? Why not let all small producers of some commodity organize and arrange to have their products sold by one of their own number or by someone whom they hire to handle such business for them? 

Western orange-growers and apple-growers, wheat-growers in several sections, and milk-producers and potato-growers in the farming states of the Middle West and the Northeast have found such methods 

---

very helpful. These are what we know as producers' co-operatives. 

One feature of recent government policies in this country has been to encourage the formation of such co-operatives among producers of farm goods.

Might not things work the same way for consumers as for producers? Indeed, perhaps they thought of it first. There is a little book called I Can Get It for You Wholesale, which was written as an example of humor. But a consumers' co-operative society can do that thing. Then the society can sell to its own members what they need at a price just enough higher than the wholesale figure to cover the cost of the salaries and other expenses necessary to make the system work. "The Equitable Pioneers of Rochdale" was the name of the first successful consumers' co-operative union. A few poor weavers living in Rochdale, a little town in England, conceived the idea. Each contributed an equal sum of money, and a small store was opened which sold necessities on a cash basis to the members almost at cost. 

Checks showing the amount of each sale were given to purchasers, and after five per cent dividends on the stock had been paid out of the profits and two and one-half per cent had been put aside for an educational fund, the rest was divided among the members in proportion to their purchases. Anyone could buy at the store, but the gains were divided among the members only. 

There were many others after it, such as the English Wholesale Society, which operated all over the world, and the Scottish Wholesale Society. In the Scandinavian countries of Europe - Denmark and especially Sweden — the government has given great encouragement to the organization of co-operative societies, and many believe they offer one of the chief reasons for the general comfortable standard of living which those countries have enjoyed. 

Members of a consumers' co-operative may get the food and clothing and farm machines and other goods they want at reduced prices because the co-operative can buy them in large quantities from the manufacturer or other original producer instead of from a retail dealer. When the profit of the retail dealer or other middleman is taken out of the final cost of the goods, the consumer may find himself considerably better off. If he can reduce his expenses, he is doing as well as if he added to his wages.

Co-operative organizations have not until recently made great headway in the United States. In emphasizing "rugged individualism," we have laid so much stress on private initiative and on everybody's duty to look out for himself that we have failed to see the other side of the picture. Besides, for a long time business co-operation among people living in scattered rural communities or small towns was not easy. Sometimes, too, co-operative associations have been failures. It might have been because of disagreement among

XIX  

People have been producing things and consuming them since the beginning of time, but as long as each family produced what its members needed, and not much else, there was little occasion for exchange of goods. Exchange, you will remember, has been defined as the transfer of the ownership or possession of goods. When people get to the point where one person can produce very much more of a certain commodity than he can use, and other people can produce a great surplus of other articles, it is only common sense for these producers to find ways to exchange their products. These practices, which we refer to today as exchange, have become very important in our economic life. 

Some Questions: 

1. How does exchange take place? 

2. What are the uses of money in the exchange of goods? 

3. On what basis are goods exchanged? 

4. How is it possible to exchange goods without the use of money? 

5. How do banks serve in carrying on the world's business? 

6. How can world-wide trade be operated? 

7. What makes business good or bad? 

226. Markets and Why We Have Them. We used to define a "market" as a meeting place for buyers and sellers, but now a market is no longer limited to a place, and the sellers often do not meet the buyers. You can buy many things by orders sent through the mail or given by telephone. A better definition of market for today might be "a region within which trade in certain commodities takes place.” 

We sometimes use the word "market" rather loosely. We speak of the “cattle market" when we mean everybody who is interested in buying or selling cattle. When we refer to the "Cleveland market" we mean to include everybody who buys or sells in and around Cleveland. When we talk about the "spring market" we mean goods that people are especially anxious to buy at that time of year. 

Markets may also vary considerably in their scope. There may be a local market for certain things for which there is demand only in a limited area. Streetcar checks, for example, would have only a 

609

local market, because they would be useless outside of the district where certain cars run. Theater tickets also have a local market. 

Certain vegetables may be much more in demand within a particular district than anywhere else.

There are also regional markets. A certain section of the country, such as the South, grows almost all the cotton that is raised in the United States. At least from the point of view of the seller, the cotton market is a southern market.

A FAMOUS MARKET 

At the foot of Fulton Street and East River in New York City is the famous Fulton Fish Market, the largest of its kind in the world. You can see that much activity goes on here, though there are some things about it some people would not like. 

A commodity may also have a national market. The flag of the 

United States would have very little sale outside of this country. 

Textbooks on United States history written in this country would have only a very limited market in any other country, but they might be sold almost anywhere in the United States.

As transportation and communication have developed, the reach of a single market has been multiplied many times. In peace times wheat grown in the United States or Russia may be sold anywhere in

the civilized world, because almost all civilized people have use for wheat. Iron, copper, and now rubber are used almost everywhere. 

Even things that have little positive value in themselves, such as diamonds, are much in demand in all parts of the world among those who have money to spend. Such commodities have a world market. 

A market is called competitive if several producers have goods to sell in that market or a considerable number of buyers are interested in these goods. A monopolistic market exists when one seller has all there is available of a certain commodity or only one person or firm will buy it. People sometimes tried to get a "corner" on gold in this country in the days when anybody could get gold who had anything to exchange for it, but now in this country all the gold that could be used for money is in the hands of the government, and the government has a monopoly of it. 

Could there be national or world markets without division of labor? Could there be national or world markets without a considerably advanced stage of civilization? Give illustrations to prove that our modern system of markets could not be carried on without the progress we have made in communication and transportation. 

227. How Exchange Takes Place. Among primitive people, few kinds of goods were produced, and the wants of all people were much alike. But even then there was some exchange of goods. 

The simplest form of exchange is, naturally, the transfer of one thing for another. A farmer may raise hens and take their eggs into town and trade them at a store for coffee or sugar. That is direct exchange of one thing for another, and is known as barter. When 

Indians first met white men, that kind of trade took place. The 

Indian might trade valuable skins or square miles of land for a few knives or a few pieces of bright cloth or perhaps "fire water."

But barter has very evident limitations. If you want a pair of shoes and the only means of getting them is by exchanging something you have already made or going to work for the shoemaker, you may wait a long time before you go far. A manufacturer of steel rails cannot live on those things. He must trade them to somebody else and perhaps make two or three other trades before he can get something to live on in exchange for his steel rails. 

The way out is, of course, to find something which everybody will take in exchange for anything that he has to dispose of. A thing that

everybody is willing to accept in exchange for goods or services we call money. With money you can buy the things you want, because the money you give to someone else he can in turn pass on to others and obtain the things he is anxious to have. 91

228. What Can We Use for Money? - We must remember that money is, after all, a thing or commodity. There is nothing magical about it. You get it because you have something to give for it, and you can get things with it because other people are willing to take it. 

Money really has three uses.

I. In the first place, and most commonly, it is a medium of exchange. 

It is a means by which trade can be carried on without the direct swapping of one thing for another.

2. Money also serves as a measure of value. We take a certain amount of money and give it a name, such as a dollar, a franc, or a pound, and then compare other things with this quantity of money. 

We say a certain thing is worth three of these units, and something else is worth fifty of them or perhaps only half of one. 

Thus we can make a comparison between things that would otherwise be hard to compare. This use of money permits trade to take place which cannot be completed until a later time. A grocer may let me have something that I want sometime during a month, expecting me, at the end of the time, to pay him an amount which we have agreed upon. This use of money is sometimes referred to as a standard for deferred payments. 

3. Money also offers a means of saving. You cannot save a gallon of milk indefinitely, not even with the modern kinds of refrigeration. 

The labor you perform as an employee of someone else cannot be saved up. Yet you are entitled to some compensation for the time and energy you have given. So money comes to the rescue, and with the money that you receive for your services, you can at some later time get something you want in exchange for the labor you gave. In the same way the farmer can dispose of his milk or his apples to someone else in exchange for money, and then either spend the money for things he needs at once or save it for future use. 

Money itself must be made of something that will last a considerable time or else it would be no more useful for savings than milk or apples. 

Besides, anything that is to be generally used as a medium of exchange will need to be something that can stand being passed from hand to hand a good many times. The best combination of qualities for money is found in metals. (Please don't ask just yet how we can have paper money.) The desirable qualities in money include the following: it must stand long usage and wear. 

1. It must be durable 

2. It must be portable — it must be easy to carry around. 

3. It should be homogeneous all parts of it should have the same qualities. That is one thing that is wrong with the use of furs or cattle for money. 

4. It must be divisible you should be able to take certain amounts of money to represent different values. (Cattle wouldn't serve here either.) 

5. It must be recognizable — the thing that we use as money should not be easily confused with something else of less value. 

---

6. It should be stable the value of the thing we use as money should not change greatly within periods of brief or moderate length. 

7. It should have value in itself— it would be hard to get people to take something in exchange for their own labor or goods which did not have any use on its own account. 

8. It should have trustworthy authority-it should be marked by an authority such as a government whose power and credit is recognized widely.

A FARMER'S MARKET 

Farmers in some sections do an extensive business selling directly to anyone who comes along. It is likely, however, that much that this man sells was not produced on his own farm. Why is money necessary to his business? And what qualities of money make a difference to him?

To meet all these requirements, nothing has been found equal to gold and silver, but they are not suitable for small sums, and we have to use nickel or copper instead.

Every country decides on a certain metal for the basis of its money system. Most countries have preferred gold for that purpose. Then it takes a certain amount of that gold and makes that its monetary unit. In peaceful, settled times, anyone who wanted could get gold money in this country and many others by exchanging some other kind of money for it. When a government is not able to permit such

exchanges, we say it is "off the gold standard." The theory still is that the dollar or the pound is the basis of the money system of the United States or Great Britain, but today you can get no gold to represent these units of money. When business conditions are bad, people are likely to get more disturbed about their money than at other times, and sometimes a country's money decreases in value very seriously if there is no likelihood of its being able to pay its debts in money that is really worth anything. 

Why not use iron for money as the ancient Spartans did? How did people pay for things in California about 1850? Why not do that way now? 

Look on the financial pages of your daily paper and see what names are used for the monetary units of different countries and what their value is today as compared with the United States dollar. Look again in a few days and see whether this "exchange value" has varied during that time. What would be meant by a statement that a country "has gone back to the gold standard"? Is the money of our country acceptable in any other country or vice versa ? 

229. Varieties of Money. Even though we have some one metal as the standard for our money system, we use several varieties of money at the same time. Let us see what some of these are. 

1. Standard money, or commodity money, is money made out of the standard metal. If that standard metal is gold, then any gold pieces in use are standard money. Just now in this country our standard money is all in the hands of the government. 

2. Representative money is that which is issued by a government in place of the actual standard money. In the United States we have coined many silver dollars, but they are rather inconvenient to carry in large amounts at least Easterners think so. So we issue paper money. One piece of paper represents one silver dollar, two silver dollars, or five silver dollars, and if we actually want the silver instead of the paper, we can probably get it. When we had gold money in circulation, there were also gold certificates which "represented" the gold in the treasury just as the silver certificates we have now represent the silver. 

3. Credit money is that which is issued by a government in the form of a promise to pay real money. It differs from representative money in that there is not enough silver, gold, or any other metal in the treasury to make it good. If a country's finances are in good shape, however, people will take a government's promise just as readily as to take money itself. On that part of our paper money which is credit money, you will see the words "United States Notes." A common nickname for them is "greenbacks.”

4. Another kind is token money, or subsidiary currency. This is money of small amounts and is issued solely for convenience. The government buys metal to make into this kind of money just as you and I might buy it if we were making something out of silver or copper, and makes as many coins as the public seems to need. All of our United States money below the dollar is of this kind. Token money never has in it quite as much value in metal as the coin is supposed to be worth, so as to discourage people from melting the coins and using the metal for something else. There is not a cent's worth of bronze in a cent, for example, yet since we can exchange token money for some other kind when we want to do so, there is little trouble about its circulation. 99 66 5. Sometimes governments have issued what is known as fiat money. 

The word comes from the Latin fiat, which means let it be done, let it be made, or let it become. Such money does not represent real money, nor does the government promise to give real money for it. It might be stamped ""ten shillings,' or printed "one franc, 99.66 one dollar,' one thousand marks," and issued for circulation from the government's treasury. Honest and well-managed governments never issue fiat money unless their countries are in extreme financial distress. Then people simply have to have something to use as money, even if it is almost valueless in itself. A notable example of this situation is the fix that the German people were in in 1923, when at one time a United States paper dollar would buy even in Germany more than you could get with a million marks in the German paper money of that year.

These explanations of different varieties of money may have suggested some of the reasons why we can have paper money. Sometimes paper money "represents" metal money, and sometimes paper money is credit money, such as our United States notes. The use of paper money makes possible a great saving of the precious metals. 

Paper money is printed in this country in figures as high as $1000 or $10,000 or even $100,000. You probably will never handle very many pieces of paper worth that much, but men who carry through big business deals sometimes have occasion to use them. Although paper money has almost no value in itself and does not wear as well as metal money, it is so convenient to handle that we are likely to use it indefinitely. If you can exchange it for other money when you need to do so, you will often prefer the "folding money" just because of its convenience.

A principle known as Gresham's Law, because an Englishman of that

name was the first to work it out, declares that when different kinds of money are in circulation, that which is really less valuable than the others (if there is a difference among them) tends to be the only kind used, and the more valuable varieties disappear from circulation. If, for instance, there were any fear that our government intended to issue enormous quantities of paper money that had nothing of value back of it, people would hold on to all the metal money that they could get their hands on. Then the only kind that would be left would be the paper money, whose value would then be very much less than it pretended to be. 

Issuing paper money in large quantities with nothing substantial to back it is known as inflation of the currency. It is dangerous business. When business conditions are not good, there are always people foolish enough to think that their government could help out by the simple process of printing a great deal more money. They do not realize that when that kind of thing is done, the money itself becomes less valuable because thinking people do not have confidence that it will ever be made good.¹

Can you imagine any conditions under which a money system could use nothing but paper? If so, what? 

230. Some Facts about Our Country's Money. In colonial days our forefathers used whatever money they could get hold of. Some English coins were in circulation, but since considerable trading was done with other countries, Spanish and French money could also be found here. 

Much more barter was carried on then than now, in proportion to the whole volume of trade, and for that reason less coined money was needed. During the Revolution our government succeeded in getting some real money by borrowing it from people in France and Holland, but they also printed a great deal of paper money which was known as continental currency. As you learned in your study of our history, its value went down so fast that "not worth a continental" became a common slang phrase. 

The Congress under the Articles of Confederation adopted our present decimal system of coinage (1784) with the dollar as the unit of value. 

The first mint was opened at Philadelphia in 1792. Our coined money is made today at the Philadelphia mint, and also at the mint in Denver. 

1 The word "inflation" is also used in other ways, often carelessly sometimes to mean an unnatural amount of lending and borrowing or a marked rise in the prices of goods. 

If you are ever talking with a person who uses the word "inflation," be sure you find out just what he has in mind.

One important question which perplexed our public officials for a long time concerned the relative value of gold and silver. We started out with a bimetallic basis for our coinage. That is, the two metals, gold and silver, were both standard money. At the beginning it was understood that the ratio between gold and silver was 15 to 1. In other words, it would take fifteen times as much silver as gold, by weight, to have a certain value. 

After a little, silver began to go down in value, so that, in 1834 a very important new law fixed the ratio between silver and gold as 16 to 1. Soon afterwards, the gold and silver dollars were required to be "fine"that is, gold or silver and alloy, that is, other metal put in to make the coin harder. That ratio of 16 to 1 has been the legal ratio between gold and silver for coinage purposes ever since. 

During the Civil War the expenses of our government jumped tremendously. To pay some of these expenses, United States notes the green- backs were issued, first in 1862. They were made legal tender for most purposes. That is, if you offered or "tendered" this money in payment of a debt, it had to be accepted. National bank notes, another kind of paper money, were also issued, beginning in 1863. Now Gresham's Law got to work. Since the treasury would not exchange good money for the greenbacks, their value went down. People who had gold money held on to it, with the result that at one time it took about $2.50 in paper to buy as much as could have been bought with $1.00 in gold. Not until the treasury was again ready to give good money for the greenbacks (January 1, 1879) did they come up to par with gold. 

For a long time after the year 1834 few silver dollars were coined, and in 1873 it was decided to drop the silver dollar from the list of coined money. 

About this time, however, vast silver mines were opened in the West, and immediately those who owned these mines demanded that the government should offer to buy silver and coin it into dollars. Some referred to the dropping of the silver dollar from the list of coins as the "crime of '73."

Our Congress yielded to the demand of the silver people enough to pass the Bland-Allison Act of 1878, which required the Secretary of the Treasury to buy and coin into silver dollars every month from $2,000,000 to $4,000,000 worth of silver. Since the country had no need of all these silver dollars, a great many of them were kept in the treasury. Then in 1890 the law was changed so as not to require the coining of the silver dollars, but the Secretary of the Treasury had to buy each month 4,500,000 ounces of silver at whatever the market price of silver was. When the business panic of the 1890's became serious, another noisy demand for the coinage of silver in large quantities arose. William J. 

Bryan, who became the Democratic candidate for President in 1896 and 1900, made this his chief battle cry. He was defeated, however, and in 

---

1900 an act was passed making gold alone the standard of our currency system. Most people believed that the currency question was settled once and for all. Monometallism, not bimetallism, was to be our policy. 

Perhaps at this point we should explain one or two terms much more on people's tongues in those days than they are today. Free coinage was one of these. If any person who has a certain metal that is used for money is privileged to take it to the United States mints and have it coined into money, there is said to be free coinage. We used to be able to do this with gold, but Bryan wanted the privilege of having that done with silver at the ratio of 16 to 1, though silver was not worth more than 30 to 1 at the time.

If this "free silver" program had succeeded, Gresham's Law would have gone into operation again and the country would, in practice, have had nothing but silver instead of gold as the standard of its money. The people who favored that kind of policy figured that, with the free coinage of silver, they could proceed to pay off their debts with money that was actually worth only about half as much as the money which they had borrowed when the debts were incurred. Naturally, the people who had lent the money did not see the beauty of any such arrangement. 

The great business depression of the 1930's upset things so seriously that many people lost their heads over the situation. Congress passed a law authorizing President Franklin Roosevelt to have much more paper money printed, or to arrange for the free coinage of silver. It also gave him the right to devalue the gold dollar that is, to cut down the amount of gold that would be called a dollar. After a time he cut down the amount of gold to be called a dollar from 23.22 grains to 13.71 grains. To put it another way, an ounce of gold had been considered worth about $20.67, but now he provided that an ounce of gold should be considered worth $35.00. All the gold in the country was called in by the government, and now a great part of the gold which we have (fourth-fifths of all the gold in the world that could be used for coinage) is kept in an immense underground vault out in Kentucky. In 1934 Congress also tried to make silver mining more profitable by providing that newly mined silver should be bought by the treasury at considerably more than the market price for silver, and that the Secretary of the Treasury should keep on buying it until one-fourth of the country's paper money was backed by silver instead of gold. This extra silver is hidden around West Point, New York, in about the same way as the gold is kept under guard in Kentucky. 

Many think that the financial policies of the Roosevelt administration were bad blunders, but it is unlikely that the gold dollar will ever be restored to its former figure. Our future policy may be to keep gold bars under the care of our Treasury to serve as a theoretical basis for

our money, and to allow this gold to get into private hands only when it is needed for shipment by bankers or business men in international trade. Gold is still the metal that most countries would like to use as the standard for their currency if conditions can ever get settled again so that they will feel able to do so. 

Since all of our money in circulation except the silver coins (dime, quarter, half dollar, and dollar), the five-cent pieces, and the cents is

1. Silver certificates, which are backed by silver dollars or silver bullion. Practically all bills below $5.00 are silver certificates, and they have been issued in denominations up to $100. 

2. United States notes or "greenbacks" which, as we have seen, are nothing but government promises to pay. They are theoretically supported by a "gold reserve" of $150,000,000. This is less than half the amount of greenbacks in circulation, but since it is very much more

than people would be likely to ask for at any one time, even if they could get it, we feel that the greenbacks are perfectly sound. 

3. Federal reserve notes are issued by federal reserve banks (§ 249) and are based on gold and bonds owned by those banks. They are issued in denominations running all the way from $5.00 to $10,000.

Other kinds of paper money that once were in fairly general circulation were the gold certificates, which represented actual gold in the treasury, and which were issued in denominations from $10 to $10,000; federal reserve bank notes issued by federal reserve banks on a slightly different basis from the federal reserve notes; and national bank notes, which national banks could issue from 1863 onward for about 70 years and which were backed by United States bonds which they owned. 

If a person has any of these kinds of paper and turns them into a bank for deposit, the bank will not reissue them to other persons. 

Be sure you watch for any new laws or other measures on the part of the government that affect our money system. How is paper money made so as to prevent counterfeiting? What features of the making of coins are intended to serve the same purpose? What changes in the form of our coin or paper money have taken place in recent years? Did you ever see any "shinplaster" currency? Why was it issued? 

231. The Meaning of Value and Price. - Here is a practical question: How much money must we give for a certain quantity of wheat or a suit of clothes or any of a thousand other things? Before we can answer that question we must make sure we understand the meaning of such terms as value and price. 

Value is a hard word to define. Sometimes it is said to be "the worth of anything with reference to the satisfying of wants." There are two kinds of value, value in use and value in exchange. The value in use of anything, like a chair, or an automobile, or a button, depends on its immediate service to us. Any of the three articles mentioned may add to our comfort or convenience. Value in exchange means the worth of anything with reference to getting something else with it. A paper dollar might have value in use as a book mark, but not for many other purposes. Its value in exchange, however, may be considerable, for with it one may obtain a variety of things. Many things, on the other hand, have a high value in use but no very great value in exchange, like a snow shovel on some winter days. The

most common function of diamonds, in use, is merely to register sentiment or show off; yet many people would like to have them, and therefore their value in exchange is high. 

Money is a means of estimating value in exchange rather than value in use. The estimate in money that we give to the exchange value of a commodity we call price. The exchange value of goods, and therefore their price, is determined in part by the two very important influences, supply and demand. By supply we mean the total amount of a commodity available for use at a given time. The whole amount of coal under the earth's surface has only a minor influence upon the price of a ton of coal. The price of coal this year will be determined both by the amount that can be mined and the demand of the public for it. Demand, as we have previously pointed out (§ 203), does not mean merely a wish that one might have something, but a desire for a thing plus the willingness and ability to get it. People who heat their homes by gas or electricity or wood fires exert no direct demand whatever for coal.

Both supply and demand are variable. The supply of strawberries varies considerably between December and June, for in June they will grow almost everywhere in this country, in December chiefly in 

Florida, Texas, or California. A girl may see a silly-looking pair of shoes in a store window. "Dad," she says, "buy me those." He would be shot before he would wear anything like them himself, but he yields to her demand. Demand and supply are often interrelated. 

When there is a high demand for a certain thing, those who can produce the commodity are stimulated to do so, and vice versa. People will not deliberately produce more of anything than they hope will be used, for unused products are simply wasted. 

If the supply of a commodity is greater than the immediate demand for it, the exchange value of any one unit of that commodity immediately falls. That is one reason why salt has always been relatively cheap. The total available supply has always been large with reference to the demand. The farmer who ships his milk in cans to a big city may get no more than a few cents a gallon for it, but in the city where the supply is limited and there are so many more people to use milk, the price goes up to fourteen cents a quart or even more. 

If either supply or demand, or both, fluctuate, price accordingly wavers up or down.

Perhaps you have seen signs like this in a store window, "Value $10, price $5." What would you think of such a statement? Give other examples of commodities for which the demand or the supply may fluctuate considerably between one period and another. 

232. What Determines Price? No one cause or influence determines what the price of anything shall be under ordinary economic conditions. During great emergencies, such as a war, a great fire, or other disaster, those who are fortunate enough to possess a supply of needed commodities may be tempted to charge unreasonable prices for them. Some, who are afraid that the supply of something they want is going to run low, will buy more than they need of it, and by this artificial demand will tend to raise its price. Then a government may need to interfere and establish the price of certain commodities, so as to make it impossible for conscienceless persons to take advantage of other people's misfortunes or unselfishness. Some people even believe in government price-fixing as a regular policy. 

But government control of prices would complicate a government's problems tremendously. If prices were all controlled by the government, there would be constant pressure on it by people who want to keep prices high for their products. On the other hand, people who want to buy things cheaply would exert all the political and other influence they could have to keep prices down. So ordinarily it is best to let everyday economic forces settle what the prices of most goods shall be. Government can always step in in emergencies. 

With government price-fixing set aside, three factors largely determine the points at which prices settle. 

First of these is the actual cost of production in land, labor, capital, and management. A grand piano simply cannot be produced for $10. 

A pair of shoes that would stand much wear could not be made for 50 cents. The raw material out of which pianos, shoes, chairs, steel rails, or anything else are made will be a considerable item in the case of manufactured articles. The wages and salaries paid to people who are employed in the business or profession will be another. Rent to the owner of needed land, and interest or dividends to the owner of capital will also come into the picture. One element of cost is that feature of management that we call overhead. That is the necessary expense for supervision and planning, for selling the product to the public, and for other general activities that play a part in the cost of

operating the business. Besides, in addition to the actual cost of production, the producer expects a profit. 

Second, the working of the laws of supply and demand is another potent influence in making prices. Indeed, prices themselves have something to do with supply and demand. If the public will not pay the cost of production of an article, it will not be produced long. 

The demand for a commodity may be elastic or inelastic — elastic if it varies considerably with the price or other attendant condition, 

Ewing Galloway AN IMPORTANT FACTOR IN HANDLING GRAIN 

This is a view of the Pillsbury Flour Mill at Buffalo. Wheat is brought to the elevators by boats on the lakes and carried directly into the mill where it is made into flour. There is a relatively inelastic demand, for instance, for bread. A demand for theatrical performances, professsional sports, and items of that kind is, on the other hand, elastic. People will attend them if they do not cost too much and if the weather and other conditions are favorable.

We often speak of market price as that which a commodity brings today or at any other given time, and normal price as a sort of average over an extended period. Market price may fluctuate above and

below this normal price, at some times widely but at others comparatively little.

Here the price would tend to settle at about 45 cents, at which point nearly 5000 units (yards, pounds, bushels, etc.) would be sold. If the price were down to 10 cents, about 7500 units of the commodity would be purchased in this market, while if it went up to 90, only about 250 would be bought. the demand line (economists generally call it a curve, whether it is a curve or not) goes in the opposite direction, and as price increases, the demand for the commodity goes down. In the diagram these two curves" intersect, and that point of intersection represents the point at which normal price tends to settle. If at any particular time the price is far away from

this normal point, somebody has guessed badly about the amount of the commodity the public is willing to pay for, or some calamity or other abnormal circumstance has entered into the situation. 

Even the prices that monopolists charge for their products are governed by the same principles that govern other prices. What is a monopolist after, except the greatest possible return for his investment or services? If he charges a price so high that few people will buy his product, he will not make nearly the profits that he would if he cut down his price and sold a much greater volume of goods. So monopoly price tends also to settle at the point that will bring in the greatest total returns to the monopolist. That does not mean that the monopolist will sell at as low a figure as he could and still make a profit, but it does mean that he will not charge more than the public in general is able and willing to pay. 

In medieval times the theory was common that there was such a thing as a "just price" which represented the cost of production plus a reasonable profit to the producer, and was the most desirable price for both producer and consumer. That principle still sounds good, but there is always room for difference of opinion as to what constitutes a reasonable profit. Some think it is perfectly reasonable to charge "what the traffic will bear." That is, to fix the price at whatever figure people will pay rather than not have the goods. Consumers naturally do not want to pay any more than is necessary to encourage the producer to stay on the job. 

The third element that enters into the fixing of prices is the amount and quality of money itself, for you remember price is simply the way we express the exchange value of goods in terms of money. There are two ways in which money itself may change in value: the volume of money might be greatly increased, or the government might deliberately change the value of the standard unit of its money. 

Taking the first alternative, suppose that at one time there are 100,000,ooo bushels of wheat within a country, and $1,000,000,000 in money in circulation. Suppose, now, that the amount of wheat and of every other thing that is bought and sold remains the same, but that by some means the amount of money in circulation has increased to $2,000,000,000. Then in accordance with this "quantity theory" of money, it will take twice as much money to correspond to a bushel of wheat or corn or a ton of steel, or whatever other unit we may think of, as it did under the first condition.

Then if it takes two dollars in money to get what one dollar would have got before, the price has doubled. For further support of this quantity theory of money, look at the prices that Germans had to pay with their inflated paper currency in 1923-10,000 marks for a pencil, 50,000,000 marks for a suit of clothes, and the like. 

If official authority changes the unit of a country's money system, somewhat similar results ought to follow. That was the purpose of the devaluation of the gold dollar in the United States in 1933 when President Roosevelt

233. Qualities and Services of Credit. - If we had all the gold in the world that could be used for money, instead of four-fifths of it, it would still be practically impossible to carry on the business of the country with it. We need something else than money to help out. 

That very helpful thing is credit.

By credit we mean the giving or receiving of a promise to pay instead of actual money payment. There must be money to use as a measure of credit, for credit is expressed in terms of whatever the monetary unit of a country is. But if we do not have to have the actual money, thousands of transactions can take place which otherwise would have to be postponed or would never occur. Credit can take many forms, and that form can be used which is most suitable to any particular 

Credit depends upon confidence. If a government's credit is good, we think that it will pay its bills even though it may be rather heavily in debt. Individual credit rests on the same basis. If we believe a person can and will pay back what he borrows of us, we say that his credit is good. We may be willing to lend him money when we would not lend it to a person whose reputation for honesty was poor, or who had no wealth or income that we knew about. 

1 Some have even suggested that we might take some system of index numbers as a means for stabilizing or "managing" our money system. If we found, for instance, that in 1938 prices were going up in comparison with 1937, we might, rather than let them continue to fluctuate, change the amount of gold in the dollar so as to correspond to the movement in the price of goods, and thus help to prevent prices from going very far from what we had decided was a fair normal figure. Others think that such a proposition is more complicated than it is worth, as a remedy for price fluctuations.

Credit renders several important services: 

I. It provides a convenient means of making payments, and makes it unnecessary for business men to carry around with them large sums of money. 

2. It permits economy in the use of the precious metals, because we do not need nearly so much gold, silver, or bronze to use for coins as we should need if every transaction had to be paid for in money. 

3. It encourages large-scale business. It would be simply out of the question to carry on such activities as those of the Standard Oil Company or the United States Steel Corporation, and even the general store in a country village would be embarrassed, if actual money had to be used for every transaction. 

4. It permits business transactions covering a considerable period of time. Because of credit, business men can make contracts for the sale of goods a year or even ten years ahead of the time the contract is made. 

5. Credit promotes saving and investment. Suppose you have saved $100. You can take your savings to a bank, leave them there, and the bank in turn may put your $100 out at interest somewhere. 

Thus that relatively small amount and many thousands of others can be used in a commercial way when otherwise it would be almost impossible to do so.

As we might expect, credit also has some disadvantages. For one thing, it may encourage extravagance. People who do not have to pay for goods at the time they get them may purchase things they really do not need and burden themselves with undesirable debt. 

Credit also may encourage speculation. You may buy something not with the idea of keeping it, but with the idea of disposing of it a little later, before you have to hand over the money for your own purchase.

Even business firms may be encouraged to undertake business expansion to an unwise extent, when they would not take the risk if they had to get cash for the expenses involved in such expansion. When business conditions are not good, people hesitate to expand their business activities, and institutions or individuals that have money to lend are a little more hesitant about lending it except on good security. 

So it is not in hard times but in easy times that credit is likely to be used most recklessly.

Besides, banks and individuals may make unwise loans if they can simply lend credit without actually handing out money (we shall speak more about this later). There can be inflation of credit that is, the making of loans on a very extensive scale as well as inflation of currency. 

Would extensive use of credit be easy in a primitive community? How can it be that in any city during a given year the total volume of business transactions measured in dollars will be many times as great as the amount of money in circulation in that community? Why is it necessary for credit to have some substantial backing? Why not set up a financial system based entirely upon credit and get along completely without money? 

234. The Use of Credit Instruments. The arrangements that are made in written form for giving or receiving credit we refer to as credit instruments. 

1. The simplest of all forms of credit is the charge account. You have an understanding at a store, for example, that allows you to receive goods without paying for them at the time. In return the store understands that you will pay for the goods you have bought whenever they send you a bill. 

Ack 

2. Even more common, perhaps, is the use of the check. To do this you have to have an account at a bank. When you want to pay or give money to someone, you may write an order on the bank, telling it to pay to this person the amount which you put down. The person whom you owe will receive it and then either pass it on to somebody else, or put it in his own bank, and that bank will ask your bank to turn over the amount mentioned in the check. 

Philip D. Gendreau

PROTECTING A CHECK 

One who desired to forge a check or change the amount which it carried would have more difficulty with one that had perforations on it specifying its value. 

3. Somewhat similar to the check is the draft. This is an order signed by a person who instructs someone who owes him to pay money to a third person. In other words, he "draws on " the party who owes him for the amount of money that is to be paid to party No. 3. The person who makes out the draft is known as the drawer, the one who is instructed to pay is the drawee, and the one who is to get the money is the payee.

4. A trade acceptance is somewhat on the principle of a draft. A person who has bought an order of goods receives a statement which is virtually the same as a bill for them, instructing him to pay the amount due at a certain time, and perhaps at a certain place. If the person who has bought the goods is satisfied with the goods, he indorses the bill with the word "accepted" and the date. Then this can be deposited in the bank by the one to whom the amount is due, and at the proper time he will get his money. 

5. Promissory notes are one of the oldest forms of credit instrument.

They are simply a statement that one person "for value received" agrees to pay to another, perhaps at a definite time and place, a certain amount with interest. A note may also be deposited in a bank by the one who is to receive the money and have it "discounted" if he wishes, that is, paid ahead of time with interest deducted from the amount due at the end of the period. 

6. A bill of exchange is a credit instrument most often used in international trade. It is somewhat like a draft on a bank, but is usually made out in three copies. As soon as any one of them is presented for payment, the other two become worthless. Certain banking firms have branches or correspondents in more than one country, and bills of exchange are usually handled through such firms. 

7. A letter of credit is used most often when one is traveling outside of his own country. He deposits a certain amount of money, perhaps $1000, with a banking firm, and then receives from them a letter saying, in effect, that he is entitled to $1000 as he needs it. If in London he needs $200, he may show his letter to the proper firm and receive the money. The fact is entered on the letter of credit, so that when he goes from London to Paris and wishes to get money there, they know that his $1000 is now reduced to $800, and whatever he gets from the banking firm in Paris is also noted on his letter of credit. He may keep on using it until he has exhausted the original $1000. 

8. A traveler's check is another credit instrument used extensively by tourists. The one who buys traveler's checks pays a fee to the bank or other firm that issues them. Traveler's checks are put up in forms representing a certain number of dollars or pounds or some other money unit. 

The person who is to use them signs his name at the top of the check, and when he wants to get cash for one of these checks, he has to sign it again. 

Then the person who is asked to cash it can compare the two signatures and see whether there has been any dishonesty. 

Personal credit is a term used with reference to an individual who borrows money for his own use, or by reason of deposits which he has made in banks or other financial organizations, is in a position to make

use of some credit instrument instead of money. Bank credit is that which is made possible by the services of banks. Sometimes when one wishes to send money to a person in a distant place who does not know him, he may get the cashier of his own bank to make out a draft which will be more readily accepted a thousand miles away than a personal check might be. Commercial credit is that resulting from business transactions which call for the use of charge accounts, promissory notes, and the like. Agricultural credit is sometimes given on the 10

235. Selling Stocks and Bonds. - Though some of us may never have occasion to make use of investment credit by purchasing stocks or bonds, we should all understand what it means. 

A bond, you remember, is a printed document representing an obligation on the part of a government or a corporation to someone who has lent it money by buying the bond. The person who buys the bond, however, does not thereby become entitled to have anything to say about the management of the concern.

Though not all stocks are on the same footing in this respect, certain kinds of stock do give the holder a voice in the direction of the business when annual or special meetings of stockholders are held. If a stockholder cannot attend a meeting himself, he usually has the right to make out a "proxy" and instruct somebody else to vote for him when occasion comes. When differences of opinion arise among stockholders as to certain business policies, even small shareholders may find their vote in demand by those who want to control those policies.

YESDAY A. F. Sozio from Gendreau THE TICKER 

Brokers' offices where an extensive business is done receive steadily, during market hours of the day, reports of sales on the stock exchange. 

Persons who make a living by buying and selling stocks and bonds sometimes call themselves investment counsel, and sometimes they are just plain, ordinary brokers. Some firms deal in both stocks and bonds; others do a bond business only. Some specialize in municipal or other government bonds; others are concerned chiefly with corporation issues.

Stocks and bonds that are expected to have a wide scale and are of substantial character usually seek to be "listed" on the New York stock exchange. The stock exchange is an organization formed for the

purpose of carrying on the buying and selling of stock. At the stock exchange only such business is done as concerns firms whose issues are listed there. 

Stocks and bonds not listed on the stock exchange are sold at what is known as the curb. so called because once deals in such securities were carried on out in the street or on the sidewalk and not under cover. Today, however, New York City has its curb exchange, which 

Keystone View Company THE NEW YORK CURB EXCHANGE 

New York's "curb exchange " used to be carried on outdoors, as the name might suggest. This is a section of the floor of the department where bonds are sold, as it looks while business is active. is a building constructed for the purpose the same as the stock exchange is. It does not follow that because some stock or bond is not listed on the stock exchange that therefore it is not good. Rarely, however, is a stock or bond that is distinctly speculative bought and sold on the stock exchange. Other large cities than New York have similar facilities for buying and selling stock. Each of them may have direct telegraph and perhaps telephone communication with the New York exchange, and when sales are made of any securities, the sale is announced, as well as the amount paid for them.

On two or three pages in the back part of most daily newspapers you will find reports of the leading sales of stock and bonds on the day when the paper is printed or on the previous day. In almost every city there are speculators who make their living by buying and selling securities. They may have some definite object in mind or may do nothing but "play the market"- which really means trying to guess in what direction the prices of various securities are going to go. 

People who are trying to bring about an increase in the price of securities are known as bulls, while those who are trying to "depress" the market are called bears.

Outsiders are sometimes carried away by the excitement of the business and risk a lifetime saving on the fluctuation of a single security. 

Some think that if a drop or rise in the price of some stock were not immediately advertised all over the country, much less disturbance and excitement would be created by the change. The securities of no really important corporation can move extensively up or down without setting in motion waves that affect many others. 

Dishonesty and misrepresentation by some dealers in securities has given some people a wrong impression of the whole business of buying and selling them. To connect a person with Wall Street is enough to damn him in some neighborhoods. Unwise speculation that helped to bring on the stock panic in the fall of 1929 and the depression that followed contributed much to the establishment by Congress of the Securities and Exchange Commission. This is composed of five persons appointed by the President, one of whom is the chairman, who have the right to set up rules under which the sale of securities shall be carried on. Any corporation that wants to issue new stock or bonds must tell the Commission why the money is desired, its own financial condition, and the terms under which the securities are offered. Though some of the Commission's regulations seem to many business men unreasonably strict, there is pretty general agreement that the net result of its work has been good.

236. Banks and What They Do. A bank didn't know as if you is an institution which takes care of money and other valuable property and provides means for the use of money and credit. There 

---

are national banks which are under the direct supervision of agencies of the federal government, and there are state banks which are chartered by a state government to do a banking business much the same as other corporations are chartered. Some such institutions are called trust companies, for in addition to their banking business they have other departments that look after estates and take care of other matters that are put under their care either by individuals or by authority of the courts.

Originally a banker's services for other people consisted chiefly in receiving money which they themselves had no means of keeping safe, and then giving the money back when it was wanted. Then bankers, instead of merely keeping the money, lent it to other people on interest, and thus made a profit. It made no difference to the depositor whether he received back exactly the same pieces of money that he left there or some others that were just as good. Now when banks make loans, instead of handing out money to a borrower, they often enter a credit account on their books and allow the borrower to write checks against it.

According to their function, banks may be classified as commercial banks, savings banks, or investment banks. Commercial banks are those that offer conveniences in regard to the handling of money, notes, checks, drafts, and the other kinds of credit instruments. Savings banks simply receive deposits, pay interest on them, and lend them so as to receive a higher interest return than they have to pay to their depositors. Investment banks supply funds for corporations through the sale of stocks and bonds. Sometimes an investment house will buy an entire issue of bonds by a corporation or will join with other institutions of the kind in doing that, and then sell the bonds to anybody who will buy them. Today banking institutions may not carry on as both commercial banks and investment banks, for fear a depositor's money might be tied up in investments and not available when the depositor needed it.

Since a bank is a corporation, there may be comparatively little difference in management between it and any other kind of corporation. But banks have such an important place in the business life of any community that what they do is no longer a purely private matter, and banks are now somewhat closely regulated by law. The ordinary commercial bank will issue stock, and the stockholders then

become the owners of the bank and elect a board of directors. Then the directors may choose a president, perhaps three or four vice-presidents, and a cashier, and arrange for other needed officers and employees.

The majority of banks are carried on for the profit of their stockholders, just as most corporations are. Some banks, however, especially certain savings banks, are known as mutual banks. Their profits do not go to outside stockholders but are distributed among the depositors the same as interest would be. In such banks the officials are simply salaried people employed to administer the affairs of the bank in the interest of depositors, and are not concerned with making private profit from any other connection they may have with the bank. 

You ought to visit a bank to see how its ordinary everyday work is carried on. Tellers receive money from depositors and pay it back to them when they ask for it. In a safe-deposit department you may rent boxes of various sizes, depending on how much you wish to store there. You may find a savings department, separate from the regular commercial department of the bank. You may find a department through which you can borrow money on a mortgage, or which may look out for property entrusted to its care. You may find a travel bureau where you can buy tickets and make arrangements for all kinds of tours. You may find a clerk in charge of a so-called Christmas 

Savings Club. Another official may look after payments on notes which have been given to the bank by persons who borrowed from it. 

Outside of keeping money safe and handing it out for use in convenient form (if you want dollar bills or nickels, you expect a bank to be able to let you have them), the services of a bank most commonly used are in the discounting of notes and the facilities for checks and drafts. John Smith has given George Brown a note for $1000 payable in three months. Brown doesn't want to wait three months for his money. He therefore may take the note to his bank and ask the bank to let him have cash right now. The bank deducts from $1000 the interest from the time the money is handed over until the note becomes due and gives Brown the difference. Then when the note does become due, it collects from John Smith.

An enormous number of checks are written in a day or a year.

IN A MODERN CITY BANK 

Things are not very lively just now, but you can see the arrangements for doing business with depositors. back when the bills are paid, if they are paid by check. The checks are kept by the bank on which they are drawn until some convenient time, when they are returned to the person who wrote the check in the first place.

If every bank in a large city had to make a direct exchange every day of checks and other transfers with every other bank, it would be a serious nuisance. So every large city has a clearing house which is maintained by co-operative action on the part of all the banks in the community. To this clearing house are sent each day the checks and

other documents which are to be transferred from one bank to another. 

They are so balanced up that a bank which has been called upon to pay out more money in a given day than it is to receive from other banks simply pays the difference to the clearing house, and the clearing house in turn pays to any member bank any surplus which may be coming to it. Small banks in a large city generally are affiliated with some large bank and do their "clearing" through the large bank rather than having a separate account at the clearing house. The total number of dollars represented by the checks which pass through a clearing house in a day or a year is a fairly good index of the condition of business at the time. 

Do the banks in your neighborhood ever pay any interest on checking accounts? If not, why not? Would there be any advantage or disadvantage in having all banks directly managed by the state or the national government? 

How much do your local banks charge for any services they render? 

237. Some Facts about Our Banking History.—Banks in the first place were private institutions carried on for profit like other businesses. If in a small community Henry Lincoln carried on a banking business, you probably went to him if you needed to borrow money. He could help you or refuse you. Bankers could be either benevolent despots or hard-hearted cutthroats, about as they preferred. 

The federal government became interested in the banking business soon after our present Constitution went into effect. Alexander Hamilton, our first Secretary of the Treasury, proposed that the government should create a United States Bank in which it would own part of the stock, and deposit its own receipts. After considerable argument as to whether the scheme was constitutional or not, the first United States Bank was set up in Philadelphia in 1792 with a charter to run for twenty years. When its charter expired, a different political party was in power, and the charter was not immediately renewed. In 1816, however, Congress chartered the second 

United States Bank, which also was to have a charter to run for twenty years. Note the difference between these United States Banks and the national banks of the present day. Though these banks were actually managed by private citizens, the federal government had a direct interest in both and used them as the sole place for depositing its own funds. Today a national bank is simply a private corporation chartered under national law, and all the thousands of national banks are on the same footing. 

When it was proposed to recharter the second United States Bank, Andrew Jackson, who was then President, vetoed a bill for that purpose. 

He thought it had worked against his election to the presidency, and believed

it was a rich man's institution and of no benefit to common people. Shortly afterward a so-called independent treasury system was set up and federal money kept in its care instead of being deposited in any banking institution. 

During the thirty years after Jackson's veto of the bank bill, banking was under no federal control. 

In 1863 the foundations were laid for our present system of national banks. The Union government, in order to sell more bonds to carry on the 

Civil War, sponsored the National Bank Act of 1863. It provided for the chartering of banking corporations which were allowed to issue national bank notes as a form of paper money, with government bonds as backing for them. Besides encouraging the sale of the bonds, it provided a new kind of paper money which was much more acceptable generally than notes issued by banks whose credit was often poor after one got a few miles away from the bank. For the next 70 years national bank notes were a common kind of paper money.

To strengthen weak spots in our banking system, an act was passed late in the year 1913 which set up the Federal Reserve System, which now has the general oversight of the country's banking operations and issues a great deal of the paper money used in the business world. Instead of having one central bank for the whole country, twelve federal reserve banks were set up. The country was divided into twelve districts, with one bank in each district, which is under the direction of a board of nine members. 

At the head of the whole system is now a board officially known as the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. It has seven members appointed by the President, so arranged that their terms, which run for fourteen years, expire two years apart. Every national bank in the country must join the Federal Reserve System or give up its charter as a national bank. Banks chartered under state laws were allowed to join, and a large number of them have done so. In addition to the reserve bank in each district, branches of that bank have been established in the larger cities, so that all the services that are rendered by the System are easily available in any part of the country. 

The reserve bank in any district does little business with individual depositors but deals with the local banks in the same way that the local bank deals with individuals. It is "a bank for banks." It issues paper money, it discounts notes for banks, it arranges transfers of funds from one bank to another, and it handles the government's own funds. 

The Federal Reserve System furnishes a tie-up between the banks of the country and the government which is of great importance. The rediscount feature of its work is important. If a local bank wants to get more money to put into circulation or to add to its own reserve funds, it may turn over to the federal reserve bank in its district notes which it has already

discounted for its patrons and have them rediscounted by the federal reserve bank. By the charge the reserve bank makes for this service of rediscounting notes, it can encourage or discourage the making of loans by means of notes and thus exercise some control over business operations in the regions served by any particular bank. 

Be sure you do not confuse the Federal Reserve System and its twelve banks with the twelve federal land banks. Back in 1916 the government organized the Federal Farm Loan System for the purpose of making it easy Seattle WASH! Portland

238. Making Banking Safe. If banks are to be chartered by the state or national government and allowed to do business with the purpose of making money for themselves, surely it is only fair that those who trust their money to these banks should be safeguarded from dishonesty or bad judgment on the part of bank employees or directors. 

Every national bank is visited at somewhat irregular times, but at least five times a year, by inspectors who go through the books of the bank to the extent that they can in the time at their disposal, and cause a statement of the financial condition of the bank to be published. In this statement you see figures as to the assets and liabilities of the bank, the amount of its capital stock, and other significant facts. If an inspector finds that something crooked has taken place, he can see to it that criminal action is taken against the guilty parties.

SAFE DEPOSIT 

One may rent at most banks a box in which he may keep important papers and securities. 

It can be opened only by the key which the renter himself keeps. The vault itself usually closes and opens only at fixed hours. 

Banks themselves have to guard against dishonesty on the part of people who do business with them. Suppose you have only $500 in your checking account with the First National Bank, but proceed to write $1000 worth of checks. What then? There are laws that provide punishment for those who knowingly write "rubber checks" - meaning checks that come back marked "NSF" (not sufficient funds). Suppose a bank lends money to someone who wishes to buy a house. It may either take a mortgage on the house or allow the

borrower to deposit with it bonds or other valuable paper as collateral. 

Then if the loan should not be paid back when due, the house in one case and the bonds in the other could be sold and the bank get what was coming to it.

Banks also have to watch what they do with their depositors' money. Most people who borrow money from a bank want to keep it for some time, at least 30, 60, or 90 days. Now suppose something happens that causes many depositors to ask for their money back at the same time. Unless the bank has a great deal of its funds "liquid," as they say, it will not be able to return all that the depositors ask, and may have to close its doors. If the impression gets out that a bank is financially embarrassed, depositors who otherwise would not ask for their money are tempted to try to get it, and a "run on the bank" results which perhaps is not at all justified by the real condition of the bank. To prevent such unhealthy events, the deposits in banks belonging to the Federal Reserve System are guaranteed in full up to $5000, and to a smaller percentage beyond that figure. This has been done by organizing the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). Banks belonging to the system are required to pay into the treasury of this corporation a certain small percentage of the amount on deposit in the banks. Then if anything happens to a particular bank so that it cannot pay its depositors from its own funds, this joint fund may be drawn upon and the depositors' money returned to them.

Bankers as a group were not very strongly in favor of the guaranteeing of bank deposits, and when this was undertaken by states it did not work any too well. But now that it is a national proposition, it seems to have been accepted as a permanent feature. There really is no more secure place to put savings than in a bank, if security is the main idea in your mind. Under present laws it is almost impossible for them to be completely lost, and certainly investing them in any enterprise carries at least as many risks as putting the money in the bank. 

At least two facts helped to bring about the closing of banks in the bad years of 1931 to 1933. One of these was too much lending of credit by bank directors to persons who ordinarily would have been able to repay the loans when they were due, but who could not do so when business conditions became so distressing. Another unfortunate element was the hysteria which seized bank depositors who had no

reason to be scared, but who got excited and by the hundreds or thousands wanted to withdraw their money. Many a bank had to close which, in the course of time, when its assets could be disposed of and the money secured, proved to have been in sufficiently sound condition so that there did not need to be any alarm.
