239. Why and What Do Nations Trade? Nations trade for the same reason that individuals do, and the same things are traded between nations as between individual persons or business organizations. Just as one individual can do certain things better than others can do them, so nations which have peculiar natural resources or other special opportunity for producing certain goods can, at least in times of peace, do that work, and others can depend on them to supply their needs. 

No nation, not even our own, is so abundantly supplied by nature with everything people want that it can be perfectly contented without using the products of other nations. What about such things as rubber, coffee, tea, and tin? Oh yes, we can use what the German calls "ersatz," or substitutes, for many of them, and maybe we can make synthetic commodities that will do fairly well. But they are seldom quite as satisfactory. 

Some people have the notion that if we buy something from other nations, we have somehow let go money which otherwise we could have given or paid to our own people. Sometimes that may be true, but if we buy nothing from other countries, we do, to that same extent, reduce their power to buy our own goods, and nobody is better off. 

Trade benefits both parties. Somebody pays $5 for a hat. Perhaps he would prefer not to pay as much as that, but can get nothing to suit him for less. So the hat really means to him more than $5 does, while the dealer prefers the $5 to the hat. In the same way, nations might wish they did not have to buy other nations' products, but if they find themselves more comfortable by doing so they are likely to keep on buying.

Once a commonly held idea in international relations was that a nation should try to sell as much as it could to other countries and buy as little as possible from them. This was a part of the so-called mercantile theory which was advocated in European countries at the time the colonization of North America was going on. Along with it was another mistaken notion that a nation is rich in proportion to the amount of gold and silver it possesses. But you can't eat or wear gold and silver or have much fun just handling these metals. You can make a considerable number of things out of them. But their greatest service comes from getting rid of them. If you cannot trade them for something else, you might almost as well not have them.

If a world war or some other calamity cut off all trade between this country and other countries, what inconvenience would be caused to your own personal customs and ways of life? Is any commodity controlled by one country to such an extent that all the rest of the world would suffer if that country should shut off the supply? 

240. Special Conditions in International Trade. For a while 

Nation X may owe more to all other nations taken collectively than those nations owe to X, but if Nation X cannot pay its debts, nations will soon refuse to sell it anything or lend any money to it. We sometimes refer to a nation which has more owed to it than it owes to others as a creditor nation, while others whose liabilities are greater than their assets, as far as international trade is concerned, are called debtor nations. 

The difference between a country's exports and imports we refer to as the balance of trade. We say a country has a favorable balance if it exports more than it imports, and unfavorable when it is the other way around. But this balance of trade is reckoned only on goods going through customhouses whose value can be estimated in money fairly easily, and on other plainly recognizable transactions. Many other things are connected with international trade. The items which are easily recognized and given money value are called visible items, and the other items not readily measured in money invisible. Let us mention a few of the latter. 

1. If our citizens invest money in the bonds of foreign governments or some other kind of property abroad, it is the same as if we bought goods abroad, for the money or something to represent it goes outside our borders. 

2. When we pay interest to citizens of foreign countries who have invested money here, money values pass to their hands. 

3. When Americans travel abroad — and citizens of the United States are said to be the greatest tourist people in the world in peace times they spend considerable money. This also goes into the "invisible" list. 

4. To a considerable extent we pay foreign shipowners English, Dutch, Norwegians, and Swedes - for carrying goods imported or exported, for normally our merchant marine does not begin to provide enough cargo room for our own exports. This amounts to the same as buying foreign goods. 

5. Money sent by immigrants back to their friends and relatives in their former homes is another invisible item of outgo as far as this country is concerned. 

---

All these items are likely to show a balance against the United States, and since this balance has been against the United States for a good many years, it helps to explain the fact that we could keep on selling more goods to foreign countries than we bought from them, because these invisible balances helped to make up the difference.

ELEMENTS IN INTERNATIONAL TRADE 

A ship is loading rubber and tin for New York at a dock in British Malaya. These are two commodities without which the United States would find it hard to get along. pile up more heavily on our side of the ledger and sometimes on the side of those with whom we trade. 

This all works out in such a way that ordinarily only a small amount of international sales and purchases is paid for in gold or other form of actual money. Germany in particular has been hard put to it in recent years to continue trading with other nations because it would not let any actual metal money go outside the country, and for that reason some countries were not anxious to sell goods to Germany. 

A number of special deals between Germany and other countries were

arranged which amounted almost to the same thing as the old-time barter, except that this time it was a government that was arranging for the exchange of one kind of goods for another. 

Before the World War, when business conditions were reasonably settled, some exchange between countries as between New York and London, for example was made by shipping gold. At any time, however, when the value of a pound or other unit of money in terms of a dollar shifts from day to day, foreign exchange becomes very much unsettled. The rate of exchange between countries varies with the idea that traders have concerning the ability or willingness of a country to pay its debts and keep its money system sound. 

Much international trade is not a direct exchange of goods between one nation and another. It may really be a sort of round-about affair which is sometimes called, for convenience, three-cornered exchange. 

The United States regularly buys more coffee from Brazil than it sells of other things to Brazil. The United States will, therefore, owe money to Brazil. Brazil may import more cotton goods from England than it sells of coffee to England, because England may have other sources of supply for coffee. Then, for the third side of the triangle, England may buy more cotton and other raw materials from the United States than it sells to the United States in the form of finished products. 

So some of the payment which United States citizens make to Brazilian citizens is paid out by them to English citizens for manufactured goods that they get from England, and some of that same money, in turn, comes back to the United States to pay for the cotton and other raw materials English manufacturers have bought from our people. 

There can be half a dozen countries engaged n this round-about exchange as well as just three. International trade, therefore, often seems rather complicated, yet some of its fundamental principles are simple enough. It is by the use of bills of exchange, trade acceptances, letters of credit, and traveler's checks that most of the payments between countries are made rather than by actual coin or gold bars.

241. Barriers Natural and Artificial. Between one country and another various obstacles and embarrassments to trade may arise which do not affect to the same extent trade within a country. 

1. The physical distances to be covered may make some difference. 

Of course it is little more trouble to ship goods from New York to Canada than from New York into Pennsylvania, but sometimes transportation of goods calls for 3000 miles or more of water travel and perhaps rail or other transportation besides. 

2. People in different countries may like different things. It is natural for people who produce goods, especially manufactured articles, to make them to suit the demand of people in their own country. If such goods are to be sold in another country, the maker or merchant must take into account that country's whims and likes or else he will do little or no business. 

3. The money systems of no two countries are exactly alike, and the prevailing language, even in neighboring countries, may be distinctly different. Such differences are a handicap to free and easy exchange of communication, and to that extent interfere with international trade. 

4. Ill feeling between the peoples of different nations, whether inherited or recently developed, may make them unwilling to buy one another's goods. In time of war ordinary trade between nations at war with each other completely stops, and even when peace is restored, it may take time for business relations to be re-established. 

5. Governments impose taxes on imported goods and may lay other restrictions upon them to promote what they think is their own advantage. 

One example is the protective tariff laws which our country and most others have. These we will discuss more at length later on (§ 263). Sometimes nations deliberately impose limits upon the quantity of certain commodities which they will permit to be received from certain nations. This kind of limitation is often referred to as establishing a quota. Any tax at all, even if only to raise revenue, can interfere somewhat with the use of the taxed goods. 

6. Occasionally the attitude of one country toward the government of another interferes with trade. After the World War a good many nations which disliked the principles of the new government which had been set up in Russia refused to recognize that government officially, or to assume any responsibility for protecting trade by their citizens with Soviet Russia.

651

After some years, the temptation to profit by such trade was too strong to resist, and nations which had had scruples against doing business with Russia concluded that they might as well not try to change the Russian government by such means. 

Some of these barriers and restrictions are inevitable. Geographical distance and differences in customs and language cannot be helped as long as human beings remain what they are. But restrictive tariff

Modern trade and business help to make nations dependent upon one another. The airplane reduces distance to its lowest point. laws and the setting up of quotas are not equally inevitable. Man and not nature must accept the blame for deliberately adopted policies that interfere with trade between nations. 

The world has been infested in recent years with certain doctrines which collectively may be called economic nationalism. It may be good judgment for a nation to plan its economic affairs so as to face emergencies intelligently, and to be able to provide for its own needs to a very large extent. But it is not equally good sense virtually to

close our doors against foreign trade, just for the sake of avoiding all dependence on other nations. 

Secretary of State Hull devoted himself earnestly and conscientiously to an opposite policy. He tried, through the making of reciprocity treaties, to encourage trade between our country and other countries.

242. In and Out of Depressions. One who studies the economic history of the United States, and indeed of any other civilized country, is struck by the alternation of good times and bad times, of prosperity and the reverse. Are such things inevitable? 

Let us glance through our own history. Conditions were poor after our war for independence — indeed, poor business conditions had considerable to do with encouraging the making of our present Constitution. In the nineteenth century, 1816-1819, 1837, 1857, 1873-1879, and 1893-1896 were years or periods when business distress was definitely marked. We used to refer to such events most often as panics, but the word "panic" ought to have a distinctive meaning of its own. In a panic there is sharp financial disorder. Good money is hard to get and business in general suddenly becomes disturbed. A depression differs from a panic in that it is drawn out over a longer period and may not be attended by a financial upset. 

On the whole, financial conditions were getting straightened out during the period of 1873 to 1879, for example, and the depression of the 1930's was not of such a character as to interfere seriously with the ability of people to get money to engage in trade if they could find anybody to hire them or buy their products.

In the twentieth century we had a money panic in 1907, a short depression just before the World War, a tremendous increase in business attending the War, another depression in 1921 and 1922, a revival which many think was unsound, and then the great depression which came upon the country in the fall of 1929 and remained with us for years. 

People who have made studies of the rise and fall of business health have found certain fairly definite steps in the course of events. We often characterize this series of steps or stages as the business cycle, going from the depth of one depression to the depth of another, or from the height of one period of prosperity to the height of another. 

To illustrate it, suppose we start with a definite period of prosperity. 

Business is booming, most people who want jobs have them, and because people have money to buy goods, prices are commonly fairly high. Then it appears that some producers have overdone their line, and piled up a stock of goods which they cannot sell. The cessation of activity in their field throws men out of work, and those people cannot buy other goods as they were doing. This drop in purchasing power soon spreads to producers of other commodities. People get alarmed, and for fear of not being able to dispose of what they do produce, restrict their activities. This brings more unemployment and

still further reduces a country's purchasing power. And so things go down until the trough of depression has reached its bottom. 

The time comes, however, when the oversupply of some kinds of goods which may have started the decline has been completely used up, as well as the limited amount that was produced while the depression was on. People must have many things and think they want many others. Then a demand develops to which business people Monthly

Since many people never learn by experience, the same mistakes are made after prosperity returns that were made in previous periods of prosperity, and in the course of time the same conditions which led to a decline begin to come into existence, and once more we are on the

way down. We have been through one cycle and have entered on another.

Can we prevent this sort of thing? We hate to think otherwise. 

If people would only keep their heads when something unusual has happened, things would not need to go to the disagreeable extremes they often do. If, when there has been a decline in general business, James Sawders

THE PAY-OFF 

"This is the day the ghost walks," as we sometimes say. After one has been out of work for a while, pay day is more welcome than ever. people who are able to purchase goods would do so, just as when everything is going well, they would provide a cushion against misfortune which would help considerably in preventing the cycle from reaching any very low point. But if those who could carry on as usual fail to do so, their failure simply adds force to the downward movement already set in motion.

How much can or ought governments to do when periods of depression come on? The administration of Franklin D. Roosevelt answered that question very differently from any that had preceded it. When

the panic of 1837 came on, President Van Buren refused to let the government be drawn into any extensive steps to interfere with the natural course which events were taking. Before long, conditions began to mend, and during most of the 1840's and 1850's there was a period which for those times seemed to be one of general prosperity. 

Historians for a long time commended Van Buren for having had the backbone to pursue a policy which for the time made him unpopular politically. Grover Cleveland met a similar problem with much the same result, and later people praised him for the way he faced a hard situation.

It is too soon to pass final judgment on the wisdom of the exactly opposite policy which Franklin D. Roosevelt pursued. Money was poured out by the billions to construct public works and provide artificially made jobs for the unemployed. The federal government assisted the states in providing "relief" in vast amounts, and the country's debt was more than doubled in six years of peace. Some believe that this policy of government generosity prolonged the depression more than it relieved it, and encouraged people not to try to help themselves out of their difficulties. The best solution of all, of course, would be to find some means of preventing these extremes of good times and bad times and reducing the difference between the top of the waves of prosperity and the bottom of the trough of depression. 

It might help considerably if we could only make every person so well informed as to what is sound and what is unsound in matters of business that as individuals we would avoid the mistakes which have contributed toward mass misfortunes for our people. 

In the early part of the depression of the 1930's it was common for some people to blame the bankers of the country for the prevailing unpleasant conditions. Was that just? Are the poor the only people who suffer in times of depression? If you were President at a time when it seemed probable that a depression period was beginning, what do you think you would do? Is it right to blame the administration in office when a depression comes? 

More foresight on the part of financial and political leaders also would help. When a war threatens or is actually upon us, we will probably exert all our energy to produce the goods necessary for national defense. But since such extreme effort will not be needed indefinitely, wise leaders will plan to have some special peaceful activity ready to take the place of war industry, or in some other way try to ease the change from abnormal to normal conditions.

XX 

The returns from production in the form of goods and services belong, in the first place, to those who do the producing. Since almost everybody can produce more of something than he can use himself, he will want much of his compensation in the form of money. How much of the return belongs to each of the factors or each of the individuals that have taken part in production? This distribution is by no means equal, and most of us would agree that some of it is not fair. It is immensely important for us to understand why this distribution occurs, and to have some reason for our opinions about proposed readjustments. 

Some Questions: 

1. What theories have been offered to explain the distribution of returns? 

2. What influences affect the return that goes to landholders? 

3. How are wages determined and how are they paid? 

4. What is the justification for interest, and what fixes its rate? 

5. To what extent may profits be justified? 

6. What changes have taken place in the relation of employers and employees? 

7. Why have labor difficulties become serious? 

8. What can be done to relieve or prevent unemployment? 

243. Some Ideas about Distribution. — Distribution, you remember, as the word is used here, does not concern the carrying of goods from one place to another. It relates to the dividing of the returns from production among those who have had a part in it. To each of the factors in production there belongs a definite return. The return to land economists call rent, to labor wages, to capital interest, and to management-profits. But the proportion of the returns that goes to the whole group of landholders, for instance, and that which goes to individual owners in the group may not correspond. 

In most industries a much larger total return goes for the wages of labor than for any other one of the factors in production, even when the returns going to any individual laborer may not be notably great. 

660

A word closely connected with distribution is income. Gross income means the total amount received from economic activity as measured in money.

Net income means the income received after the expenses incurred in production have been deducted. Money income refers to the number of dollars or pounds or francs an individual or corporation receives, and real income means the purchasing power of the money income one receives. A salary of $1000 a year, for example, meant much more in real income about 1900 than it does today, because the general standard of prices was considerably lower, and one could get many more things for his thousand dollars then than he can now. 

Each of the factors in production is affected by the law of diminishing returns, or diminishing productivity, as it is sometimes called. 

There is a limit to the returns which may be received from the use of land or labor or capital or management in a particular situation. 

Perhaps you have heard of people who were "land poor" — that is, they owned more land than they could cultivate or otherwise use profitably. Perhaps in a certain factory 500 men can work to advantage, but 600, instead of 500, might get in one another's way. Six machines of a certain kind might be used effectively in that factory, but capital in the form of three additional machines might turn out more than could be conveniently handled. 

To express the same idea a little differently, in a given situation there is a point beyond which the use of any factor of production ceases to be profitable. This so-called marginal point is that which returns to the user just enough to cover the cost of using it. Marginal land returns crops just equal to the expense for labor, capital, and planning involved in using it. The marginal worker contributes to a business just exactly what he gets as wages. Any factor whose use brings in less than that we refer to as sub-marginal. Managers will always try to get more than a marginal return from the land, labor, or capital that they use. When an intelligent manager knows that any one factor has been used up to the point where the margin has been reached, he will stop there, except in very unusual circumstances. 

Two theories for the distribution of returns from production have been offered, the productivity theory and the monopoly theory. By the productivity theory we mean that in the long run each factor tends to receive a return proportioned to the value of the services it

renders. If land, for instance, is more important than any other one factor in a particular industry or occupation, then the lion's share of the distribution will go to land. The monopoly theory says, however, that the returns that can be obtained from the use of any factor in production are determined by the extent to which an individual or group controls the supply of that factor. If a particular kind of skill or talent is needed, for example, those who hold this theory would say that workers who can provide it may get a relatively large return, not because of the value of their services one can render, but because only a few can supply them. 

The productivity theory sounds nicer, for it suggests that every individual and every contributing factor stands on his or its own merits, but the monopoly theory may come nearer the facts. Once a college diploma was a relatively rare thing, and one who had it could expect preference to be shown him in many kinds of jobs for that reason alone. 

Today, when so many more people in proportion have college degrees, the value of such a degree in getting a job has been considerably reduced. 

The force that can be exerted by an individual or group in securing returns from production is known as bargaining power. If the owner of a certain piece of land knows that no other piece of land in the same neighborhood is equally suitable for the location of a new factory, he has a bargaining power far greater than if there were half a dozen pieces of land about equally suitable. It is bargaining power that is chiefly sought by those who join unions. One does not voluntarily pay union dues just for the sake of giving union officers a soft job with a good salary. A union embracing all or a large part of the available workers may have much more to say about the returns its members are to receive in wages than if each one of them went about the matter separately. Any particular bargaining power one might have as an individual by reason of superior skill or some other personal advantage, however, might no longer operate.

Can the possessors of any particular factor in production figure out accurately in advance the potential returns they may receive, or must it be largely guesswork? What cases do you know of in which either land, labor, capital, or management were used at any time beyond the point of marginal productivity? 

244. Influences That Affect Rent. Rent is a word which the economist and the ordinary citizen do not always use in just the same

way. The economist, as you have noticed, says that rent is the return that goes to land for its services in production. The ordinary person probably thinks of rent as what has to be paid to someone else for the use of the owner's property. This latter return is called commercial rent as distinct from economic rent. If a real estate agent tells you he has a house to rent for $60 a month, he means that that is what the occupants of the house are to pay the owner. But the owner really wants to get pay not merely for the use of the land on

LOCATION AND RENT 

This is the Boulevard in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. What instances do you see here of location affecting rent, either for business purposes or for residences? which the building is situated, but for whatever capital investment he has made either in putting up the building or buying it from a previous owner, and for the cost of keeping it in condition and paying taxes on it.

Two influences very definitely affect the amount of rent, especially economic rent. These two conditions are location and productivity. 

Suppose you have a job in Cleveland. Would you care to live in 

Buffalo while holding it? If you could find a decent, convenient house in Cleveland, you would probably not be willing to pay a cent for a residence in Buffalo at the time. Market gardeners who live

near a large city and sell their product there have a "rent" coming to them that others do not whose products have to be transported several hundred miles to get to the city market. A piece of land useful in itself that is relatively easy of access will receive more rent than one that is hard to get to, whether we are thinking of economic rent or commercial rent.

The other element that chiefly contributes to rent is productivity. 

In the case of the farmer, that means fertility of soil more than anything else. Productivity may show itself in other ways, too, as in mining. Some veins of coal are, in their natural condition, worth much more than other veins. Some pieces of land which a farmer would not look at twice might be admirable as a place to set up a big building. 

There is such a thing as marginal or even sub-marginal land. It is marginal when its location or productivity adds nothing to the values obtained by its use outside of those considerations. It is sub-marginal when it does not even return as much as it costs in labor and capital to get any returns at all. Some land has actually been cultivated which in some years did not return even as much as the cost of seed used in planting the crop.

The rental worth of land might change as a result of an alteration of the original conditions. Here is a piece of city land not often visited except by those who live there. The decision is then made to lay a new main highway through that part of the city from the center of town to the country outside. What happens to the rental value of land there? More travel in that region, more opportunity for storekeepers to make sales, perhaps good sites for factories in fact a greater demand for the use of land for many purposes. For this reason intelligent public officials often keep plans under cover for the location of new public works, before the owners of land in that vicinity realize what is going to happen and put up their prices to correspond to new added rental value of their land because of its location. 

Is there any difference in the importance of economic rent as between a rural neighborhood and an urban neighborhood? Why is land in the business part of a city considered worth so very much more than land in a residential suburb or slum district? Suppose a merchant tells his customers that he has to charge high prices because his rent is high. Is that true? 

245. Problems of Landholding and Landlords. Holding land for speculative purposes has often caused unpleasant or embarrassing

situations. Somebody might either inherit or acquire in some other way a considerable piece of land, and then, without doing anything at all except paying relatively low taxes on it, find a few years later that he could sell the property for much more than it cost him. Such an increase in value not due to the activities of the holder of the land is often referred to as the unearned increment. Of course some land speculators have lost money by guessing wrong as to the possible development of certain sections, but some have made good profits. 

One of the things that years ago used to provoke the Irish people was the fact that some English landlords never came near their Irish property "absentee landlords" they were called but kept on demanding rents for the use of this property, and sometimes refused to make any allowance to the occupants of it when they made improvements on it at their own expense. Mexico has its troubles with situations growing out of the policy of landowners who kept the peons in a distressful state of serfdom. When, as the Mexican government has done in some cases, it took these lands away from their owners without giving them any compensation, it has seemed unjust. Two wrongs do not make a right, but if we know the facts about an earlier wrong it is easier to understand why the second one occurs. 

One set of people who have thought seriously about land ownership are the single taxers. Their doctrine was first made popular by Henry 

George, who in 1882 came out with a book entitled Progress and Poverty. In this he argued that land is a gift of nature and therefore rightly belongs to all the people and not to any individuals. If individuals are allowed to take pieces of land for their own use and convenience, they should pay for that use by giving over to the state the entire economic rent for that land. This, they believe, is fairer than taxing houses or other improvements and thus "punishing" people for making the improvements. Believers in this theory also maintain that revenue derived in that way would be sufficient to cover all the ordinary needs of government, and that no other tax would be needed. 

That is why the doctrine that only land values should be taxed is known as the single tax. 

The single taxer says that this isn't a tax after all, but is simply the collection by the state of the amount which the state, as the real owner of the land, has let a private individual add to the returns which his own labor earned. Some also believe that land which has been allowed to pass

under private control should be brought back to the government either by confiscation or by payment for any added values that have been put into the land by reason of the work of those who have held it. Such a policy is often referred to as land nationalization. 

Critics of such theories, even if they grant that the single taxers have an argument, maintain that it is not just to try to put upon landholders the entire burden of the cost of government. A new house or factory adds to the potential responsibility of the government of the community for fire and police protection. Why shouldn't the owner of that land with its house or factory help to meet this added cost? Besides, it is asked, how can you tell how much of the present value of a particular piece of land may be due to its original natural situation, and how much is the result of improvements made, perhaps over many years?

Single taxers deserve credit for bringing to the notice of the public the evils attending land speculation. Be sure you understand that they do not want land to be taxed on the basis of area. Land values and not land area, they insist, should be taken as the basis for what the state shall take as economic rent. In some places a compromise has been arranged between the single taxer and those who believe all real estate should be taxed, by putting a higher rate of tax upon the land value of a certain property than on the value of improvements made on the land by the owner. 

What examples, if any, can you give in your own neighborhood of “unearned increment" resulting from causes to which the holder of the land did not contribute? Do real estate agents, planners of new residential sections, and people of that character make any actual contribution to the social wellbeing of the neighborhood or community? If so, what? What might happen in your community if the single tax theory were carried out in full? 

246. Wages and How They Are Paid. We have defined wages as the return that goes to labor for its part in production. In everyday speech any payment that is made by the day, hour, or piece we are likely to call "wages," but anything paid on the basis of longer periods "salary," such as the amounts paid to ministers, teachers, or salespeople in stores. They are still wages, though, because they are a return for labor. 

Wages are not necessarily paid in money, though more often than not they are. A person working on a farm might receive house rent as a part of his compensation. A chauffeur employed by a wealthy man may live in the second floor of the garage. The sharecroppers whose doleful situation has been so much publicized in recent years get their pay out of a part of the crop that is produced.

Payments for wages in money may also take different forms. One may be paid so much per hour, week, month, or year, or in proportion to the amount of work that he does. If he manufactures some article, he may get an agreed amount for each unit he turns out. A salesman may be paid a percentage of the price of the goods he sells. 

Sometimes salespeople in a store are paid a small regular salary, plus a commission on what they sell. Sometimes an employer whose business is sufficiently profitable pays a bonus at the end of a year in addition to the regular wages or salary of employees. 

Remember that the number of dollars one receives does not necessarily indicate the value of his job from the financial standpoint. If he lives in a city where living costs are high, he may have to spend much more for such necessary items as rent and food than in some other city. Such things tend to balance themselves, however, for usually in a community or section where living costs are low, wages are also lower than in neighborhoods where it costs more to live. 

Employers pay wages because it is more profitable to pay them than not to pay them. It is true that employers have been known to keep workers when they no longer needed them, but that is not a regular procedure, nor likely to occur on an extensive scale. Usually when an employer takes on a new worker he thinks that by reason of the added service he thus obtains, he will add to his own returns more than he pays the new employee. It has been said that "the employer pays wages to labor for the same reason for which he pays interest on borrowed capital." An employee getting as low as $1000 a year would, as you can see by a little arithmetic, be costing the employer the interest on $16,6663 at 6 per cent. Sometimes, therefore, an employer may make a choice between hiring more workers and using his savings or borrowing money to buy a machine to do their work. 

Agitators sometimes misunderstand or misrepresent such facts as these. If wages are increased without any added service being rendered, the employer's profits will be cut. Then he might feel no longer any inducement to go on with his business, or might have to raise the price of his product to such an extent as to interfere with its sale. Then, in turn, profits would go down and in time men would be laid off or the business even close up. 

Why are wages by the piece more popular with some employers than time wages? Why does the average worker prefer to be paid on the time basis?

Should the work of housemaids and persons similarly employed be considered unattractive because part of their compensation comes in the form of board and room? What examples can you give of occasions when increases in wages were granted and the price of the product of the industry which was thereby affected went up? 

247. How Are Wages Determined? - No employer is entirely free to fix wages exactly at his pleasure. It is often difficult to tell in a big business how much the hiring or firing of one worker or even a

Neither can one be sure whether paying high wages and charging a high price for one's product would work out better in the long run than a lower standard of wages and prices and a larger volume of sales. 

Three theories have some bearing on this matter of the fixing of wages. The old theory, the so-called "iron law of wages," was that wages tend to be fixed at the point which would just keep the bulk of the workers from starving. That was sometimes called the subsistence theory of wages. It is a hard-hearted proposition, and few employers would ever deliberately fix their wage scales on any such 21 de 11

basis. Whether in practice, without any deliberate plan, things worked out that way in the past is another matter. 

Another theory is that the point at which wages are fixed depends on the extent of bargaining power possessed by either employer or laborer. Suppose the employer can say, "It is this job or nothing for you." Suppose, on the other hand, workmen are able to say, "You hire us or else you can't operate your business." You can figure what might happen in either case. Put this way, it sounds rather harsh, but one or the other of these situations may be the actual truth more often than most of us would wish. 

A third theory, the most generous of all, is to the effect that within certain limits paying increased wages results in better satisfied workers, and probably a greater volume and better quality of production, and therefore is good business for both the employer and the laborer. 

Besides, it is urged that the increased salary of the workers raises their own power to buy goods, and business in general is stimulated. 

There is doubtless considerable in these arguments, but we must also admit that there is a limit to what any employer can pay as wages without "going into the red."

In 1938 the railroads of the country, many of which were in bad shape financially, asked the unions to which their employees belonged to accept a 15 per cent cut. At the same time, they were asking the Interstate Commerce Commission to permit them to raise the fares that they might charge. 

The leaders of the unions refused to listen to any suggestion that they should accept a cut, and one of those leaders even went so far as to say that it was none of their business where the railroads were to get the money to pay the higher standard of wages. Give your opinion of the attitude of the parties concerned in this situation. What would the general public be likely to feel? 

We must not forget that labor has certain distinctive qualities which do not pertain to all kinds of goods. These must be taken into account in the fixing of wages along with other considerations. (1) Labor is inseparable from the laborer. A steel worker cannot contribute his services to a mill by remote control. He must be there. (2) Labor is mobile. The laborer and his services can be moved from one place to another. That is not true with a factory or a mine. (3) In two senses, labor is perishable. If you do not work today, the work you might have done never will be done. You cannot store it up. Labor is also perishable in that it is furnished by human beings who may get sick or die, and then their labor is interrupted or ended.

Like many other things wages are affected by the operation of the principles of supply and demand. When there are plenty of workers for few jobs, it is not necessary, other things being equal, to pay as high wages as when there are plenty of jobs but few workers available. 

Moreover, much labor is somewhat specialized in character, and unless a worker can furnish the particular kind of labor needed for a certain job, he will not be employed. A steel company might find that it had more office help than it needed, but only rarely could it transfer many of them out into the mills, even if more workers could be used there. The employment of laborers is also affected by the law of diminishing returns. After a certain point is reached, the employment of more laborers in the same establishment will not bring added profits in the same proportion as before. Then the decision has to be made whether additional employees will bring in enough to justify taking them on, or whether it is time to stop hiring more men. 

The possession of monopoly power may have an effect here. If a certain key part of the process of production in some industry is performed by members of a particular union and they refuse to work, they may tie up the whole industry so that nobody can earn anything. 

The manager of the world's biggest circus in the summer of 1938 discovered that the show was going to lose money right along unless the employees would accept a wage cut. The skilled performers were willing to take it rather than have the show fold up, but the "roustabouts," whose service was the providing of muscular labor and not much else, refused. Their work, though unskilled, was necessary, and the show had to close.

If everybody could do everything equally well, would there be any difference in wages? Show how the three distinctive qualities of labor affect both the employer and the employee in bargaining about wages. How has the question of seniority entered into some labor disputes? Do you think that is a fair principle? On what basis do some moving picture performers get ridiculously large salaries? 

248. Interest and Why It Is Paid. Textbooks used to define interest in this way, "Money paid for the use of money." It would be more accurate to say, "Interest is money or the equivalent of money paid for the use of money or something that money can buy." 

Still better, "Interest is the return that goes to capital for its use in production."

These pictographs tell important facts about three very important industries in the United States - coal mining, airplanes, and electric light and power. Study them so that you can get their meaning and explain why they changed as they did. 671

Why will one pay interest for the use of another's savings? Because the added amount that he can then use in his own business enables him to get a return that he otherwise could not get. He expects that by using this added capital he will obtain a return greater than what he has to pay out as interest. The Lackawanna Railroad once decided to borrow $12,000,000 and use it for the purpose of straightening out curves and improving grades on a part of their road. They figured that even though they had to pay up to 6 per cent interest on this $12,000,000, they would save enough in coal, wear and tear on their cars, and other expenditures to more than make up the interest they would pay.

The holder of capital wants to receive interest for its use, on the ground that he is denying himself the pleasure of spending it and takes some risk of losing it besides. People used to call taking interest "usury" - that is, something paid for the use of something. Today this word has an unpleasant significance and now means an unreasonable or illegal rate of interest. Lending money to relieve or assist another may benefit both the lender and the borrower; so why is there anything wrong about it? Money lenders have sometimes made themselves unpopular when they "put the screws" on those who had borrowed and either could not or would not repay what they agreed. 

Perhaps it is human nature to sympathize with the poor man rather than the rich man when the interests of the two conflict. But just because one borrows is no proof that he is therefore more honest than the one who lends.

Does capital have value if it is not receiving interest at any given time? 

If it were not possible to receive a return on invested capital, how much inducement for saving would remain? Which is better for a community, to have savings hoarded, or invested so as to bring a return in interest? 

249. What Fixes the Rate of Interest? - The same forces that operate to fix the price of anything apply to the rate of interest, for in one sense interest is the price paid for the use of capital. If capital is abundant at a given time or a given place, it can be secured at a lower interest rate than when the opposite is true. During periods of depression, interest rates go down, because there is less opportunity for capital to be invested, and those who have capital to invest are willing to accept a lower return on a safe investment rather than not to get any return at all. Risk affects the rate of interest in the

other direction. In a new or speculative business there is more danger that the capital will never come back to the investor than in the case of an industry which has an established position. So speculative industry shows higher interest rates than those industries in which the element of speculation is comparatively slight. These two reasons combined explain why interest rates in the eastern part of this country have regularly been lower than those in the western part- more savings accumulated in the more thickly settled East, coupled with risk involved in investments in the distant West.

Interest rates affect the volume of capital investments just the same as wage rates affect the cost of production of goods. If interest rates are high, the managers of businesses will not borrow extensively unless they are pretty sure of the success of their business. 

High rates of interest often have to be paid by people who do business on a small scale. People are more willing to lend to a wellestablished business or to one that is widely known than to smaller or less known ones. "Loan sharks" charge the high rates that they often do for two reasons. They think they can get them because people who have been forced to go to them for loans are often the kind who would hate to have publicity given to the fact of their borrowing. 

Besides, the lenders are not always sure of getting their money back, and want to make as much as possible on good risks in order to balance up for poor ones.

In recent years there has been a marked tendency for interest rates to go down and wage rates to go up. Some believe that this trend is healthy, because it may lead toward a more even distribution of wealth. 

They think that if one cannot get big returns by lending capital for investment, there will be less inducement to make savings, and that since more money will be spent, more will be available to pay in the form of wages. But others maintain that any tendency which has the effect of lowering the inducement for saving will, in the long run, have a harmful effect upon a country. 

If any member of your family has borrowed money, what interest did he have to pay? Why did he borrow? Why are interest rates higher in Nevada than in New York? Savings banks all over the country have reduced the rates they pay to depositors, some of them as much as from 4 per cent to less than 2 per cent. Why have they done this? Did you happen to be affected in any way?

250. Can Profits Be Justified? - Maybe your answer will depend on whether you are making any. As you know, some assert that the "profit motive" has no place in a respectable economic system, even though all economics, from the beginning of time, has been built on the idea that one had a right to benefit if he rendered service to another. 

Profits differ from wages largely in that getting them involves special

Different means of transportation are evident here. There was a time when railroads crossed streets on the level of the street. Now such grade crossings are rapidly disappearing. Each kind of transportation renders its particular service. 

Perhaps they deserve a profit for doing so. judgment and risk. If labor does a certain definite thing that it agrees to, it has no further responsibility. It is management that has the responsibility for bringing land and capital together, and of determining how many laborers are needed on a given job. 

There would be no management, and therefore no profits, if the holders of land, labor, and capital just came haphazard into the picture and did as they pleased. Economic profit represents the "wages of management" the returns that go to managers for what they have

contributed to make production successful. In popular language we often refer to profit as the difference between one's outlay and his income in a particular business or enterprise. But if this entrepreneur has invested some of his own savings in the business, if he himself has worked in the actual handling of affairs day by day, or if he owns land which has also been used in the business, he may really have been getting interest, wages, and rent in what he lumped together and called his profits. Gross profits are the excess of receipts over expendiwhat we have just described. Pure profits, on the other hand, are that part of the profits that are actually due to superior management, beyond the returns on capital, labor, or land. tures 

But are profits justifiable? What would happen if we took away the incentive to profits? Somebody must manage, for no industry will run itself. People are not going to assume the risk of failure unless there is a chance of their getting a return. If private individuals are not allowed to engage in a necessary business for profit, public officials will have to take over the work and be paid a salary for doing it. 

Our post office service could be carried on by private enterprise; but since it is a public business we have to have a Postmaster 

General, four Assistant Postmasters General, and a whole flock of postmasters and other public agents who expect salaries for running the system.

Profits may sometimes be sought through competition or through the exercise of monopoly power. In order to get business, each competitor would strive to do more for the public than the others did, and better service at lower costs would be the result so many of 

But in some us used to think, and still do to a considerable extent. kinds of competition the dishonest competitor has got the better of the honest one, and sometimes the big organization with its wealth of equipment and variety of resources has been altogether too much for a little competitor to face.

The seeker after profits through monopoly, as we have seen, does not necessarily demand unreasonable prices for his products. He determines, either by good guesswork or by actual experience, what price will bring him the greatest total returns and fixes his price at that point. This point may or may not be below the figure it would reach if there were competition, depending on the circumstances of a specific case. Theoretically, we like the idea of profits obtained.

through honest competition, but in practice we find that we may have to set up rules to regulate competition as well as monopoly. 

Does the entrepreneur's taking profits necessarily raise the price of a product to the consumer? Would inventors and discoverers have sufficient stimulus for their undertakings if profits were abolished? Are all profits really paid by the consumer of the goods that are produced? 

251. Should Profits Be Regulated? The first question might be,

Can profits be regulated? You can tell, after a fashion, how fundamental is land to the success of an enterprise. You can tell with some definiteness how much the labor of one out of a thousand workers is worth if they are all doing about the same kind of work. You can even fix by law the rate of interest which a capitalist or a banker may charge. But can you be equally definite with reference to the value of the manager's services? 

A good many elements enter into the making of profits. One is the personal ability of the manager. Under the same conditions two people might get quite different results from the same business. 

Another influence affecting profits is the general state of the business world. When business generally is active, even a very ordinary manager might be able to show profits, whereas at other times only the exceptionally talented person could do so. A third influence is luck or accident. The best manager among Illinois farmers would be up against it in a season in which there was almost no rain for a month or one in which it rained every day. A wise plant manager would carry insurance to cover damage to his factory and equipment from fire; but even so, what is going to happen to profits while repairs are being made and normal conditions re-established after a fire? 

Numerous influences work automatically to restrict profits. We have already seen that even the monopolist will find his profits restricted by the amount of his product that the public will take. When there is competition, that of itself will tend to keep profits within reason. 

One competitor thinks he will sell more goods by cutting his price. 

If that works, others will have to do so or else lose their business to the man who was keen enough to realize the limit to stupid selfishness in business management.

Profiteering does take place, of course, if by that we mean unreasonable profits gained by taking advantage of exceptional conditions to the disadvantage of the consumer. A great flood in Pittsburgh in

1936 shut off for two or three days all electric light. You can imagine what happened to the price of candles in a few neighborhoods. It is not surprising that some people took advantage of other people's misfortune, but opinions might differ as to whether you would call that a legitimate way of making profits. Profiteering of that kind is something that you can hardly hope to prevent over a brief period, but if you find that an electric light company is making 15 or 20 per cent on its investment because it has a monopoly of that business, a state can lay down regulations that will require it to keep its profits within limits that seem fair to the consumers as well as to the producers. 

To pass a law, however, that no entrepreneur should ever make more than 10 per cent profit or any other definite figure I would be dangerous. Conditions might fluctuate in the course of a year so that at some season there might be an exceptionally favorable situation for a brief period. To cut down profits arbitrarily might involve sudden adjustments in business activities that would create a great deal of confusion. Most goods will find no consumers very long if they are not worth what the producer asks, and the attempt to gain unreasonable profits will end right then and there. If the excess charge is the result of monopoly control of some essential commodity, public regulation can easily get after it. 

If you thought of starting a business not previously carried on in your community, such as the opening of a bookstore, what items would you try to take into account before you went into the proposition? What adjustments might you have to make from one year to the next? Why would it be difficult for any law to set a limit to the profits you could legally make from such a business? What would you think of the practice in vogue during the World War on government contracts, of allowing a contractor 10 per cent profit on his work? 

252. The Relations of Employers and Employees. Why do we have employers and employees, anyway? The answer is simply that some people are willing to accept the risks and the problems of carrying on a business, while others either do not wish to take such responsibilities or do not have the ability to do so. Some employees doubtless could become good executives, but find it easier to carry out instructions than to give them.

Two conditions have helped to produce an unfortunate feeling of hostility between employers and employees. The employer of a large 

---

number of workers cannot know them all personally, and most of them mean only names or numbers to him. He therefore may forget that they are human beings like himself and think of them about as he would a machine or tool which would be looked after as long as it could render useful service, but would be discarded when it showed signs of wear.

On the other side, the employee may fail to appreciate the worries of an employer or to realize the many and varied problems he must have on his mind. Not only the fixing of wages for employees, but also where to buy raw materials at the best figure and how to get the public to buy the goods that are produced, are items that the employer may have to think about at one and the same time. It may be the fault of nobody in particular that many who are connected with a business or industry cannot understand all that is involved in running the business, but it is too bad, nevertheless, that such ignorance may menace the welfare of all concerned.

Hardly ever is there a labor dispute which does not cause both sides to suffer.

Much of the unpleasantness in the labor world today is the result of the large-scale business or the factory type of organization which has brought so many benefits in other ways. Under the domestic system which prevailed during the Middle Ages, there was a close contact among workers which contributed toward good will and understanding. 

Today a man can work in a factory who terribly dislikes the owner personally, though the dislike may result from the very lack of personal acquaintance.

Besides, the head of the business may receive much bigger pay than any one worker. Suppose the head of a big industry gets $50,000 a year salary some do that and has a thousand employees. If they know what he gets while they may average $2000, they may think

that he is dreadfully overpaid. Yet if you distributed the boss's $50,000 among his employees, it would mean a little less than $1.00 a week apiece on the average for each one. That would help some, of course, but not enough to justify hating the man who founded the business and has always had to assume the manifold responsibilities of operating it. 

Would you rather be an employer or an employee if the compensation were the same? If there were not extra compensation to be obtained by accepting the responsibilities of management, would people of ability be willing to accept them? 

253. The Rise of Labor Organizations. The legal theory used to be that every individual had the right of freedom of contract. He was free to bind himself to work for a certain person under given conditions or to refuse to do so. If he did not like a particular job, he was free to quit it and take another. His wages, so it was believed, were determined by his ability to perform desired service in competition with others who could furnish similar service. 

As a matter of fact these "freedoms" seldom exist in full measure. 

A worker is not at liberty to transfer himself from one place to another whenever he wishes. Family ties or other restraints may make it hard for him to move. Besides, any one worker, unless he has exceptional talent, cannot bring much pressure to bear upon anybody else to get a situation he likes. The right of freedom of contract is another thing often more desirable in theory than in practice, for sometimes it has permitted unscrupulous employers to secure workers at far lower wages than they could afford to pay, or to work them under conditions dangerous to health or morals.

Such facts as these are back of the establishment and growth of labor organizations. When they first appeared in England, the courts treated combinations of workers as conspiracies, and it took a special law of Parliament to legalize labor unions. In this country unions first developed in the large cities, and were limited to one city and to a particular trade. After improved transportation made it easier for workers to move from one place to another, and after big business developed in industry, it became feasible for unions to be organized and to operate on a wide scale.

Not till after the Civil War did conditions become favorable for the growth of large-scale unions. One of the first labor organizations

to open its membership to workers in a great variety of activities was the Knights of Labor. This organization was harmed by getting mixed up in politics, and after rising to a membership of around 700,000 it lost strength and finally disappeared. The common types of union today organize their members on the basis of particular trades or some single industry.

Organizations of workers may, in the strict sense, be called trade unions or craft unions when they each include persons connected with some single trade or group of closely related trades. There may be a carpenters' union, a union of railroad conductors, a union of actors, and the like. 

Such a union is sometimes called a horizontal union because it may include workers who are employed in several different business organizations, and this organization then cuts across the personnel of many different business concerns. Another kind of union is the industrial union, which is sometimes called the vertical union. This includes persons employed in any capacity in connection with a certain industry, such as the United Mine 

Workers or the United Automobile Workers of America.

Harold M. Lambert SKILLED TRADESMAN 

It takes more than mere muscle work to do his job well. Do you think union membership will help him?

Strictly speaking, a labor union is one that includes in its membership workers of any kind. In common speech, however, we use it to mean an organization of workers, regardless of the particular arrangement of that organization, horizontal or vertical. The horizontal organization has its advantages when its members wish to "put the heat" on a considerable number of employers at the same time, or if its members are engaged in key activities without which a whole industry could not be operated. The industrial union has the advantage of being able to apply the full force of all its members against

particular establishments or particular industries. If a majority of the workers in the Chrysler automobile works, for instance, are organized on the industrial union basis, they can, by a majority vote, force all their members to go on strike even if a considerable number of them, and perhaps all who are employed in certain capacities, would prefer not to take such action.

The outstanding representatives of the two typical forms of labor organization today are the American Federation of Labor (the A. F. of L.) and the Congress of Industrial Organizations (the C. I. O.). The progress of the American Federation of Labor was really the result of the ability of Samuel Gompers. It is a combination of over 100 trade unions, each of which is represented in the national organization, which covers Canada as well as the United States. Gompers became its president in 1882 and, except for one year, thereafter held that office for 40 years. The Federation's policy in politics was not to affiliate directly with any political party but to support such candidates as were thought most likely to favor policies desired by the A. F. of L. Democratic candidates enjoyed the favor of the A. F. of L. more often than Republican candidates did, but though 

Gompers frequently made no bones about naming his favorites among candidates, there is no evidence that the whole Federation always followed his leadership.

The rise of the C. I. O. has been almost meteoric. John L. Lewis was the head of the United Mine Workers for a good many years. This organization in turn belonged to the American Federation of Labor. The C. I. O. was called at first the Committee for Industrial Organization. It was formed in 1935 by Lewis, Philip Murray, and a few others and aimed to organize industries vertically rather than horizontally. A particular point of attack was the steel industry, which until that time had escaped being unionized. Bitter rivalry developed not only between the two nation-wide organizations, the A. F. of L. and the C. I. O., but between John L. Lewis and William Green, who had succeeded Samuel Gompers as president of the A. F. of L. The C. I. O. not only broke away from the A. F. of L., but went hot after industries that had never before been organized. Murray succeeded Lewis as its president in 1940. 

Both the American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations usually want workers organized on a nationwide or other large-scale basis without reference to single establishments. Both look with contempt upon the so-called company union, which is made up of workers connected with some single establishment, and which is usually accused of being supported, or at least shown

favors, by the employer in that establishment. The big organizations prefer to act as if the only thing in common between the employer and the worker is the contract for work. They look with suspicion upon any co-operation between the employer and his workers unless it is carried on solely through the union organization. 

The chief object of labor organizations is to make collective bargaining effective. By collective bargaining we mean the conduct of relations between employers and workers through the officers of unions, rather than through individual contact. The unions seek to make possible united action on the part of all or most of their members. This united action may take the form of a strike or some other kind of joint pressure. Some labor organizations undertake to provide facilities for recreation, classes for study, and other means of social improvement for their members. Some unions set aside out of the dues that are paid in by their members a fund from which benefits are paid to members when they are out of work on account of a strike.

This Scotch-born labor leader rose 

C. I. O.

For many years laws passed to protect the owners of private property from the ranks to be president of the against damage were so interpreted as to make it difficult for workers to exert pressure upon employers without doing things that were definitely unlawful. The first definite concession toward the labor point of view in our national laws was seen in the Clayton Anti-Trust Act of 1914, when it was specifically declared that labor should not be considered a commodity. Strikes therefore could not be treated as conspiracies in restraint of trade. The passage of the Adamson Act by Congress in 1916 was another case of yielding to union pressure, when President Wilson himself went before Congress and asked that body to provide for the eight-hour day and make other adjustments

in connection with railroads in order to prevent a nation-wide railroad strike.

In the National Recovery measures of 1933 it was definitely provided that in any codes made under the act to govern industrial relations, workers should have the right to bargain through "representatives of their own choosing." Unionization went on fast after this, though in some cases it was promoted by employers and took the form of company unions to forestall unionization under the nation-wide labor organizations. Then in 1935 came the Wagner Labor Relations Act, which imposed very definite restrictions on what employers might do with reference to the organization of their workers, and set up the National Labor Relations Board to see that the provisions of this law were carried out. Company unions were virtually prohibited, and the Labor Board was given power to order employers to keep on their payrolls persons whom they would have preferred to "fire" because of labor union activities, and to require the holding of elections to determine what basis of representation for collective bargaining the employees of a particular establishment or group of establishments might wish. The United States Supreme Court sustained the act as within the constitutional power of Congress. 

Why might a worker prefer one type of union organization over another? 

Talk over with some employer the story of labor organization as he sees it and find out why he thinks as he does. What are the latest developments in the "war" between the A. F. of L. and the C. I. O.? 

254. Labor Controversies. Quarrels between employers and union members are often not so much the result of opposition to the existence of unions as to the methods used by union leaders, though some employers are still not reconciled to the idea of collective bargaining, especially if they have to deal with union leaders who have no connection with their own establishment. The union answer to such a feeling might be that the union's position is seriously weakened if the job of a union officer who dares to be independent is at the mercy of the employer.

The great majority of employers, however, recognize that collective bargaining is here to stay in the industries where workers are employed in considerable numbers. If union leaders show themselves anxious only to protect the just privileges of their members, an employer may

respect them and even find them useful in keeping irresponsible individuals from making trouble without sufficient grounds. 

One policy of certain unions to which some make serious objection is that of restricted apprenticeship. An apprentice is one who is learning a trade. Sometimes union workers will take on as learners only a limited number in order to keep the supply of workers in that trade down. Thus they may gain a monopoly of organization which 

Acme Photo A WAGE RATE HEARING 

One way to find who is right in a labor dispute is to hold a public hearing at which all who are interested may present their points of view. That was being done in 

Atlanta when this picture was taken. may be as undesirable as any other kind, and be used to the disadvantage of society as a whole. Some unions have been known to charge ridiculously high initiation fees to new members.

Violent disputes have arisen over demands for the closed shop. A closed shop is an establishment in which only union members are employed. An open shop is one in which persons may be employed without regard to whether they belong to a union or not. Sometimes open shops become definitely non-union shops, if union members refuse to work there. A closed shop with open union is one in which the employer may take on anybody he wishes, but as soon as one gets a

job, he must join the union. Sometimes a union which gets into its membership more than half the whole number employed in an establishment may gain "sole bargaining power" for all employees. Then all arrangements for wages, hours, and other conditions must be made through the union. In cases like this, unions generally figure that sooner or later they will be able to bring enough pressure to bear upon non-union workers so that they will join the majority. Some employers in the past have gone so far as to require, as a condition of work, that an employee would agree not to belong to a union. Such an arrangement has been referred to as a "yellow dog contract" and has been outlawed by a number of the states. 

Another policy often pursued by unions is the limiting of the amount of work that a member may do in a given time, such as the number of bricks a bricklayer may lay in eight hours. The argument for such restriction is that bosses might demand so much labor that the workers' health would be menaced, and that the only way to prevent that evil is to set a standard of work which any reasonably competent worker can meet, even though some could do more without hurting themselves.

Connected with this matter of limited output is often the question of time. Unions always insist that overtime shall be paid for at extra rates, either "time-and-a-half," or perhaps double time on Sundays and holidays. Employers sometimes wonder why workers worry about their health when considering how much they will do in eight hours, and yet are willing enough to work overtime for extra pay. 

In some states railroad unions have worked for the passage of "fullcrew" laws and provisions requiring a certain amount of work to be considered four hours, or eight hours, or some other definite length of time. Full-crew laws commonly provide that for trains of a given length a certain number of men shall be employed, or may forbid the running of trains with more than a certain number of cars in order to force the employment of more men to operate the trains that are running. Railroads object bitterly to such laws because they say they are unnecessary, and prevent them from taking advantage of improved equipment and making the economies that ought to result therefrom.

Strikes and their attendant unpleasantness cause more distress than any other feature of labor policy. Theoretically, any worker

has a right to stop work whenever he wishes if he is breaking no contract by doing so, and for the same reason, a thousand workers may stop at the same time. But what may they do after they have stopped work themselves? May they prevent people from working who wish to keep on doing so? May they prevent the employer from hiring anybody in their places? What may they do under the name of picketing? A picket, of course, is one who watches at some definite point to prevent the occurrence of something to which he objects. Please
