PICKETS 

This picture tells its own story. Sometimes, however, picket lines are composed of men who walk in close single file so that one can hardly get into a store or factory if he wants to do so.

You have all probably seen men or women parading on the sidewalk in front of some establishment wearing cards saying that this particular establishment is "unfair to organized labor." Has a picket also the right to try to prevent other workers or customers from entering the place? That kind of thing has often led to fights and bloodshed. Many who recognize the principle involved in the "right to strike" do not approve of "sit-down" strikes, in which strikers stay on their employer's property and prevent him from doing anything to protect it, even though they are refusing to work themselves. 

Another practice sometimes engaged in by workers is the boycott. 

1982 SA נס SH

This is an understanding among strikers or their sympathizers that they will refuse to use the goods produced by an employer against whom a dispute is directed, or to have any business relations with him. 

Sometimes even a secondary boycott may be undertaken, which is directed against an employer or organization simply for the purpose of forcing him or it to use pressure on some other employer who actually is in a labor difficulty. 

Keystone View Company KEEPING UP THEIR SPIRIT 

This woman is trying to strengthen the determination of these strikers to stay out. 

Sometimes workers are not so anxious to lose their wages as their leaders are to have them.

A demand often made by labor unions that employers seldom like is the check-off. This is an arrangement by which the employer deducts from a worker's wages the amount of his union dues before the wages are paid to the worker. This really makes the employer a collecting agent for the union, and brings dues into the union treasury regularly, but the practice is not always popular even with union members. 

Still another long-used means of argument in labor disputes is the publication by labor organizations of a "fair list" or "unfair list" of

employers. The unfair list, of course, includes those who have not been willing to do what the unions wanted.

Employers have sometimes combined to build up a defense against the growing power of unions. They may form associations like the 

National Association of Manufacturers, or "institutes" like the American Petroleum Institute, in which several individuals or corporations who function as employers in industry go together to promote their own interests. They may make studies of improved methods of production or may exchange information about other features of management. Their members also may co-operate in the case of extensive labor disputes.

Employers have also made use of one or two policies somewhat similar to those used by unions. They may, for instance, "lock out” their employees when there is a dispute between them and their workers and refuse to resume business until the dispute is settled. 

They may maintain a black list on which they will place the names of objectionable persons, and when such a person is dropped from one job, he may have considerable difficulty in getting another. In the past employers, when strikes were threatened or actually in progress, have gone before the courts and asked for injunctions forbidding interference with the operation of an establishment in which a dispute was going on. Several states, however, have passed laws forbidding the issuing of injunctions in labor disputes unless they would have been issued if there were no dispute going on. For instance, no injunction might issue against picketing when a strike was in process unless actual destruction of property or other serious menace was threatened.

What examples of the use of any of the labor practices mentioned in this section have come within your personal knowledge? If you were regularly employed in an industrial establishment, would you or would you not wish to be obliged to belong to a union? Which of the methods used by unions to obtain what they want do you justify? 

255. Dealing with Labor Difficulties. — Our lawmakers in many of the states and in our national government have thought it desirable to set up public agencies which would have either the right or the power to take action in the case of labor disputes. Such agencies include our national Department of Labor and similar bodies in the states. There are at least three ways by which public officials may

assist in the settlement of labor disputes- conciliation, mediation, and arbitration.

In conciliation the official simply tries to bring together the parties' in a dispute after they have abandoned efforts to settle their argument directly. He may use all kinds of arguments with them but he has no authority. In mediation he may go further and offer his services in trying to help the parties reach a settlement. He may refuse the 

Keystone View Company THE SECRETARY OF LABOR MEETS LABOR LEADERS 

Seated at the right is William Green, President of the A. F. of L. The discussion concerns a proposed plan for mediation to avert a threatened strike. The man at the left, Edward F. McGrady, has had notable success in handling labor disputes. responsibility for making the settlement himself, but he may take part in whatever discussion goes on. In arbitration one or more impartial persons, open-minded as far as the particular controversy is concerned, will listen to the arguments both sides have to present, and then try to reach a fair conclusion. Sometimes one party to the dispute may propose one or two arbitrators, the other party an equal number, and then they or some totally disinterested person will appoint a fifth. This fifth person may have to accept ultimately the whole responsibility, for too often the arbitrators named by each

side think it is their duty to support the claims of the side which nominated them.

Public officials, such as a mayor, governor, or President, sometimes try to assist in settling a labor controversy. Since such officials have chief responsibility for the enforcement of law and order, they therefore are likely to be anxious to prevent a disturbance that might be seriously harmful to public welfare, or if they cannot prevent it, to help settle it. Theodore Roosevelt was the first President to attempt anything of that kind, when he brought about a settlement of the anthracite coal strike in 1902. Wilson had a like difficulty in the bituminous coal strike of 1919. Franklin Roosevelt's administration faced similar problems, especially when the pressure of work in defense industries gave union leaders a new opportunity to make demands for higher wages and other changes. A special National Defense Mediation Board was created to deal with labor disputes that seemed likely to drag on, to the detriment of the whole country. 

Some think that the state ought to compel the parties to industrial disputes to arbitrate their differences if they cannot agree on a settlement. Canada and Australia have laws looking in that direction. 

Canada's law simply requires investigation by a government board and the publishing of its report, on the supposition that public opinion will do the rest. Labor unions have been strongly opposed, as a rule, to compulsory arbitration. They say it limits their right to strike. 

They have also argued that arbitration decisions are invariably compromises intended not to hurt either side's feelings too much. 

The "Fair Labor Standards Act" of 1938 established minimum wage provisions and maximum hour figures - "a floor for wages and a ceiling for hours," as they are often characterized. By steps changes were to take place until ultimately no worker covered by the law should have to work more than 40 hours a week or for less than 40 cents an hour. But farm workers, domestic workers, and many others were not included under its provisions. Some think that since a much larger proportion of workers in the South will be affected by the law than in the North, the advantage that southern employers have had in lower labor cost may be removed. 

The establishment of the National Labor Relations Board was a measure which did not work as smoothly as some of its advocates hoped it would. The Board has had some awkward questions to settle. For

example, coercion by employers in connection with membership or nonmembership in a labor union is forbidden. But what is coercion? Is an employer guilty of it if he makes a straightforward speech to his employees, telling them frankly what he thinks, or talks with individual employees in the same fashion, or is he simply exercising the American right of free speech? Has the employer the right to choose to

One complication in the settlement of labor disputes may come from

the fact that both sides may make statements or demands on which they do not expect ever to make good. Workers may demand higher wages than they have any idea they can get, so that later they may seem to have made concessions, while the employer may understate the wages he is willing to pay so that he may seem in turn to be reasonable. 256. Can Laborers and Employers Co-operate? They must cooperate, to some extent, else nothing will be done. If the present employers in any industry should retire, someone else must take their place. Even if you can imagine a successful industrial system without private employers, public officials would then have to play the part that employers play now. Whoever has the authority to tell other people to do this and not to do that, or to do a thing this way rather - —

TESTING A WORKER'S HEALTH 

Most large companies maintain doctors and nurses always available for the aid of the workers. than some other, will often make himself unpopular, even though he may be elected by his fellow workers to take such responsibility. 

Some employers have done considerably more than the law required in trying to make life pleasant for their employees. One means of doing this has been through what is commonly known as welfare work. 

Not only are healthful conditions while at work provided, but conveniences for social life in the form of recreation houses, lecture rooms, athletic fields, and the like. Special nurses and physicians are always

on duty to care for workers who are sick or injured while on the job, and probably help to look out for their families otherwise. The strict union man, however, cares little for welfare work. He wants the employer to distribute in the form of wages whatever it costs to provide such benefits, and then let the worker spend the money as he sees fit, or have the union carry on the welfare work instead of the employer.

Some employers have made a practice of paying bonuses, particularly at Christmas time, beyond the regular wages. The ability to pay bonuses, of course, depends upon the extent to which a business is prosperous, and that varies from year to year. When bonuses are not paid or are reduced, workers sometimes fail to understand why. 

A few employers have tried various kinds of plans often known as profit-sharing. A certain fund is set apart over and above the amount necessary to provide the standard rate of wages, and this fund is divided among workers at fixed times. As with bonuses, the success of profit-sharing depends on the prosperity of the business. What would happen in a year when there were deficits instead of profits? 

One could hardly make the workers chip in and make up a deficit. 

To aim at similar results as paying bonuses or profit-sharing, some establishments have contracts with their unions under which wages are adjusted up or down in accordance with the earnings of the business. 

Another plan to bring about mutual understanding and good will which a few years ago was more talked about than it is today was sometimes called industrial democracy. It meant simply allowing workers to be represented in bodies which they chose, which might be called a house of representatives, a senate, or council, and through which they could confer with the employer on matters of common interest. It seemed to work well in some cases, but to the union labor leader it seemed like a company union if it had any real service at all. When a union becomes strong enough to receive "sole bargaining power" in an industry, there is not much left for a "senate" or "house of representatives" to talk about. The American Federation of Labor at one time went on record in favor of industrial democracy, but it was with the understanding that the workers' side of the proposition should be handled by the regularly organized unions. 

Two other institutions which have been set up by some large employers of labor are the company store and company houses. The company

store is like any country general store or perhaps a small city department store. The chief criticisms against the company store have been that it charged more than it needed to, and that since workers could buy on credit against their regular wages, it might happen, when the time came for them to get their wages, that there was nothing left after their purchases had been accounted for. In some cases, however, the company store has rendered real convenience to workers. 

Company houses are those tenements, shacks, or respectable dwelling houses which are constructed by a coal-mining company or some other employer and rented to workers. Sometimes company houses have had nothing whatever attractive about them, and since a worker might not know how long his job was going to last, he would care little about keeping them in good condition. The rent charged might depend upon what the company thought it could get, rather than what the lodgings were actually worth. On the other side of the proposition must be mentioned the fact that such houses were usually constructed within reasonably convenient access of the workers' employment. A mining settlement was not far from the mine where the workers were employed, and a factory village was within walking distance of the factory where workers had their jobs. Sometimes, too, the houses in company towns were neat and not all just alike, and workers who lived there were encouraged to plant flowers or otherwise make their surroundings attractive.

But what if a worker who had been living in a company house lost his job and had no other job or place to go? Would the company have a right to put him out? If the worker was "fired" for inefficiency or misconduct, would he have the right to insist on living on his former employer's property? You can see how arguments might become unpleasant in such cases. 

One other question may be raised that applies to both employers and to workers. Is it desirable for them to go into politics as organizations? Should the National Association of Manufacturers, for instance, publicly announce its support of one candidate for President rather than another, or the United Mine Workers contribute money out of their union treasury to the campaign funds of a certain political party? If one has the right to do it, another has, but is it a good thing for the country to have political divisions and class line-ups mean about the same?

It certainly would be unfortunate if our public officials were chosen because it was understood they would show undeserved favors to any particular industrial group. Corporations have for years been forbidden to contribute to campaign funds, though there is no way by which you can prevent a citizen who happens to be an officer of a corporation from contributing to such a fund in his own name. Would it be desirable to have unions placed under similar limitations? Is a union leader less likely to act selfishly in public affairs than a corporation executive?

In some countries, England, for example, there has been for a number of years a separate Labor party bearing that name. They have been successful in one or two elections, and had their own Ramsay MacDonald as Prime Minister - much-loved until he discovered that as a public official he had to look at some things a little differently from the way he had looked at them before he had such responsibilities. 

In the United States there has not been, up to the present, a nationwide organization bearing the name of "labor party," although the so-called American Labor Party has cut a considerable figure in the choice of public officials in New York City and State. Would anything important be gained if our unions should attempt to imitate the English Labor Party, rather than continuing their policy of supporting the candidates of any party that seems likely to do what they want? Or would it be best of all if every employer and every worker would try to find out what solution for every problem would benefit the whole country rather than his own pocketbook? 

If you were the owner or manager of a large department store, how much welfare work would you try to do for your employees? If you were a coalminer, do you think you would make purchases at the company store and live in a company house? Are labor leaders, as you have read about them or had contact with them, inclined to consider themselves simply representatives of the members of the union, or dictators of union policy? 

257. Out of a Job. Such a condition represents happiness to some people but despair to others. Unemployment fluctuates as much as any other one element in modern economic life. It has been estimated that in the United States there may be at any time 2,000,000 people able to work and not working. Those 2,000,000 may be increased to 

6,000,000 in times of moderate business depression, or perhaps even 

12,000,000 in really bad times. Nobody can do more than guess at 

17

the total number who were out of work at any given time in the great depression of the 1930's.

The effects of extensive unemployment are disastrous. People who are out of work and have no other source of income cannot buy goods. 

People who try without success to find work may get disheartened, say to themselves, "What's the use?" and cease trying. For both the disappointed seeker after work and the loafer a sort of defeatist attitude of mind becomes habitual, and both may conclude, "They won't let me starve," and decide to live permanently on "relief."

THE UPS AND DOWNS OF EMPLOYMENT 

The solid line represents the proportionate number of persons on relief in one of our states during the period indicated. The broken line indicates the relative number who had work. The number 100 represents the average for the years 1935 to 

1939. It is evident that as industrial employment increases, the number on relief decreases. That should be the case, should it not? Can you explain the fluctuation of the lines from one year to another? 

Lack of buying power leads to poverty, with the lowering of health standards and the other unpleasant conditions that go with it. With some people poverty leads to crime, and encourages some to try to provide for their own needs by dishonest means. Governments, local, state, and now national, feel a responsibility for preventing human suffering, and politically-minded distributors of government funds do not stop with the really needy in handing them out. The cost of all this government relief has to be met sometime by taking it from the industrious and the fortunate who are willing and able to

work. In principle this is only fair, but a hard-working man hates to see people living in idleness in what seems like fair comfort if he knows they do not try to get jobs. 

The reasons why people may be out of work are numerous, and correspond somewhat to those we have given for poverty (§ 157). 

They include: 

1. General business depression the most far-reaching cause. 

2. Technological changes accompanying new methods or new machines. 

3. Disasters such as a great fire, a flood, or an earthquake. 

4. Personal illness or physical weakness. 

5. Inability to do anything well. 

6. Laziness. (The typical tramp or hobo would feel offended if somebody tried to make him take a job. Others are perfectly willing to live on the charity of their relatives, friends, or the government.) 

Some of the unemployed are really unemployable. Some are not capable of holding any permanent job, while others may be unemployable at certain lines of work. The permanently crippled are definitely limited, for instance. Those who are sick with infectious diseases should not be allowed to work where they would contaminate others. 

Make a list of the first six people you think of who are old enough to work but have no jobs. Why are they unemployed? Give examples of persons who have jobs of some kind but would be unemployable in some other positions. What is the unemployment situation in your neighborhood just now? 

258. How May We Relieve Unemployment? 

In the depression of the 1930's we met the problem by creating some jobs outright and by undertaking projects which were useful but which were not necessary to undertake at the time. Relief of the unemployment problem in that way, of course, has its limits. It can be defended as a temporary emergency measure, but it has all kinds of dangers as a permanent policy. The same is true of relief to the needy through money handouts or orders for goods- clothing, food, and the like. Few would contend that it is the duty of a government to furnish work or a comfortable living for all who are too lazy to look for work themselves. 

Unemployment insurance has received considerable attention in recent years, and is now provided for many workers through the Social Security Act of 1935 and state laws to supplement it. Workers in occupations covered by these laws must make contributions from

their own wages, and employers do the same on the basis of their own payrolls, for the support of a fund from which a worker who has contributed may get help when he is unemployed. Such funds have to be carefully safeguarded. Usually one may not call upon the unemployment insurance fund until he has been out of work at least a little while, and he may claim benefits only for a definite number of weeks or months. The purpose of such funds, when properly planned, is simply to provide a cushion for periods in between jobs and not a permanent resting place for loafers. 

Far better than mere relief is the removal of the cause of unemployment. A long-range means of improvement would be the training of every individual in school or by other means so that he is competent to do something reasonably well. Some think, in view of the constantly increasing changes in industrial methods, that it is too expensive to try to give detailed preparation for every specific trade. But at least one can get an understanding of the kinds of work that are available in this country and a knowledge of the general demands that certain classes of industry make upon workers, so that it should not take long for an experienced person to adjust himself to an available job.

Since not only unemployment but discontent on the job may lead to unsatisfactory conditions, one valuable accomplishment would be to discover and correct, as far as possible, maladjustment among workers. That does not mean that we should try to find a soft job for every worker, but that we should seek to put each worker in a place where he could do well. The economic law of least social cost declares that when an individual or a community is engaged in work for which he or it is naturally adapted, better results in volume of product and personal satisfaction follow than when other conditions prevail. If a person likes to work out of doors, why keep him inside if outdoor work is available? If he enjoys working with machinery or is skillful at office duties, why compel him to work in a mine or on a farm except when such opportunities are the only ones that are at hand? 

Perhaps school people have made a mistake in the past by saying too much about getting something else than manual work as a result of going to school, and too many people have come to think that anything else than a white-collar job is socially below standard. 

Nothing ever should be done in school or elsewhere to lead boys and

girls to think that they should never have to get their hands dirty while they work, and schools should help people to be efficient at jobs that require one to wear overalls as well as any other kind. 

Sometimes customs and practices develop in industry which unintentionally lead to the embarrassment of considerable groups of workers. 

Much has been said and written about the "45-year deadline." Many

One means of assistance to the unemployed which perhaps might be carried still further is the maintenance of employment agencies on the part of federal, state, or local governments. The individual who is out of a job and willing to work may honestly not know of opportunities where he could fit in. A public agency, with facilities for obtaining a complete knowledge of existing conditions and opportunities, can render valuable service by making such information available to workers. Private employment agencies may also be useful, but some of them have needed public inspection to make sure that they really did act in perfect honesty toward both prospective employers and employees. In these days government finds it desirable to take on authority and responsibility in almost every field of human interest. Moreover, only government can provide some of the features necessary to carry on business, such as money, and its protection is needed to guarantee safety and honesty in business relations as in other features of private life. With all these contacts between government and business, government cannot fail to influence it. When government itself goes into business, still more problems appear. 

XXI Some Questions: 

1. What is government for? 

2. How much are the operations of government like those of a private business enterprise? 

3. How does government help and how does it restrain private business? 

4. What problems connected with public utilities have stirred our government to action? 

5. How far should government go in trying to regulate or control our economic life? 

259. Government as a Factor in National Life. - Long ago we remarked that we could not get along without government. It may do us good to think back right now to what we have already observed about the services and responsibilities of government (§§ 5, 60, 162). It plays a vital and regular part in our existence, so that the old joke no longer means much that government is like the air, in that we notice it only when it is bad. Whether or not we like what has been done in 

Washington in the last decade or so, we have been forced to think about the proper place that government should take in our national life and set up some standard for determining what we ought to want government to do for us. You remember also that in this country there is a division of the activities of government which does not prevail to the same extent in most other national governments. 

705

Federal, state, and local governments have distinct organizations, and once we would have said distinct responsibilities as well. 

Some people think of government as a fifth factor in our economic life and therefore entitled to a special return of its own. Just as the landholder gets rent, the laborer wages, the capitalist interest, and the entrepreneur profits, so this kind of thinker would say government gets taxes. We prefer to look upon the government as a great service agency which we support because we get something out of it, and which charges us for the services it renders. The taxes we pay to government serve as a compensation for these services, even though we often pay a tax or take advantage of some service, without any direct connection between a tax and the service. 

Another classification of the services of government calls them protective, social, and economic. Mention some activities of federal, state, and local governments, if possible, that might come under each of these three heads. 

Is there any parallel between the steady expansion of the ministrant services of government and the habit of an individual of taking it for granted that his parents and friends who have always done things for him will keep on doing so indefinitely?

In some countries, government actually carries on business activities itself. In numerous countries some or all of the railroads are direct government activities, and in some countries telephones and telegraphs are a part of the same system that runs the post office. A country's policy in such matters is often determined by the way that activity started. If it began as a government function, it has probably stayed that way. If it began as a private enterprise, such as a railroad, electric light company, or other kind of public service corporation, the private proprietor is likely to feel that it should stay that way. 

The projects carried on under the Tennessee Valley Authority (§ 268) form the first instance in our history in which on a large scale the federal government has undertaken to reconstruct the social and economic life of an entire large section of the country. We shall know later how much more the great dams in the West Boulder, Grand Coulee, and Bonneville, for example will do than merely provide water for irrigation. Much business activity has been carried on in the field of conservation of natural resources. Just the instant a government charges for the water or power supplied by a great dam, it is as much of a business agency as a private water company or a 

---

private power company is. States and local communities also have carried on such enterprises as specially constructed highways or a public water system. Some communities definitely plan for profit from their public light and power plants. All such things we call public utilities because they render service to the people as a whole, and often require government permission or regulation if they are to be carried on by private enterprise. 

Courtesy Bureau of Reclamation GRAND COULEE 

This dam in the Columbia River in the state of Washington is sometimes called the biggest thing ever built by man. Notice the houses also put up by government agencies for workers on the dam and their families. 

Do you know of any case when a government-operated activity actually drove out of business a private organization which had been furnishing the same kind of service? If so, did it seem justifiable? In operating public utilities, what motives might influence a government that would not similarly animate private business men? 

260. Government as a Business Enterprise. There are numerous similarities between the organization and operation of a government and of private corporations. It is only natural that there should be, because each has at times patterned its organization on that of the 

---

other. Besides, any government is a corporation itself a public corporation.

The charter of a corporation is a sort of constitution under which it may operate, or to put it the other way, the constitution of a national or state government is the charter which it has obtained from the people to carry on its business. For a board of directors there may be a Congress, a state legislature, or a city council or corresponding officers in any small local government. For a general manager there may be a President, or in some countries a Prime Minister. 

Just as the manager may be removed by the board of directors in a corporation, so a Prime Minister loses his job when he no longer can control the lawmaking body. 

Governments have to charge for many of the services they render, for the same reason that department stores and manufacturing establishments do. Wages for the workers and the cost of the materials they use must be met. There may be unnecessary men and women on our public payrolls, but the great majority do some work. We the people must foot the bills. 

Governments have one great advantage over private business organizations. If they need money, they can simply levy a tax, unless they prefer to borrow the money and pay it back later. Any decent government, of course, renders services to somebody in return for the money which it collects from taxpayers. But many people have to pay school taxes who have no children or other relatives in school, and the people of a whole state may be taxed to maintain highways which many of them may never see. Besides, if a government wants land which is owned by private citizens, it usually can simply go and take it, exercising its right of eminent domain (§ 62). We have also pointed out (§ 245) that some people even favor ❝land nationalization," which means merely taking over into the hands of the government the title to all land.

Not even the government, however, has discovered any way to create wealth out of nothing. If it tried to meet payments for salaries and materials by merely printing more pieces of paper, it would not be long before that paper would not go very well. Governments which carry on business activities like water systems, electric light and power systems, often can furnish these facilities for a lower price than private corporations could furnish them and make money, because they do

not tax themselves and can, if they wish, sell their product to the public at exactly what it costs or even less. But when that happens, the revenues that might be obtained from taxing a private company have to be made up by the government in taxes on something else, or a deficit allowed to pile up. 

James Sawders

BOULDER DAM 

Most famous of all reclamation projects up to date is probably Boulder Dam, in the Colorado River. The water backed up by it is now known as Lake Mead and goes back nearly 125 miles. You are looking at the dam from the Nevada side of the river. In this case the private property that was flooded was of no great importance, but sometimes whole towns are wiped out by such projects. 

Deficits mean debts and paying debts is seldom so much fun as incurring them. Repudiation of debts- that is, simply not paying back what has been borrowed - has taken place in some of our states, but such a means of getting out of difficulty does not appeal to honest people. Besides, if a government was thought likely to do that sort of thing, it would have trouble borrowing money from anybody. A few people have asserted that our own government should meet emergencies by what they call a "capital levy." They would take the

private savings of the past and use them for government expenses now. 

Such a proposal not only is immoral, but would reduce the country's ability to meet future emergencies and set the whole people on the way not only to bankruptcy but permanent poverty. 

Too few people think deeply enough in connection with finances, either their own or their government's. Especially if a person seems to benefit by handouts which his government makes to him on the basis of borrowed money, he may be quite satisfied to continue the process. "After us, the deluge" was the saying attributed to the court of Louis XV of France in the eighteenth century. And the deluge did come later.

Economy in government is often popular to talk about, but not always to put into practice if it means throwing unneeded employees off the public payroll. Of course, there is such a thing as false economy. Sometimes it is hard to determine whether true economy in a particular case means spending a little in order to save much, or stopping an outlay to which people have become accustomed. 

Why can governments often borrow more cheaply than private citizens can? What has been the policy of your state in regard to going into debt?

If it is in debt, what have been the principal items for which borrowed money was spent? Answer the same questions for your county or other local government. 

261. Government Help to Private Business. Three different points of view have been held as to the proper relation of the government to private business. The simplest of these is the old doctrine of laissez faire,' which represents a policy of letting business take its own course. 

Government control of private business may start with the policy which we often call regulation. The great majority of us think that it is the government's duty to set up regulations as to the things that private business may or may not do. The fields in which regulation is first undertaken are naturally those which are most vital to a country's welfare, like transportation, the organization of business, and the welfare of workers. 

A third possible stage in a government's relations with business may be called the socialistic, though we do not need to infer that this third 1 The expression comes from the French and means, literally, let it do. Those who held that theory believed that it was a government's duty to let business alone. Our own 

Thomas Jefferson once declared that government governs best which governs least; but laissez faire is now largely out of date. 20

stage is inevitable. The socialist, as you know, would let private citizens own property, perhaps even land, but he would take out of their hands such activities as banking, the operation of railroads, the working of mines, and others which mean much to a people's life. 

But before going into a discussion of whether government control should go further than it has gone, let us see what government does to render help toward successful business activity.

Government agents try to prevent the carrying of harmful insects or diseased plants into regions that have not yet been infected. The Japanese beetle has made a great deal of trouble, and the efforts to stop it have not been entirely successful. (1) It offers the use of its courts to decide disputes in business and to enforce contracts when once they are made. (2) It provides for the organization of corporations and other means of conducting business and declares what shall be acceptable business methods. (3) It establishes or protects the system of money or credit without which business could not be carried on. (4) It passes bankruptcy laws to provide the conditions under which a person whose business affairs are in hopeless entanglement can get them straightened out.

(5) It sets up agencies to furnish information and give dependable advice. 

Our farmers, our seamen, and many other people profit by the information provided by the Weather Bureau. Experiment stations in our agricultural colleges and elsewhere try out new kinds of crops to see whether they are suited to our country or to some part of it. Helpful bulletins of many kinds are printed and disposed of either free or at cost. Employment agencies to bring workers and jobs together may be helpful to the business man as well as to the people who work for him. (6) Direct aid to some industries is given through money payments out of the treasury, or tariff laws intended to protect home industries from foreign competition. There has been much argument over some such payments or subsidies. We have given subsidies to railroads by money grants or gifts of land when those railroads were under construction. We have sometimes paid a "bounty" on sugar produced within the country. We will discuss separately other ways of trying to help both manufacturers and farmers.

(7) President Franklin D. 

Roosevelt's administration accepted as a duty the spending of money so as to encourage business activity which would not take place unassisted. This kind of thing was often referred to as pump-priming, since it was compared with the old practice of pouring water into a pump in order to help get it working. 

Those who favored it declared that it was not meant to be a permanent policy, but opponents of the policy asserted that it did more harm than good in setting a bad precedent before the country, and if continued would inevitably lead to national bankruptcy.

States also render many such services, as regulating and enforcing contracts, prescribing rules for the organization and conduct of business, passing bankruptcy laws, and furnishing a variety of kinds of information and advice. Many business men have not welcomed governmental interference, though most have been convinced that a

considerable amount of regulation is necessary. Everything will go. better where there is good will and mutual understanding between business leaders and government officials. There are some things that not even government officials can make business men do; on the other hand, business men who refuse to co-operate with their government cannot expect much consideration from it, even though it would be to the interest of the country for the government to go more than half way in assuring business of its good intentions. 

Do you agree with this statement: "The sole function of the government in relation to economics should be the formulation of the rules of the game and the umpiring of the game"? What is your own view of "pump-priming" in times of depression? Why is laissez faire unlikely ever again to govern the relations between governments and private business ? 

262. The Story of the Protective Tariff. — The word tariff once meant, and is sometimes still used to mean, a tax of any kind, but we have fallen into the habit of applying it specially to a tax on imported goods. Such a tax could be laid either to get money for the treasury the same as most taxes are intended to do, or to discourage the importing of goods by increasing the cost of them. A tax measure is a revenue tariff when its purpose is simply to get money for the treasury. It is a protective tariff when it aims to increase the price of foreign goods so as to encourage the production of the same goods at home. If a country cannot produce a certain commodity within its own borders, any tax on that article when imported would have to be for revenue. That is why, for example, Great Britain puts a tax on cocoa. But if Great Britain should put a tax on imports of iron and steel, they would probably be trying to keep out steel products made in the United States, Belgium, Japan, or some other place, in order to enable their own manufacturers at home to get higher prices. 

During a considerable part of her recent history—from about the middle of the nineteenth century to about 1930the British political leaders believed that a protective tariff harmed England rather than helped it. On that account Great Britain was, for more than half a century, the outstanding example of a great country that did not levy protective tariffs. If there were no tax at all on any imported goods, there would be absolute free trade. Nations have rarely gone that far in encouraging international trade. Usually the choice has been between a tariff for revenue and the protective tariff.

A protective tariff works this way. The importer adds the amount of the tariff to what he would otherwise charge for foreign-made goods. 

If a commodity costs more to produce in the United States than in some other country, it will not be readily sold in competition with the foreign-made goods if there is free trade between nations in that article. 

But if we put a tax on an imported article that is high enough to make up the difference between the cost of production here and elsewhere, then the home-made goods will sell as readily as those coming from abroad. If we put the import tax still higher, home producers may actually be able to raise their own prices and still undersell the importers. Look at the following table to see how this works in an imaginary case:
