We should keep in mind a few facts about tariff legislation: (1) If a protective tariff is so high as to exclude most or all of the imports of a certain article, little or no revenue will be obtained from it. So a high protective tariff may reduce a country's revenue rather than increase it. (2) The consumer of the goods finally pays the tariff, not the importer or the foreign producer. When a tariff keeps out foreign goods, the home producer will probably charge as much more for home-made goods as the duty on the foreign goods. (3) A high tariff does not necessarily mean good times. We have had both good and bad times under both high and moderate tariff laws. (4) No tariff law that we ever had attempted to tax all imports. 

Even under the highest of all our tariff laws the total money value of the goods that came in free was greater than of the goods that were taxed.

Alexander Hamilton did most to put the United States on the protective tariff basis. He sincerely believed in it, and some of the arguments used in his "Report on Manufactures" back in 1792 had much more force then than they would now. The duties he proposed would not be considered high today.

Tariff laws have seen many fluctuations. The Walker tariff of 1846 was a consistent low-tariff measure. The Civil War caused the levying of many new taxes, among them increased tariffs on imported goods. After the war the increased duties were kept on. President Cleveland tried to get them reduced, but without much success. President McKinley, who honestly believed in the benefits of protection, was responsible while in Congress for the tariff bill of 1890 named for him, and when President, urged the passage of the Dingley tariff of 1897, which set the highest rates that had then been known. The Payne-Aldrich tariff of 1909 reduced the duties, but did not go very far in that direction. 

After the Democrats under Wilson came into power in 1913, the Underwood Act was passed which really did reduce the tariff duties. When the 

Republicans came back, following the World War, they passed the Fordney- McCumber Act of 1922, raising the average of duties considerably, and then in 1930 the highest average of all was set by the Hawley-Smoot tariff of that year. To reduce the harmful effects on international trade that were believed to have resulted from the Hawley-Smoot Act, Congress gave 

President Franklin D. Roosevelt the authority to reduce tariff rates 50 per cent when by so doing he could make favorable trade agreements with other countries, and in 1937 and 1940 added three more years to the life of that authority.

Let us close our story of the protective tariff by summarizing the leading arguments offered by its friends and by its opponents. 

FOR 

(1) Industrial independence. A nation should be self-sufficient, as far as possible. We should therefore encourage the production of anything for which we are at all fitted, by putting a tax on imports of those commodities and thus reducing the competition from outside. (2) Security in war. A self-sufficient nation can feel less disturbance at the prospect of war in other parts of the world than one which depends upon other nations for important commodities. (3) Protection of infant industries. Infant industries, as you might guess, are those which are just getting started. There may be some logic in helping such industries get on their feet by reducing the competition from abroad.

(4) Encouragement of high wages. Because of the protection given by tariff laws American manufacturers have been able to pay the highest average wage standard of any country in the world. Other causes than the tariff, of course, assist in maintaining a high standard of wages here, but this argument is one of those which seem to be at least partly wellfounded.

AGAINST 

(1) The fostering of unsuitable industries. Each country should devote its attention to those things which it is naturally fitted to produce. If the 

United States or any other country undertakes to encourage unsuitable industries, it is harming itself. (2) Special favors to big business interests. Industries which as "infants" have been encouraged by tariffs seldom are willing to let go of the tariff when they are grown up. Sometimes our laws have enabled a producer to charge higher prices here than he actually sold his product profitably for in other countries. (3) The increased cost of living. Even though high wages may be encouraged by a protective tariff, so are higher prices of goods an inevitable result. Which is better, high wages and high prices, or moderate wages and reduced prices? (4) Harmful influence in politics. Business men and organizations have contributed to party funds because they expected their party to obtain the passage of laws that would favor their particular business through high tariff duties or otherwise.

Few of our tariff laws have been based on an intelligent understanding of what it actually cost to produce various goods here and abroad. 

Too often there has been bargaining between different interests working upon members of Congress to get the kind of tariff law that a particular pressure group might want. To come nearer doing such things wisely, Congress established in 1916 the Tariff Commission, made up of representatives of both the leading parties, which was given power to investigate the cost of commodities at home and abroad. 

The later laws of 1922 and 1930 both authorized the adjustment of certain duties up or down as compared with the rates fixed in the law, without having to change the whole law. At present the Tariff 

Commission may propose changes which will go into effect if approved by the President. 

President McKinley, a strong protectionist, and President Franklin

D. Roosevelt, who represented the Democrats, both believed in

reciprocity between nations in regard to tariff rates. If some other country would reduce the duties it imposed on goods from the United States, we might reduce our duties on certain goods coming from that country and thus find a situation that would be of advantage to both sides. Under the Roosevelt administration Secretary of State Hull was responsible for numerous such agreements. Any wholesale wiping out of the protective tariff, which, whether it should have done so or not, has become a significant factor in the development of our industrial life, would be a blunder. It would be much more sensible to correct mistakes one by one. It is too bad that so often a tariff change proposed by a member of one party has been automatically disapproved by almost everybody in the other great party. 

In the past, southerners in general opposed the protective tariff because there were few factories there. Would you expect the same attitude from southerners now? If you do find it, can you explain why? Why is it harder to protect farmers by tariff laws than manufacturers? Can you find any evidence as to whether wages are higher in industries which are benefited by protective tariffs than in those which are not? 

263. The Government and the Farmer. In recent years farmers have been just as anxious to get government support for the prices of their products as manufacturers have been in wanting a protective tariff on the goods they make. Since there are more farmers who can vote than there are manufacturers, Congressmen have been willing to listen to proposals to help the farmers for political reasons. Besides, farmers could often put up pretty good support for their argument that the laws intended to help the manufacturer might indirectly hurt the farmer, since they might result in higher prices for the farm machinery and other manufactured materials that the farmer had to use. 

Protective tariffs do not so easily work for the benefit of the farmer as they do for manufacturers. No tariff law can make soil any richer or climate any more favorable. Nature may put a limit on the amount of goods that a farmer may be able to raise. Some other procedure than protective tariffs has therefore been sought. Some of these methods of farm relief have been too complicated to explain here.

In President Hoover's administration a Federal Farm Board was established and $500,000,000 set aside for it to use in trying to keep

up the prices of the most common farm products. The price the farmer was getting was more often the cause of the grievance that he felt than any handicap that nature put in his way, but the Farm Board had no luck in its efforts to try to keep up prices by storing surplus amounts of farm products and thus keeping them off the market. 

Under President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary Henry A. 

Wallace (later Vice-President) new ideas were tried.

Through the 

Courtesy Bureau of Entomology and Plant Quarantine DUSTING COTTON AGAINST THE BOLL WEEVIL 

It is remarkable what uses can be made of the airplane these days. This is one example of government advice to farmers put into practice. 

Agricultural Adjustment Administration (the AAA) it was proposed to pay farmers for not growing as much cotton, wheat, or something else as they otherwise would grow. The money to make these payments was to come from taxes on the "processing," or preparing for market, of certain farm products. The Supreme Court threw out this idea as unconstitutional. 

The same end in part was then sought by measures carried on under the name of soil conservation. Farmers engaged in the production of a certain crop might be asked to vote on whether a limit should be

placed on the amount of the crop which they would raise. The limit would go into effect if 80% of the farmers who voted were in favor of it. Some thought that such plans as these were inconsistent, for when many people in the country were unemployed and were being paid "relief” out of the government treasury it seemed unjustifiable to destroy or otherwise limit goods that could be produced. 

Still another way of giving the farmer more money is through the system often referred to as parity payments. It has been figured that in the years 1909 to 1914 the price of farm products in comparison with those of other industries was about as favorable to the farmer as it ever was. The proposal was, therefore, put into law, with reference to some of most common agricultural commodities, that the government would lend the farmer 75% of what would be the price of those products if it were in as favorable proportion toward industrial products as farm products were in 1909 to 1914. In 1941 Congress raised this percentage to 85% and extended it to include practically all farm products instead of a limited number. 

This is the way this works out. If the farmer sells his products at a figure high enough to permit him to pay back to the government what he has borrowed, he will do so; but if he cannot get as good a price as that, he has the privilege of letting the government take his crop instead of paying back the loan. The government then would have to store the product and dispose of it in whatever way it could. 

In 1941 the situation was further complicated by the fact that there was greater activity than for many years in the industrial world and many strikes resulted, with demands for higher wages. If the price of farm goods went up, city workers had to pay more for food — and they did not like that. If, as a result of wage increases, the price of manufactured products went up, the farmer had to pay more for the things he bought that were factory-made. The whole business of trying to help one economic class or group has, you see, many entanglements. Yet one can hardly blame farmers for wishing that they could have the chance to handle a little more money than passes through the hands of the general run of farmers. 

If you have friends who are farmers, ask them how they have felt about some of the laws of the last fifteen or twenty years intended to do something for the farmer. Would it be possible for farmers to engage in the same kind

of methods that labor unions use to get benefits for themselves? If you were a Congressman from a district that included a city of 50,000 population or more and some farming country also, how do you think you would feel when you had to vote on some of the measures mentioned in this section? 

264. Governmental Restraint of Private Business. An important task of our government is to protect and encourage private business. 

But it has also done a number of things to restrain rather than to encourage it. Let's see why. 

At least two questions should have weight in matters of this kind. (1) Is the private business itself essentially helpful or harmful? If it is the latter, it ought to be restrained or suppressed. (2) Has the public been harmed through bad management or abuses of opportunities in an industry not harmful in itself? In that case, it needs not abolition but regulation. 

Public opinion often disagrees about how to regulate an industry even when regulation is plainly needed. A majority of our people at one time believed, and a large number of them still do, that the public general sale of intoxicating liquors should be prohibited, but the attempt to wipe it out did not succeed, and there is still difference of opinion about the best way to control it. There is no doubt that railroads and the steel industry have rendered very definite service to the public, and if abuses have crept into these otherwise helpful enterprises, they need regulation and not destruction. 

Outside of the creation of the Interstate Commerce Commission in 1887, the first attempt to regulate business interests on an extensive scale came with the Sherman Anti-Trust Act of 1890. This declared that combinations in restraint of trade between the states were illegal. 

Not much was done to enforce the Act until the administration of 

Theodore Roosevelt. Then the government won the Northern 

Securities case, when the Great Northern and Northern Pacific Railroads were forced to give up a project which would have meant the abandonment of competition between them in a large part of the country. Thus it was proved that big business interests could be mastered by the government if occasion required. 

There still were disputed questions arising from the vague language of the Sherman Act. When was a thing "in restraint of trade between the states," anyway? What was permissible and what was not?

The Clayton Act of 1914 answered some such questions more spe-

cifically, and it also declared, as we have learned, that labor was not to be considered a commodity concerning which there could be a "conspiracy in restraint of trade."

Other laws have extended the government's control of business operations. The Federal Trade Commission, established in 1914, was intended to bring to account business organizations that used unfair methods, including such practices as dishonest advertising and cutthroat competition. This Commission was not given power to punish individuals or firms that were found to be engaging in unfair practices, but on the evidence the Commission gathered, proceedings could be taken by the Department of Justice against those who had violated the law. Similar motives led to the establishment of the 

Securities and Exchange Commission (§ 235). 

It is unfortunate if business men or public officials get the impression that each has dishonorable designs upon the other. As far as efficiency is concerned, the chances are that private business could teach government considerable. At the same time, a fair-minded business man will admit that some among his own number have not conducted themselves honorably or with an eye to the general good. Government makes a great mistake if it assumes that private business is necessarily hostile to it, and that the way to approach it is solely by the use of the "big stick." Private business also is wrong if it assumes that all restraint or regulation is malicious. 

If you had been in the brokerage business in 1933, how do you suppose you would have reacted to the proposal to set up the Securities and Exchange Commission? What motive could a politician have in making general attacks upon business men? What examples of mistakes, misjudgments, or wrongs by business men or critics of big business have come to your attention? 

265. Problems of Public Utilities. You know how we defined public utilities (§ 260). Such business activities as railroads, bus lines, electric light companies, gas companies, water companies, and airways companies meet that definition. A considerable portion of the people of a community or a nation use them. They are usually required to obtain a franchise or grant of authority from a government before operating. Sometimes they receive the privilege of laying tracks or putting up poles and wires on the streets, or laying pipes or wires beneath them, or constructing terminal stations, or may even obtain outright grants of money or land. Sometimes they are given the

power of eminent domain, or the right to make use of water power or some other form of natural resources. 

Some of these industries make themselves vital to the people's welfare. They are "affected with the public interest," as the legal phrase goes, and it would be hard to get along without them. Once one would have laughed at a suggestion that supplying milk was a public utility. But as far as big cities are concerned, supplying milk 

PUBLIC SERVICE 

James Sawders

A PUBLIC SERVICE PRIVATELY MANAGED 

In this country a very large part of the public utility plants supplying light, heat, and power were constructed by private companies, but public regulation seems to be necessary. has become a big business and one that concerns the lives and health of its people. Street-car service, natural gas companies, and private water companies may be equally important. 

Why, then, are public utilities a problem? For several reasons. (1) Though a community needs their services, it is not good for a community to entrust its very existence to a private corporation. It must control the corporation rather than let the corporation control the community. (2) In some well-known cases, selfish men have controlled their financial management solely with the idea of making profit for

themselves rather than of benefiting the public or even the corpo ration. 

(3) The dependence of some of these utilities upon the control of natural resources or the use of streets or other property that belongs to the public gives the community or state a special interest in their management. If a city or state has given direct financial aid in getting one of these utilities started, there is all the more reason for it to feel concerned about the proper use of the privileges it has granted. (4) Sometimes public utilities have either deliberately or unintentionally passed under the control of politicians. Occasionally the franchises or grants of authority given to the utilities have been actually bought through money paid to politicians. Sometimes these franchises have given such extensive privileges to the corporation as to make it almost independent of the community which it serves. (5) The tendency toward monopoly has been a problem in connection with public utilities. Some of them are almost inevitably monopolies. In any community except a very large one, it would be a nuisance to have more than one street-car company. Even when desirable unification is brought about, underhanded methods have sometimes been used. Holding companies have been created for the sole purpose of making profit out of the ownership of stock in subsidiary companies rather than improving their management. The sale of watered stock and other evils of dishonest handling of capital have also appeared among public utilities.

The establishment of many public utilities calls for the investment of large amounts of money, and this fact alone adds new problems. 

Sometimes stock has been sold or bonds have been issued that did not represent any proper investment in the business. Sometimes, too, the ownership of the majority of the stock has passed into the hands of a very few individuals and their control of the business has shown little regard for the interests of the smaller stockholders. 

It is also important that consumers shall be satisfied with what they have to pay for services. As more and more people make use of the services the utilities render, it might be expected, other things being equal, that they could render better service than when they started, or at least equally good service at a lower cost. On the other hand, consumers do not always realize that, almost without exception, the utilities have to pay much higher wages than when they were organized,

that the cost of raw material in the form of coal or other things has gone up greatly, and that there has been a steady tendency to levy higher taxes on them.

It does not always pay to raise rates, even when the cost of operation has gone up. Nowhere nearly so many people would pay ten cents to ride on a street car as would pay five. Sometimes the boards and commissions which have authority over the utilities have prevented increases in rates or required reductions because they honestly thought it was to the interest of the corporation as well as of the public. 

Our railways, both local and national, have furnished particular problems in recent years. Street railways were developed very rapidly during the years preceding and following the beginning of the twentieth century, and for a while rendered very useful service to both city and country. Then came the automobile, and almost without warning the business of the street railways and interurban lines fell off tremendously. It was only a matter of a few years before one street railway after another went into bankruptcy. Instead of the five-cent fare which was once pretty general, six, eight, and ten cents, "three for a quarter," and other prices have been tried, none of which have been entirely satisfactory.

The same forces that brought disaster or serious competition to the street railway lines made their impression also upon the great railways of the country. Highways built at public expense were used by buses and trucks to carry passengers and freight that once went over the railroad. The railroad, which had to construct and maintain its own road, was taxed besides, and perhaps some of the tax that the railroad paid helped to build the roads for its competitors to travel over. Commuters bought autos. Some car-owners would drive three or four hundred miles in a day instead of going by train. And if the railroads raised their charges either for passenger travel or for freight, more people would buy autos or send their freight by truck. Some railroads, however, had the foresight and good judgment to use buses and trucks themselves to supplement the kinds of service they had previously been giving.

The National Association of Railroad Managers pointed out that the income they receive for five months of the year is paid out in wages, and that other expenses for coal, for necessary upkeep, and for fixed charges of various sorts leaves only five days' income out of the year to

be paid in dividends to stockholders of the railroad companies. Some railroads cannot even pay interest on their bonds, and a few of them, some of the time, do not take in as much as their day-by-day operating expenses. Nobody can stand that kind of financial strain very long. 

We cannot, for our own sakes, let either street railways or nationwide railway lines disappear without some practical substitute. But neither can we expect private capital to keep such activities going without any return.

Is capital more, or less, important in the railway business than in others? 

Does it make any difference to the public whether a railroad hands out many free passes? If the railroads of the country were completely tied up, how much would your own community be affected at the end of three weeks? 

What particular problems affecting public utilities have been of outstanding interest in your community? 

266. Agencies to Regulate Public Utilities. The first attempts to bring the "utilities" under control were made by some of the states in the 1870's. Farmers were often incensed at the kind of treatment they got from railroads in connection with the shipping of their farm products to market. The nation-wide farmers' organization commonly known as the Grange succeeded in getting some of the state legislatures to pass laws intended to make the railroads more reasonable in their methods. Things which the Grange and some other people complained about included the following: (1) One evil was discrimination - giving special rates or other favors to some people that were not given to others. Sometimes shippers who sent large amounts of goods over a road were secretly handed back in the form of rebates part of what they were supposed to pay. There was also discrimination shown between towns, for rates could be made much more acceptable to some towns than to others. (2) More was sometimes charged to transport freight between one division point and some town along the line than was charged for shipping the whole way from the division point to a larger town some distance away. That made it hard for the little town in between. 

The railroad's argument was that it cost just as much to handle the goods at the way station in between the two big ones as it did to unload perhaps the whole car at the end of a trip. But now the charging of as much or more for a "short haul" than for a longer trip over the same road in the same direction has been forbidden. 

---

(3) In order to get rid of the expense and trouble of competition, two or three railroads serving the same general territory might enter into an arrangement known as pooling (8 222). Then nobody had any inducement to improve service or otherwise attract patronage. 

The fact that in many cases a railroad could not help having a monopoly of its particular kind of transportation in a certain region was another argument for further control. A state legislature could do nothing with a railroad or any other kind of public utility outside of the limits of the state. 

Since most of the big railroads operate in several states, it was an almost impossible task to get all the states to pass the same kind of legislation about them. 

But Congress had the constitutional right to regulate "commerce between the states." In the one hundredth year after the Constitution was drawn up it finally passed the act setting up the Interstate Commerce

Commission. Its powers were mild enough, compared with what it has today, but it was a beginning. The Commission. 

was allowed to investigate complaints against railroads when cases were brought to its attention. It was at first made up of five members appointed by the 

President. Since then railroads, sleeping-car companies, bus lines, oil pipe lines, and inland waterways have come under its authority, and for some time telephone and telegraph lines were also. Its membership has been increased to eleven, and for a long time now it has had the right to investigate cases without waiting for formal complaints, and to fix a maximum rate that might be charged for service of any kind. Naturally, when the Commission decides what the maximum rate may be, that in all probability is the rate that it will be. 

Black Star A REMINDER OF THE OLD DAYS 

Once sailing vessels of this kind were fairly common. In those days there was no Panama Canal for them to be towed through, and interstate commerce offered fewer problems.

Some have found considerable fault with the I. C. C., but nobody proposes to abolish it. The railroads can neither lower wages nor raise fares without the permission of some public body, and both of those items are matters of considerable seriousness. No one can tell except by experiment whether a railroad will get more revenue these days from a 2¢ fare per mile than it will for a 2¢ fare, but one hates to try mere experiments on something so vital to the country's wellbeing as are the railroads. Several times the proposal has been offered to combine all the railroads of the country into a small number of big systems, and thus to strengthen the smaller roads, but just now neither the railroads nor the Interstate Commerce Commission is especially enthusiastic about the proposition. 

When the Federal Communications Commission was organized (1934), it took over the supervision of the telegraph and telephone lines from the Interstate Commerce Commission, and of the radio, which had been under a separate Federal Radio Commission. Its responsibility for the utilities under its control is much the same as that of the Interstate Commerce Commission over the railroads and other utilities. The radio makes the most work for this commission now, for it is still a relatively new element in our social and business life and its scope has almost no bounds. 

When the federal government decided to go into the business of regulating interstate commerce, the states did not give up regulation within the state. Most of the states have set up their own commissions, sometimes separate ones for the railroads, and sometimes commissions to deal with all kinds of public utilities. They are most often known as a Public Service Commission, a Public Utility Commission, or a Public Utilities Commission. For steam railroads, electric roads, light and power plants, and the like, they have authority within their respective states corresponding to that which the Interstate Commerce Commission has in the federal government. 

The fixing of rates, whether passenger or freight, is often no easy job. We could just say that so many cents a pound or ton of a certain kind of freight sounds reasonable and let it go at that. But the matter is nowhere nearly so simple. It seldom costs ten times as much to carry by rail a thousand pounds of goods as it costs to carry a hundred pounds. The work of handling comes when the goods are put on or off, and while the train is in motion nobody may be needed to look

after them. The cost of moving a train of ten cars may be very little more than for one of five cars. So many expenses in operating a railroad must be incurred regardless of the amount of business it does, that it is hard to set a rate per pound or ton that will be equally fair to carrier and patron all the time. Such expenses are often referred to as joint costs because they apply to the whole business and not to any particular service that is rendered. 

Another question, sometimes troublesome, relates to the valuation of the property of public utilities in considering what is a fair rate for them to earn.

Should this value be the same as the original cost, or what it would honestly cost now to replace the property if it were destroyed? Since the cost of so many things, including raw materials and labor, is so much greater today than it used to be, there might be a difference of thousands or perhaps millions of dollars between the two figures. You can readily see that there might be two very different opinions on such a matter. 

Would a railroad be likely to sell a ticket from New York to Chicago for $5.00? If so, when? Would it ever be profitable to do so? It has often been said that a railroad's policy is likely to be to charge "all the traffic will bear." Is that unreasonable? What kinds of people would make the most satisfactory members of a Public Utility Commission or Public Service Board? 

What do you think of the proposal of the F. C. C. that no radio chain should operate two networks? How much authority would you give the F. C. C. over radio stations? 

267. Government Ownership and Operation. — People who take it for granted that a government can do anything are often ready to jump at a proposal for government ownership and operation of public utilities as the answer to all the problems in that field. Many other countries have gone much further in that direction than we have. 

Not only Soviet Russia, but such nations as Germany, Italy, Switzerland, and Sweden, have government ownership and operation of their railroads and of many other activities that in this country we leave to private enterprise.

Not all industries are equally fitted for government ownership and operation. Those which are definitely new in character or depend on whims or personal likes and dislikes for their patronage must regularly be left for private enterprise, because no government will knowingly take the risk of putting goods on the market which people may not RR 17.09 DU SO ST 01 MS to .9

want or becoming unpopular for failing to supply what the people do want. It is in providing such fundamental necessities as transportation and communication, water, electricity, and the like, that a government could, with some show of success, assume responsibility. 

Whether government ownership where it has been tried is successful is one of the matters which would be mentioned in the usual debate on the subject. Sometimes it works, and sometimes it does not succeed any too well. Considerable depends upon the attitude of a people. If they are in the habit of being told by someone what to do and what not to do, they are likely to be more ready to take public operation of utilities for granted than in a country which has encouraged individual enterprise and allowed most people to choose for themselves how they want to make a living. In such projects as furnishing pure water for a community, however, people who do not generally believe in the principle of government ownership and operation of industry will go along with the idea, because the measure affects community and individual health, and that is a field in which government supervision and regulation unquestionably has a right to enter. 

The leading arguments offered in behalf of government ownership of public utilities include the following: www Inva 

James Sawders

PUBLIC SERVICE 

In Helsinki and other places of northern

Europe public telephone booths are maintained by the government for general use, in about the same way that hotels and similar places have them in this country. (1) Government operation will get rid of the element of private profit in the operation of public utilities. They can either be carried on at cost or, if there is a profit, this profit may reduce taxes that would otherwise have to be levied on some other source of income. (2) Government ownership will take the enormous capital investment in public utilities away from a few wealthy people or corporations and put

it into the hands of the representatives of the people. This would do away with the corrupting influence of big business upon government, so it is said. (3) Many public utilities depend upon sources of power and other resources that are gifts of nature and, therefore, should be operated by the whole people in the interest of all. Others are given the right to make use of streets and other public property or are granted the privilege of eminent domain. 

(4) Government ownership and operation is the surest way to control disputes between labor and capital. (5) There are numerous examples of successful government operation. 

Our own Panama Canal, the "Hydro" system of Ontario, and well-managed municipal water systems can be mentioned as instances of efficient public service in our own continent.

On the other hand, there are arguments against public ownership and operation which to many people seem strong. (1) Government operation would not be as efficient as private management. Competition, which is a spur to efficiency in private business, would be totally lacking. Public officials are notoriously shiftless and wasteful because the materials they work with are not their own and cost them nothing. (2) Taking the control of great investments out of private hands wouldsimply turn them over to political bosses. Employment on public works would then become a matter of party. (3) The great achievements of public utilities in this country have come through private development. To take over these utilities without compensation would be an outrage. To pay their present owners what their properties are worth would mean an enormous addition to the government's debt. 

(4) There is no assurance that disputes between labor and capital would be avoided if we had government ownership. Organized workers would demand control of political parties, and any defiance of their demands would lead to discontent, strikes, and even civil war. (5) In many countries where public operation prevails, people are satisfied with a poorer quality of service than our people would put up with. Besides, there is a big difference between running a municipal water system and operating a railroad stretching from coast to coast. 

In favor of government ownership are usually found unions of railroad workers and sometimes farmers' organizations. People who for any reason have an unkind feeling toward big business interests are

also likely to favor government ownership. On the other side are lined up the great majority of the business men of the country who are sure that private business is more efficient than public. Many professional men and women are also likely to oppose the government's taking over activities that could be privately operated. 

Our federal government had one big adventure into government operation. The World War caused the federal government to take over the operation of the railroads of the country, for it wanted to use them in transporting men and war materials without regard to purely private interests. Toward the end of the War period, the telephone and telegraph lines were also taken over for a little while, and some thought that the changed situation would be permanent. 

But the railroads could not make both ends meet without appropriations from the treasury, in spite of increases in freight and passenger rates. When the period of government operation was over, considerable expenditure was necessary to get the equipment of the roads in first-class shape again. During the War there were repeated increases in wages of employees to prevent them from going into private employment at higher figures. It is only fair to say, however, that this experience with the railroads gives no dependable proof of anything, for it was government operation of privately owned utilities. 

Nobody would want that permanently unless it was certain that private operation was no longer profitable, and public operation was the only way to save the railroads. 

Some years ago there was much argument over a proposal for a "physical valuation" of railroad property - that is, an effort to find out exactly what that property is worth in money. Why has such an undertaking proved of little value? What experiences has your community had with public ownership and operation of anything? 

268. Government and Natural Resources. - One hates to think that anyone can have attended modern schools for the length of time that must have been the fortune of most of the readers of this book without having learned something about the problem of conserving our natural resources, and about some of the things that have been done to accomplish this. The underlying principles applying to the subject are so easy to comprehend that any eighth-grader should be able to grasp their significance. But it would be a shame if, by failing to take a page or two to summarize the main features of this 

---

problem, we should let any reader get the impression that we did not realize its importance. 

Your study of history has told you how, until the time of Theodore Roosevelt, the appeals of those who thought we should pay attention to this problem sounded like the voice of one crying in the wilderness. 

Charles R. Van Hise, President of the University of Wisconsin, Gifford Pinchot, Chief of the United States Forest Service, and a few others, spoke and wrote on the subject, but it took the prestige of the White House in the days of Teddy Roosevelt to make people in general see its importance. We had talked about the vast riches of the country - its forests, its streams, its wealth underground, its fertile soil and thoughtlessly had acted as if these were unbounded and no harm could come from their use. Indeed, this is a matter in which the help of government is essential to its proper administration. 

Always there will be those who care more for the profits they can make today than the preservation of that source of profits for future use. 

Always there will probably be those who will not recognize mistaken methods of farming or lumbering or mining until some authority forcibly calls their mistakes to their attention, or some calamity brings home to them the error of their ways. And government has achieved enough in the field of conservation to prove that it may vitally help in promoting the general welfare of the nation. 

Theodore Roosevelt's first emphasis was on forests. As early as 1891 Congress had authorized the President to withdraw from occupation for homesteading or for sale for other purposes lands which had valuable timber. But it was Roosevelt who first took advantage of this authority on an extensive scale. He included some regions in those which he set aside which were capable of effective use in some other way, but it is easier to throw such regions open again for general use than to let land be taken up by private enterprise and then try to get it away from its private owners. Many states also have set up their forest reserves in similar fashion, along with other regions possessing geysers, waterfalls, mountain scenery, or suitable for outdoor recreation for the general public so that they would be available to all at slight cost or none at all. 

The Forest Service in the national Department of Agriculture is now in charge of the administration of the national forest reserves. 

Under its authority the cutting of trees in our national forests, the use 

ST

of some public lands for herds of cattle and sheep, and the maintenance of lookouts to watch for forests fires, are undertaken. The National 

Park Service in the Department of the Interior looks after those regions which have been set aside as national parks or national monuments.¹

Still more recent than the discovery of the need of forest conservation has come a realization that the use of land for cultivation also demands thought. Wind and rain may carry away soil that is not held in place by grass or growing crops. Especially is this true in regions where forests have been cut down which also helped in holding the rainfall and making the flow of water less rapid. The wearing away of soil we call erosion. In many parts of our country, especially in the South, we can see the great gullies that have been formed by water pouring down the hillsides and carrying away much of the good soil. We have already referred to the advantages of contour cultivation in taking proper care of the soil. We have now a Soil 

Conservation Service in the Department of Agriculture to make recommendations and give advice about such matters as these. 

Our Plains states in the Middle West suffered another unforeseen misfortune when during the World War there was a greater demand than usual for wheat, and lands were sown to wheat which probably never should have been used for that purpose. Then, after the rich profits of a season or two had passed and there was no longer the same demand for wheat, came periods of drought and heavy winds which picked up the top soil and carried it sometimes for miles. Thus came into being the so-called Dust Bowl, which threw thousands of farmers into poverty and turned some of them into restless migrants, such as the "Okies" who tried to find in California a means of living which they no longer dared to expect in their former homes. Five states in a row, from North Dakota to Oklahoma, lost from five to ten per cent of their people in the ten years between 1930 and 1940. 

Sometimes we added to our fruitful land by constructing irrigation systems with the help of dams in our rivers and ditches dug out many miles into the country. The most famous of these for a considerable time was the Roosevelt Dam in Arizona. The Shoshone Dam in 

Wyoming for a time had the reputation of being the highest of all. 

1 These are usually small areas possessing some one natural wonder or noted as being the location of some significant event which it is desired to commemorate.

A little further we mention some of the most notable recent undertakings of the kind. Some have wondered how far we should go in trying to make more land available for agriculture when we were already paying some farmers for not growing the things they otherwise would.

But just as water is needed to make the desert "blossom as the rose," so water out of place can do vast harm. Protection from floods is another activity of government which has in recent years become extensive and important. Planting forests near the sources of rivers, constructing dams and reservoirs to hold back water until it can run off slowly enough to do no harm, deepening the beds of rivers so that they can carry off more water- all these help to keep "Old Man River" and his main branches, as well as some other streams, under proper control. 

Water for transportation and water for power are other uses of one of nature's gifts. The construction of locks and dams in rivers has encouraged the use of them by steamboats, and made it possible for a boat not too large to go all the way from Pittsburgh to the mouth of the Mississippi and beyond without unloading its cargo. The 

Inland Waterways Commission has also been established, which maintains its own cargo boats on the Mississippi and a few of its main tributaries. To deal with the use of water power on our national forest reserves and in navigable streams, the Federal Power Commission of five members appointed by the President has been set up, which must give its consent before private enterprise can undertake such use of the nation's natural advantages.

From this elevated point in Pennsylvania water flows into three rivers whose mouths are far apart. There have been arguments over the question as to whether Congress has authority over the whole length of such streams just because they become navigable further along. 

---

Coal and oil are among the most valuable of nature's gifts to the United States and to some other countries also. Shall any corporation that wants to engage in the business of getting these out of the earth be allowed to do so? Or should some definite system of control be set up to prevent the unwise production of these commodities, at the same time seeing to it that they are available in quantities sufficient for our industrial needs? Just as lands were planted to wheat during the World War only to be the cause of much unpleasantness later, so coal was mined, and later on, when the demand fell off, mines were closed and miners with their families left unemployed and sometimes in danger of poverty, if not starvation. To find out what is wrong with the coal industry, the Bituminous Coal Commission was set up in Franklin Roosevelt's administration. Such states as Pennsylvania also had serious problems connected with their mining industry which involved many thousands of workers and millions of dollars of investment. We do not know yet just what is the best way to deal with the problems of our coal and oil production, but at least we know that the problems exist.

We have room only to mention the conservation of animal life, which has an importance of its own. We did not think of it soon enough to prevent the complete wiping out of the passenger pigeon and one or two other species of birds. The bison, or buffalo, almost met the same fate, though now the danger seems to be over. 

States have their fish and game laws, putting limits upon the times in which people may go out to kill specified birds and animals, either for food or for sport, and in the federal Department of the Interior we have now the Fish and Wildlife Service, which has the general oversight of our public activities of this kind. 

The most notable government enterprise resting on the idea of conservation is that undertaken by the Tennessee Valley Authority. 

During the World War the government undertook to construct a great dam across the Tennessee River in Northern Alabama at a point commonly known as Muscle Shoals. This project was not finished, and for several years after the War there was much argument as to what should be done with it.

President Franklin Roosevelt had the idea that, with the completion of the Muscle Shoals Dam as a starter, a great experiment that would cover the whole Tennessee Valley might be undertaken. So a com-

mission of three persons was appointed to take charge of this whole enterprise, which covered parts of seven states, and was operated under the name of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). The 

Wilson Dam was finished at Muscle Shoals, and others, one known as the Norris Dam, were constructed farther up in the Valley, and provisions made for disposing of power either to private power companies or directly to communities. 

THE NORRIS DAM 

This dam, a part of the Tennessee Valley Project, stores up a great volume of water. Flood control, as well as supply of power, is an objective of such projects. 

Automobiles, as you see, drive across the top of the dam. 

There was some question about the constitutional right of the federal government to go into such enterprises. The technical foundation for them rested upon the recognized authority of Congress to pass laws for improving navigable rivers. The United States Supreme 

Court decided that if, in doing this, electric power was incidentally created, it might be marketed in such a way as the federal government wishes. There has been no ruling from the Court on the right to use the activities of the TVA as a basis for social improvements. A large sum was finally paid to private capitalists who sold out their property

and rights to the TVA. An important Supreme Court decision with significant implications was rendered in December, 1940, in a case involving the New River in Virginia and West Virginia. Although it was asserted that 41 states took the opposite view, it was ruled that any river which was capable of being made navigable is subject to the authority of Congress over interstate commerce, and that a company wishing to build a dam in such a river must get a license from the Federal Power Commission. 

Similar projects for construction of dams and reservoirs have been undertaken in several parts of the country. The most notable of these are Boulder Dam in the Colorado River, and Grand Coulee and Bonneville in the Columbia River. In the case of Boulder Dam, the effort was made to keep out of unnecessary interference with or competition with private water and power companies. Some have proposed that the whole country should be divided into six or seven regions, in each of which there might be some sort of "authority" like the TVA. Others protest feelingly that it is not right for a government to ruin private investments by direct competition, and further, that if they are ruined, no more revenue will be received from taxes on them. Then new taxes on some other source of revenue will have to be introduced which may more than make up for any savings to the public in lower rates for electric power and light. 

Add to this list of activities in the field of conservation any others which you think of that pertain to the same general theme. What conservation problems are most serious in your own state? What agencies does your state government have for dealing with any of them? If you have visited any of our national parks, our great irrigation dams, or other public works of similar character, tell the class about them. You will find interesting the history of 

California's Imperial Valley. (Do not forget that some notable irrigation projects were undertaken by private companies before the federal government got into the game.) Plan a tour of the United States for a summer in which you would visit as many as possible of regions and activities discussed in this section. 

269. The Government and Prosperity. Every time in our history when there has been a serious panic or business depression, if there have been at that same time two political parties of considerable strength, the party in power has lost favor, and the opposite party profited. The financial panic of 1837 in Van Buren's administration preceded the first national victory of the Whig party. The panic of 

---

1857 preceded the defeat of the Democratic party in 1860, though this, of course, was complicated by the argument over slavery. The depression of the 1870's, coupled with the political scandals of Grant's administration, led to a great increase in the Democratic strength in the country. The depression of 1893 to 1896 overthrew the Democrats and gave the Republicans a new lease of power. The depression which began in 1929 threw out the Republicans and put the Democrats in again. Our people have acted as if any administration in power ought to keep the country prosperous.

Perhaps right here we may ask what we mean by prosperity, anyway. You recall that even in years when we thought we were prosperous as a nation, probably two million people were unemployed at any given time. When corporations in general are paying good dividends on their stock and some people are able to save considerable amounts, not everybody in the nation is likely to be contented or to feel well off. Perhaps we might properly say that a country is prosperous when poverty and low standards of living are problems of individuals or families rather than of large groups of the people.

President Franklin Roosevelt attracted considerable attention by referring to "one-third of a nation" as "ill-fed, ill-clothed, ill-housed." 

It is hard to believe, however, that except in very abnormal times anywhere nearly one person in three or one family in three thought they were ill-fed, ill-clothed, or ill-housed. Many a family has not realized that it came under those classifications until some social worker came around and told them so. 

But when unsatisfactory conditions do exist on a large scale, what, then, is the duty of the government? There are several alternatives. (1) It can co-operate with churches, lodges, and charitable societies in making needs known. (2) It can make its public employment agencies more active than ever, and can encourage those who temporarily have no job to come together and exchange services or goods to help out one another. (3) It can arrange for gifts or doles or "relief" to those who are out of work or otherwise unable to look out for themselves, and it can often provide work so as to enable the recipients to earn what they get, at least in part. (4) It can advise business men or aid them by loans to keep going as nearly normally as possible. 

A 7.8 

A 400 M 2.2

In depressions before that of the 1930's, the federal government seemed to feel that since it was private business that was in distress, things should be allowed to take their natural course until the country recovered from its economic sickness. In the latter part of Hoover's administration, the first step of a different nature was undertaken when, by setting up the RFC (Reconstruction Finance Corporation), PWA AND WPA These men were working on a project which consisted of laying a new surface for a road just south of the White House. Though probably some PWA and WPA money was wasted, worth-while things were done that would not otherwise have been done and men unemployed were given a chance to work. means were provided to aid business organizations, in the hope that when private business revived, opportunities for jobs would come back also.

Under Franklin Roosevelt, however, enormous agencies were established to provide work at public expense. We have given the main facts about the PWA, the CWA, and the WPA in Section 158. They did much to render immediate relief, but critics of such activities have raised some serious questions: (1) Is it good business, in the long run, to do at public expense and on borrowed money things that we can get along without? How will they be paid for in the future?

(2) Will the providing of work at public expense create a permanent list of dependents on the federal government, numerous enough to control any national election? (3) How should we handle such relief as may be warranted at any given time? Should a federal organization do it, or should the federal government simply turn over the money to state and local officials for distribution? (4) When workers go on strike and thus give up their regular source of income, have they the right immediately to go to the public treasury and demand to be put on relief on the ground that they are unemployed?

It is natural, but not necessarily wise, for people who think about these problems to be influenced by what seems to be their own immediate advantage. Over a long period prosperity can be maintained only if we serve the welfare of the whole community or country and

not merely of the selfish advantage of certain groups. Let us be broad-minded and thoughtful about such matters. 

As far as you have observed the operation of PWA or WPA projects, are communities permanently better off for having them done? What advantage or disadvantage do you see between making "relief" a federal proposition or one to be handled by states and local governments? Is there any moral or spiritual loss if relief of the unfortunate becomes a public proposition instead of one calling for sympathy and generosity from those who are better off? 

270. Economic Planning: What and How? - The last decade or more has witnessed a considerable amount of oratory and book writing on the general theme of economic planning. For some of this our successes in the field of conservation were responsible. Since some of the blunders of previous years were so contrary to ordinary common sense, those who had no political or financial responsibility during those tragic times became bold about telling everybody what ought to be done. Some would even give the impression that by some inherent masterful omniscience they could figure out just what ought to be done this year, and next year, and ten years ahead so that there would be no business failures, no unemployment, no bad guesses.

Should economic planning include government price-fixing? We have already pointed out some of the difficulties involved in that (232). If farmers and factory-workers alike ask higher wages or higher prices and both get them, they will both be at about the same point relatively as before. The most important question is, Does any group get less than its services really deserve? That is by no means an easy problem to solve. 

Even if a government succeeds in raising the price of some standard product within our own boundaries, what then? See what happened with the efforts to lift the price of cotton higher than the figure which the world market would naturally support. Other countries which could produce cotton more cheaply were stimulated to produce much more than they had been providing before, and naturally they could find a market for it in countries that had been buying cotton from us. 

Besides, if we try to keep prices up by destroying our surplus of some commodity like corn, or cotton, or cattle, or hogs, we may be getting rid of goods which might be used to supply human need, at the same time that we make them cost more to our own people and reduce the foreign market for them. Laws of Congress cannot repeal the laws of nature.

If a government keeps its citizens well-informed about developments either in the raising of crops, the demand for manufactured goods, or standards of living at home and abroad, intelligent people may be helped to plan their work or business more wisely than if they had no information except that which comes from their own immediate surroundings. Along with this policy we may supervise public utilities enough to see that they keep their charges down to a reasonable point. That is much easier than to fix by law a price for goods produced by strictly private agencies, or for a government to run all kinds of business itself. But if there is to be effective economic planning, it must be done by or under the direction of a government. 

If your community or some neighboring one has a public water system, on what basis does it make its charges for the water furnished through that system? What examples have you noticed recently of the fixing of rates by

Public Utility Commissions or similar bodies for goods or services furnished by them?

Regardless of objectors, it does seem as if government in the future must take a greater part in the promotion of social and economic welfare than it has taken in the past. If we were all satisfied to let everybody live as he did in the past — but few of us are! On the other hand, will private citizens, just as soon as they become public officials, cease to be selfish in looking out for the interests of those who put them in office? Will men sometimes find themselves in public office who are not qualified for important jobs in overseeing vast industries? And can we have effective planning without turning our whole system of private enterprise into a Nazified regimented state machine? Maybe we should see first how our recent activities, such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, the housing programs, our social security laws, and our labor relations acts, work out. 

Is it surprising that men who have given their lives to business management are usually hesitant about transferring to government officials any extended power over what they have been doing? Would things be better or worse if every individual or corporation who wanted to start a new industry or make extensive changes in the operation of one with which he had been connected should have to get permission of a public official? 

The proper policy of any government, of course, is the greatest good for the greatest number. Sometimes it is impossible to make reforms

without harming somebody. If a thousand people are to be helped and only one hundred injured, other things being equal, the welfare of the thousand should have first consideration. But if giving small benefits to the thousand is going to ruin the hundred, the undertaking may be neither fair nor wise.

Co-operation is the word and thought we need. Co-operation does not mean that one side must give in completely to the other except

XXII  

Economics not only tells us about the way things are done in the world of business and industry, but it has a place in our everyday lives. The kind of economic society that we want is one that will make good citizens more comfortable and contented. To bring about such a condition calls for an understanding of the means by which we may put to good use what society lets us have. Sometimes when we get into difficulty, it is because we have been too stupid or willful to do the best we can with our own opportunities.

Some Questions: 

1. How is wealth distributed in this country, and why is it distributed that way? 

2. What standards of living do our people in general desire, and with what standards do some of them put up? 

3. What elements must enter into everyone's cost of living, and what elements do enter into others'? 

4. What are some sound principles for planning our personal spending and saving? 

5. How may we use our savings to best advantage when we have any? 

271. The Distribution of Wealth. - You remember, of course, that to the economist distribution most often means, as it does here, the sharing of the returns from production among those who have taken part in it. If we were thinking of distribution from the functional standpoint, we might be trying to decide how much should go to labor as labor, or to capital as capital, or to any other impersonal factor. 

But just now we will make it personal and try to apply the principles of distribution to individuals and to families. 

The service one renders in economic activity may or may not determine the returns he will get. Some have only their daily or yearly receipts to go on. What they get this year is spent this year. Others save up something which will make things easier for them in the future, either because they are lucky enough to escape misfortune, or because they use more wisely what does come into their hands. 747

In 1938, according to the United States Bureau of Internal Revenue, there were forty-eight net incomes of $1,000,000 or more in the United States. The all-time high for such incomes was in 1929 when there were 513 reported. Forty-eight of that size means that about one person in every 3,000,000 in the United States had $1,000,000 left after paying his business bills. Yet the average income for all people "gainfully employed" in 1938 was not more than $1800, and some millions received nowhere nearly that figure but at the same time supported a family.

Naturally we need to be careful how we use such statistics. In 1938 the average person with an income of $1,000,000 or more had to turn over more than half of that in income taxes to the federal government. 

At the other end of the line, there were many people who never would receive $1800 in a year if they should live to be as old as Methuselah, and others who lived better doing nothing on relief money than they ever did when they worked for a living. If we divided up the total wealth of the country evenly, according to some reasonable estimates, there might be about $2600 or $2700 for each person. So even if we did "share the wealth" in that way nobody would be very rich. 

Much of it, too, could not possibly be shared. How would you divide up a factory, for instance, or a railroad? You could divide the income from it, perhaps, but not the wealth itself. 

Besides, it makes a tremendous difference what people do with the wealth they have. We have no reason to think that these forty-eight millionaires of 1938 were the forty-eight happiest people in the country. 

Why does the possession or lack of wealth fail to prove either comfort or contentment? How do conditions in your own community compare with those in other parts of the country in regard to the distribution of wealth? 

If any well-known rich men have recently died, what became of their wealth after their death? 

272. "Rich Man, Poor Man." - In passing judgment on the distribution of wealth we must take into account what those who had great wealth did with it. The story was told that Andrew Carnegie once said he wanted to die a poor man, and so he meant to give away all but $25,000,000. There was a time in Carnegie's life when $25,000,000 must have looked like all the money in the world. But he gave away far more than that and became one of the great benefactors of his own and other countries. Few would justify everything .

that was done in building up the Rockefeller fortune; but today 

John D. Rockefeller, Jr., is undoubtedly popular because he has tried to use the wealth which he inherited or earned for the improvement of his fellow men. Would that wealth have been equally well spent if it had been evenly distributed throughout the United States? 

Some think that great wealth in private hands has done about all that it can do for the world, and that the future policy of this or any

other country should be to prevent the amassing of great fortunes by anyone. It is for that reason, as well as to get revenue for the government, that our laws put high taxes on large incomes. Few people are willing to work hard for any kind of income if they know their increased income is going to be taken right away from them in the form of taxes.

Proposals for a redistribution of wealth quite naturally come most often from those who have nothing to redistribute. But many will

agree that a community or national life is unsound if millions of people have to live at or just above a starvation level. Moreover, it makes a big difference what any individual or family would do with added wealth or income if he knew it was coming. 

Does an increase in the number of millionaires mean a concentration or a distribution of wealth? Could a society made up of persons with small incomes carry on large-scale activities? What would you do if you received $1,000,000? 

273. Standards and Levels of Living. We may define standards of living as meaning one's ideals about the kind and quality of life experiences he would like, while we may speak of levels of living as referring to the actual conditions which a person or group is able to maintain. Or we may use the word "standards" for both those situations, and call one an ideal standard and the other an actual standard. 

Three elements have something to do with one's actual standards or levels of living. In the first place, it makes a big difference how much he wants. Some are perfectly satisfied to live in an environment and with a lack of comfort which others would find intolerable. Some act as if physical comfort was the most important thing in life, while others find more pleasure in good music, good books, and the companionship of high-minded people. One's money income is also important, for it determines the extent to which one may enjoy the material comforts and pleasures of life, and perhaps also the chance for culture and refinement.

Still a third factor is the standard of prices prevailing in a given community or at a given period. Fifty years ago $600 a year would enable a family at least to keep out of poverty and to have a reasonable amount of comfort and recreation. Today - what do you think?

It would be pretty hard in a large city, but maybe not impossible in a village or rural community. The farmer may not have as many opportunities to spend as the city man, but there are many things that cost him much less. 

Would there be a gain or loss if everybody should have the opportunity to spend money for satisfying his wants that the ordinary rich man has? 

In some countries three very definite social classes are found. At the bottom, and including by far the largest proportion of all the people, are the poor. Sometimes we refer to them as the proletariat.

They have fewer material comforts than those in the two classes above them, but generally have larger families to care for. 

The middle class, called often in a European country the bourgeoisie, includes professional people, business men and their families, and in some cases the more fortunate or successful of those who make their living by their hands. It is often said that a large and satisfied middle class is the surest basis for a sound national life. Its members are not so likely to be carried away by feelings of class injustice or to follow through ignorance the leadership of demagogues, and have a broader understanding of personal and national problems. 

The rich, of course, are distinctly the smallest class as far as number is concerned. Their influence depends often upon what money can do socially, politically, and otherwise. Sometimes it is used to sway the opinions and actions of even the poor, and sometimes to help them to better living. The middle class are sometimes accused of being too anxious to imitate the ideas and customs of the well-to-do. 

In a true democracy there may be grades of wealth, but there is also a free opportunity to move from one class to another. The movement is not always up. The expression, "From shirt sleeves to shirt sleeves in three generations," may tell the sad story of a family that rose out of humble conditions but lost its good sense, and through extravagance and folly dropped back to a station in life sadder than the grandparents knew.

In your own community, do you find this three-grade classification of people? Are conditions in this respect better or worse in your community than in other places that you know? Is there any inherited class distinction in the United States? 

274. Improving Living Conditions. Few of us would exactly agree on the items that would enter into a desirable or an undesirable standard of living. Some would differ only in minor detail, but there might be great disagreement on the kind and extent of amusement or the kind of housing one would want. Some who could afford neat and convenient homes get so much fun outside that they put up with living conditions at home that may be decidedly unattractive to others. 

The school might help us to realize what really is worth having in life, and how to adapt one's own talents to the opportunities which he enjoys or to the conditions in which he must live. We feel now that

since individual men and women differ so much, education should seek to discover individual capacities and interests and to develop those, at the same time trying to get everybody to master as much of the accumulated knowledge of the past as would help us to understand the world we are living in today. The mess hall in a railroad labor camp makes no display of luxury, but usually the men get plenty as far as quantity is concerned.

In late years governments have felt that the majority of the people wanted them to assume much responsibility for encouraging and maintaining suitable standards of living. Some say that this means that we are asking the energetic and successful to pay out of their savings so that the lazy and incompetent can live without working.

But others stress the fact that some people, no matter how hard they try, seem to be unable to obtain even a moderate degree of comfort in life, and as they look toward the future see nothing certain on which they can rely.

It may take some time before we get the perfect answer to all such questions. The same may be said of wage-hour laws covering thousands of workers and applying to a wide extent of territory. What if in some industry the employer is faced with a choice between employing a considerable number of workers at a low wage or throwing many of them out of work in order to pay fewer people higher wages? 

Rules about such matters as overtime may cause inconvenience, to say the least, and it hardly seems fair to punish a worker or an employer or both if they are mutually interested enough to put in an extra half-hour some day.

Should it be the policy of our federal government to make wages and other expenses of business operation the same all over the country? Where does government responsibility for pleasant home life begin or end?

275. Elements in the Cost of Living.

People's wants differ so much and the economic and social conditions under which they live and work are so different that one person may be able to live very comfortably on what means tough going for another. A miner, for instance, may get a higher income than a school teacher but have to spend much less for clothes and other things than the teacher. 

Yet certain general items enter into the cost of living of practically everybody. Fundamental, of course, are food, clothing, and living quarters. Among the many studies and investigations that have been made in regard to the cost of living, one of the most widely known is that made by a German named Engel in the 1850's. Some of his conclusions are referred to as Engel's Law. "As the income of a family increases, the proportionate expenditure for food decreases; that for clothing, rent, fuel, and light remains approximately the same; and that for cultural wants increases." 276. Wise Consumption. Wisdom does not always consist in seeing how little one can spend. If one is sick and he refuses to call in a doctor, he may have to spend more in the end than if he received the doctor's advice earlier. If, in order to save something for old age, one denies himself enough food of good quality and lives by choice in unhealthful surroundings, he may not live to old age to enjoy his savings. 

Wise consumption may also be called constructive consumption.

It means the spending of money for things or activities which will make the spender better or happier or benefit other people. We ought to help our fellow men by aiding in the relief of the unfortunate and contributing to the expense of righteous causes. As good citizens, we ought to keep in touch with what is going on in business, politics, literature, art, and the like. 

As we have said before, what would be wise consumption for one person or at one time might not always be so. Surely there is nothing wrong, for instance, in desiring some amusement and recreation, but what should we think of one who goes to two or three movies a week but never has a cent for the Red Cross or church? We expect a lawyer,

doctor, or teacher to look reasonably neat and to wear clothes suitable for contacts with people in any grade of society, but a farmer or miner would be foolish to keep "dressed up" all the time. H. Armstrong Roberts

ONE WAY TO WASTE MONEY 

Would you imagine that so many people would be willing to risk good money on race horses, even at Hialeah in Miami?

In a New Jersey high school of a few less than 1000 pupils, the pupils spent about $27,000 a year for ice cream, candy, "drug store drinks," chewing gum, peanuts, and that sort of thing. That same group spent in the course of a year $6300 for movies, and other outlays for amusement counted up to over $15,000 more. We cannot prove that these expenditures were actually harmful, but an average of $27 apiece in a year for things to eat and drink outside of mealtime raises considerable question. Taking the country over, two-thirds as much is spent each year for tobacco, candy, chewing gum, soft drinks, and ice cream as for public education.

These remarks may lead to a much debated question, Are expenses for luxuries justifiable? A man who has surplus cash may say, "This is mine, and I have a right to do with it as I please." In addition it is urged that expenses for luxuries provide useful work. The rich man who keeps a chauffeur and a housekeeper rather than drive his car himself or let the women of the family do something at home is helping at least two people to make an honest living. If he spends three or four times as much on his house as would be necessary for him to live comfortably, he may be encouraging business in the community to that extent. 

On the other side some plausible arguments are offered. People who are now engaged in unnecessary work might otherwise go into occupations that would benefit the whole community, instead of providing comfort for only a few. Second, expenses for luxury and display encourage among the poor a desire to imitate the well-to-do, and provoke a spirit of discontent among those who cannot do so. 

It has been said that "the cost of high living is one of the chief causes of the high cost of living." Without trying to make everybody agree about this matter, surely each of us should watch his own conduct so as to make sure that he does not imitate those who throw away their earned or inherited income on harmful amusements or be fooled by those who enjoy making a display of wealth. 

For what do you spend money that would be recognized by anyone as a luxury or should be considered such in your own case? Why did you do it?
