278. Educating the Consumer. Lately we have begun to put into our school programs courses on consumer education. Too often they have been tied up with home economics courses in such a way as to give the impression that only girls need to be educated as consumers,

and that dry goods and groceries are the only goods about which anybody could be educated. Important though such items are, consumer education is a much bigger thing than that. 

For a long time we seemed to take it for granted that people would learn through experience what was useful and worth buying. Perhaps such education is likely to be more effective than any other kind. 

But why should we require young people to have all kinds of unpleasant experiences in spending their money if they can be avoided by proper counsel ahead of time. Advertising is constantly appealing to us in one form or another, and we are often asked to buy things that we do not need or want.

Every one of us is a consumer, whether we earn any of the money that has to be used to feed and clothe us or not. Consumer education means much more than merely avoiding mistakes in buying. It actually touches the whole range of our wants and pleas- 

What ought we to want? How much should we spend? How much should we save, if we get enough to do any saving? In this chapter we can only touch the surface of the big problems. 

People who have small incomes are often the ones who use least wisely what they do receive. A rich man may be willing to pay for a better quality of cloth for a suit than the poor man, but he will probably not go twice to a tailor who does a poor job for him, nor buy a gray suit if he wants a blue one. New ideas for retail markets have reduced considerably the cost of handling the goods. 

There are several varieties, for instance, of "help-yourself stores." But some people think it is beneath their dignity to buy in such places.

an effect on the practices of others. What a pupil learns in school may be taken into the home and the knowledge used for the benefit or detriment of his family. If parents have never learned to spend money to best advantage, helpful suggestions may come from the younger members. And you never can tell how many other people of your age may justify what they are doing by referring to what you do.

Why was the business depression which began in the fall of 1929 so calamitous? One reason was that in the years preceding the break, a habit of reckless buying had been encouraged. The price not only of stocks and bonds, but of some other things, went up to unreasonable figures, and people were carried away with the idea that an era of unlimited prosperity was just ahead of the country. Then, when the bubble burst and the water blew out of these inflated stocks and bonds, people got frightened. Business men who had no need of changing their business plans hesitated to go ahead with their normal activities. They gave small orders or none at all for raw materials and discharged workers right and left in order to cut down expenses. 

All these blunders reduced the volume of business fearfully. With a proper use of common sense in buying and selling, we should neither have gone to the extremes of the decade before 1930 nor fallen into the dumps to the extent we did in 1932.

279. Avoiding Wasteful Consumption. - Now for a few more words about wise consumption. Don't buy things merely because they are cheap. The cheap goods may not last. If we buy things because they are bargains when we know we will not use the goods soon, the money we pay for them is tied up, and we may be prevented from using it for something of more real importance. This is no argument, however, against looking for real bargains or trying to get the best quality you can for the money you spend.

On the other hand, don't buy things merely because they are highpriced. Some storekeepers make it a practice to add to the price they ought to charge for an article and then tell their customers that extra quality is worth extra price. The consumer who will avoid waste needs to have some means of judging the quality of what he is getting so that he may not make a mistake in either direction. 3

That is why, at this point and elsewhere in our school work, we lay stress on the importance of wise spending and the necessity of economy if one is to live comfortably when his earning power is no longer good. 

Whether you handle much money or little, "get your money's worth" - and that doesn't mean, either, trying to get something for nothing. 

Both the merchant and the customer deserve a square deal. 

Nobody can put brains into a person's head. Nobody can do anything for those who will not take advice. Not much can be done except through bitter experience to help people who think they know it all. We can, however, do something for people who are willing to take advantage of the experience of others. Study or work groups of old or young people, or both, who want to co-operate either in finding the facts about buying and selling, or to buy and sell to better advantage as a group, can do much for themselves as individuals and for others.

If nobody spent money foolishly, what features of our community life would be less prominent or would disappear, and what ones would become more prominent? Take some common article either of food or of clothing, such as a pair of shoes, and set up standards that you could take into account in buying that article for yourself. (Each member of the class might take a different commodity.) 

280. What Advertising Does. It would be interesting, if you have not already done so, to make a list of all the different kinds of advertising that have been used in your community within your own knowledge and see what a variety of appeals are made upon people's judgment or credulity. Advertising has two main objectives. For one thing, it aims to make people want things which otherwise they would not. The first pleased user of an electric razor would tell other men about it, and the information might spread so that in the course of half a century a considerable number would learn to use that means of shaving. But how much more rapid is the expansion of the business of making and selling electric shavers if magazines devote pages to display the supposed merits of such articles? A second purpose of advertising is to give the competitor who advertises an advantage over his rivals. The advertiser wishes people to think that his make of automobile, breakfast food, or hat is so distinctly superior to others in either price or personal usefulness that the public will want to buy his brand instead of any other. 

---

A slogan you have probably heard is "It pays to advertise." Did you ask yourself whom it pays and why? Of course it pays the advertiser, or he would not keep it up indefinitely. Firms that spend several thousand dollars for one evening's radio program every week must feel that they get additional returns in the form of increased sale of the things they market. They will not keep on with such expense indefinitely just for the sake of amusing or educating the public.

Advertising also may pay the consumer. If it actually encourages him to compare one brand of goods with another or think seriously as to whether a certain article that he does not possess would be good for him to have and to use, it pays. But advertising does not pay the consumer if it encourages him to spend money for things he does not need or are of little use to him, or if it leads him to pay higher prices for goods that are not better than their competitors' but simply have benefited by more extravagant ballyhooing. 

Free speech over the radio and a free press on the advertising pages are things to be defended. But "free speech" should never be used to justify any kind of misrepresentation. Our laws give the Federal 

Trade Commission the right to investigate claims made through advertising and to issue orders against advertisers to "cease and desist" if they have been guilty of misrepresentation to the public. 

Certain manufacturers of cigarettes used to claim that smoking them would help one to "keep that girlish figure." But the Federal Trade

Commission put a stop to that, for there was not the slightest evidence that any brand of cigarettes would accomplish that result. 

Another questionable practice has been to get some prominent baseball player or other person in the limelight to sign a testimonial declaring that he used somebody's sweaters or mattresses or something else. We need not suppose that all such endorsements are knowingly dishonest, but some official should certainly have the right to protect consumers by finding out whether they are the truth. It would hardly be fair to hold publishers of newspapers and magazines responsible for the correctness of every word that an advertiser submits, but it would be reasonable to require them to refuse to publish something that gives evidence of being misleading or deliberately intended to deceive.

Privately founded organizations, such as Consumers' Research and

!

Consumers' Union, have established testing laboratories and issued publications advising their patrons as to the relative quality of commodities. Such agencies often tell their readers through their publications how to make things for themselves that have all or most of the merits of extensively advertised "package goods." 281. Learning to Be Thrifty. - Thrift and saving do not mean just the same. There can be saving of only those things that are not used up or of money received for things that are sold instead of being used by the producer. Thrift concerns things that are used as well as 

Harold M. Lambert VACATIONS FOR SOME 

This is Miami Beach. If you go there in the winter, you pay much more than in the summer.

those that are not. One definition of thrift declares that thrift is an economical use of time, labor, and money - and we should need to add "goods." The thrifty man need not be stingy. He may avoid harmful and foolish consumption and use carefully what he does have. 

Buying intelligently is still another aspect of thrift. Persons who are not willing to be free spenders may be laughed at as being "Scotch," but if they have not denied themselves the things that are essential to health and decent living, they are the ones who have the "last laugh" which the proverb says is the "best."

In school we can not only learn to be thrifty but practice it. Some people object to the practice of furnishing free textbooks and supplies to school pupils, on the ground that if they had to buy their own books and supplies, they would be much more careful of them. But if a school teaches us to use these things carefully and helps us to establish a habit of thrift that will go on with us through life, it will have done something that is worth all that it has cost the community. 

If, when one is young, he establishes habits of thrift, they are likely to stay with him when he grows older and has to look out for himself. 

The thrifty family may not go to the movies quite as often as some others, but it may be able to own a car when others are not equal to that indulgence. What is thrift for one family might not be for another, but that fact is no excuse for extravagance and wastefulness. "Thrift builds men and cities." 

Keystone View Company GETTING RID OF HIS SPARE CASH 

Pin ball machines are fairly common these days. The fellow who keeps them makes considerably more than the one who plays them. 

Give examples of acts of thrift or the opposite which you have seen yourself- for high school students, office workers, farmers, business men. Do you consider yourself thrifty? Why or why not? Will a thrifty school pupil buy an athletic ticket, own a tennis racquet, contribute to church, pay fines on library books, walk to school, go to the movies every week?

282. What to Do with Our Savings. In order to save, we must avoid spending, but not by any means all spending. Hoarding just for the sake of saving money is decidedly questionable, but saving so as to have something for future needs is thoroughly commendable. 

Saving need not prevent supporting worthy causes or contributing to the relief of those in need, though it does assume that one can live decently without spending all that he receives. 

Doubtless there are many people who, at least when times are not good, cannot save anything if they undertake to keep themselves healthy and live respectably. Unfortunately, however, the distress of some who are in deep need is the result of thoughtlessness, or even worse, in the past, and of continued extravagance. Too much of poor men's income or charity help has gone for liquor. 

But suppose we have saved something. What shall we do with it?

We could just lay it away in a bureau drawer, but a far better place for it is in the bank. Checking accounts rarely pay interest any more, but especially since the FDIC was set up, such savings are safe. 

There are also savings banks and savings departments in other banks which will take your money. If you get much interest upon it these days, you are lucky, but even half of one per cent is better than nothing. At the time this is written, the federal government is also willing and anxious to sell you bonds in denominations as low as $25 which, if kept for a period of ten years, give you the equivalent of almost three per cent interest and that is not bad, either, as interest rates are these days.

Other means of employing one's savings are investments in building and loan associations, especially if one is interested sometime in owning a house for himself, and in credit unions and other co-operative organizations which accept small deposits from their members with the intention of lending them to other members of the organization when desired. 

When one's savings approach or go beyond a thousand dollars, he may begin to be interested in bonds and stocks. Federal government bonds are, of course, about the safest thing in the world in which to place one's savings. The bonds of cities, counties, and states are, on the whole, likely to be safe, but one will do well to inquire about the habit of a local government in paying its bills or paying off its indebtedness when it comes due, before he buys its bonds. If it has

once started borrowing rather than taxing itself to meet ordinary expenses of government, one might reasonably ask questions about the likelihood of its paying back those borrowings when the time comes to do so. In fact, "Investigate before you invest" is a thoroughly desirable slogan for anyone.

Whatever amount of savings one may be able to accumulate, it is well for him to have some of them where he can get at them promptly 

TELLER Keystone View Company THE SAVINGS BANK 

These young people apparently do not spend all they earn. Savings banks no longer pay a high rate of interest, but savings on deposit there are at least not wasted. in case of need. One can never tell when he may have some special reason for using a few hundred dollars on short notice. On the other hand, one may not be so readily tempted to make unwise use of his savings if some of them have been so invested that he cannot turn them into money at any given moment. 

Do the banks in your community maintain Christmas savings funds? If so, find out how they operate. Does your school system maintain a school savings fund or some system of banking? Can or should young people who are not able to earn much for themselves be expected to plan for savings?

283. The Family Budget. The same principles that call for budget-making on the part of governments apply at least equally well to individuals and families. The only people who can safely get along without budget-making are those whose income is regularly more than they care to spend, and who have no extravagant habits. Even such people will find it an advantage to know exactly how they stand at any time. 

Keystone View Company THE FAMILY BUDGET 

This family seems to take care every month of what it will do with the family income. 

It is a good sign when all have a share in talking things over. 

Why do people fail to keep budgets, anyway? Probably the answer in most cases is that they are too lazy to sit down for an hour or so every month and do some figuring. Others were never brought up to do anything of the kind. Their own fathers and mothers drifted along from day to day with only an occasional guess as to the way things were going to turn out, and perhaps were lucky enough to get by without serious illness or other unforeseen expense. 

Perhaps it wouldn't be good business for the younger members of a

family to start in at once to reform the older ones; but if your family has not formed the habit, why not start a budget system on your own account? Then if you find that it works, you can tell the others and then get the whole group to do things in a more careful way. Plenty of people could give evidence of money troubles resulting from neglect to plan. 

Most of us who have regular jobs can tell pretty nearly what we are going to receive in a week, a month, or a year, depending on the way we are paid. If we spend more than a few dollars a year, we know fairly well what we are going to spend for at particular dates. It does not take a great deal of arithmetic to figure out how much we must spend in a month or a year, and how much there will be left for us to spend for things that are not necessities, and to save. Some banks and business corporations issue books or printed forms for the keeping of family budgets.

284. Kinds and Values of Insurance. A great deal of money is spent in this country for insurance. To some of us it may seem just a gamble. You bet, for example, that your house will burn down, and the fire insurance company bets that it won't. If it doesn't burn down, you are out what you have paid. If it does, you get back a 

---

great deal more than the amount of the premiums you have paid. 

Why are you willing to do this, if you are? Because if you are unfortunate, your loss will be wholly or partly met by what you get out of the insurance company. If you do not have a fire, you at least have been relieved from the worry that you might constantly suffer from fear of one.

Why does a fire or life insurance company take the chances it does? 

Because from the records of the past it is possible to guess with considerable accuracy how much property is going to be destroyed by fire in a given period, and how many people are going to die. Then the companies can figure out how much they will have to charge so that they can meet the demands on their treasury when they do have to make payments, and have something left over for profit and to carry on the running expenses of the organization. 

Some kinds of insurance are offered not merely to meet future misfortune but as a means of saving. You take out an insurance policy under which you agree to pay a company so many dollars a year. At the end of a given period you get back from the company either a lump sum somewhat greater than the total of what you have paid in, or receive yearly payments from the company as long as you live. (This latter plan is often referred to as an annuity.) How can the company pay you back more than you paid in? Because it has taken the money you paid and bought bonds or made some other kind of investment with it that has brought the company somewhat greater returns than it has to pay you.

Some people regard insurance agents as pests and promptly look the other way when they see one coming. The honest agent - he may prefer to be called a counselor - will not pretend that he is concerned entirely with your own welfare, for selling insurance is the way he makes his living. But he can maintain that he is proposing something that will benefit you as well as himself. Of course people can take out so much insurance in one form or another that it becomes a real burden to pay the premiums on it. We need to use judgment about this as about most other things. 

Insurance may be obtained for a great variety of purposes. A pianist may carry many thousands of dollars' worth of insurance on his hands. Charlie McCarthy is insured for $10,000. Some companies make a special business of insurance against flood and tornado,

and even crop failure, against rain on important days, against shipwreck, against illness, accidents and possible visits to hospitals, and many other possible emergencies. 

Among the many forms which life insurance may take, the following are typical — straight life, twenty-payment life, endowment. Find out the difference among these. Inquire from an insurance agent what would be the yearly premium on a life insurance policy for $1000 at your own age, at the age of 28, 38, 48, 58, under each of the plans mentioned. Which type of policy, if any, would you mention as most suitable for the ordinary person at the various ages suggested? 

A form of co-operative helpfulness which has lately received considerable attention is often referred to as a credit union. Recent laws of the federal government have encouraged the formation of such organizations, particularly for farmers. The credit union is organized somewhat like a corporation. Members of it may use their savings to buy stock in it. The money which is received is lent to members of the union for comparatively short periods when they are in special need of money for a little while. Members of the union are chosen as directors, who decide on the making of loans and other policies just as the directors of a corporation do. The union charges enough interest on its loans to cover the bookkeeping and other necessary expenses of running it and to permit stockholders to receive reasonable dividends. This kind of set-up is of special value to people of small means or small savings who prefer to have their financial interests. attended to by people of their own kind. 

If you were a farmer, would you prefer to borrow or lend money through the co-operation of other farmers or through somebody engaged in business for himself, as a banker or money lender? If any of the members of your families belong to credit unions, tell the class about them. 

285. Investment for All and Sundry. - - Investment really means putting money to work. Before there can be investment there must be savings, and then there must be some place to use the savings to bring in further returns. That is where investment has an advantage over hoarding. Hoarded savings, if they do not spoil, stay just what they were. Investment, if it is successful, adds to the savings that have already been made. 

Investments in houses and office buildings take on a more permanent character than some other forms of investment because they are not

1 so easy to dispose of on short notice as savings bank deposits or highquality bonds. And the money that you have tied up in such buildings cannot be used for any other purpose. 

One form of investment in real estate is a mortgage. When a mortgage is given, the owner of the property borrows from someone who has money to lend, and gives to the lender a claim on property which he owns. He must pay interest on the amount he has borrowed, and 

A SHORT-LIVED FAD 

Not so long ago peewee golf courses were to be seen almost anywhere. Like most fads their popularity faded. Many who put them in found that they were not a sound investment. if the interest is not paid when due or the amount which has been borrowed is not repaid at the time it is supposed to be, the mortgagee, as the one is called who lends the money, may, if necessary, take over and dispose of the property. Then he will take what is coming to him and give back the rest, if there is any. 

First mortgages on real estate are often recommended as bringing in good returns and being quite safe and reliable. But mortgaged homes and office buildings are sometimes a worry to both parties, the owner of the property who has mortgaged it and the one who has

taken the mortgage. What if the owner finds himself unable to make the fixed payments of interest, or perhaps installments on the principal of the mortgage? Sometimes the legal procedure involved in selling the property and getting the amount due on the mortgage is long and complicated, and if property values have gone down since the mortgage was taken, it may be impossible to get back the amount originally lent.

Farm mortgages have been nothing less than an economic disease in many parts of the country. Since farmers handle much smaller amounts of actual cash than many other people, it is often hard to interest city people in lending money to them. Perfectly honest farmers may find themselves unable to make payments when due, so that the lender may have to go without his interest or take over farm land which he does not know how to operate. Banks in the 

Farm Loan system (§ 237) found that out. The HOLC (§ 130) had similar experiences. Sometimes home owners found it very difficult to meet their interest charges, and some did not even try. As a result the HOLC got into the business of owning and renting property to a far greater extent than it ever intended to. 

Other kinds of investment include government bonds, corporation stock and bonds, and the like. Because holders of government bonds did not have to pay federal income tax on the interest received from them, it has been possible to sell them at lower interest rates than would otherwise have to be paid. We have previously observed that many think income from that source ought to be taxed the same as other kinds of income. Yet that would reduce the attractiveness of such bonds to buyers, and in order to sell their bonds governments might have to pay higher interest rates than now. 

Why have interest rates on almost all kinds of investment gone down in the last few years? Find out what the procedure would be if the holder of a mortgage wished to force the collection of what was due him from a home owner who had not paid his interest or principal. 

286. Features and Practices in Investment. There need not be any great mystery about buying and selling stocks and bonds. Holding stock, you remember, usually entitles one to some kind of voice in the determining of the policies of a business, though there is such a thing as "non-voting" stock which does not carry with it that right. Bonds are simply promises to pay a given amount at a given time. They 

---

are usually printed with coupons attached which are to be cut off at the times when interest is due and then cashed or deposited in a bank. 

Bonds may be issued for almost any length of time, even up to forty years or more, depending on what the issuer of the bonds thought was good business, or what he had to do in order to borrow the money. Some bonds are not "callable" until the time ends for which they have been issued that is, they cannot be paid off before that time, and the interest which they bear must be paid regularly during the entire period. 

Others are issued with the understanding that they may be "called" or "redeemed" at some earlier date than the time for which they run if the issuing government or company thinks it is to its advantage to do so. There is also a difference between a mortgage bond and a debenture. A mortgage bond carries with it a claim on the property of the corporation issuing the bond. (That may mean next to nothing as far as you and I are concerned, for what could we do with our little share of a factory building if the amount we had lent the corporation was not paid back?) A debenture is simply a promise to pay in the future. We have to depend upon the credit and reputation and business success of the corporation for the assurance that we shall get our money back. Stocks, you recall (§ 220), may be either preferred or common, and there also may be variations of these. 

H. Armstrong Roberts GETTING HIS MONTHLY INCOME 

This man owns a number of bonds. He keeps them in a safe deposit box in this bank and has come here to cut his coupons. 

It often happens that stocks and bonds are bought and sold at some other figure than their exact face value. If the corporation that issues them is doing well, its bonds will sell at par which means 100 per cent of its face value- or above par, which means more than 100 per cent. If its finances are shaky, the market price of stock or bonds may go far below par, and may even become completely worthless, if no payments of interest or dividend are made at all and there is no prospect that they ever will be resumed.

One who buys either stock or bonds ought to think of at least three 

---

considerations. The first one is, naturally, safety. Does it seem likely that you will at least get your money back when it is promised? 

The second is marketability. If for any reason you wish to dispose of stock or bonds, will you have any difficulty in doing so? A third item that may become important is diversification. It may be more sensible for most of us not to put all our savings into one form of investment. If we do thus "diversify" our "portfolio," as they call it, then if one or more of the investments go bad, we still have others that are paying. If one were lucky enough, for instance, to inherit $20,000, he might be wise to put a quarter of it in each of two wellmanaged corporations, another quarter in municipal bonds, and another in federal government bonds. 

It is common sense to do business only with those investment banks or brokers who have a reputation for sanity and honesty. Such people cannot afford to spoil their record by trying to sell you worthless securities. The broker makes his own profits by either charging you a fee for his services or by selling bonds to you at a little higher figure than he had to pay for them. A broker might, it is true, try to sell you bonds on which he would make a little more than he would make on some other kind, but if he really were honest, he would not ask you to buy anything that he did not think was safe. 

By all means, resist the temptation which frequently comes to put money into investments on which big returns are promised. If a certain type of investment were really sure of paying big returns, brokers would not have to go around and beg people with just a few thousand dollars to go into the proposition. Still further, do not invest in something that you know nothing whatever about. Of course you cannot be familiar with the details of financial conditions in Cincinnati or Smithville if you live hundreds or thousands of miles away, but you can find out how the size of their debt compares with their wealth, and whether the government of the community is usually successful in getting its taxes collected. If it is a private corporation that is offering a new series of bonds, find out what its own record has been in meeting its obligation and what its directors want to do with the money they are trying to obtain. 

Read the financial pages of some reputable newspaper and find out the meaning of terms that appear on those pages which you do not understand. 

What should you try to find out about the following kinds of stocks or bonds

before investing? A department store in your own town; a mining company in Mexico; Texas oil stock; a railroad company; the city of Philadelphia; the city of Miami. 

287. The Speculator and What He Does. Investment and specu lation are both alike and different. In investment one seeks principally to make use of his savings so that they will earn something. 

He may not care to be bothered with frequent changes resulting from buying and selling stocks, bonds, or other property. Speculation, on the other hand, is done in the hope that the property that is purchased will increase in value as well as bring in returns while this is happening. The typical speculator will buy or sell when he can make a good profit by doing so. Speculation is not necessarily dishonest, but it always involves taking a chance. So many speculators have been dishonest and have induced old folks or poor people who had saved up a little money to go into risky or outright crooked schemes that the word has, in the minds of many, come to have a bad meaning. 

How can such people get away with their dishonesty? Sometimes, as soon as promoters of dishonest propositions get the money they are after, they quietly disappear and move into another part of the country to carry on their performances, perhaps under a different name. 

Besides, one who has been tricked seldom likes to expose himself and let others know what a fool he was. Ministers and teachers, young doctors and lawyers, dislike to let others know that they are suckers or have knowingly gone into some unsound financial project. 

One of the causes of the panic of 1837, which people then looked upon as the worst ever, was speculation in land. Later, a similar fever of speculation caused people to buy land in the Northwest or in California, and still later in Florida. People bought lots at ridiculously high prices, and when the bottom dropped out of the boom lost everything. Even near old-established communities, lots are sometimes mapped out and given some fancy name, such as Sunny Acres, and then sold at unreasonable prices to people who will have to build houses on them if the land is ever to be of any real use. 

A common form of speculation is buying "on margin." One who thinks that a certain stock is going to increase in value may order his broker to buy 100 or 1000 shares of it at the current price, putting up, if necessary, part of the value of the stock to bind the sale. He has no intention of keeping the stock permanently but expects, after it

goes up a few more points, to sell it again and keep the profits he has made by doing so. If he guesses wrong and the stock goes down, he has to draw on his own funds to make up the difference between what he agreed to pay for the stock and what he was actually able to get when he sold it.

We are told that speculation when engaged in as an honest business has some good effects, however. (1) Speculation helps to stabilize prices. 

Suppose a trader thinks that cotton is going to be higher next spring than it is now, say January 1. If he buys cotton now, he thinks he can sell it for a higher price in April. So he buys, and perhaps others who think as he does also buy. This practice is called dealing in "futures." The result is to increase the demand in January, and to raise the price somewhat. 

Perhaps this same extra demand will reduce the demand in April so that the price will not go as high as it otherwise would. (2) Furthermore, speculation distributes risks more widely. If it were not for the speculator who makes this his own game, the manufacturer would himself have to be playing the market constantly. As it is, he needs only to keep an eye on the general course of events, buying as he may need the raw material to be delivered when he wants it. Be sure you understand that the speculator does not actually handle wheat, corn, or cotton himself. 

All that he buys and sells is the right to have a thousand bushels or bales or whatever it may be. He passes over this right, when he sells, to the miller or the cotton manufacturer, as the case may be. Then only are the goods actually removed from the warehouse or other place of storage to the factory. 

The stock exchange in the large cities, especially New York, supplies a constant live market for the better grade of stocks and bonds. The 

Chicago Board of Trade in a similar way is a central wheat market for the world. Through the trading at such places prices are kept nearer normal all over the world. The importance of such "commodity exchanges," dealing with wheat, cotton, or other agricultural products, led Congress in 1936 to set up the Commodity Exchange Commission, composed of the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Attorney General, with authority to regulate the trade carried on there.

Good results to other people are not the conscious purpose of the speculator. He is concerned only with the size of his own profits. 

Only the well-informed should ever hope to profit by speculation. 

The ignorant and the half-informed win only by luck, and generally lose. For most of us, sound advice is - don't do it! 

---

An editorial in a business man's magazine some years ago was entitled, "We Must Speculate." Since this magazine was not one that would deliberately encourage people to go into crooked or unsound schemes, what do you suppose the editor really meant? Is there a difference between honest speculation and gambling or buying tickets on the Irish sweepstakes?

Not all the building of new residences in late years has been done under government auspices. A number of projects have been undertaken as business ventures. community at almost any time might well hesitate about tying up his savings in a house. One whose job is uncertain or who is not sure in what neighborhood he wants to live might also think twice before buying a home.

On the other hand, one who owns the place where he lives is likely to have an inspiration to improve it or to keep it in good condition which he would not feel if he were only paying rent. The very fact that he and his family have a definite place to live may bring a sense of satisfaction and contentment which he could not have if every year the owner might raise the rent or ask him to move out. If one has bought a place through the assistance of a mortgage, there is an added

780

inducement to make savings. If one exercises proper care in selecting the neighborhood where he buys, he is sure of having something to show for his savings, even though property values may go down somewhat. Nothing less than a fire, tornado, or flood can wipe a house out of existence, and you can carry insurance, at least against fire. 

Possibly one will not actually save a great deal of money through home owning, when he considers taxes, repairs, and possible interest on his savings, but at least he can see where his savings have gone. 

The question is one that each family must answer for itself. The various housing projects which are now so much talked about are intended to provide respectable living quarters for those who could not afford to buy a place of their own. But one who has what seems like a settled job in a community that he likes may well ask himself the question, Why keep on paying $30 or more month after month and have nothing but rent receipts to show for it?

How large a mortgage on a home of average value in your community would it be wise for a family without a large income to carry? If your own family rents rather than owns the place where you live, is there any definite reason for doing so? If your family owns the place where you live, have you wished you were renting? What do you pay in an average year for taxes and repairs in comparison with what you would have to pay for rent?

XXIII 

Just as it is often a sensible policy to look back over the road we have traversed and pass judgment on our achievements and mistakes, so it is good for us to look around and look ahead and see what is in view. 

Here we are. Do we want to stay? Do we want to go back? Do we want to move on? If we do move, in what direction? We need to think seriously about some of these proposed new kinds of social order. 

We want to be able to pass fair judgment on them, and we do not want to rush hastily into something new, only to find that we are worse off than we were before.

Some Questions: 

1. What elements make up a good society? 

2. What unpleasant conditions do we find under our democratic and capitalistic system, and what achievements can we credit to it? 

3. What conditions gave rise to the proposals that have been made for radical change in social and economic life? 

4. Who are satisfied and who are dissatisfied with present conditions? 

289. Elements of a Good Society. All will agree that an ideal community should have an honest government. In the second place, most of us will agree that there should be no class distinction. In the recognition of the rights of one man or woman as against another, there should be complete equality. There need be no social snobbery and no distinction of moral merit between one honest occupation and another. A third condition in an ideal community is general intelligence, trained and expressed effectively. No community should consider itself as resting on a sound foundation if it contains any large number of people who, as one public official once said, "are too damn dumb to understand things." Besides, an ideal community would offer to everyone the chance to make the most of himself. 

A well-known social scientist whom some people look upon as rather extreme in his views has listed the following policies or activities as essential to the success of a democratic society: (1) Knowledge of the principles of sound government. (2) Organization of the people for 784

democracy. (3) A strong and efficient government. (4) Government monopoly of police and military power. (5) Complete and fair enforcement of civil rights. (6) Exposure of political propaganda. (7) Conservation of democratic temper. (8) Avoidance of

Do you think there would be much disagreement about these items?

A fair distribution of the good things of life is a reasonable desire for anyone to have. One of the foremost aims of industry, society, and government should be to secure for each and every individual his just dues. To take away from the fortunate and successful what they have, for the sole purpose of bringing them down to a common level would be most unreasonable, but we should work for such a situation as would give at least every earnest and co-operative person security from suffering and want. We should also strive for the attainment of such ideals of relationship among men as would make them all anxious for general well-being, and not merely for their own advancement. 

What makes people snobbish? Can a rich man be democratic? Are people's ideas as to the elements in a good society likely to change much or little in the course of time? 

290. Some Criticisms of Our Economic Life. (1) There is uneven and often unfair distribution of wealth. Much wealth is in such a form that to divide it would ruin it, but perhaps we could bring about a wider distribution of benefits coming from such forms of wealth. (2) There are political wrongs. Graft still occurs. Some officeholders think far more of the money they can get from the job than of the good they can do the country. And perhaps the worst of it is that "we, the people," put them there. (3) There is economic disorder and waste. Some producers aim not to provide what people really would profit by, but to make things and then induce men to buy them by high-pressure sales methods. Some workers are too anxious to reduce their hours of work, and by their attitude make it impossible for society as a whole to provide as reasonably as it might the products that could come from industry. To reduce or remove this difficulty, shall the government limit the number of people who may engage in particular business activities as it does in Germany? If so, who knows enough 

---

to plan all this, and how will we distribute these business opportunities and jobs? (4) There is lack of opportunity for many. Men and women born in what are often thought of as the lower classes in industry or society find it almost impossible to rise above their surroundings and take places of leadership. Unfavorable conditions of living lead to crime, immorality, and physical decay. 

Too many capable workers, it is asserted, live on unearned income. 

Well, what is unearned income? Shall we allow no one to profit by hiring others to work for him? Shall we refuse to let anybody have the privilege of living on the returns from inherited wealth? Shall we prevent a man from giving his children a better start in life than he had?

How would you feel about the list of debatable propositions just given if you had inherited enough so that you would not have to work for a living? 

What if you were receiving just about enough to live on? What if you had no job? 

291. What Has Capitalism Achieved? It is only fair to set off against these criticisms, which are easy enough to make, the favorable circumstances which have come into existence under a capitalistic system. We may rightly ask ourselves whether the abuses of which mention has been made are general, or whether they occur only here and there. We may inquire further, are they the result of the capitalistic system of industry, or of the ignorance, folly, and wickedness of some human beings? 

If we take the former point of view, we may feel like throwing the whole system overboard and starting again on new lines. If we conclude that the trouble is with men and women themselves, we shall rather be inclined to ask whether they would do better under some other system. Do the programs which are offered as remedies for present evils carry with them any assurance that they would actually operate without serious difficulty, or would greed and dishonesty find just as much room under some other kind of economic system as they do today?

The hope of getting ahead financially has encouraged people to work and to save, to improve ways of doing things, to bring new machinery into existence, and has made possible a much higher standard of living for the average man as well as luxurious ease for a few. Taking our

own country as an example, the average wealth of our 30,000,000 families is in all probability about $10,000. You may say that $10,000 is more than the average family ever saw at one time, and you would be quite correct. But this wealth is here somewhere and many of us get indirect benefits from its existence even though we may not have the pleasure of handling it. Under capitalism the 

Black Box Studios CAPITALISM CAN'T BE SO BAD 

The young lady is after a job, and she may need one. Our industrial system has made it possible for her and for the man to dress neatly and to converse intelligently about matters of common interest. Would any other 'ism have done more ? world has obtained, for at least the civilized part of its people, an intellectual advancement and comfortable living infinitely superior to anything that would have been accumulated without it. 

Select some one or more common industries or occupations and study it to see whether the unpleasant conditions we have mentioned are found in that occupation. If you find them there, would they be removed or reduced by a plan of organization which would not depend on private use of capital?

292. The Satisfied and the Dissatisfied. Those who see no reason for thinking that anything is seriously wrong are not likely to be greatly interested in doing things differently. Only those who are at least somewhat dissatisfied are likely to seek extensive improvements. Neither will the world move to a satisfactory level if we have nothing but faultfinders. Those who are always objecting to what someone else does seldom make any constructive contribution themselves. A cynic once said, "It is sometimes a good thing for a dog to have fleas. It helps him to overlook the fact that he is only a dog." 

But what if we all had them?

In general, there are four classes of people who are either contented with present conditions, or not willing to go to any great effort to make them different. Some are afraid of change because they fear it would spoil the good things we do have. They do not want "to jump out of the frying pan into the fire." A few have everything they want, and naturally see no reason for making changes. At the opposite end of the scale are those who are badly off but do not know it, and therefore make no effort to improve either themselves or their circumstances. And last, some people are too lazy to care about making conditions better if there would be any work in doing so. 

On the side of the dissatisfied, we find, similarly, four groups. First, there are those who have met with much distress and bad luck, and figure that any change could not make them any worse off. Another group is composed of those who have not met with social or financial success and are jealous of those who have. They will welcome a change that may either put themselves on top or at least overthrow those who have succeeded. Still others are ready to listen to the wild talk or pleasant promises of any demagogue who tells them he knows the answers. If they will only follow him, they will get $30 every Thursday, or profit by some other impossible magic. And finally, there are those who sincerely face the facts and realize that, for a great many people, conditions can be improved. They are willing to strive for improvement both for themselves and for their fellow men, but want to do it in a way that will bring with it as little unsettlement and disorder as possible.

Perhaps we cannot place a particular individual precisely in one of these eight groups. You cannot hope to satisfy some people. Former 

Governor Smith of New York once said, "I am entirely unwilling to

accept the old order of things as the best unless and until I am convinced that it cannot be made better." But when he was not willing to go the whole distance in support of changes that some people proposed, they turned on him and accused him of selling out to Wall Street. 

Is a man to be blamed or praised if he thinks much about ideal conditions which could not be obtained in his own lifetime? Can you mention any characters in history who might be listed as of that type? How were these treated by people of their own day? Why is it often easier for a demagogue to get people to follow him than one who appeals to reason and judgment? 

293. What Makes Radicals? - If one broods over the unpleasant conditions we have referred to in modern life, or if he finds a kindred spirit who can get sore at things along with him, especially if either or both think they have not had a square deal from society, there is a field for the sowing of radical ideas. The socialist (§ 191) asserts that workers are being exploited by the capitalists; therefore if fundamental industries were operated by the government, everybody would get a fair opportunity to work and a fair return for his labor. Some people of recognized ability have been socialists. In the United States 

Norman Thomas is the perennial Socialist presidential candidate. 

Socialist mayors have been elected in some cities, and in Europe Socialist parties have gained a much larger proportion of the vote at elections than they have in the United States. But nowhere has anything distressingly revolutionary been undertaken under the Socialist name, except in Russia.

The harsh government of the Czar in Russia inevitably produced hate and hostility, which was kept under cover with fair success until Russian power collapsed in the World War. The party which founded the present Russian government was at first called Bolshevist, or "those who want more." It was led by Nikolai Lenin and Leon 

Trotsky, under whose leadership the Bolshevists seized control of the Russian government in 1917. Lenin died in 1924, and Trotsky, after falling out with the other leaders, went into exile. Lenin was followed as virtual dictator of the country by the man who took the name of Joseph Stalin and is now always referred to by that title. 

Italy a few years after the World War was in serious distress and under a Socialist administration seemed to be making no improvement. 

Mussolini and his followers forced themselves into power and proceeded to reorganize the country. Step by step they did away with

anything like democracy, and abolished all political parties except the Fascist Party. Mussolini did not abolish capitalism, but put the government in entire control of industry as well as of political affairs. 

By appealing to the desire for law and order, which the average business man feels very strongly, he secured the support of the majority of business and professional men in the country and crushed any possibility of control of the state by the Socialists. Soon they too found themselves completely subject to the decrees of 

Mussolini himself.

Seeing what could be done by a determined minority headed by an unscrupulous leader, Adolf 

Hitler, in Germany, put over the same sort of program there on a far more fearful scale. In 

Germany it has been done through the agency of the socalled National Socialist party, or Nazi for short. In Germany, business men, under the guise of stopping communism, were tricked into the support of a program which soon found them at the mercy of a dictator whom they had hoped to use for their own advantage. Hitler also added to his own program a barbarous attack on the Jews, which after a time Mussolini also introduced in Italy. Then he set out to force his vicious control on all Europe or even the world. 

Some people foment discontent by openly talking about "wage wars" between the working class and the employing class. Some people who would not engage in such folly themselves encourage it by talking loudly about the "class struggle." Such tactics are intended to make the weak-minded and the unthinking ready to listen to radical agitators. Goodness knows the world will never be free from trouble if discontented groups merely set out to overthrow one class and put their own class in its place. 

James Sawders

294. The Isms in Practice. - Dictators, under whatever name, can keep themselves in power only by being able to make their subjects think that they are doing something for them. Usually, after his people have been forced or fooled into as much sacrifice as possible the dictator, in order to keep on glorifying himself, indulges in attacks, military, or economic, or both, upon other countries, as Mussolini did upon Ethiopia and Hitler upon Czechoslovakia and 

Poland, and then pours oil on the fires of nationalistic patriotism which he uses every opportunity to inflame. 1330 ADTEKA

A DRUGSTORE ON A RUSSIAN COLLECTIVE Farm 

Fascist rule in Italy did at first bring order to the country and achieve measure of outward improvement, and that made it easier for him, for a while, to keep his people quiet. Hitler could tell his subjects that the German race is destined to rule the world. When the dictator himself controls the radio and the press in his country, how could critics say much against him that his people would hear? 

In practice Russian communism worked out the same way, as far as individual rights are concerned. Instead of being a government of "workers, soldiers, and peasants," as the Bolshevist leaders proclaimed when they overthrew the Czar, it became simply another form of totalitarian rule. Stalin, who for years held no office except secretary-general of the Communist party, was merely a boss controlling the lives, property, and even thoughts of the 160,000,000 people living under the Soviet flag. Some men and women sincerely willing to see something in communist theory have gone to Russia only to come The Soviet Government in planning its collective farm system desired to make it unnecessary for people to depend on any other agency for their needs or comforts.

back disillusioned. The mass of the people under the old Russian government of the Czar were held down to such intolerable levels of life and work that almost any change had to be an improvement. 

There is no denying that the Soviet leaders have caused many of their people to learn to read and write, and to acquire an understanding of the Soviet theories of government. But they still have a considerable distance to go before enjoying as many comforts and privileges as workers are accustomed to in "capitalist" Great Britain and the United States. 

In our own country there is a recognized Communist political party which nominates its candidates for President and for governor and members of Congress and city officials. Its best-known leader, Earl 

Browder, is rather peaceful personally. The principal charge against communists is that they are in the pay of or take orders from "Moscow," and that communists, by acquiring places of leadership in labor organizations and by other means, seek to stir up trouble when it otherwise would not occur, in the hope that out of such discontent may come the opportunity for communists to seize political or economic power or both.

What is meant by "burrowing from within,” as the phrase is often used with reference to Communist activities? How different would be the status of labor unions under a Communist system from what they are today? How would you, if you had the chance to argue with a Russian worker about the respective merits of his country's program and ours, present the advantages of our system? (In defending our program, one does not need to claim perfection for it or to pretend that nothing has been achieved under Soviet rule.) 

It would be interesting if somewhere there could be tried out a pure program of moderate industrial socialism, unmixed with other radical ideas, and based on the principles of democracy. But what country is willing to play the guinea pig for such an experiment? Even if government and society were managed with perfect honesty — and such a thing is hard to imagine, in view of some things we know about politics—would not individual enterprise become stagnant because of lack of incentive, and industry itself be wrecked because its operation would depend upon the demands of politicians and the whims of incompetent public officials?

Should it be considered a reflection upon an idea to say that it is "socialistic"? Under socialism, how and by whom would a person's wages be

determined? How would socialism affect the farmer, the druggist, the teacher, the factory owner, the minister, the miner, the actor, the storekeeper, the carpenter?

Is it likely that those who never have succeeded under present conditions could rebuild the world on a better plan? Do you think if the agitators of society should somehow become well-to-do, most of them would cease to be agitators? 

295. How to Make Reforms. One thing is sure. There is no patent formula or panacea that will automatically correct unpleasant conditions overnight. In times of national distress we sometimes forget this fact. People who would not purposely do the slightest harm to anyone sometimes advocate fantastic financial schemes which might, in the end, be ruinous to the nation. 

While there is plenty of argument in favor of reasonable proposals for old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and other means of relieving the distress of those who are in difficulties through no fault of their own, it does not follow that plans for pensioning everybody over sixty years of age at a figure large enough to enable them to live in comparative luxury would be sensible. When a nation's business is in bad shape, is it more desirable to pour billions out of the government's treasury in the form of projects to do unnecessary things in order to give men work, or to try to create a situation which will encourage ordinary business to recover from fear or stagnation and go ahead under its own motion? If any large part of the people are to be taught that they may live on pensions or made work paid for by other people, is there going to be much inducement for anyone to work? 

But even such extravagances seek to right wrongs and injustices without destroying what has already been built up. They can be thwarted by argument and by the ballot, whereas revolution can be put down only by bombs and bullets. Revolution, as we have already observed (§ 109), usually changes other things as well as those that need to be corrected, and when changes come suddenly, there is almost always a violent reaction, and sometimes most of the evils which it was planned to overthrow are re-established in another form. 

It is far better to make haste slowly, if such a thing is possible. Evolution, or gradual change, brings on the new without upsetting the good things that have already been achieved. Certainly it is no more correct to assume that whatever is, is bad, than to believe that whatever is, is right.

A free speech and a free press in a free country offer the opportunity for everybody to think carefully about any kind of proposal, whoever originates it. Surely in such a country as this we all want social justice. Our differences should be, if they do exist at all, only on the best ways to bring that about. It is not social justice either to think merely about ways to protect property and wealth that have already been accumulated, or to plan for taking away what has been earned by enterprise and fair dealing in order to give it to the lazy and the ignorant. 

Is it true that what we need most is not any extensive change in our economic system, but rather a general adoption of those moral and religious principles that may be summarized in the Ten Commandments and the Golden Rule? Let us not be discouraged if we do have a considerable way to go before we can feel satisfied with what society does for all its members. 

In spite of all the blunders and crimes of which men have been guilty, our twentieth century may still offer more possibilities of general happiness and wellbeing than any previous period in human history. There is no need of listening to the prophet who declares, "The worst is yet to come," in preference to the one who maintains, "The best is yet to be." of

Close control by authority, with achievements depending upon the wisdom of the rulers.

Depends upon military force, with no regard for the rights of others.

Religion submissive to or discouraged by rulers.

Only for the rulers and those who will take orders from them.

Subject to what authorities think proper. 

Either opposed or at the mercy of the state.

Authority maintained through system of spies, summary arrest, and concentration camps. 

Carried on solely under government permission or by the government itself. 

Possession of any depends upon favor of rulers.

Improvements usually made for political effect or to promote the support by the masses of those in power.

do we want? Certainly lovers of liberty would hate to have communism introduced anywhere by the same methods by which it was forced upon the people of Russia. Can either of these happen in this country? It depends upon the intelligence, the vigilance, and the courage of those who believe that democracy, even with its weaknesses, is better than any allegedly efficient system forced upon a nation by unscrupulous rulers. We must inquire carefully into the soundness of every argument which is aimed to cause us to distrust free government and free industry, though if in communism or fascism there is anything good that can be adopted apart from the brutality of the system as a whole, we need not reject it just because of its source. 

It is up to us to work out ways for making our own life and work

more productive, efficient, and happy. There are many possible intermediate stages between a program under which a government does only what it cannot help doing, and one in which it attempts to take over the direction of everything. Democracies have made mistakes, but most of us believe that it is better to let the people make their own mistakes than to let any one man or a few party leaders make mistakes for an entire nation. If things do not go right under a democracy, the people have only themselves to blame. If they cultivate the intelligence and the enterprise of which people like those of our own country are capable, and have the open-mindedness and courage to adopt better ways when they are proved to be better, there is nothing that fascism, communism, or any other kind of ism can give which we or any other people devoted to the democratic ideal cannot have. Yes, our democracy is worth having. It is worth sacrificing for. It is worth fighting for, if that is what we must do to save it. 

What suggestions can you offer as to ways to convince doubters of the desirability of democracy? What ought we to work for, to remove any possible question about it?

EPILOGUE  

297. How Much Have We Learned? In a book which most of us ought to know better than we do, is the story of an employer who went away on a trip and turned over to his employees various sums of money to be used in business enterprise. When he came back he found that two of the three had used their money in such a way as to double it. One had simply kept it, and returned it unused. Of course, it was a little to the third man's credit that he had not squandered the money left in his charge, but he was supposed to use it in a profitable investment.

We noticed at the beginning of our study that the United States is a nation to which many talents have been intrusted natural resources, people of varied interests and capacities, and a very favorable situation. That we have used all these so as to get the highest possible service from them would surely not be true. But it has been well said, "It is always too late to be what you might have been; it is never too late to be what you may become." The fellow who always says "It can't be done" is a nuisance and a curse. 

By this time we should have a fuller and more accurate understanding of many matters than when we began our study. None of us needs to think that we know all there is to know about any of them. But something must be wrong with us if we are not better prepared than before to do our part intelligently and unselfishly. Liberty, equality of opportunity, and democracy for all, peace and order at home and abroad, good will among nations, and justice everywhere—all of these good citizens believe in. But some do not have those ideals, and we have not always realized our own responsibility to maintain them for ourselves and for all the civilized world. 

What do we mean when we talk about Americanism or the American way? 

Can you get a fairer view on public questions in school or in the outside world? 

In what spirit should one enter into a discussion of problems about which people may not all think alike? 799

298. What Are We Going to Do about It? - The people who do the most for humanity are those who have learned something about working both in groups and as individuals. They have the initiative and energy to start and carry through enterprises themselves, and they know how to co-operate with others in bringing things to pass. 

Government and business and society are not something outside of and apart from any one of us. All three have much to do in making

We may co-operate with others by voting, obeying the law, and rendering public service when the opportunity comes. Elbert Hubbard declared, "If a man write a better book, preach a better sermon, or make a better mousetrap than his neighbor, though he build his house in the woods, the world will make a beaten path to his door." 

But people will do that not merely because the man has done something better than somebody else has done it, but because his own achievement has helped other people-materially, mentally, or spiritually.

The high school or college graduate may not be as superior a person as he sometimes thinks he is, but he surely should be more capable than those who have not had his opportunities. 

If this study has made it possible for any of the boys and girls who are to be our future leaders to do better the work that will come to their hands in years ahead, it will have been well worth while.

APPENDIX A CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA PREAMBLE 

WE the people of the United States, in order to form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquillity, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves and our posterity, do ordain and establish this CoN- 

STITUTION for the United States of America. 

ARTICLE I. - LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT SECTION 1.- CONGRESS 

All legislative powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and a House of Representatives.

SECTION 2. - HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES 

1. The House of Representatives shall be composed of members chosen every second year by the people of the several States, and the electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State Legislature. 

2. No person shall be a Representative who shall not have attained to the age of twenty-five years, and been seven years a citizen of the United States, and who shall not, when elected, be an inhabitant of that State in which he shall be chosen. 

13. Representatives and direct taxes shall be apportioned among the several States which may be included within this Union, according to their respective numbers, which shall be determined by adding to the whole number of free persons, including those bound to service for a term of years, and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of all other persons. 

The actual enumeration shall be made within three years after the first

meeting of the Congress of the United States, and within every subsequent term of ten years, in such manner as they shall by law direct. The number of Representatives shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand, but each State shall have at least one representative; and until such enumeration shall be made, the State of New Hampshire shall be entitled to choose three, Massachusetts eight, Rhode Island and Providence Plantations one, Connecticut five, New York six, New Jersey four, Pennsylvania eight, Delaware one, Maryland six, Virginia ten, North Carolina five, South Carolina five, and Georgia three. 

4. When vacancies happen in the representation from any State, the 

Executive authority thereof shall issue writs of election to fill such vacan cies. 

5. The House of Representatives shall choose their Speaker and other officers; and shall have the sole power of impeachment. 

SECTION 3. - SENATE 

11. [The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen by the Legislature thereof, for six years; and each Senator shall have one vote.] 

2. Immediately after they shall be assembled in consequence of the first election, they shall be divided as equally as may be into three classes. 

The seats of the Senators of the first class shall be vacated at the expiration of the second year, of the second class at the expiration of the fourth year, and of the third class at the expiration of the sixth year, so that one third may be chosen every second year; [and if vacancies happen by resignation, or otherwise, during the recess of the Legislature of any State, the Executive thereof may make temporary appointments until the next meeting of the Legislature, which shall then fill such vacancies]. 1 3. SECTION 4.- ELECTIONS AND SESSIONS 

1. The times, places, and manner of holding elections for Senators and 

Representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof; but the Congress may at any time by law make or alter such regulations, except as to the places of choosing Senators. 

2. The Congress shall assemble at least once in every year, and such meeting shall be on the first Monday in December, unless they shall by law appoint a different day.

SECTION 5. GOVERNMENT AND RULES 

1. Each House shall be the judge of the elections, returns, and qualifications of its own members, and a majority of each shall constitute a quorum to do business; but a smaller number may adjourn from day to day, and may be authorized to compel the attendance of absent members, in such manner, and under such penalties, as each House may provide. 

2. Each House may determine the rules of its proceedings, punish its members for disorderly behavior, and, with the concurrence of two thirds, expel a member. 

3. Each House shall keep a journal of its proceedings, and from time to time publish the same, excepting such parts as may in their judgment require secrecy; and the yeas and nays of the members of either House on any question shall, at the desire of one fifth of those present, be entered on the journal.

SECTION 6. 

4. Neither House, during the session of Congress, shall, without the consent of the other, adjourn for more than three days, nor to any other place than that in which the two Houses shall be sitting. 

PRIVILEGES AND RESTRICTIONS 1. The Senators and Representatives shall receive a compensation for their services, to be ascertained by law, and paid out of the treasury of the United States. They shall in all cases, except treason, felony, and breach of the peace, be privileged from arrest during their attendance at the ses-

Appendix A 

sion of their respective Houses, and in going to and returning from the same; and for any speech or debate in either House they shall not be questioned in any other place. 

2. No Senator or Representative shall, during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the authority of the United States, which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person holding any office under the United States shall be a member of either House during his continuance in office.

SECTION 7. 

PROCESS OF LAW-MAKING 

1. All bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives; but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments as on other bills. 

2. Every bill which shall have passed the House of Representatives and the Senate shall, before it become a law, be presented to the President of the United States; if he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it with his objections to that House in which it shall have originated, who shall enter the objections at large on their journal, and proceed to reconsider it. If after such reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the bill, it shall be sent, together with the objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and, if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a law. But in all such cases the votes of both Houses shall be determined by yeas and nays, and the names of the persons voting for and against the bill shall be entered on the journal of each House respectively. If any bill shall not be returned by the President within ten days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the same shall be a law, in like manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their adjournment prevent its return, in which case it shall not be a law. 

3. Every order, resolution, or vote to which the concurrence of the 

Senate and House of Representatives may be necessary (except on a question of adjournment) shall be presented to the President of the United States; and, before the same shall take effect, shall be approved by him, or, being disapproved by him, shall be repassed by two thirds of the Senate and House of Representatives, according to the rules and limitations prescribed in the case of a bill.

SECTION 10. - POWERS DENIED TO THE STATES¹ 

1. No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make anything but gold and silver coin a tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts, or grant any title of nobility. 

2. No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws; and the net produce of all duties and imposts, laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. 

3. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty of tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war, unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay.

1. The executive power shall be vested in a President of the United

And they shall make a list of all the persons voted for, and of the number of votes for each; which list they shall sign and certify, and transmit sealed to the seat of the government of the United States, directed to the President of the Senate. The President of the Senate shall, in the presence of the Senate and House of Representatives, open all the certificates, and the votes shall then be counted.

The person having the greatest number of votes shall be the President, if

In case of the removal of the President from office, or of his death, resignation, or inability to discharge the powers and duties of the said office, the same shall devolve on the Vice-President, and the Congress may by law provide for the case of removal, death, resignation, or inability, both of the President and Vice-President, declaring what officer shall then act as President, and such officer shall act accordingly, until the disability be removed, or a President shall be elected.
